papers.abstract: In this note, we show how the exploitation of the lattice momentum balance condition allows us to envisage an analytical procedure to define the lattice pressure tensor (LPT) for the multi-phase Shan–Chen (SC) lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) with single-range potential. This construction ensures that the LPT normal component to a flat interface is constant to machine precision on each lattice node, i.e., it exactly implements the mechanical equilibrium condition on the lattice. We demonstrate the robustness of the approach by providing analytical expressions for the coexistence curves for different choices of the pseudo-potential and forcing schemes in the SC-LBM. This paper offers a novel and rigorous perspective for controlling the LPT in the SC-LBM, paving the way for its application in more general settings.

papers.title: Shear process of rock joints with two-order asperities based on the mobilizable shear strength theory
papers.abstract: Predicting shear characteristics of rock joints is crucial to the stability analysis of rock masses and early warning of pertinent engineering-geological disasters. Natural rock joints are rough with multi-scale asperities, and these asperities are degraded in the shear process with declining dilation. However, the progressive degradation of irregular asperities over shear remains thorny to quantify. Here we proposed an analytical model for the shear behavior of rock joints with two-order asperities within the framework of the mobilizable shear strength theory initiated by the first author. The asperity is shaped sinusoidal, and its geometrical properties are quantifiable by wavelet analysis of a natural profile. The degradation and dilation of each sinusoidal-shaped asperity undergoing shear are predicted by first locating the attack point of the asperity profile. The attack point is determined by equating the slope of the sinusoidal curve and the mobilizable dilation angle as a function of the accumulated elastic shear work at the end of the elastic stage. The succeeding dilation and degradation are evaluated by considering the progressive area reduction of the sinusoidal-shaped asperity as the plastic shear work accumulates. The performance of the analytical model is demonstrated by predicting the shear stress/dilation-shear displacement relationships of synthetic and natural joints with sinusoidal-shaped and irregular asperities. The new model has a great potential to predict the shear resistance of rock joints for assessing the stability of natural and engineered rock structures and joint-slip-induced disasters.

papers.title: Influence of lateral stress on stick-slip characteristics of granite fault: A true three-dimensional experimental study
papers.abstract: Understanding the stick-slip behavior of fault is crucial for studying earthquake nucleation and disaster prevention. However, experimental research on fault slip under true three-dimensional stress condition is relatively rare, particularly those focusing on the effect of lateral stress (σp) parallel to the fault plane on stick-slip characteristics. In this study, direct shear experiments under true three-dimensional stress condition were conducted to investigate the influence of σp on the mechanical and acoustic emission (AE) properties of stick-slip in granite fault. The results show that increasing σp enhances the stick-slip initiation strength (τslip) and the corresponding friction coefficient of fault, leading to an elevation in peak slip velocity and fault slip seismic parameters. The strengthening effect of σp also increases the proportion of high-energy stick-slip events, accompanied by a rise in the proportion of shear cracks during fault slip, further influencing τslip. Additionally, higher σp results in an elevated average AE b-value, indicating a gradual decrease in AE magnitudes, corresponding to the enhancement in τslip. Furthermore, b-value decline prior to stress drop can serve as a key indicator for predicting stick-slip events. These findings provide valuable theoretical insights for fault activation-induced hazards and the assessment of such hazards.

papers.title: The pyrolysis behavior and reaction mechanism of asphaltene in hydrothermal reaction
papers.abstract: High asphaltene content has been identified as the primary contributor to the high viscosity of heavy oil with its complex structure and stability posing significant challenges to both crude oil extraction and processing. In this study, the effects of reaction temperature (250–350 °C), reaction time (24–120 h), reaction pressure (11–15 MPa), and (NH4)6Mo7O24·4H2O catalyst on the hydrothermal cracking reaction were studied. The products were analyzed using elemental analysis, component analysis, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and gas chromatography techniques. Subsequently, the mechanism of hydrothermal cracking of asphaltenes was elucidated. The results showed that the optimal reaction temperature was 325 °C with the appearance of coke in the reaction products at 350 °C. The reaction reached equilibrium after 72 h and an increase in reaction pressure inhibited the hydrothermal cracking of asphaltenes. The (NH4)6Mo7O24·4H2O catalyst promoted the hydrothermal cracking of asphaltenes, and the conversion of asphaltenes increased by 5.05% at 325 °C. The C–S bond cleavage was an important reason for the increase in asphaltene conversion. The content of sulfidic and sulfoxidic sulfur decreased from 44.86% to 32.61% after the catalytic reaction. This study provides insight into the mechanism of hydrothermal cracking of asphaltenes, which can help reduce related risks in heavy oil extraction processes.

papers.title: The effects of thermal properties on interphase heat transfer between supercritical water-particle flow
papers.abstract: The interphase heat transfer of particle flow is of significant importance. This work employed the particle-resolved direct numerical simulation to calculate the interphase heat transfer of supercritical water (SCW)-particle flow. In particular, the influences of complex variations in nonlinear physical properties of SCW has been considered. The results reveal the opposing effects of nozzle effect and particle interaction on the heat transfer. The large Prandtl number (Pr) in critical zone predominantly enhances heat transfer. However, the increase in density weakens the influence of nozzle effect, diminishing the enhancing effect of larger Pr. The strength of interphase heat transfer varies under different conditions, and the influences of variations in density and Pr distribution are also different. As a result, the correlations for the normalized heat transfer coefficient N with varying constants are established. Furthermore, based on the differing dominances of nozzle effect and particle interaction, an appropriate Nusselt number (Nu) correlation for heat transfer of particle flow is developed for most cases. The correlation for SCW-particle flow interphase heat transfer Nu can be obtained by coupling the Nu and N correlations. It shows good predictive performance.

papers.title: Influences of steps on hypersonic boundary layer instability over a cone at small angle of attack
papers.abstract: The influences of the forward-facing step (FFS) and backward-facing step (BFS) on the 7° half-angle cone's boundary layer instability at different meridians are investigated at Mach 6, with step heights of 0.6 mm, and a 1° angle of attack (AoA) in a hypersonic quiet wind tunnel using the Nano-tracer-based Planar Laser Scattering techniques, and high-frequency pressure sensors. The results show that at AoA = 1°, the instability that dominates conical boundary layer transition is the second-mode wave. At a given streamwise location, as the position approaches the centerline of the leeward side, the frequency of the second-mode wave decreases while its amplitude increases, resulting in a more unstable boundary layer. Moreover, the development of the second-mode waves in the BFS model progresses faster than that in the FFS model, at different meridians. Notably, on the leeward side, the FFS stabilizes the second-mode waves, whereas the BFS model destabilizes them.

papers.title: Data-driven spatiotemporal analysis of linear and serpentine actuation for transition to turbulence
papers.abstract: The spatiotemporal Koopman decomposition (STKD) is a data-driven modal decomposition technique that provides a means to represent a flow-field as a sum of standing and traveling waves with temporal and spatial growth rates. The method involves repeated application of dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) or higher-order DMD (HODMD). In this paper, HODMD and STKD are shown to be useful in analyzing coherent structures in a flow-field perturbed by surface plasma actuation. The decomposition methods were applied to implicit large eddy simulations run with our in-house Multiscale Ionized Gas flow code which modeled a straight-edged linear and a square-serpentine shaped plasma actuators and their influence on a Mach 0.5 flow over a flat plate. The HODMD and STKD were used to compute the associated frequencies and spatiotemporal growth of the generated flow structures by decomposing snapshots of the relevant wall shear stresses. These methods were able to successfully reconstruct the variation in wall shear stress for these actuated flows with a limited number of intensifying traveling waves for both cases. For the length of the plate studied, this analysis provided more insight into the oblique wave transition caused by the serpentine actuation and the two-dimensional waves generated by the linear geometry. Ultimately, the STKD is a useful tool that could be used to improve or optimize the control mechanism since the complex transitional flow is successfully represented as a linearly evolving system.

papers.title: An acoustic backscattering mechanism of an open cylindrical shell at the air–water interface
papers.abstract: Surface ships are mostly elastic structures with curved surfaces and certain openings. The incidence of plane waves on curved surfaces excites various surface elastic waves on the shell. The presence of the air–water interface and shell openings alters the types of surface waves on the shell and their propagation paths, thereby influencing the backscattering acoustic field of partially submerged targets at a flat interface. This paper takes a partially submerged open cylindrical shell at the air–water interface as the research model, revealing the excitation and reradiation mechanisms of the flexural waves a0−, a0+, and a0 by a horizontally incident plane wave on a target at a flat interface. The influence of the immersion depth of the cylindrical shell and the size of opening on its acoustic scattering characteristics is investigated, and theoretical prediction formulas are provided, which are validated through experiments. The results indicate that the flexural waves can cross the air–water interface, be reflected at the open end of the cylindrical shell, and propagate circumferentially along the shell, forming periodic pulse echoes. By considering the multipath of flexural wave echoes, an estimation formula for the arrival times of each echo is derived. Utilizing the phase matching theory, expressions for the resonant frequencies of flexural waves and the phase conditions for mutual interference of paths are obtained. The accuracy of the prediction formulas is verified through simulations and experiments.

papers.title: A global matrix-based stability analysis of the lattice Boltzmann and gas kinetic flux solvers for the simulation of compressible flows
papers.abstract: Although the novel lattice Boltzmann and gas kinetic flux solvers have recently been proposed for effective simulation of challenging compressible flows, rigorous theoretical analysis of their stability performances is still lacking. This paper presents a matrix-based global linear stability analysis on the stability performance of lattice Boltzmann and gas kinetic flux solvers for simulating inviscid compressible flows in a wide range of Mach numbers. Five different schemes are considered, including the circular function-based gas-kinetic flux solver, the discrete gas-kinetic scheme, and the double distribution function-based discrete gas-kinetic scheme, lattice Boltzmann flux solver, and the rotated lattice Boltzmann flux solver (RLBFS). The conventional Roe scheme and Van Leer scheme are also included for comparison. With the small perturbation assumption, stability matrices for different schemes are constructed and analyzed by simulating the strong normal shock wave problem across a plane with different upstream Mach numbers. The stability phase diagram for each numerical scheme is constructed using the Mach number and grid aspect ratio (length-to-width ratio), which may provide a reference for choosing numerical schemes in practical applications. Analysis of the unstable phenomenon for these solvers has also been presented. Numerical results show that all these schemes may be unstable when the Mach number or the grid aspect ratio is large enough. The RLBFS seems to have better stability performance for all considered Mach numbers and grid aspect ratios, which may promote its application for simulating challenging compressible flows.

papers.title: Application of improved two-phase flow theory in air–water pipe flushing: Based on air-to-water ratio and cement paste rheological properties
papers.abstract: This research presents a comprehensive theoretical and practical framework for optimizing air–water pipe flushing in cemented paste backfill (CPB) systems by integrating improved two-phase flow theory with rheological analysis. Key advancements include the following: (1) establishing a novel correlation between CPB slump height and viscosity to quantify adhesion effects, (2) developing a frictional pressure drop model incorporating an equivalent diameter to account for CPB adhesion-induced pipeline roughness, and (3) identifying bubbly flow as the optimal flow pattern through rigorous analysis of air-to-water ratio impacts on shear stress and void fraction. Experimental and numerical validation demonstrates that increasing the air-to-water ratio reduces homogeneous density by up to 75% (from 1000 to 253.9 kg/m3) while enhancing flow velocity by 33% (from 6.93 to 9.24 m/s). The proposed model achieves a 10% improvement in pressure drop prediction accuracy compared to traditional methods. Field implementation in an African copper mine validated that air-to-water ratios of 2:1 reduce water consumption by 61.63% (75–28.78 m3) while maintaining flushing efficiency, addressing incomplete flushing and environmental concerns. A redesigned air–water system with sealed valve controls and pressure-adaptive compressors further ensures operational reliability. This study bridges theoretical gaps in two-phase flow modeling for non-Newtonian fluids and provides actionable strategies for sustainable mining practices.

papers.title: Optimizing injection and production parameters for enhanced thermal energy utilization in steam-assisted gravity drainage: A semi-analytical analysis
papers.abstract: This study first develops a semi-analytical model to optimize the liquid production rate or production–injection ratio throughout the steam-assisted gravity drainage (SAGD) process. Next, three semi-analytical approaches are formulated for different application scenarios. Finally, after verifying the accuracy of these approaches, we discuss their application in injection–production optimization. For ongoing projects, integrating approaches 1 and 2 effectively adjusts liquid production rates, leading to improvements in oil production and thermal energy utilization. For the Celtic Oilfield project, strategic adjustment of liquid production rates results in a 22.9% increase in oil production and an 18.6% reduction in the cumulative steam–oil ratio (CSOR) compared to the baseline. Approach 3 is particularly well suited for designing injection and production parameters for new projects. Implementing the optimized parameters from approach 3 enhances oil production and thermal energy utilization. For the SAGD project in Celtic Oilfield, this results in a 30.6% increase in cumulative oil production and a 12.9% reduction in CSOR. The optimal parameters designed for both the SAGD project in the Celtic Oilfield and in the Lvda Oilfield demonstrate the adaptability of approach 3 to varying reservoir conditions. This study presents efficient and accurate approaches for optimizing injection and production parameters to enhance thermal energy utilization in SAGD, applicable to both current and future projects.

papers.title: A projection method to symmetrize the momentum flux in a vector lattice Boltzmann formulation of hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: The standard lattice Boltzmann approach to hydrodynamics uses scalar distribution functions to represent the number densities of particles. Each particle moves with one of a small set of constant velocities. The momentum flux is the second moment of these distribution functions with respect to the particle velocities. The momentum flux is thus a symmetric tensor by construction, so the conservation law for linear momentum implies a conservation law for angular momentum. A more flexible approach uses vector distribution functions instead. Each particle carries a momentum that may not be aligned with its direction of propagation. The momentum flux tensor is in general not symmetric, so the evolution equation for angular momentum contains a source term as well as a flux. The momentum flux can be symmetrized using a more general model for collisions between particles that applies separate relaxation times to the symmetric and antisymmetric parts of the momentum flux and then sets the relaxation time for the antisymmetric part to zero. The resulting algorithm is equivalent to a projection of the momentum flux onto the space of symmetric tensors, analogous to the Chorin–Temam projection scheme for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations that projects the velocity field onto the space of divergence-free vector fields.

papers.title: Construction of a thermo-hydro-mechanical multi-field coupling model and its application in analyzing the thermal performance of hot dry rock mining
papers.abstract: Thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) coupling plays a vital role in analyzing the heat extraction efficiency of geothermal. To study the extraction performance of hot dry rock (HDR) in the Matouying Uplift area, a THM coupling model that describes the entire extraction process is first established, and then, the main controlling factors affecting the thermal performance are determined and the influence mechanism is elucidated; finally, the feasible recommendations to enhance HDR extraction efficiency are proposed. Results show that the injection temperature, pressure difference, well spacing, matrix permeability, and fracture aperture exhibit certain correlation with production well temperature, heat extraction power, heat extraction quantity, and heat extraction rate, which can be described by linear, exponential, power, binomial, and logistic functions. The low injection temperature, high-pressure difference, high matrix permeability, and appropriate well spacing and fracture aperture are most beneficial for enhancing heat extraction efficiency. In the presence of natural and artificial fractures, heat extraction is over an order of magnitude higher than in the absence of fractures. Under the same reservoir and process conditions, the thermal breakthrough time and heat extraction performance with the SCCO2 as the working fluid are 16.2% and 1–3 times of water. To achieve optimal results in HDR extraction, the following recommendations are made: first, select areas with well-developed natural fractures and conduct reservoir modification to create a dense fracture network; second, utilize SCCO2 as the working fluid for heat exchange within the reservoir; and finally, choose a higher-pressure difference, appropriate well spacing, and lower injection temperature.

papers.title: Shock train stabilization by a high-speed jet injection in an inlet isolator of a ramjet engine
papers.abstract: The ramjet engine exhibits significant potential for application due to its superior specific impulse and high-speed performance. The inlet isolator plays a critical role in decelerating and compressing the incoming flow by the internal shock system, while preventing the upstream propagation of high pressure in the combustor. Nevertheless, under hypervelocity operating conditions, the resistance of the isolator to back pressure and flow distortion will be significantly challenged. Therefore, the shock train control measures are needs to improve the performance of the isolator at high speeds. This study employs a combination of numerical simulations and experimental investigations to investigate the mechanisms and efficiency of high-speed jet injection in regulating the flow field in the inlet isolator. The results show that the jet injection enhances the velocity of airflow in the boundary layer and flow separation region to reinforce the back pressure resistance of the isolator. The injection angle, the injection pressure, and the injection flow momentum are the key factors affecting the control effect to shock trains. This study uses the downstream displacement length of the shock train after applying injection control as the metric to evaluate the control effect. Under the optimal conditions, jet injection can push the shock train downstream by no less than 13% of the isolator length (L), up to a maximum control effect of 19.20% L. A supersonic jet can further enhance the control capability and suppress the upstream propagation of the back pressure. The simulation results show that the control capability of the supersonic jet injection is not less than 26% L under suitable control conditions. This study provides critical research support for jet injection control strategies in ramjet isolators, which holds significant implications for advancing the engineering applications of flow control technologies.

papers.title: Intelligent prediction study on the seepage evolution of rock-concrete interface in compressed air energy storage artificial caverns under cyclic loading
papers.abstract: High-pressure air storage in abandoned mine roadways offers a promising approach for renewable energy utilization, but the gas-tightness of the rock-concrete interface degrades under cyclic loading. Nitrogen permeability tests on bonded sandstone-concrete and limestone-concrete interfaces under 2.5–20 MPa cyclic confining pressures yielded 146 895 data points. Results showed a cumulative increase in permeability with rising cycle counts, especially under lower pressures, characterized by slight decreases during compression and pronounced increases during unloading. The long short-term memory model, using load record values, median of loading range, interface type, and cycle counts as input features, outperformed traditional nonsequential models, achieving superior predictive performance. The accuracy and stability were further improved after the hyperparameters are optimized by the Sparrow Search Algorithm. Sensitivity analysis identified median stress amplitude as the primary factor controlling permeability evolution. This study develops a robust predictive framework and offers practical insights for optimizing the design and long-term maintenance of compressed air energy storage sealing systems under cyclic loading.

papers.title: Cellular detonation of H2–O2 mixtures propagating in media with spatially nonuniform reactivity
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effect of spatially nonuniform reactivity on the two-dimensional unsteady H2–O2 detonation characterized by the activation energy gradient. Numerical simulations reveal the front dynamics of the cellular detonation affected by the interaction of the triple points, transverse waves, and unreacted pockets. The nonhomogeneous reactivity directly affects the self-sustaining capability, which is well-demonstrated in homogeneous conditions. The average dimensions of the detonation wave and the formation of unreacted pockets formed behind the front are closely related to the reactivity gradient. As the inhomogeneity increases, the unreacted pockets in the reaction region and the extended induction length between the shock front and the flame front eventually make quenching more likely, which is also argued in this investigation.

papers.title: Approach flow effects on the wake of a circular cylinder near a bed
papers.abstract: This study numerically investigates the effect of the approaching boundary layer on flow past a circular cylinder positioned at varying distances from the bed. Two turbulent boundary layers with different thickness (thin and thick) were prescribed at the inlet boundary. The cylinder was positioned such that the gap formed between it and the bed varied from 25% to 100% of the diameter. It was noted that a reduction in the gap ratio led to increased asymmetry in the wake region, caused by the deflection of the flow exiting the gap. The change in the approaching boundary layer from thin to thick resulted in a lesser deflection of the gap flow and a smaller recirculation region along the bed. Depending on the gap ratio and the type of the approaching boundary layer, the interaction among the separated shear layers emanating from the cylinder and the bed was found to be different. At a gap ratio of 50%, with the thin boundary layer, more complex vorticity dynamics were observed, including vortex pairing between the vortices emanating from the upper cylinder side and from the bed. The analysis of the spatial two-point correlation of the velocity fluctuations revealed a significant disruption in the coherence of the structures as the gap ratio decreased. For the thick boundary layer cases, the influence of the cylinder wake was more pronounced on the downstream flow near the bed.

papers.title: Structural optimization of single-strand crucible for planar flow casting: Simulation and application study
papers.abstract: Amorphous ribbon materials are evolving to meet social development trends and commercial demands, focusing on high efficiency and stability. However, the flow of molten metal and the behavior of inclusions in the crucible during the ribbon production process significantly affect both the mechanical properties and surface quality of the ribbons. A well-designed flow control structure is crucial for optimizing molten metal flow and improving cleanliness. This study, based on computational fluid dynamics, develops a two-phase flow model and a unidirectional Discrete phase model, combined with physical simulations, to investigate the effects of different retaining wall structures on molten metal flow and inclusion removal in a single-strand crucible. The results indicate that case D, which reduces the bottom hole area and positions it 50 mm from the centerline, with 20° horizontal inclination for both upper and bottom diversion holes, and a 20° vertical inclination for the upper diversion hole, is the optimal retaining wall structure. Compared to the prototype structure, this case reduced the dead zone proportion by 18.6%, extended the mean residence time to 54 s and increased the inclusion removal rate by 20.7%. Industrial application data showed that after structural optimization, the inclusion content in the molten metal decreased by 12%, the ribbon lamination factor remained above 89.5%, and the average thickness range was reduced by 0.6. This demonstrates that numerical simulations can guide industrial optimization, enhancing the metallurgical effect of the single-strand crucible in continuous casting and improving the quality and performance of the final product.

papers.title: Gaseous slip flow through a shallow deformable microchannel
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate the fluid–structure interaction between a rarefied compressible gas flow and a long, narrow, deformable microchannel. Our approach utilizes the continuity and momentum equations to analyze the hydrodynamic field, employing an equation of state that relates density linearly to pressure. The structural analysis is based on the Kirchhoff–Love theory. The fluid flow and structural mechanics are coupled by the transverse deformation of the microchannel caused by the gauge pressure within it. We obtain the hydrodynamics using the lubrication approximation, which allows us to semi-analytically derive the flow field while accounting for the first-order slip-velocity boundary condition. Our primary findings highlight the relationship between the mass flow rate (ṁ) and the pressure drop (Δp̃). This relationship is influenced by several factors, including the compliance parameter (β̃), the dimensionless isothermal compressibility (κT), the ratio of pressure drop to atmospheric pressure (Π), and the characteristic Knudsen number (Kno). Furthermore, we derive the friction coefficient (Cf) and the associated Poiseuille number (Po). Our semi-analytical solution was compared to the experimental work of Arkilic and Schmidt [“Gaseous slip flow in long microchannels,” J. Microelectromech. Syst. 6, 167–178 (1997)], demonstrating excellent agreement for the case of a rigid microchannel. Additionally, when we consider rarefaction and a compliant microchannel, the friction factor (Cf) and pressure drop (Po) decrease. Comparing the relationship ṁ−Δp̃ for deformable and rigid microchannels reveals that for a given pressure drop, the mass flow rate can be significantly underestimated under the same conditions when rarefaction and compressibility effects are taken into account.

papers.title: Quantitative measurement of marginal regeneration of soap film
papers.abstract: The anti-gravity motion of a tadpole shaped dimple, defined as marginal regeneration, has been quantitatively described, using the large lateral shearing interferometry. The maximum film thickness is 23.06 μm and the total film volume is 1.47 ± 0.02 mm3. In the propagation stage, the area of its head gradually increases while the volume remains stable at 0.040 mm3. In the dissipation stage, both the area and volume of its head remain stable. During the lifetime, the ratio between the average film thickness and the reference film thickness at the same height, gradually increases from 0.80 to 0.93.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural network for solving the coupled Reynolds–energy equations with viscosity–temperature effects in hydrodynamic journal bearings
papers.abstract: This study presents an efficient solution framework for energy–Reynolds-coupled equations in hydrodynamic journal bearings (HJBs) incorporating the viscosity–temperature effect through a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The proposed framework is termed Reynolds-and-energy-coupled physics-informed neural network, abbreviated as RAE-PINN. Leveraging the unsupervised learning capabilities of PINN, an adaptive sampling strategy is introduced to optimize the spatial distribution of computational points. Additionally, a hard-constraint method is employed to ensure the physical consistency of boundary conditions and cavitation regions. To further enhance the generalization capability of RAE-PINN, a transfer learning strategy is implemented, enabling adaptation to variations in bearing structural parameters (such as aspect ratio, eccentricity, and radial clearance) and operating conditions (e.g., rotational speed). The results demonstrate that RAE-PINN achieves high accuracy in predicting oil film pressure and temperature distributions, closely aligning with high-fidelity finite element method (FEM) simulations. Furthermore, RAE-PINN achieves a computational speedup of over 300 times, reducing the solution time for a single bearing case from several minutes to less than one second, thereby significantly enhancing computational efficiency. Compared to traditional numerical methods, RAE-PINN not only preserves computational accuracy but also substantially reduces computational costs, providing an efficient, stable, and scalable numerical solution framework for intelligent modeling, optimized design, and real-time analysis of rotating machinery bearing systems.

papers.title: Trigger mechanism of vertical vortices at intakes with variable gate opening
papers.abstract: Suction vortices in hydraulic systems significantly impact energy loss and cavitation damage. To investigate the trigger mechanism of those suction vortices is important to improve engineering reliability, and meanwhile, the equipment life can be extended by revealing its generation mechanism and control method. Therefore, this paper numerically investigates the trigger mechanism of vertical vortices at hydraulic intakes using four real hydropower cases. Vortex evolution during gate opening is analyzed via free surface elevation, vortex core lines, vorticity, and velocity fields. The visualization results release two remarkable findings, one is that the action of gate opening indeed affects the formation and development of vertical vortex in gate chamber, while the other is that vertical vortex does not occur in Shilong radial gate opening case due to the unformed reverse pressure condition. Trigger mechanism of vertical vortex is then investigated in detail through critical submerged water depth, the Reynolds number (Re), and flow separation near pier head. The investigation shows that the results based on Gordon formula are found conflicting with numerical simulation results, which not only delayed the triggering moment of vertical vortex but also misestimated vortex occurrence in Shilong radial gate opening case. The influence of Re is an important but not dominant factor in the triggering of vertical vortex. Flow separation near pier head is considered as a key factor in the occurrence of vertical vortex at hydraulic water intake with gate opening motion.

papers.title: Time-dependent transport on the continental shelf driven by steady winds
papers.abstract: The horizontal transport on a linearly sloping continental shelf forced by time-independent wind stress is studied here in the Lagrangian framework using the adiabaticity principle, in which a potential is constructed for the cross-shelf dynamics. The dynamics is separated into fast oscillations about the potential's minimum and slow changes in the location of the minimum itself. The resulting analysis and accompanying numerical solutions show that the wind-driven transport consists of nonlinear inertial oscillations and slow net transport. As in traditional Ekman theory, the net transport is directed at 90° to the right (in the northern hemisphere) of the applied wind stress, although on the shelf the cross-shore transport is time dependent. Analytic solutions yield explicit expressions for mass conservation that imply convergence of net off-shore directed transports and divergence of net on-shore directed transports prior to reaching the shoreline.

papers.title: Using Langevin dynamics to investigate the effects of particle concentration on particle collision rate and aggregate morphology
papers.abstract: The classical Smoluchowski theory is unsuitable for analyzing particle aggregation and predicting particle collision rates because it cannot be applied under high particle concentrations and does not account for aggregate morphologies. Thus, this study developed a model based on the Langevin dynamics equation to investigate particle collisions and aggregate morphologies under varying particle concentrations [particle volume fractions (∅) of 0.001–0.3]. The results of this study indicate that an increase in ∅ accelerates the establishment of a self-preserving size distribution (SPSD) for aggregates, with the normalized size distribution function (i.e., the shape of the size distribution) remaining unchanged over time. Moreover, as ∅ increases, the equilibrium SPSD becomes broader. The collision rates in the developed model considerably exceed those predicted by Smoluchowski theory, with the enhancement factor ranging from 1.18 when ∅ = 0.001 to 24 when ∅ = 0.3. The initial particle concentration strongly influences the final aggregate structure. An increase in the number of particles (Np) causes an increase in the radius of gyration (Rg) but a decrease in the fractal dimension (Df) and shape anisotropy (A13), with these trends being more pronounced at lower ∅ values. Moreover, an increase in ∅ causes a decrease in Rg and A13 but an increase in Df. In the established model, the average Df values at ∅ values of 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 are 1.92, 2.03, 2.16, and 2.28, respectively. Low-particle-concentration systems tend to form elongated structures, whereas high-particle-concentration systems form compact clusters with strong fractal characteristics.

papers.title: The pore-network-continuum hybrid modeling of nonlinear shale gas flow in digital rocks of organic matter
papers.abstract: Organic matter (OM) serves as the primary source of gaseous hydrocarbons in shales. Fundamental understanding of its permeability and gas production characteristics is vital to optimize shale gas exploitation. The focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) imaging can resolve OM macropores with pore radii ranging from tens to hundreds of nanometers, while pore sizes of sub-resolution OM can be characterized using low-temperature gas adsorption. In this work, we focus on multiscale pore structures of OM and contribute to the development of an efficient pore-network-continuum model for simulating nonlinear gas flow in multiscale OM digital rocks, along with its fully coupled implicit numerical implementation. To demonstrate the influence of OM pore structures on its permeability and transient gas production, we select three types of OM featured by their distinct porosities, connectivity of macropores, and pore morphologies. We show that the high-porosity OM with interconnected macropores exhibits markedly different intrinsic permeability, mechanisms of apparent permeability, gas storage, and production behaviors compared to the medium-porosity and low-porosity OM. Moreover, we propose an empirical formula for OM apparent permeability with respect to an effective characterization length used in the calculation of Knudsen number, which will be the key input to the representative elementary volume (REV) size modeling of shale matrix.

papers.title: Pitch angle effects on the detachment of a prolate spheroidal particle from a wall in linear shear flow
papers.abstract: This study employs the lattice Boltzmann method to investigate hydrodynamic forces and torque on a wall-attached prolate spheroidal particle in linear shear flow. The effects of incidence angle, pitch angle, and particle aspect ratio on drag, lift, and torque coefficients under finite particle Reynolds numbers are investigated. When the pitch angle varies from 0° to 180° at a fixed incidence angle of 0°, the drag coefficient initially increases and then decreases, exhibiting asymmetry at 90°. This is because flow separation tends to develop when pitch angles are below 90°. The lift coefficient reaches its maximum at approximately a 60° pitch angle, differing from the 45° observed in unconfined shear flow. This phenomenon is attributed to the increased static pressure on the particle's upstream side. For larger aspect ratios, the torque coefficient peaks at a pitch angle less than 90°. When the incidence angle increases from 0° to 180° with a fixed pitch angle of 45°, the drag coefficient reaches its maximum at 90° due to the maximized projected area normal to the flow. The lift coefficient decreases monotonically as the particle's orientation changes from forward to backward relative to the flow. The torque coefficient decreases with increasing incidence angle, driven by a shift in the pressure center toward the particle's centroid. Rolling detachment is identified as the most effective detachment mechanism for prolate spheroidal particles. This study proposes empirical correlations for the drag, lift, and torque coefficients and an algorithm to determine the critical particle Reynolds numbers for detachment.

papers.title: Advanced wake modeling in wind farm: A physics-informed framework with virtual LiDAR measurements
papers.abstract: Active yaw control is an effective technique that mitigates wake effects by intentionally deflecting wakes away from downstream wind turbines. As flow conditions within wind farms critically influence turbine performance, precise observation and prediction of wake dynamics are essential for optimizing control strategies and maximizing energy production. This study proposes a novel wake modeling framework based on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), effectively modeling the wake field in a wind farm using measurements from sparse spatial points. Leveraging limited LiDAR measurements, the proposed framework captures complex wake dynamics, closely reflecting actual wind farm scenarios. To develop this framework, Large Eddy Simulations were first conducted to generate high-fidelity datasets of the wake field within the wind farm. Two typical scenarios were investigated: the non-yaw period, when all wind turbines align with wind direction, and the yawed period, when turbines operate at optimized yaw angles. The proposed framework was evaluated for both wake reconstruction (rebuilding flow fields within the measurement period) and prediction (forecasting beyond the measurement timeframe) using these two datasets. Results indicate that, despite limitations in reproducing small-scale turbulence, the proposed wake modeling technique accurately captures the overall wake field dynamics in the reconstruction task. In the prediction task, while the modeling results show higher errors compared to the reconstruction task, they still accurately reflect wind farm wake trajectories and power output. These results suggest that the proposed PINN-based wake modeling framework could be valuable for wind farm monitoring and wake control strategy development.

papers.title: The investigation on compressor's end wall and suction surface profiling using the surrogate model assisted optimization design method
papers.abstract: The design of non-axisymmetric end wall shapes today primarily relies on optimization methods based on surrogate models. In recent years, this approach has increasingly faced the “curse of dimensionality” due to the large number of design parameters. The key to addressing this issue lies in the choice of shaping methods. To explore more effective modeling techniques, this paper employs two different shaping methods: the lofted surface method and the surface-mapping method, to optimize the modeling of the end wall and blade. This study is based on a high-load blade cascade, where a multi-objective optimization design is conducted using the same optimization method. The study finds that the surface-mapping method exhibits a higher convergence rate during the optimization process and achieves better flow control under different incidences. Therefore, the comparison in this paper demonstrates that the surface-mapping method is more effective in addressing the “curse of dimensionality” problem.

papers.title: Investigation on improving the heat exchange efficiency of an ocean thermal engine with snowflake-like fins
papers.abstract: The low melting efficiency of ocean thermal engines limits the sampling rate of buoys driven by ocean thermal energy. To address this issue, an innovative snowflake-type fin has been integrated into the thermal unit of an ocean thermal energy conversion power generator. A numerical investigation was conducted to analyze the effects of fin configuration, bifurcation angle θ, spacing L, and length ratio α on the melting behavior and thermal storage performance, with maintaining a constant total fin volume held constant throughout the study. The results indicate that the snowflake configuration significantly reduces the complete melting time of the phase change material (PCM). Furthermore, the melting time exhibits a trend that initially decreases before subsequently increasing. Using response surface methodology, the optimal conditions for single-factor optimization with a fixed total fin volume were determined to be θ1 = 123°, θ2 = 113°, L20 = 6.78 mm, and α = 0.648, achieving the shortest melting time. Under these optimized conditions, the melting time was reduced by 34.8% compared to traditional multi-level fin configurations. This paper proposes a method for optimizing PCM melting and thermal storage performance through the utilization of a snowflake configuration.

papers.title: Mechanism of mining-induced earthquakes triggered by thick hard rock strata fracture and application of hydraulic fracturing control technology
papers.abstract: The objective of this study is to investigate the mechanisms of strong mining-induced earthquake triggered by the fracture of thick and hard rock strata and the application of hydraulic fracturing for mitigating mining-induced earthquake. A coal mine located in Shandong province, China, was selected for this case study. The mechanisms of strong mining-induced earthquake triggered by the fracture of thick and hard rock strata were revealed based on field monitoring data and the physical simulation test results. A numerical model was established to analyze the energy accumulation and release characteristics of rock strata under varying degrees of fracture, elucidating the mechanisms of seismic reduction and energy dissipation achieved by hydraulic fracturing of thick and hard rock strata. The propagation patterns of fractures during the hydraulic fracturing process were clarified, and the distribution characteristics of hydraulic fractures under different injection pressures and lateral pressure coefficients were obtained, based on numerical simulation. Field application results show that it can effectively weaken and fracture the integrity of thick and hard rock strata to reduce the occurrence of mining-induced earthquakes with large energy. A total of 21 strong mining-induced earthquake events occurred in 63upper06 working face during the advance from 0 to 500 m, significantly fewer than in the previously mined 63upper05, 63upper04, and 63upper03 working faces with reductions of 46%, 50%, and 67%, respectively. In addition, the sufficient details of hydraulic fracturing technology provided in this study can potentially be applied to coal mines with strong mining-induced earthquake.

papers.title: Revised unsteady drag force and its impact on particle dynamics at high Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: The accurate modeling of particle motion in viscous fluids at high Reynolds numbers remains a fundamental challenge, particularly under unsteady flow conditions where nonlinear effects dominate. This study introduces a revised unsteady drag formulation, extending its applicability beyond previous studies. By integrating classical solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations, the new formulation overcomes the limitations of the Maxey–Riley–Gatignol (MRG) equation, addressing non-physical memory effects associated with Basset drag and extending its applicability to higher Reynolds numbers. Through experimental comparisons and direct numerical simulations (DNS), the revised equation of motion is compared to the MRG equation, both during steady-state conditions and non-equilibrium transitions. The revised formulation exhibits consistency with observations across a board range of Reynolds numbers. Furthermore, the DNS of particle-laden turbulence reveals enhanced clustering and collision–coalescence dynamics when using the revised drag force, emphasizing the formulation's capability to capture particle interactions in turbulent flows. These findings provide critical insights into atmospheric and hydrodynamic applications, advancing our understanding of droplets settling, clustering, and growth in turbulent environments. The proposed framework holds potential for improving predictions in climate models, sediment transport, and other fields reliant on accurate particle dynamics.

papers.title: Drop spreading characteristics over a micro-pillared surface and comparison with an equivalent flat surface
papers.abstract: Low-Weber-number droplet impacts (We < 1) are crucial in applications such as dropwise condensation, microfluidics, inkjet printing, and spray coating where surface tension is dominant. The present study investigates the spreading of millimetric droplets on micro-pillared surfaces with varying pitch (15, 30, and 60 μm) and Weber numbers (0.21, 1, and 3.9), encompassing capillary, transition, and inertia-dominated regimes. Experimental observations reveal distinct jet ejection regimes, including transitions from entrapped jets to singular thin jets with increasing Weber numbers. Multiple bouncing was observed on sparsely spaced pillars at lower Weber numbers. A numerical model employing an equivalent flat surface approximation, incorporating a dynamic contact angle model for a pillared surface, was utilized to obtain droplet shapes and spreading patterns. This approach successfully predicted droplet deformation in the capillary and inertia-dominated regimes. To account for the influence of liquid penetration into the pillar spacing at higher impact velocities, the contact angle parameters were suitably modified, resulting in improved agreement between simulations and experiments across all impact regimes. These findings highlight the importance of liquid penetration between pillars for accurately predicting wetting state transitions during droplet impact dynamics on micro-pillared surfaces.

papers.title: Lattice Boltzmann method-based large eddy simulation of the influence of atmospheric stability on wind farm wake
papers.abstract: Atmospheric stability is essential for wind farm performance. In this numerical work, we investigate the behavior of wind farm wake flow under the influence of atmospheric stability through lattice Boltzmann method-based large eddy simulation. Wind turbines are conceptualized as actuator line models, and the ground momentum and thermal flux within the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) are represented using the Monin–Obukhov similarity theory. Several fundamental configurations were first simulated, including a single wind turbine under stratified ABL, and a wind farm under neutral ABL, to validate the present numerical framework. The work has then been extended to the study of wind farm performance under varying ABL conditions, including stable and convective environments. The atmospheric stability influence on wind farm performance is analyzed in detail by examining the time-averaged wake flow velocity profiles, turbulence intensity distribution, and temperature field. These quantities tend to stabilize after several turbine rows, with the wake velocity and turbulence intensity being 9% and 22% greater, respectively, in the stable case compared to the convective case. The turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) budget and vortex structure analysis reveal that the buoyancy forces dominate the TKE production in the convective condition, while vertical shear dominates under stable condition.

papers.title: The Riemann problem with delta initial data for the homogeneous pressureless hydrodynamic model
papers.abstract: During road transportation, particularly during peak hours or under specific circumstances, severe traffic congestion often occurs, significantly reducing traffic flow. Therefore, it is essential to investigate the development of severe traffic congestion. The delta shock wave is commonly employed in traffic flow models to explain severe traffic congestion. In this paper, we primarily study the development of severe traffic congestion occurring at the initial moment by investigating the initial value problem with delta initial data for the homogeneous pressureless hydrodynamic model. Depending on the local mean headway variations, the problem is categorized into four distinct cases, and the structural solutions for each case are derived. Each solution incorporates a delta shock wave that persists indefinitely, indicating that the severe traffic congestion will continue. Thus, the Transportation Management Authority must take appropriate measures to prevent severe traffic congestion, such as proactively deploying real-time traffic monitoring and adaptive signal control systems. Otherwise, mitigating severe traffic congestion will be challenging once it occurs. Moreover, we present some typical numerical results consistent with our theoretical analysis.

papers.title: A bi-variate sectional moment projection method for particle population balance dynamics
papers.abstract: A bi-variate sectional moment projection method (BVSMPM) is present in this work and applied to the solution of bi-variate population balance equations involving nucleation, growth, shrinkage, coagulation, and fragmentation. It combines the technique of sectional method and projection-based moment method in a flexible way to conserve any set of lower-order mixed moments and directly tracks the evolution of the bi-variate particle size distribution (PSD). An efficient moment-inversion algorithm, based on mixed moment decomposition technique, is developed to compute a set of moving sectional weighted particles for the moment source term closure and provide accurate reconstruction of the bi-variate PSD. Two allocation schemes for the weighted particles are proposed, and their influence on the numerical accuracy is investigated. The performance of BVSMPM is assessed using a series of test cases with different types of kernel functions and initial particle distributions. BVSMPM predicts the evolution of the bi-variate particle populations, which are almost as accurate as a high-precision solution using the direct simulation algorithm.

papers.title: Machine learning-based cavitation stage identification in an axisymmetric Venturi under bubbly shock dominance
papers.abstract: Understanding the bubbly shock mechanism in partially cavitating flows is vital for both controlling and harnessing cavitation. Venturis, due to their geometric confinement, provide an ideal platform for investigating this phenomenon. This study introduces an automatic identification method for cavitation stages in an axisymmetric Venturi dominated by bubbly shock, combining unsupervised clustering with supervised classification algorithms, requiring no prior knowledge. Using principal component analysis on high-speed photography data at σ = 0.30, three distinct cavitation stages are identified through a density peaks clustering algorithm combined with three representative classifiers: support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), and K-nearest neighbor (KNN). Stage I begins with the initial growth of the sheet cavity and ends when pressure waves first impact it, while stage II starts upon this first impact and ends when the sheet cavity first detaches. Stage III follows stage II. To ensure classification accuracy, two additional features, i.e., the difference and slope of the average gray value over a short interval, are introduced. The classification accuracies for SVM, RF, and KNN at σ = 0.30 are 99.3%, 98.8%, and 98.7%, respectively. In addition, SVM demonstrates superior generalization when tested at σ = 0.27 and 0.37, whereas RF and KNN show relatively weaker adaptability. This study presents a robust, data-driven approach for automated cavitation stage identification and offers valuable insight for analyzing and predicting complex cavitating flow structures.

papers.title: Investigation of scramjet inlet unstart/restart behavior induced by high angle of attack and dynamic isolator camber motion
papers.abstract: This study employs high-fidelity simulations, benchmarked with wind tunnel experiments at Mach 3.9, to investigate how pitching maneuvers influence unstart in a planar scramjet inlet with a Mach 2.5 shock-on-lip design and a contraction ratio of 2.14. Simulations utilize the Spalart–Allmaras unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes turbulence model to analyze unstart onset across two pitch rates (10°/s and 100°/s) over an AoA (angle of attack) range of 0°to 10°. Results indicate that unstart onset correlates with a rapid rise in exit pressure and shock detachment along the lower leading edge, with lower pitch rates producing significantly higher exit pressures. These findings highlight the sensitivity of inlet stability to the transient aerodynamics of the pitching maneuvers. A dynamic adjustment of the isolator area is introduced just before the unstart onset to evaluate the potential of this approach for unstart mitigation. This strategy enabled shock reformation and direct regulation of outlet pressure, demonstrating the potential for variable-camber inlet-isolator systems in maintaining performance under off-design conditions. In addition to physical observations, an analytical approach is presented to predict the re-acceleration of the flow due to the time rate of change of area in the isolator. An excellent alignment between the analytical equation and the simulated results is observed, indicating a useful relation for insight into inlet/isolator unstart–restart behavior, with application to future wind tunnel tests, control theory implementation, and maneuver limit studies.

papers.title: Improved Lagrangian flow network and its application to pattern evolution and mass transport in three-dimensional cavitating flow around a hydrofoil
papers.abstract: The complex behaviors of cavitation in three-dimensional (3D) cavitating vortical flow around a hydrofoil can be studied in detail using an improved Lagrangian method combined with a subgrid model. In addition, the interactions between cavitation and vortices are investigated from Lagrangian point of view. First, the 3D multiphase flow algorithm coupled with a Lagrangian subgrid model is developed to effectively capture multi-scale dynamics within the flow field. Then, the unique characteristics and dynamics of cloud and sheet cavitation phases are analyzed, emphasizing their distinct impact on fluid flow and vortex formation. In particular, the formation of the cavitation pattern in cloud cavitation is closely linked to the development of the primary vortex, with the shedding of the cavity being significantly influenced by the dynamics of the re-entrant flow. Moreover, mass transport channels are identified in Lagrangian flow network, which can be used to examine how the flow structures move and interact within the cavitating flow. Finally, an in-depth analysis is carried out to evaluate the impact of different parameter settings on the propagation and behavior of cavitation, particularly in the spanwise direction. The sources and implications of numerical errors that arise during the simulations are also discussed, and the insights gained from distinguishing between different cavitation patterns and studying their specific behaviors contribute significantly to the fields of fluid mechanics and marine engineering. In summary, this study aims to provide more reliable and accurate models for predicting and managing cavitation in practical applications, by improving the applicability of Lagrangian flow networks.

papers.title: The influence of topography on mesoscale eddy mass transport
papers.abstract: The mass transport capacity of mesoscale eddies over their long-period evolution is investigated by a series of passive tracer simulations within a numerical model. The eddy nonlinearity causes fluid parcels to be trapped within the closed potential vorticity contours, which then migrate with the eddy. The mass transport capacity of a mesoscale eddy decayed during the spontaneous generation of near-inertial waves (NIWs) and its interaction with seafloor topography. During the spontaneous NIW generation, the mass transport capacity declines due to the reduction in eddy rotational speed. The interaction between a mesoscale eddy and topography involves multiple mechanisms, resulting in a substantial decrease in the eddy radius and consequently impeding its mass transport capacity. When a mesoscale eddy encounters the topography, lee waves and submesoscale filaments are generated, and the eddy radius decreases, modulating the relative vorticity to balance the ambient vorticity variations induced by the topography. The greater the topography gradient, the more rapidly the mass transport of a mesoscale eddy decays. The leakage of mass transported by a cyclonic eddy due to the interaction between the eddy and topography is greater than that in the interaction between an anticyclonic eddy and topography. The average relative mass transport rates for both anticyclonic and cyclonic mesoscale eddies exhibit linear relationships with the topography within the range of 500–1000 m. When mesoscale eddies interact with the topography above 1100 m, baroclinic instability occurs, causing a significant fraction of the trapped fluid parcels to escape from the eddies.

papers.title: Antibubble formation on a confined liquid surface under vertical vibrations
papers.abstract: Antibubble is a unique fluid system characterized by a thin air film encapsulating a liquid core, a structure that endows them with excellent resistance to external contamination. The protective air film effectively isolates the internal liquid, demonstrating significant potential in applications such as encapsulation, controlled release, and targeted delivery in fields including medicine and materials science. However, the practical application of antibubbles has been constrained by the lack of high-throughput preparation methods. This paper presents an efficient high-throughput method for antibubble generation and systematically investigates its formation dynamics using high-speed imaging technology. Experimental results show that under vertical vibration, periodic pressure changes induce the formation of a penetrating jet within the confined bubble. The jet undergoes a pinching neck process, forming a primary droplet that subsequently experiences a collision with the bottom surface of the bubble, leading to the generation of an antibubble. Based on experimental results, this study constructs a regime map of antibubble generation behavior under different vibration frequencies, acceleration conditions, and confinement conditions. Theoretical analysis indicates that the antibubble generation frequency can reach fi = 1/2T under ideal conditions, while the maximum generation frequency measured in experiments is 12 per second, showing good agreement with theoretical predictions. This method provides a reliable framework for the large-scale production of antibubbles and lays an important foundation for further research into their properties and cross-disciplinary applications.

papers.title: Impact of local blowing and suction on controlling first-mode oblique breakdown in high-speed boundary layers
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effects of localized blowing and suction on the transition of first mode oblique breakdowns in a Mach 4.5 high-speed boundary layer using direct numerical simulations and stability theory. The linear stability theory shows that blowing enhances the amplification of first mode, while suction stabilizes the boundary layer by suppressing these disturbances. Direct numerical simulations indicate that blowing promotes the first mode oblique breakdown by increasing disturbance amplitudes. The kinetic energy budget shows that the increased amplitude of the first mode is due to the energy production term's enhancement and the weakening of the viscous term's stabilizing effect. Meanwhile, the source term of spanwise vorticity is enhanced. Conversely, suction suppresses the first mode oblique breakdown by reducing energy production and increasing viscous stabilization effects. Meanwhile, the high dissipation and negative source term of the spanwise vorticity will be caused. In summary, local suction delays the first and mode oblique breakdown, while local blowing promotes the transition of the first mode oblique breakdown.

papers.title: A mathematical model for the dynamic evolution of gas–water permeability in propped fractures due to coal fine intrusion
papers.abstract: The migration and deposition of coal fines in propped fractures directly affect the production of coalbed methane wells. This study develops a mathematical model to describe the spatiotemporal evolution of gas–water relative permeability in coal-bearing propped fractures. The key findings are as follows: As the gas–water ratio increases, the mass concentration of coal fine suspensions and the volume fraction of deposited coal fines decrease on the upstream side of a critical position, while increasing on the downstream side. At a constant gas–water ratio, an increase in flow velocity exhibits a similar effect on coal fine deposition but shifts the critical position further along the migration direction. In this case, coal fine deposition is the primary factor altering porosity and relative permeability within propped fractures. Additionally, increasing particle size leads to a higher volume fraction of deposited coal fines on the upstream side of the critical position and a lower fraction on the downstream side. Particle size does not exhibit a critical position for suspended coal fine concentration; instead, the concentration decreases consistently as particle size increases. In this scenario, the specific surface area of coal fines becomes the dominant factor influencing gas–water relative permeability. Larger coal fine particles result in a reduced specific surface area and greater porosity variation between the entrance and the far end of the propped fracture. As a combined effect, gas–water relative permeability increases across most regions of the propped fracture except near the entrance, where permeability variations become nonlinearly dependent on coal fine particle size.

papers.title: Mass and heat transfer in developing fracture-filling gas hydrate using a fractured horizontal well
papers.abstract: Natural fractures are widely distributed in hydrate reservoirs, resulting in a fracture-filling type of gas hydrate. However, the complexity of fracture networks, including both hydraulic and natural fractures, complicates the evaluations of gas well productivity. This study investigates the heat and mass transfer dynamics in fracture-filling gas hydrate reservoirs developed using a multi-stage fractured horizontal well. A coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical model was developed based on the embedded discrete fracture method, and the model was validated against a commercial numerical simulator, demonstrating high accuracy in predicting gas–water production rates and reservoir pressure, temperature, and hydrate saturation field evolution. The simulation results revealed significant insights into gas and water production rates, flux distributions, and field map distributions. Furthermore, we analyzed the impact of various hydraulic fracture parameters, including fracture numbers, angles, lengths, and morphologies. The simulation results show that fractured wells perform better than non-fractured wells, and the initial daily gas production of a multi-stage fractured horizontal well is 4.05 times that of a fractured vertical well. Besides, fracture geometry critically influences the productivity of the multi-stage fractured horizontal well. The greater the number of hydraulic fractures and the longer the fracture length, the higher the daily and cumulative gas production of the gas well due to higher drainage areas. The cumulative gas production is increased by 131.98% as the number of hydraulic fractures is increased from 3 to 9, whereas the increase is 91.66% as the fracture length is increased from 50 to 200 m. A narrower intersection angle between hydraulic fractures and the wellbore corresponds to a diminished drainage area, thereby exacerbating fracture-driven interference effects and accelerating production decline rates. The intersection density between hydraulic fractures and natural fracture systems serves as the primary determinant of drainage efficiency in fracture-filling gas hydrate reservoirs. The findings have important implications for improving gas well productivity and enhancing the efficient exploitation of fracture-filling gas hydrates.

papers.title: Enhancing seawater-lubricated radial piston pump performance via radial auxiliary support
papers.abstract: The Seawater-Lubricated Radial Piston Pump (SLRPP) serves as a critical power component for underwater equipment. To meet the demanding requirements of high working pressure and volumetric efficiency in advanced SLRPP systems, this study investigates a novel radial piston pump design incorporating an innovative radial auxiliary support mechanism. Through comprehensive static and nonlinear dynamic analysis of the piston system, conclusively identified radial force imbalance as the predominant mechanism responsible for piston misalignment. An innovative hybrid solution integrating linear rolling bearings with an auxiliary support ring was developed to optimize radial force distribution, effectively minimizing piston offset and reducing cylinder leakage. Numerical simulations and prototype testing validate the design's performance. The experimental results highlight two key achievements: (1) optimal operation efficiency (94.64%) under standard conditions (500 rpm, 1 MPa) with ideal lubrication, and (2) a dramatic 46.17% efficiency gain under demanding 15 MPa loading at 600 rpm. This performance enhancement substantially exceeds conventional SLRPP capabilities, demonstrating the transformative potential of the radial auxiliary support design. The proposed radial auxiliary support structure and its design methodology provide an effective solution for boosting SLRPP performance, offering valuable guidance for the development of similar piston pump systems. These findings present important implications for advancing high-efficiency marine hydraulic technologies.

papers.title: Enhancing computational accuracy of Savonius wind turbine: An application of shear-stress transport k – ω model with modified stress limiter
papers.abstract: This study investigates the applicability of the modified Reynolds stress limiter to improve the accuracy of the two-dimensional computational simulations of the Savonius wind turbine. The modification is applied to the shear stress transport k–ω model by incorporating the limiter strength parameters a1 and Clim. The numerical methods using User Define Function were first validated before being applied to the Savonius turbine under various flow tip speed ratios (TSRs) and configurations. The results show that increasing a1 (or decreasing Clim) strengthens the turbulent quantities, the vortex zone inside the blade, and the thin shear strain layer. These effects delay the flow attachment and separation along the blade, reduce the positive pressure force on the turbine, accelerate the vortex decay in the turbine wake, and minimize the numerical deviation. Based on the numerical analysis, a new set of limiter strength parameters (a1 = 0.45 and Clim = 0.67) is recommended, especially for high-fidelity computational results at the high TSRs, which the standard turbulence models typically overestimate. This finding is essential for accurately designing a high-efficiency Savonius turbine, which shows potential applications in urban and offshore environments.

papers.title: Analytical model for saturated nonuniform laminar flow through three-dimensional mismatched rough fractures
papers.abstract: In naturally fractured reservoirs, mismatched and heterogeneous features in the void space of fracture have been widely observed and proven to affect the transport properties significantly. However, accurate estimation of fluid flow dynamics within intricate three-dimensional fracture networks continues to pose significant challenges, thereby impeding a comprehensive understanding of how mismatched and heterogeneous geometric configurations influence system behavior. In this study, an analytical model for incompressible, nonuniform laminar flow in a single fracture with heterogeneous and anisotropic hydraulic properties is rigorously derived, which accounts for the effects of the three-dimensional local roughness, tortuosity, hydraulic inertia, and additional viscous dissipation induced by the nonuniform flow field. The model's validity was systematically evaluated through comprehensive comparisons with both numerical solutions derived from Navier–Stokes equations and experimental flow measurements conducted in three-dimensional rough-walled fractures. Quantitative analysis demonstrates that the model predictions exhibit remarkable consistency with benchmark numerical simulations (effective deviation Di range within ±5.2%, with an arithmetic mean of |Di| 1.24%) and show excellent agreement with experimental observations (an average effective deviation of 5.4%). The study reveals that the spatial heterogeneity of fractures significantly influences flow anisotropy. Hydraulic dissipation in mismatched fractures correlates strongly with the rate of aperture variation and manifests significant directional dependence. Furthermore, compared to existing modified flow models and perturbation solutions, the proposed model demonstrates superior accuracy and broader applicability, establishing a novel theoretical framework for analyzing nonuniform flow in fractures with mismatched and heterogeneous geometries.

papers.title: Experimental study on the effect of surface slip with varying zeta potential on particle migration in finite-size microchannels
papers.abstract: The slip on the fluid–solid interfaces is a crucial factor to consider in microfluidic studies of particle motion. It can alter the zeta potential, thus influencing the separation or focusing behavior of particles. Consequently, the zeta potential serves as a useful tool to study how surface slip impacts particle motion. In this work, the zeta potential of polystyrene particles modified with various surface functional groups was measured in acidic, neutral, and basic environments. The zeta potential of the microchannel wall was also considered. The particle migration trajectory in low aspect ratio microchannels was experimentally investigated under varying flow rates and pH conditions. The radial migration probability distribution and focusing regions were roughly determined through quantitative analysis. Furthermore, the variations in the peak value of radial migration density vs particle zeta potential under different flow rates were summarized. The results demonstrated that the particle radial migration in the channel differs among three surface-modified particles under varying pH conditions. Slip could affect the velocity gradient around the particle surface, qualitatively explaining these differences. Additionally, the peak value of distribution density decreases with increasing particle zeta potential, while increasing flow rate makes this variation less obvious. This study provides experimental evidence for the slip effect on particle migration in microchannels and contributes to understanding the role of slip in particle motion at the microscale.

papers.title: An insight into the correlation and coupling interactions in the vortex-induced vibration of catenary flexible riser
papers.abstract: We experimentally investigate correlation and coupling interactions of a catenary flexible riser with an aspect ratio of 125 placed within a nonlinear sheared oncoming flow, using nonintrusive high-speed camera measurement. The Reynolds number ranges from 150 to 1880 based on the depth-averaged velocity. The dynamic responses, including the response amplitude, frequency evolution, modal weight, and phase difference, are analyzed and discussed. Five correlation patterns are identified in the x- and z-directional responses based on the response frequency and phase difference, namely, strong correlation I, strong correlation II, weak correlation I-1, weak correlation I-2, and weak correlation II. It is found that the interaction between the x- and z-directional responses is sensitive to the reduced velocity. The interaction between the in-plane and out-of-plane responses, including strong coupling and weak coupling, significantly impacts the correlation response. The strong correlation I and weak correlation I-1 patterns tend to appear when the in-plane and out-of-plane responses fall into the weak coupling pattern. The weak correlation I-2 or the strong correlation II patterns are associated with the strong coupling between the in-plane and out-of-plane responses. The weak correlation II pattern is triggered when out-of-sync coupling occurs in the x- and z-directional responses. Intense competition between the coupling and correlation responses can be observed in the strong correlation II and weak correlation I-2 patterns.

papers.title: Publisher's Note: “Fluid–structure interaction in engineering based on its applications: A plenary and up-to-date review” [Phys. Fluids 36 , 101309 (2024); 37 , 019901 (2025)]
Hydroelastic dynamics of a very large floating structure of marine airport throughout aircraft landing under typhoon-driven waves: A multiphysics-coupled iterative analytical method
papers.abstract: Aircraft emergency landings on marine floating airports under typhoon conditions (induced by mechanical failures or military actions) demand precise hydroelastic analysis of a multi-module very large floating structure (VLFS). Nevertheless, traditional hydroelastic methods cannot address the complex nonlinear fluid–structure interaction (FSI) problems caused by typhoon–wave–aircraft load coupling, and existing beam/plate models fail to account for multi-body interactions and nonlinear dynamics in semi-submersible VLFS systems, particularly under connector and mooring constraints. This study developed a typhoon-driven wave spectrum using buoy measurement data and established a logarithmic wind profile based on a wind–wave equilibrium theory. A multi-rigid-body dynamics (MRBD)/finite element method (FEM) coupled solution to investigate the dynamic response of a multi-flexible-body system was proposed with decoupling between rigid body motion and elastic deformation considered. On this basis, building upon the FSI theory and computational fluid dynamics (CFD), a CFD-MRBD/FEM analytical method for hydroelastic response was established, employing a separation iteration approach to sequentially solve environmental loads, rigid body motion, and elastic deformation. The hydroelastic response throughout the aircraft landing on the eight-module marine airport under typhoon-driven waves was analyzed. The results demonstrated that the proposed method more accurately captured the nonlinear characteristics of FSI than the traditional method. These nonlinear features induced significant frequency doubling phenomena of the structural motion. The typhoon-waves condition and aircraft loads create distinct dynamic responses at different scales: large-scale rigid-body motion primarily driven by wind–wave energy and local deformations mainly caused by landing impact forces. Parametric sensitivity analysis results indicate that the elastic deformation extremum increases approximately linearly with the aircraft landing dynamic loading coefficient.
