An immersed boundary method, enhanced with a prediction-correction multi-direct forcing scheme and a smoothed discrete delta function, was employed. The inverse distance weighting interpolation was introduced to address the interpolation on a refined mesh. For two-dimensional simulation, the ground effect was divided into three regions: force enhancement, force reduction, and force recovery region. Various mechanisms, such as early or delayed vortex shedding, wall extrusion, vortex integration, and reattachment, were observed. Additionally, the vortex remained near the ground, altering the velocity difference between the wing and surrounding fluid through induced velocity. This led to a significant change in pressure on the windward side. A hysteresis phenomenon was discovered: in the force enhancement region, vertical force coefficient peaked at a later time. For three-dimensional simulation, the presence of ground resulted in a decrease in time-average vertical force coefficient. Additionally, the magnitude of this reduction diminished as the distance between the wing and ground increased. The influence of ground was primarily reflected in the more rapid growth of the vertical force coefficient during the initial stage of the downstroke, the magnitudes of its peak and trough values. These changes were attributed to alterations in the strength and state of the vortex near the wing, along with the induced effect of the rebounded vortex. It is more obvious during the downstroke that the downward velocity of the flow was enhanced, which causes the reduction of the relative inflow velocity to the wing.

papers.title: Wind energy potential of venturi-shaped roofs in building arrays with balconies
papers.abstract: Despite the effectiveness in harnessing wind energy, the use of conventional large wind turbines is limited by turbulence and the required wind speeds and directions. Instead, venturi-shaped roofs and small vertical-axis wind turbines (VAWTs) provide important solutions for achieving net-zero energy in urban areas; venturi-shaped roofs create optimal wind conditions for the efficient operation of building-integrated VAWTs. In this study, ANSYS Fluent was used to analyze the flow conditions. Four design parameters were investigated: (i) corner modifications, (ii) support structures, (iii) different VAWT arrangements on different rooftops, and (iv) wind directions in order to estimate the optimum wind conditions for venturi-shaped roof design in a typical 3 × 3 building array with balconies. The computations involved with five turbulence models were validated against the results of a wind-tunnel experiment, and the Reynolds-stress turbulence model gave the most accurate results. This study recommends round corners and an actual support-structure length of 1.8 m, which increase the wind power density (PD) and decrease the turbulence intensity in the tunnels. Under the oblique wind direction of 45°, the wind turbines produce higher average wind PD, albeit with more regions of unacceptable turbulence. The new concept is proposed to have the potential for improved wind energy capture in compact building arrays.

papers.title: A hybrid graph neural network-based framework for aerothermal prediction on hypersonic vehicles
papers.abstract: Efficient and accurate aerothermal prediction has become a crucial technology for the design of hypersonic vehicles. To enhance the generalization capability for complex geometries and reduce the cost of model training, this paper introduces a novel framework for aerothermal prediction of complex vehicles, based on a hybrid graph neural network model, named hybrid-MGNN. The model consists of three main components: normalized aerodynamic heat distribution prediction, statistical feature prediction, and flow field reconstruction. Initially, the method constructs graph-structured data from discrete mesh information, enabling precise representation of intricate geometries and flow field structures. A graph neural network model based on a message-passing mechanism establishes a nonlinear mapping from incoming flow conditions to the surface heat flux distribution of the vehicle. The model then encodes the flow conditions and global geometric features, which are fed into a feature prediction network to accurately estimate statistical features of the heat flux distribution, such as maximum values. Finally, a de-normalization technique is applied to reconstruct the aerothermal flow field on the vehicle's surface. The performance of the proposed hybrid-MGNN was validated using hypersonic double ellipsoids, blunt cones, double blunt cones, and lifting body shapes. The results show that the predicted aerodynamic heat loads have an average error of less than 6% compared to computational fluid dynamics methods, with a computational efficiency improvement of approximately 400 times. Furthermore, the hybrid-MGNN framework is highly adaptable to arbitrary mesh types and complex geometries, and transfer learning significantly reduces model training costs.

papers.title: Modeling immiscible viscous fingering in deformed multi-scale fracture-porous media
papers.abstract: Deep and ultra-deep reservoirs are widely regarded as a major substitute in onshore oil and gas exploration and development. These reservoirs typically exhibit significant geo-stress sensitivity and strong heterogeneity due to the co-existence of tight matrix and multi-scale fractures, resulting in more complicated oil-water flow patterns in deformed multi-scale media and greater challenges in enhancing hydrocarbon recovery. In order to investigate the underlying oil-water flow mechanisms in deformed multi-scale fracture-porous media, the in situ stress-loading computed tomography scanning experiment for a typical deep rock sample is conducted and three-dimensional digital rock models under different stress-loading conditions are thereafter reconstructed. By introducing a multi-relaxation color-gradient lattice Boltzmann model, immiscible viscous fingering and its effect of fluid interface evolution in deformed multi-scale fracture-porous media of deep rock samples are ultimately simulated. The results show that deformation of rock microstructure caused by stress variation can greatly affect immiscible displacement pattern. These effects are primarily characterized by pore morphology of invading phase, number of viscous fingerings and immiscible displacement efficiency. During the deformation of the core, the displacement patterns are dominated by viscous fingering, accompanied by multiple Haines jump events. The invading phase that leaves from oil-water front due to Haines jump can rapidly migrate along preferential flow paths. As the injection distance increases, the number of viscous fingerings in the deep sandstone core initially increases and then decreases. After failure, the invading phase advances rapidly along the fracture, filling larger pores in the preferential flow paths, resulting in a significant improvement in displacement efficiency.

papers.title: The differences in imbibition effects of microemulsion-forming surfactants under salinity control
papers.abstract: Research on increasing oil production in low-permeability reservoirs is challenging due to their strong heterogeneity and oil-wet properties. Microemulsion-forming surfactants can effectively mobilize the residual oil in the tight matrix by imbibition and are commonly used as stimulation measures for such reservoirs. To better understand the mechanism of microemulsion-forming surfactants, a systematic study on the imbibition process under salinity control was conducted using macroscopic and microscopic experimental methods comprehensively. Cores with identical dimensions were used to study the imbibition effect and action mode. Single-channel micromodels that can create an environment for residual oil retention were designed to study the wettability alteration and phase behavior. To characterize the size difference between fracture channels and matrix regions, fractured micromodels were fabricated for microscopic observation of imbibition phenomena. Based on the phenomenon description and quantitative analysis, the experimental studies elucidated the relationship between the dynamic phase behavior of microemulsion in porous media and the static phase changes affected by salinity. They also clarified the differences in the imbibition process of microemulsion-forming surfactants under various salinity conditions. According to the data and images from core experiments and microfluidic experiments, the microemulsion-forming surfactant showed the best imbibition effect under critical salinity, and its imbibition process was dominated by gravity. Through the diffusion of the surfactant solution and the dilution of the microemulsion, the equilibrium state among the oil phase, microemulsion, and surfactant was achieved, which significantly enhanced the ultimate imbibition recovery.

papers.title: Thermal state interplay in inclined magnetohydrodynamics convection of ternary hybrid nanofluids with saw-tooth internal cooling
papers.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive numerical investigation of inclined magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) natural convection and entropy generation in a square cavity filled with a ternary hybrid nanofluid. The enclosure contains a thermally cooled saw-tooth-shaped inner structure, and the working fluid comprises Multi-Walled Carbon Nanotubes, Copper (Cu), and Ferric Oxide (Fe3O4) nanoparticles suspended in water. An external magnetic field with varying inclination angles is applied to evaluate its impact on heat and flow characteristics. The governing nonlinear partial differential equations for mass, momentum, energy, and entropy transport are solved using the Finite Volume Method, accelerated by a Full Multigrid Algorithm for computational efficiency. Key parameters including the magnetic inclination angle (χ), Hartmann number (Ha), Rayleigh number (Ra), nanoparticle volume fraction (ϕ), and four distinct thermal boundary states are systematically analyzed to understand their effects on flow behavior and thermodynamic irreversibility. The results highlight that state 3, combined with moderate Ha and χ (≈60°), offers an optimal trade-off between thermal performance and entropy generation. The study emphasizes the importance of integrating geometric design, magnetic control, and thermal boundary configuration to enhance the thermofluidic performance of MHD nanofluid systems. Future work may incorporate multi-objective optimization techniques, such as Pareto front analysis, to further refine this balance for practical engineering applications.

papers.title: Large eddy simulation of the cavitating flow in an annular jet pump with special emphasis on the cavitation–vortex interactions
papers.abstract: The annular jet pump (AJP) has garnered significant attention in nondestructive conveying, but cavitation can severely impact its performance. Large Eddy simulation was used to investigate the unsteady three-dimensional cavitating flow in an AJP under various operating conditions. The results, validated against experimental data, revealed the onset and evolution of shear cavitation at low flow ratios and low-pressure cavitation at high flow ratios. The results show that cavitation under low flow ratios mainly occurs in the suction chamber's shear layer, initially forming a ring-shaped structure dominated by intense shear effect between high-speed primary flow and low-speed secondary flow. The evolution of ring-shaped cavitation demonstrates clear periodicity, progressing through four distinct stages: initiation, twisting deformation, recirculation, and collapse, with its development closely linked to vortex structure evolution. Under large flow ratios, cavitation primarily develops in the throat and diffuser, manifesting as two distinct types: (1) jet shear layer cavitation induced by vortex structures and throat low pressure and (2) wall shear cavitation driven by boundary layer effects. In contrast to low flow ratio conditions, cavitation at large flow ratios exhibits no clear periodicity but remains strongly correlated with vortex structure evolution, particularly in the diffuser, where cavitation collapse coincides with vortex formation. Furthermore, analysis of the vorticity transport equation revealed a strong coupling between cavitation and vortex structure, with cavitation significantly impacting vorticity distribution and generation. The results indicate that the vortex stretching term is the primary contributor to vorticity transport, while the baroclinic torque term exhibits strong spatial correlation with cavitation.

papers.title: Various approximations of mathematical models of internal gravity waves in the stratified atmosphere
papers.abstract: Two new mathematical models describing the propagation of internal gravity waves (IGWs) in a stratified atmosphere are proposed in this paper. The first model is called the non-Boussinesq gas approximation. It differs from the well-known incompressible fluid model in that the dynamics of the buoyancy force is not described by the continuity equation but by the heat conduction equation. The obtained dispersion relation differs from the dispersion relations in the incompressible fluid and anelastic gas approximations. In the second proposed model, called the general model, we abandon the Boussinesq approximation, and the system of equations includes both the continuity equation with density disturbance and the heat conduction equation. The analysis of the proposed model has shown that in the general case the maximum frequency of IGW's oscillations is equal to the Brunt–Väisälä buoyancy frequency, i.e., the results coincide with the results of the compressible fluid approximation (adiabatic approximation). However, the fundamental difference of our model is that the amplitude of acoustic waves in the adiabatic approximation decays with height, whereas in the general case it grows with height.

papers.title: Similarity solution for magnetogasdynamic shock wave in a non-ideal dusty rotating gas with gravitational field
papers.abstract: In this paper, we use the method of the Lie group of transformations to obtain similarity solutions for a quasi-linear hyperbolic system of partial differential equations (PDEs). This system of PDEs pertains to the shock wave dynamics in a rotational axisymmetric non-ideal dusty gas, including magnetic and gravitational fields. We investigate both adiabatic and isothermal flows to discuss all possible cases of the similarity solutions for the considered problem. The generators of the Lie group of transformations contain arbitrary constants, leading to a range of solutions with power-law and exponential-law shock paths. However, similarity solutions are identified only for the case of the exponential-law shock path in both isothermal and adiabatic flows. The shock strength and flow field behind the shock front are analyzed with respect to the variation in parameters like non-ideal parameter (b¯), gravitational parameter (G0), adiabatic exponent (γ), mass fraction of the solid particles (Kp), the ratio of the density of solid particles to the initial density of the gas (μ1), and Alfvén Mach number (MA−2). Out of these parameters γ, b¯, and MA−2 are found to have a decaying effect on shock strength, while μ1 and Kp have an increasing effect on shock strength.

papers.title: Turbulent transport over a wavy disk rotating in a forced flow
papers.abstract: The influence of an imposed outer flow on momentum and heat transport in a fully turbulent flow over a rotating non-flat disk is investigated. Transport enhancement in a turbulent boundary layer over a sinusoidal wavy disk has already been witnessed. In particular, considering potential applications of a wavy disk in turbomachinery, a situation further closer to the realistic one is considered. An imposed outer cross-flow serves the purpose, also from the perspective of existing studies for the sake of comparison. Numerical modeling is based on the boundary layer equations modeled in a body-fitted curvilinear coordinate system. An in-house developed finite-difference code, written in MATLAB, is utilized for a numerical solution of the equations. The Cebeci–Smith turbulence model, which utilizes the eddy viscosity concept, is employed to model the Reynolds stresses and the turbulent heat flux. Calculations have been carried out up to a Reynolds number of Rer=2.85×109, using a non-uniform mesh, dense near the disk and gradually getting coarser away from the disk. The non-dimensional parameter (a/ω) serves to examine the impact of the outer cross-flow on the flow and heat transfer characteristics. The presence of an outer cross-flow limits the influence of the number of sinusoids (N), which has been seen to play an important role, otherwise. The impact of the number of sinusoids N on the transport process is quite pronounced up to N=2 and becomes insignificant for larger values of N. The results reveal that in the presence of an external cross-flow, the velocity and temperature gradients increase significantly, thereby enhancing the shear stresses and the heat transfer rate. The average radial and circumferential skin-friction coefficients, the Nusselt number, and the moment coefficient increase by up to 1196.89%, 66.39%, 52.75%, and 66.75%, respectively, compared to a flat disk when the surface undulation ratio is 0.2, the number of sinusoids is equal to 2.0, and a forced flow parameter equals 1.0.

papers.title: Effects of silt clay content on rheology and filter cake characteristics of water–bentonite slurry in slurry shield tunneling
papers.abstract: Water–bentonite slurry is widely used in slurry shield tunneling due to its ability to stabilize the tunnel face and transport excavated soils. As the shield advances, natural soil is eaten by the cutting teeth and inevitably mixes with fresh water–bentonite slurry, among which silt clay-sized soil particles are difficult to remove, impeding reuse of the slurry and posing challenges for tunneling safety and efficiency. Therefore, it is crucial to evaluate the performance and adaptability of slurry containing silt clay soil. In this study, non-swelling silt clay (kaolin) was added to water–bentonite slurries of varying bentonite concentrations, creating water–bentonite–kaolin slurries with densities ranging from 1019 to 1200 kg/m3. The rheological properties of these slurries were evaluated using a concentric cylinder rheometer, while the hydraulic characteristics of the resulting filter cakes were examined via modified fluid loss tests. The results showed that due to the addition of kaolin, higher-density slurries displayed increased rheological parameters. Slurries with higher bentonite concentrations showed pronounced non-linear rheological profiles, attributed to bentonite's strong thixotropic properties. Both higher bentonite concentrations and slurry densities produced thicker filter cakes with extremely low hydraulic conductivities (approximately 10−9 m/s). Pure bentonite slurries formed filter cakes with the highest void ratios and greater water retention, whereas denser slurries exhibited reduced pore space. Furthermore, pressure gradients under laminar flow conditions in a specific pipe were quantified, and a reference chart was developed to preliminarily determine the slurry's capacity to suspend soil particles. The implications for slurry shield tunneling practices were discussed.

papers.title: Research and application of self-suspending proppants based on block copolymer modification in coalbed methane wells
papers.abstract: Conventional proppants exhibit limited sand-carrying capacity and incomplete gel breaking below 60 °C, resulting in inadequate fracture support and reduced stimulated reservoir volume. In this study, a self-suspending, high-salinity-resistant block copolymer was synthesized by precisely controlling the copolymer composition and topology. Based on this, a novel self-suspending proppant fracturing fluid system was developed. Its sand-carrying capacity, gel-breaking behavior, friction reduction, salt resistance, and transport performance were systematically evaluated and compared with those of emulsion polymer-based fracturing fluids. The self-suspending proppant achieved complete dispersion within 45 s and maintained suspension stability for over 25 h. It supported sand loadings up to 60%, and a small amount of proppant could carry more than ten times its weight in quartz sand. The friction reduction rate exceeded 71%, averaging 2.32% higher than that of emulsion polymer systems. The self-suspending fluid demonstrated minimal proppant settling during transport, resulting in improved placement and fracture conductivity. In contrast, emulsion polymer-based systems suffered from poor dispersion, emulsion formation, and reduced viscosity and transport distance. Field trials in the Linxing coalbed methane reservoir showed that a mixture of 10% self-suspending proppant with 26% conventional quartz sand enabled stable injection and doubled gas production compared to wells treated with emulsion polymer-based fluids. These results demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of self-suspending proppant-based fracturing fluids for use in coalbed and shale reservoirs.

papers.title: Capillary waves on the liquid film of a Taylor bubble in vertical countercurrent flow
papers.abstract: This study reports the identification of a previously uncharacterized type of capillary wave on the moving interface of a Taylor bubble in vertical countercurrent flow. In our experiments, the buoyancy of the Taylor bubble is precisely balanced by a downward laminar water flow (Re = 1400) within a 12.4 mm diameter glass pipe. These previously uncharacterized waves appear at a height one-fourth to one-half of the pipe diameter above the bubble's tail and remain stationary in the laboratory frame, implying that their upward propagation speed exactly matches the downward motion of the interface. The waves persist for 5–10 wavelengths, spanning one-fifth to one-third of the pipe diameter. We measured their wavelength for bubbles of different lengths (1.5–11 pipe diameters) and determined the liquid film thickness at the wave location. From the measured mass flow rate, we calculated the laminar velocity profile in the liquid film and the interface velocity. We have shown that the measured wave propagation speeds align with the interface velocities computed from the film thickness, confirming their capillary nature within experimental uncertainty. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the underlying physics: these capillary waves originate from a newly formed toroidal vortex near the bubble tail that rotates opposite to the primary air vortex inside the bubble, consistent with previous computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations and our new observations.

papers.title: Advances in flow and civil structures
papers.abstract: The Flow and Civil Structures special collection is one of the earliest and largest efforts to consolidate transformative research bridging fluid mechanics and civil engineering. It addresses mutual and escalating challenges posed by extreme environmental loads and rapid urbanization, linking these two massive research fields. With nearly 200 papers, contributions span fluid–structure interactions in bridges, building, and high-speed railways; hydrodynamic resilience of offshore infrastructure; granular flows in urban drainage systems; turbulence-driven pollutant dispersion; and much beyond. The collection features advances in experiments, numerical simulations, field measurements, and analytical methods to improve predictions of wind-induced vibrations, optimize wave-resistant design, and mitigate urban flooding hazards. By integrating artificial intelligence and machine learning analysis, it advances infrastructure resilience for compound hazards in an increasingly dynamic climate, addressing both global and local scales.

papers.title: Correlation analysis of entropy production and vorticity characteristics of pressure swirl nozzles
papers.abstract: Interactions among characteristic vortices in pressure swirl nozzles lead to significant energy dissipation. This study focused on entropy-driven energy loss and the identification of coherent vortical structures and established a quantitative framework linking rigid vorticity transport to entropy production. Based on this framework, the spatial correlations between hydraulic loss and four sub-components of rigid vorticity transport strength were analyzed to identify the dominant mechanisms through which coherent vortices induce localized energy dissipation. The results revealed that turbulent dissipative entropy production predominated in the overall hydraulic loss of pressure swirl nozzles. Direct dissipative entropy production was primarily governed by shear enstrophy. In contrast, turbulent dissipative entropy production showed strong correlations with both total vorticity transport strength and shear enstrophy, but both turbulent and direct dissipative entropy production had weak correlations with rigid enstrophy. Further decomposition of the rigid vorticity transport revealed that direct dissipative entropy production was closely associated with the pseudo-Lamb term, whereas turbulent dissipative entropy production was largely driven by the viscous term and exhibited minimal dependence on the pseudo-Lamb term. Additionally, both shear and total vorticity transport strength were dominated by the pseudo-Lamb mechanism, while shear vorticity transport was mainly influenced by viscous effects. These findings deepened the understanding of energy dissipation and vortex transport dynamics in pressure swirl nozzles, offering new insights for performance optimization and flow control.

papers.title: Numerical investigation on aerodynamic performance of vertical axis wind turbine based on cycloidal pitch control strategy
papers.abstract: To address the inherent limitations of fixed-pitch VAWTs (vertical axis wind turbines), particularly the aerodynamic efficiency degradation caused by dynamic stall effects, this study proposes a novel active flow control methodology termed CPCS (cycloidal pitch control strategy). The investigation employs a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 0021 airfoil (NACA0021) symmetric airfoil-based aerodynamic model, utilizing unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations coupled with the shear stress transport k-ω turbulence model to resolve complex flow phenomena. Through systematic parametric analysis, the correlation between eccentricity ratio and energy harvesting characteristics was quantitatively established, with particular emphasis on vortex evolution mechanisms. Numerical results demonstrate that CPCS implementation effectively enhances the Cp (power coefficient) in the low tip speed ratio region, achieving a maximum Cp improvement of 6.8% compared to conventional fixed-pitch VAWT. This performance enhancement is primarily attributed to the torque amplification effect resulting from the dynamic optimization of attack angles in the downwind region of the blade.

papers.title: Characteristics of torsional vortex-induced vibration for blunt body sections at high angles of attack
papers.abstract: To enhance the understanding of the mechanisms driving torsional vortex-induced vibrations (VIVs) at high angles of attack (AoAs), a systematic investigation of the vibrational characteristics was conducted during the evolution process from a rectangular section to a bare bridge section at ±5° AoAs. The research was facilitated through simultaneous vibration-pressure measurement testing. Furthermore, the spatial distribution characteristics of the surface pressure were assessed by employing the Higuchi method, framed within the context of fractal theory. The research indicates that the torsional VIV observed in sections with a width-to-height ratio of 10 is primarily driven by a single-side impinging lead-edge vortex at ±5° AoAs. The superposition of AoAs and the gravity effect will result in different vibration responses of the symmetrical section. Furthermore, the critical zones of induced vibration can be effectively characterized through the statistical parameters of surface pressure. During the initial stage of the lock-in region, the surface pressure near the leading-edge shear layer becomes aligned with the torsional natural frequency, when only minimal vibrations occur. Additionally, in the lock-in region, the interaction between the structure and the incoming flow encompasses three distinct modes of energy conversion: energy absorption, energy dissipation, and energy exchange.

papers.title: Radiation spectra of the Martian atmosphere behind shock wave at 6–9 km/s
papers.abstract: For Mars entry, shock layer radiation will contribute a significant portion of the total heat flux at the peak heating point in the entry trajectory, and the low-density gases are likely to be in a thermochemical non-equilibrium state. In this work, one-dimensional spatially resolved imaging spectroscopy is designed and built to perform imaging spectroscopy on shock waves created in a detonation driven shock tube to investigate the thermochemical non-equilibrium flow behind shock waves. The spatially resolved radiance spectra of the Martian simulant (96% CO2, 4% N2) atmosphere were investigated in the velocity range of 6–9 km/s and the wavelength range of ultraviolet to visible. The non-equilibrium post-shock excitation and relaxation dynamics of spectral features were captured. The results show that the thermal equilibrium is reached at 2.2 cm for the 8.11 km/s condition and at 3.1 cm for 8.93 km/s behind the shock front. The evolution of vibrational and rotational temperatures of the cyano radical behind the shock wave was obtained by two-temperature spectrum fitting. Comparisons with numerical predictions were conducted, and the experimental temperature curves showed a good match with the predicted ones.

papers.title: Continuous fabrication of oriented rubber nanocomposites with improved thermal conductivity via torsion-induced extrusion processing
papers.abstract: Thermal conductive nanocomposites are increasingly important for dissipating unwanted heat and ensuring long-term thermal stability in highly integrated electronic devices. Herein, we report a new continuous torsion extrusion strategy that induces torsion-spiral flow to inexpensively prepare oriented thermal conductive nanocomposites with multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) as the thermal conductive fillers and ethylene-propylene-diene monomer (EPDM) as the rubber matrix. The torsion-spiral flow was tailored though newly designed torsion screws to facilitate effective de-agglomeration and uniform dispersion of MWCNTs during extrusion process and to induce them to arrange in an orderly manner. A comprehensive evaluation of the torsion extrusion method was carried out through experiments and simulations, to demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving uniform mixing and directional dispersion of particles. The impact of screw configuration on the microstructures, thermal and mechanical properties of the prepared composites was analyzed. Our work indicates that the screw structures highly affect the dispersion morphology of the particles, thereby affecting the overall performances of composites. The EPDM/MWCNTs composites fabricated by the torsion screw with dispersedly arranged torsion elements perform both high thermal conductivity and mechanical properties due to its excellent uniform mixing and directional dispersion. These results suggest that the novel torsion extrusion process has potential value in practice to fabricate directional high-thermal-conductivity polymer materials.

papers.title: Dynamic evolution of fluid energy in gas extraction: Insights from physical simulation and mathematical modeling
papers.abstract: The efficient exploitation of coalbed methane (CBM) is pivotal for supporting the goals of peaking carbon emissions and achieving carbon neutrality. The fluid energy within a CBM reservoir is a critical parameter influencing gas migration. However, current research predominantly addresses the evolution of coupled physical fields, such as thermo-hydro-mechanical processes, while the dynamic behavior of fluid energy itself receives comparatively less attention. This study conducted a systematic analysis of the energy storage characteristics of reservoir fluids. A mathematical model was developed for calculating the energy of gas, liquid, and solid three-phase fluids, thereby resolving the prior inability to separately quantify the energy of adsorbed and free gas phases. Physical simulation experiments were conducted to examine multi-seam CBM production under various pressure differentials. Results indicate that reservoir energy can be classified into three types and six stages, each associated with specific gas migration behaviors. High-pressure coal seams exhibited negative reservoir energy throughout the production process with the near-wellbore region identified as a low-pressure zone. As the reservoir pressure difference increased from 0.2 to 0.4 and 0.6 MPa, the peak energy correspondingly rose from 0.23 to 0.66 and 2.65 kJ/t with complete energy dissipation (0 kJ/t) occurring at 10.79, 14.84, and 21.9 minutes, respectively. Reservoir energy was positively correlated with distance from the wellbore center. Conversely, low-pressure coal seams displayed positive reservoir energy with higher energy levels near the wellbore and decreasing energy at greater distances. Energy transfer from the near-wellbore area to the deeper reservoir occurred in an approximately ellipsoidal pattern.

papers.title: Enhanced microparticle focusing in a serpentine microchannel integrated on a lab-on-a-disk platform using combined inertial and dielectrophoretic forces
papers.abstract: Precise focusing of microparticles is a key issue in microfluidic systems, playing a key role in applications such as particle separation, cell sorting, biomedical diagnostics, and lab-on-a-chip technologies. Achieving high-particle separation efficiency with minimal focus width remains a significant challenge in this field. Among various designs, serpentine microchannels are widely employed to induce secondary flows, particularly Dean flow. In this work, formalism was developed and simulations conducted in a serpentine microchannel integrated in a lab-on-disk (LOD) platform to leverage rotational forces—including centrifugal and Coriolis forces—alongside Dean flow and enhance particle focusing, taking macrophage cells as a model system. To further refine and improve cell focusing, multiple electrodes were incorporated to generate an electric field, introducing a dielectrophoretic (DEP) force to the process. Numerical simulations were conducted to analyze the effects of key parameters on fluid flow profiles, including flow rate (u), number of microchannel turns (UN), rotation speed and angular velocity (ω), configuration and number (Ne) of electrodes, frequency of applied field (f), and applied voltage (V). The governing Navier–Stokes equations for fluid flow, the equation of rotational motion, and the continuity equation for flow density were implemented to model particle behavior within the system. The results demonstrated that increasing the number of turns and the applied field voltage significantly enhanced process performance. At UN = 15 and/or V = 200 V, about 100% of the particles exited through a single outlet, while the focusing width (Wf) was reduced from 90 to 13.8 μm and 6.6 μm, respectively. Additionally, the optimal system parameters were determined as u = 0.025 m/s, ω = 100 rad/s, f = 100 kHz, and Ne = 12. This study highlights the synergy between inertial forces and DEP in LOD platforms, demonstrating its potential for high-precision particle manipulation, including sorting, focusing, and cell separation applications.

papers.title: Compressible Kelvin–Helmholtz instability with nonequilibrium effect under external force
papers.abstract: The impact of external force on compressible Kelvin–Helmholtz (KH) instability, considering hydrodynamic and thermodynamic nonequilibrium (TNE) effects during its evolution, is analyzed using a two-component discrete Boltzmann method. The results show that stronger external forces lead to a more complex evolution of the KH instability, causing significant changes in physical gradients, material mixing, and TNE behaviors. Physically, a higher external force amplifies compressive and rarefactive effects and disturbance waves, which in turn makes the KH evolution more intricate. Additionally, when the direction of external force aligns with the one of the initial density gradient, the KH vortex is resisted; otherwise, the KH and Rayleigh–Taylor instabilities are promoted. These results enrich our understanding of the mixing behavior in the compressible KH instability under external forces and provide a new perspective for experimental research and macroscopic model improvement.

papers.title: Simulations of a Lamb–Oseen vortex in the presence of a concentrated region of polymeric fluid
papers.abstract: Direct numerical simulations are performed to study the effects of spatially non-uniform polymer concentration on a Lamb–Oseen vortex. This simplified problem relates to turbulent drag reduction using polymer additives and is a step toward optimizing polymer drag reduction strategies. Previous work has examined spatially uniform polymer concentrations; however, this study investigates how the localized distribution of polymer affects a single vortex. The goal of the study is to determine the optimal polymer placement relative to the vortex core and to relate this positioning to identifiable flow features that maximize the enstrophy dissipation. The simulations reveal a strong correlation between regions of high strain rate around the initial vortex and the most effective polymer placement. Key results indicate that placing the polymer approximately 39% beyond the vortex core radius yields the greatest enstrophy dissipation, aligning closely with regions of maximum strain rate at the initial conditions.

papers.title: Preferential concentration of particles in a decaying isotropic turbulence in the dilute regime
papers.abstract: The gravitational settling of small solid particles in an incompressible decaying turbulence is investigated using the Eulerian–Lagrangian framework. We were able to reach a Taylor microscale-based Reynolds number, Reλ=71, on a mesh size of 1283. There is an increase in the mean settling velocity of the particles in a turbulent flow compared to that in a static flow. This increase in the settling velocity decreases with time in the case of decaying turbulence. The particle dynamics is found to be modified by the decaying turbulent flow, resulting in a relatively uniform distribution. The highest decay rate of particles is observed when St=O(1). Consequently, the de-clustering of the particles is also found to be peaked at St=1. The trademark columnar accumulation of particles also disappears at low Froude numbers when the turbulence decays over time. For light particles, the distribution correlates well with low-vorticity regions, which disappears for heavy particles as gravity dominates the distribution for heavy particles in both forced and decaying turbulence. We have also analyzed the distribution quantitatively by plotting the Voronoi tessellation. We have found the distribution of Voronoi cell areas to be highly skewed to very low values due to the effect of clustering of particles.

papers.title: Investigation of bubble dynamics near a semicylindrical protrusion within a confined space
papers.abstract: The present paper investigates the bubble collapse deformation and jet characteristics near a semicylindrical protrusion within confined spaces. Based on the high-speed photography experiments, typical phenomena of the bubble collapse splitting are explored, and their parameterized partitioning is conducted. The underlying physical mechanisms are analyzed through the Kelvin impulse theory. In addition, a quantitative analysis is conducted on the characteristics of the collapsing jet, as well as the corresponding liquid velocity and Kelvin impulse. The main conclusions are given as follows: (1) four typical bubble collapse morphologies are observed: fang-shaped and semicircular collapses in the bubble unequal splitting region; B-shaped and heart-shaped collapses in the equal splitting region. (2) As the bubble position approaches the intersection of the semicylinder and the flat wall, the collapsing jet width increases. (3) The inconsistency between the bubble centroid movement and collapsing jet directions leads to the unequal splitting of the bubble.

papers.title: Integrated laboratory and field testing of gas fracturing for permeability improvement in coal seams
papers.abstract: Gas fracturing technology has emerged as a promising method for enhancing coalbed methane (CBM) extraction in low-permeability coal seams. This study combines laboratory experiments and field tests to investigate the mechanical response, crack propagation mechanisms, and permeability enhancement effects of gas fracturing under complex stress conditions. Laboratory experiments used triaxial stress simulations and acoustic emission (AE) monitoring to analyze coal samples under varying axial and confining pressures. Results revealed that gas fracturing significantly improves permeability by generating fracture networks, with permeability increases correlating strongly with volumetric strain and AE activity. Specimens subjected to lower confining pressure (20 MPa) and higher axial pressure (8 MPa) exhibited weaker fracturing resistance, higher crack density, and a 29.9% permeability increase compared to samples under higher confining pressure (25 MPa). Field tests in the Pingmei Group's Eighth Mine demonstrated that gas fracturing extended the permeability enhancement radius beyond 9 m, achieving a 75.7% maximum gas flow increase and sustaining efficient extraction for 40 days within a 6 m radius. These findings highlight the critical role of stress-state optimization in gas fracturing design and provide practical insights for improving CBM extraction efficiency in low-permeability coal seams.

papers.title: Compressibility effects of supersonic isentropic mixing layers
papers.abstract: Compressibility effects are described as a stabilizing effect due to compressibility. The compressibility effects of supersonic mixing layers are numerically investigated using two thermodynamic models. One model is derived from the Crocco–Busemann relation, and the other is derived from the isentropic condition of layers. In mixing layers, the growth rates of the former condition are consistent with those obtained from linear stability theory and previous experiments. The growth rates of the latter condition are larger than those of the former condition, and the isentropic condition reduces compressibility effects at high convective Mach numbers. Therefore, the isentropic mixing layer shows potential for solving supersonic mixing problems.

papers.title: A layered liquid crystal metastructure with polarization encoding and information encryption functions
papers.abstract: Encoding and encryption are essential parts of information transmission based on electromagnetic (EM) waves, where the traditional methods related to encoding and encryption often need complex structures like special-shaped channels and unit arrays. To reduce the limitation of mass manufacture of encoding and encryption devices, a layered metastructure (LM), based on the interference of EM waves, is designed for the function of encoding and encryption, which is composed of indium arsenide (InAs) and E7 liquid crystal (LC). Assuming the phase difference between EM waves, elected as linear polarization waves, incident from the front and back terms of the LM as ΔΦ, the magnetic field B (0.8 or 3.30 T) and ΔΦ (180° of 9°) can serve as the first and second input logic levels to control the certain polarization conversion in the range of 15.733–16.095 Terahertz (THz), where the InAs has the tunability of the B. By the combinations of the logic levels, an information relationship is established between the external parameters and output polarization forms. When the supersaturation bias voltage (190 V) is applied, the long axis in E7 LC will be rotated, meaning that the correspondence relationship between logic levels and polarization output is destroyed to obtain the effect of encryption in the coverage of 15.733–16.095 THz. Therefore, the proposed LM can realize the function of encoding and encryption with excellent application possibility and value, benefiting the mass production of encoding and encryption devices of EM waves.

papers.title: Wave breaking characteristics around a wedge-shaped bow: High-fidelity simulation of water–air–bubble mixed flow
papers.abstract: Wave breaking is a complex and widely occurring phenomenon around marine structures, characterized by the coexistence of water, air, bubbles, and spray, as well as its inherently multiphase, multiscale, and multi-physics nature. This paper investigates the wave breaking of a wedge-shaped bow under various yaw angles (γ= 0°, 10°, 15°, 20°, and 30°) through high-fidelity numerical simulations. A direct forcing immersed boundary method is adopted to model the presence of the wedge-shaped bow, enabling accurate treatment of solid–fluid interaction as the structure pierces the free surface. The study employs a coupled level-set and volume-of-fluid method, along with adaptive mesh refinement techniques, to capture the severe deformation of the free surface and the characteristics of the water–air–bubble multiphase flow. The influence of yaw angle on large-scale flow structures such as wave elevation, air tube evolution, and liquid film tearing, and small-scale microstructures such as droplet splashing, air entrainment, and bubble motion is analyzed. The results show that increasing the yaw angle significantly enhances the nonlinear characteristics of bow wave breaking, leading to more intense liquid film tearing, an expanded range of air tube distribution, and the formation of secondary splashing and bubble wake mixing. The number and volume of droplets increase markedly with yaw angle, with their size distribution following a power law of −4.5. The bubble distribution is primarily influenced by vortex shear and buoyancy, with the size spectrum transitioning from −10/3 to −4.5 as the bubble size increases. This study reveals that yaw angle, by altering the flooding angle, impacts the bow wave-breaking mechanism, providing insights into optimizing ship hydrodynamic performance and understanding marine spray and water–air–bubble wake dynamics.

papers.title: Influence mechanism of disk surface roughness on the flow characteristics of low-speed marine gas turbine rotor–stator cavity
papers.abstract: In marine gas turbines, surface roughness on both rotating and stationary disk surfaces can markedly alter flow structures within the rotor–stator cavity, leading to energy losses that remain poorly quantified in the literature. This study presents the first systematic computational fluid dynamics investigation of centripetal through-flow rotor–stator cavities subject to rotor roughness (RR), stator roughness (RS), and combined rotor–stator roughness (RRS) across six rotational speeds (n = 1000–4000 rpm) and a broad roughness range (equivalent surface roughness ks = 0–76.81 μm). Numerical simulations are rigorously validated against bench-scale measurements, ensuring high fidelity of the predicted flow fields and performance metrics. Our results demonstrate that rotor roughness dominantly amplifies boundary-layer disturbances, expands the core vortex region, and induces local vortical structures, whereas stator roughness exerts a secondary influence. Under RRS conditions, cavity performance trends align closely with the RR case. Quantitatively, rotor torque coefficient increases by up to 35% and axial thrust coefficient by up to 18% at ks = 76.81 μm. Finally, we derive and validate empirical correlations incorporating roughness terms for rapid estimation of torque and thrust variations in engineering practice. This work provides actionable insights and practical tools for predicting and mitigating performance penalties due to disk surface roughness in marine gas turbine rotor–stator cavities.

papers.title: Steam ablation needles based on porous radiation clusters
papers.abstract: Steam thermal ablation (STA) is an emerging minimally invasive treatment technique that utilizes the energy of high-temperature steam to treat diseased tissues. Compared to traditional techniques such as microwave ablation and radio-frequency ablation, STA has the advantages of lower temperature in the ablation center area and avoiding tissue carbonization. However, the current design of steam ablation needles still faces challenges such as poor controllability of steam flow, uneven heating, and difficult to accurately predict the area of tissue ablation. In response to this issue, this article studies and designs several porous radiation clusters–steam ablation needles (PRC–SAN), and investigates their steam flow characteristics, temperature distribution, and tissue ablation effects. This article designs three PRC–SAN, establishes corresponding fluid dynamics models, analyzes the flow state of steam inside the needle tube, and verifies its ablation effect on tissues through experiments. The research results indicate that different arrangements of porous radiation clusters significantly affect the steam flow rate and outlet temperature distribution, thereby determining the shape and range of the ablation area. The experimental verification used pig liver tissue as the ablation object and recorded the morphology of the ablation area and temperature changes in the tissue. The results indicate that the optimized design of PRC–SAN can provide a more uniform thermal field distribution, improve ablation accuracy, reduce nontarget tissue damage, and avoid carbonization caused by local overheating. In addition, this article also explores the correlation between the steam flow rate at the outlet of the ablation needle and temperature, and finds that the two are positively correlated on a large scale. However, due to the influence of heat loss and pore distribution during steam transmission, there may be small deviations in local areas. The experimental results indicate that optimizing the aperture and spacing of porous radiation clusters can improve ablation efficiency and enhance the controllability of ablation shape. This study provides important theoretical basis and experimental support for the application of STA in precision therapy. In the future, design parameters can be further optimized to meet different clinical needs.

papers.title: Material point method to simulate stress effects during rock breaking by pulsed water jet
papers.abstract: Numerical simulation is an effective approach to studying the mechanism of water jet rock breaking. However, pulsed water jet (PWJ) rock breaking causes complex stress conditions that traditional numerical simulation methods cannot deal with adequately due to high-speed collisions, material deformation, and failure. Thus, the instantaneous rock-breaking mechanism of a PWJ remains unclear. In this study, we compared the impact damage process of a continuous water jet (CWJ) and a PWJ on granite using jet impact experiments and material point method (MPM) simulations. The following results were obtained: (1) A comparison of the two water jet methods demonstrates that the MPM is an ideal tool for studying high-pressure water jet rock breaking. It can simulate the complex physical processes occurring during the water jet impact. (2) The PWJ achieves a greater erosion depth than the CWJ, and the latter causes more severe damage around the impact area, resulting in a larger erosion volume and smaller erosion depth. (3) The highest water hammer pressure occurs when the water column impacts the rock. The PWJ is less affected by the water cushion effect and returns water in erosion holes, generating high stress during each pulse impact. Therefore, the PWJ has higher energy use efficiency, water hammer pressure, and better rock-breaking performance. The rock-breaking mechanism is intermittent high stress concentration failure and fatigue damage.

papers.title: Aerodynamic performance of a ducted fan in high-altitude, high-speed electric aircraft via a data-driven method
papers.abstract: Studying the propulsion performance of ducted fans in electric aircraft is crucial for achieving zero emissions in next-generation electrically propelled general aviation. Existing research lacks an understanding of aerodynamic performance regulation for high-altitude, high-speed electric propulsion systems. This study examines the impact of blade pitch angle (BPA) on the aerodynamic performance and unsteady flow behaviors in high-speed ducted fans. The results show that as true airspeed increases from 0 to 300 km/h, the effective angle of attack decreases from 10° to 3°, and the total thrust drops from 1784.43 N to 234.53 N (an 86.86% reduction). Increasing the BPA significantly enhances total thrust under high True Airspeed with a 1096.70 N increase when adjusting from 0° to 20°. Meanwhile, the BPA significantly affects the evolution of flow disturbance characteristics. As the BPA increases from 0° to 10°, the dominant disturbance frequency increases from 168.076 to 193.375 Hz. For the case of 0°, the first-order dynamic mode decomposition mode aligns closely with the blade tip vortex structure. For the case of 10°, leading-edge flow separation becomes the main disturbance source, overshadowing tip leakage unsteadiness. When the BPA increases to 20°, the frequency drops sharply to 101.783 Hz due to flow reattachment and the restoration of tip leakage dominance. The competition between leading-edge separation and tip leakage intensity determines unsteady disturbance characteristics under BPA adjustments. This study aims to provide theoretical foundations for adaptive variable-pitch control of ducted fans, advancing the design of high-stability electric propulsion systems.

papers.title: Coupled effects of rough wall and horizontal vibration on heat transfer characteristics of turbulent Rayleigh–Bénard convection
papers.abstract: In this paper, the coupled effects of rough wall and horizontal vibration on flow and heat transfer characteristics of turbulent Rayleigh–Bénard (RB) convection are studied at a Rayleigh number of 108 by double distribution thermal lattice Boltzmann method. Our numerical results indicate that the recirculation zone of the roughness gap is effectively disrupted, and the thickness of the temperature boundary layer is effectively reduced by the high-frequency horizontal vibration, which effectively enhances heat transfer. Horizontal vibration accelerates the flow of fluids, which is conducive to the full mixing of cold and hot fluids. The time-averaged Nusselt number of vibrating RB convection under rough walls is significantly increased by 206% compared with that of traditional RB convection at a roughness height of 0.05 and a vibrational frequency of 1000. However, the time-averaged Nusselt number of RB convection under rough walls is significantly increased by 23%, and the time-averaged Nusselt number of vibrating RB convection is increased by 169% compared with that of traditional RB convection, which reveals that the coupling effect of two factors is greater than the simple superposition effect of a single factor. Due to the promoting effect of plumes generated by horizontal vibrations on large-scale circulation and the inhibitory effect of increased roughness height on large-scale circulation, different vibration frequencies result in different monotonicity of normalized Reynolds number on roughness height.

papers.title: Hybrid physics-data-driven deep learning for pore-scale transport in microfluidic system
papers.abstract: Microfluidic platforms serve as powerful tools for pore-scale transport studies, generating datasets ideal for data-driven modeling. While conventional physics-driven models dominate flow characterization, their simplified two-dimensional (2D) implementations introduce substantial bias despite computational efficiency. Conversely, pure data-driven approaches face generalization limitations. To address both challenges, we developed a hybrid framework embedding physical transport mechanisms into neural networks. Through microfluidic experiments comparing four modeling approaches (pure data-driven, hybrid, 2D physics-based, and 2D depth-averaged models), we demonstrated that the hybrid model achieved consistent predictive accuracy across temporal scales. It outperformed traditional 2D physics-based models, which exhibited significant prediction bias. The model generalized well at different flow rates, as evidenced by the accurate reconstruction of the concentration field. Both hybrid and data-driven models performed comparably in short-term forecasting with sufficient data, but the hybrid framework uniquely maintained long-term prediction reliability. Quantitative analysis revealed monotonic accuracy improvements with increased experimental data in hybrid model bias correction. This work establishes the first experimental validation of hybrid modeling for pore-scale solute transport in microfluidic systems, bridging microscale observations with deep learning for enhanced porous media transport prediction.

papers.title: Influence of seabed irregularity on the wake of a tidal turbine
papers.abstract: Bathymetric features at tidal sites can introduce complex flow phenomena, such as pressure gradients and bed-induced turbulence. Understanding how these modify tidal-stream turbine wakes is critical to the design and operation of turbine arrays. Large-eddy simulations are performed to characterize the wakes of a tidal-stream turbine operating over a rough bed generated as a self-affine surface with roughness statistically similar to those found at a real tidal site. Comparison is drawn to smooth-bed conditions, both without and with a localized Gaussian ridge. The rough bathymetry enhances near-bed turbulence generation and increases vertical shear. Different wake center propagation and vertical wake expansion are observed for four transverse turbine positions, while lateral wake expansion is similar. Disk-averaged velocities and turbulence intensity in the wake region are always higher for the rough-bed cases. The ridge with a smooth bed leads to coherent turbulence structures, but these are suppressed by the higher turbulence occurring over the rough bed. Similar wake recovery rates are seen for all cases. However, lateral wake expansion is larger for the smooth bed, especially in the far-wake. The irregular bathymetry leads to an uneven streamwise variation of pressure transport and streamwise convection terms of turbulent kinetic energy budget. The ridge's adverse pressure gradient increased the contribution of the vertical convection term, counterbalanced by larger vertical turbulent transport and turbulent production. These findings highlight that realistic bathymetry notably impacts turbine wake recovery, with smooth-bed conditions underestimating downstream velocity and overestimating wake expansion.

papers.title: A comprehensive review on analysis of permeability measurements and surfactant enhanced oil recovery in shale
papers.abstract: Shale permeability measurements are usually conducted under steady state (SSM) and unsteady state (USM). Nevertheless, research has shown that USM is faster and produces better results than SSM. Because of this, numerous works have used USM with pulse decay (PDM) and gas research institute (GRI), being the most common methods utilized in many studies to investigate core plug and crushed sample permeabilities, respectively. Therefore, in this review, the reports on SSM, PDM, and GRI are presented. In addition, key parameters affecting permeability changes in shale were discussed. Moreover, it is no news that primary and secondary recoveries in shale have not been successful because of the permeability contrast between the matrix and fracture. Poor recoveries from these mechanisms could also be attributed to rock wettability and interfacial tension (IFT). Therefore, in the second part of this review, we focused on the recent studies on surfactants and surfactants + CO2 as enhanced oil recovery (EOR) agents in shale. This is necessary because both have been reported to be among the most effective EOR technologies for shale based on experimental, simulation, and field trials. Surfactants are primarily utilized for IFT and wettability alteration. However, some results showed that a combination of CO2 and surfactant would provide a stronger wettability change, some revealed that surfactant reduced the minimum miscibility pressure of CO2 and oil, many reported an increase in oil displacement efficiency with a CO2 + surfactant mixture, and a few studies recommended CO2 huff and puff after surfactant-assisted imbibition as hybrid EOR for shale.

papers.title: Graphics processing unit-accelerated updated Lagrangian particle hydrodynamics modeling of heat conduction and convection problems
papers.abstract: In this paper, an updated Lagrangian particle hydrodynamics (ULPH) method incorporating high-order nonlocal differential operators is employed to simulate fluid heat conduction and natural convection processes. The introduction of high-order matrix inversion significantly increases computational demand. Therefore, graphics processing unit (GPU) parallel acceleration was implemented within the ULPH framework. We have conducted several simulations, including natural convection within a cubic cavity and between concentric cylinders. The results show that the ULPH method aligns well with existing literature, and the GPU acceleration efficiency improves with the increase in computational scale. This method exhibits inherent accuracy and convergence, making it promising for simulating complex fluid dynamics scenarios.

papers.title: Dynamic behavior of droplet impinging on a superhydrophobic inclined cylindrical surface
papers.abstract: Droplet impinging on an inclined cylinder is different from that on a horizontal one in some ways. However, there is still a lack of in-depth study on its dynamic behavior. In this study, a numerical model of droplet impinging on a superhydrophobic inclined cylindrical surface was established by incorporating a dynamic contact angle model. Droplet motion patterns, sliding behavior, spreading and shrinking behavior, and contact time after droplet impinging were discussed under the influences of inclination angle and Weber number. Results show that under different conditions, droplets may exhibit four motion patterns: full rebound, pure slide, fragmentation, and oscillation. Pure slide is an inherent motion pattern for droplet impinging on an inclined surface, and full rebound is caused by the different sliding velocities of leading and trailing edges. Leading edge's sliding distance curve is convex and trailing edge's one is concave. The dimensionless sliding distance of the droplet rises with Weber number and inclination angle, and the effect of Weber number on it lessens at small inclination angles. The time for the droplet to reach maximal spreading length in axial direction gradually exceeds that in circumferential direction with the increase in inclination angle, and the non-monotonicity of the axial spreading length during the shrinking process disappears when an inclination angle is introduced. When the Weber number is less than 15.28 and the inclination angle rises from 0° to 80°, the contact time increases by 58.8%. This growth is even more pronounced when the Weber number is larger.

papers.title: Effect of fuel distribution strategies on combustion performance in a core burning scramjet combustor
papers.abstract: Optimizing fuel distribution strategies in scramjets is crucial for efficient supersonic combustion, thermal management, and performance enhancement. Existing research has overlooked the potential to enhance combustion performance while reducing heat load through fundamental fuel distribution strategies. This study investigates the effect of core-to-mainstream fuel distribution on the combustion performance of a core burning scramjet combustor under hypersonic inflow conditions (Mach 2.8, total temperature 1400 K, and total pressure 1.5 MPa) through experiments and numerical simulations. The findings demonstrate that the core burning scramjet combustor achieves self-sustained combustion of kerosene fuel. A fuel distribution strategy with a low core equivalence ratio and high mainstream equivalence ratio enhances combustion efficiency and total pressure recovery coefficient. The detailed flow field analysis reveals low wall heat load characteristics, with high-temperature regions concentrated downstream of the core burning chamber and at the center of the main combustion chamber. By integrating these findings, this research advances the understanding of fuel distribution strategies for the core burning scramjet combustor and offers practical guidance for optimizing combustion performance and thermal management in hypersonic propulsion systems.

papers.title: Enhanced architecture with adaptive sampling method for solving elliptic partial differential equations
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks have made significant progress in solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, challenges remain in handling high-frequency oscillatory components and singularities in the solutions. This paper proposes two types of multi-scale deep neural networks (DNNs): the multi-scale DNN and an optimized fully connected DNN with a custom network structure. Both utilize the Fourier transform as the activation function of the first hidden layer, effectively enhancing the capability of DNNs to address high-frequency problems. Additionally, this paper introduces an adaptive sampling algorithm that leverages the gradient of the solution to guide the distribution of sampling points, making them more suited to the specific characteristics of the problem. By solving elliptic equations with singularities and multi-scale features, the results demonstrate that this method effectively tackles singularity and multi-scale PDE problems, fully validating its effectiveness.

papers.title: Direct numerical simulation and an empirical model of effective thermal conductivity for hybrid compounded phase change materials by an integrated enthalpy-based lattice Boltzmann model
papers.abstract: The effective thermal conductivity (ETC) of composite phase change materials (CPCMs) determines the design and performance of the phase change heat exchanger. Direct simulation at the pore scale explores the main factors that influence ETC and gets an empirical model of ETC about pore structure parameters and thermal contact resistances (TCRs). Based on an integrated enthalpy-based lattice Boltzmann model with TCRs developed by our group, a double distribution function lattice Boltzmann model is built to describe the flow, phase change, and heat transfer processes for hybrid CPCMs at the pore scale. The geometry model for the phase change material (PCM) particle location is randomly generated by elastic collision between particles. Aiming at the hybrid CPCMs' unique composite way, the effects of the shape and size of PCM particles and TCRs between base and PCM particles on the characteristics of flow, heat transfer, and phase change processes are systematically investigated. The mechanism of phase change heat transfer for hybrid CPCMs is analyzed, and the variation principles of ETC with the shape and size of PCM particles and TCRs are summarized. Finally, an ETC empirical model of hybrid CPCMs, including the PCM particle properties and TCRs, is fitted, which may provide the theoretical basis and guidance for the directional design and optimized preparation of hybrid CPCMs.

papers.title: Time-marching throughflow method for inverse design of multistage compressors via characteristics-driven mesh adaptation
papers.abstract: Throughflow design plays a pivotal role in the aerodynamic design of modern turbomachinery. This paper proposes a time-marching throughflow method for the inverse design of multistage compressors. To accurately model the inviscid blade force, a mesh adaptation technique dynamically aligns the streamwise grid lines with the evolving streamlines. The method of characteristics directly solves the surface-flow slip equation, eliminating iterative steps and enhancing computational stability and efficiency. Empirical loss correlations are incorporated to capture loss effects. The Euler equations, discretized via finite volume method, are advanced using an implicit time-marching scheme. The inverse design procedure is validated by reconstructing a high-turning blade and a real-world transonic rotor from a prescribed tangential velocity distribution, achieving close agreement with the original one. A multistage compressor designed with this method achieved an isentropic efficiency of 87.69% at the design pressure ratio. The compressor demonstrated a wide operating range with efficiencies exceeding 88.0% at 80% and 90% of design speed. Results show that, while further performance improvements are possible, the developed design methodology proved effective for the aerodynamic design of multistage axial-flow compressors.

papers.title: Unsteady aerodynamic characteristics of a flying wing aircraft with variable-sweep morphing
papers.abstract: In this paper, numerical simulation method was used to solve the unsteady aerodynamic characteristics of a flying wing aircraft with variable-sweep morphing, and the influences of the shear morphing rate, angle of attack, and Mach number on the unsteady aerodynamic characteristics were analyzed. The results indicate that the best flight performance of the aircraft can be achieved by adjusting the wing sweep angle under various flight conditions. The unsteady aerodynamic coefficients exhibit dynamic hysteresis loops relative to the corresponding static-state data in the varying sweep process. Due to the influence of additional velocity effect and hysteresis effect, the surface pressure and shear stress distribution of the aircraft during the sweep forward and backward processes are significantly different from the static state, especially near the wingtip. As the shear morphing rate increases, the influences of the unsteady effects become more pronounced. The dynamic deviation of aerodynamic coefficients and the areas of hysteresis loops are approximately proportional to the shear morphing rate. As the angle of attack increases, flow separation occurs on the upper surface of the wing, intensifying the hysteresis effects of the flow structures. As the Mach number increases, the wing's sweep morphing influences the shock position and strength. This work provides a reference for the aerodynamic optimization and dynamic control strategy of variable configuration aircraft in a wide speed range.

papers.title: Non-uniform matrix deformation reshaping fluid diffusion properties and its effect on the supervision assessment of CO2 safety sequestration
papers.abstract: The CO2 sequestration capacity of deep coalbeds is profoundly governed by the fluid diffusion properties. However, the role of non-uniform matrix deformation in reshaping diffusion pathways remains inadequately understood. This urgently requires attention to the effect of fluid diffusion behavior on CO2 sequestration under the control of non-uniform matrix deformation. Based on the non-uniform matrix deformation coefficient and integrating the multivariate physical property parameters of Shenmu Runbang coal samples, this study investigates the evolution of matrix width under the regulation of non-uniform matrix deformation. By elucidating the evolution characteristics of binary gas adsorption–desorption, gas concentration, and diffusion rate, this study reveals the mechanism by which non-uniform deformation influences fluid diffusion behavior. Furthermore, it clarifies the impact mechanism of fluid diffusion behavior on deep coal seam CO2 storage under the control of non-uniform matrix deformation characteristics. The findings reveal that the influence of non-uniform matrix deformation on matrix width exhibits the nonlinear characteristic of a significant biphasic transition, and it significantly attenuates the fluid diffusion within the matrix. Furthermore, binary gas-induced non-uniform matrix deformation significantly suppresses matrix width. In the process of CO2 sequestration in deep coal seams, this effect notably mitigates matrix swelling induced by CO2, thereby enhancing the dual regulatory role of matrix width and fracture aperture in diffusion capacity, and further enhances the positive effect of diffusion capacity on CO2 sequestration, providing theoretical support for the technological innovation of deep coal seam CO2 safety sequestration and effectively contributing to the realization of dual-carbon supervision assessment goals.

papers.title: Gas slug frequency measurement and modeling based on acoustic emission and machine learning
papers.abstract: Slug flow is a typical intermittent gas–liquid two-phase flow that often occurs in petroleum extraction, chemical industry, etc. The gas slug frequency serves as a core quantitative indicator of slug flow dynamics, directly reflecting the wave dynamics and interphase interaction mechanisms. Accurate prediction of slug frequency holds significant value for advancing theoretical models of multiphase flow and analyzing the evolution of operational conditions. An acoustic emission measurement system is designed to capture the dynamic flow information of slug flow in real time. A window-optimized Savitzky-Golay filtering algorithm is utilized to suppress the non-stationary noise, while the power spectrum density method is utilized to extract the characteristic frequency information. A dimensionless parameter system (including Remix,β,Wel, Frl, X) is constructed based on the Strouhal number(St), in where Pearson correlation analysis is employed to elucidate the synergistic effects on the St. Subsequently, a gas-slug frequency prediction model is developed using gradient boosting regression. Experimental results demonstrate that, within the range of 0.4 < βg < 0.8, the model achieves a relative error of less than 30%, indicating high prediction accuracy. Verification tests under varying pipe diameters (25–76 mm) and liquid viscosities (1–181 mPa·s) reveal a mean absolute percentage error of less than 30%, with 70% of experimental data points exhibiting relative errors within ±30%, confirming the model's robust extrapolation capability. This study provides a novel methodology for gas–liquid two-phase flow parameter measurement.

papers.title: Quantitative assessment of coal seepage characteristics and pore–fracture structures using micro-computed tomography under stress–seepage coupling effects
papers.abstract: The study of coal permeability is essential for ensuring coal mine safety and the efficient extraction of coalbed methane (CBM). This research investigated coal permeability evolution and pore–fracture structural dynamics under stress–permeability coupling using a flow–solid coupling evaluation system and high-resolution micro-computed tomography (Micro-CT). Results reveal that coal permeability demonstrates nonlinear “suppression-activation” behavior controlled by effective stress. Under low confining pressure (<3 MPa), osmotic pressure triggers fracture expansion, yielding a 366.4% permeability surge. Conversely, high confining pressure (>3 MPa) intensifies pore closure, constraining permeability enhancement. Hydraulic treatments prove most effective at low effective stress (<3 MPa), where crack volume increases by 429.2% in volume growth rate, accompanied by 230.8% and 428.6% rises in fractal dimension and connected porosity, respectively. Large pores expand to 6.2%, forming interconnected flow channels. Under high effective stress, homogeneous pore–throat structures develop, compressing flow paths and restoring near-original permeability levels. Finite element simulations demonstrate enhanced coal anisotropy post-treatment, with axial permeability increasing 217.5%, improving directional flow capacity. These findings highlight stress-dependent permeability regulation mechanisms, suggesting optimal hydraulic fracturing parameters should prioritize low effective stress conditions to maximize fracture network connectivity in deep CBM reservoirs. This study elucidates the regulatory mechanisms of stress–permeability coupling on the microstructure of coal, providing a theoretical foundation for optimizing hydraulic fracturing parameters in deep CBM extraction.

papers.title: Investigation and revision of the viscous torque formula based on inertial effects and nonlinear dissipative effects
papers.abstract: The hydro-viscous drive clutch, a speed-regulating device utilizing oil film shear to transmit torque, exhibits discrepancies between traditional viscous torque models and experimental results due to the neglect of radial flow and rotational inertial effects. This study revises the conventional torque model based on Couette flow by re-deriving it from the Navier–Stokes equations in cylindrical coordinates, accounting for the coupled effects of radial and rotational flows. Through a detailed analysis of the convective acceleration and viscous diffusion terms, a novel viscous torque model is proposed, comprising three components: the viscous shear term (representing pure shear), the nonlinear term (capturing radial inertial effects), and the dissipation term (reflecting angular-flow coupling). Computational fluid dynamics simulations with mesh independence verification validate the model. Results show that within typical operating ranges—flow rate (Q = 0–30 l/min), oil film thickness (h = 0.1–0.5 mm), and angular velocity difference (Δω = 10–100 rad/s)—the revised model improves torque prediction accuracy by up to 28% compared to traditional formulations. Pressure contours and velocity streamline analyses reveal shear stress distributions dominated by inertial effects, highlighting the role of radial momentum transport in rotational energy dissipation. This work establishes a refined theoretical framework for accurate torque estimation and efficiency optimization in hydro-viscous drive systems operating under high-speed, variable-flow conditions.

papers.title: Experimental studies on flow noise interference mechanism of tandem shallow cavities with different spacings at subsonic speeds
papers.abstract: Regarding the flow noise interference mechanism of tandem shallow cavities, experimental research on the near-field flow field characteristics and far-field acoustic field characteristics of two cavities of the same size along the flow direction in tandem was carried out. The incoming flow velocity was adjusted from 60 to 80 m/s at the intervals of 5 m/s, which corresponded to Reynolds numbers from 6.6 × 105 to 8.8 × 105.
