By redesigning the nonlinear weights, the scheme now regains full third-order accuracy whenever a discontinuity contaminates only the 5-point stencil, whereas the original formulation collapsed to first order in that situation. Second, exploiting the compact stencils near boundaries, we devise four nearly one-sided nonlinear interpolation schemes without directly using cross-interface data. The resulting boundary scheme is high-order accurate in smooth, distorted grids and stays sharp and non-oscillatory when a shock lies on the interface. Finally, to achieve global integral conservation of the conserved variables, we propose a hybrid conservative difference scheme that combines face-to-cell and cell-to-cell stencils, driving conservation errors to machine precision. At last, the proposed schemes are validated through a series of numerical tests. The results demonstrate that even with grid distortion across block interfaces, the proposed scheme ensures the desired order of accuracy in smooth flow and avoids oscillations near shock locations.

papers.title: Double-diffusive stability analysis of micropolar fluid-saturated horizontal porous layers in the presence of a concentration-based internal heat source
papers.abstract: Concentration-based internal heat sources significantly influence the stability of micropolar fluid flow, playing a vital role in biomedical engineering by accounting for metabolic heat in drug delivery and tissue engineering and in chemical reactors and polymer processing by preventing thermal instability due to exothermic reactions or ion gradients. This article analyzes the stability of a micropolar fluid-saturated porous layer with a concentration-based internal heat source and vertical throughflow. Linear stability is assessed using the normal mode technique, while nonlinear stability is investigated through an energy method. Numerical solutions are obtained using MATLAB's bvp4c routine. The effects of vertical throughflow direction (Péclet number, Pe) and parameters, such as the Darcy number (Da), Lewis number (Le), micropolar parameter (m2), coupling number (N1), and solutal Rayleigh number (Rs), are examined. A comparison of linear and nonlinear thresholds identifies regions of subcritical instability. The study reveals that the internal heat source enhances stability during upward throughflow but promotes instability during downward throughflow. Additionally, at high Péclet numbers, its effect on downward flow becomes negligible.

papers.title: Mechanism of hydrodynamic properties affecting sector gate force behavior during dynamic water closure
papers.abstract: This study aims to provide a deeper analysis of the mechanical effects induced by turbulent flow characteristics in the gate recess on the sector gate during dynamic water closure. A full-scale three-dimensional geometric model focusing on the gate body was constructed using actual dimensional data. The third-generation Liutex-Omega vortex identification criterion was employed to clarify the evolution of vortex structures and quantify vortex intensity. The temporal variation of forces acting on the nose and skin plate was systematically analyzed through shear effects and stagnation pressure characteristics, revealing the interaction mechanisms between the gate and the flow during closure. The results demonstrate that the absolute vortex intensity near the central nose and side noses alternates in dominance, with two instances of equal intensity. The vortex evolution within the gate recess progresses through eight distinct stages. During the primary vortex attenuation and dissipation stage, transient peak operating forces arise due to a short moment arm, strong shear forces, and a resultant force near the side nose that tends to open the gate. The force peak occurs at gate openings ranging from 0.20 to 0.25, and exhibits an exponential relationship with the chamber flow velocity. This study offers novel insights into the force behavior characterization of sector gates under hydrodynamic operating conditions.

papers.title: The interaction mechanism between detonation wave and liquid kerosene
papers.abstract: Rotating detonation engine has garnered increasing attention due to their remarkable advantages, including pressure gain during the transition from reactants to products, accelerated heat release, reduced entropy generation, and enhanced thrust. Nonetheless, the interaction between the two-phase jets and the detonation wave has not been explored. This study aims to investigate the effects of the interaction process on the detonation wave and two-phase fuel jets. A novel experimental apparatus based on optical diagnostics was developed and rigorous two-dimensional numerical simulations were validated to facilitate the visualization of rotating detonation flow fields, which can be used to obtain the microscopic behavior of liquid kerosene in detail. The results of this study indicated that the interaction process of the detonation wave and liquid kerosene is divided into three stages: the leading shock heating stage, the evaporation, and the combustion stage, followed by the complete combustion stage. Moreover, parametric studies demonstrate that elevated kerosene inlet temperatures enhance droplet evaporation but accelerate detonation wave decay. Similarly, increased inlet pressure improves combustion efficiency within optimal ranges, whereas excessive pressure result in negligible detonation intensity improvement. Finally, a comparison between experimental observations and numerical simulations revealed strong consistency in droplet evaporation dynamics and interactions with detonation waves, which provide critical insights into the combustion and flow characteristics of the two-phase rotating detonation engine.

papers.title: Gas viscosity from first principles: A case study on nitrogen
papers.abstract: Gas viscosity is a critical parameter in aerodynamics. However, the underlying mechanisms have not been fully uncovered, especially for the bulk viscosity. Viscosity of typical diatomic gas nitrogen (N2) was investigated from a microscopic perspective. An equilibrium molecular dynamics (EMD) method was programmed, where an essential high-precision potential energy surface (PES) was constructed by fitting justified density functional theory calculations. The achieved PES was effectively validated by comparing with the CCSD(T) potential. The research was conducted at a medium temperature range from 100 to 1100 K, which minimized the influence from vibrational energy generation in molecular collisions. Based on the first principles calculation and successively the EMD study, Green–Kubo formula was applied to compute the shear and bulk viscosities. Results from the established micro-to-macro transcale model were compared with various experimental and theoretical values from the literature and were essentially validated. The bulk viscosity turns out to demonstrate a novel nonlinear pseudo-exponential trend with temperature, relative to traditional methods with different approximations or errors. Nonetheless, a linearized fitting to the achieved shear viscosity shows another highlight, compared to the generally applied Sutherland's equation.

papers.title: Pressure drop characteristics of gas–liquid flow in a horizontal butterfly valve
papers.abstract: Butterfly valves are standard components in pipeline systems for a wide range of industries, including chemical, water conveyance, and petrochemical. Special attention should be paid to the pressure drop caused by the complex two-phase flow through butterfly valves. In this paper, an experimental platform for gas–liquid flow was designed and constructed to investigate the pressure drop characteristics across a horizontal butterfly valve. Focusing on the intermittent flow patterns, including elongated bubble and slug flow, the effects of valve openings and gas–liquid superficial velocities on pressure drop were analyzed through experimental research under different operating conditions. It is found that the two-phase flow exhibited substantial asymmetry within the horizontal butterfly valve, leading to intensified local friction and flow separation, as well as enhanced breakup and merging of the gas–liquid phase interface. The pressure drop caused by gas phase is significant, especially under high valve opening, and the pressure drop multiplier shows a higher growth rate with the increase in gas phase proportion. A parametric model of the two-phase pressure drop multiplier for horizontal butterfly valves is proposed by equivalently describing the flow of gas and liquid phases using a Venturi tube and a thin orifice plate, respectively. The calculated results of the proposed model are consistent with the experimental data, verifying the effectiveness of the model. Compared with existing correlations, the proposed model demonstrates enhanced predictive accuracy of the two-phase flow pressure drop multiplier of horizontal butterfly valves.

papers.title: Vector quantization variational autoencoder for turbulent flow images
papers.abstract: This study explores, for the first time, the application of vector-quantized variational autoencoders to reconstruct and analyze flow images from fluid dynamics simulations across varying resolutions. The method demonstrates effective reconstruction performance, achieving meaningful quantitative results, such as mean squared error, peak signal-to-noise ratio, and structural similarity index measure. These metrics indicate that the method effectively captures and preserves key flow patterns relative to reference images. However, experiments with latent space interpolation reveal that direct linear interpolation between coarse and fine latents produces lower-quality medium-resolution reconstructions than the reference data, highlighting the need for additional conditioning or constraints. Despite this limitation, the interpolation results outperform naive pixel-based methods, suggesting that the technique encodes meaningful and structured latent representations of flow images. The potential applications of the proposed method in fluid dynamics are significant. By conditioning latent representations with specific flow parameters, the technique can synthesize flow images for novel fluid dynamics scenarios, including intermediate states or parameterized datasets. This capability opens avenues for generating flow states that may not be achievable through direct simulations or experiments, such as scenarios involving dynamically changing boundary conditions–a situation typical in atmospheric, oceanographic, or engineered flows. Moreover, generating such synthetic data could considerably expand the accessible parameter space while reducing the computational cost of running extensive simulations or experiments. These features position the proposed method as a promising tool for compressing, reconstructing, and synthesizing flow data for fluid dynamics research and applications.

papers.title: Flow boiling heat transfer characteristics of de-ionized water in superhydrophobic microchannels under electrowetting actuation
papers.abstract: Surface wettability is a critical factor influencing microchannel boiling phase-change heat transfer. Most current methods produce surfaces with unitary hydrophilic or hydrophobic properties, which cannot dynamically adjust wall wettability in response to boiling characteristics. The electrowetting effect offers the advantage of real-time surface wettability modulation. This study experimentally investigates the impact of the electrowetting effect on flow boiling in superhydrophobic microchannels, exhibiting a static contact angle of 153.4° ± 1.5°. Experimental results reveal that the electrowetting exerts a greater influence on wall temperature when large bubbles dominate the flow boiling process compared to scenarios with smaller bubbles. In the voltage range of 60–100 Vrms, higher voltages intensify vapor–liquid interface oscillations and promote rewetting of dry-out regions, leading to enhanced wall cooling. However, as the heating power increases, the cooling effect exhibits a non-monotonic trend due to competing interfacial forces: evaporation momentum forces generated during bubble nucleation and growth progressively surpass electrowetting-induced liquid film movement, diminishing interfacial modulation. At flow rates of 0.3–0.8 ml/min, higher flow rates reduce bubble nucleation sites while accelerating bubble detachment, limiting both the spatial extent and temporal duration of electrowetting-induced interfacial interactions, consequently reducing wall cooling performance. At a low flow rate of 0.3 ml/min and a low heating power of 4.77 W, applying a high voltage of 100 Vrms reduces the local wall temperature up to 13 °C and increases the local and average heat transfer coefficients by 180.9% and 31.0%, respectively. This study provides significant insights for advancing applied research on electrowetting-enhanced boiling heat transfer in microchannels.

papers.title: A parameter-optimized reinforcement iterative learning control method for enhancing passenger pressure comfort and air quality in high-speed trains traversing extreme tunnels
papers.abstract: When high-speed trains traverse tunnels with characteristics such as high altitude, steep gradients, and substantial lengths, intense tunnel pressure waves are generated. These pressure waves induce pressure fluctuations within the carriage, adversely affecting passenger pressure comfort. However, when trains pass through extra-long tunnels or tunnel groups, maintaining a balance between passenger pressure comfort and air quality becomes challenging. This is because the existing passive control strategy—closing ventilation ducts for a certain duration—fails to match the tunnel pressure wave characteristics. Therefore, an iterative learning control (ILC) algorithm that matches the tunnel pressure waves is employed to suppress interior pressure fluctuations. However, the learning parameters in existing ILC algorithms for interior pressure control are fixed and cannot adapt based on control performance, thereby lacking adaptive tuning capabilities. To tackle these issues, this paper integrates reinforcement learning (RL) into the ILC framework and proposes a parameter-optimized reinforcement iterative learning control (PORILC) scheme for managing interior pressure fluctuations within the vehicle. Specifically, the RL-based adaptive gain adjustment scheme is developed. A performance-related weighting factor is introduced to combine the decreasing gain of ILC with the powerful exploration capability of RL. Finally, simulation results demonstrate that, compared with traditional passive control and conventional ILC methods, the proposed PORILC scheme ensures both passenger pressure comfort and air quality within the carriage, with enhanced tracking accuracy. Experimental results suggest that the PORILC scheme contributes to improved pressure comfort for vehicle occupants under extreme tunnel pressure wave excitation.

papers.title: Differences in thermal characteristics of longitudinally ventilated tunnel fires induced by fire location
papers.abstract: Tunnel fires are high-risk incidents in confined spaces. However, the impact of fire location randomness on fire development and smoke control has not been fully explored. This study experimentally analyzed how fire location influences tunnel fire characteristics under longitudinal ventilation. The findings revealed distinct differences when the fire was near the entrance (S/d ≤ 2, where S was the distance from fire source to tunnel entrance and d was the side length of pool fires) vs inside (S/d > 2). When the fire source was located inside the tunnel, the fully developed and thick smoke layer generates stronger airflow by its compression effect, which significantly affected flame tilt. This led to a steeper flame tilt angle, a reduced flame height, and an intensified radiative heat flux to the tunnel floor. However, when the fire was near the entrance, the maximum ceiling gas temperature might not be fully captured, and smoke was more easily exhausted, leading to a reduction in smoke backlayering length and critical velocity. Incorporating fire location effects, characterization models were developed for key parameters of flame behavior, including flame geometries and radiation heat flux, and smoke control, including smoke backlayering length and critical velocity. This work enhances insights into the stochastic nature of tunnel fires, expands fire dynamics research frameworks, and supports improved thermal safety in tunnels.

papers.title: Research on bioinspired groove design for low-frequency flow noise suppression in towed cable
papers.abstract: This study addresses the critical challenge of low-frequency flow noise in turbulent boundary layers (TBL) during the towed cable operations. Inspired by the biomechanical principles of sharkskin structures, we propose bioinspired microgrooved surface design for low-frequency flow noise suppression. By integrating the Stress-Blended Eddy Simulation method with the Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings acoustic analogy theory, a coupled fluid–acoustic numerical model was developed to analyze spectral discrepancies. The hybrid model's accuracy was validated through successive grid refinement iterations, and the spectral characteristic error of numerical prediction was reduced. Four bioinspired groove configurations (rectangular, trapezoidal, triangular, and sinusoidal) were systematically investigated using high-fidelity numerical simulations. The results reveal that the grooves effectively disrupt large-scale vortex coherence, achieving a reduction in wall pressure fluctuation intensity. The rectangular groove exhibited optimal performance at 14 knots, reducing sound pressure levels within the towed cable by 11.92% and 14.5% at 100 and 700 Hz, respectively. Near-field noise attenuation rates reached 21.21% and 20.5% at the corresponding frequencies. Notably, flow noise reduction efficacy was strongly correlated with towing velocity, with microvortex energy dissipation mechanisms becoming dominant in high-speed regimes (>8 knots).

papers.title: Study on the influence of excavation footage on gas concentration prediction based on the Transformer model
papers.abstract: Coal mine gas disasters pose a serious threat to mine safety. Thus, enhancing the accuracy of gas concentration prediction in mines is vital for preventing coal mine accidents effectively. Conventional gas concentration prediction methods typically focus solely on gas concentration variations, overlooking other environmental factors that impact gas outburst amounts. This oversight leads to low prediction accuracy. This study introduces a Transformer-based prediction model, which innovatively integrates mine excavation footage data as an input feature. Unlike traditional approaches, this method more effectively captures gas concentration variations. The experiment utilized gas concentration and excavation footage data from a Hebei Province coal mine, which exhibited diverse data characteristics, for prediction analysis. Comparative experiments were carried out with the traditional long short-term memory and gated recurrent unit models. The results demonstrated that combining excavation footage data with gas concentration data as model inputs yielded lower root mean squared error and mean absolute error values. It also substantially improved the R-Square (R2) for predictions compared to using only gas concentration data. Moreover, the Transformer model exhibited higher prediction accuracy across different datasets than other models, highlighting its superior adaptability and effectiveness. This method is significant for gas concentration prediction and risk warning in coal mine working faces.

papers.title: The aerodynamic mechanism of the effect of gap width on the vertical vortex-induced vibration of the triple-box girders
papers.abstract: The triple-box girder is prone to vortex-induced vibration (VIV). However, the effect of gap width on vertical VIV and its underlying aerodynamic mechanism remains unclear. Based on wind tunnel tests and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, this study investigates the aerodynamic mechanism of the effect of gap width on the vertical VIV performance of the triple-box girders. Four groups of girder models with varying gap widths were tested experimentally to elucidate the relationship between gap width and the vertical VIV performance. The CFD simulations were used to explore the effects of gap width on flow characteristics and pressure distribution under peak amplitude of VIV conditions, while the energy distribution of distributed aerodynamic forces was analyzed to systematically discuss the aerodynamic mechanisms involved. Results indicate that gap width significantly influences the vertical response of VIV of the triple-box girder. The peak amplitude of VIV increases with gap width, though the growth rate diminishes as gap width expands. Increasing gap width enhances the intensity of vortex shedding between gap regions, leading to a marked rise in fluctuating pressures on the local surfaces of midstream and downstream boxes, while mean pressure distributions remain relatively stable. As the gap width increases, the positive energy contribution region progressively expands from the lower surfaces and the trailing edges of the upper surface of the downstream box to encompass the lower surfaces and the trailing edges of the upper surface of the upstream and midstream boxes, thereby enhancing the peak amplitude of VIV. These findings provide valuable insights for understanding the aerodynamic mechanisms of triple-box girders subject to VIV and optimizing the aerodynamic shape.

papers.title: Study on the effect of type and content of hardness-indicator ions within fluids on the wettability and microstructure of coal dusts
papers.abstract: The traditional evaluation system for coal dust wettability does not adequately account for highly mineralized water environments. Therefore, it is essential to systematically investigate the effects of hardness-indicator ions (Ca2+/Mg2+) in aqueous solutions on coal dust wettability and microstructure. This study employed wettability experiments (surface tension, contact angle measurements, and sedimentation tests) to analyze the influence of ion type and concentration on coal–water interfacial behavior. Results demonstrate that the surface tension of solutions containing only Ca2+ or Mg2+ initially decreased and then increased with rising hardness levels, with hardness thresholds observed at 500 and 700 ppm, respectively. This trend was consistently reflected in parameters such as droplet contact angle, spreading coefficient, and coal dust immersion time. Furthermore, microscopic characterization techniques, including low-temperature nitrogen adsorption, Fourier-transform infrared, and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, revealed significant impacts of ion type and concentration on coal dust pore characteristics, functional group distribution, and hydrophilic/hydrophobic element content. Specifically, low-hardness levels [≤500 ppm (Ca2+) and ≤700 ppm (Mg2+)] synergistically enhanced wettability, whereas high-hardness levels [>500 ppm (Ca2+) and >700 ppm (Mg2+)] suppressed it. The divergent effects of Ca2+ and Mg2+ were attributed to differences in their charge-to-ionic radius ratios. These findings provide theoretical support for the effective mitigation of coal dust pollution in mining environments.

papers.title: Research on sensitivity analysis methods for production dynamics in heavy oil polymer flooding using proxy model
papers.abstract: In heavy oil polymer flooding development, accurately identifying dominant control parameters and their impacts on production performance is crucial for enhancing development efficiency. To overcome the limitations of conventional numerical simulation methods characterized by time-consuming computations and low efficiency, this study employs a random search-optimized multilayer perceptron (RS-MLP) proxy model as its foundation. Through comprehensive comparison of eXtreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) and random forest (RF) algorithm performance, XGBoost was selected for feature importance analysis, utilizing information gain to quantitatively evaluate the influence of both static and dynamic parameters on oil rate, water cut, oil recovery factor, and pressure maintenance level. The study shows that nonlinear connections between parameters are well captured by the XGBoost model. While porosity largely controls fluctuations in oil output and water cut, oil saturation has the biggest effect on oil recovery factor and oil rate among static characteristics. With an average sensitivity of 0.265 across water cut, oil recovery factor, and pressure distribution, injection rate exhibits significant regulatory impacts on displacement dynamics for dynamic parameters. In comparison to traditional numerical simulation, the created RS-MLP proxy model improves computational efficiency by two orders of magnitude while achieving good prediction accuracy (R2 = 0.96) with a mean absolute error of 1.98. This study shows that, in some situations, data-driven techniques can successfully take the place of traditional numerical simulations to produce quick and precise sensitivity analysis. The method has great practical relevance for achieving intelligent reservoir management and offers a novel technical way for optimizing polymer flooding development in heavy oil reservoirs.

papers.title: Effects of interfacial rheology on solutocapillary convection near the air–liquid interface
papers.abstract: The roles of interfacial rheology in solutocapillary convection near the air–liquid interface driven by a point mass source are investigated. First, the assumption of the conically similar viscous flow is successfully extended to treat the effects of interfacial rheology on solutocapillary convection near the air–liquid interface. By taking the surface viscosity as a small parameter, the steady solutocapillary convection is analyzed by applying the matched asymptotic expansion method. For small Re numbers and small/large Sc numbers, the exact solutions of the solutocapillary convection are shown. It is found that, to generate the first-order surface tension, the interfacial rheology related to the leading order solution is more dominant than the first-order concentration gradient of surfactant. Moreover, for general physical parameters, the governing equations of the solutocapillary convection for the perturbation solutions are numerically solved by applying the shooting method. In comparison with basic solutions for the solutocapillary convection near the air–liquid interface without the interfacial rheology, the interfacial rheology enhances both the divergent flow near the interface and the convergent flow far from the interface. Its effects on the distribution of surfactant depend on Pe number. For small/large Pe numbers, the interfacial rheology slightly/greatly increases the distribution of the surfactant near the interface and slightly/greatly decreases the distribution of the surfactant near the symmetric axis.

papers.title: NOx reduction and stability enhancement in high-pressure ammonia swirling combustion through multiphysical fields collaboration
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effects of pressure variations on NOx emissions during ammonia combustion in a stratified swirling vortex-tube combustor, utilizing stratified vortex combustion (SVC) technology. The results reveal a significant inverse correlation between rising pressure (from 0.1 to 2.0 MPa) and emissions of NOx, NH3, and H2, with NOx concentrations decreasing from 0.103 to 0.066 g/kg for NO and from 0.880 to 0.540 g/kg for N2O. Peak formation rates of nitric oxide (NO) and nitrous oxide (N2O) also decline substantially from 39.95 to 10.15 mol/(kg s) and 27.85 to 21.45 mol/(kg s), respectively, while their reduction rates shift from −6.15 to −3.03 mol/(kg s) for NO and −38.57 to −31.48 mol/(kg s) for N2O. The SVC technology enhances NO reduction, suppresses N2O formation, and inhibits ammonia conversion to nitroxyl (HNO)—a key NO precursor—through the synergistic optimization of multiphysics fields (e.g., velocity, temperature, and composition fields) under elevated pressures. The observed reduction in peak NO concentration is driven by lower temperatures (e.g., from 1808 to 1756 K at peak NO formation zones) and decreased levels of reactive intermediates (e.g., OH drops from 4.67 × 10−4 to 1.40 × 10−4, HNO from 1.3 × 10−4 to 9.623 × 10−5) in the NOx formation zone. Notably, while NH2 and H concentrations decline at higher pressures, the high-temperature region in the NO and N2O reduction zones expands by approximately 20% at 1.5 MPa, providing a larger domain for effective emission reduction. These findings, supported by chemical kinetics analysis, demonstrate SVC's potential for stable, efficient, and low-emission ammonia combustion across varying pressure conditions, offering critical insight for its industrial application as a clean fuel technology.

papers.title: Role of bubble size on hollow droplet collision onto thin liquid film
papers.abstract: The present work numerically explores the behavior of hollow droplet collision on a thin film surface by considering pertinent factors. Dimensionless quantities, such as diameter ratio (d/D), Weber number (We), Ohnesorge number (Oh), and film thickness Ho/D are employed to characterize the impingement mechanism of hollow droplets onto thin films. Characterization of radial spreading (f/D), edge jet (h/D), and central counter jet (L/D) is understood through a qualitative approach using numerical contours. Thus, temporal growth of f/D, h/D, and L/D are predicted for different values of We, d/D, and Ho/D. Similarly, predictions are extended for maximum spreading (fmax/D), maximum edge jet (hmax/D), and maximum central counter jet (Lmax/D) to enrich the characterization of insightful physics of hollow droplet collision on thin film surface. The reduction gradient of fmax/D with d/D is anticipated to be steeper at a higher We than a lower We. It is noticed that the gaseous bubble does not burst at a higher magnitude of Oh. Thus, a regime map on Oh−d/D plane is anticipated to distinguish two separate regimes, such as bursting and no-bursting zones. Fluidic behavior of impingement mechanism is elucidated using velocity vectors. Finally, we have also proposed relevant correlations to predict the maximum spread fmax*=fmax/D, maximum edge jet hmax*=hmax/D, and maximum central jet Lmax*=Lmax/D in terms of different pertinent input parameters.

papers.title: Supersonic turbulent pipe flow at computationally moderate Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: Well-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) of supersonic turbulent pipe flow at centerline Mach numbers of 1.6 and 1.8 and moderate friction Reynolds numbers of 1000 and 2200 are performed. The present LES of the supersonic pipe flow at friction Reynolds number 2200 is the first in the literature for which no direct numerical simulation (DNS) data are available. The statistics of the lower Reynolds number pipe flow agree quite well with those of the existing DNS by Modesti and Pirozzoli, “Direct numerical simulation of supersonic pipe flow at moderate Reynolds number,” Int. J. Heat Fluid Flow 76, 100–112 (2019), at similar Mach and Reynolds numbers. A distinct low wavenumber k−1 region in the streamwise velocity spectra, appearing due to the presence of large-scale motions (LSM) and very large-scale motions (VLSM), is observed along with a distinct logarithmic region in mean velocity. Other well-known high Reynolds number features such as a bimodal behavior of the premultiplied spectra of streamwise velocity fluctuations and a second outer peak in the Reynolds stresses are seen, which are compared with those found in incompressible pipe flows. A logarithmic variation of azimuthal velocity variance is also observed in a region away from the wall, as predicted by Townsend's attached eddy hypothesis [Townsend, The Structure of Turbulent Shear Flow, 2nd ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1976)].

papers.title: An experimental study on two-phase flashing R134a spray cooling performance with multiple nozzles
papers.abstract: Low-boiling-point R134a spray cooling effectively reduces surface temperatures rapidly, with applications in chip cooling, automotive air conditioning, and laser biomedicine. Multiple nozzles have a larger spray coverage and liquid film spreading area compared to a single nozzle, allowing for enhanced convective and phase-change heat transfer, leading to large-area uniform cooling and flexible adjustment of cooling capacity. An experimental apparatus for cryogen spray cooling was set up to analyze the effects of various factors, including nozzle inner diameter, spray distance, spray pressure, spurt duration, and cooling substrate, on the surface heat transfer characteristics. The results indicate that the lowest surface temperature is primarily influenced by the nozzle inner diameter and spray distance, while the peak heat flux is mainly affected by the spray distance and the cooling substrate. The heat flux with copper surface is ∼38 times that of an epoxy resin block (qmax = 8179.94 kW/m2). Nozzle diameter has the most significant impact on the uniformity of surface cooling, whereas spray pressure and duration have the weakest effects on surface heat transfer characteristics. When the cooling substrate is an epoxy resin block, appropriate spray conditions (Nozzle diameter D = 0.4 mm, spray pressure P = 1.9 MPa, spray distance H = 10 mm, and spurt duration ts= 50 ms) allow droplets to fully atomize and distribute reasonably across the surface, achieving the lowest cooling temperature (Tmin = −40.13 °C) and the highest heat flux (qmax = 217.76 kW/m2) as well as realizing a longer effective cooling time.

papers.title: Yaw angle impact on high-speed train–flat box girder aerodynamics
papers.abstract: Flat box girders are widely used in large-span bridges to accommodate high-speed trains, owing to their cost-effectiveness and vibration stability. However, their aerodynamic stability remains a critical issue that has received relatively little attention, especially when coupled with a train to form a train–flat box girder (train/bridge) system. Therefore, this study conducted a numerical simulation of a train/bridge system to analyze the flow field, drag coefficient (CD), lift coefficient (CL), and moment coefficient (CM) of the train. Numerical results revealed complex and significant aerodynamic interactions within the system, with stronger disturbances and more pronounced flow separation when the train was positioned on the windward side of the bridge. Both CD and CL of the head and middle cars increased with yaw angle, showing two distinct phases: a gentle variation interval (0°–15°) and a linear increase interval (20°–70°). However, in the 75°–90°-range, the CD of the middle car on the windward side of the bridge surged abruptly, whereas CL dropped sharply. Meanwhile, the CM of the head and middle cars gradually decreased with increasing yaw angle; however, the CM of the middle car on the windward side suddenly decreased when the yaw angle exceeded 75°.

papers.title: The hydrodynamic performance of multi-hydrofoil formations in plain river networks based on fish schooling dynamics
papers.abstract: To address the challenge of insufficient hydrodynamic performance in plain river networks, this paper proposes a multi-hydrofoil formation pumping method inspired by fish schooling, building on prior research into the water-pushing performance of a single hydrofoil. Using the finite volume method and overlapping mesh technology, this study conducted a numerical analysis of the hydrodynamic performance for three hydrofoil formations: parallel, positive-triangle, and negative-triangle. The results show that under different spacing configurations, the vortices exhibit significant reorganization phenomena during the development process of the wake flow field, leading to substantial differences in hydrodynamic performance. The optimal spatial parameters for each formation are as follows: parallel hydrofoil formation: D/c=1.4 (D represents the lateral spacing, and c represents the chord length); positive-triangle hydrofoil formation: D/c=1.8 and G/c=0.4 (G represents the longitudinal spacing); and negative-triangle hydrofoil formation: D/c=1.0 and G/c=0.8. Across different oscillation frequencies, each sub-hydrofoil in the multi-hydrofoil system required an increase in input power by 3%–32% compared to a single-hydrofoil system. However, the average flow rate was enhanced by 100%–152% and the average pressure difference increased significantly by 301%–525%. With pump efficiency calculated using the formula: (average flow rate × average pressure difference)/input power, the multi-hydrofoil system achieved a significant efficiency improvement of 144%–327%. The characteristic curves of different hydrofoil formations resemble those of traditional axial flow pumps, exhibiting a head decrease with increasing flow rate and a pumping efficiency trend of initial rise followed by decline as flow rate increases. This similarity suggests potential applications of multi-hydrofoil formations in pump design for plain river networks.

papers.title: Structured nonlinear cascades bridging macroscopic fluid scales and molecular vibrations
papers.abstract: I propose and theoretically analyze a novel approach to selectively excite molecular vibrational modes through structured fluid dynamics guided by generalized symmetry-based transformations of the Navier–Stokes equations. By encoding specific molecular resonance information into structured macroscopic fluid perturbations and using iterative nonlinear cascades, I demonstrate numerically that energy can coherently transfer from macroscopic scales down to molecular vibrational frequencies. This structured cascade, described by a generalized Gelfand transform and associated nonlinear structure constants, ensures resonance conditions at molecular scales, significantly delaying thermalization and enabling precise quantum state manipulation in fluids. Numerical simulations explicitly targeting the asymmetric vibrational mode of CO2 validate this methodology, highlighting its potential applications in controlled molecular excitation and coherent fluid-based quantum manipulation. The novelty of this work explicitly lies in introducing generalized symmetry-adapted nonlinear cascades, carefully designed to achieve coherent and selective molecular-scale energy excitation from structured macroscopic fluid perturbations, a significant departure from traditional turbulent cascades.

papers.title: Aerodynamic research of a high-load turbine with novel leading edge fillet considering rim seal
papers.abstract: The rim seal can effectively prevent the ingress of high-temperature gas into the gap between the stator and rotor passages. However, the blending of the sealing air and the mainstream will change the flow state in the passage, reducing the turbine efficiency. To improve the flow field and increase efficiency, the PW-E3 incorporates a newly designed fillet at the leading edge of rotor blade, with the fillet bending in the opposite direction to the blade. This leading edge fillet (LEF) organizes the sealing of air in the passage. The variations of the total pressure coefficient (Cpt), pressure coefficient (Cp), and the passage vortex are discussed to evaluate the effect of the fillet at different mass flow ratios. The numerical results show that the application of a LEF effectively mitigates flow losses and subsequently increases the stage efficiency. Moreover, as the fillet height is incremented, there is an observable augmentation in the increasing rate of the stage efficiency. The efficiency growth rate is the largest at a fillet height of 3, with a value of 0.45%. The streamwise total pressure coefficient is decreased under the effects of LEF. And the spanwise total pressure coefficient decreases in the vicinity of the hub end wall. The increasing mass flow ratio of the sealing air reduces the improvement caused by the fillet. The passage vortex is also investigated in depth. It is found that the passage vortex experiences an upward displacement as the LEF lifts the sealing air. As the mass flow ratio of the sealing air intensifies, the scale of the passage vortex undergoes an expansion. Consequently, this elevation of the passage vortex restrains the expansion of the separation bubble on the suction side.

papers.title: Investigating tip-speed ratio balancing for enhanced hydrodynamic performance of counter-rotating marine current turbine
papers.abstract: Counter-rotating marine current turbines demonstrate significant potential for tidal power extraction. However, existing studies neglect the critical interaction between upstream (λ1) and downstream (λ2) tip-speed ratios (TSRs) within rotating wake environments. This work systematically investigates TSR balancing strategy via coupled analytical (momentum theory with wake rotation) and numerical methods (ANSYS 2022 R1, SST k-ω turbulence model) across a broad TSR design range (λ1, λ2: 0.5–9.7). Results reveal that the rear rotor exhibits greater sensitivity to TSR changes. Contrary to conventional design paradigms, novel geometries with λ2/λ1 ≤ 1.3 can still achieve a competitive power coefficient, indicating the potential for efficient operation under such conditions and exceeding the performance of a single-rotor configuration. Analytical solutions show that momentum theory underpredicts power performance at high TSRs due to tip losses, while numerical simulations identify optimal TSR intervals, yielding a 9.3% efficiency gain over a single-rotor system. Furthermore, increasing λ1 accelerates the onset of negative torque in the rear rotor, as λ2 approaches its operational limit. This study challenges prevailing assumptions by demonstrating that rear rotor can efficiently operate at elevated TSRs (λ2/λ1) under stabilized axial induction factors, offering actionable insights for optimizing high-output marine energy systems.

papers.title: Study on the cavitation characteristics and noise mechanisms of a propeller under non-uniform inflow
papers.abstract: In propeller-driven propulsion applications, the influence of non-uniform inflow on propeller cavitation processes and noise characteristics is inevitable. To further elucidate the mechanisms by which hydrofoil wake vortices affect propeller surface cavitation behavior and noise propagation, this study systematically investigates propeller operation under various hydrofoil angles of attack using numerical simulations. The complex interaction mechanisms among hydrofoil wake vortices, propeller blade tip vortices, and the propeller itself are explored. The results show that hydrofoil wake vortices, by altering the local inflow velocity magnitude and direction, exert opposite effects on the cavitation behavior of blades at different positions. Additionally, under the influence of hydrofoil wake vortices, the strength of the propeller blade tip vortices is significantly reduced, and the onset of instability occurs earlier. It is also found that the overall noise intensity and radiation characteristics of the propeller are notably affected by non-uniform inflow conditions.

papers.title: Sedimentation of a charged hydrophobic colloid with physisorbed surface charge and similarity with a charged droplet
papers.abstract: The sedimentation of a charged hydrophobic rigid colloid by considering a surface charge-dependent slip condition is studied by numerical simulation alongside a simplified model. The primary aim is to elucidate the effect of the lateral mobility of ions adsorbed on the surface of the hydrophobic rigid colloid and establish an identity with the sedimentation of a charged liquid droplet. For the hydrophobic surface with mobile adsorbed charge, an additional electric force and a frictional force are produced by the physisorbed ions to create an alteration of the conventional slip boundary condition and the slip length. We have also considered separately the sedimentation of the liquid droplet by considering a stress balance condition at the charged interface, which includes a non-zero tangential component of the electric stress. The governing electrokinetic equations for the hydrophobic rigid particle as well as the droplet are solved numerically. We have also constructed a simplified model based on a first-order perturbation from equilibrium. The mobility of the physisorbed surface charge enhances the sedimentation velocity of the hydrophobic colloid by creating an enhanced slip velocity. The sedimentation velocity generally diminishes as the surface charge density increases. However, for a fully mobile surface charge, the velocity of the hydrophobic rigid colloid increases with the rise in surface charge density at an elevated value of the slip length. The numerical findings and the semi-analytical solution establish that the sedimentation of a hydrophobic particle with a fully mobile surface charge resembles that of a liquid droplet, wherein the viscosity of the droplet relates to the slip length of the hydrophobic particle.

papers.title: Effect of vortex generator spanwise width on vortex size and aero-optical effects in backward-facing step flow field
papers.abstract: Flow control is required to suppress aero-optical effects for optical windows with backward-facing steps. This study investigates the impact of vortex generator (VG) spanwise width on vortical breakdown and aero-optical distortions in a Mach 3 flow field over a backward-facing step, using the nano-tracer planar laser scattering technique. Vortex evolution is quantified through fractal dimension analysis and two-point spatial correlation, while aero-optical effects are evaluated via gray-density calibration and ray-tracing methodology. Experimental results indicate that VG with larger spanwise widths facilitate accelerated vortical structure breakdown. However, excessive spanwise widths of VGs lead to a reduction in the global fractal dimension of the flow field and an increase in vortex size. Enhanced interaction between VG wakes and lower-wall turbulent boundary layers (TBLs) is observed for wider VGs. For spanwise widths of 24 and 18 mm, wake-induced TBL vortex size initially decreases before increasing along the streamwise direction. Time-averaged density fields further reveal a closer proximity of wake structures to the lower-wall TBL with increased spanwise widths of VGs. Optical path difference (OPD) in the computational domain initially increases, then decreases, and eventually stabilizes due to vortex breakdown and TBL/wake development. Notably, the 18 mm VG configuration exhibits a higher root mean square deviation of the OPD than other cases. This parametric study offers insights into optimizing optical window flow control strategies to mitigate aero-optical distortions.

papers.title: Visualization study of viscous fingering and its implications in acid fracturing with multistage alternating injection
papers.abstract: Multistage alternating acid fracturing enhances non-uniform acid etching and fracture conductivity by promoting viscous fingering, thereby improving carbonate reservoir productivity. However, the evolution of viscous fingering under varying injection conditions remains insufficiently understood, limiting the optimization design of injection parameters. This study employs a visualized experimental setup to examine the effects of viscosity contrast, injection rate, fracture width, and the number of alternating stages on viscous fingering morphology and acid-etching patterns. Quantitative metrics, including fractal dimension and fingering area, were utilized to characterize non-uniform etching induced by fingering. Results indicate that higher viscosity contrast suppresses piston-like displacement and promotes fingering bifurcation, increasing etching non-uniformity and fracture conductivity. Injection rate and fracture width jointly affect the inlet acid velocity. Fingering complexity initially increases with acid velocity but declines beyond a critical threshold, suggesting the existence of an optimal injection rate for a given treatment. Increasing the number of alternating stages deepens etched channels and enhances fingering complexity, improving the fracture conductivity. However, with a fixed acid volume, more stages reduce per-stage acid volume, shortening the effective penetration distance. Thus, a balance between acid penetration and non-uniform etching is critical for optimal multistage alternating acid fracturing design.

papers.title: Successive droplets impacting on non-wetting surfaces: Impact force and contact time
papers.abstract: Successive droplet impact on non-wetting surfaces (NWSs) remains poorly understood compared to single droplet impact. In this work, the impact outcomes, contact time, and impact forces of successive droplets impacting NWSs are investigated via direct numerical simulations. Four typical outcomes, including single bounce, double bounce, spindle-shaped, and arrow-shaped jets, were observed by varying the droplet impact spacing, Weber number (We), and Ohnesorge number. A positive correlation between the contact time and both the impact spacing and We was revealed. It was found that, unlike the single droplet impact process, the force evolution over time in the successive droplet impact process showed a trimodal peak characteristic. The generation mechanism of the two peak forces (F1* and F2*) among these is similar to that of single droplet impact, while the another peak force originates from the appearance of the trailing droplet. Interestingly, the variation of impact spacing does not change the F1* but intensifies or suppresses the F2*. Additionally, the energy analysis shows that the collision process is highly dissipative, and the viscous dissipation of the whole process can account for up to 80% of the total initial energy. Meanwhile, it is observed that the post-collision viscous dissipation increases with increasing impact spacing. These findings reveal the dynamic and mechanical characteristics of successive droplets impacting on NWSs and provide an important theoretical basis for a deeper understanding of multi-droplet interactions.

papers.title: Model and data-driven hydrodynamic identification and prediction for underwater gliders
papers.abstract: Accurate real-time estimation and prediction of hydrodynamic parameters are critical for precise control of underwater gliders (UGs) in ocean observation missions. However, the time-varying oceanic environment introduces significant uncertainties, making it difficult for existing measurement methods to capture the inherent nonlinearities and spatiotemporal dependencies in hydrodynamic data. This study presents a comprehensive hydrodynamic identification, preprocessing, and prediction framework driven by model and data-based approaches. Initially, the hydrodynamic data are identified by integrating the UG motion model with sea trial data using an internal penalty function. Next, the identified hydrodynamic data are decomposed with an optimized variational mode decomposition method, and the resulting intrinsic mode functions are clustered via hierarchical analysis to improve interpretability. Subsequently, a hybrid neural network combining convolutional neural network (CNN), bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM), and LSTM is developed to establish an offline-enhanced real-time hydrodynamic prediction model. Testing results show that the CNN-LSTM model enhanced with CNN-BiLSTM feature extraction significantly improves error control and noise robustness, achieving reductions of 26.25% in root mean square error and 27.74% in mean absolute error, compared to the baseline CNN-LSTM model. Finally, the trained enhanced CNN-LSTM model is applied to real-time hydrodynamic prediction during the sea trial, achieving a coefficient of determination of 0.9756 and 0.9839 for drag and lift data, respectively, while also demonstrating excellent performance across all other evaluation metrics. Briefly, this study contributes valuable insights into the processing and measurement of complex UG data in dynamic marine environments.

papers.title: Gated recurrent unit-informer with mixture of experts: A novel architecture for real-time drill string vibration monitoring via surface-downhole parameter fusion
papers.abstract: Real-time and precise monitoring of drill string vibration states is crucial for ensuring the safe and efficient drilling of complex oil and gas wells. However, limited by the high cost and poor timeliness of downhole measurement data acquisition, existing methods predominantly rely on single-source parameters, making it difficult to precisely monitor vibration modes. A novel architecture for real-time drill string vibration monitoring via surface-downhole parameter fusion was designed. First, a downhole three-axial acceleration prediction model was established based on the gated recurrent unit (GRU) to provide real-time downhole data for the model. Second, the variational modal decomposition (VMD) method is introduced to extract the multicomponent frequency domain features of downhole vibration signals. Third, a hybrid network architecture with the GRU and Informer models in parallel is designed to capture and fuse the multidimensional and multiscale features of the surface-downhole information. Finally, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture is introduced to synthesize the coupled correlations between vibrations to improve the computational efficiency and accuracy of the model. The results demonstrate that GRU-Informer with MoE outperforms current models, achieving an accuracy of 0.912 and a precision of 0.820. Compared to the models with separate inputs of surface mud logging and downhole vibration data, the model's accuracy was improved by 15.59% and 11.08%, respectively. Comparative studies validate the contributions of VMD, GRU-Informer structure, and MoE, emphasizing the critical role of the designed framework in improving the model adaptability and performance. This work provides significant theoretical support for mitigating drilling risks and enhancing operational efficiency.

papers.title: Aerodynamic shape effects on fluid–structure coupling vibration of train tail inside a small cross section tunnel
papers.abstract: Inside small cross section single-track tunnels, the ride comfort for drivers and passengers has been considerably impacted by the sustained lateral swaying in the tail car of the 160 km/h power-concentrated electric multiple unit (EMU). Nevertheless, previous studies have mostly focused on unilateral train aerodynamics or vehicle dynamics. Systematic investigations into the mechanisms governing fluid–structure coupling vibrations in trains inside tunnels remain insufficiently explored. Therefore, a fluid-structure coupling simulation platform for 9-car marshaling train aerodynamics and vehicle dynamics is constructed, and the accuracy and efficacy of the coupling method are validated through on-track tests. On this basis, aerodynamic loads and dynamic responses of the carbody while EMUs traverse tunnels are investigated. Furthermore, the effects of differing carbody lengths and head shapes on coupling characteristics are examined. The results indicate that the front and rear ends of the carbody are subjected to aerodynamic loads, which induce carbody lateral displacement and rotational motion. The coupling effect alters the amplitude and frequency of aerodynamic loads with aerodynamic load frequencies synchronized to carbody vibration frequencies. Harmonic vibration is obviously detected at both the front and rear ends of the carbody with the rear end exhibiting greater intensity. The aerodynamic shape of the tail car predominantly affects the intensity of aerodynamic loads. The vibration frequency of the carbody is primarily influenced by two factors: the train's running velocity and the interplay between the carbody's dynamic response and the surrounding flow field. This work can provide a reference for the aerodynamic shape optimization of trains traversing tunnels.

papers.title: Numerical treatment of electrical properties in two-phase electrohydrodynamic systems
papers.abstract: Generation and manipulation of micrometer-sized liquid jets is highly relevant for applications like sample delivery in serial femtosecond crystallography. A promising method combines gas flow focusing with electrospraying but remains underexplored due to numerical limitations regarding high interfacial electric property gradients. This study addresses this challenge by assessing different approaches for electrohydrodynamic (EHD) numerical treatment of two-phase interfaces within the finite volume method and the volume-of-fluid framework. A new geometric mean interpolation technique was developed to address the limitations of high electric conductivity-ratio gas–liquid systems. The technique was related to the established EHD modeling approaches, comprising two electric force implementations and two electric property interpolation methods. Three verification tests involving no flow conditions demonstrated consistent performance of all solvers regarding the electric equations, and they were charge-conservative. Validation on a free boundary problem experiment revealed varying levels of agreement. Results show that the Coulomb-polarization force implementation combined with weighted harmonic mean interpolation provides the most accurate and physically consistent modeling of electric forces at fluid interfaces, followed by the novel geometric mean technique. The model based on the Coulomb-polarization force is applied to simulate electro-flow-focused jets, capturing the complex interplay of hydrodynamic and electrostatic forces in a high-velocity co-flow configuration. While weighted harmonic mean interpolation yields the highest fidelity regarding the electric force magnitude and electric charge position, it fails for extremely low gas conductivities. The proposed geometric mean interpolation provides a stable alternative for simulating EHD two-phase flows, particularly in configurations with large interfacial electric property gradients.

papers.title: Formation mechanisms and morphological transitions of compound droplets in ferrofluid systems
papers.abstract: This study develops an axisymmetric multiphase flow model for non-conducting ferrofluids in cylindrical coordinates, based on Maxwell's equations and the phase field method. The governing equations are solved using a high-accuracy spectral element method. The model is validated through a series of benchmark simulations, including Laplace's law for stationary droplets, the deformation of non-magnetic droplets under uniform magnetic fields, and the coalescence of bubble pairs. Subsequent simulations investigate the effects of surface tension ratio, magnetic field strength, droplet size, and density ratio on the formation of compound droplets composed of magnetic and non-magnetic droplets in a non-magnetic fluid. Results indicate that the surface tension ratio is the primary determinant of droplet morphology, yielding three distinct morphologies under varying ratios: dumbbell-shaped structures, magnetic droplet encapsulating non-magnetic droplet, and the inverse encapsulation. For a surface tension ratio of 1:1:1, the contact time between droplets first decreases and then increases with increasing magnetic field strength. When the surface tension ratio is set to 3:1:1, reducing either the radius of the non-magnetic droplet radius or the density ratio slows the ascent velocity of the non-magnetic droplet, thus shortening contact time. When the two droplets have identical densities, decreasing the radius of the non-magnetic droplet slightly enhances encapsulation. Furthermore, simultaneous reduction of both the density ratio and non-magnetic droplet radius drives the compound droplet morphology to transition from semi-encapsulation to full encapsulation. The formation of fully encapsulated compound droplets primarily depends on surface tension ratios, with synergistic contributions from droplet sizes and density ratios.

papers.title: Shear-layer instabilities and vortex evolution in disk wakes at subcritical Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: This study investigates the shear-layer instabilities and vortex evolution at subcritical Reynolds number (Re=3000) using an advanced anisotropic hybrid Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes and Large-Eddy Simulation model, enhancing the theoretical framework of disk wake dynamics by systematically resolving the spatial and spectral signatures of three interrelated instability mechanisms. Quantitative analysis reveals a radial variation in vortex shedding intensity (StV=0.146–0.148), with the most prominent spectral peaks consistently observed at an intermediate radial location (y/D=0.31). This radial asymmetry highlights the spatially inhomogeneous response of the near wake to shear-layer excitation. Subsequently, detailed spectral analysis confirms and extends previous observations of ultra-low-frequency oscillations (StL=0.01–0.07), demonstrating their established but complex relationship with recirculation bubble dynamics, adverse pressure gradient modulation, and synchronized force fluctuations. Finally, combined vorticity–spectral analysis provides the first quantitative determination of Kelvin–Helmholtz instability extent (Ls≈0.7D) while revealing higher-order harmonics (up to StKH4=5–6.5), offering new evidence of nonlinear energy transfer in separating shear layers. These findings advance the theoretical framework for subcritical wake transitions by establishing quantitative relationships between multi-scale instabilities and their governing physical mechanisms, providing insights for practical wake control and industrial design strategies.

papers.title: Multi-grid graph neural networks with self-attention for computational mechanics
papers.abstract: Combining computational mechanics with machine learning has recently attracted a lot of attention, especially in computational mechanics, where researchers aim to improve the accuracy and computational cost of the simulations. While convolutional neural networks have been used to turn mesh data into images, newer methods now use graph neural networks to work directly with mesh structures. In this work, we introduce a new multigrid graph neural network framework, designed for time-dependent three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics simulations. The proposed method uses self-attention within the message-passing steps to better understand the solution behavior across both space and time. It also uses attention scores to dynamically prune and refine meshes, making it possible to handle large-scale simulations efficiently without losing accuracy. Inspired by Bidirectional Encoder (BERT), we also add a self-supervised training method tailored for graphs, which helps the model generalize better. Tests on benchmark datasets show that the method performs better than current state-of-the-art approaches, even on larger and more complex meshes. Codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/DonsetPG/graph-physics.

papers.title: Microorganisms swimming in Giesekus viscoelastic fluids at finite Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: Using the immersed boundary method, we numerically investigate the locomotion of microorganisms in Giesekus fluids at finite Reynolds numbers, focusing on swimmers with asymmetric strokes and varying stiffness. The kicker stroke, based on the Caenorhabditis elegans, has larger undulations at the tail, while the burrower stroke has larger undulations at the head. Our results show that soft swimmers can swim faster in viscoelastic fluids than in Newtonian fluids at small Reynolds numbers. At finite Reynolds numbers, however, both stiff and soft swimmers experience lower speeds in viscoelastic fluids, with fluid inertia further reducing their speed and efficiency. We find that it is associated with hydrodynamic forces: the pressure force propels the swimmer, while the viscous and polymer forces resist motion. At small Reynolds numbers, increased pressure in viscoelastic fluids enhances speed, but at finite Reynolds numbers, pressure decreases with increasing Weissenberg number, causing deceleration. Additionally, it is observed that fluid shear-thinning properties have minimal impact on the swimming behavior of both kicker and burrower in this complex environment.

papers.title: Shock wave attenuation characteristics in the Tesla valve
papers.abstract: A Tesla valve is a passive unidirectional flow conduit designed with specialized geometric. For reverse flow, the interaction between the channel and fluid results in energy dissipation and pressure reduction. As a kind of fluid characterized by high Reynolds numbers, a shock wave can also be attenuated by Tesla valves. If this attenuation can be controlled, it will offer a new approach to solving the challenge of measuring high-pressure shock wave parameters in near-field explosions. We use numerical methods to investigate the attenuation characteristics of shock waves within the Tesla valve, clarifying the influence of different Tesla valve geometric and load parameters on the attenuation effect. The results show that a Tesla valve with two basic units produces two pressure peaks at its inlet and four peaks at the outlet. We also found that reducing the inner diameter d and increasing the incident load intensity both improve the attenuation rate and the diodicity. However, increasing the diversion angle α results in a higher pressure attenuation rate but lower diodicity. In addition, increasing α also prolongs the time interval between the overpressure and the flow velocity reaching the maximum value, respectively, thus realizing the effect of decoupling the overpressure and the dynamic pressure in time. This paper identifies the relationship between the geometric parameters of the Tesla valve and the shock wave pressure attenuation rate and diodicity. These findings provide valuable references for the optimized design and performance prediction of Tesla valves in controlling the attenuation of shock waves.

papers.title: Aerodynamic repellency of impacting water drops on inclined superhydrophobic surfaces
papers.abstract: Understanding the dynamics of drop impact on surfaces is of great interest due to its prevalence in nature and practical applications. Previous studies have observed that when a drop impacts an inclined superhydrophobic surface, it exhibits asymmetric bouncing with elongation along the surface, and the maximum spreading diameter and contact time depend on both the drop impact velocity and the tilt angle of the surface. However, the underlying mechanisms behind these scenarios have yet to be fully understood. Inspired by the work of Zhan et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett., 126, 234503 (2021)], which revealed the critical role of an air layer in drop impingement on moving superhydrophobic surfaces, we extend this investigation to drop impingement on inclined superhydrophobic surfaces, revealing this to be a more general phenomenon. Our experiments provide clear evidence demonstrating that a thin air film becomes trapped between the drop and the substrate during impact. This is supported by interference patterns observed between the impinging drop and the substrate, with the air layer serving as a lubricant for the sliding drop. By analyzing the morphological evolution of the drop and conducting a simple scaling analysis, we reveal that this air film between the drop and the surface generates a viscous force that competes with capillary and inertial forces. This interplay results in the asymmetric elongation of the drop and an unexpected reduction in contact time. Furthermore, we discuss the displacement of the drop as it slides along the inclined surface during impingement, emphasizing the dominant role of the inertial force. Our findings provide novel insights into the interaction between drops and superhydrophobic surfaces.

papers.title: Motion of three geostrophic vortices on a sphere
papers.abstract: Accurately approximating and applying geophysical phenomena requires considering geostrophic vortices on spherical or sphere-like curved surfaces. Accordingly, this study explores the dynamics of geostrophic fluid vortices on the surface of a sphere. The geostrophic vortex model incorporates the effects of stratification and planetary rotation and is relevant to large-scale atmospheric phenomena. The governing equations of the model are expressed in terms of the Legendre functions and systematically formulated along with the corresponding Hamiltonian. We focus on the three-vortex case and investigate its dynamics, identifying the fixed and relative equilibria of the vortices. The general dynamics is analyzed using the phase diagram based on trilinear coordinates. Notably, we demonstrate the occurrence of the non-self-similar collapse of the three geostrophic vortices. This result significantly differs from that of the point vortex on a sphere, where the collapse is always self-similar. Numerical computations for the trajectories of vortices with various initial configurations reveal regular and irregular patterns of vortex motion depending on the strength and initial location of the vortices. Remarkably, we find a recurring motion of vortices converging toward and diverging from a relative equilibrium.

papers.title: The influence of gravity on heat transfer and flow structure in centrifugal convection under low rotation
papers.abstract: We investigated the influence of gravity on heat transfer and flow structure in centrifugal convection under low rotation. The study focused on the role of the Froude number (Fr) under conditions of either constant axial Rayleigh number (Rag) or constant total Rayleigh number (Rat). Our findings indicate that, at constant Rag, the Nusselt number (Nu) initially decreases with increasing Fr, reaching a peak around Fr≈0.2. In contrast, under constant Rat, Nu exhibits a slight initial decrease followed by a gradual increase with increasing Fr. For Fr≤0.2, buoyancy due to gravity dominates thermal driving, resulting in an inclined temperature boundary layer. As Fr increases beyond 0.2, the centrifugal force becomes dominant, enhancing heat transfer and promoting a more uniform temperature boundary layer. At Fr≥5, the system exhibits characteristics similar to classical Rayleigh–Bénard convection, primarily influenced by strong centrifugal effects and weak axial flows. These insights enhance our understanding of heat transfer mechanisms influenced by combined gravity and rotation, offering potential optimizations for industrial heat transfer system designs and performance.

papers.title: Self-healing movable gel for enhanced heavy oil recovery in harsh fractured reservoirs
papers.abstract: Fractured heavy oil reservoirs are characterized by deep burial depth and complex fracture networks, leading to significant heat loss during thermal recovery processes. However, the existing cold production oil-flooding agent has insufficient performance and low viscosity retention rate in high-temperature and high-salinity environments. Based on the strong hydrogen bonding of hydroxylamine organic compounds, a N-methylglucamine functionalized movable oil-flooding gel (N-MG@MFG) is synthesized via a one-pot method for improving fluidity, temperature tolerance, and salt resistance in heavy oil reservoir. N-MG@MFG with various viscosity (ranged from 221 to 854 mPa s) was successfully prepared by using ternary copolymers P(AM/ACMO/AMPS) as gel skeleton, phenolic resin as a cross-linking system and N-methylglucamine as a functional modifier. This novel gel exhibits unprecedented stability, retaining a high viscosity exceeding 200 mPa·s at 150 °C and 22 × 104mg/l salinity, outperforming current agents by a significant margin. By fitting the Arrhenius equation, it is revealed that N-MG@MFG can retain its original molecular structure under extreme conditions. Notably, its resistance to dilution and shear force is groundbreaking: the viscosity retention rate remains above 69.8% after 85% dilution and surpasses 86.3% post three shear cycles, showcasing remarkable self-healing capabilities. Cryo-scanning electron microscopy, proton nuclear magnetic resonance, and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveal a unique mechanism where N-methylglucamine, via hydrogen bonding, modulates polymer cross-linking density to endow fluidity, a feature absent in traditional gels. In oil flooding experiments, N-MG@MFG achieves a remarkable 75% oil recovery rate in pure gel flooding and 71% in slug flooding of fractured cores, representing a significant leap in efficiency. This study not only fills the gap in developing high-performance oil flooding agents for extreme reservoir conditions but also offers an innovative molecular design concept, opening up new avenues for heavy oil reservoir exploitation.

papers.title: Study on dynamics of droplet impacting on the zirconium alloy tube surface and the modeling of maximum spreading factor
papers.abstract: To reduce scratches caused during the assembly of fuel assemblies, an ice film can be prepared on the zirconium alloy tube surface before assembly to reduce or even prevent scratches. The quality of the ice film is directly affected by the maximum spreading factor. For this purpose, it is crucial to describe the relationship between droplet parameters and the maximum factor. In this study, first, the high-speed camera technology was used to investigate the droplet impact dynamic behavior on zirconium alloy tubes and the effect of droplet parameters on the spreading process. Then, the theoretical model of the maximum spreading factor is established based on energy conservation and combined with rotational momentum and cylindrical anisotropy, and the polynomial regression and intelligent algorithms were used for comparison. The results show that the deviation is within ±10%. Still, the evaluation indicators of the model established in this study are superior to the other models. The results show that the theoretical model can accurately reflect the non-linear relationship between the droplet parameters and the maximum spreading factor. This study provides data support and a theoretical basis for subsequent control of the liquid film shape and the preparation of high-quality ice films.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of downburst-induced wind loads on rectangular high-rise buildings: Influence of geometric features
papers.abstract: Downbursts are intense, short-duration wind events commonly associated with thunderstorms and are known to generate highly localized, near-ground wind loads that can significantly affect the structural safety of high-rise buildings. Despite their destructive potential, the aerodynamic effects of downbursts have not been fully incorporated into conventional design practices. This study investigates the surface pressure distribution and aerodynamic force characteristics of high-rise buildings subjected to steady-state downburst wind fields, with a specific focus on the influence of geometric parameters—namely, height-to-width (H/B) and depth-to-width (D/B) ratios. Experiments were conducted using an impinging jet wind tunnel system capable of reproducing localized, near-ground peak wind features typical of thunderstorm downbursts. Eight rigid building models with systematic variations in H/B and D/B were tested across multiple radial locations. Surface pressure data were used to compute both local and overall aerodynamic force coefficients. The results show that the peak horizontal wind speed occurs at a radial distance of r/Djet = 1.0. The turbulence intensity exhibits an inverse relationship with the mean wind speed and follows a vertical trend of first decreasing and then increasing with height. Increasing H/B significantly reduces mean and fluctuating drag forces and results in smoother lateral load distributions, while D/B modulates suction intensity on roof and rear façades. The findings enhance the understanding of shape-dependent aerodynamic behavior in downburst conditions and provide practical insights for wind-resistant design of high-rise buildings in thunderstorm-prone regions.

papers.title: Thermal and bioconvective transport in Casson-based trimetallic nanofluid flow over a moving surface with gyrotactic microorganisms and thermophysical effects
papers.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of steady, two-dimensional Casson fluid flow embedded with trimetallic nanoparticles copper (Cu), nickel (Ni), and zinc (Zn) suspended in engine oil over a stretching surface. The model incorporates the combined influences of thermal radiation, Joule heating, viscous dissipation, chemical reaction, and bioconvection due to gyrotactic microorganisms. Employing similarity transformations, the governing partial differential equations are reduced to a system of ordinary differential equations and solved numerically using a robust fourth-fifth order Runge–Kutta–Fehlberg method with a shooting technique. This study investigates the effects of key non-dimensional parameters, including the Casson parameter, magnetic field strength, porous medium permeability, mixed convection, buoyancy ratio, and Rayleigh number, on the velocity, temperature, solutal, and motile micro-organism distributions. Results show that increasing the Casson parameter and magnetic field intensity suppresses the velocity, while thermal and concentration profiles are significantly enhanced by thermal radiation and Eckert number. The influence of Schmidt numbers and bioconvection parameters on Sherwood and motile density numbers is also evaluated. The present results are found to be in good agreement with existing literature, confirming the validity of the proposed model. The outcomes of this work provide valuable insight into optimizing thermal and mass transport in nano-biofluid systems with implications in industrial coating, biomedical transport, and thermal energy harvesting applications.

papers.title: Nonlinear decay in turbine endwall film cooling induced by mainstream oscillation: High-frequency excitation effects on suction-side flow separation and suppression strategies
papers.abstract: Thermal protection of gas turbine components under dynamic flow conditions is critically challenged by two intertwined mechanisms that govern film cooling performance degradation: intensified turbulence mixing at the mainstream–coolant interface and diminished coolant retention near the wall due to momentum redistribution. Large-eddy simulations were implemented to systematically elucidate the interdependent mechanism between mainstream oscillation and end wall crossflow in film cooling. It was revealed that high-frequency mainstream oscillations (>130 Hz) amplify turbulent kinetic energy at the interface by 4.5 times compared to low-frequency conditions, significantly disrupting coolant film stability. This enhanced mixing is attributed to the breakdown of coherent vortex structures.
