The effects of these parameters on four different flow zones as well as on the threshold (supercritical and subcritical) amplitudes ςa and nonlinear phase speed Ncr are explored in detail. The explosive unstable flow zone of this flow problem increases or decreases accordingly as the increase in E or M and φ, irrespective of the values of Re, We, and θ, which confirm the destabilizing role of E and the stabilizing influence of M and φ on this flow dynamics as well. The analysis reveals the necessary conditions for the nonexistence of unconditional stable zone (kj≤kc) as well as the existence of four different flow zones (kj > kc) and the second explosive unstable zone (kj < kc) of this flow problem which are essentially the relations between the cut-off wavenumbers kc (for which ωi+ is zero) and kj (for which J2 is zero) depending upon the values of E, M, Re, We, θ, and φ.

papers.title: A physics- and data-based method for sloshing active control
papers.abstract: This study presents an experimentally validated physics- and data-based approach to optimize piston-type actuator amplitudes in shipboard pools for active control of sloshing-induced wave elevations under resonance conditions. The piston actuators, installed at both ends of a pool, are driven periodically to counteract waves generated by the pool's motion. Building upon our previously validated linear numerical method that accurately predicts non-resonant wave dynamics using actuators, we established an efficient framework to determine optimal actuator thresholds. Experimental investigations in two scaled pool configurations at the sloshing laboratory of the University of Duisburg-Essen confirmed the numerical method's effectiveness in identifying critical actuator amplitudes for resonance mitigation, despite inherent limitations in modeling nonlinear wave phenomena. To address nonlinear characteristics in resonant regimes, we implemented a data-driven Kolmogorov-Arnold Network trained on experimental wave profile data. This hybrid method demonstrated exceptional computational efficiency, enabling rapid optimization of wave mitigation systems using piston-type actuators. Experimental results validated both the reliability and the practical feasibility of the proposed hybrid method to optimize piston-type actuator motions for resonance control in confined waters. This work established a baseline method for active sloshing control system design, combining computational efficiency with experimental verification. The proposed approach bridged linear system analysis with nonlinear dynamic responses through synergistic physics-data integration, suggesting pathways for enhanced nonlinear coupling analyses in future research developments.

papers.title: Exploring the effect of different exercise intensities on hemodynamics of abdominal aortic aneurysm based on multiscale computational fluid dynamics simulations
papers.abstract: Exercise has been shown to provide cardiovascular benefits for patients with abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA). However, the relationship between AAA hemodynamics and exercise intensities is unclear. The present study aims to use multiscale computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to investigate how different intensities affect the AAA hemodynamics, hoping to help patients' daily exercise management. A patient-specific AAA model was established based on magnetic resonance angiography. The hemodynamic environment under resting and five intensity exercise states was obtained using multiscale CFD simulations. The required heart rate, cardiac output, and blood pressure were calculated from the metabolic equivalent (MET). The results show that: (1) The shape of the AAA flow waveform during exercise is different from that at rest. (2) The reverse velocity vectors are always concentrated on one side of the AAA. Exercise increases the flow velocity, but the systolic flow patterns become chaotic during moderate- and high-intensity exercises. (3) As the intensity increases, the proportions of time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) <0.4 Pa area are 34.58, 6.81, 2.68, 0.53, 0.25, and 0.07%, and those of TAWSS >4 Pa are 0, 0.21, 2.40, 9.53, 14.84, and 31.56%. Compared with the resting state, the proportions of oscillatory shear index >0.3 area decrease 1.50, 2.23, 2.29, 2.33, and 3.65 times. For this patient, the recommended exercise plan maintains 1.75–2.5 METs with a heart rate of 75–83 bpm. Multiscale CFD simulations can effectively display the hemodynamic environment within AAA during exercise. It has the potential to provide concrete insights into vague exercise intensity, benefiting specific AAA patients.

papers.title: Predicting the width of the recirculation zone at an ice-covered confluence
papers.abstract: In a confluence channel, the recirculation zone, due to its relatively low flow velocity, might be a primary site for pollutant accumulation, sediment deposition, and aquatic organism activity. While the maximum width of the recirculation zone in a confluence can be estimated, models to predict the width of the recirculation zone in an ice-covered confluence are lacking. A one-dimensional semi-analytical model was developed based on the momentum equation, incorporating a ratio function to represent longitudinal acceleration induced by hydrostatic pressure gradients and shear stresses. An empirical expression for this ratio function was obtained via polynomial fitting. Finally, the model was validated using three-dimensional numerical results and laboratory-scale confluence experimental data, demonstrating its ability to accurately quantify variations in the depth-averaged width of the recirculation zone.

papers.title: Characterization of shock–turbulent structures within shock/cloud interaction in astrophysical galactic outflows
papers.abstract: In this article, the numerical simulation of three-dimensional hydrodynamic (HD) shock/cloud interaction in galactic outflows has been carried out by solving compressible HD equations [Banda-Barragán et al., “Shock–multicloud interactions in galactic outflows—I. Cloud layers with lognormal density distributions,” Mon. Not. R. Astron. Soc. 499, 2173–2195 (2020)] in the computer code PLUTO [Mignone et al., “PLUTO: A numerical code for computational astrophysics,” Astrophys. J., Suppl. Ser. 170, 228 (2007)], using higher-order finite volume method. The detailed flow features involved in complex shock/cloud interaction have been discussed thoroughly in this present study. Furthermore, the invariants (P, Q, and R) of the velocity gradient tensor (∂ui∂xj) reveal the local flow topology [Chong et al., “A general classification of three-dimensional flow fields,” Phys. Fluids A 2, 765–777 (1990); Suman and Girimaji, “Velocity gradient invariants and local flow-field topology in compressible turbulence,” J. Turbul. 11, N2 (2010); Thaker et al., “Invariants of the velocity gradient tensor in a spatially developing compressible round jet,” J. Fluid Mech. 971, A18 (2023)] due to shock/turbulence interaction. The joint probability density function of Q–R obtained from numerical data depicts the presence of turbulent sheet-like unstable-focus-compressing (UFC) and turbulent tube-like stable-focus-compressing (SFC)-like structures during the shock/cloud interaction for both compressive and solenoidal clouds, respectively. Furthermore, the distinct behaviors of the identified turbulent structures (both UFC and SFC) have been examined in great detail, offering valuable insights into the mechanisms that govern star formation following shock/cloud interactions.

papers.title: Fractal modeling and numerical simulation of ablative surfaces under non-uniform diffusion in carbon fiber materials
papers.abstract: During atmospheric reentry, spacecrafts are subjected to intense aerodynamic heating, necessitating ablative thermal protection systems (TPS) as a primary safeguard. Although severe ablation typically occurs in continuum or near-continuum flow regimes, many advanced TPS materials under development feature carbon fiber-based porous microstructures. In such cases, gas diffusion can still be dominated by Knudsen diffusion, where the diffusion coefficient depends strongly on the pore diameter. Traditional models often neglect the non-uniformity of pore distribution within fiber preforms, leading to errors in ablation rate prediction. In this study, fractal theory is employed to characterize the mesoscale pore structure of random carbon fiber materials, and a fractal-based diffusion model is developed that accounts for the non-uniform distribution of pores. Analysis reveals that the pore distribution plays a critical role in accurate diffusion modeling. Assuming uniform pore distribution can severely overestimate the diffusion coefficient—by up to 1.8 times compared to the fractal model. Furthermore, the Weierstrass–Mandelbrot function is employed to reconstruct the rough ablation surface induced by non-uniform diffusion in a fractal manner, and an analytical expression for the surface area is derived. Based on the reconstructed surface, the ablation process of a reentry spacecraft with a rough wall is simulated using the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method. This approach provides an efficient means of incorporating mesoscale roughness into DSMC simulations, avoiding the excessive computational cost associated with mesh refinement down to the roughness scale.

papers.title: An open channel with one-sided rectangular vegetation patches: Regulatory effects and turbulence structure analysis
papers.abstract: The arrangement of vegetation patches in rivers creates critical habitats, but the hydrodynamics of alternating patch-cavity systems are not fully understood. This study investigates the flow structure and turbulence in an open channel with one-sided rectangular vegetation patches of two densities (solid volume fraction ϕ = 0.10 and 0.05). Three-dimensional velocity data were collected using an acoustic Doppler velocimeter. We found that the downstream flow adjustment distance (Xeq) was negatively correlated with vegetation density ϕ. In the developed equilibrium region, the flow field consists of a low-velocity cavity and a high-velocity mainstream, separated by a turbulent mixing layer. Flow visualization revealed two distinct exchange mechanisms: weak internal circulation driven by shear-layer eddies in the dense case and suppressed eddy penetration due to strong “bleed flow” through the patch in the sparse case. At the cavity-mainstream interface, quadrant analysis showed that momentum exchange was dominated by ejection (Q2) and sweep (Q4) events with sweeps being the most intense contributors to Reynolds stress. These findings provide a quantitative basis for designing patch-cavity systems to create specific ecological functions, such as refugia or dispersal corridors, in river restoration projects.

papers.title: Steady flow of Jeffery–Hamel Casson hybrid nanofluid for thermal enhancement with impacts of Soret–Dufour
papers.abstract: Improving thermal performance in modern heat exchanger systems is crucial for meeting the growing demands of energy efficiency and advanced thermal control. In this context, the present study delves into the thermophysical behavior of a steady, two-dimensional flow of Casson-based hybrid nanofluid comprising copper and graphene oxide nanoparticles within a converging/diverging channel. The model accounts for multiple interrelated physical phenomena, including the effects of viscous dissipation, internal heat generation, linear thermal radiation, Soret and Dufour mechanisms, and a magnetically influenced Darcy–Forchheimer porous medium. The core objective is to systematically analyze how these parameters influence heat and mass transfer characteristics in a confined, non-Newtonian flow domain. Through similarity transformations, the governing nonlinear partial differential equations are simplified into ordinary differential form, and the resulting boundary value problem is addressed using the Optimal Homotopy Analysis Method, known for its adaptability and precision in handling strongly nonlinear systems. Numerical interpretations reveal that an increase in approximately 4.36% in the heat transfer rate is observed within the converging channel as the radiation parameter rises highlighting the positive influence of thermal radiation on enhancing heat transfer.

papers.title: Wall boundary conditions for lattice Boltzmann simulations of turbulent flows with wall functions
papers.abstract: This paper investigates wall boundary condition schemes for the simulation of turbulent flows using the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) coupled to turbulence models with wall functions. The analysis focuses on two schemes: a regularized boundary scheme with third-order reconstruction of the velocity gradients using wall function data and a slip-velocity bounce-back scheme. The LBM solver is coupled to the Spalart–Allmaras turbulence model and uses a model consistent wall function. The performance of the wall boundary schemes is assessed in two canonical turbulent flow cases, a fully developed channel flow and a zero-pressure-gradient flat plate boundary layer, selected specifically to isolate and analyze the impact of wall boundary treatments on turbulence modeling. The analysis shows that, for the selected test cases, the slip-velocity bounce-back approach, which has received relatively little attention within the context of LBM coupled to Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes turbulence models with wall functions, behaves fairly consistently in terms of both accuracy and mesh convergence. The regularized-based approach, on the other hand, appears to be highly sensitive to the reconstruction of the wall-normal velocity gradient, even in simple geometries, such as flat walls, where no interpolation is required. This dependency of the regularized boundary schemes on near-wall gradients, which had been noted before in the literature, requires the use of ad hoc gradient reconstruction techniques, requirements that are not present in the slip-velocity bounce-back method. A hybrid regularized boundary scheme that blends two different gradient reconstruction techniques but requires calibration is introduced as a tool to investigate this effect.

papers.title: A general ablation model for composites based on a coupled direct simulation Monte Carlo and mass-consistent marching cubes approach
papers.abstract: A general ablation model based on a coupled direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) and mass-consistent marching cubes (MCMC) approach is presented. MCMC is a novel surface reconstruction algorithm that ensures consistency between the simulated surface recession rate and mass flux. The DSMC-MCMC ablation framework has also been expanded for composites by allowing for unique per-grid-point mass densities and per-cell surface reaction sets. A carbon–carbon composite composed of a square array of cylinders embedded in a matrix is ablated. For a sufficiently high reaction probability on the fiber surface, a counter-intuitive behavior is observed where high pore velocities coincide with reduced permeability and slower ablation. The DSMC-MCMC method is also applied to a more realistic thermal protection system sample which is generated from a tomographic scan.

papers.title: Advancing the Cercignani–Lampis–Lord model and its application in direct simulation Monte Carlo calculations
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting the aerodynamics of hypersonic vehicles in rarefied gas regime requires a gas–surface interaction (GSI) model with high fidelity. The Cercignani–Lampis–Lord (CLL) model was regarded as one of the most accurate GSI models and commonly employed in rarefied gas flow studies. However, systematic molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the normal scattering kernel of the CLL model fails under certain hypersonic conditions, since the normal energy accommodation coefficient exceeds the permissible range of [0, 1]. This issue frequently arises when the incident gas molecules have substantial energy difference along the tangential and normal directions. To overcome this limitation, a modified CLL model (mCLL) is proposed in this work by introducing two independent coefficients σn and γn in the normal scattering kernel. This modification extends the applicable range and enhances the accuracy of the GSI model. Validation against the wind tunnel experimental data in slip regime confirms that the mCLL model possesses better accuracy in predicting both the wall pressure and heat flux distributions. Moreover, in direct simulation Monte Carlo calculations of highly rarefied gas flow, the mCLL model exhibits pronounced discrepancies in aerodynamic force and heat compared to the Maxwell and CLL models. Consequently, the mCLL model provides an advanced boundary condition, which is particularly important for hypersonic rarefied gas flow study.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical evaluation of chambered porous barriers in the presence of seawall
papers.abstract: The gravity wave scattering phenomena attributed to porous breakwaters are analyzed using experimental and numerical investigations. Three different configurations, such as traditional Jarlan-type, single-chambered, and dual-chambered porous breakwaters (modified Jarlan-type), are explored for their energy damping across the range of design parameters. The experimental findings are utilized to validate the numerical model developed using the dual boundary element method within the framework of linear wave theory. Linear and quadratic pressure drop boundary conditions are employed to capture the energy loss due to viscous and inertial effects. Notably, the dual-chambered porous breakwater excels in performance over the presented alternatives, which is plausibly predicted by the quadratic pressure drop boundary condition. Furthermore, the present study leverages the benefits of a partially extended vertical inner barrier to develop the dual-chambered breakwater system, and it shows the minimum reflection (KR) of 0.133 as the porosity is confined to 0.2. The energy dissipation (KD) for the relative horizontal plate submergence (S/h) of 0.375 remains high across most wavelengths, with a peak of 0.98. The dual-chambered breakwater having 0.2 porosity shows a 55% enhanced reduction in wave reflection compared to the 0.4 porosity and a 51% better reduction in wave reflection compared to the conventional Jarlan-type breakwater of 0.2 porosity. Overall, the analysis concludes that the dual-chambered porous breakwater could be a highly effective coastal protection structure, due to its substantial attenuation of incident wave impact.

papers.title: Modeling and analysis of two-phase flow maldistribution in the dead-ended anode channels for proton exchange membrane fuel cells with parallel flow fields
papers.abstract: In the dead-end anode (DEA) mode, parallel flow fields are more prone to flooding, which can significantly impair the performance of proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC). To further explore the flooding phenomena in parallel flow fields operating in the DEA mode, the water dynamics within parallel flow fields is investigated using volume of fluid method in this study. Specifically, the effects of constant vs variable manifold widths on the gas–liquid two-phase flow are investigated, focusing on key performance indicators including water removal efficiency, gas distribution uniformity, and water coverage in the flow field. The results indicate that increasing the constant manifold width effectively reduces flooding frequency and significantly affects water dynamics. For the flow fields with a constant 7.5 mm manifold width, the water removal rate is 0.8336, the gas uniformity index is 0.7323, and the average water coverage rates at the bottom, sides, and top of the flow field are 0.034, 0.123, and 0.109, respectively. Compared to the flow fields with a constant 7.5 mm manifold width, the flow field with 1.6–7.5 mm variable manifold width has the same water removal and coverage and slightly lower gas distribution uniformity. However, the variable manifold width flow field accelerates the drainage of water from the outlet manifold, improving water removal efficiency by 18.2%. Furthermore, excessively small blind ends can cause flooding in the outlet manifold in the flow field with variable manifold width. This study provides valuable insights into the efficiency and performance improvement of PEMFCs operating in DEA mode.

papers.title: Impact of mining-induced fault filling activation on lagging water inrush based on porosity evolution
papers.abstract: Coal mine water inrush exhibits high complexity and diversity, with fault-induced water inrush and its seepage-related parameters playing a critical role in evolutionary studies. This study investigates the hysteresis characteristics of fault-induced water inrush using numerical simulation, differing from conventional methods by first simulating stress-damage field evolution to derive porosity variations. These porosity values are then fed back into multi-field coupling simulations (e.g., seepage field analysis). Key findings reveal that porosity evolution significantly influences the time-lag effect of fault-induced water inrush. When incorporated, it induces plastic damage at each stage, altering seepage-related physical properties. Specifically, porosity feedback drives fault-filling body collapse, accumulation, and compaction under coupled seepage-damage conditions. By optimizing damage weakening and water-induced weakening parameters, the model self-interprets hysteresis mechanisms, as evidenced by porosity evolution feedback. The refined simulations better match real-world conditions, improving practical applicability and scientific rigor.

papers.title: Vortex convection velocity determination methods and application in the flow near airfoil trailing edge
papers.abstract: The convection velocity is an important parameter for characterizing traveling vortices in turbulent flow, and its calculation methods are evolving with the measurement technologies. Using high-frequency particle image velocimetry and the synchronized far field sound pressure measurements, different methods are explored to calculate the convection velocity, i.e., the velocity decomposition, the velocity cross correlation, the vortex time trajectory, the frequency-wave number contour, as well as the time delay between velocity and noise signal methods. The methods have been applied on a test case of airfoil trailing edge with vortex shedding, which includes laminar separation bubble, acoustic feedback loop, and tonal noise generation phenomena. A relative standard deviation of 2.71% of the convection velocities has been noticed from the five methods under the same flow condition. The cross correlation methods show the advantage of convection velocity determination along the chordwise direction. The frequency-wave number method seems the most robust method for its global calculation in terms of spatial and time domain. At the end, all the methods have been applied to investigate the trend of convection velocity vs free stream velocity and angle of attack. The convection velocity increases as the angle of attack decreases and flow speed increases, which is ascribed to the separation bubble moving upstream.

papers.title: Sensitivity analysis of rock dynamic response based on a multi-scale parameter model
papers.abstract: The micro-stiffness ratio plays a significant role in the dynamic response characteristics of rock materials when analyzed using particle flow code. In this study, a macro–micro parameter model is developed to relate the micro-stiffness ratio to the macro-Poisson's ratio, revealing the relationships between multi-scale parameters. Large-scale split Hopkinson pressure bar numerical simulations are conducted to investigate the sensitivity of the dynamic mechanical characteristics of limestone to variations in the micro-stiffness ratio. The results indicate that, under impact loading, the force chain gradually concentrates toward the center of the specimen, forming a symmetrical saddle-shaped boundary. As the micro-stiffness ratio increases, both the normal peak stress and elastic modulus decrease, while the normal strain rate and strain acceleration increase. Axial and radial stresses exhibit similar sensitivity to the micro-stiffness ratio. The proportion of axial dissipated energy increases with the micro-stiffness ratio, whereas the proportion of radial dissipated energy decreases. The initiation time of damage evolution is significantly correlated with the micro-stiffness ratio: higher ratios lead to earlier initiation of damage evolution but slower damage accumulation. Consequently, the failure mode transitions from sudden brittle failure to slow and gradual failure.

papers.title: Stratified to annular flow transition due to drop entrainment in a flat minichannel
papers.abstract: This study deals with the experimental and numerical investigation of the transition from stratified to annular flow in a flat minichannel over a wide range of gas and liquid velocities, including turbulent conditions. It was established that the transition to annular flow at high phase flow rates occurred not only due to sidewall wetting, as reported in the literature, but also as a result of drop entrainment. Moreover, when the contact between the liquid and the side walls of the channel was eliminated, the transition to annular flow at high liquid and gas flow rates occurred solely due to drop entrainment. To study the droplet entrainment mechanisms in a minichannel, numerical simulations were performed in both two- and three-dimensional problems using volume of fluid and coupled volume of fluid with level-set methods. It was found that the mechanism of the disturbance wave formation in the minichannel does not differ from that in large-scale channels and is associated with the merging of initial waves near the liquid inlet. However, compared to large-scale channels, in a minichannel, the wave frequencies increase significantly, while the longitudinal wave size decreases (by about an order of magnitude). The primary cause of drop entrainment was pulsations, in particular vortices, in the gas phase which induced oscillations in the vertical pressure gradient above the disturbance waves. These oscillations could lead to vertical wave growth, eventually resulting in liquid ligament formation and its subsequent breakup. An additional factor increasing the likelihood of instability with drop entrainment was wave coalescence.

papers.title: Transient fluid flow simulation and optimization of cleanup in offshore low-permeability wells: Integration of core flooding and nuclear magnetic resonance characterization
papers.abstract: Drilling fluid invasion into low-permeability gas reservoir pores results in a water block effect. The cleanup operation is essential at the start of gas well production, as it helps displace near-wellbore invaded fluids via gas flowback to restore reservoir productivity. However, a few studies have attempted to optimize the cleanup operations, and post-cleanup gas production rates often decline below expectations due to a lack of understanding of transient fluid flow mechanisms. The purpose of this paper is to clarify the physics of drilling fluid flow in near-wellbore porous media and provide effective designs for cleanup operations. To optimize the cleanup design, we first clarified the critical conditions for fluid mobilization across pore scales. By combining core flooding experiments with nuclear magnetic resonance analysis, this study revealed a hierarchical pore-size displacement mechanism: larger pores (>1 μm) are activated first, followed by intermediate pores (0.1–1 μm), while smaller pores (<0.1 μm) remain immobile. This pore-size-dependent mobilization results in a pressure gradient-dependent flow characteristic of invaded fluids in porous media. Accordingly, a transient gas flow model incorporating dynamic permeability was developed to describe the transient displacement behavior. Numerical simulations demonstrate that once the flowback gas rate exceeds a critical threshold (corresponding to the minimum pressure gradient for 0.1 μm pore activation) and cleanup time is also sufficient, all invaded fluids can be thoroughly cleared. This study provides a quantitative framework to optimize cleanup operations, particularly in offshore low-permeability gas reservoirs. The findings enable operators to balance flowback rates and duration, reducing near-wellbore damage and restoring formation productivity.

papers.title: In-depth analysis of flow field aerodynamic mechanism in integrated combustor–turbine structure for heavy-duty gas turbine
papers.abstract: In future heavy-duty gas turbines, to achieve higher output power and efficiency, cutting aerodynamic losses and cooling air use is key. This paper puts forward a novel integrated combustor-turbine module (ICTM) for heavy-duty gas turbines, using an innovative integrated design approach to boost aerodynamic efficiency. The ICTM consolidates the combustor liner, transition duct, and first-stage nozzle guide vanes into a single module, utilizing low-solidity composite blade profiles. Three configurations (N18, N20, and N24) were developed and tested. Advanced diagnostic techniques, including pressure-sensitive paint, particle image velocimetry, and five-hole probe measurements, were employed to investigate the aerodynamic characteristics. Numerical simulations complemented the experimental study, providing detailed insights into the flow mechanisms. Results indicate that the ICTM demonstrates excellent aerodynamic performance with minimal secondary flows. The total pressure loss coefficient for the N20 configuration was 0.0486, representing a 31.3% improvement over traditional designs. This research offers a promising new direction for gas turbine performance optimization by enhancing fluid dynamics, implementing effective flow control strategies, and reducing total pressure loss.

papers.title: On theoretical modeling of underdriven oblique detonation phenomenon
papers.abstract: Polar analysis is an important theoretical method in shock and detonation fields. However, a detonation polar is fundamentally different from the well-established shock polar due to not only the reaction heat release but also its involvement of a so-called underdriven oblique detonation wave (ODW) with a flow deflection angle θ smaller than the Chapman–Jouguet (CJ) angle θCJ, whose traditional modeling is recognized as non-physical in the literature. In this study, a far-field physical model of underdriven ODWs neglecting the initiation zone, as a CJ ODW surface followed by a centered expansion fan, is proposed based on the numerical observations of the flow features of a wedge-induced ODW at θ < θCJ simulated using a finite-rate two-step chain-branching reaction model. Accordingly, the polar segment of underdriven ODWs in terms of pressure p and θ, i.e., the p–θ relation, is quantitatively constructed using a combination of the theoretical solution of a CJ ODW and the Prandtl–Meyer isentropic expansion relation. Thereafter, such physical and mathematical modeling of underdriven ODWs from a far-field perspective is well verified with a series of numerical cases simulated using a quasi-equilibrium reaction model. Finally, a sensitivity analysis is carried out to evaluate the effects of the viscous boundary layer developed on the wedge surface. The results showed that the initiation zone of viscous wedge-induced underdriven ODWs is significantly shorter than that of the inviscid counterparts, but the viscosity effect is negligible from the far-field perspective. This work advances the fundamental understanding of underdriven ODWs and supplements the theoretical modeling of the oblique detonation phenomenon.

papers.title: Hydrodynamics of wave-induced fluid resonance in a recessed moonpool
papers.abstract: The hydrodynamics of wave-induced fluid resonance in a recessed moonpool are numerically investigated using both a multiphase viscous flow solver and a fully nonlinear potential flow solver. This study aims to investigate the nonlinear resonance phenomena inherent to the recessed moonpool configuration, with particular attention to the associated reflection, transmission, and radiation waves. Emphasis is also placed on assessing the predictive accuracy of the potential flow solver and elucidating the physical mechanisms underlying its deviations from the viscous flow results. The quasi-steady amplitude- and phase-frequency responses of fluid oscillations are first examined to identify the characteristic multi-peak resonance behavior. Frequency-domain harmonic analysis and spatial modal decomposition are then employed to provide physical insight into the observed resonance features. Furthermore, the transient evolution of nonlinear superharmonic resonances induced by sloshing modes is analyzed in terms of phase dynamics, time-varying wavelet energy spectra, and the spatiotemporal development of modal interactions. Radiation damping energy transfer mechanisms associated with piston- and sloshing-mode resonances are elucidated, revealing frequency-dependent reflection and transmission behavior. The role of viscous energy dissipation is investigated through analysis of the vorticity field. The predictive performance of the potential flow model is critically evaluated based on both transient dynamics and quasi-steady hydrodynamic responses. The physical insights obtained in this study contribute to a deeper understanding of nonlinear, transient, multi-frequency, and multi-mode fluid resonance in recessed moonpools, and provide valuable guidance for the application and limitations of potential flow solvers.

papers.title: Reconstruction of the mean velocity, pressure, and turbulent viscosity fields from background-oriented schlieren measurements using a physics-informed neural network
papers.abstract: A data assimilation technique for turbulent flows, based on the use of the physics-informed neural network (PINN), is presented. Mean temperature fields, measured with the nonintrusive background-oriented schlieren (BOS) method, and sparse velocity measurements are used as input data. The velocity, pressure, turbulent viscosity, and thermal conductivity fields are reconstructed using PINN. PINN searches for the flow field, which approximately satisfies the governing equations while remaining close to the available experimental data. Reconstruction is performed for the free and impinging subsonic axisymmetric turbulent jets of hot air. The results are compared with conventional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations. The feasibility of taking into account the spatial variation of the turbulent Prandtl number is demonstrated. However, due to a large number of unknown parameters, accurate reconstruction of the turbulent Prandtl number field requires velocity data measured with high spatial resolution.

papers.title: Analytical study of water wave interaction with a vertical cylinder surrounded by a non-concentric cylindrical perforated wall
papers.abstract: The wave interaction between water waves and concentric cylindrical structures received extensive attention, but analytical investigations on the hydrodynamic problems of non-concentric structures were rarely reported. In this study, a vertical cylinder surrounded by a non-concentric cylindrical perforated wall is taken as an example, where the vertical cylinder can be regarded as a platform and the perforated wall can serve as a protective facility. An analytical method for the hydrodynamic problems of non-concentric cylindrical structures is developed in the context of the potential flow theory. In the analytical process, the entire fluid domain is divided into two regions, and the velocity potentials of the fluid motion are expressed by the Bessel–Fourier series. Graft's addition theorem is used to address the problem caused by hybrid coordinate systems, and the expansion coefficients in the velocity potentials are determined through the boundary condition on the perforated wall. The linear wave forces and mean drift forces on the cylinder and the perforated wall are obtained, and the calculation expression of the dissipated wave power of the perforated wall is given. The analytical solution converges rapidly, and the calculated results are consistent with the numerical results of the boundary element method. Typical examples are presented to examine the effects of the wave frequency, the cylinder position, and the porous effect parameter on the hydrodynamic quantities. The results show that the wave forces on the inner cylinder and the perforated wall are sensitive to the cylinder position, and there exists an optimal geometric porosity to maximize the energy-dissipating performance of the perforated wall. The present analytical scheme can provide a basic reference for wave-induced hydrodynamic problems of other complicated non-concentric structures.

papers.title: Vortex-induced vibrations of inclined and curved flexible cylinders with a strip-theory-based discrete vortex method
papers.abstract: Non-vertical flexible structures, such as inclined and curved cylinders, are encountered in deep-sea applications and exhibit more complex vortex-induced vibration (VIV) responses than vertical cylinders due to geometric non-uniformity and flow-curvature interaction. These complexities challenge both full-scale computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and reduced-order models, emphasizing the need for an accurate and efficient CFD-based approach. This study presents a meshless numerical methodology employing strip-theory-based discrete vortex method (SDVM) to simulate the VIV in non-vertical flexible cylinders. The full-scale flow is approximated by a sequence of flow strips, each resolved using SDVM without empirical hydrodynamic coefficients. Structural dynamics are modeled using a tensioned Bernoulli–Euler beam and solved in time domain. The methodology is validated against two benchmark experiments: an inclined flexible cylinder and a steel catenary riser (SCR) in uniform flow. Simulations verify the independence principle up to 60° inclination. For the SCR, a mixed standing-traveling wave pattern is observed, with downward energy transfer from the top. Additionally, a novel modal group switching behavior, characterized by abrupt shifts in the dominant frequency and amplitude, is also identified over a broad range of incoming flow velocities. The proposed methodology offers an efficient and accurate tool for simulating VIV in complex offshore structures, bridging the gap between simplified reduced-order models and full-scale CFD simulations.

papers.title: Pore-scale flow mechanisms in three-dimensional heterogeneous porous channels: Topology optimization and critical pore diameter effects
papers.abstract: This paper presents a method for modeling three-dimensional heterogeneous porous channels using the variable density topology optimization technique. This approach allows for parametric control over porosity and pore throat dimensions, enabling the creation of a highly accurate geometric model. Additionally, the Navier–Stokes equations are employed to examine the pore-scale flow behavior, revealing the microscopic mechanisms through which pore structure parameters affect flow velocity, pressure drop, and nonlinear flow transition characteristics. Ultimately, a revised model for effective permeability (Keff) is introduced, enhancing the precision of macroscopic models in the cross-scale analysis of flow in porous media. The results indicate that the method of generating porous flow channels through topology optimization demonstrates high accuracy. The design error decreases as the porosity increases, reaching a minimum of 0.2% at a porosity of 0.5. It has been found that a critical pore diameter of 150 μm maximizes fluid flow velocity and minimizes critical mass flux. The effect of pore diameter on fluid velocity and vortex strength is significant, while the influence of porosity becomes apparent only at the critical pore diameter. As mass flux increases, effective permeability continuously decreases, whereas the number of vortex structures initially increases before stabilizing. The modified Keff model links pore-scale structure with macroscopic predictions, reducing the prediction error of the pressure gradient to 0.04% in cross-scale simulations. These findings provide new insights for optimizing porous media in microfluidic and energy applications.

papers.title: High-order simulations of non-ideal flows with efficient control of temporal and spatial accuracy
papers.abstract: This work presents the simulation of complex transonic/supersonic viscous flows with non-ideal compressible conditions with a high-order accuracy both in time and space. The computational efficiency of a solver based on a discontinuous Galerkin spatial discretization is increased with algorithms to adapt the polynomial degree of the solution over the mesh and the time step-size during the simulation, i.e., the p- and Δt-adaptation algorithms. The proposed implementation of these algorithms and non-ideal equations of state allows a further decrease in the computational cost of the simulations. The look-up-tables are used instead of the direct resolution of the non-ideal equations of state and are generated after each adaptation of the polynomial degree of the solution to increase the accuracy of the interpolation of the thermodynamic variables/derivatives. If the flow phenomenon is steady, the Δt-adaptation algorithm is able to reach the convergence of pseudo-unsteady simulations with a computational cost comparable to that of steady simulations and an efficient time integration. Furthermore, a spectral filter is used on the dual graph of the mesh after each adaptation of the polynomial degree of the solution to decrease the differences in the polynomial degree between neighboring elements. The accuracy and computational efficiency of different variables used in the error estimator for the p-adaptation algorithm, i.e., pressure, temperature, velocity magnitude, speed of sound, entropy, and the fundamental derivative of gas dynamics, are compared on simulations with different free-stream and wall conditions, equations of state, and governing equations. The results also demonstrate the influence of negative values of the fundamental derivative of gas dynamics and cold-wall conditions on flow phenomena such as shock/boundary-layer interaction and buffet/vortex shedding.

papers.title: Viscoplastic flows in narrow channels: Herschel–Bulkley model versus its regularizations
papers.abstract: We investigated the two-dimensional flows of a viscoplastic fluid in symmetric channels with impermeable walls under no-slip boundary conditions. As response functions for the Cauchy stress tensor, we considered both the celebrated Herschel–Bulkley model and a very general class C of its regularizations that depend on a positive parameter known as the regularization parameter. The regularized models in C admit smooth response functions for the viscosity that tend to the non-smooth Herschel–Bulkley viscosity function as the regularization parameter tends to zero. To make the equations governing the flow amenable to analysis, we considered channels with small aspect ratio so that the lubrication approximation can be used. In this way, we were able to obtain analytical solutions, perform an asymptotic analysis of the regularized solutions, and compare the results predicted by the Herschel–Bulkley model and its regularizations. We found that for any given channel, the regularized flows predicted by the regularizations in C tend to the same velocity field in the limit as the regularization parameter tends to zero. The asymptotic flow coincides with that predicted by the Herschel–Bulkley model only if the viscoplastic fluid flows in plane channels. Instead, in channels with curved walls, the results are markedly different.

papers.title: Study on oil–water two-phase flow characteristics and influencing factors in fractured-cavity reservoirs considering hydraulic-mechanical coupling
papers.abstract: Fractured-cavity reservoirs are highly inhomogeneous with coexisting matrix, fractures, and cavities, making it extremely difficult to characterize fluid flow, and posing a significant challenge to efficient development. In this study, the hydraulic-mechanical coupling model of oil–water seepage-free flow for fractured-cavity reservoirs was constructed, and the correctness was verified by physical model experiments. Then, through numerical simulation, the influences of cavity parameters (quantity, size, and distribution) and fracture-cavity combination patterns were analyzed, revealing the controlling mechanisms of fracture-cavity patterns on oil–water flow characteristics. The results showed that with increasing quantity and diameter of cavities, the shielding effect and dominant role became increasingly pronounced, leading to reduced reservoir connectivity and difficulty in forming significant dominant flow channels. The cavities and fractures along the direction connecting injection and production wells formed favorable dominant flow channels with superior connectivity. Remote cavity distributions from production wells could accelerate water breakthrough time, while proximal cavity clusters near production wells tended to form localized isolation zones with lower displacement efficiency and reduced water cut. The connectivity of fracture-cavity combination models followed this descending order: Series–parallel type > parallel type > series type. Furthermore, the water cut levels of the three models showed consistent ranking with their connectivity patterns. The results provide theoretical support for the evaluation of oil–water distribution and the optimization design of development plans in fractured-cavity reservoirs.

papers.title: Erratum: “Assessing the influence of design variables on serpentine duct intake performance using surrogate-based sensitivity analysis” [Phys. Fluids 37 (6), 066127 (2025)]
Mechanism of cross-vane flow influence on the hydraulic performance of centrifugal pumps with half vaned diffuser
papers.abstract: Half vaned diffuser has been shown to improve the efficiency of centrifugal pumps and shift the high-efficiency zone toward higher flow rates compared to full-height vaned diffuser. However, the mechanism underlying this performance enhancement remains unclear. This study integrates experimental data and numerical simulations to investigate how cross-vane flow influences the hydraulic performance of centrifugal pumps. Results indicate that using half vaned diffuser increases the maximum pump efficiency from 55.1% to 57.0% and broadens the high-efficiency flow rate range from 30.42–40.08 to 37.63–48.61 m3/h. Half vaned diffuser modifies the internal flow field of the volute by modifying its own flow characteristics, thereby substantially reducing the hydraulic losses of the volute. The mechanism by which half vaned diffuser reduces hydraulic losses lies in the presence of leakage flow and leakage vortices induced by cross-vane flow. These structures mitigate velocity and total pressure difference between pressure and suction surface, promote momentum exchange between end clearance and vaned region, and suppress and eliminate flow separation on the suction surface. Consequently, the formation of main vortex structure and backflow near the volute tongue is effectively eliminated, resulting in improved flow uniformity and reduced energy losses. Furthermore, cross-vane flow mitigates the non-uniform distribution of vorticity stretching and tilting term, and viscous diffusion term within the diffuser, weakening their influence on the formation of main vortex structure with a blocking effect in the volute. The viscous effect of the end face play an important role in improving the internal flow characteristics of half vaned diffuser-particularly within the end clearance-thereby enhancing the flow field near the volute tongue and suppressing the development of main vortex structures in the volute. These findings provide new insights into the flow physics of half vaned diffuser and offer guidance for improving centrifugal pump performance through diffuser design.

papers.title: Publisher's Note: “Compressible fluid leading to deterministic quantum mechanics. II. The linearized temporal-azimuthal wave solution” [Phys. Fluids 37 , 086124 (2025)]
Machine learning analysis of boiling regimes and spreading dynamics in liquid nitrogen droplet impact on superheated surfaces
papers.abstract: The impact of liquid nitrogen droplets on superheated surfaces involves a complex interplay of transient fluid flow, heat transfer, and phase change phenomena, all of which critically influence the efficiency of spray cooling systems. To investigate this behavior, we develop two machine learning models: one for classifying boiling regimes upon droplet impact and another for predicting spreading dynamics across the regimes. A dataset of 5274 experimentally obtained impact images is used to evaluate seven convolutional neural network architectures with ResNet-18 achieving the highest classification accuracy of 99.8%. Based on this classification, a multilayer perceptron model is trained using five key parameters—Reynolds number, Weber number, Ohnesorge number, Capillary number, and surface temperature—to predict the maximum spreading coefficient and spreading time. Compared to traditional empirical methods, our models significantly improve predictive accuracy, reducing errors to below 4.8% and 8.4% for the respective parameters. In addition to deepening the fundamental understanding of cryogenic droplet dynamics, this machine learning-based framework offers valuable potential for optimizing the design and performance of cryogenic cooling systems.

papers.title: Multiscale dynamics in cryogenic cavitating flows: A coupled thermodynamic-population balance model and mechanism analysis
papers.abstract: This study presents a novel cryogenic cavitation prediction framework that integrates bubble coalescence-breakup dynamics with a thermodynamically enhanced mass transfer model using a population balance model (PBM) approach. Validated against Hord's experiments, the developed PBM-Modified Zwart–Gerber–Belamri (PMZGB) model demonstrates 28% higher predictive accuracy than the conventional Zwart–Gerber–Belamri (ZGB) model, achieving a 19% relative error in cavitation length prediction while precisely resolving interfacial pressure-temperature distributions. Multiscale analysis reveals dual cavitation mechanisms: millimeter-scale cavity shedding is governed by low-frequency pressure pulsations (dominant mode at 499.57 Hz), whereas micrometer-scale bubble collapse is modulated by high-frequency dynamics (>1060.67 Hz). Characteristic bimodal bubble size distributions emerge, with micrometer-scale bubbles (0.001–0.5 mm) constituting over 50% of the population. Thermodynamic feedback through bubble coalescence and breakup emerges as a critical regulator of cavitation intensity, while millimeter-scale cavities (>3 mm) display pressure-dependent cyclic growth-decay patterns that dominate low-frequency pressure instabilities. The study elucidates how the dynamic equilibrium between coalescence and breakup mechanisms intrinsically controls cavitation cycles under varying flow conditions. Furthermore, the identified regulatory mechanisms involving vapor volume fraction (αv) and turbulent dissipation rate (ε) provide new insights for cavitation suppression strategies in cryogenic fluid machinery.

papers.title: Theoretical analysis of the dynamic characteristics of a spatial three-bubble system
papers.abstract: The coupling effects and energy transfer mechanisms in multi-bubble systems have been long-standing focal points in fluid dynamics research. In this study, we theoretically investigate the dynamics of a spatial three-bubble system using a compressible bubble dynamics model that incorporates phase transition and migration effects. The dynamic behaviors and energy conversion processes are analyzed for different spatial configurations. Validation is performed through a series of spark-generated bubble experiments. Energy distribution and dissipation characteristics are compared across three experimental cases: two non-collinear arrangements with different initial dimensionless distances, and a linear arrangement. The results show that for bubbles positioned symmetrically, the interaction is governed by both dimensionless distance and arrangement shape. Furthermore, using a dimensionless framework, the effects of spatial configuration and flow field compressibility on system dynamics are examined. In particular, when the three bubbles are symmetrically arranged, fluid compressibility dominates the central bubble's energy dissipation.

papers.title: Dispersion of tumbling microswimmers in a plane poiseuille flow
papers.abstract: Active tumbling plays a key role in microswimmer transport. Using a continuum model based on the Smoluchowski equation, moment method, and generalized Taylor dispersion theory, the dispersion process of tumbling microswimmers is analyzed and characterized by a case study for a plane Poiseuille flow. The Galerkin spectral solutions are validated through comparison with individual-based simulations, showing good consistency between the two approaches. The study is primarily concerned with the cross-sectional concentration, orientation distribution, and effective dispersion coefficients in narrow channels, and reveals how key parameters influence long-time transport behavior. The results indicate that, in most cases, tumbling promotes the uniformity of the cross-sectional concentration distribution, suppresses shear-induced orientation polarization, and reduces both the drift velocity and the dispersivity. Strong shear weakens the influence of tumbling, the swimming ability of microswimmers enhances cross-stream migration, and translational diffusion promotes the uniformity of the cross-sectional concentration distribution. These findings help understand the tumbling effect in microswimmer transport in confined environments.

papers.title: Proposal of a turbulent Prandtl number model for predicting heat transfer deterioration in supercritical flows
papers.abstract: The supercritical heat transfer is characterized by abnormal heat transfer modes due to significant variation in thermophysical properties near the pseudocritical temperature. The sharp difference in the density sets up strong buoyancy forces, especially in vertical flows, causing severe heat transfer deterioration (HTD). The prediction of the onset of this HTD and wall temperature peaks is overpredicted with the existing Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) models, where the turbulent Prandtl number is taken as a constant. The upward flow of supercritical fluids, viz., water, carbon dioxide, and n-decane, through circular pipes undergoing HTD is considered in this study. The components of the turbulent Prandtl number are analyzed to determine the effect of the variable turbulent Prandtl number model on predicting the peak wall temperature and its position, and to understand its impact on the heat transfer behavior. The increase in turbulent Prandtl number in the buffer region tends to suppress turbulence near the wall and improves the HTD, thus acting as a correction factor for RANS models in predicting the onset of HTD at supercritical conditions. Compared with available experimental data, the results improve significantly with the variable turbulent Prandtl number model, with a maximum error of 9.5%. The buoyancy production models are also varied for different cases, and their influence on turbulent heat flux calculation is compared with that of the variable Prt model.

papers.title: Multi-cycle dynamics and vortex structures of the cavitation bubble in the circular tube
papers.abstract: Revealing the bubble dynamics within the tube facilitates precise control of bubble positioning, thereby offering potential improvements in targeted drug delivery and the operational efficiency of inertial micropumps. This study focuses on an in-depth investigation of the multi-cycle dynamics of the cavitation bubble and the associated vortex behavior within a circular tube. The reliability and accuracy of the current model were validated through comparisons with three sets of experiments. A comprehensive analysis was conducted to investigate the effects of the relative position (δ) and tube diameter (γ) on bubble dynamics, vortex structures, and wall shear stress. The results show that the cavitation bubble exhibits different jet patterns depending on the δ: bidirectional jets occur at the pipe center (δ = 0), the unidirectional jet appears when the bubble is positioned off-center, and a high-speed unidirectional jet is observed near the tube port. The vortex structures induced by cavitation bubble collapse and their effects on wall shear stress exhibit significant variations under different γ. Two distinct regions are observed according to whether the localized high wall shear stress regions occur or not. The localized high wall shear stress is observed in the range 0.4 < γ ≤ 1.3, whereas no such high-shear regions are present when 1.3 < γ ≤ 1.6. As δ increases, the bubble collapse time in the first two cycles increases. In contrast, a decrease in γ leads to a reduction in the maximum bubble radius, while both the collapse time and peak wall pressure increase.

papers.title: Effects of labyrinth cavity angles and non-axisymmetric end wall on the performance of the shrouded stator at different inlet boundary layer thicknesses
papers.abstract: The interplay between leakage flow and secondary flow markedly impairs the aerodynamic efficacy of shrouded stators within axial compressors. However, the synergistic influence of inlet boundary layer thickness, cavity angles, and non-axisymmetric end wall contouring remains insufficiently understood. This study employs numerical simulations to systematically investigate the underlying mechanisms by which these factors influence the flow in a high-pressure compressor cascade, while innovatively integrating variations in labyrinth cavity angles with non-axisymmetric end wall design to enhance stator performance. Results reveal that thicker inlet boundary layers increase total pressure and entropy loss coefficients by over 12.03% and 10.71%, respectively. Notably, increasing rotational speed leads to a reduction in the entropy loss coefficient until the escalating losses caused by temperature gradients begin to offset this benefit. Among five cavity angle designs, structure 4, featuring an inlet angle opposing the mainstream and an outlet angle aligned with it, achieves optimal performance at 0 rpm by minimizing leakage and mixing losses. The incorporation of non-axisymmetric end wall with structure 4 further reduces total pressure and entropy loss coefficients by 5.09% and 2.66% at 0 rpm, respectively. However, its effectiveness diminishes at higher speeds due to overlapping effects with circumferential momentum. This study provides a pioneering exploration of the coupled control mechanisms involving cavity angles and non-axisymmetric end wall design, offering valuable insights for enhancing stator efficiency under complex operating conditions and establishing a theoretical foundation for advanced turbomachinery design.

papers.title: Aerodynamic modeling of wind turbine blade considering bending deformation: A modified vortex cylinder model
papers.abstract: With the increasing size and flexibility of modern wind turbine blades, blade bending deformation has become more pronounced, making its aerodynamic effects non-negligible. This study investigates the aerodynamic impact of blade bending deformation and proposes a modified vortex cylinder model considering bending deformation (VC-BD). Compared to the blade element momentum, lifting line method (LLM), and high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods, the VC-BD model captures both geometric and wake-induced effects induced by blade bending and responses more accurately under various bending conditions. A vortex-theoretical analysis identifies two main categories of bending-induced aerodynamic effects: geometric changes altering local angle of attack and loading, and aerodynamic induction effects involving bound vortex self-induction, wake redistribution, and trajectory distortion. The proposed VC-BD model accurately captures the aerodynamic effects of blade bending, showing strong agreement with CFD and LLM results while maintaining a favorable balance between fidelity and computational cost. It provides a practical and efficient tool for early-stage design and aeroelastic analysis of flexible blades.

papers.title: Numerical study on energy harvesting from flow-induced vibrations of dual-interfering-cylinders in ocean currents
papers.abstract: Ocean energy resources have abundant reserves and play an important role in addressing energy crises. The study simulated flow-induced vibration energy harvesting in an isosceles triangular structure composed of upstream fixed dual interfering cylinders and a downstream single-degree-of-freedom vibrating energy-harvesting cylinder, revealing that the presence of upstream interfering cylinders enhances marine energy capture. With the Reynolds number and spacing ratio fixed at 150 and L/D = 2, respectively, numerical simulations were performed for cases with different diameter ratios (D* = 1.0, 0.8, and 0.6), and wake visualization analysis was employed to illustrate the influence of vortex structures on structural vibrations. Parallel numerical analyses of a single energy-harvesting cylinder configuration were conducted to highlight the advantages of the dual interfering cylinder configuration in wake-excited energy harvesting. The results demonstrated that, under the wake excitation effects of the dual interfering cylinders, the dual interfering configuration exhibited significantly stronger flow-induced vibration energy-harvesting responses compared to the single energy-harvesting configuration, along with maintaining higher dimensionless amplitudes at elevated reduced velocities. Regarding energy harvesting performance, the dual interfering configuration showed high sensitivity-to-diameter ratio variations: The D* = 0.6 case achieved optimal energy-harvesting power and efficiency at reduced velocity (Ur) < 7, while at Ur > 7, the optimal diameter ratio shifted, with the D* = 1.0 configuration demonstrating superior capabilities. This research elucidates the influence mechanisms between multi-bluff-body wake-excited energy harvesting and diameter ratios, emphasizing the advantages of wake excitation in flow-induced vibration energy harvesting and establishes a technical foundation for the design of renewable marine energy harvesting devices based on multi-bluff-body wake excitation.

papers.title: Flow state transition and heat transfer characteristics in radiative Rayleigh–Bénard convection
papers.abstract: The Rayleigh–Bénard (RB) convection under the influence of thermal radiation holds paramount importance in both natural systems and engineering applications, like advanced energy storage systems, renewable energy conversion technologies, and high-efficiency power generation systems, etc. Remarkably, thermal radiation significantly modifies flow dynamics and heat transport in RB convection. In this paper, direct numerical simulations of two-dimensional radiative RB convection in a square cavity have been conducted within the range of Rayleigh number Ra = 5 × 105–5 × 109, Planck number Pl = 0.005–0.16, and optical thickness τ = 0.01–50. By incorporating radiative heat transfer mechanisms into the classical buoyancy-driven convection framework, we elucidate the coupled effects of thermal radiation and fluid motion on heat transport efficiency and flow structure evolution. The simulation results reveal that thermal radiation imposes a stabilizing effect on the flow state of RB convection, promoting the transition from disordered chaotic flow to organized steady-state circulation. The impact of thermal radiation on convective heat transfer is complex and can be stratified into three distinct regimes, i.e., radiation-sensitive regime, transition regime, and buoyancy-dominated regime. The evolution of flow structures influenced by thermal radiation varies distinctly across different regimes, thereby exerting a profound influence on convective heat transfer. Conversely, the radiative and total heat transfer always decrease continuously with the attenuation of thermal radiation. These findings advance understanding of radiation-convection coupling in complex systems.

papers.title: Radial flow force reduction in a hydraulic spool valve using balanced through-hole design
papers.abstract: The hydraulic spool valve (HSV) represents the core control element in the fluid power system by virtue of its precise flow and pressure regulation abilities. Unbalanced radial flow force (RFF) is a major contributor to spool instability and friction-induced failure in HSVs, particularly in open-neutral configurations where flow field asymmetry is prominent. Conventional assumptions often overlook RFF due to structural symmetry, yet practical designs constrained by standard port layouts frequently induce asymmetrical pressure and velocity distributions. To address this issue, a novel through-hole design is proposed and integrated into the mid-shoulder of the HSV spool. Specifically, the study employs a combined approach of computational fluid dynamics-based numerical simulations and experimental bench testing to evaluate RFF generation and suppression mechanisms. The Realizable k–ε turbulence model is used to capture turbulent flow features and assess the contribution of pressure and viscous forces. Various through-hole angles are analyzed to determine the optimal configuration. Results indicate that RFF is predominantly pressure-driven (accounting for over 85% of total force), with significant asymmetries localized around the mid-shoulder region. Incorporating a 15° inclined dual through-hole structure reduces RFF on the mid-shoulder by 45.5% and total spool RFF by 29.9%, improving flow symmetry and minimizing pressure gradients. The optimized structure also enhances performance stability under varying spool displacements, achieving a maximum total spool RFF reduction of 55.5% at −1.5 mm displacement.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal distribution of the intraglottal pressure and vocal fold contact pressure in excised larynges
papers.abstract: The contact pressure experienced by the vocal folds during phonation is considered a major factor contributing to vocal fold injuries and lesions. Understanding the spatiotemporal distribution of vocal fold contact pressure across the medial surface and its dependence on laryngeal geometrical and mechanical properties (such as glottal gap, vocal fold vertical thickness, vocal fold length, and vocal fold stiffness) is essential to identifying strategies that minimize contact pressure and reduce the risk of vocal injury. This study aims to characterize the spatiotemporal distribution of intraglottal pressure across the medial surface in excised larynges. The intraglottal pressure was measured using a modified probe microphone at different locations within the vertical plane containing the glottal centerline (mid-sagittal plane), following a grid-like pattern. The resulting pressure distribution maps indicate small variations of intraglottal pressure in the anterior–posterior dimension, but large, complex variations in the vertical dimension. A criterion, derived from applying Bernoulli's equation to vocal fold vibration with prescribed vocal fold contact, was developed to identify the contact pressure peak as a rapid increase in the intraglottal pressure preceded by a negative pressure in the intraglottal pressure waveform. This criterion also allows estimation of the vertical span of vocal fold contact (by extension the vocal fold vertical thickness) and the mucosal wave speed. The preliminary results from this study indicate that the vocal fold vertical thickness has a large impact on the peak contact pressure value, which corroborates findings from previous computational studies.

papers.title: The different types of vortex-induced vibration and galloping interference and distinguish them through forced motion
papers.abstract: This study investigates the interference mechanism between vortex-induced vibration (VIV) and galloping at low mass ratios through numerical simulations of three prismatic sections at a Reynolds number of 200. Three distinct modes of VIV-galloping interference are identified, exhibiting characteristic variations in the vibration amplitude vs reduced velocity relationship across different mass ratios: (i) in the VIV-dominant mode, galloping is suppressed below a critical mass ratio; (ii) the galloping-dominant mode demonstrates increasing galloping amplitude with decreasing mass ratio at a given reduced velocity, with no observable critical mass ratio; (iii) the reattachment-suppressed mode involves boundary layer separation followed by reattachment, which weakly suppresses galloping, consequently, increased damping thereby reinstates galloping vibrations. The three modes exhibit different numbers of inflection points in their respective force coefficient vs angle of attack curves under quasi-steady theory. However, quasi-steady theory is limited in quantifying the influence of mass ratio, necessitating the adoption of the forced motion method incorporating energy transfer for further analysis. Results demonstrate that the single-frequency forced motion method accurately predicts the free vibration response at high mass ratios. However, it fails to adequately represent the pronounced vibration effects induced by significant vortex shedding on the prism at low mass ratios. Incorporating the amplitude component at the vortex shedding frequency enables effective characterization of the distinct VIV-galloping interference behaviors observed under low mass ratio conditions.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic mechanisms of deformable bubble pair interactions at varying Weber and Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: The two-bubble system provides an ideal framework for investigating the fundamental interaction mechanisms within bubble swarms. Using a coupled front-tracking and proportional-integral-derivative control simulation framework, we systematically investigate the hydrodynamic interactions between bubble pairs across a wide range of Reynolds numbers (Re), Weber numbers (We), and spatial configurations. Our results reveal a stark dichotomy in interaction regimes dictated by the Weber number. At low Weber numbers, where bubbles remain nearly spherical, tandem pairs exhibit a drag reversal: with increasing Reynolds number, the interaction transitions from a shielded, attractive state to an inertia-driven repulsive one, while side-by-side pairs experience attraction. In contrast, at high Weber numbers, pronounced bubble deformation leads to persistent attractive interactions for tandem pairs across all tested Reynolds numbers, whereas side-by-side configurations become repulsive. Furthermore, a critical inclination angle range of 30°–45° is identified, marking a transition in the interaction regime, characterized by a reversal in lift force direction. The rotational dynamics also show strong Weber number dependence: at low We, the torque consistently promotes horizontal alignment, consistent with predictions for spherical bubbles, whereas at high We, the torque reverses within the same critical angle range, actively promoting vertical alignment for highly deformable bubbles. These findings provide new insights into the dynamics of bubble pairs and advance our understanding of multiphase flow behavior in bubble swarms.

papers.title: Control of incident shock wave/boundary layer interaction by concave surface
papers.abstract: The separation induced by incident shock wave/boundary layer interaction (ISWBLI) in supersonic/hypersonic inlets significantly degrades aerodynamic performance. This study proposes a novel passive control method for ISWBLI by using a concave surface. Numerical simulations were employed to elucidate the flowfield under the influence of the concave surface, thereby validating the effectiveness of the control method. The results demonstrate that the concave surface generates beneficial expansion waves and precompression effects, which collectively attenuate the separation region both upstream and downstream of the shock impingement point. Specifically, the results show substantial separation size reduction, with upstream concave surface placement achieving 49.1% suppression and downstream configuration yielding 39% reduction. The near wall airflow exhibits distinct interaction patterns depending on geometric positioning. The effectiveness of control is observed in two distinct regions. The first effective region occurs when the initial position of the concave surface is located upstream of the reattachment point of the separation region, extending until the shock impingement point reaches the leeward expansion side. The second region is characterized by the shock impingement point being situated on the windward expansion side, continuing until the end position of the concave surface is downstream of the separation point. Conversely, shock impingement on the concave compression surface intensifies shock strength and exacerbates separation. A critical finding reveals that maximal mitigation of the adverse pressure gradient occurs when the shock impingement point is displaced a distance d1 from the initiation point of the concave surface, or proximate to the end of the concave surface.

papers.title: Optimization of hydrogen acoustic microfluidic pump based on loss function-enhanced physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: The coupling design of acoustic streaming effects and sharp-edged array structures within a microfluidic pump is essential for enhancing hydrogen transport performance. This study introduces an enhanced physics-informed neural network (PINN) that combines multiple loss functions, including gradients and partial differential equation (PDE) residual losses. A detailed analysis of the impact on both nonlinear fitting accuracy and optimization efficiency is provided to achieve efficient optimization of the acoustic field, flow field, and structure. The results indicate that enhancing the PDE residual loss in PINNs contributes most significantly to improving fitting accuracy, establishing it as the central component in Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. A notable interaction is observed between the PDE residual loss and the Sobolev gradient loss, indicating that a well-balanced combination of different loss terms can substantially enhance the accuracy of surrogate models. The enhanced PINN reduces the sample size required for fitting a nine-dimensional Ackley function by 86% compared to a conventional PINN while maintaining high fitting accuracy with an R2 value of 0.99. Although different optimization algorithms yielded consistent optimal results, the enhanced PINN reduced the number of iterations by 41.2% compared to the standard PINN, exhibiting superior stability, robustness, and faster convergence toward the optimal solution. The optimized asymmetric sharp-edged array structure increases hydrogen flow by 68.3%, minimizes the impact of vortices on the main flow, and generates a stronger driving force through an unobstructed Rayleigh–Schlichting flow. These findings provide critical engineering insights for optimizing hydrogen transport designs.

papers.title: Two-way interactions of a rigid sphere and the vortical flow in an X-shaped microchannel
papers.abstract: The X-shaped microchannel is an effective microfluidic device for particle processing, where a particle's residence time and oscillation frequency in the junction are key factors. This study quantitatively examines their dependence on the flow Reynolds number (Re), channel aspect ratio (AR), and particle blockage ratio (β) using direct numerical simulations via an immersed boundary–lattice Boltzmann method. Our simulations cover the ranges 60≤Re≤160, 0.5≤AR≤1, and 0.2≤β≤0.5. The particle's lateral entry position is fixed near the channel centerline, ensuring interaction with the vortical flow. It is known that a steady spiral vortex forms for 48<Re<300, with vortex breakdown (VB) occurring at Re>100. The results at AR=1 reveal two competing effects: (1) vortical flow weakening due to particle blockage, which reduces residence time; and (2) vortical flow augmentation due to VB shrinkage caused by the particle, which increases residence time. For Re<100, VB does not occur, and only the first effect is present, leading to a decrease in residence time as β increases. At Re>130 with β=0.2, the second effect dominates, increasing residence time relative to a massless point particle, with this increase further amplified at higher Re. A larger β favors the first effect. Frequency decreases with higher β (all Re, AR) and lower AR (for Re<100 only). At Re>100, lower AR shrinks VB simultaneously, fixing frequency approximately.

papers.title: Many-body dissipative particle dynamics simulation of droplet dynamic behavior on stripe-patterned surfaces
papers.abstract: The motion of droplets on solid substrates represented a ubiquitous phenomenon in hydrocarbon exploitation. Effective regulation of droplet dynamics was of great scientific significance for enhancing fluid mobility. In this work, several different surfaces, including homogeneous surfaces and stripe-patterned surfaces, were constructed. Subsequently, droplet motion processes were simulated using the numerical method of many-body dissipative particle dynamics (MDPD). On homogeneous surfaces, the contact angle increased from ∼43° to ∼152° as the attractive parameter between the droplet and substrate increased within the range of −40 to −12.5. The droplet spontaneously migrated toward the hydrophilic region, and at the same attraction parameter, contact angles on different wetting surfaces deviated from those on homogeneous surfaces. However, the contact angle difference decreased with increasing attractive parameter. Findings revealed that the larger the attractive parameter between them, the more spherical the final morphology of the droplet became. The threshold force required to overcome adhesion and repulsion for droplet motion decreased from ∼0.05 to ∼0.0004 MDPD units as the attractive parameter increased from −40 to −15. On stripe-patterned surfaces, droplet motion in directions parallel and orthogonal to the stripes was investigated. As the magnitude of external force and simulation time increased, the displacements and velocities in both directions increased accordingly. The motion behavior and morphology of the droplet on solid surfaces were dependent on surface wettability, external forces, and stripe-patterned distribution. This work provided new and sound perspectives for the understanding of droplet motion and brought deep insight into enhancing flowability.

papers.title: Deep learning enhanced particle tri-view image extraction and three-dimensional reconstruction for trichromatic mask particle image velocimetry
