Infrared thermography was employed to visualize streak structures induced by stationary crossflow vortices on both the smooth and porous surfaces. Compared to the solid wall, the porous surface slightly enhances the intensity of the stationary crossflow vortices. However, it significantly suppresses high-frequency instabilities while stimulating the low-frequency instabilities, especially the traveling crossflow vortices in the yawed cone boundary layer. The PSE results demonstrate that the high-frequency oblique modes have a higher growth rate than the Mack modes of a sharp cone at a 6° angle of attack. The continuous wavelet transform analysis reveals two high-frequency unstable modes (y-mode and z-mode) on the solid wall, while only one is present on the porous surface. Through bispectrum analysis, it is found that the porous surface exhibits stronger interactions between high-frequency and low-frequency unstable modes, with no observed self-interactions among high-frequency modes.

papers.title: Spanwise resolution effects on flow simulations around a square cylinder at the critical angle
papers.abstract: In large-eddy simulations or direct numerical simulations of flows past bluff bodies, the spanwise resolution significantly increases the total cell count and, consequently, the computational cost. The spanwise resolution dz is normalized by the characteristic length scale D (width or diameter), yielding the nondimensional form dz/D. This study investigates the influence of dz/D on the separating–reattaching flows around an infinitely long square cylinder at the critical incidence angle of 14° and at a high Reynolds number of 2.2×104. Simulations span dz/D=0.013–0.08 to systematically evaluate resolution effects. The results demonstrate significant effects of dz/D on aerodynamic forces, surface pressures, and the flow statistics, even at spanwise resolutions finer than those employed in most previous studies. Coarser resolutions (dz/D>0.013) yield higher mean drag, larger rms pressure and force fluctuations, and a shorter, narrower recirculation zone behind the cylinder. As dz/D is refined, the shear layer evolves to exhibit both spanwise and streamwise vortices, enhancing its spanwise coherence and resilience to external disturbances. A detailed comparison with fully separated flows reveals both similarities and distinctions in spanwise resolution effects. Key differences include the trailing-edge effects, a markedly higher frequency of the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability, and pronounced low-frequency unsteadiness inherent to separating–reattaching flows.

papers.title: Cavitation erosion in Venturi pipe and erosion optimization of four-stage pump
papers.abstract: Cavitation erosion is a prevalent and challenging phenomenon in hydraulic machinery, which can cause flow-induced failure. In this study, we investigate the mechanisms and mitigation of cavitation erosion through a combined experimental and numerical approach. High-speed visualization experiments were conducted in a Venturi-type pipe to capture the transient evolution of cavitation structures and correlate them with erosion-prone regions. Simultaneously, numerical simulations based on the large eddy simulation (LES) method coupled with a volume of fluid (VOF) model were used to resolve the cavitating flow field. A local erosion aggressiveness indicator was developed to quantitatively evaluate cavitation-induced material damage. The proposed erosion prediction model is verified against the experimental results, and the erosion attributes of the specimens are investigated under varying expansion angles. The findings indicate that the formulated cavitation prediction model adeptly delineates the distribution characteristics of cavitation across the surface of the specimen. Under conditions of constant flow rate, there is a discernible decline in cavitation intensity concurrent with the augmentation of the expansion angle. Building on this observation, a numerical simulation is conducted to examine the cavitation erosion in a four-stage high-pressure circulating pump. By increasing the diffusion angle of the leading-edge twisted blades, the cavity distribution is altered, resulting in an increased distance between the cavitation bubble collapse center and the blade surface. This adjustment reduced the impact of pressure waves on the blade surface, thereby mitigating the risk of cavitation erosion.

papers.title: Failure mechanism and performance deterioration of bentonite suspensions in drilling fluids under CO2-thermal coupling conditions
papers.abstract: Deep acidic gas reservoirs have emerged as promising geological CO2 storage sites, driven by global carbon neutrality goals and advancements in carbon capture, utilization, and storage technologies. However, during drilling operations in these reservoirs, water-based drilling fluids are frequently contaminated by acidic gases like CO2, leading to severe rheological and filtration abnormalities that jeopardize wellbore stability. As the dispersion state of bentonite governs the performance of such fluids, this study investigates the structural and colloidal stability of bentonite suspensions under CO2-thermal coupling conditions, simulating contamination at 0.2–1 MPa and temperatures of 80–150 °C. Macroscopic fluid performance, colloidal stability, surface chemistry, and microstructural evolution were systematically analyzed. Results reveal a two-stage evolutionary mechanism: under mild CO2 intrusion, slight protonation of particle surfaces enhances the three-dimensional network, improving rheological and filtration properties. In contrast, severe contamination disrupts electrostatic equilibrium, triggering particle aggregation dominated by van der Waals forces and causing performance deterioration—a process exacerbated by elevated temperatures that accelerate particle migration. These findings elucidate the microstructural degradation pathways of bentonite under CO2-thermal coupling, offering theoretical insights for designing contamination-resistant drilling fluids in deep acidic gas reservoirs.

papers.title: Exploring the application of pressure balance concept on flow-induced force minimization for the tooth-on-rotor type labyrinth seal in turbomachines
papers.abstract: Although labyrinth seals primarily suppress the clearance leakage in turbomachines, its complicated internal flow also generates significant flow-induced force (tangential force) exciting the rotor vibration. This problem is particularly severe for the tooth-on-rotor type labyrinth seal. To counter this problem, this study explores the application of pressure balance concept on tangential force minimization, thereby proposing a pressure balanced type labyrinth seal. On the outer side of the tooth-on-rotor type, one central chamber and several pressure balance pipes are designed. These pressure balance pipes enable the flow transfer between the innermost seal cavity and outermost central chamber. Based on the computational fluid dynamic method, the performance of the pressure balanced type is obtained. Compared with the tooth-on-rotor type, the pressure balanced type further reduces the leakage through increasing the kinetic energy dissipation and flow resistance. The pressure difference between both sides of the eccentricity direction is reduced. The tangential force is minimized form the root. The pressure balanced type's tangential force is independent of preswirl ratio. This is highly important for high/ultra-high speed turbomachines. The effect of pressure difference on the tangential force is also largely reduced. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of the pressure balance concept on tangential force minimization, and provides a useful alternative for modern seal design.

papers.title: Size effect of mode II fracture characteristics of a typical sandstone using the short beam compression specimens
papers.abstract: Shear-sliding mode fracture, i.e., mode II fracture, is a very common rupture mode of rocks. The size effect on the mode II fracture of rocks is critical yet remains underexplored. This study investigates the size effect on the mode II fracture behavior of sandstone using short beam compression specimens with four different lengths. Uniaxial compression tests combined with digital image correlation (DIC) were employed to characterize the mode II fracture toughness (KIIC and KIIC0; the former is defined as the experimentally measured mode II fracture toughness, and the latter as the actual mode II fracture toughness without the confinement effect) and fracture process zone (FPZ) evolution. Results revealed that KIIC increased significantly with specimen size, where KIIC increased by approximately 97% as the specimen length expanded from 10 to 50 mm. The FPZ length measured via DIC increased from 1.77 to 5.25 mm as the specimen size increased, while the normalized FPZ length decreased from 0.89 to 0.53, indicating reduced relative influence of the FPZ on fracture behavior for larger specimens. The analysis of strain evolution during crack propagation revealed that smaller specimens formed a continuous high strain band at an earlier loading stage compared to larger specimens. Additionally, comparative analysis showed FPZ lengths obtained by DIC were larger than the finite element model and stress intensity factor method predictions due to inelastic damage evolution and stress redistribution in the FPZ during loading. These findings are essential in evaluating the safety and stability of rock engineering structures.

papers.title: Large-scale forced drag control in compressible channels
papers.abstract: This study explores drag reduction in compressible turbulent channel flows via large-scale streamwise swirls induced by spanwise opposing wall-jet forcing (SOJF). Direct numerical simulations of the compressible Navier–Stokes equations are performed at a bulk Reynolds number of Reb=2800 for both subsonic (Mab=0.8) and supersonic (Mab=1.5) cases. The control parameters are fixed at A+≈0.015 and λ+≈1200, while two different control heights for large-scale swirls are examined, i.e., yc+=10 and 30. We find that SOJF achieves a drag reduction of 14.0% at Mab=0.8 and 6.8% at Mab=1.5 for yc+=30, higher than 8.1% (Ma=0.8) and 0.6% (Ma=1.5) for yc+=10. The better performance of a larger yc+ is found to be caused by a more effective suppression of near-wall velocity streaks and streamwise vortices, associated with a greater reduction of Reynolds shear stress and turbulence production. Moreover, the degraded control efficacy at higher Mach numbers originates from the intrinsically elevated near-wall density in compressible flows, further intensified by SOJF-induced wall-normal ejections. The results indicate that to enhance drag reduction in high-speed flow regimes, it is important to address the density stratification for developing a Mach-number-adaptive control manner.

papers.title: Sub-cavity induced passive control of confined supersonic cavity flows across varying freestream Mach numbers
papers.abstract: The self-sustaining cavity oscillations enhance fluid mixing, promoting energy and momentum transport. Despite their utility, the associated oscillation frequencies can amplify acoustic loading, potentially damaging structures that house cavities. Understanding cavity flow dynamics across various geometries and freestream conditions is, therefore, crucial, along with devising strategies to regulate these oscillations without compromising performance. In this study, we investigate the role of sub-cavities placed at the front and aft walls of a cavity confined by a top wall with a deflection angle of 2.29°, under freestream Mach numbers M∞=2 and 3. We perform large-eddy simulations (LES) using OpenFOAM for each configuration and analyze the unsteady pressure signals through spectral methods. The results show that the aft-wall sub-cavity most effectively suppresses the dominant oscillation frequency at the lower Mach number (M∞=2), while the front-wall sub-cavity achieves the greatest suppression at the higher Mach number (M∞=3). We examine the density gradient contours (numerical schlieren), vorticity fields, normalized acoustic impedance, and global wavelet power to identify the flow mechanisms responsible for frequency attenuation. At M∞=2, the aft-wall sub-cavity entrains mass and interrupts the convectively driven feedback loop. At M∞=3, the front-wall sub-cavity weakens the hydrodynamic–acoustic coupling between the cavity pressure waves and the shear layer near the leading edge, thereby disrupting the compressibility-driven feedback loop. We observe that these configurations suppress the major oscillation frequencies by 5.45% and 23.4% for M∞=2 and 3, respectively. We further validate these findings by computing the cross correlation between pressure probes located near the front and aft edges and by analyzing the spatiotemporal coherence in pressure and velocity fields using dynamic mode decomposition, which confirms the mechanisms behind the observed frequency suppression.

papers.title: Gas–solid flow-based capture of nascent tire-wear particles emitted from heavy container-truck tractors through porous filtration media
papers.abstract: Heavy container trucks generate disproportionately large quantities of tire-wear particles (TWPs) owing to their high axle loads, dual tires and long duty cycles. We investigate the gas–solid two-phase-flow capture of freshly emitted TWPs from the tractor unit using a porous filter that spans the full cross section of the collection duct. Porous filter placement together with inlet-outlet geometry was optimized through a coupled Eulerian–Lagrangian multiphase flow framework and verified with a 1:24 physical model on a bespoke test rig. The results showed that a suitably designed triangular inlet promotes the entrainment of TWPs into the capture duct, driven by the pressure differential between the internal and external flow regions. The optimal top angle of the triangular inlet was found to be 50°. The rear outlet, incorporating an overhead cavity, effectively suppresses air backflow within the capture duct by reducing the static pressure in the vicinity of the outlet. Under the integrated front–rear configuration, the average capture ratios reached approximately 31.4% at 30 km/h, 44.1% at 60 km/h, and 50.9% at 90 km/h. An analogous comparison across studies suggests that the porous filter achieves approximately 6.7% higher capture efficiency than the adhesive method at 90 km/h. The experimental and simulation results exhibit good agreement both qualitatively and quantitatively. The proposed methodology offers guidance for mitigating secondary hazards associated with tire-wear emissions from the tractors of heavy container trucks.

papers.title: First-order long-time convergence of fully discrete methods for viscoelastic flow with tempered power-law kernel
papers.abstract: This work presents a rigorous analysis of fully discrete numerical schemes for a viscoelastic flow model with memory effects governed by a tempered power-law kernel. The finite element method is employed for spatial discretization, and a backward Euler method is adopted for time discretization. Two discretization strategies are considered: a fully implicit scheme and a semi-implicit scheme, each incorporating a convolution quadrature rule tailored to the tempered fractional integral. Regularity results for the spatially semi-discrete solutions are established. Optimal error estimates with respect to both time and space are derived, with particular attention to their long-time behavior. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical convergence results of the schemes and to explore the influence of the viscoelastic parameter ρ on the numerical solutions.

papers.title: Phase behaviors of CO2-enriched oil system with aqueous phase under high-pressure conditions: An integrated experimental and theoretical study
papers.abstract: Under the globally advocated initiative of carbon capture, utilization, and storage, CO2-enhanced oil recovery has emerged as the preferred injection strategy for tight or shale oil reservoirs. The CO2–oil–water interactions induce complex multiphase behavior in reservoirs, yet previous studies regarded the aqueous phase as an inert phase, largely neglecting or underestimating its impact on CO2–oil systems. This study designed and conducted pressure–volume–temperature cross-experiments with varying CO2-to-water ratios to simulate reservoir multiphase conditions, elucidating aqueous phase effects on CO2–oil systems by phase behavior perspective. The phase behavior modeling of water-bearing CO2–oil systems was achieved by coupling the Soave–Redlich–Kwong equation of state (SRK EOS) with the Cubic Plus Association (CPA) term and Huron–Vidal (H–V) mixing rules. The results show that the SRK-CPA EOS model achieves satisfactory accuracy in describing the phase behavior of water-bearing oil systems compared to the classical SRK EOS. CO2 injection exhibits greater potential for viscosity reduction due to its higher solubility. However, this mechanism is suppressed when the aqueous phase is considered due to the partitioning dissolution of CO2 in water. In CO2–oil–water systems, a rising water cut weakens CO2's viscosity-reducing effect, simultaneously resulting in greater solubility loss in water compared to CH4, a more pronounced decline in the three-phase hydrocarbon boundary line, and contraction of the three-phase region in the phase envelope. In contrast, the two-phase hydrocarbon boundary line contracts inward, which is completely opposite to that observed in oil–water systems in previous experiments. Finally, the critical water saturation threshold can be quantified by analyzing the rate of change in key parameters, such as saturation pressure. The findings of this study provide valuable insights for evaluating multiphase behavior, CO2 storage potential, injection parameter optimization, and solubility loss in water-bearing reservoirs during CO2 flooding.

papers.title: Coalescence-induced droplet jumping on nanodimpled surfaces: A molecular dynamics study
papers.abstract: Coalescence-induced droplet jumping on structured surfaces is strongly influenced by surface morphology and has been shown to enhance jumping velocities for droplets within millimeter to micrometer scales. However, at the nanoscale, increased viscous dissipation would hinder jumping, and the critical droplet size and radius ratios of coalescence-induced droplet jumping remain controversial. This work investigates the coalescence of water droplets located on adjacent nanodimples of the same surfaces via molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The results indicate that increasing the surface hydrophilicity enhances both adhesion energy and viscous dissipation, resulting in three typical post-coalescence outcomes: coalescence-induced jumping, departure from the nanodimple of the surface via wetting transition, and formation of larger Wenzel droplets adhering to nanodimpled surfaces. For coalescence-induced droplets jumping, the liquid bridge radius with coalesced time satisfies Rb ∼ tc1/2, consistent with an inertial-limited-viscous mechanism. Increasing droplet size leads to a mismatch with nanodimpled geometry, causing disordered internal flow and elevated viscous losses, which significantly reduce the jumping kinetic energy. For example, when the droplet size increases from 3 to 9 nm, the energy conversion efficiency decreases markedly from 6.1% to 0.6%. Furthermore, decreasing droplet radius ratios would make the smaller droplet retract earlier under the action of the surface tension, and coalescence-induced jumping occurs only when the droplet radius ratio ranges between 0.65 and 1.

papers.title: The turbulent/non-turbulent interface in wall-jets
papers.abstract: The present study addresses the turbulent/non-turbulent interface (TNTI) in turbulent wall-jet flow using direct numerical simulation data. Three detection methods are investigated based on the vorticity, passive, and active scalars. In these methods, TNTI is detected as an isosurface of the scalar value, with a proper identification of the scalar threshold. Performance of the detection methods is assessed and compared qualitatively and quantitatively, and the most suitable one is determined. The intermittency parameter and probability density function for the location of the TNTIs are computed and analyzed using different methods. The TNTIs obtained from the passive and active scalar methods exhibit similar geometrical features, and both can reliably detect the TNTI in wall-jet flows. This is evidenced by an abrupt change in the conditional mean profile of turbulent kinetic energy and a small peak in the vorticity at the interface. While both passive and active scalar methods effectively detect the interface, the vorticity method tends to mark the interface at a higher position. The TNTI is not a simple monofractal but has a non-uniform geometry defined by a continuous spectrum of fractal dimensions. Additionally, local entrainment velocity at the TNTI is evaluated. Although detrainment is found to be more significant in turbulent wall jets compared to turbulent free jets and turbulent boundary layers, entrainment has been demonstrated to remain the dominant overall mechanism. It is demonstrated that local entrainment velocity is influenced by the interface curvature, with faster entrainment observed at regions of extreme mean curvatures, regardless of the sign.

papers.title: Research on the energy loss characteristics in the double-hump region of a pump-turbine
papers.abstract: With the large-scale integration of renewable energy, pumped storage, as a globally recognized reliable peak-shaving power source, has become increasingly prominent. However, frequent operating condition transitions inevitably force pump-turbines to pass through the hump region, or even the double-hump region during start-stop or load regulation processes, which seriously affects the stable operation of the unit. In this study, to reveal the formation mechanism of double-hump region, the energy loss characteristics of a pump-turbine are thoroughly investigated by a combination of experiment and unsteady simulations. The characteristics of energy conversion, pressure fluctuation, and internal flow in the double-hump region are also elaborated in detail. The results show that the decline rate of unit hydraulic loss energy curve increases significantly under the double-hump conditions. The runner work energy curve initially shows a downward trend in the first hump region, and then the energy coefficient continues to increase rapidly with the decrease in flow rate. The characteristic frequencies in the double-hump region exhibit complex evolutionary patterns. In the first hump region, the pressure fluctuation frequencies in the runner disperse across multiple frequency bands with enhanced nonlinear superposition effects. In the second hump region, the pressure fluctuation amplitudes in the guide vane increase significantly. Additionally, the formation of the first hump region is primarily attributed to the emergence of a large-scale flow separation region near the band side of the runner inlet. This leads to a sharp increase in runner's energy losses, acting as the primary factor, and a decline in its work capacity, both of which contribute to the formation of the first hump region. The formation of the second hump region is mainly due to the significant increase in rotating stall intensity within the guide vane. The dynamic evolution of Dean vortices in the draft tube also has a certain promoting effect on its formation.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of the flow characteristics in a semicircular S-shape inlet duct with large offset for boundary layer ingestion propulsion system
papers.abstract: The boundary layer ingestion (BLI) propulsion system is mostly partially or fully embedded into the aircraft fuselage. To adapt to the irregular geometrical shape of the blended wing body aircraft surface, a semicircular-to-circular S-shape inlet duct is preferably utilized as an intermediate to connect the fuselage and the BLI fan. With the intensive requirement of a compact inlet duct and fan propulsor, the designed offset-to-length ratio of an S-duct is continuously increased, which poses a great challenge to internal flow inside the S-duct. Moreover, our previous explorations have revealed that when the offset-to-length ratio of an S-duct reaches a certain value, a significantly distinct flow feature is noticed in a large offset-to-length ratio semicircular-to-circular S-duct compared with that in a conventional circular-to-circular S-duct. In this study, numerical simulations are conducted to investigate the influence of offset-to-length ratio on the internal flow characteristics in a semicircular-to-circular S-shape inlet duct. Results have shown that compared with the conventional circular-to-circular S-duct, another vortex pair occurs near the lower wall, except for the well-known vortex pair induced by the low-momentum wall-around flow. It is found that this new vortex pair originates mainly from the central pressure differential-driven flow and is located adjacent to the low-momentum wall-around flow-induced vortex pair. As the offset-to-length ratio is increased, the circumferential total pressure distortion and the swirl distortion are intensified at the aerodynamic interface plane, while the radial total pressure distortion intensity is decreased. The number of swirl pairs increases with the offset-to-length ratio. Moreover, the vortex formed by the central pressure differential-driven flow demonstrates greater stability than the vortex formed by the low-momentum wall-around flow, leading to a “siege” phenomenon. Both of the vortices generated by the low-momentum wall-around flow and the central pressure differential-driven flow are intensified as the offset-to-length ratio grows. Since the flow characteristics at the outlet of an S-duct could have great impacts on the aerodynamic performances of the downstream fan propulsion system, the results can provide hidden guidelines for high-performance design of a compact inlet duct and fan propulsor system.

papers.title: Wake topology and vortex structure evolution of a marine propeller with a fractured blade
papers.abstract: This study investigates the wake evolution and vortex instability mechanisms of a marine propeller under blade fracture conditions, with the objective of understanding how severe structural damage alters propulsive flow dynamics. High-fidelity simulations were conducted using the improved delayed detached-eddy simulation approach on a grid of 66.9 × 106 cells. A comparative analysis with an intact propeller was performed to evaluate the impact of fracture on wake topology and flow behavior. The results reveal that blade fracture significantly modifies the tip vortex system, leading to two distinct and successive vortex merging events at different downstream and radial locations. These merging processes are driven by mutual inductance and exhibit a leap-frogging mechanism, in which smaller vortices overtake and merge with larger ones. This sequence substantially enhances turbulence intensity and alters energy transfer within the wake. The instability of the tip vortex system was also found to directly influence the development of hub vortex instability, which was suppressed following the completion of tip vortex merging. These findings provide theoretical insights into the fluid dynamics of damaged marine propulsors and offer a physical reference for developing predictive tools and safety assessment strategies under extreme operating conditions.

papers.title: Fluid effects on the dilatancy of two-phase gravity-driven granular flows
papers.abstract: Volume fraction of solid grains plays a critical role in determining the dynamics of granular flows. The evolution of volume fraction is governed by flow dilatancy depending on the rheological behavior of solid–fluid mixtures and, hence, the pore fluid effects, which are dominated by apparent cohesion and viscous drag in unsaturated and saturated flows, respectively. Prevailing approaches for predicting volume fraction in wet granular flows using two-phase flow models have been proven valid for submerged granular flows or suspensions that conform to visco-inertial rheology. However, for unsaturated granular flows, widely accepted methods for volume fraction modeling remain lacking, due to the cohesive interaction mechanisms not yet being fully described. In this study, we conducted small-scale flume experiments using uniform pseudo-spherical ceramic beads, with initial water content progressively varied from dry to oversaturated states. The dynamics of the experimental flows were captured by sensor measurements and image processing techniques, with solid volume fraction evolution obtained by particle tracking velocimetry. We incorporated our experimental data into the μK (visco-inertial) and μIm (extended inertial) rheological frameworks constructed for two-phase flows and then contrasted the fitting performance of the two corresponding volume fraction scaling models, ΦK and ΦIm, through error analysis. We demonstrate here for the first time the excellent validity of ΦIm scaling for both unsaturated and saturated granular flows in which the dominated fluid effect ranges from apparent cohesion to viscous shear; by contrast, ΦK scaling shows significantly better applicability to saturated granular flows than to unsaturated flows.

papers.title: A methodology for predicting choked compressible gas flow in pores using dimensional analysis
papers.abstract: High-velocity compressible gas flow in porous media has been reported in several subsurface geological environments. As gases migrate through pore throats under high pressure gradient conditions, the velocity can increase to sonic levels and choked flow can occur, which affects the flow behaviors. In this study, pore-scale numerical simulations and dimensional analysis of the results have been carried out to describe the choking conditions. Two different numerical simulators have been prepared for two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) geometries, and relevant simulations have been designed, performed, and post-processed. It has been proved that both simulators can capture the unique behaviors of the process, and their result's accuracy has been validated using the available analytical solutions. A detailed dimensional analysis using the Buckingham π theorem has been performed to investigate the physics of the choking process. Quantification of different mechanisms has produced several dimensionless groups describing the interplay of various driving forces. Accordingly, different equations have been developed to determine the critical pressure ratio that choked flow occurs, and the maximum mass flow rates that pass through choked capillaries. The accuracy of the equations has been tested against the results of the 2D and 3D numerical simulations with satisfactory agreement.

papers.title: High-frequency nonlinear electromagnetic waves in magnetized electron–ion plasmas
papers.abstract: This work investigates the nonlinear propagation of high-frequency electromagnetic waves in a magnetized electron-ion plasma. By applying a multiple-scale perturbation method to the Maxwell–fluid system, we derive a nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) that governs the evolution of the wave envelope. Dispersion analysis reveals multiple solution branches, among which a stable low-frequency mode emerges, which makes it particularly suited for supporting localized nonlinear structures. To verify the theory, we examine three representative exact solutions of the NLSE, the Kuznetsov–Ma (K–M) breather, the bright soliton, and the Akhmediev breather, and validate them through three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations. The numerical results closely match the analytical predictions in both waveform structure and parameter dependence. We find that the amplitude and group velocity of the waveforms can be effectively tuned via plasma density and magnetic field strength, while the envelope width remains nearly constant, albeit with distinct values for each solution type. These findings demonstrate the existence, stability, and tunability of nonlinear electromagnetic structures in magnetized plasmas, providing a robust theoretical framework for experimental realization and potential applications in energy transport and wave-based diagnostics in both space and laboratory plasma environments.

papers.title: Insight into the molecular level detachment process of crude oil from the calcite surface by CO2 and CO2/N2 gas injection
papers.abstract: CO2 flooding and CO2/N2 mixed flooding have demonstrated great potential in enhancing oil and gas recovery. However, the molecular-level mechanistic details, especially within complex systems involving specific mineral surfaces like calcite, require further clarification. To clarify these processes, we employed molecular dynamics simulations to examine oil phase adsorption on calcite and the microscopic interactions among gas, oil, and calcite walls. The findings reveal that the highly polar compounds, like benzoic acid and n-heptanoic acid, exhibit stronger and more stable adsorption to the calcite surface, making them less prone to removal by pure CO2. In contrast, less polar hydrocarbons like n-heptane and n-dodecane form oil films that are more easily stripped. Additionally, during the mixed oil phase adsorption, polar compounds tend to localize closer to the wall. The gas phase (CO2, CO2/N2) displaces oil molecules primarily through competitive adsorption on calcite and dissolution of oil molecules. The interaction between gas and oil is stronger than that between oil and calcite, highlighting a key condition for effective oil detachment. CO2 exhibits stronger adsorption on calcite and greater oil solubility than N2. Accordingly, the interaction between the gas and oil phases, along with the oil stripping efficiency, increases with the CO2 content. van der Waals energy dominates interactions between CO2/N2 and hydrocarbons, as well as between calcite and these hydrocarbons. In contrast, electrostatic energy governs interactions between calcite and polar compounds. These findings offer molecular-level insights to guide gas injection strategies for enhanced oil recovery in carbonate formation.

papers.title: Numerical investigations on hydrogen-enriched fuel–air mixing characteristics in a single micromix nozzle for the gas turbine combustor
papers.abstract: Efficient hydrogen-enriched fuel–air mixing in a micromix combustor is a key factor that influences the combustion process, flow dynamics, and NOx formation. This study focuses on a single nozzle within a hydrogen-enriched micromix combustor to identify optimal fuel–air mixing strategies and explore the mixing mechanism. Through detailed numerical investigations of gas flow and geometric parameters by Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stoke and large eddy simulation, the influence on the cold-flow field and mixing performance is analyzed. The results indicate that the momentum ratio significantly affects the initial jet trajectory and vorticity magnitude; an optimal momentum ratio of approximately 30 yielded the best mixing characteristics. Preheating the air to 575 K was observed to increase turbulent viscosity and molecular kinetic energy, thereby promoting more effective momentum and mass diffusion rates. Increasing the number of fuel tubes and reducing the tube diameter expanded the diffusion region, improving hydrogen-enriched fuel–air interaction. In addition, higher mass flow rates resulted in deeper jet penetration, while the jet angle significantly influenced the spatial fuel distribution and vortex structure within the premixing tube. A properly adjusted jet angle of 30° led to the breakdown of large vortices into smaller structures, thereby maximizing the contact surface between hydrogen-enriched fuel and air and, thus, enhancing the mixing characteristics. Overall, the micromix combustor demonstrates strong potential for achieving efficient, small-scale fuel–air mixing, which is essential for clean, low-emission combustion.

papers.title: Numerical investigations on a tethered undulating foil near free surface using a smoothed-particle hydrodynamics method
papers.abstract: Research on biomimetic propulsion near the free surface offers valuable insights into the design and control of underwater biomimetic vehicles. This study employs the smoothed-particle hydrodynamics method to examine the propulsion of an undulating hydrofoil near the free surface, focusing on the effects of the Froude number (Fr) and the dimensionless submergence depth (H/L) on hydrodynamic performance, and analyzing results alongside vortex structures and free surface deformation. The main results indicate that the time-averaged thrust generated by the undulating hydrofoil tends to decrease with decreasing H/L and increasing Fr. At Re=4000, when H/L<1.5, the hydrofoil achieves the locally optimal propulsion efficiency at Fr=0.2, while for 1.5<H/L<2.5, it reaches its optimal efficiency at Fr=0.4. The hydrofoil is attracted to the free surface when Fr=0.2 and 0.4, whereas it experiences a repulsive force away from the surface when Fr=0.6. Additionally, a “P + S” type vortex street forms in the wake when the hydrofoil travels near the free surface. As Re increases, the variation trend of the hydrofoil's hydrodynamic characteristics with respect to H/L remains nearly consistent, while the number of small vortices in the wake gradually increases. The present method provides an effective approach for simulating bionic hydrodynamic problems near the free surface.

papers.title: Investigation on collapse dynamics of ice-sand bi-frictional mixtures using material point method
papers.abstract: Climate warming is associated with increased activity and significantly larger magnitudes of ice-rock avalanches in high-altitude mountainous regions. The contrasting physical properties of ice and rock contribute to the distinctive dynamics of ice-rock avalanches. In this study, the dynamics and packing characteristics of ice-rock avalanches were explored through numerical column collapse of ice-sand bi-frictional mixtures using the material point method with a concentration-dependent rheology model. The findings revealed that ice content and resistance-reducing effect of ice grains significantly affect the run-out distance. An effective initial aspect ratio (defined as the ratio of the initial height to the initial radius of the column) is scaled exponentially with ice content to derive a unified scaling relationship. Such a coefficient can be used to predict the flow regime, taking into account the influence of ice contents. This study concludes that ice-sand mixtures primarily exhibit inertial and liquid-like flow regimes as a result of low-friction interactions, thereby contributing to enhanced mobility. Finite-size analysis shows similarities with natural geophysical mass flows and can be extended to the prevention and mitigation of ice-rock avalanches.

papers.title: Janus drop impact on inclined non-wettable ridged surface
papers.abstract: The impact dynamics of Janus drops on inclined non-wettable ridged surfaces are systematically investigated using numerical simulations and theoretical models. The Janus configuration comprises two immiscible phases: a low-viscosity water part (W) and a high-viscosity glycerin–water solution part (G), with a stable interface. The combined effects of viscosity ratio, impact inertia, and surface inclination on separation behavior are analyzed by varying the normal (Wen) and tangential (Wet) Weber numbers. Higher viscosity ratios suppress tangential retraction of the G part, promoting asymmetric lateral retraction of the W part and facilitating separation. Regime maps are constructed for different viscosity ratios, presenting the separation conditions as functions of Wen and Wet. The normal Weber number primarily controls residence time by setting the initial spreading extent, while the tangential Weber number generates the morphological asymmetry (tangential deformation) that drives separation. Furthermore, a theoretical retraction model is developed to predict the residence time and demonstrates strong agreement with simulation results. This combined framework offers predictive understanding of Janus drop splitting dynamics and provides design guidelines for applications requiring efficient phase separation.

papers.title: Effects of confined boundaries on hovering flight using the unsteady vortex lattice method
papers.abstract: Insect flight adjacent to single or multiple walls during hovering or approaching perching is common in nature. The aerodynamic forces of insects flying near multiple surfaces may deviate significantly from those experienced during normal hover over a single ground. This work investigates the effects of multiple walls on a three-dimensional hovering wing. The aerodynamics of the hovering wing is calculated by the unsteady vortex lattice method (UVLM). To handle the flow instabilities associated with strong wing-wake and wake-wake interactions in hover, a novel treatment of wake straining is incorporated with a vortex core growth model that stabilizes the numerical simulation and avoid numerical dispersion. The treatment significantly extends the capability of the UVLM and improves its accuracy in the modeling of wings during hovering flight. The ground effects are modeled by a lattice of bound vortices. To study the effects of multiple walls, two cases are considered: a pair of hovering wings in a U-shaped channel and between top and bottom walls. The lift coefficients and the flow fields are analyzed by varying the distance between the wing and the walls. Three typical regimes are identified due to the walls: force enhancement, force reduction and force recovery. The lift coefficient of the wing in the U-shaped channel is lower than the wing hovering over a single ground, while that of the wing between the top and the bottom walls is higher. These observations are closely related to the changes in wake and vortex structures causing changes in the downwash and effective angle of attack of the wing.

papers.title: Nonlinear bifurcation dynamics of laser-induced encapsulated microbubbles under acoustic cavitation: Influence of thermal and viscoelastic parameters
papers.abstract: This study investigates the nonlinear dynamics of laser-induced encapsulated microbubbles under acoustic cavitation, focusing on the bifurcation behavior of the bubble expansion ratio. A high-precision laser radiation technique is employed to heat the surrounding fluid locally to a critical temperature, triggering controlled bubble nucleation and subsequent oscillatory dynamics. By analyzing the bifurcation diagrams of the radial expansion ratio against key control parameters, such as laser intensity, fluid viscosity, and encapsulation properties, we characterize the transition between stable oscillations, period-doubling bifurcation, and chaotic regimes. The results reveal how viscoelastic encapsulation influences damping mechanisms and stability thresholds, offering insights into optimizing microbubble performance in biomedical and industrial applications, including ultrasound contrast imaging and targeted drug delivery. In particular, increased shell viscosity and acoustic frequency were found to suppress chaotic oscillations, while elevated temperature and low-frequency driving promote bifurcation and instability. These findings provide practical design guidelines for tuning acoustic and thermal parameters to ensure controlled cavitation and enhance the efficacy and safety of microbubble-assisted therapies.

papers.title: Experimental study on seepage characteristics of soil–rock mixtures with different fractal dimensions of particle size in fault zone
papers.abstract: This paper takes the Sanshan Island fault zone as the engineering background, conducts permeability tests, and combines fractal theory to study the permeability characteristics of soil–rock mixtures (S-RMs) with different rock-block proportions (20%, 30%, 40%, 50%, 60%, and 70%) in the fault zone and their corresponding relationship with fractal dimensions of particle size (FDPS). The main conclusions drawn are as follows: (1) The S-RM within the Sanshan Island fault zone exhibits fractal characteristics, with FDPS ranging from 2.05 to 2.59 for both soil and rock-block particles. (2) The linear fitting degree between the rock-block proportion of the S-RM and the fractal dimensions of particle size of the rock-block particles reaches 0.92, which can be used as a bridge to study the permeability characteristics of S-RM with different fractal dimensions of particle size. (3) As the seepage pressure increases, the permeability coefficient of the S-RM gradually increases, and the relationship between seepage pressure and permeability coefficient can be described by a power function. (4) As the FDPS increases, the permeability coefficient of S-RM shows a trend of first decreasing and then increasing. When the seepage pressure is 0.03 MPa, the FDPS increases from 2.227 to 2.647, and the permeability coefficient decreases from 5.47 × 10−6 to 3.14 × 10−6 cm/s. During the process of increasing the FDPS from 2.647 to 2.899, the permeability coefficient increased from 3.14 × 10−6 to 4.97 × 10−6 cm/s. (5) For S-RM with the same rock-block proportion, as the particle size and distribution range of the rock blocks increase, the fractal dimension of the particle size of the S-RM gradually increases, and the permeability coefficient gradually decreases.

papers.title: Measuring the critical length scale of percolation of fine particles under vibration using discrete element method
papers.abstract: Understanding percolation is vital for improving transport and mixing in multiple industrial applications. The vibrated packed bed system is ideal for studying percolation as it provides good control over various parameters. Dynamic voids refer to the continuously evolving gaps within the vibrated granular system. These gaps play an active role in determining the extent of percolation. To quantify the impact of these dynamic voids, a novel index, the critical length scale of percolation, is introduced. This index is defined by a new 80–20 criterion representing the maximum void size that allows free particle percolation at a steady state. The results reveal that non-spherical particles have a lower critical length scale of percolation. Increasing the fine particle composition or adding intermediate particles reduces the critical length scale of percolation. Multiple machine learning models—including Linear Regression, Polynomial Regression, Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Random Forest (RF), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)—are trained on data from Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations to predict the percentage of percolated fine. A subsequent error analysis identified the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model as the top performer, achieving R2 value of 0.97. The model confirmed that the particle size ratio is a more dominant factor than sphericity in governing percolation. This machine learning model effectively generalizes the Discrete Element Method (DEM) findings, providing a powerful and accurate predictive tool for industrial applications.

papers.title: Study on droplet breakup characteristics in the Y-shaped microchannel based on the accelerated volumetric lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: The advancement of point-of-care testing (POCT) microfluidic systems critically relies on the rational design of topologically complex microchannel networks governed by multiphase flow dynamics. This study develops an approach based on the Graphics Processing Unit accelerated volumetric lattice Boltzmann method with the Shan–Chen multiphase model to investigate the droplet breakup characteristics in benchmark Y-shaped microchannels, revealing: (1) three universal stages—compression, compression-stretching, and rapid rupture (capillary dominance); (2) spatiotemporal characteristics (breakup time, T*, daughter droplet volume ratio, Vr) affected by the geometrical parameters and capillary numbers; and (3) critical transition at Cacritical=0.108 where external dominance (Ca>Cacritical) yields slight T* reduction (enhanced by deformation at Ca>0.135) with stable Vr, while internal dominance (Ca<Cacritical) causes sharp decreases in both; (4) parabolic Vr/T* vs initial position relationships showing minimal T* at the symmetric center; and (5) T* follows a parabolic law minimized at RB=0.294 ± 0.009, and Vr adheres to power-law scaling, both with angle-dependent coefficients. These insights establish essential parametric dependencies for POCT topology optimization.

papers.title: Effect of upper end wall boundary layer suction on high-load helium compressor performance in thorium molten salt reactors
papers.abstract: The performance of the helium compressor is a crucial factor in determining the efficiency of thermal-to-work conversion in thorium molten salt reactors. The high-load design approach can efficiently increase the pressure ratio while minimizing the number of compressor stages. However, due to this design technique, compressor flow passages become narrower with short blades. Consequently, the impact of the end wall boundary layer on the compressor's performance becomes a point of concern. The end wall boundary layer can be effectively controlled and regulated through the suction technique. This paper investigates the effect of suction holes at various positions and angles impacting the performance characteristic of multi-stage high-load helium compressors. This research concluded that the optimum suction axial position is at 0.3 of the suction-side arc length, the optimum circumferential position is 2.0 mm, and an angle of 120° can decrease the total-pressure loss coefficient by 10.47%. Moreover, due to the suction effect, the efficiency and total pressure ratio at the design point can be improved up to 0.29% and 0.129%, respectively.

papers.title: Control of monodisperse droplet size in microfluidics: A combined experimental and numerical investigation
papers.abstract: Monodisperse droplets, characterized by their uniform size distribution and well-controlled physicochemical properties, have found extensive applications in drug delivery, bioengineering, and food science. However, experimentally tuning droplet size typically requires multiple rounds of photomask design and microfluidic chip fabrication, which is costly and inefficient. To address this, we developed a numerical model for droplet generation in microfluidics based on the Volume of Fluid method in Fluent. The model was experimentally validated, achieving a maximum relative error below 5.43%. We systematically investigated the droplet formation mechanism, with a particular focus on the influence of structural and operational parameters on the control of droplet size. Three flow-focusing chips with dispersed phase inlet widths of 20, 40, and 70 μm enabled controlled modulation of droplet diameters ranging from 13.6 to 108.55 μm. Pressure variations at the geometric center of the flow-focusing structure inlet region revealed four distinct stages of droplet formation: lagging, filling, necking, and detachment. The associated pressure curves exhibited periodic oscillations, serving as a reliable indicator of monodispersity and generation stability. Structural parameters significantly affected both droplet size and frequency. The chip with a 20 μm inlet generated droplets at frequencies ranging from 625 to 7695 Hz, markedly higher than those of the 70 μm inlet (66.67–715 Hz). This study demonstrates the capability of high-precision, low-cost control of droplet size via numerical simulation. The findings provide theoretical insights for the design of microfluidic chips and practical guidance for applications in drug formulation, cell encapsulation, and microcapsule synthesis.

papers.title: Propeller noise performance prediction based on artificial intelligence method and rotor modal relationships
papers.abstract: Efficient acquisition of high-confidence noise performance data is essential for optimizing propeller noise characteristics. A machine learning-based model, referred to as the Propeller Noise Spectrum Deep Learning (PNSDL) model, has been proposed for the prediction of propeller noise. This algorithm integrates the Noise Spectrum Deep Learning (NSDL) model to identify and predict the deep spectral noise features of the propeller, while a CNN-MHA(CM) model, based on rotor modal relationships, is employed to predict and correct the pure tone noise features of the propeller. Based on the flow field and noise mechanism of counter-rotating propellers calculated using the nonlinear harmonic method, this study conducts a quantitative analysis and discussion of the model's prediction performance based on wind tunnel noise test data. The results demonstrate that the PNSDL, by rotor modal relationships, substantially enhances the NSDL's ability to recognize and predict complex propeller noise features. For the prediction of single-rotor propeller spectral noise, 85% of the predicted conditions exhibit a relative error of less than 5%, while for counter-rotating propellers, 87.17% of the predicted conditions show a relative error of less than 5%. A primary cause of prediction errors in the PNSDL for certain propeller pure tone noises lies in the limited explanatory power of the rotor modal relationships for complex propeller noise features. Continued exploration of more intricate noise mechanisms and their integration into the model is expected to further enhance the model's prediction accuracy.

papers.title: Multiscale analysis of diffusioosmotic transport of micropolar fluids in microchannels
papers.abstract: The ability of the applied chemical concentration gradients to move the fluid, i.e., diffusioosmosis, requires a more robust mathematical model to predict the interdependency of the solute dispersion and the fluid movement. The present work illustrates the influence of applied concentration gradient on the movement of micropolar fluid within the microchannel using the mathematical model of diffusioosmosis. The model consists of a rectangular channel filled with micropolar fluid in which the solute concentration gradient is imposed, having a standard Gaussian distribution. The model for combined advection-diffusion, i.e., Taylor's dispersion model, is employed to regulate the solute distribution. The diffusioosmotic pressure gradient purely drives the micropolar fluid through the diffusioosmotic slip flow at the wall. A multi-timescale approach is utilized to obtain the closed-form solution of the flow and concentration profiles. The combined approach of homogenization and the Laplace transformation is used to find the analytical expressions of the concentration profile. The pure diffusion and the solute wall interaction induce the slip flow at the wall, which further contributes to solute dispersion by advection, leading to the combined advection-diffusion process. The two different boundary constraints for microrotation at the wall, including no-spin (NS) and no-couple stress (NCS), have been thoroughly studied. The graphical illustrations of the various dynamic quantities provide a comprehensive analysis of their physical behavior under the influence of relevant flow parameters. It is noted that for stronger diffusioosmosis, all the dynamic quantities, including the velocity profile, rotational velocity, effective diffusivity, wall shear stress (WSS), and mean concentration, are sensitive to micropolar fluid parameters like micro-scale parameter and coupling number. It is observed that the velocity profile and mean concentration show less variation concerning different parameters for no-couple stress at the wall, compared to the no spin of the microparticles at the wall. Further, the outcomes from the mathematical model advance the understanding of fluid flow induced by concentration gradients, which can assist the researchers in analyzing drug delivery, the separation process, and various species transport applications in the novel framework of diffusioosmosis.

papers.title: A novel model of unsteady fluctuations of supersonic mainstream influenced by a forward-facing-step-induced shock
papers.abstract: To develop the noise reduction strategies required for constructing a quiet wind tunnel, this paper focuses on the critical mechanism of noise amplification in the supersonic mainstream across shock waves, which are often generated by uneven wall surfaces in the wind tunnel, such as a forward-facing step (FFS). Supported by datasets from experiments and Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS), a novel theoretical model has been proposed for predicting post-shock mainstream fluctuations based on the given signals upstream of the shock. This model successfully incorporates the unsteadiness of moving shock waves. It is derived by decomposing the shock wave relationships using Reynolds decomposition and reveals that pre-shock fluctuations of pressure, Mach number, and shock angle collectively contribute to the post-shock levels of pressure fluctuations. The conclusions obtained from the theoretical analysis have been verified experimentally. Assessments demonstrate that this model can predict the amplitude of post-shock pressure fluctuations with high accuracy, with an uncertainty level below 0.21%. Meanwhile, the frequency spectrum is also a critical parameter for characterizing pressure fluctuations. The characteristic frequencies of post-shock pressure fluctuations, as derived from pre-multiplied spectral analysis, show close agreement between the theoretical predictions and DNS results. This is crucial for accurately quantifying and suppressing unsteady wave disturbances in the design of quiet wind tunnels. The unsteady oscillation characteristics of the shock induced by the FFS, as well as the disturbance characteristics in the mainstream, were studied using high-frequency pressure sensors in the experiments. The experimental pre-multiplied spectra reveal the coexistence of two distinct peaks in the mainstream fluctuations, for the current micro-step case (h/δ = 0.058). One peak corresponds to a low-frequency signal at St = 0.016 (679.8 Hz), which is attributed to the unsteady motion of the shock wave. The other is a high-frequency peak at St = 0.38 × (15.75 kHz), in close agreement with DNS results, corresponding to disturbances in the boundary layer propagating into the mainstream along the Mach line.

papers.title: Quantitative study of the influence of masks on airflow dynamics during breathing using particle image velocimetry
papers.abstract: The dynamics of airflow are critical to respiratory disease transmission, particularly in indoor environments and industrial settings with high particulate matter, where airflow governs the dispersion and inhalation of infectious aerosols and dust. This study uses particle image velocimetry to perform a quantitative analysis of airflow during breathing, with and without face masks, using live human participants. We investigate three scenarios: no mask, a 2-ply cloth mask, and a filtering face piece 2 (FFP2) mask with an exhalation valve. Results show that cloth masks reduce mean exhalation velocity by 70% and maximum jet velocity from 4.2 m/s to under 2 m/s, while FFP2 masks with valves reduce peak velocities by 45.2% and redirect airflow downward. Directional analysis reveals that cloth masks deflect exhaled air forward and upward (30°–90°), increasing the potential for long-range droplet suspension, whereas valved FFP2 masks direct flow downward (330°), limiting forward dispersion. We further adapt multiphase puff models to quantify the transport of respiratory droplets ranging from 5 to 50 μm. These adapted models, which incorporate drag and entrainment effects, show that omitting drag can overestimate droplet travel by up to 1.5 orders of magnitude (e.g., 5 μm droplets can travel 15 m vs 0.5–1.5 m when drag is included). During inhalation, we find that droplets up to 10 μm can be drawn into the respiratory tract from distances up to 40 cm. These findings demonstrate the significant influence of mask type on airflow and droplet dispersion patterns, providing critical insights for public health guidelines and mask design in airborne disease mitigation.

papers.title: A matrix preconditioning framework for physics-informed neural networks based on the adjoint method
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a popular approach for solving forward and inverse problems involving partial differential equations (PDEs). Compared to fully connected neural networks, PINNs based on convolutional neural networks (PICNNs) offer advantages in the hard enforcement of boundary conditions and in reducing the computational cost of partial derivatives. However, PICNNs still struggle with slow convergence and even failure in some scenarios. In this study, we propose a matrix preconditioning method to improve the convergence of PICNNs. Specifically, we combine automatic differentiation with matrix coloring to compute the Jacobian matrix of the PDE system, which is used to construct the preconditioner via incomplete lower-upper factorization. We subsequently use the preconditioner to scale the PDE residual in the loss function to reduce the condition number of the Jacobian matrix, which is key to improving the convergence of PICNNs. To overcome the incompatibility between automatic differentiation and triangular solves in the preconditioning, we also design a framework based on the adjoint method to compute the gradients of the loss function with respect to the network parameters. By numerical experiments, we validate that the proposed method significantly accelerates the convergence of PICNNs and successfully solves the multi-scale problem and the high Reynolds number problem, in both of which PICNNs fail to produce satisfactory results.

papers.title: Electrohydrodynamic breakup of a leaky dielectric drop in pressure-driven flow
papers.abstract: We numerically investigate the breakup dynamics of a leaky dielectric droplet migrating through a confined microchannel under the combined influence of Poiseuille flow and a transverse electric field. The multiphase flow problem has been modeled using a coupled Navier–Stokes equation and phase-field method. Deformation and breakup behavior of the drop have been studied extensively for wide ranges of electrical capillary number (Cae), capillary number (Ca), electrical conductivity ratio (R), and electrical permittivity ratio (S). Five distinct breakup modes are observed: equatorial breakup (EB), equatorial polar breakup (EPB), polar breakup (PB), oblate fish breakup (OFB), and oblate breakup unstable (OBU). The novel EB regime is characterized by the bending of the prolate-deforming droplet (R > S) and its subsequent disintegration into identical twins exactly at the channel centerline as a collective consequence of higher viscous force (high Ca) and strong electric field (high Cae). The EPB mode demonstrates characteristics of both EB and PB regimes at high R and moderate to low S. For an oblate deforming droplet (S > R), at large Cae, we identify an intriguing OFB mode, marked by a wavy interfacial morphology mimicking fish motion, which eventually breaks from crest and trough locations. Further increase in Cae accelerates this breakup process to such an extent that it transforms to an entirely unstable disintegration mode (OBU). Finally, the regime diagram predicted by our study reveals how the interplay of pertinent forces and electrical properties governs droplet breakup, offering insight and useful design criteria for microfluidic applications.

papers.title: Mechanism of tip clearance leakage vortex evolution and energy loss characteristics in gas–liquid multiphase pumps based on vortex dynamics theory
papers.abstract: In the extremely complex environment of offshore extraction, the stability and reliability of the helical–axial multiphase pump have become a critical focus in both practical engineering and theoretical research. The tip clearance leakage flow induced by the tip clearance between the impeller blades and the pump casing is one of the key factors constraining the performance of multiphase pumps. Building upon existing research, this paper proposes the Reynolds-averaged transport equation for the enstrophy of the rigid vorticity based on gas–liquid two-phase flow. This equation is coupled with the mean kinetic energy transport equation to systematically analyze the energy loss mechanisms and vortex dynamics characteristics caused by the generation and dissipation processes of the tip clearance leakage vortex. The study found that the tip clearance region exhibits a high turbulence kinetic energy generation rate, accounting for 34% to 44% of the total flow loss within the impeller, due to the strong shear interaction between the leakage flow and the main flow. Vorticity diagnostics revealed that the liquid phase continuously dominates the flow in this region due to centrifugal gas–liquid separation, intensifying viscous dissipation. Analysis based on the Reynolds-averaged transport equation for the enstrophy of the rigid vorticity indicates that the evolution of rigid vorticity in the main flow passage is dominated by the Coriolis Force Term; the generation of shear vorticity is controlled by the Vorticity Stretching Term; and the Baroclinic Torque Term couples with the gas–liquid density gradient to synergistically influence the vortex structure. The application of this equation effectively elucidates the gas–liquid two-phase regulation laws governing Tip clearance flow within multiphase pumps. The research results provide an important theoretical basis for optimizing the structural design of the tip clearance in multiphase pumps and enhancing their hydraulic performance and operational stability.

papers.title: Mesoscopic kinetic model of wettability: From molecular dynamics to thermodynamics
papers.abstract: We present a mesoscopic kinetic model for the wettability of the liquid–vapor fluids on a solid substrate by handling microscopic molecular interactions. The fluid internal potential energy is refined to incorporate the solid–fluid molecular interaction, and then the usual macroscopic thermodynamic quantities are consistently found. An effective solid density containing microscopic details is identified to determine the macroscopic state of complete drying, partial wetting, or complete wetting. Furthermore, a concise graphical rule is derived for the contact angle in the partial wetting state. This mesoscopic kinetic model of wettability, validated by consistent lattice Boltzmann modeling, successfully bridges microscopic molecular interactions and macroscopic thermodynamic properties.

papers.title: Channel-assisted Fourier neural operator for high-fidelity far-wake prediction of a wind turbine under yawed conditions
papers.abstract: The channel-assisted Fourier neural operator (CFNO) for real-time, high-resolution, long-horizon prediction of yawed wind-turbine far wakes is introduced. CFNO injects yaw through a channel-assisted layer and combines a post-channel-mixing depthwise-separable spectral convolution (DSSC) with real-valued weights and residual-enhanced Fourier layers. These choices stabilize long autoregressive predictions and reduce parameters to about 23% of the Fourier neural operator (FNO) and about 50% of DSSC-FNO. CFNO is trained and validated on large-eddy simulation (LES) produced with an actuator-disk model with rotation (ADM-R), which closely reproduces far-wake behavior. It achieves 0.89% error on a 180 × 70 high-fidelity far-wake grid (up to x/D=12), exceeds an FNO baseline, and runs at millisecond-to-sub-second latency on a single GPU. These capabilities enable digital-twin-assisted wake steering and differentiable, yaw-based model-predictive control with potential to reduce wake losses, moderate cyclic loads, and stabilize aggregate power.

papers.title: Supersonic to hypersonic transition of magnetized shocks with viscous dissipation
papers.abstract: This study presents a rigorous numerical investigation into the interplay between magnetic fields and high-speed flow dynamics across supersonic and hypersonic flow regimes. Employing advanced computational techniques, we quantify the impact of varying Mach (M) and Reynolds (Re) numbers on flow discontinuities, with particular focus on shock wave behavior under magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) conditions. The key solutions are derived for critical physical parameters such as compression rate (κ), Mach number ratio (M2M1), Cowling number ratio (C2C1), Reynolds number ratio (Re2Re1), pressure ratio (p2p1), magnetic pressure ratio (h2h1), and entropy production (S2−S1) across the shock wave. This study analyzes the combined effects of magnetic fields and viscous dissipation on shock waves in supersonic and hypersonic ideal MHD flows. A 1D model, solved using Rankine–Hugoniot conditions, reveals that stronger magnetic fields reduce post-shock pressure ratios by up to 20% while increasing downstream Mach numbers and generation. Notably, viscous, inviscid, and ideal gas flow simulations, both with and without magnetic coupling, exhibit strong alignment with the benchmark studies of Cavus [“On the effects of viscosity on the shock waves for a hydrodynamical case—Part I: Basic mechanism,” Adv. Astron. 2013, 1 (2013)], corroborating the numerical fidelity of our approach. This work validates its novel approach through rigorous statistical comparison with established studies, employing percentage change analysis, mean value differences, standard deviation measurements, and 95% confidence intervals. The results demonstrate significantly enhanced predictive capability relative to prior methods. Furthermore, the analysis reveals a previously under-characterized phenomenon: magnetic field effects exhibit pronounced Mach number dependence, becoming substantially more influential in hypersonic regimes compared to supersonic conditions. This finding addresses a critical gap in existing shock wave literature. This consistency underscores the robustness of our methodology in capturing MHD flow interactions under extreme velocity conditions.

papers.title: Spiral tumor cell particle inertial focusing device based on secondary flow structure enhancement
papers.abstract: The isolation of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) from blood is critical for clinical treatment, disease prediction, and numerous other applications. The use of rectangular cross section spirals for CTCs isolation has been reported extensively. But a high Reynolds numbers (Re) is required to achieve high target cell separation purity for the existing device. The present work proposes a novel microfluidic platform that combines a single-loop rectangular cross section spiral channel with an innovative array of convex structures, enabling continuous and highly effective separation of two types of CTCs [(human breast cancer cells (MCF-7) and A549 (human lung cancer cells)] from blood cells at lower Re. The array of convex structures enables to evaluate the focusing of target cells because an extra certain lift force is generated. The COMSOL Multiphysics 6.0 software and the finite element method were utilized to achieve the optimization of the geometries of array in detail. Additionally, the particle trajectory was studied under the distinct Re. The polymethyl methacrylate was utilized to construct the chip with an engraving machine. The polystyrene beads (24 μm), which imitate the MCF-7 cells, were used to verify the device performance. In the simulation, the optimized design with a single loop achieved 100% separation (24 , 15 , 10 , and 8 μm) at a Re of 68. Thus, this device holds promising potential as a sample pretreatment tool for clinical diagnosis.

papers.title: Capture–release dynamics of nanoparticles in a viscoelastic hydrogel under an oscillating magnetic field
papers.abstract: A study was conducted to understand the effect of superparamagnetic nanoparticles on a viscoelastic hydrogel subject to an oscillating magnetic field directed tangent to the hydrogel surface. A capture–release kinetic model was formulated for the dynamic transition of nanoparticles between a freely oscillating state in the Newtonian solvent and a hydrogel-bound captured state. The viscoelastic hydrogel is modeled as an Oldroyd-B fluid. A parametric analysis was conducted to understand regimes of system behavior in terms of key dimensionless parameters. Increasing the viscous-to-thermal work ratio enhances detachment, while higher adhesion energy promotes particle retention by the hydrogel. The magnetic field amplitude controls both uptake rate and oscillatory strength, and the relative matrix-solvent velocity shapes the harmonic content of the response. A bifurcation was observed at a critical value of the ratio of retardation to relaxation times. For values of this ratio less than the critical value, the system exhibits multi-periodic elastic-regime responses, whereas for values of the ratio above the critical ratio, the system collapses into mono-periodic viscous-regime behavior. The capture rate coefficient includes an absolute value, so its product with sinusoidal magnetic forcing yields only odd harmonics in the response. Elastic waves propagate from the no-slip base, and height-averaged particle counts oscillate at twice the driving frequency. These findings elucidate how nonlinear capture–release kinetics and viscoelastic memory produce multi-periodic and odd-harmonic-dominated dynamics, informing the design of switchable smart materials for on-demand drug delivery and biofilm control.

papers.title: Flow and aeroacoustics control of an inclined wall-mounted cylinder using porous coatings
papers.abstract: This study investigates the evolution of flow structures and aerodynamic noise generation around inclined wall-mounted cylinders (FWMCs) at a Reynolds number of 50 000 using large eddy simulation (LES) and the Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings acoustic analogy. The influence of inclination angles on flow dynamics and acoustic responses is examined in detail, with a particular focus on the control effects of porous coatings under various inclinations. The analysis covers aerodynamic forces, shear layer evolution, wake reconstruction, and the development of three-dimensional (3D) vortex structures, highlighting how inclination modifies wake behavior and the distribution of unsteady acoustic sources. The results show that inclination angle significantly alters vortex shedding modes and wake deflection characteristics. Forward inclinations enhance surface attachment and induce asymmetric wake dynamics, while backward inclinations promote vortex flattening. These effects lead to nonlinear changes in drag and noise generation. The introduction of porous coatings improves wall permeability and enhances the dissipation of flow disturbances, effectively suppressing shear layer instabilities and weakening large-scale vortex shedding and noise radiation. Under inclination angles of θ=0° and θ=−45°, the peak sound pressure levels (SPLs) are reduced by 26.5% and 25.9%, respectively, indicating improved wake stability and more localized noise sources. Furthermore, in the backward inclination scenario, excellent noise reduction performance is observed, with a maximum peak sound pressure level reduction of 29.7% at θ=45°. These findings demonstrate that changes in inclination induce more complex three-dimensional flow-acoustic coupling around FWMCs, confirming the effectiveness of porous materials in modulating the flow field and suppressing aerodynamic noise under intricate three-dimensional (3D) wake conditions. The outcomes offer valuable theoretical support for the passive flow control design of bluff-body structures in practical engineering applications.

papers.title: Investigation on the liquid phase diffusion of an acid dye in aqueous solution by employing a novel diaphragm cell method
papers.abstract: In order to investigate and enhance the diffusion process of dyes to fiber, the liquid phase diffusion behavior of the C.I. Acid Red 134 (AR-134) dye was investigated by employing a novel diaphragm cell method. The effects of process factors on the dye liquid phase diffusion properties were systematically discussed and a theoretical model of the relationship between diffusion coefficient and process factors was established. Meanwhile, an Arrhenius model and a polynomial model were established to explore the relationship between temperature, concentration of the dye, and liquid phase diffusion coefficients of the dye. Moreover, the isothermal diffusion rate curve of the dye was built, and liquid phase diffusion dynamics of the dye were illustrated. The results indicate that in order to improve the dye liquid phase diffusion properties, the flow rate and temperature should be properly increased, and the concentration of Peragal O and sodium sulfate should be decreased. Meanwhile, the relationship between dye liquid phase diffusion coefficients and temperature conforms to the Arrhenius equation under the same concentration of the dye. In addition, dye liquid diffusion coefficients at the same temperature can be expressed as concentration polynomials. Particularly, the liquid phase diffusion behavior of the dye was more consistent with a quasi-first-order kinetic model and was not controlled by a chemical adsorption mechanism. The obtained results supplemented traditional dyeing theories on the liquid phase diffusion process of acid dyes, providing an application foundation for new ideas and methods in the research and development of green and high-efficiency dyeing technology.

papers.title: Wetted area of droplet impact onto micropillar arrays with various pillar geometries
papers.abstract: This study utilizes the volume of fluid method and dynamic contact angle model to numerically investigate the wetted area dynamics during droplet impact on square, cylindrical, and triangular pillar arrays. User-defined functions are implemented to real-time monitor wetted areas on the array substrate, pillar side surfaces, and pillar top surfaces with dimensionless parameters like the wetted area ratio (maximum to steady-state wetted area ratio) defined for analysis. The influences of Weber number (We) and static wall contact angle (θ) on wetted area are systematically examined. The results show that in triangular pillar arrays, the pinning effect restricts droplet spreading and retraction, yielding the smallest wetted area ratio. However, the side surface wetted area and steady-state total wetted area are the largest among the arrays studied. In square pillar arrays, the groove-driven effect dominates to produce the largest wetted area. Cylindrical pillar arrays, with smooth surface curvature facilitating flow division, exhibit the optimal bottom surface wetting and relatively rapid droplet retraction. Although the top surface wetted area is minimal, a pinning–depinning–repinning cycle occurs at low θ. The side surface wetted area constitutes the primary component of the total wetted area, accounting for the highest proportion.
