Micropillar geometry predominantly dictates the fractional distribution of wetted areas, with We and θ exerting weak influence. These findings furnish both quantitative foundations and engineering insights for designing hydrophilic microstructure surfaces.

papers.title: Characteristics of overburden fracture spatial distribution in abandoned mines goaf group
papers.abstract: Developing and utilizing the remaining methane resources in abandoned mines could reduce resource waste, protect the environment, and promote the sustainable development of the coal industry. However, determining the distribution characteristics of the fracture space in abandoned mines was the prerequisite and basis for the effective identification of methane-enriched areas and the precise development and utilization of resources. At present, most abandoned mines had goaf group. Compared with the mining of a single working face, the distribution patterns of their overburden fracture fields might be different. Based on this, taking the east area of Panji No.1 Coal Mine in Huainan as the research background, the three-dimension distinct element code discrete element software was used to construct a three-dimensional numerical model of the stope. A calculation program for the fractal dimension of overburden fractures in goaf group was proposed, and the fractal characteristics of the overburden fracture field were analyzed. The coal-rock strata in the dip direction of the goaf group were divided into three zones: the concentrated fracture-development zone (I), the recompaction zone (II), and the top-separation zone (III). The distribution range of the dominant channels for methane migration was determined. Meanwhile, based on the bulking characteristics of the caved rocks in the caved zone and the subsidence characteristics of the overburden in the fractured zone, the fracture porosity distribution function was obtained, and the three-dimensional distribution law of the overburden fracture porosity in goaf group was expounded. The research results indicated that: for each goaf within the goaf group, the fracture porosity of the caved zone decreased continuously under the influence of repeated mining. Its distribution presented a “shovel” shape, with a higher fracture porosity around the goaf and a lower one in the middle of the goaf. The peak value of the fracture porosity reached 32.5% and was located at the upper and lower corners of each goaf. The fracture porosity in the fractured zone continuously increased under the influence of repeated mining. The distribution of fracture porosity in the middle presented a “double-hump” shape. The fracture porosity was large in the outer convex areas and small in the inner concave areas, with a peak fracture porosity reaching 14.3%. The distribution of fracture porosity at the top presented a “single-peak” shape. The fracture porosity was small around the goaf and large in the middle of the goaf, with a peak fracture porosity of 16.7%. The fractal dimension values of overburden fractures and the distribution of fracture porosity on the side of the section coal pillar increased significantly compared with those on the side of the boundary coal pillar. The fractures in the caved zones on both sides of the section coal pillar penetrated each other, forming a fracture-intensive area, which served as the dominant channel for methane migration in the goaf group of abandoned mines. The research results provided a basis for the precise identification of methane-enriched areas in the east area of Panji No.1 Coal Mine and laid a theoretical foundation for the evaluation of methane resources in abandoned mines.

papers.title: Experimental study of quasi-static collapse and flow dynamics in low-saturation wet granular columns
papers.abstract: The transient collapse behavior of low-saturation wet granular materials under quasi-static conditions is crucial for geophysical and engineering applications but remains poorly understood. This study investigates the collapse dynamics of wet granular columns using two-dimensional and three-dimensional experiments with precisely controlled release velocities. A servo-driven lifting mechanism enables accurate regulation of release conditions, and a flow-state identification approach based on the advancing front velocity is proposed to distinguish between quasi-static and inertial flow states. Three distinct quasi-static collapse regimes—delayed transient collapse, intermittent collapse, and prolonged collapse—are identified, with transitions governed primarily by initial column height and release velocity, forming well-defined regions in the proposed phase diagram. A theoretical model is developed to predict the restabilizing height at which the collapsed material temporarily stabilizes, and its predictions, incorporating a velocity-dependent failure angle, show strong agreement with experimental results. Additionally, particle size is found to significantly influence capillary cohesion and collapse regime boundaries. The proposed framework captures the combined effects of column geometry, release velocity, and particle size, offering a predictive tool for wet granular flows and advancing the understanding of their behavior in both natural and engineered systems.

papers.title: Tribute to Dr. John Michael Dealy and special collection in Physics of Fluids
Thermodynamically consistent numerical method for two-phase carbonate acidizing with capillarity effects
papers.abstract: Matrix acidizing is an effective technique to promote the porosity and permeability in carbonate formations, thereby enhancing the oil production rate. In oil-saturated reservoirs, the carbonate acidizing process could be a typical oil–water two-phase flow rather than the widely investigated single-phase flow. The existence of capillarity effects makes numerical modeling of the coupled two-phase carbonate acidizing process more complicated and challenging compared to the single-phase flow. In this paper, we first introduce the concept of free energies for reactive two-phase flow with capillarity, and then, guided by the second law of thermodynamics, we establish a thermodynamically consistent mathematical model for the coupled two-phase carbonate acidizing process, which satisfies an energy dissipation law. Due to the complexity of the physical process, the model consists of a number of strongly nonlinear and fully coupled equations. To efficiently solve this model in practice, we further propose a linearized and decoupled numerical method that is able to inherit the thermodynamical consistency, i.e., the energy dissipation law. Numerical results are also provided to show the potential applicability of the model and numerical method, especially demonstrating that capillarity between binary fluids has significant effects on the carbonate acidizing process.

papers.title: Atmospheric stability effect on wind farm flow and performance
papers.abstract: Large-eddy simulations are used to investigate how surface-layer stability (from strongly stable to strongly unstable) and free-atmosphere stratification influence wind farm flow and power output. Increased stability reduces turbulence intensity (TI), limiting wake recovery and decreasing power to downstream turbines. These effects are amplified under strong free-atmosphere stratification, which confines the internal boundary layer, suppresses vertical mixing, and reduces momentum entrainment, leading to stronger velocity deficits and greater power losses. Blockage effects, including entrance-region wind speed reduction, also intensify with increasing stratification—more so in the free atmosphere than in the surface layer. In strongly stratified cases with low Froude numbers (Fr ≲ 1.2), pronounced standing gravity waves form, accelerating the flow in the exit region and near wake, but slowing wake recovery further downstream due to reduced ambient TI. While wake recovery is generally delayed under stronger stratification, wind speed recovers more slowly than TI, particularly when free-atmosphere stratification is strong. Overall, the results highlight the need to consider both surface-layer and free-atmosphere stability when assessing wind farm aerodynamics and performance.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal distribution of liquid mass in transient sprays using X-ray tomography from a laser-driven plasma accelerator
papers.abstract: We present time-resolved three-dimensional measurements of the averaged liquid mass distribution generated by the Spray M from the Engine Combustion Network. The operating condition corresponds to a non-reacting early injection case for spray-guided gasoline injection during the first 200 μs. Few-femtosecond X-rays from a compact laser wakefield accelerator, enable quantitative spray measurements, from the nozzle tip to the spray front. Spray cone angles, plume directionality, and mass redistribution are quantified with spatial resolution of the order of 15 μm. Results show that the eight plumes exhibit a similar spatial distribution of liquid volume fraction. In addition, the distribution of liquid volume fraction changes over time, with maxima starting from the external periphery and moving toward the internal periphery of the plumes. This experiment demonstrates the possibility of studying the time-resolved three-dimensional liquid mass distribution of challenging multi-hole transient sprays running at high injection pressures. This opens new opportunities for validating spray simulations and advancing fuel injection technologies in next-generation combustion systems.

papers.title: Confined staggered jet array impingement on moving surface: Hydrodynamics and heat transfer in turbulent regime
papers.abstract: Impinging jets on moving surface under confined space experience strong crossflow flow, which generates adverse flow field that can suppress the influence of jets' momentum at high surface velocities [S. Shah, V. Kumar, and K. D. P. Nigam, “Turbulent jet arrays impinging on moving surface: Effect of surface motion and wall confinement on heat transfer,” Int. J. Therm. Sci. 204, 109213, (2024)]. To understand the heat transfer mechanism under such conditions, a parametric study was conducted where a staggered array of 27 turbulent jets (3 × 9) impinged on moving surface under confinement numerically. The surface velocity varied based on the surface-to-jet velocity ratio (Vr) from 0 to 2, the jet-to-surface distance (H) varied from 4 to 8 times the jet hydraulic diameter (D), and the jet Reynolds number (Re) varied from 8000 to 28 000. A two-equation eddy viscosity-based model, shear stress transport k-ω model, was used to close the Reynolds averaged Navier–Stokes equations of flowing fluid. The effect of different parameters on heat transfer is represented through local (Nu) and average (Nuavg) Nusselt numbers at moving surface while flow fields are shown by mean velocity fields (U) and turbulence kinetic energy. The crossflow is quantified by normalized mass fluxes (φ) at the outlets. It is observed that the heat transfer is governed by jet momentum for Vr≤ 0.6, after that surface driven flow dominates. The crossflow suppresses the momentum of end jets nearer to right outlet, eliminating their effect on stagnation region heat transfer. A power law correlation for Nuavg has been derived from the current parametric study as a function of all parameters considered. It is recommended to operate the jet array for low Vr values to control the heat transfer through jet momentum under such conditions.

papers.title: Fast multipole boundary element method with subdivision surface for acoustic analysis under seabed and sea surface reflection conditions
papers.abstract: This study proposes a novel method for simulating sound scattering that accounts for the combined reflection effects of both the seabed and sea surface. The target geometry is modeled using isogeometric analysis to minimize geometric errors. The boundary element method incorporating a half-space fundamental solution is then employed to numerically simulate the external acoustic field in an infinite domain, incorporating the composite reflections from the sea surface and seabed. To enhance computational efficiency, the fast multipole method is implemented in the sound scattering model, significantly reducing computational time and memory requirements. The accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm are validated through numerical examples.

papers.title: Phase-field lattice Boltzmann method for two-phase electrohydrodynamic flows induced by Onsager-Wien effect
papers.abstract: The leaky dielectric model is widely used in simulating two-phase electrohydrodynamic (EHD) flows. One critical issue with this classical model is the assumption of Ohmic conduction, which makes it inadequate for describing the newly discovered EHD flows caused by the Onsager-Wien effect [Ryu et al., “New electrohydrodynamic flow caused by the Onsager effect,” Phys. Rev. Lett. 104(10), 104502 (2010)]. In this paper, we proposed a phase-field lattice Boltzmann (LB) method for two-phase EHD flows induced by the Onsager-Wien effect. In this scheme, two LB equations are employed to resolve the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations and the conservative Allen-Cahn equation, while another three LB equations are used for solving the ionic concentration equations and the electric potential equation. After we validate the developed LB method, we perform a series of numerical simulations of droplet deformation under EHD conduction phenomena. Our numerical results indicate that the presence of the Onsager-Wien effect has a significant impact on droplet deformation and charge distribution. Also, it is interesting to note that, apart from the heterocharge layers near the electrodes, a charge cloud may form between the droplet interface and the electrode in some cases. To thoroughly understand the droplet dynamics, the effects of the reference length d, the applied voltage Δψ, the permittivity ratio εr, and the ionic mobility ratio μr on droplet deformation and charge distribution are all investigated in detail.

papers.title: Aerodynamics and aeroacoustics of da Vinci's aerial screw
papers.abstract: Leonardo da Vinci's aerial screw, conceived in the 15th century, represents one of the earliest conceptualizations of lift-generating rotary flight. Despite its historical significance, the aerodynamic and aeroacoustic performance of this rotor has received limited scientific attention. In this study, we employ direct numerical simulations to analyze the aerodynamic forces and acoustic emissions of a modernized da Vinci aerial screw design across a range of Reynolds numbers (2000, 4000, 8000, and 16000). These results are compared against those from a canonical two-bladed rotor producing similar lift. The aerial screw demonstrates 42.2% lower mechanical power consumption and 72.3% lower acoustic intensity per unit lift, primarily due to its larger wetted area and correspondingly lower rotational speed. Although the aerial screw exhibits a lower lift coefficient and much of its surface contributes minimally to lift generation, the net performance under iso-lift conditions highlights its efficiency and reduced noise signature. The continuous spiral geometry of the aerial screw also helps suppress blade–vortex interaction noise common in multi-bladed systems. These findings support previous scaling analyses and point toward unconventional rotor designs as viable options for low-noise aerial platforms.

papers.title: The aerodynamic performance of cycloidal propellers with dynamic pitch regulations
papers.abstract: The cycloidal propellers, as a multi-degree-of-freedom propulsion system, achieve omnidirectional thrust vectoring through the periodic pitching of blades and exhibit significant potential for vertical takeoff and landing applications. However, in hover conditions, their aerodynamic performance is highly sensitive to dynamic pitch parameters, necessitating a systematic parametric framework to reveal these coupling relationships. This study developed a non-symmetric pitch-control model and investigated the influences of pitch amplitude, phase shift, and motion power exponent on lift, power consumption, and lift-to-power ratio (LPR). Numerical results showed that inter-blade aerodynamic interactions, especially leading-edge vortex interactions, induced pronounced unsteady aerodynamic loading. Total lift grew nonlinearly with increasing pitch amplitude, with optimal efficiency (peak LPR) occurring at 20°. Moreover, imposing different pitch amplitudes between upper and lower half-cycles enhanced performance: reducing amplitude in the upper half-cycle increased total lift, whereas enlarging amplitude in the upper half-cycle (relative to the lower) improved energy efficiency.

papers.title: Investigation of the collapse behavior of a cavitation bubble near double cylinders within a narrow gap
papers.abstract: Cavitation occurring near critical components of hydraulic machinery with complex boundaries can seriously affect its safe and stable operation. Employing the OpenFOAM platform, this work analyzes cavitation bubble oscillation behavior near double cylinders within a narrow gap. Specifically, the cavitation bubble collapse features and symmetry evolution are evaluated vs bubble–cylinder distances, and the pressure changes caused by jets and shock waves on cylinder surfaces are discussed. The results show that cavitation bubble evolution exhibits three characteristic collapse patterns based on jet formation: (1) three-jet, (2) two-jet, and (3) single-jet patterns. During collapse, increasing the bubble–cylinder distance reduces interfacial asymmetry and decreases the lateral protrusion of the bubble wall, which in turn reduces the number of jet types. In addition, during the collapse stage, pressure monitoring along the cylindrical axis reveals two distinct regions: a central zone dominated by the jet and shock wave, and an edge region governed by boundary reflection effects. As the axial distance from the center increases, the influence of boundary reflections intensifies significantly.

papers.title: A comparative study on vortex shedding dynamics of forced oscillating splitter-plate with or without cylinders
papers.abstract: This study explores the vortex shedding dynamics of oscillating cylinder with splitter plate compared to pure plate, emphasizing its impact on propulsive performance. Conducted at a Reynolds number of 3000, the investigation combines particle image velocimetry and force measurements to analyze thrust, lift, and vortex evolution across a range of Strouhal numbers (St: 0.12–0.72) and non-dimensional amplitudes (A*: 0.175–2.5). The results reveal that the oscillating cylinder with a splitter plate significantly enhances propulsive efficiency compared to the pure plate, particularly under reverse 2S flow conditions. At high St and low A*, the splitter-plate configuration achieves an efficiency improvement of 29.8%, driven by augmented vortex formation, reattachment, and fusion. The findings highlight the critical role of flow regime transitions and geometric design in optimizing fluid–structure interactions, offering insights for bio-inspired propulsion systems and advanced marine engineering technologies.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of energy dissipation and vortex characteristics of a pump-turbine with splitter blades under the influence of rotating stall in the hump region
papers.abstract: Under the current scenario of large-scale renewable energy integration into the grid, pumped storage power stations serve as critical components for peak shaving and frequency regulation. The pump-turbine as a core component of these stations needs frequent operational condition changes during operation. Unstable internal flow phenomena can significantly impact unit stability, particularly the rotating stall issue under off-design conditions. This study employs numerical simulations combined with entropy production analysis and vorticity transport equation analysis to investigate the transient flow characteristics within the hump region of a pump-turbine designed with splitter blades. The results indicate that rotating stall originates from flow separation within the guide vane passages. This propagates circumferentially through interactions between vortex structures, triggering reverse flow, and sudden pressure gradient changes. The development of unsteady vortex structures, such as the separation vortex on the guide vane suction surface and the circumferential vortex in the vaneless region, is closely correlated with a sharp increase in turbulent entropy production rate, constituting the dominant factor in hydraulic losses. Analysis based on the vorticity transport equation reveals the influence of relative vorticity stretching and Coriolis force on the evolution of the stall. This research deepens the understanding of transient flow phenomena within the hump region of splitter-blade pump-turbines and provides valuable insights for enhancing the operational stability of pumped storage units and optimizing internal flow design.

papers.title: Experimental study on the occurrence law of shock-outburst coupled dynamic disasters
papers.abstract: To explore the characteristics of the coupling occurrence and mutual induction of rock burst in deep mining and coal and gas disasters, a shock-outburst coupled dynamic disaster test was designed through a self-developed physical simulation test device. The velocity calibration of ejected coal particles, the calculation of ejected energy, the analysis of regional energy distribution, and the discussion of the fractal dimensions of the two types of disasters were carried out. The results show that during the coupled dynamic disaster test, the movement of coal particles will all go through three stages: the initial accelerated migration stage of coal particles, the deceleration movement stage under the gas–solid dynamic equilibrium, and the particle deposition stability stage. It is concluded that the total ejection energy of the impact-induced test varies as a quadratic function with the air pressure, while that of the protruding induced test varies exponentially. Based on the dynamic allocation model of the system's stored energy and dissipated energy, the disaster energy criterion with the proportion of residual energy Q as the core is proposed; the regional fractal characteristics of the coal lumps after the disaster were analyzed, and it was concluded that the impact-induced “large” particles occupied the dominant position. The fractal dimension D increased significantly with the increase in gas pressure. The highlight is the feature that induced “small” particles are dominant, and D decreases with the increase in gas pressure. The test results can provide certain theoretical support for the prediction and prevention and control of coupled dynamic disasters.

papers.title: Dynamic evolution of oil droplet population in non-Newtonian swirling flow field
papers.abstract: Polymer flooding is widely applied in offshore oil recovery, but the resulting non-Newtonian, high-viscosity mixtures pose challenges for rapid oil–water separation in compact vane-type swirl separators. To investigate the dynamic evolution of oil droplet clusters in such complex flows and improve separation efficiency, this study developed a coupled simulation model integrating the Eulerian multiphase model, power-law rheological model, population balance model, and Reynolds stress model turbulence model. The model captures the breakup and coalescence behavior of oil droplets in non-Newtonian swirling flow fields under varying polymer viscosity coefficient, rheological index, inlet liquid velocity, and inlet oil-phase concentration. The results show that increasing the polymer viscosity coefficient leads to larger average droplet diameters (D32, D90, D5) across the pipe section, but a gradual decrease in centerline D32. A lower rheological index reduces average D32 and D5, but increases centerline D32 and slightly increases average D90. As inlet liquid velocity rises, average D32 increases, while centerline D32 and D90 first rise then fall, peaking at 1.2 m/s; D5 decreases steadily. Higher inlet oil-phase concentration enhances collision frequency, resulting in an overall increase in droplet sizes. These findings elucidate the interaction between rheology and flow conditions in governing droplet cluster dynamics within swirling flows, thereby enabling the directional optimization of swirl-vane separators for non-Newtonian fluids.

papers.title: Effect of different types of vortex generators on delaying flow separation
papers.abstract: Under crosswind conditions, ensuring the safe operation of high-speed trains is a top priority. The crosswind-induced separated flow on the train roof may form large-scale vortical structures on the leeward side, increasing the risk of overturning. Because of their scalability and ability to energize the flow, vortex generators (VGs) are regarded as a promising control measure when installed on high-speed trains. Therefore, it is essential to evaluate the effectiveness of vortex generators in delaying flow separation on the train roof. In this study, three-dimensional structured grids were constructed for the Baseline case, as well as for rectangular, triangular, and wedge-shaped VGs. Large eddy simulation was employed for numerical simulations. The comparative analysis leads to the following conclusions: the vortices generated by the VGs are located at the interface between the boundary layer and the free stream. The induced downwash flow effectively transports momentum from the free stream into the boundary layer, thereby reducing its thickness, enhancing attachment, and delaying separation. The delayed flow, shifted downward, weakens the shear layer characterized by υ′w′¯ on the train's leeward side. This suppresses the unsteady growth of large-scale vortical structures by reducing energy uptake from the free stream, ultimately contributing to improved crosswind stability of the train.

papers.title: The aerodynamic and acoustic performance of a bumblebee-inspired micro-air vehicle in Martian atmosphere
papers.abstract: Micro-air vehicles (MAVs) based on flapping wings have been identified as a potential means for Mars exploration due to their high performance in low-Reynolds-number environments. The low-density atmosphere on Mars and the small scales of MAVs impose challenges in their operation due to rarefaction and compressibility effects. This study numerically investigates the aerodynamic and acoustic performance of a bumblebee-inspired MAV in compressible, rarefied flows. To decouple the effects of rarefaction and compressibility, the average wingtip Mach number (Ma) varies from 0.6 to 1.4, and the Knudsen number (Kn) varies from 0 to 0.05 with a second-order slip model implemented for Kn≥0.01. The numerical results show that rarefaction offers an improvement in the lift coefficient mainly attributed to a decrease in the viscous force, while the increase in Mach number results in a lift reduction due to the pressure variations. The introduction of the slip boundary results in some minor changes in pressure forces due to a change in the formation and development of the vortex structures at the leading edge of the wing. Acoustic signatures are a function of Ma due to the appearance, propagation, and interaction of shock waves. The variation in shock strength results in an increase in sound pressure, while the shock shape and shock interactions during stroke reversal phases result in the shift of the secondary harmonic frequency profile from a quad-pole source at Ma=0.6 to a hex-pole source at Ma=1.4.

papers.title: Optimizing gas diffusion layer perforation and microporous layer coverage for enhanced mass transport in proton exchange membrane fuel cells: A lattice Boltzmann study
papers.abstract: To improve mass transport performance of the gas diffusion layer (GDL) in proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), a GDL structural optimization scheme is implemented, considering various perforation diameters (Dp=35–210 μm) and microporous layer (MPL) coverage ratios (e=3%–21%). A three-dimensional pseudopotential multiphase lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) is employed to simulate gas–liquid two-phase transport at the pore scale. Key transport parameters, including water saturation, oxygen concentration distributions, longitudinal dispersion coefficients, and Péclet numbers, are comprehensively evaluated. The result identifies an optimal perforation diameter of 105–140 µm and MPL coverage ratios of 12%–18%, which achieves lower liquid water saturation, faster breakthrough, enhanced oxygen diffusion, and more stable gas–liquid separation. Liquid water converges and forms stable pathways at an intermediate Dp=105–140 μm, which reduces water retention time, prevents gas blockage, and improves drainage and gas transport efficiency. However, excessive large Dp inhibits water drainage speed primarily due to inadequate capillary driving forces. Meanwhile, larger perforations also extend oxygen diffusion pathways, delaying localized oxygen replenishment. In addition, a moderate e, ranging from 0.12 to 0.18, ensures stable, interconnected capillary pathways, and thereby improves drainage efficiency. Uncontrolled lateral water spreading occurs when e < 0.12, whereas excessive water accumulation and poor drainage are discovered when e > 0.18. These findings offer critical insight into pore-scale gas–liquid transport interactions, providing practical guidance for optimizing GDL structure design.

papers.title: Numerical investigation on swirl flow and mixing behavior in a hexagonal-arranged dense-lattice helical cruciform fuel assembly
papers.abstract: The forced convective heat transfer capacity of fluid-solid conjugate heating surfaces is closely related to the evolution behavior of the fluid flow field. The strong shear flow induced by complex non-canonical structures can promote the generation of vortices, thereby enhancing the heat transfer capacity and improving the safety margin of the heat exchanger. In recent years, helical cruciform fuel (HCF) has received extensive attention in the design of small modular reactors due to its high-power density, compact arrangement, and complex non-canonical structure. To investigate the refined swirling flow field and mixing behavior under complex twisted structure, based on the validation results of the mixing experiment, flow resistance experiment, and applicability analysis of turbulence models, the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation on a 19-rod hexagonal-arranged dense-lattice HCF assembly was conducted. The causes of strong shear flows and swirling vortex distributions in the rod bundle flow field were analyzed. Meanwhile, quantitative analyses of transverse mixing and flow resistance characteristics of the HCF assembly with different flow rates were carried out. Different from cylindrical rods, the mixing coefficient of the helical fuel doesn't exhibit a monotonic variation trend with Reynolds number; instead, it mainly manifests as forced flow sweeping along complex twisted structures. The average mixing parameters of the central, side, and corner channels are 0.028, 0.027, and 0.04, respectively. Furthermore, the flow resistance model of HCF assembly based on Rehme's theory and a refined mixing model is developed, with an average prediction accuracy improved by 44.8%.

papers.title: A novel post-streaming interpolation scheme for thermal boundary treatment in the double multiple-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: This study proposes a robust and accurate thermal boundary treatment scheme within the double distribution function and multiple-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann framework, aimed at enhancing the precision and generality of incompressible thermal flow simulations. A novel post-streaming equilibrium decomposition interpolation algorithm is developed to address the limitations of conventional piecewise extrapolation methods. Unlike traditional approaches, the proposed method eliminates the need for velocity interpolation at boundary nodes, thereby avoiding temperature discontinuities and preserving second-order spatial accuracy. The effectiveness and generality of the model are validated through a series of benchmark tests, including thermal Couette flow, flow past a circular cylinder under various thermal boundary conditions (Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin), natural convection in a square cavity with an embedded cylinder, and three-dimensional flow and heat transfer around a moving sphere. The simulation results show excellent agreement with analytical solutions and experimental data, demonstrating the model's high accuracy, stability, and adaptability across diverse thermal flow problems. This work develops a high-accuracy computational framework for simulating complex thermal systems involving curved and moving boundaries. Although only a single-sphere model is considered in this study, the proposed method can be easily extended to multi-body simulations with arbitrarily shaped geometries, thus laying a solid foundation for future research on heat and mass transfer in multi-physics environments.

papers.title: Coalescence dynamics of two coaxially rising bubbles: Modeling and semi-empirical analysis of drainage time
papers.abstract: Drainage models are crucial for bubble coalescence efficiency, with drainage time being a key parameter. However, existing theoretical models often assume planar liquid films, ignoring bubble deformation effects during coalescence, which reduces their practical applicability and predictive accuracy. To address this limitation, we employ a coupled volume of fluid method and the continuum surface force model to systematically investigate the coalescence dynamics of two coaxially rising gaseous bubbles covering a wide range of operating conditions with Weber numbers (We) of 0.0316–2.5708, Morton numbers (Mo) of 6.895 × 10−9–0.3664, Galileo numbers (Ga) of 6.83–222.92, and Eötvös numbers (Eo) of 1.22–8.7. Through a mechanistic analysis of the dynamic processes involving leading and trailing bubbles, along with the associated variations in the interfacial liquid film thickness during coalescence, we define the contact moment as the characteristic transition point in the vertex velocity of the trailing bubble's upper interface. The initial liquid film thickness and drainage time are systematically quantified based on this definition and a semi-empirical predictive model correlating the initial liquid film thickness with We and Mo is developed. Furthermore, a Ga-Eo phase diagram is constructed to quantify the trailing bubble's shape at the contact moment. Moreover, a systematic assessment and subsequent modification of Chesters model, originally derived under the planar film assumption, are performed. Finally, novel semi-empirical drainage time models are developed by incorporating effects of bubble shape and central symmetry, significantly enhancing predictive accuracy and extending applicability.

papers.title: Dependency of optimal jet control position on Reynolds-number in cylinder flow via resolvent analysis
papers.abstract: Flow around a circular cylinder is a typical unstable separated flow, and its unsteady loads control has been a key research focus in fluid mechanics. This paper proposes a feature-driven flow control position design methodology based on resolvent analysis effective gain, and studies the Reynolds number dependence of the optimal control position. Resolvent analysis is first conducted on the time-averaged flow, with the effective gain quantitatively characterizing the sensitivity to tangential jet excitation on the cylinder surface. By applying steady jet control at the position corresponding to peak effective gain, complete suppression of unsteady vortex shedding is achieved. Subsequently, a relationship between the optimal control position and Reynolds number is proposed: θopt=−154.26Re−0.5+87.59 (47≤Re≤200). The Re−0.5 power-law dependency fundamentally originates from viscosity-dominated boundary layer dynamics. This relationship reveals a critical physical law: the optimal tangential jet position consistently resides at Δθ=9.1° upstream of the flow separation position. Finally, we propose a variable of the effective range of the Coanda effect, explaining the viscous wall-attachment physics mechanism that maintains this fixed upstream offset. Flow field analysis further demonstrates that the optimal control position invariably coincides with 12.4% of the maximum surface vorticity in the uncontrolled case. This study indicates that the separation position of cylinder flow is a key feature, providing important guidance for the design of control positions.

papers.title: Systematic evaluation of PANS-based turbulence models in separated flows at different resolved scales
papers.abstract: Accurately simulating flow separation across multiple scales remains a major challenge in computational fluid dynamics, primarily due to the complex interactions of multi-scale vortex structures and transitional processes within the boundary layer. The Partially Averaged Navier–Stokes (PANS) method is employed in this study to investigate two representative separated flow cases: the backward-facing step flow and the flow around a square cylinder. The predictive performance of the PANS k-ε and PANS k-ω turbulence models is evaluated under various values of the unresolved-to-total kinetic energy ratio fk. Results show that with appropriate mesh resolution and cutoff scales, the PANS method can effectively capture key characteristics of multi-scale flow separation and coherent wake, while offering improved computational efficiency. For the backward-facing step flow, both models are able to reproduce the velocity distribution. In the near-wall region (y<1.5H), however, the PANS k-ω model provides better agreement with experimental data, attributed to its treatment of adverse pressure gradients. For large-scale separated flows, the PANS method is capable of accurately resolving the majority of turbulence development within the wake region. The main discrepancies arise near the initial vortex formation zone, where the flow structure is inherently complex and unsteady. In addition, by reducing the cutoff parameter below a critical threshold, the coexistence of the dominant Kármán vortex shedding frequency (fvs) and the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability frequency (fKH) can be captured when the fk values is reduced below a critical threshold.

papers.title: Wave attenuation by flexible suspended aquaculture canopies: Insights from experiments and theoretical analysis
papers.abstract: Suspended longline aquaculture systems, extensively used for cultivating algae and shellfish in China, contribute significantly to global food supply and blue carbon sequestration. Understanding the hydrodynamic processes within these culture regions is critical for ensuring structural safety, maintaining product quality, and managing ecological impacts. However, the flexible connections and dynamic deformations of longline structures introduce significant complexity to the study of the coupling mechanisms between these structures and waves. This study investigates wave propagation through flexible suspended aquaculture canopies using a combination of physical model experiments and simplified theoretical modeling. Laboratory experiments are conducted for two representative forms of longline aquacultural structures, in which the soft connections of the structure components and mooring systems are reasonably modeled to reproduce the wave–canopy interactions. A simplified theoretical model is developed to predict wave transmission, incorporating a bulk drag coefficient adjusted for shielding effects and an effective canopy height to account for canopy flexibility. The experimental and modeled results reveal that wave transmission through suspended canopies is influenced by multiple interacting parameters. Transmitted wave height decreases with increasing wave steepness, and the impact diminishes at higher steepness levels. Shallower water depths result in lower wave transmission through the canopy. A non-monotonic relationship between relative canopy width (B/L) and wave transmission is observed, with a local transmission peak around B/L=0.6–0.7. Increased canopy density, vertical placement, stiffness of individual culture units, and the ratio of canopy height-to-water depth all contribute to reduced wave transmission, whereas anchoring angle has a comparatively limited effect. Additionally, the spatial distribution of culture units affects the degree of energy dissipation due to varying shielding effects. Spectral analysis indicates that most wave energy dissipation occurs at the fundamental frequency, with rigid canopies showing greater dissipation at higher harmonics. The proposed theoretical model and the findings provide valuable theoretical support for optimizing the aquacultural structure design and spatial layout in marine ranching.

papers.title: Investigating directional flow-induced non-Fickian transport in rough-walled fractures with variable roughness characteristics
papers.abstract: How the combined effects of flow direction and surface roughness parameters govern anisotropic flow and non-Fickian transport have not yet been fully understood. In this study, we aim to investigate the directional flow-induced non-Fickian transport mechanism in rough-walled fractures. Flow direction is systematically varied in 15° increments from 0° to 345°, yielding 24 orientations for each fracture model. To examine its interaction with fracture roughness, the fluid flow and solute transport simulations were performed in OpenGeoSys-6 across combinations of Hurst exponent (H = 0.4–0.8) and roughness amplitude (σ2 = 0.1–0.3). The results show that flow direction strongly controls solute transport in rough-walled fractures. In the representative case (H = 0.4, σ2 = 0.3), preferential high-velocity channels and fingered plumes form along specific orientations, while other directions produce dispersed flow. Breakthrough curve analyses across 24 directions yield mean deviations of 3.203% and standard deviations of 1.811%, indicating substantial variability. Arrival time (tarrival) and saturation time (tsaturation) reveal that rapid breakthrough coincides with prolonged saturation, whereas delayed arrival yields shorter saturation and more uniform distribution. The combined effects of H and σ2 further regulate anisotropy: at H = 0.4, the mean tarrival is 0.287 and tsaturation is 2.612, exhibiting the largest directional variability with coefficients of variation (COV) of 0.243 and 0.118, respectively; as H increases to 0.8, tarrival increases to 0.316, tsaturation decreases to 1.993, and corresponding COV drops to 0.006/0.004, indicating smoother fractures promote more consistent transport behavior with reduced directional sensitivity. Besides, fractures with low H and high σ2 exhibit broad distributions and significant directional asymmetry, while those with high H and low σ2 show nearly isotropic transport. These findings emphasize the strong coupling between flow direction and fracture roughness, and demonstrate that non-Fickian transport is not solely a result of geometric disorder but also a direction–dependent phenomenon. The results underline the importance of incorporating directional heterogeneity into predictive transport models for fractured media.

papers.title: Erratum: “Centrifugally driven spherical gap convection with polar angle-dependent boundary condition: Can the Nusselt number fall below Unity?” [Phys. Fluids 37 , 083618 (2025)]
New insights into bridge flutter evolution: Flutter type classification, phase difference, amplitude ratio, and torsional center
papers.abstract: Flutter mode shape, describing the relative motion relationships between different degrees of freedom (DOFs), plays an important role in understanding bridge flutter phenomena. However, its evolution mechanism has long been obscured by numerous interconnected parameters. This study investigates the evolution mechanism of the bridge flutter mode shape for a heaving-lateral-torsional 3DOF system using explicit expressions. A new classification method is proposed by dividing flutter into three types based on amplitude ratio criteria: torsion-dominated flutter, heaving-dominated flutter, and branch-switching flutter. A unified expression for nominal torsional center (NTC) is developed, with its practical applications demonstrated. The theoretical sensitivity expressions of amplitude ratio are derived regarding the influence on various system parameters. Numerical examples of different rectangular sections and a streamlined bridge section are presented. The results reveal that the phase difference expression consists of three parts approximately proportional to U−1, U, and U3 (U: wind speed), respectively, explaining its non-monotonic behavior with wind speed. The NTC position is mainly governed by H3* and the gap between uncoupled heaving and torsional frequencies. A theoretical proof is provided for the forward movement of the torsional center, which would occur if H3* < 0 and torsional-to-heaving frequency ratio > 1. The sensitivity analysis shows that the amplitude ratio at flutter onset is sensitive to torsional frequency, wind speed, H3*, and A3*, in descending order of sensitivity. For the rectangular sections, the flutter indicators (amplitude ratio, phase difference, and wind speed at flutter onset) generally increase with increasing width/height ratio, with the NTC position moving away from the center. Branch-switching flutter could occur for the thin plate section at very high wind speeds.

papers.title: Direct numerical simulations of boundary layer transition caused by impinging particles
papers.abstract: Environmental effects such as rainfall can degrade airfoil performance through bypass transition to turbulence, which has significant implications to the safety of helicopters, urban air mobility, and unmanned aerial vehicles. This study examines the fundamental mechanisms by which dynamic impacts affect the flow through the lens of vorticity and local instability. Various scenarios of droplet impacts abstracted as particles were simulated as time-evolving body forces and studied using pseudo-spectral direct numerical simulations. These impact scenarios involve the creation and evolution of large-scale flow features such as turbulent spots, wedges, and low-speed streaks, and the interactions between them. This paper demonstrates that there exist meaningful interactions between “static” elements such as low-speed streaks and turbulent wedges, and transient disturbances such as impact initiated turbulent spots, with instances of localized suppression of turbulence being present. Also discussed are the effects of roughness Reynolds number Rekk associated with the part of the droplet that remains on the surface after impact. It is found that even impacts of droplets that are generally classified as “subcritical” can display a meaningful increase to the turbulence and time-averaged shear stress. These findings are expected to advance modeling and mitigation techniques of airfoil performance due to environmental factors involving transient impacts.

papers.title: Insight into the oil–water seepage mechanism based on shale stress deformation: A numerical simulation approach
papers.abstract: In shale reservoirs, organic matter (OM) and inorganic matter exhibit different deformation behaviors under stress. Their heterogeneous distribution leads to complex oil–water flow during the fracturing production process. In this study, a conceptual shale model with varying total organic matter content (TOC) is developed. A novel aspect is the consideration of shale stress deformation coupled with fluid flow, based on which the oil–water seepage mechanism is investigated. Simulation results demonstrate that the high TOC matrix swept by water during the soaking stage can be effectively mobilized, and the flow rate of oil briefly increases. During the soaking stage, pore pressure in the shale matrix increases. The fluid-induced stress on OM leads to deformation, which expands additional oil–water flow channels and creates favorable conditions for fluid exchange between isolated or small pores within the matrix. The elastic energy stored in deformed OM is released during production, which provides energy supplement for the flow of shale oil and helps to maintain a higher oil production in the later stage. Additionally, the influences of Young's modulus, shale permeability, fracture spacing, and matrix distribution on oil recovery efficiency are analyzed. The results are expected to provide a deeper understanding of the oil–water seepage mechanism and clarify the favorable conditions for hydraulic fracturing exploitation.

papers.title: Design and sensitivity analysis of the targeted-docking model for autonomous aerial refueling based on convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: As the preferred method for unmanned autonomous aerial refueling, soft aerial refueling technology has drawn the attention of scholars worldwide. Existing research mainly focuses on solving the problems related to the hose-drogue assembly or on vision-based drogue positioning and tracking. However, there is currently no precise and efficient docking model or strategy that can effectively guide the docking path of the receiver. Based on earlier research findings, this paper proposes a targeted-docking approach. It constructs a dataset using the bow wave model and the Kriging interpolation method. Leveraging the advantage of convolutional neural networks in extracting deep features from data, a targeted-docking model is established for the first time. Traditional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations require extensive computation time about 2 days to solve the detailed flow field characteristics, but the targeted-docking model realized the prediction of the successful docking range under any steady-flow refueling condition within 10–15 s, meeting the key requirements of the aerial refueling mission. Subsequently, by comparing with the original data obtained from CFD simulations, the accuracy and practicality of the model are verified. Finally, the Sobol method is adopted to conduct a sensitivity analysis of variables under different refueling conditions, identifying the parameters that significantly influence the refueling success rate. This result enhances the interpretability of the model and provides theoretical guidance for the design of docking schemes for unmanned autonomous refueling.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of deep bed filtration in electrically charged porous media
papers.abstract: We study the inertial capture of fine particles in laminar flow through a granular filter by means of computational fluid dynamics with consideration of electrostatic interactions. During their flow through the filter, the suspended particles are subjected to an attractive electrostatic interaction with the filter grains, which is modeled by means of the Yukawa potential, while gravity is neglected in the simulations. We find that the fraction of uncaptured particles reaching the end of the filter undergoes a phase transition at a porosity-dependent critical Stokes number Stc∼ϵ−β, where β=4.880 ± 0.015. Above this critical Stokes number, nearly all particles are captured. Moreover, we find that the amount of suspended particles in the medium decays exponentially with downstream flow distance in the filter and propose a phase diagram for the filter efficiency. Our results indicate that, in the presence of the Yukawa potential, the filter efficiency decreases with the intensity of the electrostatic interaction, A. This result is consistent with the observed decrease in the penetration length of the particles with increasing A and opens applications for improving filter efficiency through the design of electrically charged filter structures.

papers.title: Hydraulic fracture cross-layer propagation characteristics in the interlayered sand-shale reservoir
papers.abstract: China's continental shale oil reserves face geological challenges from complex, weak structural planes (i.e., lithology interfaces and bedding planes) and discontinuous interlayers (i.e., shale and sandstone), which limit the effective stimulation of multiple pay layers. This study investigates hydraulic fracture (HF) cross-layer propagation behaviors in the Chang 7 Member sand-shale reservoirs, integrating fracturing experiments and numerical simulations to analyze impact of vertical stress difference (KV), interlayer stress contrast (Δσh), injection rate (Q), fluid viscosity (μ), weak plane shear strength (IS), weak plane tensile strength (IT), and cyclic injection. Results reveal that HF height extension is governed by interlayer obstruction and weak plane activation, forming three fracture propagation patterns: activated bedding planes, passivated fractures, and cross-layer fractures. Enhanced HF penetration occurs with higher KV, Q, μ, IS, IT, and reduced Δσh. Conversely, fractures become passivated with the weak plane activation. The dominant factor of fracture height is Δσh, followed by the IS, IT, KV, Q, and μ. Compared with conventional injection, cyclic injection improves fracture height and fracture area by 200% and 23%, respectively. Reduced cyclic amplitude or extended cycle duration promotes bedding activation. To achieve vertical connection of multiple pay layers, it is recommended to perform hydraulic fracturing with 30 mPa s guar gum at a flow rate above 8.3 m3/min. These findings are expected to provide hydraulic fracturing guidance for the interlayered shale oil reservoirs.

papers.title: On flow unsteadiness in strongly separated high-speed ramp flows using kinetic and data-driven methods
papers.abstract: The gas dynamics of high-speed flows over several compression–expansion ramp geometries with large separation regions were investigated using a particle-kinetic approach and data-driven methods. These large separation regions allow study of the role of scaled angle predicted by triple deck theory on recirculation strength, separation size, and appearance of secondary recirculation regions, all of which lead to flow unsteadiness. Examining four different free-stream conditions for the same geometry using the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) approach, we show that the stability of single recirculation in the separation region is more sensitive to wall temperature and free-stream velocity than physical ramp angle. Stability in this context refers to appearance of secondary separation regions. In addition, configurations with similar types of recirculation regions from literature considered, we find that general trends regarding unsteadiness, such as appearance of secondary recirculation regions, mostly hold; however, the flows are too complex to be characterized by only scaled angle. Thus, stochastic flowfields generated by DSMC were investigated using data-driven methods, namely, spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) and dynamic mode decomposition (DMD). We found that both methods yield similar frequency components and mode shapes for spatiotemporal coherent structures of unsteady DSMC flows. With the help of these structures, the main mechanisms of unsteadiness were identified as oscillations of the reattachment shock, Kelvin–Helmholtz-like instability of the shear layer, and c-shaped mode of the separation bubble. This is the first time SPOD has been applied to a DSMC generated flowfield and compared with DMD.

papers.title: Full-scale experimental study on tunnel pressure waves caused by an urban train with various air-intake statuses of air-conditioning units
papers.abstract: Urban railways alleviate traffic congestion and enhance transportation efficiency. The operation of trains in tunnels can cause significant pressure waves, resulting in passenger discomfort and auditory damage. Therefore, airtight train configurations were employed to mitigate interior pressure fluctuation. To ensure interior air quality, controlled ventilation through air-conditioning units (ACUs) is required. However, during tunnel operations, pressure waves enter the carriage through ACUs, thereby affecting the interior pressure. Considering that the on-off plates of air intakes may malfunction, the influence of tunnel pressure waves on the auditory comfort of passengers is worth investigating. In this study, a full-scale test was conducted to investigate the spatiotemporal distribution characteristics of the interior/exterior pressure variation induced by trains with different lengths passing through tunnels at multiple speeds. The ACU air intake operates in three states: automatic control (closed), 1/4 open, and fully open. An inverse correlation was observed between train length and interior/exterior pressure variation. Compared with the driver's cab, the interior pressure of the passenger compartments was more affected by the train length (with a difference of approximately 30%). The operational state of ACU air intakes significantly impacts interior pressure variations, with closed intakes effectively reducing fluctuations, whereas opening size demonstrated limited influence. Both the amplitude and variation of the interior/exterior pressure exhibited positive correlations with train speed. These findings inform optimized ACU intake control strategies for enhancing passenger auditory comfort.

papers.title: Lubrication characteristics and rapid evaluation of squeeze film damper under non-circular whirl trajectory
papers.abstract: The influence of non-circular whirl trajectory parameters on the dynamic characteristics of squeeze film damper has not been well understood. In this study, a fluid domain model was established to analyze the influence of whirl trajectory parameters on lubrication characteristics under different structure and working condition parameters, revealing the underlying evolution mechanism. Four machine learning models were established to enable rapid evaluation of dynamic behavior. The results show that non-circular whirl trajectories cause lubrication characteristics to vary sinusoidally with the whirl angle. The whirl trajectory has the most pronounced effect on the maximum pressure, the average value, and amplitude of the steam volume fraction. With increase in the whirl trajectory parameters, the stability of the dynamic characteristics decreases. Under most operating conditions, when the non-circular whirl trajectory parameter is 2.5, the amplitude increase in dynamic characteristics fluctuation is more than 10 times compared with the circular whirl trajectory. The sensitivity of width to damping is the highest for conventional parameters. Among the four machine learning models, the particle swarm optimization-backpropagation neural network algorithm has the best prediction performance, with R2-values exceeding 0.93. The research results provide a new approach for rapid evaluation of dynamic coefficients in squeeze film dampers under non-circular whirl conditions.

papers.title: Study on vortex-induced vibration characteristics of side box π -shaped cross sections with different aspect ratios
papers.abstract: The π-shaped cross sections with aspect ratios of 6, 8, and 10 were selected as research objects to investigate the influence of aspect ratio on vortex-induced vibration (VIV) characteristics. Wind tunnel vibration tests were conducted at angles of attack (AOA) of 0° and ±3°. In addition, for the cross section with a 10:1 aspect ratio, concurrent vibration and surface pressure measurements, as well as numerical simulations, were performed to provide detailed insight into the flow–structure interactions. Surface pressure characteristics under different AOAs are systematically analyzed using the partition method, energy method, and correlation coefficient method. Based on the correlation coefficient method, the concept of wave crest distance was proposed. The results demonstrate that an increasing trend in maximum vibration amplitude was observed with increasing aspect ratio. A delay of VIV response was observed in the lock-in region as the AOA shifted from negative to positive. From the perspective of correlation coefficients, as the AOA transitions from negative to positive values, the wave crest distance between the correlation coefficients of upper and lower surfaces gradually decreases. Correspondingly, the maximum VIV amplitude in the second lock-in region of vertical bending increases with the reduction of wave crest distance. The second lock-in region at 0° AOA is associated with the “long-tail” vortex shedding; however, when the AOA is not at 0°, the long-tail vortex shedding pattern transitions to a “thick-tail” pattern.

papers.title: Diffusion–diversion wind barrier for high-speed train protection passing real terrain
papers.abstract: This study, based on real terrain in Xinjiang, China, examines a novel wind barrier known as the diffusible diversion case (DDC) and compares its effectiveness in protecting moving trains from crosswinds to that of the original porous case. It utilizes the Unsteady Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes equations along with the Trimmed Mesher for numerical simulations. Two-stage wind tunnel experiments are conducted to verify the method's accuracy, and the movement of the train is achieved through a sliding mesh. Results show that upon reaching the maximum crosswind speed point, the DDC reduces side forces on the head, middle, and tail cars by 22.76%, 8.44%, and 30.38%, respectively, due to decreased pressure differences. During this moment, the pressure differences between the windward and leeward sides of the head, middle, and tail cars drop by 24.48%, 25.95%, and 14.44%, respectively. Meanwhile, with DDC's assistance, the airflow on the windward side of the train undergoes a three-stage redirection, becoming constrained to the bridge deck area and slowing down. The airflow entering the bogie cavity shifts from predominantly horizontal to predominantly vertical, with lateral components decreasing by 60.93% and 69.33%. The intense negative pressure zones on the leeward side fade and rapidly separate from the train body. Moreover, the DDC releases crosswind energy from the wake flow either on the windward side of the train region or outside it. The separation line, which shifts toward the windward side along with an expanded reverse flow area, indicates the optimization of asymmetric vortex shedding in the wake.

papers.title: Linear stability of buoyant convection in horizontally heated porous layers
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the onset and nature of natural convection instabilities within elongated cavities filled with a Newtonian, incompressible fluid saturating a homogeneous and isotropic porous medium. The study begins by deriving an exact analytical solution for the base flow, which takes the form of a one-dimensional motion between two horizontal, thermally conducting parallel plates. To capture inertial effects beyond the Darcy regime, the base flow is subsequently extended through numerical simulations incorporating the nonlinear Forchheimer correction. All analyses are carried out under the assumption of an effective Prandtl number equal to unity (Pr=1) and perfectly conducting thermal boundary conditions. A comprehensive linear stability analysis is then performed to assess how the porous medium characteristics, namely, the Darcy number Da, porosity ε, and the Forchheimer drag coefficient CF, influence the emergence and nature of flow instabilities. The results reveal a rich spectrum of convective modes, comprising both stationary (ST-2D and SL-3D) and oscillatory (OT-2D and OL-3D) behaviors. The existence and structure of these disturbances are shown to depend sensitively on the interplay between diffusive, inertial, and buoyant effects modulated by the governing parameters Da, ε, and CF. To elucidate the physical mechanisms underlying the bifurcations, an energy budget analysis is conducted at the critical thresholds. This reveals that the instabilities may be driven by shear, buoyancy, or a synergistic combination of both, depending on the mode and parameter regime. Altogether, the findings provide new insight into the intricate dynamics of convective flows in porous media, with implications for both fundamental science and a variety of practical applications.

papers.title: Structural design and experimental study of composite disc magnetorheological brake
papers.abstract: To make up for the lack of braking torque (BT) and stability of the magnetorheological brake (MRB), an innovative composite disk magnetorheological brake design is proposed in this paper. This design combines a multi-disk and T-shaped disk layout and uses a dual-coil excitation mode to boost the magnetic field strength in the working area. Based on the Bingham model, a torque model dominated by magnetic force torque is derived. Via electromagnetic field simulation analysis, the influence patterns of current, coil turns, working gap, brake disk radius, and magnetic shielding ring thickness on BT are clarified, verifying the rationality of the magnetic circuit design. Experimental findings indicate that at an initial braking speed of 100 km/h with a 2.8 A current applied, the measured maximum BT reaches 270 N·m, and the output torque increases with current and rotational speed. This structure provides an effective solution for the design of high-torque-density MRB.

papers.title: Rarefaction-induced Rayleigh–Taylor growth for a light gas layer
papers.abstract: The Rayleigh–Taylor (RT) interface evolution within a light fluid layer subjected to rarefaction-driven flows is investigated through rarefaction-tube experiments and numerical simulations, with focus on initial condition effects. Rarefaction-induced acceleration yields distinct RT instability responses at the two interfaces: the upstream interface (I1) becomes RT-unstable while the downstream interface (I2) remains RT-stable. This contrast drives interface coupling that reduces perturbation growth for in-phase configurations but weakly suppresses or promotes growth for anti-phase configurations. To resolve these distinct behaviors, Mikaelian's linear model [Phys. Fluids, 7, 888–890 (1995)] is modified through incorporating a phase correction factor. The modified model accurately predicts linear amplitude evolution for both interfaces across layer widths, with validity further confirmed through comparison with prior heavy fluid layer results. Increasing I2's initial amplitude or reducing layer width modulates I1 growth, suppressing it for in-phase cases while amplifying it for anti-phase cases, where layer width reduction proves more effective. A higher Atwood number at I2 intensifies the reflected rarefaction wave, thereby reducing I1 growth; however, it simultaneously enhances interface coupling, enlarging the growth disparity at I1 between in-phase and anti-phase configurations. These findings provide insights for manipulating perturbation growth through tailored initial conditions.

papers.title: The onset of long-wave oscillatory thermosolutal instability in a heated layer of a moderately dense nanofluid
papers.abstract: We investigate the thermosolutal Marangoni instability in a moderately dense nanoparticle suspension (nanofluid). The nanofluid layer deposited on a solid substrate and subjected to a specified constant heat flux is exposed to the ambient atmosphere at the air–liquid deformable interface. The effects of thermophoresis and gravity are considered. Using the method of asymptotic expansions, we investigate the oscillatory long-wave thermosolutocapillary instabilities, taking into consideration the dependence of the thermophysical properties of the nanofluid on the local nanoparticle concentration. Variations in the threshold of the long-wave oscillatory thermocapillary instability with the heat transfer rate at the interface and the interface deformability are obtained. We find a transition from monotonic to oscillatory thermosolutal Marangoni instability with a codimension-two point bifurcation. An excellent agreement is obtained between the results of the asymptotic analysis and those of the numerical solution of the full eigenvalue problem, in terms of the critical values of the Marangoni number, the wavenumber, and the frequency.

papers.title: Effect of concentric surface roughness on traveling disturbances in the rotating disk boundary layer
papers.abstract: The linear stability of the rotating disk boundary layer with surface roughness is investigated, building upon the earlier work by Harris [“Stability of the flow over a rough rotating disk,” Ph.D. thesis (University of Warwick, 2013)] and Garrett et al. [“On the stability of von Kármán rotating-disk boundary layers with radial anisotropic surface roughness,” Phys. Fluids 28, 014104 (2016)]. The study employs the Yoon et al. [“Flow and heat transfer over a rotating disk with surface roughness,” Int. J. Heat Fluid Flow 28, 262–267 (2007)] approach for modeling concentric surface roughness, where the roughness is defined as a function of the radial direction coupled with a spatial-averaging of the base flow. Neutral stability curves and critical conditions for linear instability are computed for varying roughness factors and for traveling wave disturbances with temporal frequencies ω¯∈[−10,10]. The results demonstrate that surface roughness stabilizes the type-I crossflow instability and destabilizes the type-II Coriolis instability. Finally, a high-Reynolds number asymptotic analysis is undertaken for the upper branch of the neutral stability curve associated with the crossflow instability.

papers.title: The effect of top surface boundary conditions on internal solitary waves in numerical simulations
papers.abstract: Numerical simulations of internal solitary wave (ISW) propagation are extensively employed to assess their impact on marine structures and ecosystems. In such simulations, rigid-lid and free-surface boundary conditions are commonly implemented at the top computational boundary. While the rigid-lid condition simplifies model setup and reduces computational cost by fixing the upper surface, the free-surface condition more accurately represents ocean surface physics. This study quantitatively evaluates the influence of these surface boundary conditions on ISW dynamics using a fully nonlinear numerical model. Comparative simulations are conducted across varying density differences, initial wave amplitudes, and depth ratios. Results reveal that under large density differences, the choice of boundary condition (rigid-lid vs free-surface) significantly alters ISW wave profiles, phase speeds, and flow fields. However, for a small density difference close to the real ocean (e.g., ρ1/ρ2=1000/1025), both conditions yield indistinguishable results across key ISW characteristics. Furthermore, under these realistic density differences, the effects of top boundary conditions remain negligible regardless of variations in initial wave amplitude or depth ratio. Consequently, for oceanographically relevant scenarios, the rigid-lid condition achieves comparable accuracy to the free-surface condition in predicting ISW characteristics. This supports its utility in simplifying ISW propagation and evolution simulations when surface wave interactions are not of primary interest. Additionally, the Miyata–Choi–Camassa theory solution proves suitable as an initial wave profile condition, applicable for both small and large wave amplitudes.

papers.title: Modulatory role of coronary flow in aortic valve hemodynamics: A fluid–structure interaction study
papers.abstract: Aortic valve stenosis has a high complication rate with coronary artery disease, and angina due to coronary ischemia often resolves rapidly after aortic valve replacement. These clinical observations suggest a close anatomical and physiological connection between aortic valve function and coronary arteries, but the mechanism of mechanical coupling between them is still not fully recognized. Based on high-resolution fluid–structure interaction simulations, we systematically evaluate the modulation mechanisms of coronary drainage on leaflet motion and downstream turbulent structures. Results demonstrate that the coronary arteries are not simply passive anatomical features but also act as active hemodynamic modulators. Coronary flow markedly alters the spatiotemporal evolution of vortex structures within the sinus, suppresses the energy spectrum amplitude at low wavenumbers to stabilize the jet core, and reduces global entropy by approximately 10%. Leaflet flutter characteristics migrated from low-frequency high-amplitude to high-frequency low-amplitude, suggesting an underlying bioprotective mechanism. The comprehensive evaluation of relevant hemodynamic metrics indicated that neglecting coronary arteries in numerical simulations may lead to systematic misinterpretation. These findings emphasize that coronary flow not only facilitates myocardial perfusion but also plays a critical role in regulating local valvular hemodynamics, with potential implications for prosthetic design and patient-specific modeling.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic analysis and stabilization mechanisms of a Novel Flying Wing Anchor® under free-fall and ocean current conditions
papers.abstract: The Flying Wing Anchor® (FWA®) is an innovative hybrid dynamically installed anchor designed for efficient self-weight installation, offering high kinetic efficiency and enhanced directional stability, qualities that make it well suited for deep-sea mooring applications. However, its hydrodynamic behavior during the free-fall phase, particularly under varying geometric configurations and ocean current conditions, remains inadequately understood. This study employs both static and dynamic simulations to investigate the influence of geometric design, self-correction capability, and ocean current effects on the hydrodynamic performance of the FWAs®. The numerical results elucidate the roles of steady flow fin geometry and flying wing size in determining drag characteristics and directional stability, confirm the anchor's self-correcting behavior during descent, and quantify the effects of different ocean current scenarios. Additionally, a time-dependent analytical model for drag coefficient and added mass during free fall is developed and validated against numerical simulations.

papers.title: A three-phase fluid–structure interaction algorithm for compressible flows and thin-walled structures based on the extended ghost fluid method
papers.abstract: Numerical simulations of fluid–structure interactions involving compressible fluids and thin-walled structures often encounter numerical oscillation issues. First, the numerical solution of two-phase flows with high density and pressure ratios suffers from discrete errors, which can induce nonphysical oscillations at the fluid–structure interaction interface. Second, the added mass effect causes a mismatch in wave impedance between the solid elastic wave and the fluid pressure wave, resulting in the continuous back-and-forth propagation of elastic waves within the thin-walled structure. This induces nonphysical oscillations at the fluid–structure interaction interface. This study proposes a three-phase fluid–structure interaction algorithm based on the extended ghost fluid method to effectively eliminate these numerical oscillations. First, the fifth-order weighted essentially nonoscillatory finite difference method is employed to solve the flow of compressible two-phase fluids. Meanwhile, the finite element method is used to solve the motion of thin-walled structural deformations. Subsequently, the ghost fluid method is extended and enhanced for application to interactions between compressible fluids and thin-walled structures. Meanwhile, coupling rules between fluid grid nodes and solid hexahedral finite elements are established to effectively mitigate nonphysical oscillations. Comparisons between numerical and experimental results, the numerical accuracy at the fluid–structure interface, and the mass conservation in the fluid domain collectively demonstrate that the extended ghost fluid method, combined with the proposed fluid–structure coupling rules, is robustly applicable to simulations involving compressible flows and thin-walled structures.

papers.title: Effects of submersion depth on the dynamics and deposition of lock-release turbidity currents
papers.abstract: This study investigates the influence of the submersion depth on the propagation dynamics and the deposition patterns of turbidity currents using the lock-release configuration. While previous studies have investigated the effects of submersion depth on conservative density currents, its impact on non-conservative, particle-laden currents has received comparatively less attention. To address this, we employed a set of high-fidelity numerical simulations based on the implicit large eddy simulation methodology to analyze the behavior of turbidity currents generated with different particle diameters and submersion depths. The analysis focused on key propagation parameters, including front position, front velocity, turbulent structures, and deposit patterns, enabling the estimation of the run-out distance. The results highlight a significant impact of the submersion depth on the evolution of the current and its depositional characteristics, demonstrating that increased submersion leads to extended run-out distances and changes in the deposit distribution. The evolution of coherent turbulent structures, such as Kelvin–Helmholtz billows and vortex shedding, was found to be strongly influenced by vertical confinement. Reduced confinement promoted the formation of larger, more organized turbulent structures, leading to higher shear stress near the bed and a more pronounced current separation. A threshold depth was identified beyond which further submersion produces diminishing changes, revealing an asymptotic behavior in flow characteristics and deposition patterns.

papers.title: K-nearest neighbors-enhanced shared time information multivariate proper orthogonal decomposition: Insights into particle migration in fluid flows
papers.abstract: Multiscale spatiotemporal feature analysis of three-dimensional particle migration is crucial for elucidating the mechanisms between settling dynamics and fluid flow. To fully understand this complex system, we propose a multi-stage, multivariable analysis framework that combines an improved modal decomposition with low-dimensional dynamical modeling. In particular, by integrating a K-nearest neighbors algorithm into the shared time-information multivariable proper orthogonal decomposition, the K-nearest neighbors-enhanced shared time information multivariable proper orthogonal decomposition is used to enhance mode reconstruction accuracy and ensure consistent physical interpretation across velocity, pressure, and vorticity fields. Based on this low-dimensional representation of the flow, we then apply the sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics method to derive a system of ordinary differential equations that accurately captures the flow's underlying dynamics, enabling high-fidelity multivariable time-series prediction.
