papers.abstract: The effects of a stepped seabed on the interaction between linear long waves and a flexible, horizontal, and submerged plate are theoretically analyzed. The reflected and transmitted wave energies, together with the wave flux energy concentrated below and above the plate, are characterized. The mechanical response of the structure is obtained from the Kirchhoff-Love thin plate theory. Wave hydrodynamics are analyzed under the assumption of potential flow theory. The geometry of the seabed can exhibit different configurations, ranging from a uniform seabed to finite and infinite steps, vertical walls, and trenches. The plate length can be much larger than or of the same order of magnitude as the wavelength. Two boundary conditions are analyzed for the edge of the plate: when they have free displacement and when they are clamped. When the plate length is of the same order of magnitude as the wavelength, the energy flow above and below it is almost equal; however, for very long plates, the most significant energy flow occurs above it. This analytical solution allows for the characterization of the effects of a stepped seabed on the energy flux enhancement induced by the long-waves–flexible plate interaction.

papers.title: Drag enhancement by turbulence on a fixed cylinder: Effects of aspect ratio and inclination angle
papers.abstract: Direct numerical simulations are conducted to investigate the effects of height-to-diameter aspect ratio (H/D) and inclination angle on turbulence-induced drag enhancement for fixed cylindrical particles in laminar and turbulent flows. When the cylinder axis is perpendicular to the flow, drag enhancement decreases with decreasing aspect ratio due to the competing effects of (i) turbulence-induced pressure reduction on the rounded surface and (ii) reduced drag enhancement near the sharp edges. The trends in pressure and viscous drag enhancements are consistent with those of the total drag, with the downstream low-pressure region contributing more significantly to drag enhancement when it is located away from the sharp edge. Among various inclination angles, the influence of aspect ratio is most pronounced when the cylinder axis is normal to the flow. When the axis is aligned with the flow, drag decomposition reveals distinct trends depending on the aspect ratio: for short cylinders, pressure drag enhancement dominates due to the streamwise advection of low-pressure regions along the rounded surface; for long cylinders, viscous drag enhancement prevails, driven by the accumulation of large velocity gradients along the streamwise direction.

papers.title: The collapse behavior and acoustic characteristics of bubble clusters with varied layers and fractions under the wall's shielding effect
papers.abstract: This paper studies the effects of the wall on the noise spectrum of bubble clusters during near-wall collapse. Applying direct numerical simulations and the Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings method to evaluate sound pressure (SP), the acoustic characteristic of layered clusters with varied layers and fractions is investigated. Preliminarily knowing about “the wall's shielding effect” on cavitation bubble collapse, we discussed how its strength and action mechanism change in detail. The results reveal that the greater the number of layers is, the more obvious “the wall's shielding effect” will exceed the interlayer shielding effect, resulting in more significant collapse asymmetry and larger disparities of sound pressure (SP) between internal bubbles. The wall imposes minor enhancement or suppression on the time-domain SP peaks and improves the overall sound pressure levels (SPLs) of the multi-layer bubble clusters. For the different-fraction clusters, the wall significantly delays the collapse of the dense cluster, as well as increasing its frequency-domain sound pressure level (SPL), but has slight effects on the SP peaks and SPL decay rates of both the dense and sparse clusters. The decay rates of α = 37.4%, 7.16%, and 0.98% bubble clusters with more than four layers roughly stabilize at 2.4, 4.0, and 5.2 dB/octave, respectively. Inside the sparser cluster, “the wall's shielding effect” is more even but predominant for individual bubbles. These conclusions provide a concrete discussion of the effect mechanism of the wall on the acoustic radiation of bubble clusters with varied layers and fractions, thereby laying a solid foundation for the practical evaluation of cavitation noise.

papers.title: Aerodynamic study of dihedral angle configurations on a hexacopter during horizontal airflow disturbances
papers.abstract: Multi-rotor Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) often experience horizontal incoming flow disturbances during hovering, which can compromise both mission accuracy and stability. This study investigates the aerodynamic performance of a hexacopter with dihedral angle configurations, which is capable of resisting interference from horizontal flows, unlike planar hexacopters. The effects of four yaw angles and three rotor dihedral angles were systematically examined using both test bench experiments and computational fluid dynamics simulations under varied operating conditions. The aerodynamic performance of the propellers was analyzed in terms of upwash, downwash flow, and rotor angle of attack. Results demonstrate that the direction of rotation of the front rotor significantly influences the thrust distribution of adjacent rotors in the presence of incoming flow. Among the yaw angles studied, a yaw angle of 60° generated higher lift and pitching moments compared to a yaw angle of 0°, while yaw angles of 30° and 90° induced additional rolling moments. The study also reveals that differences in the rotor dihedral angle significantly affect the pitching moment and positional drift of the hexacopter, respectively. These findings provide insights into optimizing the performance of multi-rotor UAVs under wind disturbances.

papers.title: Wall slip effect on the squeeze flow of a viscoelastic fluid confined between two parallel disks or between a sphere and a disk
papers.abstract: Squeeze flow refers to the fluid flow between two parallel or near-parallel surfaces that converge toward each other, allowing the fluid to move relative to the surface. This phenomenon is important in various applications, including lubrication systems, biological systems, and microfluidic devices, where conventional no-slip boundary conditions are not always valid, especially at small scales. This study examines the effect of wall slip on the squeeze flow behavior of an upper-convected Maxwell fluid confined between two parallel disks or between a sphere and a disk. The lubrication approximation is used to obtain the expressions for the pressure distribution and the normal squeeze force in the disk–disk configuration. The introduction of slip changes the flow dynamics, reducing viscous resistance and allowing faster fluid drainage between the surfaces. Furthermore, this analysis is extended to a sphere-disk configuration. The effects of wall slip on the pressure distribution, film thickness, and flow rate are analyzed. The key findings suggest that slip has a major impact on flow behavior in areas with high shear and tight spaces. In general, wall slip improves the lubrication efficiency and could lead to new engineering applications in nanofluidics and soft materials.

papers.title: Effect of droplet loading on multiphase flow past a circular cylinder at low Mach numbers
papers.abstract: The aerodynamic characteristics of droplet-laden flows past a circular cylinder are investigated using a compressible multiphase flow solver based on the six-equation model. The numerical framework is validated against benchmark cases for both multiphase and single-phase flows. Unlike prior studies that have primarily examined compressibility effects in single-phase flows or multiphase interactions at higher Reynolds numbers, this work is the first to systematically analyze the combined influence of compressibility and droplet–gas coupling in the low-Mach, laminar regime. The study explores the effects of droplet size, volume fraction, and Mach number on flow unsteadiness, droplet distribution, and aerodynamic forces. Results reveal that increasing the droplet volume fraction suppresses vortex shedding and promotes a transition to steady flow, primarily through enhanced interphase drag. Droplets preferentially accumulate in the front stagnation region, with minimal penetration into the wake, particularly under high inertial loading. The mean drag increases with droplet concentration, while the lift initially rises and then diminishes as unsteady behavior is suppressed, accompanied by a corresponding decrease in Strouhal number. At higher Mach numbers, smaller droplets contribute more significantly to drag due to stronger coupling with the compressible gas phase. Overall, the study provides new physical insights into the interplay between compressibility and multiphase dynamics in laminar flows, a regime that has remained largely unexplored.

papers.title: Flow and mist explosion coupling process of liquid fuel from storage tank under explosion
papers.abstract: Liquid fuel storage tanks are important targets in warfare and terrorist attacks, and their safety assessment forms the basis of effective protection. The prediction of the harmful effects in the area outside the tank after rupture under explosive load is essential for effectively preventing chain explosion processes. This paper examined energy output in the coupling of dispersal and detonation of liquid fuel under explosion load using numerical simulation. The results show that the detonation occurs at the same time as the liquid fuel disperses to form a cloud in the cylindrical device of the JP10 liquid or JP10/IPN mixed liquid fuel under the explosion load of the central explosive charge. For 0.5 kg JP10 in a cylindrical device, the times for the chemical reaction to start are 0.43, 0.27, 0.08, and 0.06 ms, and the locations for the chemical reaction to start are 0.22, 0.20, 0.12, and 0.09 m, respectively, for the center-charge/fuel mass ratio of 5%, 10%, 15%, and 21%. At the center-charge/fuel mass ratio of 15%, the peak explosion pressure of the 0.5/0.5 JP10/IPN mixture reaches its maximum at the far field among the examined mass ratios 0.3/0.7, 0.5/0.5, and 0.7/0.3 of JP10/IPN.

papers.title: Soot distribution and particle emissionsin a swirl combustor at elevated temperaturesand pressures
papers.abstract: An experimental investigation is conducted to examine soot distribution and particulate matter (PM) emissions in the pilot swirl flame of a centrally staged combustor at elevated temperatures (up to 650 K) and pressures (up to 0.5 MPa). The study employs comprehensive optical diagnostics, including two-dimensional laser-induced incandescence, particle image velocimetry, and simultaneous OH/kerosene planar laser-induced fluorescence, complemented by the scanning mobility particle sizer measurements. Results demonstrate that soot predominantly forms near the inner shear layer of the primary recirculation zone but is suppressed by high flow velocities and OH oxidation. Increasing combustor inlet pressure and temperature significantly enhances soot formation, triggering a distribution transition from hollow cone mode to solid cone mode. Under transitional operating conditions, intermittent shifts between these modes correlate with the sporadic presence of OH radicals in the primary recirculation zone. Statistical analysis of exhaust PM reveals nucleation mode dominance in the size distribution, with particle number concentrations and geometric mean diameters increasing at higher pressures. Both in-flame soot and exit PM volume fractions exhibit power-law relationships with pressure, though their temperature sensitivities differ, potentially due to distinct post-flame soot evolution processes. This work highlights the critical role of turbulence−soot interactions in governing soot formation and PM emissions, providing vital insights under engine-relevant conditions.

papers.title: Effects of cavitation bubble dynamics near a free surface on gas layer stability and impact loading of biomimetic microstructured surfaces
papers.abstract: The dynamics of cavitation bubbles critically affect the stability of gas layers and induce intense impact forces on adjacent surfaces. This study numerically investigates the complex interaction mechanisms among a cavitation bubble, a free surface, and three representative biomimetic gas–entrapping microstructured surfaces. A compressible volume of fluid multiphase model with equations of state is developed and validated against experimental observations of bubble morphology, gas layer evolution, and free surface deformation. The effects of bubble–surface (γf = 0.25–1.0) and bubble–wall (γw = 0.8–1.5) stand–off distances are systematically examined, focusing on liquid jet characteristics, shock wave propagation, wall shear stress, and the resulting force and impulse on the microstructured surface. The results reveal that the hierarchical microstructure provides superior gas layer retention, sustaining a higher gas volume fraction (αg = 0.87) and attenuating impact loading (p/p* = 45) compared to micropillar and re-entrant microstructures. The evolution of wall shear stress shows alternating outward and inward patterns driven by bubble-induced radial flows, with peak values of 282 kPa (outward) and 89 kPa (inward) for the hierarchical microstructure. Furthermore, variations in γf and γw significantly influence the jet dynamics, modify the spatial distribution of wall pressure and shear stress, and determine the resulting force and impulse on the microstructured surface. These findings offer theoretical insight into mitigating cavitation-induced erosion and enhancing gas layer stability in marine hydrodynamics and fluid machinery.

papers.title: Tangential combustion instability and flame dynamics of a shear injector in a model rocket engine combustor
papers.abstract: To investigate the tangential combustion instability of coaxial shear injectors, an experimental study on self-excited tangential combustion instability under high-speed and high-temperature inlet conditions was conducted in a model rocket engine combustor. The experiment captured time-series data of oscillating pressures and transient CH* chemiluminescence images of the flame, which were subsequently analyzed to determine the pressure and flame oscillation modes. The results indicate that self-excited tangential combustion instability can be achieved through an off-center injector configuration. The oscillation frequency within the combustion chamber was observed to switch from 2100 to 2700 Hz as the oxidizer velocity increased. Based on the analysis of pressure phase relationships and three-dimensional acoustic simulations, the oscillation modes were identified as 1T1L and 2T0L, respectively. In both cases, the flame exhibited a lifted state, where variations in lift height altered the phase relationship between heat release and acoustic oscillations, thereby influencing the instability conditions. Regardless of the specific tangential oscillation mode, the flame from a single injector consistently exhibits a symmetric longitudinal unstable mode, and the repeated formation and collapse of heat release clusters drive synchronized combustion oscillations.

papers.title: Effects of acoustic liners' nonlinear characteristics on attenuating self-sustained combustion oscillations in a bluff-body flame
papers.abstract: Acoustic liners are key passive dampers for reducing self-sustained combustion oscillations in gas turbine combustors and afterburners. This study experimentally and numerically explores how acoustic liners mitigate longitudinal combustion oscillations in a combustor featuring a bluff-body diffusion flame. Combustion tests measured oscillation suppression using liners with varying porosities, complemented by acoustic simulations clarifying liner operating mechanisms. Results indicate that optimizing the maximum sound absorption coefficient alone does not yield optimal oscillation attenuation. Instead, lowering the acoustic impedance (dimensionless impedance <0.5) significantly enhances suppression effectiveness. Additionally, attenuating combustion oscillations reduces their frequency by up to 40 Hz, explaining why maximizing absorption and minimizing oscillation intensity cannot be simultaneously optimized. Liners with larger aperture ratios exhibit better suppression performance under identical backing cavity conditions, owing to reduced oscillating velocity within the holes, which lowers the nonlinear acoustic resistance. When the peak sound absorption frequency is approximately 70 Hz lower than the self-sustained oscillation frequency, the liner can reduce the pressure oscillation amplitude by 81% (equivalent to 14.5 dB). This work offers new insights into acoustic liner design for passive control of combustion oscillations in afterburners.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of transverse flow-induced vibrations of a D-section cylinder at low Reynolds number with varying angles of attack
papers.abstract: Flow-induced vibrations (FIVs) of noncircular cylinders, particularly D-section bodies, frequently occur under low Reynolds number and low mass ratio conditions in applications, such as cables, risers, and microscale structures. Compared to circular cylinders, these configurations exhibit greater dynamic complexity and higher safety risks. At low Reynolds numbers, the interaction and transition between vortex-induced vibration (VIV) and galloping are still not sufficiently understood. This study numerically investigates the transverse FIV of a D-section cylinder at a Reynolds number of 100 and a mass ratio of 10, through reduced velocities from 2 to 20 and angles of attack from 0° to 180°. Five distinct vibration regimes are identified: typical VIV; transitional response I; small-amplitude VIV (S-VIV); transitional response II; and galloping. The results reveal that increasing the angle of attack progressively drives the system through multiple vibration regimes, transitioning from typical VIV, through intermediate states, to galloping. Lock-in, beating phenomena, and 2S vortex shedding dominate in the VIV regimes, while galloping exhibits persistent frequency separation, rising amplitudes, and multiple vortex shedding within one vibration cycle. Energetic analysis shows strong coupling between vibration and wake evolution, with frequency harmonics inducing anomalous amplitude peaks. These findings elucidate the underlying mechanisms that govern VIV–galloping transitions and underscore the critical role of angle of attack in determining the dynamic response.

papers.title: Non-axisymmetric oscillating water column wave energy converter: A semi-analytical study
papers.abstract: A non-axisymmetric floating oscillating water column (OWC) wave energy converter (WEC) is proposed in this paper. In contrast to the traditional bottom opening used in axisymmetric OWCs, the newly proposed OWC WEC has a submerged opening positioned on the front cylindrical wall. A semi-analytical coupled hydrodynamic–pneumatic model is developed to investigate the power extraction of the proposed OWC, where the hydrodynamic model is established using the matching eigenfunction expansions and method of separation of variables. Following the model validation against general theoretical identities, the model is first applied to a stationary offshore OWC to study the effects of the chamber breadth and submerged opening geometry on power extraction under a series of regular waves with varying wave periods and incident directions, and then to an elastically constrained floating OWC WEC with six degree-of-freedom motion under both regular and irregular waves. The numerical results show that in comparison with axisymmetric OWCs, the proposed non-axisymmetric configuration significantly broadens the effective frequency bandwidth and increases the capture width ratio by up to three times with normal incidence of both regular and irregular waves. For floating OWCs, the free-sway motion emerges as a detrimental factor, negatively affecting both power extraction and safe operation.

papers.title: Thermosolutal stability analysis of Brinkman porous layer under local thermal non-equilibrium situation in the presence of viscous dissipation
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting local thermal non-equilibrium (LTNE) behavior between fluid and solid phases in weakly conducting, highly viscous flows is essential for numerous engineering applications, including electronic cooling and thermochemical energy storage systems. Motivated by these considerations, we investigate the instability mechanisms of double-diffusive convection influenced by viscous dissipation within a horizontal porous layer under LTNE conditions. A mathematical model is formulated wherein the momentum equation incorporates the Brinkman extension of Darcy's law to account for viscous effects. The thermal boundary conditions assume an adiabatic lower surface and a constant temperature upper surface. A linear stability analysis is conducted by introducing normal mode perturbations to the base state, resulting in an eigenvalue problem that is solved numerically. The study accounts for arbitrarily oriented oblique roll disturbances and reveals that the primary instability mode corresponds to longitudinal rolls (P=0 or δ=π/2), where the roll axis aligns with the primary flow direction. The onset of convection is characterized by determining the critical solutal Rayleigh number (Rc) and associated wavenumber (ac) for both longitudinal and oblique rolls. These results are illustrated graphically for varying values of the interphase heat transfer coefficient (H) and viscous dissipation parameter (ξ). It has been observed that the viscous dissipation parameter and the porosity-modified conductivity ratio exert a destabilizing influence, whereas the interphase heat transfer coefficient contributes to system stabilization over a certain intermediate range.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical analysis of rotating detonation in liquid hypergolic propellants
papers.abstract: This study employed an impinging-jet injector with 62 impinging pairs and an annular combustion chamber to conduct experiments on rotating detonation using liquid monomethylhydrazine (MMH) and nitrogen tetroxide (NTO). The experiments successfully achieved self-sustained rotating detonation waves spontaneously formed by hypergolic propellants, and observed detonation initiation, single-wave mode, and dual-wave mode. Furthermore, numerical simulations based on the Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes/large eddy simulation hybrid model and the discrete phase model were performed, successfully reproducing the hypergolic rotating detonation phenomenon. Experimental results revealed low-amplitude pressure oscillations in the combustion chamber prior to rotating detonation formation. The detonation waves in liquid MMH–NTO were found to develop from low-amplitude combustion instability, with the deflagration-to-detonation transition process exhibiting progressive characteristics. Numerical simulations revealed a transient deflagration process following the detonation wave. As the upstream droplets evaporated and absorbed heat, the temperature drop weakened the deflagration. Prior to the subsequent detonation wave arrival, the deflagration intensity attenuates to its minimum level, thereby storing energy to sustain stable detonation propagation while effectively suppressing the pre-wave deflagration characteristic. Energy release in hypergolic rotating detonation concentrates in the high-density droplet zone at the combustor head, exhibiting peak combustion intensity. The detonation wave triggers abrupt pressure and temperature surges that induce rapid propellant droplet evaporation and reactant compression. The compressed reactants undergo near-constant-volume combustion with fast energy release, driving supersonic detonation wave propagation.

papers.title: Stability mechanism of oil-swollen surfactant micelles: Insights from surfactant escape free energy
papers.abstract: The stability of oil-swollen surfactant micelles is critically important in fields such as drug delivery, environmental remediation, and crude oil extraction. Nevertheless, the microscopic mechanisms underlying their structural stability remain unclear. Here, we employ coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations coupled with umbrella sampling to study the structural characteristics of oil-swollen surfactant micelles composed of varying numbers of sodium dodecyl sulfate molecules (NSDS) and decane molecules (NDEC). By analyzing the escape process of surfactant molecules from the micelles, we explore the microscopic mechanisms through which NSDS and NDEC influence oil-swollen micellar stability. The results show that increasing NSDS results in structural imbalance of oil-swollen micelles, while increasing NDEC enhances micellar compactness and stability. Both the escape free energy and escape time of surfactant molecules from oil-swollen micelles exhibit non-monotonic trends with NDEC increasing, which are attributed to the balance between intermolecular interactions (oil-surfactant and surfactant-surfactant). Moreover, we identify the critical ranges for NSDS and NDEC that maintain micellar stability and determine the optimal decane-to-surfactant ratio of stable oil-swollen micelles. These results could provide effective guidance for optimizing the formulation design of swollen micellar solutions from free energy viewpoints.

papers.title: Optimized semi-flexible supersonic nozzle design using exact throat solution with characteristic inversion and Bézier Mach distribution
papers.abstract: Supersonic semi-flexible wall nozzles with the ability to continuously vary the Mach number have become a key configuration for advanced supersonic wind tunnels, with their contour design typically based on the Sivells method. However, this method faces two persistent challenges in its application: (i) suboptimal flow field uniformity, particularly during continuous Mach number variation, and (ii) localized Mach number depression (“dimples”) along the nozzle axis. This paper presents an enhanced design methodology to overcome these challenges. The proposed improvements incorporate two key elements: (1) exact analytical solutions for transonic flow to replace the conventional source-flow approximation used in the Sivells method at the throat section, and (2) a Bézier-optimized characteristic method for expansion contour design. Experimental results demonstrated that the improved design method significantly enhanced performance even in a small 0.3 m-scale wind tunnel: flow field uniformity reached 0.0010–0.0053 in fixed-geometry mode (Ma = 1.2–3.0), while dynamic flow uniformity was maintained at 0.002–0.010 in continuous morphing mode (Ma = 1.5–3.0). These research outcomes provide a reliable technical approach for designing supersonic wind tunnel semi-flexible nozzles.

papers.title: Wave interaction with two-dimensional submerged perforated thin-plate structures: Effects of structure shape
papers.abstract: Perforated thin-plate structures, which can effectively dissipate wave energy and also serve as base structures for growing corals in nature-based solutions to shore protection problems, can be promising alternatives to traditional rubble-mound breakwaters for shore protection. The growth of corals may be affected by the geometrical shapes of the base structures. This study investigates wave interaction with one or multiple submerged perforated thin-plate structures, emphasizing effects of structure's shapes on wave transmission and wave loading. Using a multi-domain boundary element method (BEM) and a parameterization of the pressure drop across a perforated thin plate, six cross-sectional shapes that belong to the following four types are considered for different ratios of structure height to water depth: rectangular, trapezoidal, triangular, and semi-circular shapes. For the purpose of verifying the BEM codes, an analytical solution was also developed for a single structure with a rectangular shape. The results show that for a given number of structures, the rectangular and trapezoidal shapes are more effective in reducing wave energy transmission, providing protection across a range of wave periods. The reduction of wave energy in the transmitted waves is controlled mainly by the energy dissipation into turbulence. Resonant reflection, found when multiple structures are used, can only slightly affect wave transmission in the frequency range of practical relevance. The wave loading on the structures for promising designs is studied. The results reported here are useful for marine biologists and coastal engineers to choose a suitable shape for the base structures for reducing wave energy and growing corals and geotechnical engineers to design foundations and anchoring schemes.

papers.title: Start-up process of the ground vortex ahead of the engine intake with crosswind
papers.abstract: The ground vortex formed within the crosswind degrades the power output of the aero-engine and threatens the flight takeoff safety. Considerable amounts of experiments have been conducted to investigate the flow mechanism for the formation of the ground vortex. However, the detailed transient start-up process of the ground vortex is still unclear due to the limitations of the measurement techniques. In this work, high-fidelity delayed detached eddy simulations are performed to investigate the underlying mechanism of the ground vortex formation ahead of the intake with the occurrence of crosswind. A thorough validation is conducted first to compare the simulation against the experimental data. By gradually increasing the mass flow into the intake, a near-ground shear vortex formed around the intake due to its blockage to the crosswind is enhanced by the suction of the intake and gradually approaches the highlight plane. Multiple ground vortex filaments are generated from the shear vortex at the boundary between the crosswind and the suction flow. The vortex filaments merge into one single ground vortex, and it moves upwind along the intake lip together with the lower trailing vortex. It takes 0.9–1.0 s for the ground vortex to be formed with a velocity ratio of 4.7–5.0. The formation process found in this study is different from previous research in which the ground vortex is evolved from the trailing vortex or the ambient vorticity.

papers.title: Periodic softening–hardening damage mechanism of sandstone under cyclic water immersion
papers.abstract: The stability of the surrounding rock in underground tunnels is vital for the safe extraction of coal. Groundwater seepage, in conjunction with rock–water interactions, triggers progressive degradation, which is a primary cause of surrounding rock instability. This degradation leads to damage, posing a serious threat to the safe operation of the coal mine. In this study, cyclic loading and unloading experiments and computed tomography (CT) scanning were conducted on sandstone specimens subjected to varying cyclic water immersion heights. The results demonstrate that increasing the cyclic immersion height and immersion height differential significantly reduces the ultimate bearing capacity of sandstone. This reduction corresponds to a diminished capacity for elastic energy storage and an accelerated rate of energy dissipation associated with crack propagation, as evidenced by an increasing proportion of dissipated energy. Combined with CT scanning analysis, both the three-dimensional fracture volume ratio and the fractal dimension rise with cyclic immersion height, indicating more complex fracture development. Additionally, the study reveals the periodic softening–hardening damage mechanism of sandstone under cyclic water immersion. During the cyclic water immersion process, the periodic loss and replenishment of moisture within the sandstone induce softening–hardening effects on its structure. This alternating process promotes progressive fracture initiation and propagation, accelerates internal damage accumulation, and leads to the degradation of mechanical integrity, ultimately rendering the sandstone more vulnerable to failure. These findings provide valuable insights for the study of surrounding rock stability in coal mine tunnels.

papers.title: Investigation of noise prediction for a five-bladed propeller under edgewise flow using permeable Ffowcs Williams and Hawkings surfaces
papers.abstract: This study presents a computational investigation of far-field propeller noise under edgewise inflow using Detached Eddy Simulation coupled with the Ffowcs–Williams and Hawkings formulation. The primary contribution lies in evaluating and validating surface size—with and without end cap—and end-cap correction strategies for permeable surfaces, along with a theoretical model for optimal end-cap spacing based on equations from jet-noise theory and Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition. To assess these effects, smaller and larger surfaces with open ends, a single end cap, and two correction approaches—JetEnd and SPODEnd—are tested on a five-bladed propeller configuration and compared against experimental measurements. Results show that open-ended permeable surfaces substantially underpredict noise in the downstream region due to vortex leakage, whereas closed-end configurations significantly improve accuracy, with up to 97% of downstream microphones falling within 10 dB of experimental data (vs 33% for open-end). JetEnd correction provides only minor additional changes(less than 2.3 dB), indicating that spurious noise from end caps is small and largely confined to low frequencies. Both JetEnd and SPODEnd methods yield nearly identical predictions, confirming that a single end cap can predict sufficiently well. A simplified convective-spacing model is shown to align with dominant pressure-fluctuation structures extracted via Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, which means that, if correction is needed, JetEnd can be used. Limitations associated with smaller permeable surfaces highlight the need for future development of lateral boundary corrections to reduce contamination from side-edge vortex escape. While the findings are demonstrated on a specific case, the same physical reasoning suggests applicability to other propeller cases.

papers.title: Graphics processing unit accelerated high-order moment-encoded lattice Boltzmann method for liquid–vapor phase-change simulations
papers.abstract: Although visually appealing, the simulation of the liquid–vapor phase-change flows faces numerous challenges in accurately reproducing complex bubble dynamics (nucleation, growth, coalescence, departure and breakup, etc.). Recently, a cascaded lattice Boltzmann method (CLBM) was proposed to solve the liquid–vapor phase-change process, which is based on the three-dimensional nineteen-velocity (D3Q19) lattice. Although this method has faithfully reproduced complete boiling regimes, it systematically comes at the price of a substantial memory requirement: double D3Q19 discretizations for the LB equation requires more variables per grid node and makes it hard to run higher resolution simulations on a laptop or workstation. To open up kinetic-based liquid-vapor phase-change simulation to industrial applications, we employ the recent high-order moment-encoded LBM (HOME-LBM) framework for solving the pseudopotential multiphase model with a memory footprint reduction by a factor of two while coupling with the temperature solved by a three-times faster lightweight finite difference method through a non-ideal equation of state. We show that our HOME-LBM phase-change solver can get similar accuracy and lower computing costs on numerical simulations of several canonical problems than CLBM. It is verified that the resulting solver can simulate both the isothermal multiphase flow and the liquid–vapor phase-change process. In addition, we present more challenging examples to demonstrate our solver's visual complexity, accuracy, and realism.

papers.title: A novel quasi-two-dimensional multi-streamline performance calculation method for transonic fans
papers.abstract: Conventional one-dimensional mean-line methods struggle to accurately predict the performance of low hub-to-tip ratio transonic fans due to spanwise flow gradients, while two-dimensional methods are computationally costly and require excessive geometric parameters, making them unsuitable for preliminary design phases. This study proposes a quasi-two-dimensional multi-streamline approach that reduces both computational cost and geometric complexity relative to full through-flow solutions, without sacrificing radial flow resolution. By incorporating multiple streamlines under simplified radial equilibrium, it accounts for non-uniform radial distributions during preliminary design. Key innovations include a streamlined resettling algorithm, a stream tube choking model and flow redistribution scheme, and a meridional curvature correction scheme. Validation using single-stage and two-stage transonic fans shows that the method significantly improves prediction accuracy. Compared to traditional streamline curvature through-flow methods, it achieves about 100-fold speedup with the same number of streamlines and closely matches full three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics results in radial aerodynamic parameter distributions. This novel framework reconciles accuracy and computational efficiency, effectively addressing radial flow non-uniformities in the preliminary design phase. It streamlines the fan/compressor design process and enhances performance prediction reliability, offering significant advantages for high-performance turbomachinery development.

papers.title: Suppression of the aerodynamic forces and vortex-induced vibration of a circular cylinder by bypass channels
papers.abstract: Numerical investigations are conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of bypass channels in suppressing the aerodynamic coefficients of a stationary circular cylinder. The aerodynamic coefficients, which vary with the geometric shape, thickness, entrance location, and exit location of bypass channels, are given attention. Compared with the bare cylinder, the flow from bypass channels can weaken the cross-communication between the bilateral shear layers of the cylinder and suppress the alternating vortex shedding in the wake. Under the optimal parameters, the root mean square lift coefficient (Clrms) of a stationary cylinder can be reduced by more than 83.7% with a 60.1% reduction in the mean drag coefficient (Cdmean). Then, the vortex-induced vibrations (VIVs) of a single-degree-of-freedom spring-mounted cylinder are investigated under the optimal parameters. The results show that bypass channels are able to alter the vortex shedding pattern in the wake, disrupting the periodicity of lift fluctuations. Eventually, the maximal VIV amplitude of the cylinder with bypass channels can be reduced by 94.87%.

papers.title: Heat transport and ionic dynamics in pure and mixed molten salts
papers.abstract: Heat transfer in liquids is challenging as it combines competing effects of oscillations, which dominate heat capacity, and diffusion, which enables hydrodynamic flow. This is compounded by the junior state of liquid thermodynamics theories. Nevertheless, molten salts play an increasingly important role in industrial and energy applications and there is a pressing need to understand the mechanisms behind their transport processes. We use molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the heat transport of three molten salts: LiCl, KCl, and their mixture. In multi-component fluids, the distinction between conduction and convection is confounded by the presence of partial mass currents. We therefore calculate different susceptibilities, which include and exclude heat carried by partial currents. We find that, while the heat advected by mass currents in the mixture increases with increasing temperature, the heat transferred by collective vibrational motion decreases with increasing temperature. This causes a maximum in the heat transport in the mixtures only—in pure salts the vibrational and diffusive components decrease monotonically with temperature. We attribute this anomaly to the extra freedom of collective ionic motion in mixtures—in pure salts the motion of cations and anions is bound by conservation of momentum. In mixtures, the introduction of a new species releases this condition and enables a coherent but diffusive collective motion. We tentatively ascribe this motion to “diffusive” phonons, previously used to explain similar anomalies in solid thermal conductivity. These results indicate the rich relationship between ionic dynamics and transport in molten salt mixtures.

papers.title: Extending the trapping theorem to provide local stability guarantees for quadratically nonlinear models
papers.abstract: The Navier–Stokes equations are partial differential equations to describe the nonlinear convective motion of fluids and they are computationally expensive to simulate because of their high nonlinearity and variables being fully coupled. Reduced-order models (ROMs) are simpler models for evolving the flows by capturing only the dominant behaviors of a system and can be used to design controllers for high-dimensional systems. However it is challenging to guarantee the stability of these models either globally or locally. Ensuring the stability of ROMs can improve the interpretability of the behavior of the dynamics and help develop effective system control strategies. For quadratically nonlinear systems that represent many fluid flows, the Schlegel and Noack trapping theorem [Schlegel and Noack, “On long-term boundedness of Galerkin models,” J. Fluid Mech. 765, 325–352 (2015)] can be used to check if ROMs are globally stable (long-term bounded). This theorem was subsequently incorporated into system identification techniques that determine models directly from data [Kaptanoglu et al., “Promoting global stability in data-driven models of quadratic nonlinear dynamics,” Phys. Rev. Fluids 6, 094401 (2021)]. While the Schlegel and Noack trapping theorem provides global stability criteria for systems with strictly energy-preserving nonlinearities, many physical systems, including those with inflow/outflow boundary conditions, exhibit weakly relaxed energy-preserving structures. This work introduces two key advances: (1) a theorem establishing analytical stability bounds for linear-quadratic systems under relaxed energy-preserving constraints, explicitly quantifying the local stability radius, and (2) the extended trapping SINDy algorithm, which embeds these theoretical guarantees into data-driven system identification. By integrating Lyapunov's direct method with the trapping theorem framework, our approach enables the first provably locally stable models for quadratic dynamics with weakly broken energy-preserving nonlinearities. Several examples are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed algorithm.

papers.title: Acoustic performance of a meta-liner based on an extended slit-neck resonator and a perforated panel under grazing flow
papers.abstract: This study proposes a low-frequency broadband meta-liner (extended-slit resonator meta-liner, ERML) based on an extended slit-neck resonator and a perforated panel. A theoretical impedance model under grazing flow and a semi-analytical numerical model with equivalent impedance boundary conditions were established. The noise reduction performance and sound absorption characteristics under different typical low Mach number grazing flow conditions were comprehensively investigated. The ERML achieves broadband noise reduction below 500 Hz at grazing flow velocities ranging from 0 to 0.15 Ma, achieving the thickness-to-wavelength ratio of 1/24. Under static conditions, the measured average transmission loss within 150–500 Hz reaches 7 dB, while at Ma = 0.15, the corresponding value is 6.2 dB, suggesting that the presence of grazing flow reduces the sound attenuation performance of ERML. This reduction in sound attenuation can be attributed to the interaction between the grazing flow and the meta-surface, which affects the acoustic energy dissipation capability of ERML, leading to a slight decline in overall efficiency. Comparative analysis confirms that the integration of a perforated panel stabilizes the acoustic performance of ERML under grazing flow, enhancing its adaptability to complex flow fields. Finally, experimental samples were fabricated and tested in a flow duct to evaluate acoustic performance under grazing flow, validating the effectiveness of the theoretical model and numerical method. The ERML demonstrates outstanding low-frequency broadband noise suppression, strong adaptability to actual flow environments, along with advantages in structural simplicity and manufacturability, exhibiting promising prospects for noise control applications.

papers.title: Study of squeezed ferrofluid flow through fibrous porous media
papers.abstract: This study explores the unsteady squeezed flow of ferrofluid through a fibrous porous medium confined between two circular disks. The lower disk remains stationary, while the upper disk undergoes sinusoidal oscillations in the axial direction, inducing time-periodic compression of the porous matrix. The variation in the inter-disk gap drives transient deformation, altering porosity and permeability over time. A normalized Kozeny–Carman relation is employed to model the deformation-dependent permeability, effectively capturing the relationship between porosity evolution and flow resistance. The combined influence of oscillatory squeezing motion, fibrous microstructure, and magnetic effects significantly alters flow resistance, mixing behavior, and heat transfer characteristics. A similarity transformation reduces the governing momentum and energy equations to a set of coupled nonlinear ordinary differential equations, which are solved numerically using the MATLAB built-in boundary value problem solver (bvp5c). The results reveal that increasing the squeezing parameter intensifies axial flow and enhances thermal transport, while stronger ferromagnetic interactions redirect streamlines radially and suppress vertical compression, contributing to flow stabilization. The overall velocity magnitude increases under stronger compression of the porous medium, enhancing ferrofluid displacement and axial pumping effects. The heat transfer of ferrofluid is found to be damped by augmented ferromagnetic interactions, whereas it is enhanced with increasing oscillatory compression. The skin friction coefficient and Nusselt numbers on both disks exhibit distinct oscillatory patterns, with sharp peaks occurring during early compression phases. These insights provide a foundation for engineering adaptive thermal and lubrication systems, where oscillatory compression and magnetic field are harnessed to regulate transport and stability.

papers.title: A phenomenological model for predicting bedload transport in vegetated channels using near-bed turbulent kinetic energy
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of bedload transport in vegetated riverbeds is critical for wetland protection and ecological restoration. This study develops a novel turbulence-based theoretical model for bedload transport in vegetated flows. The near-bed turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) is derived from the phenomenological theory of turbulence through quantitative analysis of multiscale turbulent eddy structures. For rigid vegetation, the proposed model provides a unified framework for estimating near-bed TKE across diverse configurations, including uniform distribution, patchy clusters, random arrangements with variable diameters, and vertically heterogeneous morphologies, improving upon previous empirical superposition approaches. The predicted near-bed TKE exhibits a robust correlation with measured bedload transport rates compiled from 358 experimental datasets, supporting its validity as a physically meaningful predictor. Following the operators of formulas developed for unvegetated beds, a refined TKE-based bedload transport formulation for vegetated flow is derived using symbolic regression, calibrated on datasets with uniformly distributed cylindrical vegetation. Validation demonstrates that the proposed transport model maintains high accuracy while effectively generalizing to more complex rigid vegetation scenarios. Compared to existing literature models, our formulation shows improved predictive precision and broader applicability.

papers.title: Modeling microchannel flow of Phan–Thien–Tanner fluids using hybrid skip-physics informed neural network
papers.abstract: This study investigates the combined electroosmotic and pressure-driven flow of viscoelastic fluids in a parallel-plate microchannel, emphasizing the interplay of flow and thermal transport under realistic electrokinetic conditions. The simplified Phan–Thien–Tanner model is used to characterize nonlinear rheology, while the electric double-layer potential is evaluated using the full Poisson–Boltzmann formulation, beyond the Debye–Hückel approximation. Closed-form solutions are obtained for the velocity field, flow rate, and stress distribution under hydrodynamically fully developed conditions. The thermally developing regime is analyzed through the energy equation, considering Joule heating and viscous dissipation. To improve predictive accuracy, a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework is integrated with the governing equations to reconstruct velocity and temperature profiles from sparse data without mesh generation. Multiple PINN architectures were investigated, with skip connections shown to significantly enhance convergence in deeper networks. A hybrid training strategy, combining physics-constrained learning with data-driven fine-tuning, outperforms conventional neural networks. A Hybrid Skip-PINN (five hidden layers) achieves the best performance with mean squared error of 1.3783 × 10−6 and demonstrates robustness against noisy data. Parametric studies highlight the effects of viscoelastic, Brinkman, Peclet, and surface potential parameters. The proposed hybrid framework offers a robust methodology for design and optimization of microfluidic systems.

papers.title: Three-dimensional two-phase smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulation of bubble/droplet rise and coalescence at moderate Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: Bubble and droplet dynamics play pivotal roles in diverse industrial and scientific applications. This study presents an advanced three-dimensional (3D) Lagrangian framework for two-phase flow simulation that combines Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) with the Continuum Surface Force method to solve the Navier–Stokes equations. The developed model incorporates two key innovations: a density-independent formulation using Rusanov-flux-inspired artificial diffusion and an implicit 3D advection velocity correction scheme. The specialized simulator accurately captures bubble rise and coalescence dynamics across moderate Reynolds numbers (23≤Re≤135) and a broad range of Eötvös numbers (5≤Eo≤1000), while systematically evaluating critical numerical parameters, including particle resolution effects, boundary interactions, and density/viscosity ratio dependencies. Validation against experimental data and established numerical benchmarks confirms the model's precision in predicting both isolated bubble behavior and complex coalescence processes. The 3D SPH approach successfully reproduces diverse bubble morphologies, from oblate ellipsoids to skirted configurations, while maintaining numerical stability throughout all stages of coalescence, from initial approach to final interface rupture. Additionally, 3D streamline visualizations based on the velocity field reveal vortex dynamics and their influence on the wake structure and surrounding flow. These patterns highlight how vortex cores shift and evolve in response to changes in bubble morphology and proximity to sidewalls during rising and merging. Overall, the results demonstrate the robustness of the proposed framework for modeling complex interfacial flow phenomena, with strong potential for both fundamental research and industrial applications involving multiphase systems.

papers.title: Impact of the square rib on flow dynamics and thermal performance in the microchannel
papers.abstract: A three-dimensional numerical investigation of flow and heat transfer has been carried out within a microchannel containing a square rib, focusing on flow separation, recirculation, and vortex shedding over the range of the Reynolds number (Re) from 12 to 1000. The study explores the impact of rib orientation, channel aspect ratios, and Re on the formation of recirculation bubbles, flow symmetry, and boundary layer behavior with a detailed impact of wall shear stress. At low Re, steady flow is observed with minimal recirculation behind the rib. As Re increases, flow separation occurs, leading to the formation of recirculation bubbles in the rib wake and along the sidewalls. Particularly for the rib with two sidewalls parallel to the vertical mid-plane of the channel and at Re = 85, flow separation initiates on the sidewalls of the rib but reattaches immediately. At 101 ≤ Re ≤ 400, the flow separation occurs on both sidewalls and the wake of the rib. A further increase in 400 < Re ≤ 900 leads to the merging of recirculation bubbles of the rib sidewalls and wake, with the recirculation bubbles center shifted to the saddle point. The wall shear stress highlights the flow separation near the sidewalls and wake of the rib. The critical Reynolds number (Rec) for flow transition is identified between 900 < Re ≤ 1000, where unsteady flow is characterized by the change of vortex shedding with time. Additionally, by applying heat flux to the bottom wall of the microchannel, the influence of varying Re on the average Nusselt number, friction factor, local heat transfer coefficient, wall shear stress, and vortex formations is analyzed.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical study of metal droplet splashing effects on direct current air arc interruption
papers.abstract: To investigate the interaction between metal droplet motion and arc plasma dynamics during direct current interruption, an improved bidirectionally coupled model is developed based on magnetohydrodynamic theory. By incorporating the volume force exerted by the metal droplet into the momentum conservation equation, the model enables dynamic feedback between the air arc flow field and the metal droplet trajectories. The influence of droplet splashing (DS)-under varying velocities and particle sizes-on the flow field distribution within the contact gap is analyzed, and the mechanism of flow field reconstruction induced by metal droplet motion is revealed. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that DS typically occurs under conditions such as current oscillation, which induces localized vortices in the flow field and inhibits the directional motion of the arc. Furthermore, metal droplets with larger diameters and higher velocities cause more severe disturbances to the arc-induced flow field.

papers.title: Hydraulic fracture propagation in thick conglomerate formations: Insights from acid-induced weakening
papers.abstract: Conglomerate formations are characterized by strong heterogeneity, high mechanical strength, and a high resistance to fracturing. To address the challenges associated with effectively controlling fracture propagation trajectories and fracture zones—stemming from the pronounced heterogeneity and strength variations within thick conglomerate layers—both experimental testing and the finite element method were employed to simulate the propagation behavior of hydraulic fractures during acid-composite fracturing. The study systematically investigated the influence of acidizing duration, in situ stress conditions, gravel physical properties, and fracturing process parameters on fracture initiation and propagation. The results indicate that acid treatment significantly reduces the mechanical strength of the conglomerate by weakening the cementation between particles. Acid fracturing promotes a higher incidence of deflected fractures, leading to increased fracture width and extension distance. The particle size and content of gravel exert a direct influence on fracture trajectories. When fractures encounter large gravel, they tend to deviate from the direction of the maximum horizontal principal stress. As the gravel diameter decreases, the extent of fracture deviation diminishes, and propagation aligns more closely with the principal stress direction. Furthermore, excessive fracturing fluid injection rates and high fluid viscosities can adversely affect fracture width and propagation extent. The optimization of fracturing parameters is essential for achieving effective stimulation and favorable engineering outcomes in conglomerate formations.

papers.title: Study on the dynamics of underwater explosion bubbles near elastic–plastic cylindrical shells
papers.abstract: The dynamic behavior of underwater explosion bubbles is largely dependent on their boundary conditions. The pulsation behavior of bubbles near free surfaces or rigid boundaries has been extensively studied, while the rich mechanical mechanisms behind the pulsation behavior and jet development of bubbles near elastic–plastic boundaries have not yet been systematically investigated. In this paper, underwater explosion bubbles are first generated using experimental methods, and their pulsation behaviors under different conditions are recorded using high-speed photography. Subsequently, the arbitrary Lagrange–Euler method and the Cowper–Symonds material model are employed to accurately simulate the pulsation process of the bubbles and the dynamic response of the structures. It is shown that the pulsation behavior of bubbles near elastic–plastic cylindrical shells has been categorized into six distinct types based on varying dimensionless distance parameter γL. With an increase in γL from 0.01 to 3.20, the maximum bubble dimensionless volume V* increased from 0.75 to 0.93, while the pulsation dimensionless period T* increased from 0.78 to 1.00. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that jets are generated by bubbles in proximity to an elastic–plastic cylindrical shell, and these jets propel away from the shell. During the developmental phase of these jets, two broader jets with a dimensionless speed v* of 0.82 have been observed to converge and form a narrower jet with a dimensionless speed v* of 5.45, resulting in an escalation of energy within the narrower jet. This phenomenon elucidates the mechanical mechanism underlying the rapid acceleration of bubble jet velocity to tens of meters per second. Additionally, the effects of buoyancy parameters and boundary conditions on both bubble pulsation and jet velocity have been examined, providing valuable insights for investigations into the pulsation of underwater explosion bubbles in the vicinity of cylindrical shells.

papers.title: Aerodynamic characteristic of small-scale and hyper-rotated plane Couette flow with contracted cross section
papers.abstract: Aerodynamic gas bearings, which leverage their hyper-rotational speed and lightweight attributes, have emerged as pivotal components in turbines and compressor turbomachinery. The gas film flow field of aerodynamic gas thrust bearings (AGTBs) is characterized by a small-scale, hyper-rotated plane Couette flow with a contracted cross section. However, the flow dynamics under rotor motion, variable clearance cross sections, and ambient leakage remain unclear. This study investigates the aerodynamic characteristics of plane Couette flow with clearance heights ranging from 30 to 200 μm through numerical simulations and experimental measurements. The key findings reveal that the circumferential contraction and sudden expansion of the gas film channel lead to an alternating distribution of high- and low-pressure zones. A large-scale recirculation zone forms near the backward-facing step owing to flow channel expansion. The hyper-rotated flow is predominantly governed by the interaction between the self-acting pressure difference force and centrifugal force, driven by rotor motion. The pressure difference force induces secondary flow deflection from the inner to outer diameter, whereas the centrifugal force causes fluid inhalation near low-pressure zones and exhalation near high-pressure zones. In addition, the dynamic compression effect of the plane Couette flow correlates positively with the rotational speed and negatively with the clearance height. The centrifugal force, which is amplified by higher rotational speeds, strengthens the secondary flow deflection. The dynamic compression effect diminishes and becomes negligible when the clearance height exceeds 100 μm. An optimal pitch ratio of 0.5 maximizes the dynamic compression effect. This study elucidates the mechanism of a high-speed, small-scale plane Couette flow and offers theoretical insights into AGTB design and optimization.

papers.title: Study on the influence of perforation on vndirectional hydraulic fracturing from the roof
papers.abstract: To solve the problems that gas outburst accidents are prone to occur in the mining process of broken and soft outburst coal seam, and the existing research on the directional roof hydraulic fracturing of broken soft outburst coal seam lacks the analysis of roof bedding and perforation design, this paper uses the method of combining experiment with particle flow code (PFC), investigates the influence of perforation on the directional hydraulic fracturing of roof, and defines the optimal perforation layout scheme under the joint action of bedding and perforation. The results reveal that hydraulic fracture propagation is significantly influenced by the bedding angle and in situ stress conditions of the rock mass. During roof fracturing, once fractures propagate to the coal-rock interface, they induce the formation of a complex fracture network within the coal seam, effectively enhancing its permeability. PFC has accuracy and engineering adaptability in hydraulic fracturing numerical simulation. Under the conditions of different bedding angles, the directional hydraulic fracturing perforation should be arranged in different ways, a vertical perforation configuration is recommended for bedding angles of 0°–15°, while for angles of 30°–60°, perforations should be oriented perpendicular to the bedding direction. At 45°–60°, perforations should avoid alignment with the bedding plane and instead adopt a large-angle orientation. Under the parameter combination of “three perforations-optimized angle-suitable bedding,” the effect of directional hydraulic fracturing of bedding rock broken soft coal seam roof is the best. This perforation scheme offers an effective strategy for gas control in outburst-prone soft coal seams.

papers.title: Disentangling chaotic laminar and turbulent flow components in a weakly curved square duct flow
papers.abstract: For straight duct flows, the transition to turbulence results from perturbations of finite amplitude, characteristic of a subcritical bifurcation depending on the Reynolds number, and the resulting dynamics are abruptly chaotic in space and time. On the other hand, for slightly curved duct flows, the laminar solution is subject to successive supercritical bifurcations, from steady state to temporal chaos, for increasing Dean number. The present article investigates the coexistence of these two scenarios. The method is based on the separate computation of the laminar solution and the turbulent deviation. Assuming a relatively weak curvature, the equations are expressed in Cartesian coordinates; the equations for the laminar component are governed by the Dean number, while the turbulent deviation is not directly sensitive to the curvature and governed by the Reynolds number. The separation between the laminar, temporally complex solution and turbulent disturbances is fundamentally different from the Reynolds decomposition and allows us to distinguish the concomitant effects of the curvature and the Reynolds stress. The results are illustrated, for the case of square duct flow, with the secondary flow in accordance with Prandtl's classification and with the head losses.

papers.title: Experimental study on the characteristics of hydrogen sulfide-containing gas leakage jets using schlieren technique
papers.abstract: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is a major by-product in both primary energy extraction and enhanced recovery operations. Uncontrolled leakage of H2S-containing gases during transportation poses severe threats to human safety and environmental integrity in the vicinity. Consequently, research into the dynamic characteristics of H2S-containing gas leakage jets is of significant importance. Given that the jet phase of leaking H2S-containing gas is influenced by multiple factors, this study employs schlieren apparatus and high-speed videography to conduct experimental investigations on the leakage jets of H2S-containing gas mixtures. The effects of H2S concentration, leakage orifice diameter, and internal gas flow velocity on the jet behavior of the gas mixture were analyzed. The results indicate that, under the combined influence of internal/external pressure differentials, gradual kinetic energy dissipation, and the molar mass of the gas itself, the leaking gas exhibits distinct phenomena, including vortex formation, kinetic energy dissipation, and plume diffusion. The influence of H2S concentration, leakage orifice diameter, and internal gas flow velocity on the jet distance of the leaking gas was quantified, elucidating the relationships between these factors and the jet distance. Furthermore, the relative impact of these multiple factors on the jet behavior was quantified, establishing the hierarchy of influence as leakage orifice diameter > leakage flow velocity > concentration ratio. This work supplements the existing body of research on H2S-containing gas leakage jets from an experimental perspective.

papers.title: Experimental and staged simulation investigation of sympathetic detonation behavior in unconfined explosive charges
papers.abstract: Sympathetic detonation (SD)—the unintended ignition of an explosive (acceptor) caused by the detonation of a nearby charge (donor)—poses critical risks in explosive storage and deployment. This study integrates near-field experiments with staged high-fidelity numerical simulations to investigate SD behavior in unconfined tri-nitrotoluene charges in air. Experiments under two initiation configurations reveal that detonation direction and stand-off distance significantly affect SD occurrence, with measured transmission distances of 40 mm (axial) and 15 mm (lateral), and corresponding safety distances of 100 and 30 mm. A three-dimensional direct numerical simulation framework employing high-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory schemes and multi-stage solvers resolves the coupled shock-to-detonation processes. The ignition and growth model is used to describe chemical kinetics, allowing the simulation of ignition phenomena otherwise undetectable in experiments. Numerical results align well with experimental data and uncover key near-field behaviors, including partial detonations, backblast-induced overpressure spikes, and ignition without macroscopic detonation. These findings highlight the limitations of traditional flow-field-based SD criteria and emphasize the importance of micro-scale reaction modeling in defining accurate safety margins. This multiscale approach offers a robust methodology for evaluating SD hazards and optimizing safety design in explosive systems.

papers.title: Film flow characteristics of molten slag on rotary disk atomizer at commercial scale and implications for slag granule production
papers.abstract: Centrifugal-granulation-assisted thermal energy recovery (CGATER), which produces small, hot granules from bulk molten slag for further waste-heat recovery, has emerged as a promising route to treat high-temperature molten slag in the iron and steel industry. However, scaling up CGATER remains challenging due to limited granulation data at the commercial scale. One viable solution is to approach the slag film flow characteristics by modeling and, thus, infer the granulation performance. Herein, we carried out the first computational fluid dynamics modeling of the film flow on the atomizer at the commercial scale, as enabled by the newly developed multiphase, heat transfer model. Orthogonal cases were set for modeling to systematically understand the effects of operation parameters and thermophysical properties on film flow. It is found that heat transfer affects the total film thickness by up to 220.1% but only has a minor effect on the liquid film thickness (13.4% on average). The rotary speed proves the most effective way to adjust the thin liquid thickness at the commercial scale. A cross-validation was implemented to evaluate the correlations comprehensively, which highlights the acceptably good accuracy of our correlation by R2 = 0.85. Finally, we quantified the correlation between the slag film thickness and the slag granule size, enabling fast yet accurate prediction of the centrifugal granulation performance. This work not only explores the film flow characteristics of molten slag at the commercial scale for the first time but also provides a rational pathway to predict granulation performance for the scale-up of CGATER technology.

papers.title: A multiscale Boltzmann equation for complex systems of neutral gases across all flow regimes
papers.abstract: A multiscale Boltzmann equation (MBE) is found from the gas-kinetic theory as the master equation for complex physical systems of neutral gases across all flow regimes, which span from the continuum limit to the free-molecular limit, covering a vast range of applications such as hypersonic flows over near-space vehicles and delicate flows around micro-electromechanical systems. A key feature of this MBE is the introduction of the observation scale into the master equation, which distinguishes the MBE from single-scale master (or governing) equations where fixed observation scales are implied in their basic assumptions. The fundamental properties of MBE, such as the asymptotic preserving property, are proved theoretically, and a concise numerical scheme is developed for MBE to demonstrate its validity on benchmark multiscale problems.

papers.title: Hydraulic hysteresis in turbulent wakes under a free surface
papers.abstract: It is well known that a turbulent wake behind an obstacle placed beneath a free surface can show two completely different flow states. One is a supercritical flow with a discontinuous surface, while the other is a subcritical flow with a smooth surface. In the present study, we aim to quantitatively capture a hydraulic hysteresis around these bistable states. For this purpose, we conduct experiments of the wake behind a square plate placed beneath a free surface, and we measure the velocity fields using particle image velocimetry and the drag force using a load cell. The results show that the hysteresis loop can be captured around the Froude number of unity, both when changing the plate depth at a fixed inflow velocity and when changing the inflow velocity at a fixed plate depth. We also conduct experiments varying the plate size L to show the condition (depth≲0.4L) under which the hydraulic hysteresis appears.

papers.title: A point cloud network-embedded multi-fidelity surrogate model for fast aerothermal prediction of hypersonic vehicles with variable configurations
papers.abstract: Fast and accurate aerothermal prediction is essential for hypersonic vehicles. In this study, a Point Cloud-Embedded Multi-Fidelity Network (PC-MFNet) is proposed for aerothermal prediction with variable configurations. Within this framework, low-fidelity heat flux data generated by Eckert's reference enthalpy method are embedded into a point cloud neural network, enabling effective multi-fidelity data fusion to enhance prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. To construct the multi-fidelity dataset, four representative hypersonic configurations—the double ellipsoid, blunt cone, blunt biconic, and lifting body—were selected based on computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations and engineering calculations. The generalization performance of PC-MFNet was evaluated through multi-dimensional test cases with totally different configurations. Results show that PC-MFNet maintains prediction errors below 4% under various angles of attack and Mach numbers for the trained configurations. For unseen configurations outside the training set, the model achieves average prediction errors for heat flux below 14%, demonstrating strong generalization performance. Moreover, PC-MFNet requires only 0.2% of the prediction time compared to CFD simulations while maintaining near-CFD-level accuracy.

papers.title: Compressible and viscous flow over a heated cylinder with varying thermal effects: Aerodynamics and heat transfer
papers.abstract: This study numerically investigates the effects of the surface-to-free-stream temperature ratio on aerodynamics and heat transfer in compressible flow over a two-dimensional heated circular cylinder. Wall-resolved simulations with fully compressible Navier–Stokes equations are performed at Reynolds number, Re, ranging from 20 to 150 and free-stream Mach number, M∞, of 0.2 and 0.4, which are both defined based on the free-stream values and cylinder diameter. The effects of temperature ratio, TR, between the cylinder surface and free-stream are investigated at neutral (1.0), low (1.1), moderate (1.5), and high (3.0) TR that cover the Boussinesq (neutral and low TR) and non-Boussinesq (moderate and high TR) regimes. The rigid cylinder is represented using a second-order robust ghost cell immersed boundary method. This study extends previous literature by exploring higher TR effects on steady and unsteady aerodynamics, vortex shedding, flow separation, and heat transfer. An increase in TR stabilizes the flow and can completely suppress vortex shedding. Although at low TR, the time-averaged local Nusselt number distribution at the cylinder surface is sensitive to M∞ due to the aerodynamic heating, at higher TR, it becomes insensitive to M∞. The effects of fluid transport coefficient model choice are also examined using constant and temperature-dependent (power-law) coefficients. Both models provide similar results for aerodynamics in the Boussinesq regime; however, the constant fluid transport coefficient model fails to capture the underlying flow physics in the non-Boussinesq regime. The temperature-dependent transport coefficient model is essential even within the Boussinesq regime for accurate heat transfer predictions and analysis.

papers.title: Wave propagation and transformation over double submerged breakwater based on smoothed particle hydrodynamics method
papers.abstract: Double submerged breakwaters play a vital role in coastal protection by dissipating wave energy and mitigating shoreline erosion. Traditional grid-based numerical methods often struggle in capturing the complex, nonlinear wave process around such structures. In this study, a smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) approach is used to simulate nonlinear wave propagation and transformation over double submerged breakwaters. Model validations against extensive experimental data demonstrated excellent agreement in the wave elevations and velocity fields. Results showed that the double submerged breakwater configuration significantly reduces wave crests, enhances wave dispersion, and increases energy dissipation. Analysis of fluid fields revealed strong turbulence and localized vortices behind the structures, providing insight into the energy dissipation mechanisms. The results confirm the effectiveness of the SPH method for simulating wave–structure interactions and offer valuable guidance for the design and application of submerged breakwaters.

papers.title: Reverse bouncing mechanisms: Droplet rebound on surfaces with spacing-gradient grooves
papers.abstract: Understanding droplet rebound dynamics plays a crucial role in guiding technological applications such as inkjet printing, drug delivery, and microfluidics. This study investigates the complex directional rebound behaviors of droplets impacting on grooved surfaces with gradient spacing through a chemical potential lattice Boltzmann method. Through systematic observation of contact angle evolution, contact line pinning/depinning dynamics, force variations, internal momentum distribution, and velocity vector fields during rebound processes, a comparative analysis is performed for two distinct directional rebound modes, revealing the mechanisms underlying reverse bouncing. The results show that at lower Weber number (We = 42.4), droplets complete spreading and rebound along the wettability gradient after contraction. With the increase in Weber number, liquid penetration into grooves enhances, resulting in pinning at the right contact line and consequent asymmetrical droplet deformation. This pinning effect generates a hysteresis force that drives partial droplet contraction accompanied by rightward centroid migration, ultimately leading to rebound against the wettability gradient. Analysis of groove structure effects shows that an increase in the base value of the groove spacing d facilitates reverse droplet bouncing. And when H*(groove height-to-radius ratio) < 1, bottom contact promotes liquid column ascent, avoiding contact line pinning and enabling droplet rebound along the wetting gradient direction. This work provides insights for designing microstructure surfaces to control droplet motion.

papers.title: Meniscus dynamics and jetting transitions in pulsatile flow electrosprays
papers.abstract: Jetting in electrosprays results from the interplay of surface tension and electrostatic forces acting on a liquid meniscus. Rayleigh-type capillary waves govern interfacial dynamics of classical pulsating electrosprays and synchronize jetting with meniscus extrusion. We have been using a resonant mechanical actuation of the electrospray emitter to generate periodic pressure waves and produce controllable meniscus deformation, while a superimposed electric field assists in driving singularity formation. It is suggested that the mechanical actuation across various pulsatile flow fields [governed by the Womersley number, WO=R*(ωρ/μ)1/2, where ω is the angular frequency of flow fields, ρ and μare the density and viscosity of the liquid, and R is the nozzle radius] would modulate interfacial behavior under combined hydrodynamic and electrostatic effects. To explore meniscus response across distinct inertial–viscous regimes, a piezoelectric actuator was used to generate pulsatile flow at three representative Womersley numbers. Jetting frequencies, liquid volume deposition, and liquid jet morphologies were studied across small, intermediate, and large Womersley numbers. The electric field remained below the jetting threshold in the absence of flow.
