Valve flapping induces high-intensity turbulent pulsed airflow, while pulsed injection triggers intense entrainment of Kelvin–Helmholtz (K–H) vortices, enhancing the penetration depth and mixing zone area of fuel jets. Their synergistic interactions may promote efficient and homogeneous mixing, thereby supporting high-intensity, rapid PGC within a short distance.

papers.title: Study of energy dissipation dynamics and pressure fluctuation response during pump-turbine startup in pump mode
papers.abstract: Under pump startup conditions, rapid parameter fluctuations in pump-turbines lead to unstable flow and significant pressure pulsations, which compromise power plant safety. This study performs numerical simulations of the transient flow field during the startup process of a mixed-flow pump-turbine within a pumped storage power station. Analyses were carried out at discrete guide vane opening (GVO) positions. The main conclusions are as follows: Entropy production analysis indicates that the total entropy generation decreases nonlinearly as the guide vane opening increases. Pressure pulsation in the runner synchronizes with changes in guide vane opening, and pulsation intensity increases in the bladeless area. Both fast Fourier transform (FFT) and short-time Fourier transform (STFT) analysis reveal that the predominant frequency of pressure fluctuations across all regions is the blade passing frequency (5.5 Hz) and its harmonics, attributed to rotor–stator interaction.

papers.title: Baroclinic shift of hypersonic heating streaks over an ablating compression ramp
papers.abstract: We present novel observations from direct numerical simulations of transitional Mach 8 flow over a 15° compression ramp ablator. Heating streaks over the ramp are seen to undergo a half-wavelength shift near the location of transition from laminar to turbulent boundary layer flow. This phenomenon leads to an intriguing pattern of ablation grooves on the surface. Our analysis shows that the underlying mechanism is driven by the baroclinic torque in the strongly stratified near-wall region. We discuss the impact of this baroclinic shift for a surface undergoing ablative recession and assess its sensitivity to different thermal boundary conditions and perturbation amplitudes.

papers.title: Coupled imbibition-flowback behavior in shale pore-fractures networks using the lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: During fracturing operations, high-pressure injected fluids flow through complex fracture network and micro-nano pores within shale formations. The coupled effects of capillary forces, viscous forces, and rock surface wettability drive forced imbibition processes, ultimately influencing reservoir recovery efficiency. Based on the Shan–Chen multi-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann model, the study conducts an oil–-water two-phase flow/imbibition simulation in reconstructed shale pore-fracture networks, clarifying flow mechanisms under waterflooding and systematically probing the roles of bedding fractures, wettability, and pressure gradients. The results demonstrate that bedding fractures significantly enhance oil mobilization by connecting blind-end pores and reducing viscous and capillary resistance, leading to an 8.7% increase in recovery. Strongly water-wet conditions produce continuous displacement fronts and improve oil recovery by 6.9% compared to oil-wet cases. Increasing the capillary number, representative of higher injection pressure, accelerates the advancement of the imbibition front and improves sweep efficiency, raising recovery by 7.1%. These findings provide theoretical insight for optimizing shale oil development strategies, including wettability modification, pressure regulation, and fracture design.

papers.title: Applying 8-foci imaging to instantaneous three-dimensional flow field reconstruction
papers.abstract: Advances in microfluidics have enabled the exploration of complex fluid dynamics within intricate geometries, facilitating both the fabrication of sophisticated microchannels and the study of realistic three-dimensional (3D) flow environments. However, capturing 3D flow fields with high spatial and temporal resolution still remains a significant challenge due to the limitations of current experimental techniques. Here, we introduce a novel approach using widefield multifocus microscopy to achieve instantaneous 3D flow reconstruction by simultaneously imaging eight axial planes. This technique was applied to investigate particle dynamics in microchannels engineered to replicate vascular bifurcations. In cylindrical channels mimicking blood vessels, we observed radial particle migration toward the channel center, reminiscent of margination in blood flow. At bifurcation points, particle collisions and deceleration were localized at the apex, followed by redistribution into downstream branches. Our 3D imaging further revealed complex transport phenomena, including non-Gaussian lateral displacements, Lévy flight–like behavior, and net migration away from channel walls. These findings underscore the importance of true volumetric flow measurements for elucidating particle–wall interactions and the behavior of biological fluids in both physiological and engineered 3D microenvironments.

papers.title: Scalar transport during miscible viscous fingering experiments in consolidated porous media
papers.abstract: Miscible viscous fingering, driven by the viscosity contrast between displacing and displaced fluids, significantly impacts subsurface processes in energy and environmental applications. Prior experimental studies that relied on synthetic porous media, such as sand packs or Hele–Shaw cells, do not fully represent the impact of fingering on pressure and concentration distribution in three-dimensional geological media. In this study, we perform experiments of scalar transport during viscous fingering in consolidated Berea Sandstone cores to capture fingering dynamics. Pressure profiles are monitored using high-resolution transducers along the core length. Scalar concentrations are measured using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy, enabling ultra-sensitive detection of fingering-induced effects in the scalar breakthrough curve. Impacts of viscosity contrast and injection flow rate on the pressure drop profile through the domain and the scalar breakthrough profile at the outlet are analyzed. Channeling of the less viscous fluid at high viscosity contrasts is identified as the primary reason for deviations between classical models and the experimental results. A numerical model calibrated with experimental data of breakthrough and pressure profiles reproduces in situ finger dynamics, enabling further investigation of mixing and spreading processes and the synthesis of an effective transverse diffusivity in terms of the transverse variance and dissipation rate of the scalar. We propose a novel workflow utilizing temporal, longitudinal, and transverse spatial moments of the concentration distribution, previously unexplored in viscous fingering studies, to systematically quantify stochastic dispersive characteristics. Ultimately, this work improves predictive modeling capabilities essential for efficient management of subsurface resources.

papers.title: Experimental measurements and potential flow simulations for ship roll response coupling with internal sloshing flow under wave actions
papers.abstract: This study investigates the coupling effects between ship roll response and internal sloshing through combined experimental measurements and potential flow simulations. The roll motion response of a ship with internal sloshing is characterized by a two-peak variation with incident wave periods. The periods at the peaks correspond to the first and second ship roll resonant periods. Systematic experiments demonstrate the transition of dominant roll amplitudes from the second to the first resonant period with increasing filling depth, governed by sloshing-induced restoring and overturning moments. A conceptual oscillator model is further introduced to interpret the two-peak variation in roll motion. The findings provide a new physical and theoretical basis for predicting roll resonance of ships with internal sloshing, offering valuable insights for the design of offshore structures.

papers.title: Drop impact on a heated pre-wetted wall: Deposition-on-crater splash regime
papers.abstract: The impact of a liquid drop with high Reynolds and Weber numbers on a wet solid surface typically results in the emergence, rising, and expansion of a corona-like thin jet. This phenomenon is explained by the propagation of a kinematic discontinuity within the wall film. Conventional theories suggest that the corona-forming liquid jet comprises material from the impacting drop and wall film. In this study, the impact of a drop on a wall film is observed using a high-speed video system. Simultaneously, the distribution of the contact temperature at the substrate surface is measured with a high-speed infrared system. The results reveal that heat transfer predominantly occurs within the thin thermal boundary layers in the drop and substrate. Moreover, our experiments show that under our specific conditions, the drop deposits at the base of the crater, while only the wall film produces the corona and splashes. Correspondingly, the secondary drops consist only of the heated material of the wall film. This regime has not been previously reported in the literature. The validated models for the diameter of the cold spot, the characteristic time, and the contact temperature developed in this study can be potentially useful for reliable modeling of spray cooling.

papers.title: The arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian coupled finite element-discontinuous Galerkin method for the non-Newtonian two phase fluid structure interaction via the phase field model
papers.abstract: In this work, we establish a coupled finite element-discontinuous Galerkin (FEM-DG) method in the arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian (ALE) computational framework for the challenging non-Newtonian two phase fluid structure interaction problems. The moving interface between two different fluids is described via the phase field model. The flow field governing equations are written in a unified form according to the ALE description. The elastodynamics equation of the solid is written in the Lagrangian formulation. The numerical solution of non-Newtonian two phase Navier–Stokes equations is accomplished via the coupled finite element and discontinuous Galerkin method. The Cahn–Hilliard equation is solved according to the streamline upwind Petrov–Galerkin (SUPG) method and the governing equation of solid structure is solved based on the standard finite element method. The deformation of the fluid domain mesh is managed using a mesh moving technique. A semi-implicit partitioned coupling scheme is designed to combine these four solvers efficiently and stably. The flow through a fixed cylinder with an elastic rod is investigated to demonstrate the convergence and validity of our combined computational algorithm. It is the first time that the non-Newtonian two phase dam break flow impacting a flexible rod is studied in detail. The development of the interface between two fluids and the deformation of the elastic rod with different Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids are all fully analyzed.

papers.title: Experimental study on the motion behavior of multi-sized bubbles in a continuous casting mold
papers.abstract: A 1:3 scaled water model experimental system was established based on the similarity principle. High-speed cameras and particle image velocimetry were employed to capture bubble images, and ImageJ was used for image processing to extract bubble trajectories, size distribution, and gas volume fraction. The motion behavior of multi-sized bubbles in the continuous casting mold was systematically investigated. The experimental results indicate that the casting speed, flow rate, mold size, and slag layer all have significant effects on the movement and distribution patterns of multi-sized bubble-like flows within the mold. First, small bubbles exhibit a distinct fan-shaped flow pattern, whereas large bubbles remain confined near the submerged entry nozzle, rising almost vertically. Both casting speed and gas flow rate influence the strength of the upper recirculating flow, which in turn affects the spatial distribution and movement behavior of bubbles. Moreover, the width of the mold influences bubble trajectories by altering the jet impingement area. As the mold width increases from 1050 to 1750 mm, the trajectories of small bubbles gradually evolve into a fan-shaped flow. Consequently, fewer bubbles follow the downward flow into the deeper region of the mold, and the gas volume fraction decreases from 6.52% to 4.26%. In addition, due to its inherent viscous resistance and surface tension, the slag significantly suppresses the gas–liquid two-phase flow. As the slag thickness increases from 0 to 2 cm, the rising velocity of bubbles decreases, and the overall gas volume fraction drops from 5.29% to 2.62%.

papers.title: Wake prediction of a fully coupled floating wind turbine using dynamic mode decomposition and bidirectional long short-term memory method
papers.abstract: Floating offshore wind farms require rapid, accurate wake predictions to support control and layout optimization, yet fully coupled large-eddy simulations (LES) remain prohibitively expensive. This study proposes an integrated combining LES, dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) workflow for short-term wake forecasting around floating offshore wind turbines. First, LES coupled with the MoorDyn dynamic-mooring model resolves six degrees of freedom platform motions for the offshore code comparison collaboration continuation-DeepCwind semi-submersible floating wind turbine under combined wind-wave-current loading. DMD compresses the resulting flow fields into a set of spatial modes associated with distinct frequencies, and a BiLSTM network learns the temporal evolution of the leading coefficients. The framework is benchmarked on canonical cylinder flow and then applied to the floating wind turbine. Retaining the first 27 DMD modes captures >98% of wake energy, while the BiLSTM achieves mean absolute and root-mean-square errors below 1% and 1.5%, respectively, over a 5 s prediction horizon (one rotor revolution), with R2 > 0.96. Compared with full LES cases, the surrogate achieves an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost without compromising key wake features such as velocity deficit recovery and vortex shedding dynamics. The proposed DMD-BiLSTM model offers a physics-informed, real-time capable tool for wake prediction, providing a physics-informed surrogate that supports advanced control strategies and provides high-fidelity input for dense farm layout optimization.

papers.title: Aerodynamic performance and flow dynamics of High-Speed train under crosswind: Effect of turbulence model
papers.abstract: This study employs Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS), improved delayed detached eddy simulation (IDDES), scale-resolving hybrid (SRH), and large eddy simulation (LES) turbulence models to conduct a comparative numerical analysis of the aerodynamic load characteristics and surrounding flow field structure of a high-speed train at a Reynolds number of 250 000 and a yaw angle of 30°. The influence of the Gamma Re-Theta transition model and grid resolution on the computational results is investigated. The findings indicate that the LES method based on the wall-adapting local eddy-viscosity (WALE) model performs well with sufficiently refined grids, exhibiting small errors compared to wind tunnel tests. Without using a transition model, the RANS, IDDES, and SRH turbulence models are unable to accurately capture the near-wall flow characteristics at any grid resolution, consequently failing to accurately predict the pressure and pressure fluctuation distribution on the train surface. This fundamental deficiency stems from the models' difficulty in capturing instabilities within the free shear layer. When a transition model was employed, both the IDDES and SRH turbulence models demonstrated improved capability in predicting the train's aerodynamic performance. Furthermore, SRH exhibited superior grid adaptability, and it maintained excellent performance even on coarse grids and achieved computational accuracy comparable to that of the LES model. The core conclusion of this study confirms that the SRH model, leveraging its robust performance and potential for significant computational cost reduction, emerges as a promising approach for studying highly separated external flows at high Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: A second-order particle Fokker–Planck–Master method for diatomic gas flows
papers.abstract: The direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method is widely used to describe rarefied gas flows. The DSMC method accounts for the transport and collisions of computational particles, resulting in higher computational costs in the continuum regime. The Fokker–Planck (FP) model approximates particle collisions as Brownian motion to reduce computational cost. Advanced FP models have been developed to enhance physical fidelity, ensuring the correct Prandtl number and the H-theorem. The FP model has further been extended to handle diatomic gases, such as the Fokker–Planck–Master (FPM) model. Alongside these developments in modeling, computational efficiency has also been improved by achieving second-order spatial and temporal accuracy, as demonstrated in the unified stochastic particle FP (USP-FP) method. However, these accuracy improvements have not yet been extended to diatomic gases, which are essential for engineering applications such as atmospheric reentry. This study proposes a unified stochastic particle Fokker–Planck–Master (USP-FPM) method for diatomic gases that achieves second-order accuracy in both time and space. Temporal accuracy is enhanced by reproducing second-order energy, viscous stress, and heat flux relaxations. Spatial accuracy is improved by employing a first-order polynomial reconstruction method. Three test cases are investigated: homogeneous relaxation, Poiseuille flow, and hypersonic flow around a cylinder. The results show that the USP-FPM method provides accurate solutions even with coarser cell sizes and larger time steps compared to the DSMC and FPM methods. In particular, for the hypersonic flow around a cylinder, the USP-FPM method achieves a speed-up factor of 28 compared to the DSMC method, while maintaining accuracy.

papers.title: Influence of gravity modulation on the initiation of Rayleigh–Bénard convection in ferro-nanofluids
papers.abstract: The study investigates the influence of sinusoidal (sine wave) and non-sinusoidal (square wave, triangular wave, and sawtooth wave) gravity modulation on Rayleigh–Bénard Convection in ferro-nanofluids (FNF) using both linear and nonlinear stability analyses. Controlled fluid systems are important in application situations, and hence, we have considered gravity modulation approach to control. The linear analysis based on the Venezian method is performed to determine the Rayleigh number of the problem, while the nonlinear analysis is carried out by solving the non-autonomous Lorenz equations to evaluate the heat transfer coefficient through the Nusselt number. Free-free and rigid-rigid boundary conditions for both upper and lower plates are considered along with isothermal and iso-nano concentration conditions. The purpose of the present study is to investigate the influence of initiation of convection and heat transfer in FNFs. This research focuses on analyzing the effects of various dimensionless parameters on the onset of convection and heat transfer. The results indicate that the magnetization parameters destabilize the system and enhance heat transfer. Among the four wave forms considered, square wave gravity modulation is found to facilitate greater heat transport compared to other forms of gravity modulation. In addition, the presence of ferro-nanoparticles advances the initiation of convection and enhances heat transfer. The novelty of this study lies in analyzing unconsidered aspects of gravity modulation, together with magnetic effects and nanoparticles, on the onset of convection and heat transfer in FNFs using both linear and nonlinear stability approaches.

papers.title: Investigation of the instability of electrified viscoelastic jets in electromagnetic fields
papers.abstract: The regulation of electromagnetic fields on the mechanical behavior of jets holds substantial academic and engineering significance for pivotal technological processes. Nevertheless, the cross-scale coupling mechanism governing the interactions among electromagnetic fields, rheological stress, and interface instability in this multi-physical field system remains inadequately elucidated, which restricts the precise control of jet dynamic behavior in practical applications. To address this issue, a novel theoretical model was established based on linear stability theory, with the integration of the continuity equation, Navier–Stokes equations, and electromagnetic field-induced effects. Leveraging this model, a systematic investigation was conducted to characterize the instability behaviors of viscoelastic jets under the action of electromagnetic fields. The results demonstrate that under the condition of identical shear viscosity, the growth amplitude of boundary disturbances in jets exposed to an electromagnetic composite field was 4.1% higher than that in a single-field environment. Notably, the electromagnetic coupling effect exerted a significant regulatory impact on the attenuation characteristics of boundary layer disturbances; specifically, as the Reynolds number increased, the curve corresponding to the maximum disturbance growth rate exhibited a gradual flattening trend, indicating a weakened sensitivity of disturbance evolution to Reynolds number variations. Furthermore, it was verified that boundary disturbances of viscoelastic jets propagated and grew at an accelerated rate in the electromagnetic composite field. This phenomenon was expected to provide a feasible technical pathway for addressing atomization challenges under special operating conditions. This study clarifies the intrinsic instability mechanism of jets under the synergistic action of electromagnetic fields and rheological stress. Moreover, it establishes novel theoretical criteria, which lay a solid theoretical foundation for the active regulation of jet morphology in typical engineering applications, including electromagnetic atomization, polymer injection molding, and aerospace propellant atomization.

papers.title: Exploring infodynamics in the study of human aerosol droplet size distributions
papers.abstract: Human respiratory aerosols have a significant influence on disease transmission and public health. However, the intrinsic mechanisms driving their size distribution remain poorly understood. This study introduces an infodynamic analysis to quantify the informational content (infodiversity) of aerosol size distributions from different respiratory activities (breathing, speaking, and coughing). By integrating experimental measurements with probabilistic physical modeling, this study reveals that human aerosols predominantly exhibit lognormal characteristics, often requiring multimodal representations involving mixtures of Lognormal, Gamma, and Weibull distributions. The results indicate that Lognormal distributions dominate aerosol size characterization (64.5%), followed by Weibull (21%), and Gamma (14.5%) distributions, quantified through differential informature values ranging from 0.21 to 5.48 nats. A novel composite normalized infodynamic gap metric was introduced, with a threshold of 0.01, to identify the best mechanistic convergence between the data and statistical models. These findings contribute to aerosol science by providing a rigorous theoretical framework to link microscopic aerosol production mechanisms to macroscopic health-relevant outcomes, thereby guiding future experimental and numerical studies aimed at disease mitigation.

papers.title: Effect of coupled surge–pitch motions on the wake characteristics of floating offshore wind turbines under atmospheric boundary layer inflows
papers.abstract: This study presents a numerical investigation of floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs) subjected to coupled surge–pitch motions under atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) inflows. Large eddy simulation combined with the actuator line model is used to simulate FOWTs, with a focus on analyzing aerodynamic performance and wake characteristics. Results indicate that platform motion has a limited impact on time-averaged power and thrust but causes pronounced fluctuations in instantaneous power and thrust. Compared to fixed-bottom wind turbines, FOWTs exhibit faster wake recovery under ABL conditions, particularly within 6D (D represents the rotor diameter) downstream. Gaussian fitting shows that FOWTs with larger platform motion amplitudes and higher frequencies exhibit smaller standard deviations and larger centerline displacements. Phase-averaged vorticity analysis reveals that platform motion induces periodic vortex structures near the shear layer, which remain coherent within the first 4D downstream. Dynamic mode decomposition analysis is performed to examine the unsteady evolution of FOWT wakes. The results show that the dominant modes are primarily influenced by inflow turbulence, while platform motion excites response modes with periodic spatial structures. Although the energy contribution of these motion-induced modes is generally limited, low-frequency motions tend to induce higher-energy modes and more pronounced wake responses. These findings provide valuable insight for analytical wake models, reduced-order modeling, and future studies on complex platform motions and multi-turbine interactions.

papers.title: A novel nanoparticle-enhanced magnetic fluid for low-temperature sealing application
papers.abstract: The large starting torque of magnetic fluid seals at low temperatures is a key challenge hindering their application in low-temperature environments. Numerous studies have shown that there is an inherent contradiction between reducing starting torque and maintaining pressure resistance, making it difficult to achieve both simultaneously. In this study, a detachable magnetic fluid sealing device and a sealing testing bench were designed to measure the pressure resistance and starting torque of the magnetic fluid seal at low temperatures. We found that as the temperature decreased, the starting torque increased exponentially. Further experiments revealed that adding hydrophilic silica nanoparticles to the magnetic fluid significantly reduced the starting torque of the sealing device. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that the formation of large-scale, field-induced structures in the magnetic fluid at low temperature is the key reason for the increase in starting torque. The silica nanoparticles can hinder the formation of these structures, thereby reducing the starting torque without significantly affecting the pressure resistance of the sealing device. Our research is of great significance for solving the low-temperature sealing problem in high-end equipment.

papers.title: Characterization of wind–dust pressure distribution in the near-wall region of a trough solar collector
papers.abstract: Desert regions provide abundant solar irradiance and are thus attractive locations for utility-scale solar thermal plants; however, wind-driven dust loads generated by intense sandstorms pose a serious hazard to the safe operation of parabolic trough collectors (PTCs). Accordingly, investigating dust-mitigation design for PTCs under sandstorm conditions is essential. This study employs numerical simulation to assess how variations in installation tilt, wind-direction orientation, incoming wind speed, and dust volume fraction influence vortex characteristics and wind–dust pressure distributions around PTCs. The results show that, across the examined range of installation tilts, the drag and lift coefficients associated with wind–dust loads are relatively large, while dust-induced moment components in the X and Y directions remain comparatively small. Under oblique wind conditions, asymmetric pressure fields and convex conical vortices amplify overturning moments, with mean dust moments in the X and Y directions approximately 27 and 3 times greater than those under vertical wind, respectively. Further analysis indicates that variations in incoming wind speed and dust volume fraction induce wind–dust load fluctuations of only about 1%–5%. Therefore, dust-mitigation measures for the reflectors should primarily target drag and lift. Anti-overturning design should concentrate on oblique wind scenarios within the 45°–75° range and account for abrupt moment changes induced by asymmetric vortices. This work provides a theoretical framework to inform dust-mitigation design criteria and overturning protection systems for PTCs deployed in desert solar thermal plants.

papers.title: Anisotropy evolution and gas transport characteristics of coal structure under tectonic stress: Insights into multiscale microstructural controls on methane desorption and diffusion
papers.abstract: The pore architecture within coal media critically influences gas emission behavior. This study used fluid injection and photoelectric radiation methods to systematically analyze the microporous structures of primary and tectonic coals across nanometer to micrometer scales. It reveals how tectonic stress-induced anisotropic evolution of coal pore structures affects gas desorption and diffusion mechanisms. The results show that tectonic activity significantly accelerates pore formation in macropore and mesopore regimes. In macropores, surfaces become smoother and migration pathways simplify, while mesopores feature rougher surfaces that provide more gas adsorption sites and simpler spatial structures that offer favorable migration channels—collectively promoting efficient free gas transport. At the micrometer scale, tectonic coal's primary fracture network is disrupted, forming a more extensive network of micrometer-scale fractures. This leads to a significant increase in pore throats and cavities, with a reduction in long-sized throats and development of short-sized ones, effectively shortening gas migration paths. In primary coal, throats show a preferred orientation (270°–330°), reflecting strong anisotropy. In contrast, tectonic coal exhibits reduced tortuosity, with throat orientation angles distributed across multiple directions, weakened anisotropy, and enhanced pore connectivity. Tectonic deformation enhances gas transport capacity through synergistic optimization across scales: creating more efficient pathways at the nanoscale (via modifications to surface and spatial configurations) and significantly improving connectivity at the microscale (through reorganization of fracture networks). This synergistic effect weakens the overall structural anisotropy of the coal matrix, leading to markedly higher methane desorption and diffusion rates. The comparative study of coal microstructure characteristics provides critical theoretical insights for understanding gas emission in tectonic coal, offering scientific guidance for coal mine gas disaster prevention and coalbed methane exploitation.

papers.title: Odd viscosity effect on interfacial instability of droplet on a heated substrate driven by surface acoustic waves
papers.abstract: The rapid generation of aerosol droplets with micrometer- and sub micrometer-scale diameters is enabled by surface acoustic wave (SAW) atomization. In this study, a theoretical analysis is performed for the first time to investigate the impact of the odd viscosity effect on a droplet placed on a heated substrate under SAW actuation. From the governing equations, a droplet evolution equation is derived that incorporates the effects of the acoustic capillary number E, the thermal Marangoni number MaT, and the odd viscosity coefficient μ. The method of lines was employed to numerically simulate the droplet evolution process. μ plays a crucial role in droplet behavior under SAW excitation. At low E, increasing μ reduces the droplet's aspect ratio ε, while at higher E, the influence of μ on reducing the droplet's aspect ratio becomes weaker, and acoustic forces dominate. Atomization occurs when the capillary waves induced by SAWs reach a critical amplitude. At early times, capillary waves elongate slightly with increasing μ, with a modest rise in elongation of the capillary waves l and peak count. However, this does not trigger atomization. At higher E, the effect of μ on capillary waves elongation becomes more noticeable, though atomization conditions are still not met. As time progresses, the elongation of capillary waves becomes more pronounced, and atomization occurs at E = 30 and E = 70. Interestingly, when μ surpasses a certain threshold, odd viscosity dominates and prevents atomization. The influence of Bi on the droplet's aspect ratio ε becomes weaker as E increases.

papers.title: Numerical investigation on dissolved oxygen destratification under the coexistence of planar water jet and regular wave
papers.abstract: The dissolved oxygen concentration (DOC) and its vertical distribution are essential to ensuring seawater quality and fish growth. In this study, a two-dimensional (2D) numerical model consisting of a numerical water tank and dissolved oxygen (DO) transport is conducted to investigate the DO destratification process under the coexistence of a planar water jet and regular waves. The effects of the wave and jet parameters are analyzed using the destratification ratio (DR) of the DOC, as well as the stratification index at the initial time (SI0) and sampling time (SI1). It was found that SI1 decreases and DR increases as the wave height increases and the DOC of the injected water decreases. As the wave period increases, SI1 first decreases and then increases, and DR exhibits the opposite trend. Both SI1 and DR increase with increasing SI0. A symbolic regression algorithm is used to obtain an empirical equation for predicting DR with relatively high accuracy.

papers.title: Chaotic mixing inside microdroplets in microchannel with slanted grooves and staggered-herringbone grooves
papers.abstract: The present study employed simulation methods to investigate droplet-mixing-based chaos in microchannels with slanted grooves and staggered-herringbone grooves. The microdroplets rotate under the influence of transverse flow, generating two asymmetrical circulating vortices internally to enhance the mass transfer between the two halves of the droplet with mixed components. Compared to the slanted groove micromixer (SGM) with a 60° slanted angle, the SGM with a 45° slanted angle exhibited a more obvious difference in vortex size, resulting in higher mixing efficiency. The droplets rotate and stretch inside the staggered-herringbone groove micromixer (SHGM). Due to the influence of the interlaced structure, the internal vortex state exhibits continuous variation, thereby significantly enhancing the mixing efficiency. For SHGM, when the inlet velocities of the discrete phase and the continuous phase are 0.001 and 0.003 m/s, respectively, over 90% mixing efficiency is achieved after the droplet travels a distance of 0.6 mm, corresponding to an effective mixing time of 60 μs. Further studies were conducted on the effects of parameters such as two-phase flow velocity, surface tension, viscosity, contact angle on the thickness of the continuous liquid film, and the size of the corner flow, as well as on the variation pattern of the mixing efficiency of microdroplets. For SHGM, the time required to achieve complete mixing can be reduced to the order of tens of microseconds, with the ability to adjust the mixing time by modifying the control parameters.

papers.title: Nonlinear bifurcation analysis of self-excited thermoacoustic oscillations in diffusion flames
papers.abstract: Self-excited thermoacoustic instability arises from the nonlinear coupling between unsteady heat release, acoustic perturbations, and flow velocity oscillations. While extensively studied in premixed configurations, the nonlinear bifurcation characteristics of such instabilities in diffusion flames remain less explored. This study employs a Rijke tube apparatus with self-priming double-row diffusion flames to systematically investigate these dynamics. Synchronized acoustic and optical diagnostics, including the application of a digital flame color discrimination method for flame dynamics analysis, are utilized. The key findings demonstrate that the system exhibits subcritical Hopf bifurcation with marked hysteresis in response to flow rate and tube length variations, indicating inherent bistability and a risk of abrupt instability onset. In contrast, varying the flame position induces no significant hysteresis, as its influence is primarily a linear modification of the acoustic–flame phase relation. Local Rayleigh index calculation further identifies the flame base as the core instability driver and reveals that thermoacoustic coupling enhances local combustion completeness, evidenced by blue intensity of red–green–blue color model. These findings may hold significant value for analyzing the prediction of thermoacoustic instability in diffusion flame-based combustors.

papers.title: Effect of temperature-dependent viscosity on the stability of natural convection in a vertical layer of porous medium
papers.abstract: The study investigates the effect of temperature-dependent viscosity on the stability of natural convection in a vertical layer of porous medium. The Lapwood–Brinkman model is used to describe the flow in a porous medium. Linear stability analysis is applied using the normal mode technique to analyze the effect of temperature-dependent viscosity. The system of equations forms a generalized eigenvalue problem, which is solved numerically using the Chebyshev collocation method. The critical values for the Darcy–Rayleigh number, wave number, and wave speed are computed for a wide range of values of the Darcy–Brinkman number, Darcy–Prandtl number, and viscosity variation parameters Γ1 and Γ2, showing the novelty of our solutions. The main cause of instability is the presence of the inertial effects. For both Γ1=0 and Γ2=0, instability occurs in both stationary and traveling wave modes depending on the values of physical parameters. But for non-zero values of Γ1 and Γ2, instability occurs through the traveling wave mode only. For some fixed values of Prd, DaB, the effect of decrease in the viscosity shows a destabilizing effect on the system. For some fixed value of DaB, the critical wave speed cc shows linear dependence on Prd up to some particular value of Prd, and this value of Prd increases with decrease in the value of Γ1(=Γ2). For some fixed values of Prd, DaB, the decreasing order of system stability for Γ1 and Γ2 follows as Γ1>Γ2, Γ1=Γ2, and Γ1<Γ2.

papers.title: An asymptotic solution of wave interaction with a spatially varying elastic plate
papers.abstract: The present article addresses a coupled potential flow and thin plate model of water-wave scattering influenced by an elastic plate with spatial variations. The scattering problem is solved mathematically using asymptotic expansion and the Fourier transform approach. The paper develops a first-order asymptotic solution, which significantly illustrates the hydrodynamic coefficients and emphasizes wave diffraction phenomena. Based on the real-life scenarios, we consider the sinusoidal ripple-type shape function of the elastic plate and analyze the Bragg resonance in wave reflection. The number of ripples and the wavenumber of the shape function affect the most reflected wave components, and the energy of reflected waves is increased due to wave action conservation. A deeper understanding of resonance phenomena, the influence of plate geometry, the roles of compressive force, and flexural rigidity, as well as the intricate interplay between wave characteristics and structural parameters, is obtained through the combined numerical analyses conducted in this study. Examining plate deflection reveals that the deflection amplitude is substantially higher near the variation region of the elastic plate. Findings of this study can assist in the design and optimization of very large floating structures and coastal protection systems by enabling the prediction and control of wave amplification, suppression, and transmission through the strategic tuning of structural geometry, rigidity, and compressive force.

papers.title: Reduced-order modeling of sessile droplet evaporation in binary liquid systems
papers.abstract: We develop a reduced-order model (ROM) to describe the quasi-steady, diffusion-limited evaporation of a sessile droplet of a binary liquid mixture on a solid surface. First, we implement a finite element model (FEM) of diffusion of liquid vapor of a binary droplet in two-dimensional, axisymmetric coordinates. The model incorporates modified Raoult's law with activity coefficients to capture the non-ideal behavior of binary liquids. Second, ROM is constructed using analytical expressions for the evaporation of pure liquid droplets, extended to binary mixtures. We evaluate the accuracy of the ROM by comparing it with FEM predictions over a wide range of initial alcohol volume fractions. The ROM agrees well with FEM results, with discrepancies less than 5%, while offering significantly lower computational cost. Finally, to validate the ROM, we conduct side-view visualization experiments on the evaporation of pure liquids (water, isopropanol) and binary mixtures (water–ethanol) on PDMS-coated surfaces. The ROM predictions of time-varying droplet volume, wetted radius, and contact angle show good agreement with experimental data, with minor deviations explained based on model assumptions.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of mean and turbulent characteristics of a free air rectangular jet with/without lip length
papers.abstract: The influence of geometric modifications to a rectangular nozzle on the flow structure of a free jet was investigated experimentally. In this work, an adaptable nozzle was employed, featuring exchangeable upper and lower plates that could be replaced to achieve the desired lip length, while the remaining geometry was unchanged. This study aims to assess the effect of lip length on flow structure by comparing a nozzle with equal lip length, serving as a reference, to configurations with 10 and 20 mm lower lip extensions. Both the mean and turbulent properties of the jet were characterized along the streamwise and spanwise directions using a 2-dimensional hot-wire system. In addition, particle image velocimetry (PIV) was utilized for flow visualization, assessment of air entrainment, and proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) analysis. The findings indicate that increasing the lip length broadens the radial spread of the mean axial and radial velocity distributions and amplifies velocity fluctuations, resulting in enhanced mixing. Furthermore, a longer lip increases the centerline velocity decay rate and enhances velocity fluctuations along the centerline, producing a reduced potential core length relative to the equal-length configuration. It also produces a wider shear stress distribution and increases the turbulent transport of normal and shear stresses via radial velocity fluctuations. PIV imaging and POD analysis further demonstrated asymmetric vortex roll-up and mixing with ambient fluid. The newly explored lip length effect has potential applications in flow control and could be relevant to a wide range of industrial free turbulent jet technologies.

papers.title: Aerodynamic noise reduction of small unmanned aerial vehicle rotors via steady suction and blowing control
papers.abstract: To address the pronounced noise generated by the rotors of a small-scale unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) during hover, this study investigates two active boundary-layer control schemes—BR-S (baseline rotor with suction) and BR-SB (baseline rotor with combined suction and blowing). Three-dimensional large-eddy simulations capture the near-field unsteady flow, while the Ffowcs-Williams–Hawkings acoustic analogy predicts the far-field noise. Across rotational speeds of 2000–7000 rpm and suction–blowing velocities of 0–12 m/s, overall sound-pressure level and spectral characteristics are systematically evaluated. Results show that BR-SB markedly outperforms BR-S, achieving up to 6.5 dB reduction at lateral microphones and mean reductions of 3.21 dB (aft) and 5.38 dB (lateral). By contrast, BR-S suppresses low-order blade-passing-frequency peaks but introduces localized mid-frequency sidebands. Flow-physics analysis reveals that leading-edge suction delays boundary-layer separation, whereas trailing-edge blowing persistently perturbs the shear layer and fragments nascent vortex structures, thereby attenuating both discrete harmonics and broadband turbulent noise. Overall, the combined suction–blowing strategy offers an effective and practically feasible pathway toward quieter operation of small UAV rotors.

papers.title: Gramian angular field imaging and texture analysis for identifying instability precursors in compressor unsteady flows
papers.abstract: We present an image-based approach for early detection of surge precursors in a centrifugal compressor. One-dimensional pressure signals are mapped to Gramian angular field images, from which Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix correlation is computed as the primary indicator using fixed windowing and gray-level quantization. On a single test rig at 60 000 and 70 000 rpm, the correlation trace rises prior to measured surge onset and follows the approach–surge–recovery evolution (e.g., a surge interval near 19.41–19.51 s at 60 000 rpm), enabling a baseline-referenced threshold for monitoring. To stabilize short-window fluctuations, a lightweight exponentially weighted moving average (α = 0.1) produces smoother yet responsive trajectories without resorting to black-box training. In the stable operating map, correlation exhibits a V-shaped variation with decreasing mass flow—coherent at overload, weakest near peak efficiency, and strengthening again as surge is approached—providing a physically interpretable trend. Within this scope, the study is a compressor-focused proof-of-concept; extension to other unsteady-flow problems is plausible but will require problem-specific tuning and independent validation.

papers.title: Study on the flow field characteristics of kerosene-fueled oblique detonation engine
papers.abstract: A nine-species, twelve reaction steps surrogate-kerosene model was employed to investigate the flow field characteristics of a kerosene-fueled oblique detonation engine. Validation against both numerical and experimental results confirms the model's validity; on this basis, the flow field characteristics of combustor and influencing factors are investigated. Research results indicate that: (1) Typical wave structure within the combustor is characterized by the presence of oblique shock wave, oblique detonation wave, separation shock wave, reattachment shock wave, reflected shock wave, and separation zone. (2) Shock and expansion waves affect the species distribution, with the expansion process facilitating the transformation of intermediate products into final products. (3) As flight altitude increases, the separation shock wave and oblique detonation wave angles decrease, enlarging the separation zone scale and displacing the reattachment shock wave origin downstream, and the reflected shock wave vanishes entirely. (4) As the equivalence ratio is increased from 0.8 to 1.2, both the separation shock wave and oblique detonation wave angles enlarge and the reattachment shock wave migrates upstream. With the equivalence ratio further increased, a counter-trend emerges. (5) Wave structure oscillations at a frequence identical to that of the incoming flow, while the reflected shock wave are repeatedly generated and annihilated as the separation zone contracts and expands. Oscillatory waveforms of pressure and density within the separation zone deviate markedly from the incoming flow. (6) Spatial non-uniformities in fuel mixing exert a virtually negligible influence on the wave structure.

papers.title: Force model for a freely moving spherical particle interacting with a planar shock
papers.abstract: This study evaluates different forms of the inviscid-unsteady and viscous-unsteady forces in the Annamalai–Balachandar model for predicting the force on a freely moving spherical particle interacting with a planar shock wave under viscous conditions, based on particle-resolved simulations with a ghost-point immersed boundary method. Three particle dimensionless densities 1, 10, and 1000, representing low, moderate, and high particle densities, respectively, and three incident shock Mach numbers 1.22, 1.75, and 2.51 (corresponding to post-shock Mach numbers 0.31, 0.8, and 1.2 and representing low, moderate, and high Mach numbers) are considered. We examine two forms for both inviscid-unsteady and viscous-unsteady forces: Form I averages the relative momentum before computing its material derivative, while Form II reverses the order. The startup motion of a particle in compressible flows is numerically simulated. Key particle behaviors observed include sustained acceleration for moderate-to-high density particles, velocity overshoot (initial increase followed by decrease) for low-density particles at low-to-moderate Mach numbers, and moving with the shock wave for the low-density particle at high Mach numbers studied. Our results show that, for the viscous-unsteady force, Forms I and II yield nearly identical results for all cases. For the inviscid-unsteady force, the prediction accuracy for the total force using Form I is better for the low-density particle, comparable for the moderate density particle, and worse for the high-density particle, compared to Form II. Form I of the inviscid-unsteady force is overall better for the prediction of the impulse and the peak force on the particle.

papers.title: Equilibrium states of a periodically forced spheroid in oscillating shear flows
papers.abstract: We present a study on the properties of equilibrium solutions and their bifurcations of the non-autonomous equations resulting from the dynamics of periodically forced spheroids in an oscillating shear flow. This is an extension of the earlier work by Kurian et al. [“Dynamics of a driven spheroid in a slow oscillating creeping shear flow,” Phys. Fluids 36, 083356 (2024)]. The orientations trace Jeffery orbits in oscillating shear flows with an angular displacement. However, an external torque causes a drift of the orbit in simple shear flows. Flow oscillations enhance this drift and angular displacement, and prolate spheroids exhibit a stronger response than oblate spheroids. Real-valued equilibrium states exist up to a critical torque k2c(re), where re is the particle aspect ratio. These states are static and neutrally stable nonlinear centers confined to a two-dimensional plane. At k2c(re), these centers merge into a center when the flow oscillations are in resonance with the external periodic torque, i.e., the non-Brownian spheroid undergoes a new type of bifurcation—the collision of two centers. On crossing k2c(re), the orientation vector transitions into periodic orbits. This resonance solution represents a physically realizable system that permits equilibrium solutions in non-autonomous equations. In contrast, the neutrally stable nonlinear centers reappear as an unstable node at k2c(re), resulting in a center-node bifurcation when the torque is constant in simple shear flow. On increasing the torque, the unstable node emerges as a complex conjugate pair, leading to a ghost phenomenon, and moves to new orientations which finally align along the external torque for sufficiently large torques.

papers.title: A morphological prediction of gaseous detonation shock front under lateral divergence effect
papers.abstract: In this study, the detonation shock dynamics (DSD) theory is employed to predict the propagation behavior and front morphology of gaseous detonation wave in a two-dimensional channel partially filled with a C2H2/O2/Ar premixed gas and partially with an inert gas. In the DSD theory, the relationship between the propagating velocity normal to wave front Dn and the curvature κ of the front, determined based on the generalized Zel'dovich–von Neumann–Döring (ZND) model, is used to account for the effect of lateral divergence on detonation wave propagation. Additionally, a shock polar approach is employed to determine the boundary conditions used in the DSD calculations. The predictive capability of the method was validated against two-dimensional numerical simulations of detonation wave propagation in the same configuration. The results demonstrate that the DSD framework, originally developed for condensed-phase detonations, can be effectively extended to gaseous detonation systems and can accurately capture the shape of the detonation shock front (DSF) during steady propagation under the condition of lateral divergence. The smaller reactive gas layer height and equivalence ratio, larger inert gas dilution ratio, and lower initial pressure can lead to more curved DSF and higher velocity deficit of the propagating detonation wave under the lateral divergence effect. The results also reveal that the choice of inert gas does not affect the shape of DSF due to the blockage effect of the sonic locus. This work provides an efficient and low-cost theoretical prediction tool for gaining deeper insight into the propagation characteristics of gaseous curved detonation waves.

papers.title: A moments-based regularized lattice Boltzmann method: Incompressible curved boundary implementation and validation in two dimensions
papers.abstract: We develop a curved-boundary condition for the moments-based regularized lattice Boltzmann method in two dimensions, combining the computational efficiency of Cartesian grids with accurate curved-boundary representation through moment regularization and extrapolation. Using the Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook collision model with D2Q9 lattice stencils, we implement the boundary treatment on uniform Cartesian grids with stair-case lattice nodes and employ an extrapolation technique to accurately impose wall boundary conditions on curved surfaces. Validated via flow past a cylinder at moderate Reynolds numbers (Re=10−200), the method shows excellent agreement with benchmarks (≤2% error in pressure and force coefficients). Global time-averaged lift and drag coefficients, surface pressure coefficients, pressure recovery ratio, velocity deficit in the wake downstream, and vortex dynamics are rigorously investigated and compared with literature data. Distinct flow regimes emerge: (1) for Re≤50, viscous dominance creates steady wakes with slow momentum recovery (20% at x≈25D); (2) for Re>50, vortex shedding enhances mixing, accelerating wake recovery (20% by x≈6D at Re≥100), but reducing pressure recovery to 15.6% at Re=200 due to increased dissipation. The accuracy of the developed method in capturing regime transitions and wake dynamics demonstrates its potential for complex-geometry simulations.

papers.title: Observation-guided generative flow field reconstruction of rotating detonation combustor
papers.abstract: Acquiring high-resolution flow field data in reacting flow systems is essential for understanding their underlying mechanisms. However, it still remains challenging due to experimental limitations in capturing full-dimensional high-resolution measurements. This study introduces a novel observation-guided generative diffusion model and takes the rotating detonation combustor as a case study to reconstruct detailed flow fields from sparse or incomplete observations. Compared to discriminative models, the generative model demonstrates robust generalization across different observation configurations without the need for retraining. Results also indicate that the proposed observation-gradient-guided strategy surpasses existing flow field reconstruction studies in accuracy and consistency. The model operates effectively in scenarios including incomplete velocity fields and sparse pressure fields. Furthermore, the model can generate higher-resolution flow fields through a cascaded adaptive refinement reconstruction. This study provides a model with strong generative performance and generalization capability for flow field reconstruction research. As a surrogate model, it has the potential for flow field visualization and analysis in scientific research and engineering applications.

papers.title: Discontinuous phase dynamics in a constricted capillary channel with rough surface
papers.abstract: The dynamics of droplets in capillary channels with constrictions play a crucial role in various fields. While previous studies have extensively explored the behavior of droplets in smooth channels, the effect of surface roughness combined with constricted geometries has remained less understood. This work investigates the effects of roughness on droplet dynamics as they pass through a constricted capillary channel. Using three-dimensional numerical simulations, we analyzed how rough surfaces influence droplet deformation, pressure drop, interfacial area changes, and surface energy during passage. We demonstrate that surface roughness introduces a distinct interface pinning and jumping mechanism, quantified by an average pinning duration of 0.0002 s, which fundamentally alters droplet deformation and leads to a significant increase in the required pressure drop. This effect is most pronounced in channels with pillars, where we also observe oscillatory variations in the fluid–fluid interfacial area caused by dynamic groove filling and emptying. Furthermore, we introduce a roughness-dependent critical length (Lc) as a new geometric criterion for droplet confinement. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of multiphase flow in complex channels, emphasizing the importance of considering both geometric constraints and surface characteristics for better predictive models and efficient system designs.

papers.title: Vortex energy cascade regulation in dual-shaft rigid-flexible reactors: Multiscale fragmentation via flexible excitation for high-efficiency mixing
papers.abstract: In a dual-shaft rigid mixing system, strong vortex zones intensify energy dissipation, adversely affecting mixing performance. To address this issue, the present study investigates a dual-shaft rigid-flexible combined mixing system and conducts a comparative study against three existing systems. By analyzing the mixing time and power consumption, as well as conducting wavelet analysis, flow field simulations, and fast Fourier transform analysis, we find that the proposed dual-shaft rigid-flexible combined mixing system significantly enhances the mixing performance, with a maximum improvement of 74.36%, and optimizes the distribution of multiscale vortices. This improvement stems from flexible ribbons that adjust the flow field structure and redistribute energy, effectively reducing the energy dissipation in strong vortex zones. The core mechanism is identified as flexible vibration → vortex fragmentation → reduced dissipation. This work provides a reference for the design of large-scale mixing equipment and offers new perspectives for research on vortex control and energy optimization in fluid dynamics.

papers.title: Unsteady two-dimensional concentration distribution in an ice-covered channel with temperature dependent settling velocity
papers.abstract: The health of coastal ecosystems is closely linked to the transport of suspended sediments from rivers to estuaries. This transport is significantly influenced by water temperature; however, its impact, particularly in ice-covered channels, remains poorly explored. This study presents a comprehensive two-dimensional sediment transport model in ice-covered channels, incorporating temperature dependent settling velocity. The model captures spatial and temporal variations in sediment concentration by employing an energy conservation based formulation to derive a temperature dependent settling velocity profile. The governing advection–diffusion equation is solved using the Alternating Direction Implicit method. While the steady state concentration is achieved rapidly with a vertically decreasing profile, thermal stratification produces an inverse relationship between temperature and settling velocity, with the latter decreasing by up to 64.3% as temperature increases from 0 °C to 3.6 °C. Consequently, sediment concentration close to the surface rises by nearly 99%, indicating enhanced suspension at higher temperatures. The model also predicts lower vertically averaged sediment concentrations under ice-covered conditions compared to open channel flows. Sensitivity analysis reveals that a ±30% change in inverse of turbulent Schmidt number alters predicted averaged concentrations by nearly 28.6%, while variation in roughness scaling parameter changes vertical averaged concentration profiles by 72.3%. Model predictions show good agreement with experimental data under steady conditions, confirming its reliability. Overall, the findings emphasize the critical need to incorporate temperature variability in modeling sediment dynamics in cold region hydrodynamic systems, especially under changing climatic conditions.

papers.title: Wake flow separation control on a notchback Ahmed body using sawtooth plasma actuators
papers.abstract: This study experimentally investigates plasma streamwise vortex generators (PSVGs) applied to a notchback Ahmed body with an effective backlight angle βeff = 21° for wake control. Wind tunnel experiments were performed at Reynolds numbers ranging from 5 × 103 to 7 × 104 based on the square root of the model frontal area. Smoke flow visualization and particle image velocimetry (PIV) results demonstrate that PSVGs positioned upstream of the slant substantially modify the deck separation flow. The upstream-induced flow strengthens boundary layer momentum, marginally reducing the separation and drag. Conversely, the activation located at the slant-leading-edge nearly eliminates central large-scale separation, facilitating the shear layer reattachment to the deck surface. This reattachment leads to a consequential intensification of the C-pillar vortices, diverting their trajectories outward and increasing the drag. The results indicate PSVGs' potential for automotive wake control, with activation locations producing distinct flow structures and a control mechanism.

papers.title: Optimization of Laval nozzle structure for gas mixture of NH3–O2 combustion products and CO2–H2O by response surface methodology
papers.abstract: Ammonia is a promising alternative fuel, and the nozzle plays a critical role as a core component in ammonia-fueled hypersonic propulsion systems. This study combines response surface methodology (RSM) with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to optimize the geometric configuration and combustion performance of the ammonia-fueled Laval nozzle. The RSM is adopted for optimizing the thrust by adjusting the nozzle's geometric parameters and the inlet parameters of the Laval nozzle. The CFD's results demonstrate that the quadratic effect of the throat radius and the interaction between the inlet and throat radii are critical for thrust optimization. The response surface models have demonstrated significant potential in enhancing nozzle thrust. The thrust is increased by 2% through adjusting the geometric parameter of the nozzle. Optimizing inlet parameters indicates that higher inlet temperatures (1073.15 K) and higher oxygen concentrations (12%) enhance the chemical kinetics efficiency of ammonia combustion, thereby improving the conversion of thermal energy into kinetic energy. The thrust increased by 37% under the optimal inlet parameters obtained through response surface optimization. The effectiveness of RSM in multi-variable optimization is verified, and the mechanism of multi-parameter coupling effects on hypersonic ammonia combustion dynamics is revealed.

papers.title: Influence of wetting step surfaces on bubble drag reduction
papers.abstract: Wetting step surface is beneficial for the maintenance of bubbles and therefore has potential to enhance the bubble drag reduction (DR) effect. To clarify this issue, the influences of wetting step surfaces on bubble drag reduction are studied. This numerical investigation employs the mixture model to study bubble drag reduction mechanisms on flat plates with different surface wettability. The research systematically compares uniformly wetting surfaces against a novel wettability step design featuring adjacent hydrophobic (170° contact angle) and hydrophilic (80° contact angle) regions. Key findings demonstrate that while uniform superhydrophobic surfaces achieve above 90% DR at low Reynolds numbers with high gas injection, their performance degrades severely ( >20% DR loss) at moderate flow velocities (4 m/s) due to turbulent disruption of ultrathin gas layers. The proposed wetting step surface overcomes this limitation by maintaining near-optimal DR efficiency (96.5%) across flow regimes (1–5 m/s) and angles of attack (±10°), outperforming uniform surfaces by up to 27% at higher speeds. Results show that strategically patterned wettability enables robust DR performance unattainable with homogeneous surfaces. This work provides foundational insights for marine energy applications, particularly the design of next-generation energy-saving ship hulls integrating active bubble injection with surface microengineering.

papers.title: Phase-resolved wave prediction from radar observations based on a multi-scale Fourier neural operator
papers.abstract: Phase-resolved ocean wave prediction is a vitally important but challenging task in ocean engineering. Any algorithm used for real-time reconstruction of the wave field must be both efficient and accurate. With this aim in mind, we propose a novel pipeline for phase-resolved wave prediction based on radar observations. The core architecture is based on a multi-scale version of the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO), which enhances the modeling of high-frequency components. Numerical simulations of nonlinear wave fields and their corresponding radar images are then used to train and test the proposed models. It is demonstrated that the proposed method achieves high accuracy and efficiency in wave prediction, with the multi-scale FNO model reducing prediction errors by approximately 14% compared to the standard FNO model. The method also exhibits robustness to noise and can be generalized to unseen sea conditions. Overall, the proposed technique is promising for real-time, phase-resolved wave prediction for use in ocean engineering practice.

papers.title: Phase transition seepage mechanism and heat/mass transfer characteristics of liquid nitrogen in loose media within confined spaces
papers.abstract: Spontaneous combustion of coal in goafs poses a significant threat to coal mine safety. The complex heat and mass transfer process during liquid nitrogen (LN2) injection in goafs is critical in determining its fire prevention and extinguishing efficiency. To investigate this process and the influence of injection rate, a large-scale experimental platform was established to visualize LN2 migration and inerting processes. Additionally, a numerical model was developed. This model was then validated against experimental data. This study identified and elucidated a secondary cooling phenomenon exclusively occurring in the middle layer, attributing it to local vortices generated by the coupled action of thermal buoyancy, gravity, and vaporization expansion force. These vortices induce instantaneous LN2 migration and redistribution, thereby revealing the complex phase-change seepage mechanism within porous media. Furthermore, the cooling and inerting effects of LN2 within the loose medium were quantified, indicating that the inerting zone radius is approximately 2–3 times that of the cooling zone. The research clearly demonstrated that increasing the injection rate significantly enhances the seepage velocity and extends the LN2 migration range, thereby effectively improving the cooling and inerting effectiveness in distal regions. These findings deepen the understanding of the phase-change seepage mechanisms of cryogenic fluids in loose media and provide a theoretical basis for optimizing parameters in LN2 fire prevention and extinguishing technologies.

papers.title: Immersed boundary method in the TELEMAC three-dimensional model for a diversion-wall lateral intake
papers.abstract: Submerged diversion structures are commonly employed in lateral water withdrawal projects to enhance flow patterns and stability. In numerical simulations, terrain elevation methods are traditionally adopted to represent submerged obstacles. However, such simplifications cannot accurately reproduce underwater structures with vertical sidewalls. To address this limitation, an improved immersed boundary method (IBM) is developed and integrated within the TELEMAC hydrodynamic modeling software (TELEMAC) via its three-dimensional hydrodynamic module (TELEMAC-3D). The method is assessed for a lateral water intake at the Rong River Estuary. First, the submerged diversion wall is simulated using IBM boundary conditions, and numerical results exhibit strong agreement with experimental data, with most relative errors with 4%. Subsequently, simulations comparing the classical mesh-deletion method, the terrain-elevation method, and IBM are conducted for conditions where the diversion wall height matches the water surface elevation. The deficiencies inherent in the terrain-elevation approach are highlighted through these comparisons. Furthermore, by systematically refining mesh quality, the comparative analysis underscores IBM's superior capability to accurately simulate vertical underwater structures. Notably, the IBM approach achieves equivalent simulation accuracy while reducing computational time by approximately 80%. These findings indicate that IBM significantly enhances numerical modeling efficiency and accuracy for submerged hydraulic structures.

papers.title: Application of multi-factor flow field simulation to extruder safety assessment
papers.abstract: During the processing of energetic materials in extruders, thermomechanical coupling effects may trigger material decomposition or deflagration. Existing safety assessments predominantly rely on macroscopic computational fluid dynamics with millimeter-scale resolution, which fails to resolve critical micron-scale hotspot evolution driven by localized thermal–mechanical interactions. A multi-scale modeling framework is proposed in this study integrating MATLAB-based micron-scale simulations with Fluent-based macroscopic flow field analysis. A novel time-discretization scheme is developed to enhance convergence efficiency, achieving convergence times of only 24.4% and 26.8% compared to explicit and implicit formats, respectively, under identical iteration speeds. Multi-factor flow field simulations are calibrated through sensitivity testing and coupled with extruder operational data to establish safety threshold. The framework bridges the resolution gap between energetic material hotspot dynamics (micron-scale) and device-level flow behavior, enabling risk prediction. This predictive tool identifies high-risk zones, quantifies safety thresholds, and analyzes the impact of key structural parameters, offering a transformative approach for real-time extruder safety monitoring and design optimization in industrial environments.

papers.title: Atomization characteristics of gas–liquid internal mixing of non-Newtonian fluids
papers.abstract: Non-Newtonian fluids play a significant role in aerospace propulsion, yet the atomization strongly depends on nozzle structure, influencing combustion efficiency. However, existing studies have offered limited comparisons of how nozzle structure affects the atomization behavior. This study provides a comprehensive structural comparison of non-Newtonian spray nozzles and identifies their distinct atomization characteristics, aiming to provide new insights for optimizing non-Newtonian atomization systems. Nine nozzle configurations were designed, including external mixing straight/helical groove and internal mixing straight/helical groove nozzles with different sleeve outlet diameters (0.3, 0.4, and 0.5 mm) and Y-jet nozzles. Three representative fluids (glycerol–water solution, xanthan gum, and polyethylene oxide solutions) were tested. The results show that internal mixing nozzles generally achieve superior atomization, while external mixing designs are limited by pressure constraints. The Y-jet nozzle is characterized by a bimodal droplet size distribution, containing both extremely small and extremely large droplets. Moreover, in internal mixing nozzles, helical groove nozzles widen the spray angle by nearly 50% and reduce the Sauter mean diameter of shear-thinning fluids by about 40% compared with straight groove designs. For Newtonian fluids, reducing the sleeve outlet diameter promotes jet instability, whereas viscoelastic fluids require larger outlets to mitigate clogging. Furthermore, viscoelasticity suppresses jet breakup, necessitating higher gas pressures to disrupt molecular chains.

papers.title: Coupled effects of swirl flow and drill-string vibration on deepwater wellbore temperature and cooling optimization
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of the wellbore temperature field in deepwater drilling is essential for operational safety. A few existing studies have considered the coupled effects of swirling flow and drill-string vibration, making it difficult to accurately characterize the downhole thermal environment. Based on wellbore heat transfer and drill-string dynamics, with the coupled effects of drill-string rotation–vibration accounted for, a transient heat-transfer model for deepwater drilling was developed. The sensitivity of bottom-hole temperature (BHT) in deepwater drilling to various factors was evaluated using a Plackett–Burman (P–B) screening design, followed by the proposal of targeted cooling methods. Compared to DRILLBENCH and models ignoring coupling effects, this model predicts annular temperatures closer to actual conditions, with a relative error of 1.02%, demonstrating higher accuracy and improved stability. An optimal insulation coating thickness can reduce BHT by up to 23 °C. Additional methods, such as adjusting the drill string rotation–vibration coupling factor and increasing fluid displacement, can lower BHT by 5–7 °C. The effectiveness of surface cooling methods exhibits pronounced diminishing marginal returns, with cooling capacity becoming increasingly limited as depth increases. Given the limited efficacy of individual cooling strategies, an integrated approach that combines multiple methods is recommended to achieve effective wellbore temperature reduction. The efficiency of surface-based cooling exhibits pronounced diminishing marginal returns. As well depth increases, its cooling capacity becomes increasingly limited. Given the limited effect of a single method, it is recommended to integrate multiple cooling techniques to effectively reduce wellbore temperature. The research results provide practical guidance for predicting and controlling wellbore temperature in deepwater drilling.

papers.title: Effect of non-uniform surface wettability on dynamics of a slender axisymmetric body during oblique water entry
papers.abstract: This paper numerically investigates the effect of non-uniform surface wettability on the dynamics of a slender axisymmetric body during oblique water entry. The body surface consists of hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts, with hydrophilic stripes distributed on either the upstream or downstream side. Meanwhile, different inclination angles are also considered. By analyzing cavity evolution, pressure distribution on the body surface, and vortex structures in the surrounding flow field, it is concluded that the distribution of hydrophilic stripes on the upstream or downstream sides significantly affects cavity formation. The generation and collapse of the cavity significantly influence rotation behavior. As the inclination angle decreases, the effect of upstream wettability on motion becomes less pronounced. Compared to cavities formed by hydrophobic surfaces, the rotation and shear effects within cavities generated by the shielding effect are more chaotic. The current research provides a significant understanding of how varying surface wettability can be utilized in oblique water entry scenarios, offering practical strategies for managing the passive movement of objects.

papers.title: Transition in the scaling laws of droplet-impact contact time
papers.abstract: Contact time has become a central focus in recent studies of droplet impact dynamics because of its relevance to anti-icing and self-cleaning. At the macroscale and nanoscale, distinct scaling laws for contact time have been proposed; however, the transition between them remains unresolved because of a lack of systematic investigations at the intermediate microscale. In this work, many-body dissipative particle dynamics simulations are employed to explore droplet impacts at the microscale. The results reveal two regimes of contact-time evolution: a velocity-dependent regime consistent with the Hertz elasticity theory, and a velocity-independent regime exhibiting pronounced scale effects. By decoupling the contributions of slip and viscous effects to the scale effects, it is found that varying slip length does not significantly alter the contact time, whereas increasing the Ohnesorge number markedly and nonlinearly prolongs it. When Oh > 0.3, viscous effects begin to significantly affect the contact time, and it can increase to more than 1.5 times that of droplets in the velocity-independent regime. These findings clarify that the change in bouncing dynamics induced by decreasing droplet size is mediated by viscous effects. To describe such scale effects, a full-scale scaling law for contact time is proposed, achieving an average error of <10% over the parameter range involved in this paper. Moreover, a boundary equation between the velocity-dependent and velocity-independent regimes is further established based on the insights into these regimes. By bridging the microscale gap, this study provides cross-scale insight into the bouncing dynamics of droplets impacting solid surfaces.

papers.title: Unsteady aerodynamic loads and wake dynamics of twin floating vertical axis wind turbines under asynchronous phase rolling excitation
papers.abstract: The operational phase difference between twin floating vertical axis wind turbines (FVAWT) serves as a key variable in regulating their asynchronous motion patterns, directly influencing the strength of aerodynamic interference and the coupled behavior of wake structures.
