This study reveals the significant influence of triaxial stress variation during cyclic injection–production on the thermal response, providing new experimental evidence and technical support for improving the heat extraction efficiency of EGS.

papers.title: Recent advances in fluid dynamics and its applications
papers.abstract: Fluid dynamics stands at the intersection of classical science and modern technological innovation, encompassing applications that extend from industrial manufacturing and biomedical systems to sustainable energy, climate modeling, and environmental processes. Its inherent complexity and versatility make it a cornerstone discipline for addressing many of today's most significant scientific and engineering challenges. This special issue on “Recent Advances in Fluid Dynamics and Its Applications” presents a collection of selected papers originating from the International Conference on Applications of Fluid Dynamics 2024. The contributions highlight the interdisciplinary nature of contemporary fluid mechanics through studies spanning turbulence and multiphase flow, transport phenomena, thermal and mass transfer processes, and magnetohydrodynamics, as well as emerging topics in biofluid dynamics, renewable energy, and environmental modeling. Emphasis is placed on both fundamental investigations and applied analyzes that translate theoretical insights into practical innovation. By showcasing these recent developments, this special issue reflects the dynamic evolution of fluid dynamics research and underscores its vital role in shaping future technologies and sustainable solutions. It is intended to serve as a resource and inspiration for researchers, engineers, and practitioners engaged in advancing the science and applications of fluid mechanics.

papers.title: Applicability criteria for equivalent continuum modeling of multiscale fracture networks in porous media
papers.abstract: The equivalent continuum model is a widely used approach for simplifying simulations of small-scale fracture seepage. However, its applicability has long been constrained by ambiguous scale boundaries and heterogeneous fracture distributions. In this study, numerical models with varying scale ratios (model size to fracture size) and degrees of distribution homogeneity are systematically developed to clarify how these factors constrain the accuracy of the equivalent continuum model. The results show that the pressure difference decreases significantly with the scale ratio, from the order of 10−1 MPa to 10−3 MPa as the scale ratio increases to 103. Fracture distribution homogeneity controls the spatial extent of the pressure difference. At a homogeneity level of 1, the region with a significant pressure difference (ΔP > 0.1 MPa) accounts for only 3.42% of the total area. Based on these findings, this study establishes an applicability chart for the equivalent continuum model that clearly delineates the criteria by incorporating both scale ratio and homogeneity. The chart clearly identifies an “equivalent region” (scale ratio ≥103 and homogeneity ≥0.8) and a “transition region” (scale ratio ≥102 and homogeneity ≥0.4208), together with quantified error expectations. This applicability chart provides explicit quantitative criteria and a solid theoretical basis for the accurate use of the equivalent continuum model.

papers.title: Cluster-level proppant transport and placement in propagating multi-cluster fractures: A computational-fluid-dynamics-based wellbore–perforation–fracture coupling method
papers.abstract: Multi-cluster hydraulic fractures originate from wellbores and perforations, where stress–shadow interactions significantly alter fracture geometry and slurry hydrodynamics—making cluster-level proppant placement a highly dynamic process. Understanding this transport and placement is essential for effective multi-cluster fracturing, yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear due to complex fluid–proppant flow within the integrated wellbore–perforation–multi-fracture system. A reliable predictive model is crucial for forecasting production gains and optimizing fracturing design. To address this gap, we developed a CFD-based (computational-fluid-dynamics-based) dimensionless model of perforation-to-fracture transport efficiency via nonlinear regression, which accounts for differences in proppant and fluid allocation. This model is coupled with a 3D multi-planar fracture model based on the displacement discontinuity method and fracture mechanics to quantify slurry and proppant distribution during multi-fracture propagation. Simulation results show bidirectional stress shadows shorten mid-cluster fractures, promoting heel-biased bedload transport and limiting proppant placement in central clusters. Raising injection rate expands propped area and coverage: increasing from 8 to 10 m3·min−1 boosts propped area by 43.1% and coverage by 13.9%, with diminishing returns at 14–16 m3·min−1. Lower proppant concentrations (∼5%) enhance long-range transport and inter-cluster uniformity; 5%–10% raises propped area by 84.2% and coverage by 82.6%, while ∼25% causes interaction-dominated settling and toe-region under-propping. Enlarging proppant size (50–150 μm) intensifies heel accumulation, cutting propped area by 5.2%. Proppant density effects weaken at >14 m3·min−1 due to dominant kinetic energy. This study guides “rate–concentration–size–density” selection to balance cluster effectiveness and long-term conductivity in reservoir stimulation.

papers.title: Early-stage impact dynamics in dense suspensions of millimeter-sized particles
papers.abstract: We investigate the early-stage impact dynamics in dense suspensions composed of millimeter-sized particles. While traditional models based on the Stokes flow are typically applicable to suspensions of micrometer-sized particles, their validity for larger particles remains uncertain. Through controlled impact experiments, we examine the maximum drag force Fmax acting on a projectile as a function of impact speed u0. We have successfully conducted experiments using these suspensions and confirmed the relation Fmax∼u03/2 for relatively large u0 as observed in the previous studies of suspensions of micrometer-sized particles. Our results demonstrate that the floating model—equivalent to the viscous model—successfully captures the early-stage dynamics even in suspensions with larger particles. This finding suggests that viscous-dominated behavior persists under certain conditions, extending the applicability of the floating model or the viscous model to new regimes. Our work provides experimental validation for theoretical predictions and contributes to a deeper understanding of impact-induced responses in dense suspensions.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of acoustically forced helium jet in crossflow using shadowgraphy and modal analysis
papers.abstract: This study presents an experimental investigation of helium jet in a crossflow of air, with an objective to understand the influence of acoustic forcing on jet behavior and mixing. Unforced and sinusoidally forced jets are studied. High-speed shadowgraphy is used to capture instantaneous jet images. These images are further processed using the Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) algorithm to provide insights into the spatiotemporal behavior. Schlieren Imaging Velocimetry (SIV) is also used to understand jet entrainment and identify regions of low and high velocities. Moreover, an interface tracking method is used to obtain interface location oscillations for near nozzle and far field locations. The energy spectrum of these oscillations is obtained through a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) analysis. The unforced jet is observed for different jet-to-crossflow velocity ratios (R), and it is observed that the jet penetration increases with R. Unforced cases show a broadband spectrum, indicating the absence of any dominant frequency, except for the lowest velocity ratio case. The instability in unforced cases is limited to shear layer oscillations. For the forced cases, a clear dominant frequency corresponding to the forcing frequency (and occasionally their harmonics) is recorded. It is observed that the impact of forcing function is not the same for all the frequencies, and the jet response is observed to be much more pronounced for a higher frequency as compared to a lower frequency forcing. Two typical cases, highlighting the effect of frequency response, are compared in detail using image analysis, interface tracking, POD, and SIV.

papers.title: Unsteady flow past rounded rectangular cylinder in power-law fluid: OpenFOAM simulations with proper orthogonal decomposition
papers.abstract: This study presents a numerical investigation of unsteady flow past rectangular cylinders with rounded corners in power-law fluids at Reynolds number Re=150 (based on bulk inlet velocity U∞ and cylinder height D), corresponding to the unsteady laminar vortex-shedding regime under confinement and blockage ratio D/LH=0.2. Simulations were performed using the nonNewtonianIcoFoam solver in OpenFOAM for two aspect ratios (AR = 1 and 2), three corner radii (R/D=0, 0.25, 0.50), and three power-law indices (n=0.6, 1.0, 1.4) representing shear-thinning, Newtonian, and shear-thickening behaviors. The results demonstrate that increasing the corner radius significantly modifies the wake dynamics and reduces drag. For AR = 1 and n=0.6, the total drag coefficient decreased by up to 46.7% from R/D=0 to 0.5. At n=0.6, the Strouhal number exhibits a 55.4% increase as the corner radius ratio R/D rises from 0 to 0.5, indicating that corner rounding enhances wake stability and promotes more regular vortex shedding. Time-averaged pressure coefficient (Cp) contours showed enhanced base pressure recovery and shortened recirculation zones. Vorticity and Q-criterion fields revealed suppression of vortex shedding and wake unsteadiness at higher R/D and lower n. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) analysis showed that the first two modes captured over 85% of the total energy for rounded geometries, indicating dominance of coherent structures and enhanced flow regularity. The novelty of this work lies in its combined analysis of non-Newtonian effects, geometric rounding, and modal decomposition under confined unsteady conditions.

papers.title: Mixed convection in horizontal channel with unstable stratification for low-Prandtl-number fluids
papers.abstract: Mixed convection with unstable stratification for low-Prandtl-number fluids is an important momentum and energy coupling transport process, which attracts growing interest in engineering practical scenarios. In this study, a series of scale-resolving implicit large-eddy simulations is conducted with high-pass filter technique in high-order spectral element method. The nominal friction Reynolds number is up to Reτ,N=1020 for engineering practical use. The range of the Richardson number is 0≤Ri≤10 and the Prandtl number is fixed at Pr=0.025 to investigate mixed convection for liquid metals under different buoyancy conditions. The quasi-streamwise longitudinal counter-rotating rollers with streamwise meandering fulfill the entire channel width to enhance turbulent heat transfer. The flow pattern similarity is quantitatively discussed through Reynolds stress invariants and Monin–Obukhov (MO) similarity, finding that the flow pattern is mainly controlled by the Richardson number. A new scaling of MO length scale is proposed, and the results show that the buoyant effect is more pronounced for low-Prandtl-number fluids. Furthermore, the power-law Businger–Dyer–Panofsky flux profile relationship is still applicable to MO universal functions for low-Prandtl-number fluids. New empirical correlations and scaling are proposed for friction drag and heat transfer with the average maximum relative deviation no larger than 25%. The premultiplied co-spectra of friction drag and heat transfer indicate that flow similarity also exhibits in statistical wavenumber space with the typical streamwise wavelength λx≈8h of buoyancy-induced large-scale motions. The extension of Fukagata–Iwamoto–Kasagi identity is conducted to study the contributions of shear turbulent motions and buoyancy-induced large-scale motions on friction drag and heat transfer. The results show that buoyancy-induced large-scale motions only cost 20%–25% friction drag loss, but contribute nearly 60% heat transfer, showing good profits on less friction and more heat transfer.

papers.title: Hydrodynamics around a circular collared cylinder system on a rigid bed
papers.abstract: This study employs large eddy simulation to investigate the hydrodynamics around a collared cylinder system. To achieve this objective, both experiment and numerical simulations were conducted. The experimental study was performed for bare cylinder and cylinder with a collar at bed level using an acoustic Doppler velocimetry to validate the simulation results. In the numerical simulation, four cases were analyzed: an isolated cylinder (without collar), a cylinder with a collar at the bed level (z/H=0), and cylinder with collar at elevated positions of z/H= 0.25 and z/H= 0.5, where z represents the vertical position of the collar from the rigid bed and H is the flow depth. From the simulation results, various hydrodynamic parameters were analyzed, including mean velocities, streamlines, turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), Q-criterion, rotational tensor, and normalized Reynolds shear stress (RSS). Additionally, peak RSS, peak TKE, Strouhal number variation with collar elevation positions, integrated turbulent momentum fluxes (ITMFs), and vortical structures were investigated. It was observed that the collar placed at the bed level significantly modifies the flow field by reducing both streamwise and vertical velocities and weakening the streamline patterns around the cylinder. The results show clear recirculation zone forms downstream of the cylinder, while a marginal attenuation of TKE and Q-criterion, indicating reduced turbulence intensity and coherent structures. From the RSS components and ITMFs, it is observed that the cylinder with a collar at bed level suppresses near-bed turbulence, exhibiting the lowest magnitudes of streamwise lateral RSS (−u′v′)¯. Furthermore, vortical structure analysis revealed that the presence of the collar enhancing shear-layer instabilities, vortex shedding, fragments the flow into multiple layers, influencing the complexity and strength of vortical interactions around the cylinder.

papers.title: Turbulence and coherent structures in fully developed open-channel flows beneath periodic surface submergence
papers.abstract: Periodic surface submergence, which frequently occurs in floating installations such as solar farms and aquaculture systems, induce a surface boundary with roughness heterogeneity that fundamentally disrupts the boundary layer characteristics and reshapes underlying turbulence. This study experimentally investigates the turbulent structures and free-surface dynamics induced by periodic submergence in a fully developed flow using high-resolution particle image velocimetry. Spanwise-oriented semi-submerged bars with 70% open spacing were deployed periodically in the streamwise direction, at submergence depths ranging from 1% to 12%, which represents realistic prototype scenarios. Time-averaged results of the instantaneous measurements revealed that the flow asymmetry increased with the submergence depth together with turbulence intensification near the surface. At higher submergence, streamwise velocity fluctuations reached up to 18% of the local maximum velocity, while both the velocity peak and zero-shear-stress position shifted downward, reaching up to 15% of the flow depth. Two-point correlation analysis showed that the streamwise and wall-normal extent, as well as the inclination of hairpin packets, also increased with submergence, surpassing those induced by traditional two-dimensional rough walls. Spectral analysis identified a consistent dominant Strouhal number of St=0.11 for all test cases. Dynamic mode decomposition revealed dominant coherent structures aligned with the harmonics of this frequency, which became more pronounced and elongated with increasing submergence. Strong free-surface oscillations also emerged under high submergence, exhibiting amplitudes up to 0.5 times the submergence depth. These findings underscore the distinct turbulence mechanisms underneath periodic surface submergence and improve the physical understanding toward hydrodynamic assessments.

papers.title: Dynamics of hydroelastic wavetrains with plate inertia
papers.abstract: In the linear theory of hydroelastic waves, the inertial effects of thin plates are often neglected due to their minimal impact on the dispersion relation. This assumption also persists in many nonlinear studies. For instance, existing research that uses the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation to describe finite-amplitude responses near the critical velocity (the phase speed minimum) typically does not consider inertia. However, such a defocusing-type model fails to explain the fully localized responses observed experimentally in deep water. Our main contribution is demonstrating that incorporating plate inertia fundamentally alters the nonlinear hydroelastic wave dynamics. Specifically, when the areal density of the plates exceeds a critical threshold—determined by water density, gravity, and flexural rigidity—the deep-water NLS equation changes from a defocusing type to a focusing type. This transition enables solutions that decay in the far field. Through multiple-scale analyses, we also illustrate that inertia modifies the intensities of nonlinear wave–wave interactions. Our theoretical predictions align closely with numerical results derived from potential flow theory, and this agreement is further validated by a novel reformulation of time-dependent conformal mapping that takes the inertia term into account.

papers.title: Experimental study on water entry of Janus spheres with asymmetric wettability
papers.abstract: This study focused on the water entry of Janus spheres with asymmetric wettability. The effects of impact velocity and sphere size on splash behaviors, cavity dynamics, and trajectory deviations are experimentally investigated using high-speed imaging techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that wettability contrast drives distinct contact-line dynamics, resulting in three-phase line pinning and sliding behavior that generates pronounced asymmetry in the splash curtain. Enhanced rupture occurs on hydrophilic surfaces while splash height attenuates with rising velocity. Cavity formation demonstrates profound asymmetry, redirected toward hydrophilic hemispheres by orthogonal pressure gradients established through divergent contact-line motion and Marangoni flows. By converting kinetic energy into tangential momentum, implosion energy reversal drives transverse jetting at hydrophobic interfaces. Heterogeneous wettability preserves inertial scaling of cavity pinch-off times. Resultant hydrodynamic attraction asymmetries mediate trajectory deviation toward hydrophilic regions, with deflection trajectory scaling with impact velocity. The findings establish wettability patterning as a mechanism for passive trajectory control through engineered flow separation.

papers.title: Onset of thermal convection in the Brinkman porous layer under local thermal non-equilibrium with gravity variation and viscous dissipation
papers.abstract: This paper aims to study the commencement of convective motion in a Brinkman porous enclosure under local thermal non-equilibrium conditions, and how it is influenced by varying gravity fields, vertical throughflow, and viscous dissipation. Four types of gravity variation—linear, quadratic, cubic, and exponential—are considered, each characterized by the gravity variation parameter (λ). The upper and lower boundaries of the layer are maintained at a constant temperature. Applying the normal mode technique, the resulting eigenvalue problem was solved numerically. The stability characteristics are analyzed through graphs and tables, illustrating the effects of the throughflow parameter (Q), Darcy number (Da), viscous dissipation (Ge), interphase heat transfer parameter (H), and gravity variation parameter (λ). It is observed that the system tends toward local thermal equilibrium for both very high and very small values of the interphase heat transfer parameter. The gravity variation parameter, throughflow, and interphase heat transfer parameter enhance system stability, whereas the porosity-modified conductivity ratio promotes instability; however, for γ≥10, the effect of H becomes negligible. Among the four gravity variations, the exponential form provides the strongest stabilization, followed by linear, quadratic, and cubic variations. In the exponential case, the critical Rayleigh number (Rac) increases markedly from about 450 to nearly 3250 as λ rises from 0 to 1.5. In contrast, viscous dissipation contributes only marginally to instability; the maximum reduction of Rac is merely 1.11% when Ge increases from 0 to 1 under linear gravity variation.

papers.title: Effects of streamline-blunted aerodynamic braking plates on turbulent flow around a high-speed train with and without yaw angle
papers.abstract: This study employs the improved delayed detached eddy simulation (IDDES) method to investigate the aerodynamic characteristics of a high-speed train (HST) equipped with streamlined-blunted aerodynamic braking devices under crosswind conditions at yaw angles of 0° and 15°, with a Reynolds number of 5.0 × 105. The accuracy and reliability of the numerical simulations were validated against scaled wind tunnel experiments conducted at the same Reynolds number. Aerodynamic forces, pressure distributions, and flow field characteristics were systematically compared and analyzed for four cases: 0° OC, 0° BC, 15° OC, and 15° BC. The results indicate that IDDES provides a reliable tool for numerically evaluating the aerodynamic performance of braking devices under both open-air and crosswind conditions. At a yaw angle of 0°, deploying aerodynamic braking plates significantly enhanced the positive pressure distribution on the head car and the negative pressure distribution on the tail car. Consequently, the overall pressure drag increased substantially, leading to a marked rise in aerodynamic drag. Compared with the original configuration (OC), the drag coefficients of the head and tail cars increased by approximately 364.65% and 354.46%, respectively, resulting in an overall aerodynamic drag increase in about 235.4%. At a yaw angle of 15°, owing to reduced interference among some braking plates, the braking plates contributed even more to aerodynamic drag than in the 0° yaw case. Specifically, relative to the 0° yaw case, the drag increments of the head and tail cars further increased by approximately 103.15% and 60.63%, respectively, resulting in a total aerodynamic drag increase in about 334.47%. Moreover, crosswind conditions significantly altered the surface pressure distribution on the original high-speed train, producing positive pressure on the windward side and negative pressure on the leeward side and roof. With the deployment of braking plates, the total lateral force on the train increased by approximately 13.67% compared with the original configuration, while the lift force decreased by about 5.04%.

papers.title: Flame stabilization enhancement in a supersonic combustor by multi-scale cavities combination
papers.abstract: This study investigates an enhanced passive control strategy for suppressing combustion oscillations in scramjet engines by introducing an auxiliary small cavity upstream of the primary flameholder. Experimental tests conducted on a direct-connect rig with Mach 3 inflow demonstrate that the staged-cavity design achieves remarkable stability improvements across equivalence ratios (Φ = 0.34–1.2). Key findings include: (1) 48.9% and 47.2% reduction in pressure oscillations at Φ = 1.2 and 0.6, respectively, with the mean normalized pressure increasing by approximately 8.57%; (2) Expansion of flammability limits (lean ignition at Φ = 0.34 vs baseline Φ = 0.48); (3) 81.2% suppression of flame front fluctuations through standing flame anchoring. Mechanistic analysis reveals five synergistic effects: (i) pre-combustion in the auxiliary cavity decentralizes heat release, (ii) the small cavity's shear layer sustains a persistent pilot flame without additional injectors, (iii) boundary layer stabilization prevents separation-induced oscillations, (iv) enhanced fuel–air mixing creates localized premixed zones within the diffusion flame, and (v) shock restructuring maintains flame anchoring despite pressure variations. High-speed imaging and schlieren visualization confirm the design's ability to maintain stable jet-like flames while eliminating chaotic combustion modes observed in conventional configurations. The auxiliary cavity approach demonstrates simultaneous improvements in combustion stability (oscillation suppression), performance (thrust increase), and operational envelope (extended ignition limits), providing a practical passive control solution for scramjet combustors. Residual low-frequency fluctuations (4%–5% amplitude) suggest future optimization opportunities in cavity-flowfield integration. These findings establish staged cavity combustion as an effective strategy for next-generation hypersonic propulsion systems.

papers.title: The mass transfer behaviors and mechanisms of CO2–oil phase in quartz confined nano-space: Insights from molecular dynamics simulations
papers.abstract: The mass transfer process of CO2 multiphase systems constitutes a core physical mechanism governing both oil recovery and sequestration performance, involving complex interactions between CO2 and oil under reservoir conditions. However, the mass transfer behavior of CO2 multiphase systems at the nanoscale remains insufficiently elucidated. This study investigates the transport and mass transfer processes of CO2 multiphase systems within nanopores using molecular dynamics simulations, specifically focusing on the underlying CO2–oil interaction mechanisms and the influence of various factors. The results demonstrate that the energy difference between CO2–oil phase and oil phase–pore wall interactions serves as the decisive factor for mass transfer behaviors, with larger energy differences correlating to enhanced miscibility effects. Van der Waals energy dominates the CO2–oil interaction energy and acts as the primary driving force for interphase mass transfer. Elevated temperature and pressure significantly promote the mass transfer process. CO2 exhibits superior mass transfer behaviors with nonpolar oil molecules compared to polar counterparts, and shorter-chain nonpolar molecules achieve better miscibility with CO2. Hydrocarbon gases can promote the mass transfer process between CO2 and C8H18, and impurity gases inhibit mass transfer. The mass transfer degree of CO2 and C8H18 increases with nanopore size and reaches higher levels in hydrophilic pores. These findings provide molecular-level insights into CO2–oil mass transfer behaviors, offering theoretical guidance for optimizing CO2-enhanced oil recovery and geological sequestration strategies.

papers.title: Interfacial transport of CO2/CH4 in hydroxylated silica nanopores: Implications for CO2-enhanced gas recovery
papers.abstract: CO2-enhanced gas recovery (CO2-EGR) requires knowledge of how interfacial interactions regulate gas transport in nanoporous reservoirs. Molecular dynamics simulations of a 6 nm hydroxylated silica slit pore at 20 MPa were conducted to assess the coupled effects of surface hydroxyl density (2.30–9.58 OH/nm2), water saturation (17%–50%), and temperature (313.15–363.15 K) on CO2/CH4 transport. A consistent three-layer organization emerges: bound water films adjacent to pore walls, interfacial enrichment of CO2, and CH4 occupying the pore center with greater mobility. Moderate hydroxylation stabilizes water films while maintaining accessible pathways, whereas higher hydroxylation enhances CO2 binding but restricts transport channels. Water saturation exerts a nonmonotonic influence: at intermediate levels, laterally continuous interfacial pathways enhance CO2 diffusivity and CO2/CH4 selectivity; at high saturation, bulk-like aqueous domains form, weakening selectivity and suppressing gas mobility. Temperature raises diffusivities more strongly for CO2 than for CH4 and follows Arrhenius behavior with activation energies ordered CH4 < CO2 < H2O. Concurrently, heating reduces CO2 adsorption, reflecting a competition between interfacial residence and in-plane migration. These findings, while bounded by the studied geometry, pressure, and force fields, elucidate general mechanisms of nanoconfined transport and provide a physical basis for understanding the trade-off between displacement efficiency and storage security in CO2-EGR.

papers.title: Moving mesh fluid–structure interaction approach for vortex-induced vibration simulation based on the discontinuous Galerkin method with adaptive mesh refinement technique
papers.abstract: Vortex-induced vibration (VIV) remains a fundamental yet computationally challenging problem in computational fluid dynamics. This study develops a moving mesh fluid–structure interaction approach within a Runge–Kutta discontinuous Galerkin adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) framework. The viscous term in the compressible Navier–Stokes equations is discretized using the high-order interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin (IPDG) method. In addition to the above, key numerical advancements encompass the rigorous derivation of the Lax–Friedrichs (L–F) numerical flux formulation tailored for moving mesh, an enhanced AMR-driven nodal correction methodology designed for curved surface geometries, and the implementation of a ghost-node boundary condition treatment scheme to address dynamic mesh motion. Numerical validation proceeds through three phases: first, the Couette flow simulations confirm the IPDG method's spatial convergence order. Subsequent analysis of an unsteady flow past a cylinder demonstrates the AMR framework's efficacy in resolving vortex-dominated flow. Finally, six VIV benchmark cases are simulated using the third-order IPDG discretization, establishing the proposed FSI approach's accuracy. Furthermore, synthetic jets (SJs) flow control is investigated through four frequency-variant SJs configurations. The results reveal that the SJs can achieve complete VIV suppression at a low actuation frequency, while higher actuation frequencies reduce suppression efficiency because the energy of the SJs is more in the form of acoustic waves.

papers.title: Erratum: “Pore-scale insight into the impact of heterogeneity in porous media on CO2–oil immiscible displacement” [Phys. Fluids 37 , 102014 (2025)]
Relationship between unpredictability and intermittency in shell models of turbulence and experiments
papers.abstract: We study the predictability of turbulent velocity signals using probabilistic analog forecasting. Here, predictability is defined by the accuracy of forecasts and the associated uncertainties. We study the Gledzer–Ohkitani–Yamada (GOY) shell model of turbulence as well as experimental measurements from a fully developed turbulent flow. In both cases, we identify the extreme values of velocity at small scales as localized unpredictable events that lead to a loss of predictability: worse mean predictions and an increase in their uncertainties. The GOY model, with its explicit scale separation, allows us to evaluate the prediction performance at individual scales to better relate the intensity of extreme events and the loss of forecast performance. Results show that predictability decreases systematically from large to small scales. These findings establish a statistical connection between predictability loss across scales and intermittency in turbulent flows.

papers.title: Turbulent flow past a finite wall-mounted cylinder at various degrees of upstream sheltering: Effects of the number of upstream cylinders
papers.abstract: Turbulent flow over tandem low-aspect-ratio finite wall-mounted circular cylinders (FWMCCs) was experimentally investigated using planar particle image velocimetry. The FWMCCs occupied less than 20% of the incoming turbulent boundary layer thickness and were arranged at streamwise spacings l/d=2 and 6 and height ratios hu/hd=0.5 and 1; here, l is the center-to-center streamwise spacing, d is the diameter, hu is the height of the upstream FWMCCs, and hd is the height of the downstream FWMCC. Four distinct configurations were considered: configuration 1 (l/d=2, hu/hd=0.5), configuration 2 (l/d=2, hu/hd=1), configuration 3 (l/d=6, hu/hd=0.5), and configuration 4 (l/d=6, hu/hd=1). For each configuration, the dependency of the downstream FWMCC wake on the number of upstream sheltering FWMCCs n was examined for n=0 (i.e., isolated FWMCC) to n=4 (i.e., sheltering by four upstream FWMCCs). The time-averaged streamwise and wall-normal velocities, in-plane turbulent kinetic energy and its production, Reynolds shear stress and its quadrant decomposition, and two-point correlations were examined for each configuration. The results support an independence threshold of n=3 for configurations 1, 3, and 4, past which the downstream FWMCC wake mean flow and turbulence are independent of n for the overwhelming majority of reviewed flow quantities. For configuration 2, the results suggest that the downstream FWMCC wake approaches independence; however, investigations with n>4 are recommended to pinpoint the independence threshold for this configuration.

papers.title: A robust intermittency equation formulation for transition modeling in Spalart–Allmaras simulations of airfoil flows over a wide range of Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a new robust formulation for local correlation-based laminar-to-turbulent transition models. This mechanism is incorporated into Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes equations, coupled with the Spalart–Allmaras (SA) turbulence model, considering both γ and γ–Rẽθ,t transition frameworks. In this context, special attention is placed on numerical stabilization of the γ transport equation, which is identified as the root cause of instabilities observed in both γ and γ–Rẽθ,t-based models. To this end, the intermittency equation is reformulated in logarithmic form and further stabilized through an energy-based limiting to bound excessively high positive values. In order to suppress unphysical pressure oscillations in the transition region, a gradient-driven artificial viscosity is also introduced. Additionally, the SA equation is augmented with strain-rate-modulated production and rotation correction terms. The presented approach has demonstrated consistent effectiveness and robustness in the simulation of flow fields around airfoils over a wide range of Reynolds numbers, making it suitable for practical aerodynamic design applications.

papers.title: Bio-inspired technologies for enhanced wave energy converter: A review
papers.abstract: Over the past two decades, significant growth in global energy consumption has driven the exploration of clean and renewable energy sources, among which ocean wave energy stands out as a vast and largely untapped resource. In addition to traditional electromagnetic generators, triboelectric nanogenerators and piezoelectric power generation technologies have emerged as viable options for low-frequency wave energy harvesting. This review demonstrates that bio-inspired designs substantially improve energy conversion performance, with representative cases achieving up to 30%–40% enhancement in capture factor or several-fold increases in power density over conventional counterparts. By categorizing and quantitatively analyzing bio-inspired wave energy harvesting devices into four types—bio-inspired electromagnetic, triboelectric, piezoelectric, and hybrid systems—this work not only summarizes the current state-of-the-art but also critically assesses key performance metrics, identifies persistent challenges in scalability and durability, and outlines future research directions. The quantitative analysis presented in this review underscores the significant potential of bio-inspired strategies in advancing wave energy harvesting toward practical and competitive renewable energy solutions.

papers.title: An experimental study of the evolution characteristics of the air-mass-near-the-tube-carrying-type shoulder cavity and the attached tail cavity
papers.abstract: The attached shoulder-tail cavities of an underwater vehicle are accompanied by complex flow phenomena and determine its motion and loading characteristics. The evolution of underwater vehicle-attached cavities is studied. The ability of the solid wall to carry the air mass near the tube is focused on. The evolutionary properties of cavity collapse and tailing surges are studied. The effects caused by the cavitation number and the Froude number are discussed. The study showed that the air mass near the tube-carrying-type shoulder cavity is prone to form disintegration before leaving the water when Frl ≤ 6.42. During vehicle traversing the free surface, the shattered shoulder cavity forms a splash jet impacting the tail cavity. As the Fr increased, the position of the disintegration point is progressively closer to the free surface, and the convex fluctuation point occurs near the leading edge of the cavity. The umbilical tailing surges gradually converge. Until Frl = 10.41, no significant disintegration of the cavity is observed. At low cavitation numbers, the ability to carry the air mass near the tube out of the tube is better than at high Fr. When Frl = 11.88, the maximum value of L¯1 is 0.5L. When Pdifference = 16.8, the maximum value of L¯1 is 0.72L. The high pressure ratio reduces the splashing effect of the jet. When the vehicle is completely above the free surface, L¯J−D8 = 6.28, L¯J−D9 = 4.75, and L¯J−D10 = 2.80. The tail cavity is pulled from the jet to form a tailing surge.

papers.title: Impact of differentiating factors on the hemodynamics of umbrella-shaped and fusiform-shaped inferior vena cava filters: A computational fluid dynamics simulation study
papers.abstract: This work applies computational fluid dynamics to carry out a systematic investigation of two representative inferior vena cava filters (IVCFs): the umbrella-shaped Denali and the fusiform-shaped OptEase IVCFs. The study emphasizes how blood rheology, inferior vena cava (IVC) diameter, and flow rate influence the hemodynamic environment surrounding these devices. The simulations indicate that although the Newtonian assumption preserves the global flow pattern, it largely exaggerates the downstream stagnation region (roughly twice that predicted by non-Newtonian models) and reduces the overall velocity magnitude (centerline velocity drops by about 30%). It also weakens the acceleration inside the filter and underestimates both wall shear stress (WSS) and flow resistance. Such discrepancies could mislead clinical evaluation and structural safety assessments. Among the five non-Newtonian rheological models examined, all yield similar flow field distributions, but clear variations appear in WSS and resistance. The simplified cross model predicts the largest values, whereas the Carreau model provides intermediate results, thus offering a more representative choice. A smaller IVC diameter markedly lengthens the post-filter stagnation zone (at 15 mm, nearly twice that at 25 mm) and substantially increases filter-surface WSS, which may enhance thrombus trapping and dissolution yet simultaneously elevate resistance and fracture risk. Higher inflow rates exert effects comparable to a reduced vessel diameter, intensifying resistance and promoting local disturbances. Overall, these findings highlight that clinical application of IVCFs may incorporate imaging data to select filter type and geometry tailored to patient-specific IVC size and flow rate, thereby achieving effective embolus interception while limiting complications.

papers.title: Perturbation solution for jet noise reduction via an air–water curtain
papers.abstract: The attenuation of jet-generated noise through multiphase curtains offers a promising passive mitigation strategy. This study develops a perturbation-based framework to quantify the interaction of acoustic waves with an air–water droplet curtain placed around a jet. Starting from the volume-averaged multiphase equations, linearized perturbation solutions are derived for two configurations: (i) suspended droplets in quiescent air and (ii) dispersed droplets subjected to the influence of ambient flow. For the suspended case, both asymptotic and numerical solutions are obtained, showing that attenuation increases with droplet volume fraction and that there exists an optimal droplet to jet nozzle diameter ratio for maximum reduction. Comparisons with previous experimental data confirm the ability of the model to capture frequency-dependent absorption trends. The dispersed case reveals that interphase slip reduces peak attenuation and shifts it toward higher frequencies. Parametric studies highlight the roles of volume fractions, Strouhal number, droplet size, and slip velocity in the regulation of attenuation. The results demonstrate that a curtain on the order of one jet nozzle diameter can provide significant noise reduction without affecting thrust.

papers.title: Study on hydrate formation and plugging mechanisms in mineral oil–methane–water bubble flow systems without emulsifiers
papers.abstract: Gas hydrate formation poses a significant flow assurance challenge in oil and gas production under extreme environmental conditions. This study specifically investigates the kinetics of methane hydrate formation and the associated plugging mechanisms in multiphase flow systems containing waxy oil. Experiments were conducted in a visual flow loop under various pressure (5.2–8.2 MPa) and temperature (−1 to −3 °C) conditions. The results demonstrate that the presence of waxy oil is a critical factor for pipeline plugging, as it significantly promotes hydrate nucleation—reducing the onset time by up to 53.66%—and fosters particle aggregation, leading to a dramatic increase in slurry apparent viscosity (up to 2067%). In contrast, hydrate slurries in a pure methane–water system flowed smoothly without blockage. Visual observations revealed the macroscopic process from initial hydrate formation and viewing window coverage to aggregate-induced plugging and subsequent hydrate aging and deposition. Higher initial pressure and lower temperature accelerated hydrate formation kinetics and shortened the time to plugging. A key finding is that plugging, which occurred before or after hydrate formation ceased, was primarily due to the aggregation of hydrate particles rather than to a high hydrate volume fraction. These findings highlight the severe synergistic risk posed by hydrates and waxy oils in flow assurance.

papers.title: The natural -conformation tensor constitutive laws
papers.abstract: In this work, we revisit the seminal work of Renardy [M. Renardy, J. Non-Newtonian Fluid Mech. 52(1), 91–95 (1994)] on the reformulation of the stress tensor in its “natural” basis and present a generic framework for the natural-conformation tensor for a large class of differential constitutive models. We show that the proposed dyadic transformation can be equated as an orthogonal transformation of the conformation tensor into a streamlined orthonormal basis given by a rotation tensor expressed in terms of the unit velocity vectors. We also show that the natural-conformation tensor formulation is a particular sub-case of the kernel-conformation tensor transformation [A. M. Afonso, F. T. Pinho, M. A. Alves, J. Non-Newtonian Fluid Mech. 167–168, 30–37 (2012)] with the kernel function acting on the rotation of the eigenvectors rather than on the magnitude of the extension of the conformation tensor.

papers.title: Large heavy particles in turbulent pipe flows: Skin friction drag, turbulence modulation and preferential particle distribution
papers.abstract: Previous studies on particle-laden flows have focused mainly on either small, heavy particles or large, and weakly buoyant particles. We present measurements in the regime of large and heavy particles, investigating the particle-turbulence dynamics over a parameter space covering a wide range of particle volume fractions, Stokes and Froude numbers at low to moderate Reynolds numbers. We consider the flow in a vertical pipe, thus allowing for the investigation of the two-way coupling between particles and the carrier phase turbulence while excluding the effect of gravity-induced settling on the wall-normal migration of particles. Pressure drop measurements indicate a linear increase in the skin friction coefficient with the volume fraction of particles. The growth rate of the skin friction coefficient was found to scale inversely with the Froude number. Using time-resolved particle image velocimetry measurements, we show that the carrier phase turbulence is modulated even at particle concentrations as low as 0.3%, indicating that particle-induced stresses due to the distortion of fluid streamlines cannot be neglected. Additionally, using Voronoi tessellations to quantify the particle concentration field, we observe a strong deviation from the Poisson behavior for cases both with and without turbophoresis. The results of particle tracking show that the particles move in roughly straight-line trajectories, which deviate from the flow streamlines with a mean angle of about 2° and a maximum angle of about 9°. The particles were also observed to be situated away from vortex cores indicating the occurrence of the centrifuge mechanism.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical investigation of the aerodynamic performances of the salsify seed
papers.abstract: Wind-dispersed plant seeds exhibit excellent aerodynamic performance. For example, Taraxacum officinale (dandelion) seed achieves long-distance dispersal through its unique pappus structure. However, its micro-scale structure limits the potential for bio-inspired engineering applications. To explore more scalable pappus structures, this study focuses on the Tragopogon sp. (salsify) seed, with a pappus structure similar to the dandelion seed but at larger physical dimensions. Key geometric features of the salsify pappus structure were extracted and abstracted into a porous disk model. Wind tunnel tests and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were conducted on three comparative models: a dandelion pappus model, a salsify pappus model, and a solid disk model with the same projected area as the salsify pappus. The numerical results were obtained by solving the incompressible steady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations with the Spalart–Allmaras turbulence model using Ansys Fluent software platform. Results of wind tunnel tests show that these models can generate separated vortex rings in the airflow. The separated vortex ring formed by the salsify porous model is the largest and most elongated. CFD simulations further validated these findings and revealed that the salsify pappus structure is the most effective model in suppressing reverse flow and smoothing pressure gradients. These merits can reduce wake diffusion and enhance wake stability. This study offers valuable insights for further investigation of the larger-scale pappus structure and provides a novel insight into the bio-inspired applications.

papers.title: The effects of vegetation on gravity currents propagating in channels of general cross-sections
papers.abstract: This study presents a mathematical model to investigate the dynamics of gravity currents in channels with vegetation and varying cross section (CS) geometries. The model, based on a system of shallow-water equations, incorporates a vegetation-induced drag force of the form Fd∼|u|λ (where u is the current speed and λ is constant) allowing for the analysis of flow behavior under different configurations, including fixed volume (lock-release) and constant influx conditions. We focused on power-law CSs defined by f(z)=zγ and explored the influence of both the channel geometry and the drag parameter, λ, through analytical similarity solutions and numerical computations. Our findings reveal a complex interplay between drag and channel shape. For fixed-volume flows, the propagation distance of the current increases with γ, while for certain constant-influx cases, the trend is inverted, with the fastest propagation occurring in rectangular channels (γ=0). The propagation rate for the constant-height influx case and the Boussinesq lock-exchange problem was found to be dependent solely on the drag parameter λ and independent of the channel's geometry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that flows with non-constant drag can be accurately approximated using an averaged drag value. Ultimately, this study establishes a quantitative relationship that is essential for accurately modeling and controlling the propagation of density-driven flows in complex environments where both channel geometry and vegetation-induced drag are variable.

papers.title: Experimental study on phase behavior of the CO2–oil–saltwater system in a high gas–oil ratio offshore carbonate reservoir
papers.abstract: The application of seawater alternating CO2 miscible flooding technology in offshore carbonate reservoirs shows promising potential. However, the impact of saltwater on the interactions between CO2 and oil remains unclear. In this paper, the multi-component dynamic mass transfer experiments of the CO2–oil–saltwater three-phases system were conducted by using the research method of pressure-volume-temperature analyzer, gas chromatography and high-resolution microscope. The influence of oil–water ratio and salinity on the component exchange law between oil and gas miscible multilayer transition zones is explored. The influence mechanism of saltwater on mass transfer between CO2 and oil is revealed. The results show that the ability of oil to dissolve CO2, the degree of oil expansion and gas injection viscosity reduction under bubble point pressure decrease with the increase in water content under constant total volume oil and water. Minimum miscible pressure (MMP) is increased due to the increase in water content. The extraction and mass transfer capacity of CO2 is reduced. Conversely, under a constant oil–water ratio, the ability of oil to dissolve CO2, the degree of oil expansion and gas injection viscosity reduction under bubble point pressure are enhanced with the increase in salinity. MMP is reduced due to the increase in salinity. The ability of CO2 extraction and mass transfer is enhanced. The mechanism of saltwater affecting the mass transfer of CO2–oil includes water resistance, CO2 consumption, and space competition between inorganic salt ions and CO2 molecules. The above research provides theoretical guidance for optimizing injection and production parameters of seawater alternating CO2 miscible flooding to improve oil recovery.

papers.title: Flow characteristics of a rear-wall-expansion cavity flameholder in an augmented/ramjet combustor
papers.abstract: A reliable pilot-flameholder in an augmented/ramjet combustor is extremely important for the continued extension of flight envelope. The application of the rear-wall-expansion cavity as a central pilot-flameholder is proposed to meet more challenges. The rear-wall-expansion cavity combines the advantages of large total pressure recovery coefficient of the step and long residence time of the conventional cavity. To fully understand the flow behavior of the rear-wall-expansion cavity flameholder, the effects of the inlet condition and structural parameters on the flow characteristics of the central flameholders (including the step, rear–wall–expansion cavity, and conventional cavity) are investigated comprehensively via numerical simulation. Results show that different structural parameters have different effects on the flow characteristics of the flameholders. The same structural parameter has different effects on the flow characteristics of different flameholders. Particularly, the forward diffusion angle and length-to-height ratio are significant structural parameters that make it difficult to predict the flow characteristics. Additionally, results of the orthogonal experimental design for flow and structure are summarized. According to different flow characteristics, the priority of structural parameters, which should be considered, is obviously different. Furthermore, as a transitional configuration between the step and the conventional cavity, the rear-wall-expansion cavity has the smallest change rate of the flow characteristics at 50–200 m/s. Hence, the rear-wall-expansion cavity flameholder has more stable flow performance over a wide speed range.

papers.title: Directed autonomous motion of active Janus particles induced by wall–particle alignment interactions
papers.abstract: We propose a highly efficient mechanism to rectify the motion of active particles by exploiting particle–wall alignment interactions. Through numerical simulations of active particles' dynamics in a narrow channel, we demonstrate that a slight difference in alignment strength between the top and bottom walls or a small gravitational drag suffices to break upside-down symmetry, leading to rectifying the motion of chiral active particles with over 60% efficiency. In contrast, for achiral swimmers to achieve rectified motion using this protocol, an unbiased fluid flow is necessary that can induce orbiting motion in the particle's dynamics. Thus, an achiral particle subject to Couette flow exhibits spontaneous directed motion due to an upside-down asymmetry in particle–wall alignment interaction. The rectification effects caused by the alignment we report are robust against variations in self-propulsion properties, particle's chirality, and the most stable orientation of self-propulsion velocities relative to the walls. Our findings provide key insights into the controlled transport of active matter and demonstrate a novel strategy for sorting both artificial microswimmers and natural biological species—such as bacteria and sperm cells—based on their intrinsic chirality and self-propulsion velocities.

papers.title: The interfering flow-induced vibration (FIV) characteristics of three unequal-diameter flexible risers in right-triangle arrangement
papers.abstract: Because of hydrodynamic interference among risers, riser bundles exhibit more complex flow-induced vibration (FIV) than single riser. This study experimentally investigates the FIV characteristics of three flexible risers with unequal diameters in right-triangle arrangement under uniform flow. The larger-diameter riser (LR) is placed tandem to smaller-diameter riser 1 (SR1) and side-by-side with smaller-diameter riser 2 (SR2). Within Reynolds number (Re) ranges of 2832−11 328 (LR) and 1805−7220 (SR1/SR2), the FIV response characteristics of riser models in the cross-flow (CF) and in-line (IL) directions are further analyzed using modal superposition and fatigue damage estimation methods. The strain and displacement of SR2 exhibit significant amplitude amplification in the CF direction due to the proximity interference from LR and SR1, leading to substantially increased fatigue damage in prototype riser. In the tandem pair of LR and SR1, frequency capture of SR1 by LR is observed, along with reduced mean drag displacement and increased vibration amplitudes in both CF and IL directions. Additionally, higher pretension reduces CF vibration amplitudes, further affecting fatigue damage.

papers.title: Characterization of centrifugal compressor vaneless diffuser performance and stability using high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics
papers.abstract: Turbocharging technology has become indispensable in modern internal combustion engines, enabling greater power density and contributing to emission reductions. As a critical component of a turbocharger, the centrifugal compressor directly influences overall system performance. Within centrifugal compressors, the vaneless diffuser plays a pivotal role in determining both performance and stability, especially near surge limit conditions. Using a validated, high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model, this paper investigates the impact of hub side recess sizes on diffuser performance and stability. By comparing diffuser performance parameters and performing flow field visualization, such as dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) techniques, it was revealed that the enlarged diffuser recess caused the absolute flow angle on the hub side to become more radial by dampening the impeller discharge flow. This modification significantly mitigated flow separation losses on the hub side in the vicinity of the diffuser exit region. Further analysis of circumferentially averaged absolute flow angle distributions under surge limit conditions, across different speedlines for various geometry configurations, confirmed the occurrence of diffuser-dominated instability at high rotational speeds. Additionally, a novel non-uniformity parameter, ϡ, was introduced to effectively quantify the influence of circumferential and axial non-uniformity of the flow. Incorporating both the limiting flow angle and the non-uniformity parameter, the results further support the authors' previous inference that the diffuser became the dominant component governing compressor stage stability at high rotational speeds. This study provides insights into centrifugal compressor stage stability, with the methods developed to characterize diffuser stability offering guidance for diffuser design optimization.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic performance study of a self-propelled manta-like vehicle employing non-sinusoidal flapping
papers.abstract: To fill the gap in the research on the self-propelled swimming process of underwater bionic vehicles with non-sinusoidal flapping, this study established non-sinusoidal flapping equations for the vehicle, and a deformation-kinematic coupling code was developed based on a user-defined function in the computational fluid dynamics software FLUENT. A two-degree-of-freedom self-propelled numerical strategy has been developed, and the effects of non-sinusoidal flapping on the kinematic characteristics, hydrodynamic performance, and vortex evolution mechanisms of bionic vehicles, along with their underlying mechanisms, have been revealed. The following conclusions are drawn: Compared to sinusoidal flapping, square-wave flapping significantly increases peak thrust, enhancing the vehicle's maneuverability. When the non-sinusoidal parameter K = 1.3, the peak thrust increases by up to 99.3%. The sawtooth wave flapping enhances the vehicle's cruise efficiency. When K = −0.9, the cruising efficiency increases by 9.3%. The flapping waveform dominates thrust discrepancy by influencing the intensity and distribution of the shear layers. As swimming velocity increases, this mechanism gradually shifts to a combined effect of the flapping waveform and swimming velocity acting on the evolution of the leading-edge vortex, thereby affecting thrust. The discrepancy in energy dissipation power generated by flapping waveforms is also influenced by swimming velocity, shifting from a combined influence of the fin-tip vortex (TV) and trailing-edge vortex to the dominance of the TV. The above findings reveal the fluid mechanisms underlying non-sinusoidal flapping in vehicles and provide a reference for developing vehicle control strategies.

papers.title: Simulation of nonstationary longitudinal wind fields using adaptive and improved two-dimensional Hermite time–frequency interpolation
papers.abstract: The wind fields in extreme wind areas have highly nonstationary characteristics, so the accurate simulation of nonstationary wind fields is a fundamental concern in the buffeting analysis of large-span bridges in these areas. Due to the time-varying coherence, classical spectral representation method (SRM) needs for extensive Cholesky decomposition and harmonic superposition. To improve efficiency, interpolation schemes are introduced into the decomposition, and time–frequency decoupling methods are employed to apply the fast Fourier transform. However, the frequency and time interpolation node distribution schemes are complicated and lack adaptive ability. Meanwhile, the traditional two-dimensional (2D) time–frequency interpolation method is less efficient. Therefore, new adaptive frequency and time interpolation-enhanced schemes and an improved 2D Hermite interpolation method are proposed in this study, aimed to improve the accuracy and efficiency of simulating nonstationary wind fields. The frequency interpolation scheme takes the wind spectrum derivative as an index and sets the interpolation node distribution adaptively. In addition, the time interpolation scheme sets time interpolation nodes based on the peak and trough locations in time-varying mean wind speed. Then, the improved 2D Hermite interpolation method is conducted to decrease the Cholesky decomposition and decouple the time–frequency spectrum, and time-domain basis functions in the same frequency-domain region are summed, to further reduce the computational effort of this interpolation method. Finally, the interpolation scheme and the proposed method are validated through parametric analysis and numerical examples to assess their accuracy and efficiency.

papers.title: Control of sliding droplet movement through electrowetting on dielectrics
papers.abstract: Through the electrowetting on dielectric effect, we attempted to control the movement of a droplet sliding on an inclined plate owing to gravity. The electrode boundary of the substrate was deflected from the in-plane gravitational direction, and the behavior of a droplet sliding on the substrate was investigated. The maximum volume that could slide along the electrode boundary was obtained theoretically from the force balance between the surface tension acting on the contact line and the gravitational force. The calculated results were in good agreement with the experimental results. For the substrate manufactured in this experiment, a maximum deflection angle of 55° was obtained for a 28 μL droplet. We created a device to sort the volume of droplets from different sliding paths depending on each volume. By installing electrode boundaries with different inclinations on the substrate, it was confirmed that the droplets actually slid in different paths and were classified in a predetermined position according to their volumes.

papers.title: Vorticity shedding and acoustic resonance excitation in a tube array with different compactness
papers.abstract: This study experimentally investigates the mechanism of flow-excited acoustic resonance in an inline tube array, with emphasis on the effect of the number of tubes in the transverse and streamwise directions on triggering and sustaining acoustic resonance. The results show that the number of tubes in the transverse direction makes the tube array more susceptible to acoustic resonance excitation. While the number of tube rows in the streamwise direction contributes to the development of distinct flow structures, a minimum requirement of four tube rows to reproduce the aeroacoustic behavior expected in a full tube array configuration. Particle image velocimetry measurements using both phase-locked and modal decomposition techniques reveal intrinsic flow structures, dominated by low and high frequencies flow periodicities, and how they are influenced by the excitation of different acoustic cross-modes. Under off-resonance conditions, a dominant jet-like flow develops between the tube lanes, characterized by a symmetric vortex structure about the jet centerline. When resonance is excited by the higher-frequency periodicity, a co-shedding flow pattern emerges, sustaining organized jet flow. In contrast, excitation by the lower-frequency periodicity results in a quasi-single-body shedding pattern that suppresses jet formation. The results presented in this paper show clear evidence of the critical role that acoustic particle velocity plays in organizing the vorticity shedding in the tube array with respect to the excited acoustic cross-modes. These insights provide the foundation for implementing effective control strategies to mitigate flow-excited acoustic resonance in tube arrays.

papers.title: Electro-osmotic creeping physiological propulsion between uniform and non-uniform microtubes with transversely deflecting walls
papers.abstract: This work focuses on the mathematical modeling of a flow situation that arises from the interaction of two flow mechanisms, such as peristalsis and electro-osmosis, through an annular space between a non-uniform microtube (a physiological vessel) with non-zero wall surface roughness and a microtube (an artificially designed peristaltic endoscope) with uniform cross section and zero wall surface roughness. The authors have modeled the roughness of the outer microtube's wall as a sinusoidal structure to represent the roughness found in a physiological microtube. The flow setup is mathematically modeled using conservation laws like the continuity equation, Cauchy equations of motion, and the Poisson equation. To explore the kinematics of the present flow model, the governing equations are simplified by taking certain approximations, such as the Debye–Hückel approximations and lubrication approach, and obtained the axial velocity profile of the fluid flow and electric potential function. To ensure the correctness and reliability of the present model, the authors also provided a graphical validation. Furthermore, authors have plotted the illustrative figures to describe the effect of control parameters, including the Debye–Hückel parameter and Helmholtz–Smoluchowski velocity, non-uniformity and wall surface roughness of the outer microtube, radius ratio and peristalsis generating factor (occlusion), and fluid rheology (Jeffrey fluid parameter) on the hydrodynamic quantities. The findings reveal that a higher surface roughness parameter increases wall shear stress at the outer non-uniform microtube, reducing flow velocity, whereas electro-osmotic forces enhance fluid propulsion by overcoming flow resistance. Furthermore, increasing the non-uniformity of the outer microtube restricts both electric potential and wall shear stress at its wall, while simultaneously enhancing the profile of instantaneous flow rate and axial velocity. The results and insights of this research work may be beneficial in exploring the physiological propulsion of physiological fluids, such as urine, blood, cervical mucus, and embryos, as well as in designing and manufacturing microfluidic tools, advanced endoscopes, and bio-microfluidic devices.

papers.title: Full-range drift-flux model for upward two-phase flows in vertical rectangular channels
papers.abstract: Two-phase flow in rectangular channels is critical in thermal-fluid systems, necessitating accurate two-phase flow analysis for performance optimization. The drift-flux correlation, a key element in two-phase flow analysis, is often limited to specific flow regimes or channel geometries. This study developed a full-range drift-flux correlation for rectangular channels, covering the entire void fraction range from zero to unity. The critical area-averaged void fraction distinguishing between pure-dispersed and beyond-dispersed flows was analytically modeled by the assumed void fraction distributions. In the pure-dispersed flow, the experimentally determined distribution parameter correlation has been well accepted. This study developed a distribution parameter model from the pure-dispersed two-phase flow to the gas single-phase flow based on the approximated void fraction and mixture volumetric flux. In the pure-dispersed flow, the reliable drift velocity correlation was available. This study developed a model of the drift velocity from the pure-dispersed two-phase flow to the gas single-phase flow based on the momentum balance between the gas core and the liquid film. The model validation was conducted using 225 adiabatic and 332 boiling two-phase flow data sourced from 22 experimental studies. The developed full-range drift-flux correlation achieved a mean relative error of −2.18% and a mean absolute relative error of 11.9%, demonstrating robust predictive capability across all flow regimes, under a void fraction of 0.007 70–0.897, a superficial liquid velocity of 0–10.5 m/s, and a superficial gas velocity of 0.006 89–23.9 m/s. The correlation was applicable to rectangular channels with an aspect ratio (= channel gap divided by channel width) of 0.05–1.00.

papers.title: On the consistency of dynamic procedure in improved delayed detached-eddy simulation
papers.abstract: Dynamic procedures, typically motivated by scale-similarity concepts, have proven highly successful and are widely used in Large Eddy Simulation (LES) for determining model coefficients. However, in hybrid Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS)/LES approaches, excessively coarse grids can undermine scale-similarity-based dynamic procedures: the turbulence mode implied by the test filter scale may be inconsistent with that of the grid filter. In this study, we derive a consistent dynamic model (CDM) by minimizing dependence of stress on the turbulence-resolution length scale, thereby ensuring consistency between RANS and LES modes. The CDM is capable of recovering the standard dynamic model (SDM) in regions far from the wall, while smoothly transitioning to the RANS mode near the wall. A priori tests in homogeneous isotropic turbulence show that, as filter width increases, the SDM coefficient quickly decays toward zero, whereas the CDM remains consistent with Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS)-calibrated values, demonstrating broader applicability. A posteriori tests in turbulent channel flow confirm that the CDM avoids underprediction of CDES near the wall and accurately distinguishes between RANS and LES regions without additional wall treatments. Consequently, mean and fluctuating quantities predicted on coarse grids agree better with experimental data and scaling laws than those from LES and the SDM. In periodic hill simulations, the CDM also predicts separation and reattachment points closer to high-resolution LES, further validating its ability to capture separated flows on coarse grids.

papers.title: Effect of perturbation parameters on utilizable satellite droplet generated by Rayleigh instability
papers.abstract: Generating ultra-high frequency micro-droplets with smaller diameters by Rayleigh instability is valuable in the fields of material fabrication and semiconductor process. The traditional method of reducing the orifice diameter to generate smaller droplets faces severe challenges in high-quality manufacture of extremely small orifices. To address these challenges, a method of obtaining extremely small droplets under a large, easily manufactured orifice by utilizing satellite droplets was proposed. As a prerequisite to utilize satellite droplets, the perturbation effect on satellite droplet generation, motion characteristics, and size is investigated in this paper. First, the aspect ratio (λ) of the ligament, which is measured by extracting the potential neck contraction points, is proposed to identify satellite generation transition lines with switching dimensionless wavenumbers (k′). Second, we investigate the motion state of the satellites with fixed wavenumber and switching perturbation amplitude, which shows that there is an amplitude difference (ΔA) between the symmetric pinch-off of the ligament and the state of the stable satellites. By considering the velocity-corrected satellite droplet, we point out that the relationship between relative motion velocity and neck contraction point diameter is the basis for identifying the stable satellites. Finally, we explored the Fourier series expansion of jet surface waves to explain satellite droplet size variations, especially the stable satellites. It is pointed out that the fundamental wave and second-harmonic wave ratios mainly influence the size and generation regimes of the satellites. Our work can provide systematical guidance for utilizing satellite droplets generated by Rayleigh instability in various applications.

papers.title: A weakly compressible discontinuous Galerkin method for incompressible fluid flow and heat transfer problems
papers.abstract: The weakly compressible approach offers a promising alternative to traditional incompressible solvers by preserving a simplified hyperbolic structure, enabling explicit time integration, and avoiding the solution of the pressure Poisson equation. Motivated by these advantages, this study integrates the weakly compressible formulation within a high-order discontinuous Galerkin framework to simulate incompressible flow and heat transfer problems. An exact Riemann solver is derived to account for buoyancy effects under the Boussinesq approximation, ensuring stable and accurate treatment of thermally driven flows. In addition, consistent boundary conditions, including Riemann far-field, isothermal/adiabatic wall, is developed to accommodate a wide range of flow and heat transfer configurations. A series of benchmark tests, covering steady and unsteady, inviscid and viscous cases, as well as natural and forced convection problems, demonstrate the method's high-order accuracy, robustness, and agreement with reference solutions. The numerical results elucidate the correlation between the artificial sound speed c0 and the underlying physical parameters.

papers.title: Symmetry-based investigation of transport enhanced blood flow model
papers.abstract: To study the blood flow circulation dynamics, the present work thoroughly investigates the one-dimensional blood flow and transport in arteries and veins. We construct the one-dimensional optimum subalgebra and provide exact solutions of the governing equations using Lie symmetry analysis. A systematic framework is developed to generate a network of nonlocally related partial differential equation systems. These systems, constructed from local conservation laws and symmetry-based approaches, yield nonlocal symmetries that are classified and applied to obtain further exact solutions. One such solution is used to study the evolution of weak discontinuity waves. The findings shed light on blood circulation dynamics and suggest potential uses in hemodynamic modeling and analysis.

papers.title: Lattice Boltzmann model for transonic flows
papers.abstract: The hydrodynamic limit of a discrete kinetic equation is intrinsically connected with the symmetry of the lattices used in construction of a discrete velocity model. On mixed lattices composed of standard lattices the sixth-order (and higher) moment is often not isotropic and thus they are insufficient to ensure correct imposition of the hydrodynamic moments. This makes the task of developing lattice Boltzmann model for transonic flows quite challenging. We address this by decoupling the physical space lattice from the velocity space lattice to construct a lattice Boltzmann model with very high isotropy. The model operates fully on-lattice, achieves Mach 2 with only 81 discrete velocities, and generalizes the isothermal equilibrium distribution. We also present a number of realistic benchmark problems to show that the lattice Boltzmann model with a limited number of velocities is not only feasible for transonic flow but is also quite simple and efficient like its subsonic counterpart.

papers.title: Response of sediment cloud dynamics to initial discharge and ambient flow conditions
papers.abstract: When the bulk volume of dredged sediments is released into the water within a relatively short time, the sediment cloud exhibits complex diffusion and settling characteristics, which can negatively impact the water quality in the disposal area. In this study, the computational fluid dynamics-discrete element method coupling model and experiments were used to investigate the influence of particle size, inlet cross-sectional geometry, and cross-flow on sediment cloud behavior. The results reveal that the movement characteristics of the sediment cloud are sensitive to particle sizes prior to seafloor impingement, with sustained discharge developing a quasi-steady sediment-laden jet. The cross-sectional geometry of the inlet also significantly affects the plume center velocity, with the influence zone extending approximately ten times the equivalent diameter downstream. Specifically, non-circular inlets (square, triangular) induce flow asymmetry and enhance near-field fluid entrainment, while the coaxial annular inlet exhibits the smallest spread due to the shielding effect of the outer annular flow. The presence of cross-flow promotes lateral spreading. Among the different cross-sectional geometries tested, the coaxial annular inlet demonstrates the optimal cross-flow penetration depth (minimal deflection) due to its protective outer flow. The triangular inlet generates the largest lateral spread by enhancing mixing with the ambient fluid. While the spread of the square inlet is smaller than the triangular inlet, its final diffusion pattern under cross-flow converges toward that of the circular inlet.

papers.title: Dynamic stall of a pitching airfoil under reverse flow conditions
papers.abstract: This study experimentally investigates the dynamic stall of a pitching NACA 643418 airfoil under reverse flow conditions, whereby the geometric trailing edge is located upstream of the geometric leading edge. The investigation focuses on the correlation between surface pressure, aerodynamic forces, and the evolution of the dynamic stall vortex (DSV) and the aerodynamic trailing edge vortex (TEV). A range of mean angles of attack from 5° to 25°, pitching amplitudes from 5° to 15°, and reduced frequencies between 0.05 and 0.21 were tested on an airfoil using a combination of particle image velocimetry (PIV) and surface pressure measurements. The results reveal a distinct dynamic stall mechanism in reverse flow conditions: multiple flow separations occur during both the upstroke and downstroke periods, yet the DSV maintains partial attachment. While the outer layer of the DSV sheds into the flow, its inner core remains anchored and is subsequently reinforced by shear layer feeding. This sustained vorticity injection leads to periodic DSV re-growth, which manifests in the force hysteresis loop as multiple distinct peak regions. In addition, it is also found that the largest difference between conventional and reverse flow dynamic stall lies in the initial stage of the DSV development. For reverse flow dynamic stall cases, the initial flow separation near the leading edge causes a gradual decrease in the pressure coefficient. However, for conventional dynamic stall cases, the laminar separation bubbles that occur before the DSV cause the maximum suction on the airfoil surface.
