Specifically, a scaling factor (r) is introduced to proportionally adjust the third-stage isentropic compression surface, thereby establishing opposite-family interaction between the compression waves and the cowl shock. To validate this wave configuration methodology for hypersonic inlets, six inward-deflecting-cowl hypersonic inlets featuring geometrically distinct third-stage compression surfaces were designed through controlled variations of both compression method and scaling factor magnitude. Comprehensive numerical simulations characterized their aerodynamic performance and flowfield structures under design (Ma0 = 7.0) and off-design (Ma0 = 6.0, 6.5) conditions. The numerical results reveal that, compared with conventional shock-on-lip (SOL) configurations, the cowl shock progressively attenuates with increasing r, resulting in a remarkable reduction in the scale of the separation bubble induced by the cowl shock and a significant improvement in the total-pressure recovery coefficient. At the design condition, an increase in the scaling factor results in a 32.52%–53.36% enhancement in throat total-pressure recovery coefficient, an 18.55%–30.57% reduction in entropy rise, and a 18.33%–72.01% decrease in the bleeding ratio. The inlet also demonstrates significantly enhanced aerodynamic performance under off-design conditions. Specifically, the mass flow ratio increases notably: at Mach 6.5 and 6.0, it rises by 4.29%–4.70% and 7.25%–8.46%, respectively, compared to the SOL configuration. The consistency in flowfield structures and throat-section aerodynamic parameters between the three-dimensional and two-dimensional inlets further confirms the applicability of the wave-configuration method under three-dimensional conditions. An optimal scaling factor range of 1.50–1.75 is identified, which effectively balances the performance metrics, substantially improving total-pressure recovery coefficient and minimizing the bleeding ratio without significantly compromising the pressure ratio characteristics.

papers.title: Analysis of the tumbling dynamics of highly resolved polymer chains in shear flow with hydrodynamic interactions through Brownian dynamics simulations on graphics processing units
papers.abstract: Predictions of the scaling of chain end-over-end tumbling times in shear flow exist for long chains under dominant hydrodynamic interaction (HI) conditions. However, these have never been examined by simulations for highly resolved chains, to level of single Kuhn step. Brownian dynamics (BD) simulations of fairly long, highly detailed polymer chains, at the resolution of a single Kuhn step, remains computationally prohibitive even on the modern processors. This is especially true when the beads on the chain experience HI, which requires the usage of methods like Cholesky decomposition of large matrices at every time step. In this study, we perform BD simulations, with HI, of reasonably long and highly resolved polymer chains on modern graphics processing units (GPUs). First, we present the details of a highly scalable, parallel hybrid code implemented on a GPU for BD simulations of chains resolved to a single Kuhn step. In this hybrid code using compute unified device architecture (CU) and message passing interface (MPI), we have incorporated HI using the Cholesky decomposition method. Quite remarkably, our GPU implementation shows a scaling of ∼N1.2 and ∼N2.2 of the computational times for shorter and longer chains in the modern GPUs, respectively, which is significantly lower than the theoretically expected ∼N3. Furthermore, we use the BD simulations with HI using GPUs to validate predictions for chain tumbling times in shear flow. Our results clearly show the scalings of ratio of tumbling time and number of springs, N with respect to Wi are Wi−2/3 and Wi−3/4 with and without HI, respectively, for a long and highly resolved chain. However, equivalent bead-spring model fails to show any sensitivity to HI, thereby further showing the need of finely resolved models for rheological studies.

papers.title: Effect of electric field on the linear stability of an inclined oscillatory film flow
papers.abstract: The linear stability of a liquid film flowing down an oscillating inclined plane with an electric field acting normal to the plane is found for disturbances of arbitrary wavenumbers. Utilizing the long-wave perturbation method and Floquet theory, the analytical solutions of the time-dependent perturbation equations are solved. The asymptotic solution reveals that the Floquet exponent is independent of the wall-normal oscillation amplitude. The combined effects of the inclined angle, the electric field, and the oscillating amplitude on the stability of liquid film are described. Moreover, the physical mechanism of the destabilized effect of electric field in the long-wave regime is discussed briefly. For finite-wavelength instability, the time-dependent Floquet system is resolved numerically based on the Chebyshev spectral collocation. Both the effects of wall-normal oscillation and streamwise oscillation on the stability are considered. The results of wall-normal oscillation show that the presence of an electric field increases the critical amplitude and the cutoff wavenumber for the regions of subharmonic and harmonic instabilities, and the gravitational instability extends to larger wavenumbers. For the streamwise oscillation, a new island-like unstable region is observed in the contour of growth rate, leading to the breaking of the neutral curve. When considering the effect of electric field, the gravitational unstable region continuously expand to lower oscillation frequencies, and the stable region only exists within closed neutral curves. This demonstrates the destabilizing effect of electric field on oscillating liquid film.

papers.title: Numerical study of flow structure and aerodynamic noise characteristics of rectangular jets with different nozzle shapes at low Mach number
papers.abstract: This study numerically investigates the flow and aeroacoustic characteristics of rectangular jets with different nozzle geometries but with the same mass flow rate. Turbulence statistics in the near field are compared, and the influence of nozzle shape on jet dynamics and associated noise is assessed. The configurations analyzed include a planar nozzle and orifice-type nozzles with square, beveled, and filleted edges. The Reynolds number based on the nozzle height is 1.1×104 and the maximum Mach number is approximately 0.17. Flow fields are computed using Delayed Detached Eddy Simulation with the Spalart–Allmaras turbulence model, while far-field noise is obtained using Farrasat's 1A formulation from permeable integration surfaces. The numerical framework is validated against experimental data. Results demonstrate that square and beveled orifices induce the vena contraction effect by their sharp edges, resulting in higher exit velocities and elevated near-field turbulence. In contrast, planar and filleted nozzles exhibit weaker turbulence, delayed shear layer roll-up, and longer potential cores. The beveled orifice in particular exhibits pronounced tonal noise peaks at 4.3, 8.5, and 12.7 kHz in the turbulent velocity spectrum. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition identified dominant energetic modes near the potential core boundary where vortex roll-up and shear-layer interaction occur. The sharp-edged orifices produce overall sound pressure levels approximately 10 dB higher when integrating across the full frequency spectrum (including the tones) and 7 dB higher for the broadband component, compared to the planar and filleted nozzles. These findings underscore the trade-off between jet mixing and noise mitigation in nozzle design, offering insights for optimizing rectangular jets for engineering.

papers.title: Heat-flux-enhanced thermoelectric self-driven flow of liquid metal in an annular channel
papers.abstract: A temperature gradient across dissimilar metals can induce a thermoelectric effect, which in turn drives the flow of liquid metal under a magnetic field. In this study, a thermoelectric self-driven liquid metal flow was realized using gallium–indium–tin and constantan, achieving a maximum velocity of 0.2 m/s. The flow behavior was systematically investigated. In the weak magnetic field regime, the flow accelerates with increasing magnetic field strength and heat flux, and a pronounced near-bottom higher velocity forms at the bottom. In the strong magnetic field regime, however, the enhancement of induced current leads to dominant Lorentz damping, resulting in a more uniform velocity profile. The variation of average flow velocity with the Hartmann number (Ha) exhibits a single-peak behavior characterized by “enhancement at low fields and suppression at high fields,” revealing the dual role of the magnetic field. Heat flux consistently promotes the flow, with the maximum average flow rate showing a linear dependence on the temperature difference, while the optimal Hartmann number (Haopt) increases in a nonlinear manner. Finally, a segmented predictive model based on dimensionless heat flux, the thermoelectric number (Te), and the Ha was proposed, achieving a fitting accuracy of over 92%. This model effectively characterizes the velocity evolution governed by the competition between thermoelectric driving and magnetic damping. The present study not only elucidates the fundamental mechanisms of thermoelectric magnetohydrodynamic flow but also provides theoretical and experimental support for the application of liquid metals in energy storage and thermal management.

papers.title: Sparse-sensor reconstruction of oblique detonation-wave temperature fields using a diffusion-guided residual coordinate-attention U-shaped network
papers.abstract: Oblique detonation engines (ODEs) hold significant promise for hypersonic propulsion, where accurate sensing of the internal flow field is critical for achieving optimal performance. However, reconstructing the full flow field from sparse, incomplete, and irregular wall temperature measurements remains a formidable challenge. To address this, we propose the diffusion-guided residual coordinate-attention U-shaped network (DRC-UNet), which is designed to recover the global combustion chamber temperature field. DRC-UNet integrates three key components: a score-based diffusion model (SDM) for robust data completion, residual connections to enhance deep feature propagation, and coordinate attention for improved spatial localization. Using only 36 uniformly distributed wall-temperature sensors, DRC-UNet outperforms the baseline U-shaped network (U-Net) by improving the average structural similarity index measure (SSIM) from 0.95 to 0.99 and increasing the average peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) from 28.31 to 41.81 dB, while better recovering shock fronts. Furthermore, under extreme data sparsity—where only 12 randomly distributed wall sensors (approximately 2% of the total measurement points) are available—DRC-UNet still achieves high-fidelity reconstructions, maintaining a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) below 1.5%. In contrast, conventional end-to-end networks often struggle under such conditions, as they rely on fixed sensor layouts and require retraining to adapt to varying data sparsity. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a robust and generalizable solution for intelligent sensing, capable of accurately reconstructing complex flow fields from incomplete or irregular data. This study provides a foundation for advanced diagnostics and control in oblique detonation engines by enabling temperature field reconstruction from sparse sensors.

papers.title: Research on velocity distribution models in compound channels based on modified Tsallis entropy and Renyi entropy
papers.abstract: Accurately understanding the velocity distribution in compound channels is of great theoretical and engineering significance, as it enhances the calculation accuracy of hydraulic parameters, improves simulations of sediment transport, and supports ecological restoration projects. This study focuses on a compound channel with a deep main channel and symmetric two-layered floodplains. By incorporating the composite momentum thickness, eddy viscosity coefficient, and velocity inflection point into the Tsallis and Renyi entropy frameworks, an improved cumulative distribution function is derived. This model effectively captures the abrupt changes in the velocity profile resulting from the effects of secondary flows and shear layers. Furthermore, by analyzing the intrinsic relationship between the momentum thickness of the mixing layer and the flow characteristics, a quantitative correlation with the dimensionless hydraulic parameter (Fr/Dr) was established, thereby enhancing the model's overall capability to describe complex flow structures. Research results indicate that both entropy-based models demonstrate satisfactory performance in predicting the depth-averaged velocity within both the main channel and the floodplain. However, the modified Tsallis entropy model exhibits superior predictive accuracy and stability under high-velocity gradient conditions in the floodplain and during high-discharge scenarios. This study provides a novel theoretical approach for predicting flow velocity distributions in complex cross-sectional morphologies, and offers a scientific basis for hydraulic computations and comprehensive river regulation in practical engineering applications.

papers.title: Rotor–stator interaction and its induced noise suppression in a centrifugal pump with the staggered impeller
papers.abstract: The staggered impeller (SI) is an effective strategy for enhancing flow stability, improving energy efficiency, and suppressing pressure pulsations in double-suction pumps. In the present paper, SI in an end-suction centrifugal pump is proposed. Its effect on the acoustic signature is investigated using an acoustic analogy method combined with the broadband noise source model. The correlation between flow structures and acoustic responses is clarified by integrating the λ2 criterion and the Lamb vector analysis, thereby revealing the noise reduction mechanism associated with the SI design. These results demonstrate that, compared to the normal impeller, the SI leads to a significant reduction in acoustic power on the blade surfaces, particularly on the pressure side, while the contribution from quadrupole sources remains negligible. The staggered configuration exhibits a pronounced effect in suppressing low-frequency noise. The reductions in sound pressure level at the blade-passing frequency reach 21% at the pump inlet and 20.9% at the outlet. Across the entire frequency range, the average reduction in overall sound pressure level is 13.9%, with the most significant decrease observed in the intensity of the volute dipole. The internal flow analysis confirms that the periodic shedding of wake flow and its interaction with the tongue are the dominant excitation source of pump noise. The interaction between the wake shed from staggered blades not only improves the circumferential uniformity of velocity distribution at impeller outlet and weakens the shedding intensity of the wake flow, but also alters the pattern of rotor–stator interaction, ultimately achieving the effective suppression of flow-induced noise.

papers.title: Static freezing characteristics of saline droplets on flat substrates
papers.abstract: Sea spray icing remains a critical hazard jeopardizing the maritime safety of vessels. To advance the mechanistic understanding of sea spray icing at the microscale, this study experimentally investigates the morphological evolution during static freezing of individual saline droplets on flat substrates. Utilizing a custom-built droplet freezing platform coupled with high-speed videography, this work systematically investigates the effects of droplet salinity, volume, and substrate temperature on volume expansion, height evolution, and contact angle variation during static freezing of saline droplets. The experimental measurements elucidate parametric influences on freezing characteristics. The results demonstrate: (1) Compared to pure water, saline droplet solidification requires an additional ‘salt precipitation’ stage; (2) at substrate temperatures ≤−24 °C, eutectic reactions during freezing significantly influence volume expansion; (3) salinity dominates droplet height evolution, with post-freezing height variations remaining below 5.3% when altering droplet volume or substrate temperature at fixed salinity. In addition, based on the experimental data, this paper proposed an empirical relationship between the morphological changes of saline droplets and the droplet salinity, droplet volume, and substrate temperature. Therefore, this study can not only be applied to practical engineering predictions under specified conditions but also help deepen the understanding of the microscopic mechanisms of saline droplet freezing.

papers.title: Study on the mechanism and microstructural testing of acid-induced hydrothermal phase-change fluid fracturing
papers.abstract: Coalbed methane (CBM) has excellent prospects and value for extraction, and hydrothermal fracturing technology can produce a complex fracture network conducive to gas recovery. Hydrothermal treatment of coal dust specimens with different initial solutions was designed in this study, with slick water and fracturing fluid used as comparison group experiments, and microanalysis of the treated coal dust was carried out. The main research results were as follows: (1) The best pore expansion effect was achieved by using an acid solution as the hydrothermal initial fluid to treat the coal powder; the largest amount of minerals was removed, and the acidified hydrothermal treatment obtained the best CBM resolution effect. (2) The reason for mineral loss in coal was explained through the establishment of the acidified mineral dissolution model, and the concentration and diffusion rate of the acid solution affect the mineral decomposition effect. (3) The energy spectrum analysis reflects that the pore blockage was not only caused by mineral particles but also by coal particles, thus establishing the acid dissolution mineral model, which explains the principle of penetration enhancement by acidified hydrothermal impact. (4) The hydrothermal shock effect prompted the transformation of micropores into mesopores within coal, forming new flow pathways. This manifested as a systematic reduction in fractal dimension, revealing a synergistic enhancement of permeability alongside a diminishing complexity of the pore network.

papers.title: Microfluidic study on the pore scale displacement behaviors of CO2 and oil under miscible or immiscible conditions
papers.abstract: CO2 injection into reservoirs presents an effective method for achieving greenhouse gas sequestration while enhancing oil recovery. Pore scale CO2 displacement behavior is crucial for understanding the oil recovery enhancing mechanism. In this study, CO2 flooding experiments were carried out in a microfluidic chip under miscible or immiscible conditions to investigate the flow dynamics and oil distributions. Dynamic oil recovery efficiency was quantified, and the effects of pressure and temperature on residual oil morphology were analyzed. Experimental result demonstrates that the elevation of temperature and pressure significantly enhances the displacement efficiency. As the pressure and the temperature increased from 4.0 to 8.0 MPa and from 40 to 60 °C, the CO2 displacement efficiency increased from 31.81% to 88.32% and from 33.99% to 51.27%, respectively. Under immiscible conditions, CO2 tends to flow preferentially through larger pores, leading to pronounced gas channeling and low displacement sweep efficiency. Concurrently, the CO2 bubble is snapped off when it passes through narrow throats and is confined by capillary force. Upon reaching the minimum miscibility pressure, gas channeling is suppressed, and a stable piston-like displacement front develops, resulting in a higher sweep efficiency compared to immiscible conditions. It is also found that the residual oil cluster contributed dominantly to the oil recovery rate. As pressure increased from 4.0 to 6.0 MPa, the proportion of oil cluster decreased significantly from 49.7% to 20.3%.

papers.title: Calibration of a roughness function model for ship simulations in the transitionally rough regime
papers.abstract: In this paper, the impact of different equivalent sand-grain roughness sizes on the KRISO Container Ship (KCS) is quantitatively evaluated. Numerical uncertainty was assessed using the least squares method and the Grid Convergence Index. Subsequently, validation was performed against experimental data to demonstrate the accuracy of the simulations in reproducing hydrodynamic phenomena around the ship. Compared to previous studies, this research evaluates and analyzes a greater number of data points. The focus of this paper is on the transitional roughness regime to address the existing gap in prior research. Since ship coatings may fall within the transitional roughness regime, and given that previous calibrations have been primarily focused on the fully rough regime, lacking sufficient accuracy in the transitional range, this study performs renewed calibration based on a genetic algorithm to derive new, validated model coefficients specifically for the transitional regime. The newly calibrated model was then applied to the KCS and its predictions were compared against those of previous models to quantify improvements in the transitional roughness range.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of hydraulic lifting of multi-sized coarse particles in laterally vibrated pipe for deep-sea mining
papers.abstract: In deep-sea mining, the efficient and stable transportation of coarse particles in the vertical riser is a key technical challenge to ensure the safe operation of the system. Based on the coupled method of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and the discrete element method (DEM), this paper studies the transport behavior of multi-sized coarse particles under transverse vibration conditions and focuses on exploring the effects of the standard deviation of particle size distribution, vibration parameters, and feed concentration on the flow characteristics of solid–liquid two-phase flow. The results show that the pipe vibration induces the periodic transverse migration of particles, and at a specific phase, a near-wall aggregation layer is formed. The disturbed boundary layer structure leads to a directional difference in wall friction. As the standard deviation of the particle size distribution increased from 0 to 0.001, the average axial velocity fluctuation of the particle group was reduced by 35%, improving the stability of the transport system. However, it also leads to an increase in pressure drop and energy consumption. At low amplitudes and frequencies, it is more advantageous to use single-size particles for conveying. At high amplitudes and frequencies, the increased inertial force causes the particle group to gradually aggregate from the center of the pipe toward the wall. In addition, increasing the feeding concentration can enhance the conveying efficiency, but it will also exacerbate the risk of energy loss and equipment wear.

papers.title: Assessing the effects of viaduct configurations on traffic pollutant transport: A large-eddy simulation study comparing quasi-two-dimensional and three-dimensional urban canyons
papers.abstract: Viaducts are widely used across high-density urban environments. Although their influence on pollutant dispersion has been studied, the majority of studies use quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) street canyon models, with few directly comparing them to three-dimensional (3D) ones. This study explores these differences by conducting large-eddy simulations using both quasi-2D and 3D models to assess traffic pollutant dispersion in street canyons with urban viaduct configurations under perpendicular approaching wind. Four configurations are examined, including ground-level roads only, viaducts without noise barriers, and viaducts with bilateral noise barriers of 2 or 4 m in height. Five important parameters, including mean wind velocity, pollutant concentration, indoor personal intake fraction (PIF), vertical mass fluxes, and pollutant exchange velocity, are employed to evaluate the differences between quasi-2D and 3D models. The findings show that quasi-2D models with various viaduct configurations yield mean indoor PIF for buildings away from the road and overall street canyon pollutant concentrations comparable to those from 3D models. However, quasi-2D models with viaduct configurations tend to overestimate spatially averaged pollutant concentrations at pedestrian-level zones by up to 1.8 times and overestimate mean indoor PIF in near-road buildings by as much as 54.8% compared to the 3D cases with viaduct configurations being investigated. Moreover, 3D models with viaduct configurations exhibit better pollutant removal efficiency, with the dimensionless pollutant exchange velocity through the roof level up to 33.6% higher than in quasi-2D models.

papers.title: Investigation of sheet to cloud cavitation dynamics using modal decomposition
papers.abstract: The objective of this study is to apply modal decomposition methods to numerical simulations of sheet to cloud cavitation over a wedge. A homogeneous mixture model is employed, and the numerical method is first validated against experimental measurements, showing good agreement across a range of cavitation numbers. The simulations capture the two primary mechanisms known to destabilize the sheet cavity: the re-entrant jet mechanism and the condensation front mechanism. The results confirm that a homogeneous mixture model composed of incompressible liquid and vapor phases is adequate to capture the formation of a condensation front, suggesting that individual phase compressibility is not an essential condition for its formation. Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) are then used to analyze dominant flow structures within a single cavity shedding cycle. The modal analysis shows distinct spatial modes delineating the two instability routes. At relatively low cavitation numbers, the leading POD mode and DMD mode capture a wall-detached vapor structure that travels upstream as a condensation front, accompanied by pressure variations inside the partial cavity. At higher cavitation numbers, the dominant modes show a thin, wall-attached vapor structure that advances upstream as a re-entrant jet accompanied by pressure variations outside the partial cavity. The identification of these dominant spatial modes for each of the mechanisms presents an opportunity to design appropriate control strategies to modulate sheet to cloud cavitation transition at different cavitation numbers.

papers.title: Analysis of bubble distribution and energy gradient in impeller of multiphase pump
papers.abstract: To elucidate the mechanisms of bubble breakup, transport, and size evolution in gas–liquid two-phase flow within multiphase pumps, this study employs a numerical approach based on the population balance model to investigate the axial and radial distributions of gas volume fraction under various inlet gas volume fractions and flow rate condition. Flow instability and bubble breakup hotspots are analyzed using the energy gradient theory. Results show that, regardless of operating conditions, the volume fraction of small bubbles consistently increases along the spanwise direction, while medium and large bubbles gradually decrease, indicating a continuous breakup process from larger to smaller bubbles within the impeller passage. This radial gradient in bubble size evolution is identified as a fundamental characteristic of multiphase flow in such pumps. At impeller outlet section, the proportion of small bubbles consistently follows the pattern of 0.9Q > 1.0Q > 1.1Q, and this trend remains consistent across the entire gas volume fraction range. Furthermore, analysis based on the energy gradient reveals that bubble breakup primarily occurs near the blade leading edge, after which bubbles migrate toward flow-stable regions.

papers.title: Finite element and machine learning modeling of vortex-induced vibrations of the upstream cylinder in tandem configurations: Effects of wake interference and geometry
papers.abstract: Wake interference influence on the transverse vibrations of an elastically mounted upstream cylinder in tandem configurations is investigated using finite-element simulations and a data-driven surrogate model at Reynolds number Re=150 over a reduced-velocity range U*=3–20. Three cross sections are considered: square, circular, and diamond (square rotated by 45°), with streamwise spacing varied from Lx=3B–10B (or 3D–10D for the circular case). For the square cylinder, gaps Lx≤5B confine the interstitial shear layers, intensifying vortex shedding, strengthening fluid–structure energy transfer, and producing large-amplitude lock-in. Circular cylinders, with smoother separation, exhibit weaker sensitivity to spacing, whereas the diamond geometry shows intermediate behavior: synchronization dominates the lock-in response, but wake interference controls vibrations once synchronization is lost. To assess three-dimensional effects, simulations of the square-cylinder configuration at Re=1000 and U*=10 reveal that small gaps suppress spanwise instabilities, preserve wake coherence, and amplify oscillations. The results demonstrate that streamwise spacing systematically modulates upstream wake coherence, providing a mechanism to either enhance or mitigate vibrations in tandem arrangements.

papers.title: Improved delayed detached eddy simulation investigation of the effect of crosswind yaw angle and knuckle state on aerodynamic characteristics of a pantograph
papers.abstract: The expansion of high-speed rail networks into coastal regions, where monsoons and extreme crosswinds are frequent, poses a significant challenge. These winds can severely degrade the pantograph's flow field, leading to abrupt changes in aerodynamic forces. This can compromise the pantograph–catenary system's current collection quality and endanger train operational safety. However, most existing research has focused on conventional crosswind conditions. Consequently, a detailed understanding of the pantograph's aerodynamic characteristics and the evolution of its flow field under extreme crosswinds yaw angle is currently lacking. Using the improved delayed detached eddy simulation method, this paper systematically investigates the influence of varying extreme crosswinds yaw angles on the pantograph. The results indicate that the aerodynamic coefficients and the overall flow field of the pantograph components exhibit a complex variation with wind angle in both the knuckle-upstream and knuckle-downstream configurations. The influence of the operational state on the lift of individual components is significant, whereas its impact on drag is comparatively limited. Overall, the lift and lift-to-drag coefficients generally show a non-linear trend, characterized by an initial increase followed by a subsequent decrease. The aerodynamic forces on the pantograph components exhibit sharp non-linearities at yaw angles of 10°, 30°, and 50°. Specifically, at 30° and 50°, the flow fields are the most complex, and the aerodynamic characteristics are the most adverse. This is also the point where a synergistic increase in both lift and drag is triggered. This study provides a detailed explanation of the unsteady aerodynamic flow field characteristics of the pantograph under extreme crosswinds and varying yaw angles. The findings provide theoretical support for the wind-resistant design optimization of pantographs and for enhancing the operational safety of high-speed trains under extreme weather conditions.

papers.title: Differential dissolution of multiple carbonate minerals: Impacts on pore network evolution and permeability
papers.abstract: A substantial body of research has been conducted to explore the multi-scale dynamic evolution and nonlinear coupling relationships from microstructure to macroscopic properties of carbonate rocks under reactive solute transport at the pore scale. However, these studies primarily focus on single-mineral systems, neglecting the influence of mineralogical diversity. This study examined the dissolution characteristics of calcite and dolomite under varying hydrodynamic conditions and introduced a pore-scale reaction transport model. The kinetic mechanism of mineral dissolution, microscopic pore network evolution and macroscopic seepage response were systematically analyzed. Results demonstrated that the calcite dissolution rate substantially exceeded that of dolomite, leading to heterogeneous features including discretized pore size distributions and distorted hydraulic pathways in a multi-mineral system. Low-velocity flow regimes shift the dissolution process from reaction-limited to mass-transfer-limited, further exacerbating dissolution unevenness and promoting the development of irregular pore geometries. By integrating pore-scale simulations with quantitative characterization of pore size distributions and pore shape parameters from natural carbonate rock samples, this study confirms the critical role of mineral composition and hydrodynamic conditions in governing the evolution of pore network heterogeneity. These heterogeneous features significantly impede fluid transport efficiency. Enhanced mineralogical complexity and reduced hydrodynamic conditions amplify the heterogeneity of pore structures during ongoing dissolution, consequently constraining the extent of permeability improvement. Furthermore, under low-velocity flow regimes, dissolution tends to concentrate in pore spaces that contribute less to permeability.

papers.title: A novel dynamic-modeling framework for assessing the hydrodynamic installation of dynamically installed anchors under combined ocean current and mooring line effects
papers.abstract: This study introduces a dynamic model analysis framework to simulate the hydrodynamic installation of dynamically installed anchors (DIAs) under the coupled effects of ocean current and operational mooring lines. The key innovations of this framework lie in its dynamic evaluation of the anchor's directional stability during descent and its integrated treatment of environmental and operational mooring loads. Unlike traditional static approaches, the proposed dynamic model updates the hydrodynamic forces, center of gravity, and applied moment of DIAs at each time step through a six-degree-of-freedom motion calculation module, thereby enabling continuous tracking of the restoration moment coefficient and instantaneous inclination angle. The MoorDyn library, based on the lumped-mass method, is applied to simulate mooring dynamics, and the overset grid technique is employed to facilitate the transfer of information related to fluid–structure interaction. The framework yields critical performance indicators, including directional stability, inclination angle, offset distance, impact velocity, and drag coefficient under the coupling influence of ocean currents and mooring lines. Validation cases confirm the model's robustness and reliability. The verified framework is subsequently applied to investigate the installation characteristics of torpedo- and plate-shaped dynamically installed anchors, with a specific focus on the impact of mooring line configurations and current-line coupling effects on the torpedo anchor performance. Results show that the mooring line reduces the falling velocity of the DIAs and increases their drag coefficient. Current action increases the inclination angle and offset distance of the DIAs, affecting their directional stability. The coupling effect between the two further exacerbates this adverse impact.

papers.title: An efficient, moments-based approximation for deviation propagators of recurrent flows
papers.abstract: A simple, data-assisted and physics-based approach for recurrent fluid dynamics is presented, and approximations for the application to macroscopic problems are developed. Large-step predictions are built upon sufficiently similar reference states in a precomputed database around which the Navier–Stokes equations are linearized. Hence, the deviation of any flow field from its nearest reference state obeys a linear propagator, and its evolution over a large time step can be calculated by the convolution with this propagator. An efficient, Gaussian approximation for these operators is constructed from their leading-order moments, which can be obtained along with the set of reference states with little overhead costs. The methodology is applied to two- and three-dimensional vortex shedding after a cylinder at Re = 200. Validation is carried out via a comparison of field time series, temporal means and variances, autocorrelation functions at selected locations, and global balances of momentum and kinetic energy. Results for cases with boundary conditions outside the reference set are of mostly (very) good accuracy, with speed-ups of about two orders of magnitude compared to classical computational fluid dynamics simulations. While the propagator simulations do not reach real-time capability for large-scale, three-dimensional flows, they might serve as a data augmentation method in connection with machine learning approaches.

papers.title: Tumbling time of rimmed disk in incompressible fluid
papers.abstract: We examined the impact of adding a rim to a disk on its sedimentation dynamics. In the limits of vanishingly small or very large rims, the behavior closely resembles that of a disk or rod, respectively. However, for intermediate rim heights, the dynamics undergo substantial changes. One particular configuration is energetically favorable, causing the system to spontaneously transition toward this state when released from an unstable position. The rotation time exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the rim to base height ratio, with configurations where the rim height equals the base width yielding the shortest rotation times. Our experimental findings were corroborated by simulations, which identified the presence of vortex structures, playing a critical role in the three dimensional rotation dynamics. To further substantiate these results, we developed a three-dimensional model describing the rotation of the vial within its self-generated vortex structures, demonstrating the same non-monotonic behavior.

papers.title: Understanding the role of sample preparation parameters on gelation of a colloidal dispersion
papers.abstract: Colloidal gels have been of interest for several years due to their central role in the design of products and technologies across pharmaceuticals to cosmetics, coatings, and advanced materials. Particularly, hydrophilic clay gels are widely studied owing to their tunable rheological properties and rich phase behavior. In this work, we perform a study on Laponite® (a synthetic clay) dispersion to investigate the underappreciated yet critical role of preparation protocols on gelation behavior of colloidal gels. We perform rheological experiments to monitor the effect of preparation parameters, such as drying, stirring time, stirring speed, stirring technique, salt purity, sample volume, and rheometer geometry on the gelation behavior of Laponite dispersion. The aqueous dispersion of Laponite unanimously exhibits all rheological signatures of sol–gel transition across multiple sample preparation protocols adopted in this study. The attractive gel microstructure is also confirmed by Small-Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS). Our findings indicate that variations in these preparation parameters lead to differences in the gelation behavior and are related to the surface and edge charge acquired by the particle upon dispersion in aqueous media. We also perform Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA), Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FE-SEM), and Powder X-Ray Diffractometer (PXRD) measurements to have insights into the thermal stability and particle-level architecture. The findings highlight the importance of preparation parameters in determining gelation behavior and provide a framework for improving the reproducibility of Laponite-based colloidal gels.

papers.title: Suppression of tower-wake-induced vibrations of suspenders through installing small-scale wind turbines on bridge towers
papers.abstract: Flexible suspenders of long-span suspension bridges are prone to wind-induced vibrations. Different from the vibration caused by the wake of the suspender itself, longer suspenders nearby the bridge tower may suffer from the tower-wake-induced vibration (TWIV). To suppress the TWIV of suspenders, this study attempts to improve the flow field around the bridge tower from a new perspective. After understanding the separated flow characteristics for bridge towers with different corners, a pair of small-scale vertical-axis wind turbines (VAWTs) was installed on the tower column considering different positions. The changes in separated flow characteristics were discussed. Subsequently, different tip speed ratios of the VAWTs were simulated, and the aerodynamic performance of nearby suspenders was studied. The results showed that the separated flow characteristics around the bridge tower are closely related to the corner shape. For the bridge tower with circular corners, the installation of VAWTs on the leeward corners effectively weakens the vortices shed from the tower column and improves the wake flow field. Thus, the fluctuation of aerodynamic forces of the nearby suspenders significantly decreases, reducing the possibility of TWIVs. On the other hand, the maximum power coefficient of the VAWTs in the tower wake is also increased.

papers.title: Effects of wind barriers on vortex-induced vibrations and vehicle aerodynamics of a steel Box–Truss girder
papers.abstract: The steel box–truss composite girder is a newly developed structural form characterized by high stiffness and small mid-span deflection, and it has been increasingly applied in long-span high-speed railway bridges. However, due to complex aerodynamic interactions between the truss members and the box girder, its aerodynamic performance remains difficult to evaluate. Wind barriers, commonly installed to improve train operational stability, further complicate the aerodynamic coupling within the train–bridge system. This study, based on a long-span steel box–truss cable-stayed bridge, conducted 1:47 scale wind tunnel tests to analyze the effects of wind barrier parameters (height and porosity) on train aerodynamic coefficients and the vortex-induced vibration (VIV) performance of the bridge girder. Results show that the girder exhibits good resistance to VIV without wind barriers, but noticeable VIV responses may occur after their installation. Wind barriers also significantly affect the aerodynamic forces acting on the train. At a fixed porosity, increasing the barrier height leads to a reduction in the overturning moment coefficient, while increasing the porosity causes a slight increase in the overturning moment. Adding vertical stabilizing plates to the girder's inclined webs or bottom plate effectively suppresses VIV. Increased porosity further reduces vibration amplitude. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations reveal that these measures help disrupt periodic vortex shedding at the girder's trailing edge, providing an effective VIV mitigation strategy.

papers.title: Shock-driven flow physics of Richtmyer–Meshkov instability in tandem light cylindrical interfaces
papers.abstract: The Richtmyer–Meshkov instability (RMI) arises when a shock wave impulsively accelerates a perturbed density interface, generating baroclinic vorticity and driving complex interface evolution. This study presents high-fidelity numerical simulations of shock-driven RMI in tandem light cylindrical interfaces, examining the influence of center-to-center spacing, shock Mach number, and interface size. An in-house high-order modal discontinuous Galerkin solver is employed to resolve multi-scale wave interactions, vortex dynamics, and deformation processes. The results show that reduced spacing strongly enhances instability growth, vorticity generation, and mixing through interfacial coupling, with baroclinic vorticity dominating at late times. Increasing Mach number amplifies both dilatational and baroclinic contributions, accelerating transition to small-scale turbulence. Interface-size variations not only reveal that larger radii strengthen initial vortex generation but also alter downstream response via shock focusing and flow deflection. Comparative analyses with single-interface cases confirm that multi-interface coupling sustains instability growth, modifies circulation dynamics, and enhances turbulent mixing. Furthermore, comparisons between tandem light- and heavy-gas configurations highlight reversed baroclinic vorticity deposition and distinct coupling pathways in light gases, leading to earlier turbulence onset and enhanced small-scale structures. These findings highlight tandem light-cylinder RMI as a distinct regime with implications for shock-driven mixing layers, supersonic combustion, and inertial confinement fusion.

papers.title: Determining aeration properties over vegetated embankments
papers.abstract: This study examines the air–water flow characteristics of overflowing vegetated embankments through laboratory experiments with submerged natural vegetation of varying heights (3–12 cm) on an 18° slope. Double-tip conductivity probe measurements at 50 kHz and high-speed imaging were used to determine aeration properties, the inception point of air entrainment, and vegetation-induced roughness and velocities. The results show that flow-induced vegetation deflection governs roughness, with taller vegetation reaching maximum deflection even at lower flow rates, while shorter vegetation bends progressively with increasing discharge. The resulting friction factor and roughness parameter decreased with decreasing bending ratios (hd/hi). Increasing vegetation height shifted the inception point upstream under lower flow rates and enhanced air entrainment deeper into the flow. Differences in air entrainment between vegetation heights, despite similar friction factors, were linked to observed swaying motions of the deflected vegetation blades, which intensified turbulence, bubble count frequency, and interfacial area. Bubble size distributions indicated larger bubbles near the inception point and progressive breakup downstream. Findings highlight the interplay between vegetation dynamics, roughness, and aeration, and suggest further investigation into turbulence and velocity profiles within the vegetated layer to better understand swaying and bending effects on air entrainment.

papers.title: Study on the coupling characteristics of flow and heat transfer in transcritical channel flows at low Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: In micro-scale cooling passages such as microchips, turbulent heat transfer must be achieved at low Reynolds numbers, and transcritical flows are particularly attractive because their drastic thermodynamic properties variations near the pseudo-critical point can trigger and sustain turbulence at these conditions. To quantify the pronounced sensitivity of thermodynamic properties to temperature variations, direct numerical simulation of supercritical channel flows at low Reynolds numbers was conducted to identify the dominant mechanisms. A comprehensive analysis has shown that turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) transport is governed by production, dissipation, and diffusion, with mean properties (density, viscosity) playing a dominant role in the production, dissipation term, and property fluctuations significantly influencing the diffusion term. Similarly, second-order momentum can be accurately scaled without accounting for fluctuating properties, an insight that drastically simplifies turbulence modeling for supercritical fluids where such properties fluctuations (density) are large. Crucially, density fluctuations are identified as the universal source of Reynolds stress generation, thereby pinpointing why the Morkovin hypothesis fails in transcritical flows. Budget analyses further reveal that pressure–strain redistribution dominates Reynolds-stress transport, while baroclinic torque governs vorticity dynamics, jointly dictating the turbulence anisotropy sustained by intense density gradients. Leveraging this finding, new scaling laws are derived for streamwise velocity, Reynolds stresses, and vorticity (the dominant component of TKE dissipation). The revised laws collapse the data across a wide range of wall-temperature differences, confirming their superior universality and predictive accuracy. These revised correlations improve the predictive accuracy for thermal performance in energy systems operating at transcritical conditions, providing critical insights for optimizing high-pressure fluid engineering applications.

papers.title: Activity gradient-induced crossflow filtration in a perivascular space
papers.abstract: In active fluids, the micro-structural elements convert the chemical energy into mechanical energy by activating their molecular motors to move their flagella (or pili). When the activity of the microorganisms decreases or increases, the overall fluid motion can develop without any external force. In this analytical study, we have investigated the transport characteristics in a micro-vasculature consisting of a core region filled with an active liquid, surrounded by a porous perivascular region filled with a non-active liquid, considering the decreasing activity of the microorganisms. We have obtained the velocity field and volume flow rate across the core layer and perivascular layer of fluids, considering the liquids in both regions as Newtonian, and they carry similar fluid properties. A creeping flow analysis is carried out for the core layer, and a Darcy model is employed for the porous outer layer. It has been observed that a significant amount of mass transport is occurring in the perivascular space due to activity gradient-induced core flow. Depending upon the porosity and sinusoidal behavior of the perivascular space, significant differences in the flow rate are observed. This study may have significant applications in biomedical engineering, including targeted drug delivery, thrombus removal, and real-time vascular diagnostics. The use of self-propelled micro-swimmers enables precise navigation in the blood flow, enhancing therapeutic efficacy with minimal invasiveness.

papers.title: Topology optimization for supercritical fluids in multi-reference frames
papers.abstract: Supercritical gases can be efficiently transported due to their high density and low viscosity; however, their modeling is typically based on tabulated thermodynamic data that are non-differentiable, making them unsuitable for gradient-based optimization. This research proposes a novel topology optimization framework tailored for compressible supercritical fluid flows. The framework combines a multiple reference frame formulation for steady-state treatment of rotor–stator interactions, a compressible adjoint-based optimization scheme enhanced with automatic differentiation, and a polynomial-based thermodynamic model valid over predefined ranges of temperature and pressure, thereby avoiding reliance on non-differentiable thermodynamic tables. This formulation enables efficient gradient computation while supporting multi-objective optimization, balancing competing factors such as energy dissipation and vorticity generation. The method is applied to the optimization of a rotor–stator device operating with supercritical carbon dioxide, and several tests are conducted to demonstrate the framework's ability to generate innovative geometries and adapt to varying operational conditions, including different flow rates and rotational speeds. The effect of volume fraction is characterized in the rotor–stator optimization, showing its sensitivity in influencing blade size. Furthermore, the results demonstrate how relying on the vorticity-based objective function introduces suitable modifications to the initial design, while the energy dissipation objective promotes the formation of connected blades that generate more efficient flow passages. This work establishes a computationally feasible and versatile approach for advancing the design of efficient supercritical fluid systems.

papers.title: Dynamic response of the self-propelled underwater vehicle interacting with internal solitary waves
papers.abstract: Internal solitary waves (ISWs) generate unsteady loads that pose significant risks to the safety of underwater vehicles. In this study, a numerical model for simulating the interaction between ISWs and an underwater vehicle is established based on the N–S equation combined with the shear stress transport k−ω turbulence model and initialization wave-making. By numerical simulation, the relationship between ISWs-vehicle of initial velocity and recovery stiffness, the planar trajectories and load characteristics of underwater vehicles encountering ISWs are investigated. The results show that at lower initial velocities, the underwater vehicle's trajectory is primarily waveform; as the initial velocity increases, it transitions to fluttering and finally to a diving trajectory. For a higher initial velocity condition, the lift loss of the vehicle with Δh*=0.05 is 2.98 times larger than that with Δh*=0.2. As dimensionless initial velocity u0*>1.47, the vehicle is in danger of “falling deep.”

papers.title: Unsteady flow characteristics in the double-tongue volute of an open-type pump based on modal decomposition
papers.abstract: The open-type pump represents a key technological innovation for achieving pipeline-free cleaning systems, however, the complexity of its internal flow dynamics remains incompletely elucidated. To reveal the unsteady flow characteristics within the double-tongue volute of an open-type pump, proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), and POD-based DMD methods were employed to analyze the evolution of vortex structures and pressure pulsations. The results reveal complex vortex structures featuring multiple frequency couplings within the double-tongue volute. All three model decomposition methods can effectively identify the spatiotemporal evolution characteristics of vortex structures. The dominant energy distribution is characterized by large-scale, alternating quasi-ordered structures at the volute inlet, associated with the blade-passing frequency. Under design condition, vortex shedding occurs at a frequency of 1.5 times the shaft rotational frequency. Under off-design conditions, a significant energy concentration is observed near the tongue, indicating that the energy loss in this region has a great impact on pump efficiency. In contrast, higher-order harmonic frequencies correspond to smaller-scale, alternating quasi-ordered structures that contribute to energy dissipation. The reconstructed flow fields based on the first 20 modes yield root mean square errors of 0.24% (POD), 0.37% (DMD), and 0.28% (POD-based DMD), demonstrating the feasibility of these methods for constructing surrogate models of the flow field and realizing optimization in the open-type pump.

papers.title: A divergence-free synthetic inflow turbulence generator for large eddy simulation of compressible turbulent boundary layers
papers.abstract: We propose the Compressible Discretizing and Synthesizing Random Flow Generation (C-DSRFG) method, a divergence-free inflow turbulence generator for large eddy simulations (LES) of compressible boundary layers. As an extension of the incompressible DSRFG framework by Huang et al. [“A general inflow turbulence generator for large eddy simulation,” J. Wind Eng. Ind. Aerodyn. 98(10), 600–617 (2010)], C-DSRFG explicitly enforces the divergence-free condition on velocity fluctuations (∇·u′=0), a constraint whose significance is theoretically analyzed herein and has been largely overlooked in conventional compressible inflow generators. Validation through LES of a supersonic (M∞=2.33) flat-plate turbulent boundary layer demonstrates that enforcing this condition reduces the required turbulence adjustment length by over 40% compared to its non-divergence-free counterpart. Furthermore, the method's robustness and applicability are confirmed through simulations of a weakly compressible (M∞=0.5) boundary layer and a typical engineering problem—a shock-wave/turbulent boundary-layer interaction on a compression ramp. For all cases, key turbulence statistics—including velocity fluctuations, mean velocity profiles, friction coefficient, and spectral distribution—are compared with available datasets. The results reveal a consistent agreement with properties established in the literature, which fully validates the proposed method's physical realizability and its applicability to complex compressible flow engineering scenarios.

papers.title: A front-tracking immersed boundary method for dynamics of three-dimensional capsules in multiphase flow systems involving viscoelastic fluids
papers.abstract: This paper presents a front-tracking immersed boundary method (IBM) for simulating the dynamics of three-dimensional capsules in multiphase viscoelastic flows. The approach couples the lattice Boltzmann method for solving fluid and constitutive equations with the finite element method for capsule membrane mechanics, while fluid–structure interaction and interface tracking are handled using the immersed boundary (IBM) and front-tracking (FTM) techniques, respectively. The solver is validated through several benchmark cases—including spherical and biconcave capsules in Newtonian shear flows, capsules in Newtonian/Oldroyd-B multiphase flows, and compound capsules in Newtonian shear—showing excellent agreement with existing numerical results. The method is further applied to investigate biconcave and compound capsules in Newtonian/Oldroyd-B multiphase shear flows. For biconcave capsules (modeling red blood cells), results show that internal viscoelasticity negligibly affects tumbling motion but significantly alters swinging dynamics, reducing deformation at moderate Weissenberg numbers while increasing it at high values. For compound capsules, the outer membrane exhibits non-monotonic deformation with increasing viscoelasticity, while the inner membrane shows monotonic reduction (low volume fraction) or minimal response (high volume fraction). This work establishes a robust numerical framework for studying capsule dynamics in viscoelastic multiphase environments and provides valuable benchmarks for biomedical and microfluidic applications.

papers.title: Aerodynamic characteristics of flow past tandem wing
papers.abstract: Numerical simulations are conducted to investigate the effects of tandem wing on vortex shedding, three-dimensional instabilities, and aerodynamic force coefficients at Re=1000. The angle of attack of the tail wing, denoted by αtw, is varied between 0° and 14°, whereas the main wing is fixed at αmw=14°. For a single wing, the wake transitions from a two-dimensional to a three-dimensional state via mode C instability, accompanied by hairpin vortices. The tandem configuration suppresses the formation of hairpin vortex structures, and the wake exhibits quasi-periodic and periodic three-dimensional modes with spanwise wavelengths nearly three times than that of mode C instability. The tandem configuration increases the frequency of streamwise vortex generation. Unlike a single wing, where each vortex shedding cycle produces a single streamwise vortex, pairs of streamwise vortices of opposite polarity are generated in tandem wing wake. The three-dimensionality becomes weaker with a decrease in αtw, yielding two-dimensional vortex shedding and a steady-state wake for αtw<2°. The lift and drag coefficients of the main wing remain fairly constant with αtw. The tail wing experiences reduction in the lift and drag due to the main wing wake. The tail wing exhibits a drag inversion phenomenon. The pressure and the suction on the tail wing undergo a reduction due to the wake interaction, and the maximum pressure is seen near the mid-chord region of the tail wing. A separation bubble is formed on the upper surface of the tail wing for αtw≥6°. The weak vortex shedding due to the tandem configuration causes a significant reduction in the unsteadiness.

papers.title: Evaluation of Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes models for simulating vortex-induced vibration in high Reynolds number flow
papers.abstract: This study considers the simulation of turbulent two-dimensional vortex-induced vibrations of a spring-mounted cylinder in cross-flow. It focuses on a Reynolds number range of 5×104–105, with spring stiffness 1200 N/m2 and damping coefficients from 28 to 50 Ns/m, for which experimental data are available. Three original outcomes are identified. First, the use of moving overset meshes to track the oscillating cylinder, reduces grid-size requirements and maintains high-quality near-wall resolution even at large oscillation amplitudes. Second, making the turbulent viscosity coefficient of the k−ε model sensitive to the strain rate invariant results in the correct predictions of vibration amplitude and frequency over the available dataset, thus offering a cost-effective approach. Finally, further simulations decouple the effects of the Reynolds number from those of a previously overlooked dimensionless parameter involving the spring constant, and reveal that this second dimensionless parameter exerts a far stronger influence on fluid velocity and flow-induced vibrations than the Reynolds number.

papers.title: Tribo-dynamic modeling of main shaft journal bearings in wind turbines for improved startup and reduced friction wear
papers.abstract: As wind turbine capacities increase, sliding bearings have been increasingly adopted for their cost-effectiveness and reliability. However, unsteady rotational speeds and complex main shaft motions under transient wind conditions often lead to inadequate lubrication and edge wear, thereby increasing the risk of bearing failure. Existing simulation models fail to simultaneously capture the multi-degree-of-freedom (DOF) dynamics of the main shaft, the tribological characteristics at the bearing interfaces, and the interactive effects among multiple bearings, thereby limiting a comprehensive understanding of the friction and wear mechanisms. To address this, a coupled tribo-dynamic framework for multi-bearing main shaft systems is developed, which fully accounts for the 6-DOF dynamics of the main shaft and the mixed elastohydrodynamic lubrication behavior of segmented bearing pads. Numerical results show that stochastic wind loads induce slow shaft rotation and significant tilting, which aggravate lubrication degradation. Increasing oil supply pressure improves lubrication performance and shaft acceleration, while appropriate pad-edge modifications mitigate localized contact, thereby reducing friction and wear. The proposed approach provides a systematic tool for evaluating friction- and wear-related risks and offers design guidelines to enhance the reliability of large-scale wind turbine bearings.

papers.title: Hydraulic jumps influenced airflow in a partially filled circular pipe
papers.abstract: A hydraulic jump is one of the most common hydraulic features in open channel flow, inducing extra turbulence. The generation and release of hazardous gases, such as H2S and CH4, can be largely affected by the air movement induced by hydraulic jumps, posing corrosion and health risks in urban drainage systems. Despite extensive research on hydraulic jumps in open channels, gaps persist in understanding air–water interactions in partially filled circular pipes. This study experimentally examines the characteristics of hydraulic jumps and the associated air motion in a partially filled pipe. Experiments were performed in a 0.3 m diameter pipe, with water flow rates ranging from 8 to 21 l/s. Air flowrates and air pressure gradients along the pipe were measured to quantify relative air demand, drag coefficients, and momentum transfer. These results show that the relative air demand β, defined as a ratio of air to water flow rate, increases with the Froude number (Fr) of water flow, especially for Fr < 2, reaching 0.015–0.058 under partially filled conditions, substantially higher than that one for downstream full pipe flow cases. Across the hydraulic jump region, pressure gradients are 20%–80% greater than the ones at upstream or downstream sections, driven by rapid momentum flux changes and intensified turbulent dissipation. Drag forces and pressure gradients are identified as the dominant drivers of air motion, while wall friction is negligible. Drag coefficients decrease with increasing Fr. These findings improve the understanding of air–water interactions in partially filled circular pipes.

papers.title: Analysis of flow field characteristics of pseudoplastic fluid mixing based on lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: Pseudoplastic fluid mixing is essential for homogenization in chemical industrial processes. This study validates a lattice Boltzmann method program and investigates the effects of impeller speed and rheological parameters on mixing flow fields. Results indicate that the consistency coefficient has limited influence, mainly confined to high-shear zones near the impeller. In contrast, reducing the flow index from 0.52 to 0.10 induces significant spatial heterogeneity: shear rate and velocity increase by up to 1.7 times and 0.035 times near the impeller, but decrease by 0.90 and 0.75 times in far-field regions, respectively. Increasing the initial yield stress markedly reduces the active mixing volume by 29.6%, severely impairing efficiency. While higher rotational speed enhances mixing via shear thinning, its effect saturates beyond a critical point. Similarly, in Newtonian fluids, flow stabilizes beyond a critical Reynolds number of 80. This study establishes quantitative relationships among rheological parameters, operational conditions, and mixing efficiency, providing a theoretical basis for process optimization.

papers.title: Numerical study on the steady self-diffusiophoresis of a spherical Janus particle in a Brinkman medium
papers.abstract: The locomotion of a self-diffusiophoretic Janus particle in a complex medium is crucial for biomedical applications. In this work, the self-propulsion of a spherical Janus particle in a Brinkman medium is studied by developing a coupled mathematical model integrating solute diffusion with Brinkman flow equations. Notably, the law of the particle's self-diffusiophoretic speed, power dissipation, and swimming efficiency are investigated with the surface coverage and swimming resistance. Numerical results show that the distribution of propulsion speed is symmetric regarding the surface coverage, and the relative propulsion speed is independent of surface coverage. The relative power dissipation is increased significantly with swimming resistance when the swimming resistance exceeds a critical value. Additionally, swimming efficiency demonstrates non-monotonic behavior with variations of resistance. Our numerical results may further guide the design of synthetic active particles capable of efficient operation within complex physiological environments.

papers.title: Analysis of sub-atmospheric pressure effects on flow characteristics of a twin-stage swirler combustor
papers.abstract: Understanding of flow characteristics of combustor under sub-atmospheric conditions is critical for plateau ignition and high-altitude relight of aero-engine. In this study, the impacts of sub-atmospheric operating pressure pop on flow characteristics of a twin-stage swirler combustor have been experimentally and numerically investigated. Specifically, two reference velocities Vref, i.e., 3.0 and 5.5 m/s, are considered. The sub-atmospheric pop ranges from 0.08 to 0.02 MPa, while the pop of 0.11 MPa represents an atmospheric condition. Results show that as the pop decreases from the atmospheric pressure to sub-atmospheric ones, there exist two flow patterns, i.e., Y- and V-type. The critical pressure of their transition is associated with the Vref. A higher Vref has a lower critical pressure, indicating its higher capacity to withstand the sub-atmospheric pressure effect. A non-linear map between the radial pressure difference across the second stage swirler airflow and the pop is observed, except in the region near the swirler exit. The flow pattern transforming from Y-type to V-type leads to an expansion of the central toroidal recirculation zone and an increase in the reflux ratio. Further, the simplified force balance analysis by reductio for swirl flow shows that both the centrifugal and pressure differential forces should reduce linearly as decreasing the pop, but the pressure differential force actually decreases non-linearly and more rapidly than the centrifugal force when the pop approaches some certain value. Consequently, the swirl flow expands radially outward for force balances, accounting for the transition of the flow pattern from Y-type to V-type.

papers.title: Extreme water hammer pressure of spiral case in hydropower station with super long headrace tunnel and surge tank during load rejection: Mechanism analysis and improvement measures
papers.abstract: The hydropower station with superlong headrace tunnel (HSSLHT) is a key form of hydropower development. However, HSSLHTs exhibit substantial water flow inertia and large surge wave amplitudes, which make the transient characteristics different from those of conventional short headrace tunnel hydropower stations. Therefore, the conventional water hammer pressure reduction measures for short headrace tunnel hydropower stations cannot be fully applicable to HSSLHTs. This study aims to clarify the mechanism responsible for the maximum spiral case pressure (SCP) in HSSLHTs and to propose corresponding improvement measures. The mathematical model of the HSSLHT is first developed using the method of characteristics and validated through prototype testing. Subsequently, the “double-peak” characteristic of SCP fluctuations is revealed, where the maximum SCP occurs at either the first or second peak. Finally, engineering measures are proposed to mitigate the maximum SCP. Results indicate that the first peak of the SCP occurs earlier, arising from water hammer pressure induced by the rapid closure of the guide vane, while the second peak of the SCP occurs later, coinciding with peak surge in the surge tank resulting from water level oscillations. The first peak can be reduced by enlarging the surge tank shaft diameter, increasing the impedance orifice diameter, extending guide vane closure time, and reducing the headrace tunnel diameter. The second peak can be reduced by enlarging the surge tank shaft diameter and decreasing the impedance orifice diameter. Overall, these findings provide guidance for engineering design and operational safety of HSSLHTs.

papers.title: The along-flow-path dynamic adsorption behavior of polymers on mineral surfaces with different roughness
papers.abstract: During enhanced oil recovery, polymer adsorption onto reservoir surfaces reduces displacement efficiency and can cause formation damage. To address this, we combined core flooding experiments on natural clay-rich cores from the Daqing P Block with molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the adsorption behavior of four polyacrylamide-based polymers: polyacrylamide (PAM), neutralized polyacrylamide (NPAM), hydrolyzed polyacrylamide (HPAM), and sulfonated polyacrylamide (SPAM). Experiments showed that HPAM and SPAM exhibit weak adsorption, whereas PAM and NPAM are strongly retained. Simulations reveal that this contrast arises from differences in polymer charge and surface interactions. HPAM adsorption decreases with increasing surface roughness due to enhanced electrostatic repulsion from negatively charged clay surfaces. In contrast, PAM and NPAM adsorb more readily on rougher surfaces, where cavities and hydroxyl groups promote anchoring via van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonding—NPAM shows the strongest response owing to its higher polarity. SPAM displays only a marginal increase in adsorption at high roughness, likely due to limited mechanical trapping in deep pores. Overall, polymer adsorption is governed by electrostatics, chain polarity, surface chemistry, and surface topography.

papers.title: Theoretical analysis of frequency shift on resonant interaction induced by steady free-surface flow over rippled bottoms
papers.abstract: We theoretically investigate the resonant frequency shift behaviors on triad resonance induced by steady free-surface flow over rippled bottoms. This triad resonance involves two free-surface propagating wave components and one bottom fixed topographic profile wave component. The perturbation analysis of the boundary value problems for free-surface steady uniform flow over a finite rippled patch is applied in this study up to the third order by substituting the perturbation expansion series of the frequency term. Then, we derive the high-order terms in the frequency expansion series quantitatively by considering the third-order nonlinear inhomogeneous forcing terms from both free-surface and bottom boundary conditions. For the theoretical frequency shift solution obtained in this study, we compare it with flume experiment results of one representative triad resonant phenomenon, which is induced by a specific triad resonant combination (k1−k2=kb) and also known as upstream-propagating waves. Within the generation parameters (Fr and kbh) domain of upstream-propagating waves, the theoretical solutions reveal that both the resonant frequency upshift and downshift exist, and the free-surface nonlinearity is the dominant factor of the frequency shift terms. This work will provide the theoretical references for the complex free-surface resonant interaction above a rippled patch in ambient flow.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of combustion pattern formation in cavity-stabilized supersonic flows
papers.abstract: Scramjet engines utilize cavity-based stabilization mechanisms to maintain combustion within millisecond-scale residence times under extreme flow conditions. However, the interaction between complex physical processes within the system frequently drives the system into combustion instabilities, thereby reducing performance and threatening structural integrity. This study experimentally investigates the formation of combustion patterns in a cavity-stabilized supersonic combustor. Through high-speed pressure and CH* measurements, we identify distinct combustion states as the global equivalence ratio (Φ) increases: aperiodic oscillation at low Φ (0.3), intermittent oscillation at intermediate Φ (0.6), and synchronized periodic oscillation at high Φ (0.9). Cross wavelet transform reveals distinct transient phase coherence between pressure and heat release rate, while convergent cross mapping establishes causal relationships, confirming bidirectional causality at high Φ. High-speed flame imaging visually corroborates the transition from aperiodic to synchronized combustion via the intermittent state. The dynamics are interpreted via the Kuramoto model, which successfully characterized the intermittent synchronization behavior phenomenologically, illustrating that the supersonic combustion in scramjets constitutes a multi-oscillator system. Similar transition patterns have been reported in subsonic combustors, suggesting potentially universal synchronization mechanisms.

papers.title: A new perspective on nonlinear flow evolution: The inference of the ideal curve and the establishment of the process hydraulic aperture
papers.abstract: Nonlinear flow in rock fractures is often described by the Forchheimer equation; however, there are still flaws and contradictions in the understanding of the Forchheimer equation and nonlinear evolution mechanisms, such as differing interpretations of various hydraulic apertures and the factors affecting the linear and nonlinear coefficients. This study utilizes wavelet analysis filtering and reconstruction techniques to investigate the impact of roughness at different scales on nonlinear seepage. It further provides new insights into the Forchheimer equation and hydraulic aperture by introducing the concepts of the ideal curve, the ideal Reynolds number, and process hydraulic aperture, along with the proposed criteria for determining them. A new mathematical model, incorporating geometric characteristics and Reynolds number effects, is developed and validated, effectively describing hydraulic aperture variations during nonlinear flow. The findings clarify the evolution of hydraulic aperture and flow coefficients, resolve previous contradictions, and advance understanding of nonlinear seepage mechanisms.

papers.title: Research on the three-dimensional turbulent jet mechanism and refined characteristic parameters of the deflector jet hydraulic amplifier
papers.abstract: The structure of the deflector jet hydraulic amplifier is intricate and involves various dimensional size factors. The internal flow field undergoes intricate physical processes with multiple energy conversion stages, leading to insufficient research on the mechanism of the internal flow field and its static characteristics. This paper considers boundary layer effects and momentum loss, proposing a calculation method where the isovelocity contours of the jet cross section exhibit an arch shape. The velocity distribution within the jet space is derived, and a three-dimensional nonlinear velocity diffusion model for the deflector jet hydraulic amplifier is established. Based on this, theoretical and numerical models of the static pressure characteristics of the receiver port are established, aiming to narrow the gap between conventional theory and actual system behavior. To verify the model, the pressure characteristics of the deflector jet hydraulic amplifier are evaluated through performance testing. The results show that the three-dimensional theoretical data are in good agreement with the experimental data, with a maximum deviation of 6%. The numerical simulation combining the Yang-Shih low-Reynolds number model and multiphase flow model exhibits a maximum deviation of 8% from experimental data. The two-dimensional theoretical model, which neglects momentum loss along the thickness direction, results in calculated values higher than those of the three-dimensional model, and exhibits a maximum deviation of 14% from experimental data. Additionally, this study employs theoretical and numerical methods to analyze the influence of refined characteristic parameters on pressure performance, providing theoretical and numerical guidance for servo valve design and performance improvement.

papers.title: Impact of personalized blood viscosity on left atrial thrombus formation: A computational fluid dynamics study
