papers.abstract: During an episode of atrial fibrillation, the effective contractile function of the left atrium (LA) is lost, increasing the risk of thrombus formation. Notably, blood, as a typical non-Newtonian fluid, exhibits pronounced shear-thinning behavior, a phenomenon that is particularly evident in the low shear rate flow environment within the left atrial appendage (LAA). However, the predictions of existing non-Newtonian blood models show considerable differences in the low shear rate range, which brings challenges to the accurate simulation of thrombus formation risk in patient-specific LAA. This study constructs a personalized blood model based on clinical data from different patients. Using the same LA geometry, the simulation results of the personalized model were compared with those of two general non-Newtonian models, the Carreau–Yasuda model and the Cross model. The differences in thrombus risk prediction were evaluated through non-Newtonian rheological properties, from the aspects of blood stasis and endothelial damage. The results indicate that general non-Newtonian blood models have significant limitations in the precise assessment of thrombotic risk in the LAA. Meanwhile, for the same LA model, as blood viscosity increases, both the risks of blood stasis and endothelial damage increase, resulting in a higher thrombotic risk. These findings demonstrate that patient-specific non-Newtonian blood properties are critically important in hemodynamic simulations and hold significant implications for advancing precision medicine.

papers.title: High-resolution analysis of hydraulic response characteristics of groundwater infiltration-defective stormwater pipeline-manholes in urban catchments using machine learning and fluid–structure coupling methods
papers.abstract: Current research focuses on isolated physical fields, neglecting systematic studies of hydraulic responses under multi-field coupling from groundwater infiltration and pipeline defects. This study integrates computational fluid dynamics (CFD), discrete element method (DEM), generalized adaptive smoothing method (GASM), improved genetic algorithm (IGA), global sensitivity analysis (GSA), Bayesian optimization (BO), convolutional long short-term memory (ConvLSTM), and dynamic temporal convolutional networks (DTCNs) to formulate GASM-ConvLSTM-DTCN, IGA-BO-GSA, and CFD-DEM based high-resolution numerical models to analyze combined effects of groundwater infiltration and hydraulic scouring in defective stormwater pipelines. First, GASM and CFD-DEM reconstructed the incomplete flow field. Key physical processes of the defected pipe-manhole system were then analyzed with a three-level (microscale, mesoscale, macroscale) feature extraction network. On this basis, spatiotemporal attention mechanisms and mass-momentum conservation gating techniques were introduced to effectively integrate multi-scale features and construct a GASM-ConvLSTM-TCN-based early warning model for manhole water-level prediction. To quantify the non-linear interactions between groundwater level and pipe inlet velocity on outflow dynamics, a hybrid fluid-structure coupling framework was developed based on IGA-BO-GSA. Numerical simulations and scaled-down experimental analyses indicate that the main effect index of the groundwater level (68.4%) was considerably higher than that of pipeline inlet velocity (49.7%). Furthermore, a non-linear interaction effect of 23.5% existed between groundwater level and pipeline inlet velocity. Nash efficiency coefficient of the manhole water-level early warning model remained stable within the range of [0.80, 0.84], demonstrating a reduction in the fluctuation amplitude of over 40% compared with the benchmark model. These findings provide scientific evidence on drainage pipeline failure.

papers.title: The origin of the self-sustained oscillations in fluidic oscillators and the role of some internal dimensions
papers.abstract: Fluidic oscillators (FOs) are commonly used in active flow control (AFC) applications to delay the boundary layer separation from any bluff-body. These devices are also employed in combustion chambers to enhance mixing, or in heat transfer applications to promote the generation of a turbulent boundary layer and therefore enhance cooling. The frequency associated with the self-sustained oscillations generated by the FO depends on the Reynolds number and the internal dimensions of the oscillator. In fact, this work aims to clarify which are the most relevant FO internal dimensions capable of modifying the outlet flow frequency and which is the origin of the self-sustained oscillations. Two main internal modifications were considered. Initially, the feedback channel (FC) width is modified, but differently from previous research papers, then in the present study, each FC width is associated with a different mixing chamber (MC) inlet width, and this small modification in the inlet width is proved to have large implications in the FO outlet frequency. In fact, the influence of the MC inlet width is found to be more relevant than the modification in the FC width. The modification of the MC outlet inclination wall is also addressed in the present study. The MC pressure and the interaction between the main jet and the reverse mass flow jet are highly influenced by this particular modification. When analyzing the forces acting on the main jet as it enters the MC, it is observed that, regardless of the internal modification performed, the pressure forces play the most important role; therefore, we conclude that for the present FO configuration, the self-sustained oscillations are pressure driven.

papers.title: Impact of viscous droplets on soap bubbles: Coalescence suppresses bubble bursting in viscous regime
papers.abstract: The impact of a viscous droplet on various surfaces is a fundamental physical process in nature and numerous technological fields. Despite the significant progress on understanding the impact dynamics of viscous droplets on solid surfaces and liquid films, the impact of viscous droplets on bubbles, especially the influence of droplet viscosity, is still poorly understood. Here, the impact dynamics of water-glycerol droplets with different viscosity on soap bubbles has been experimentally studied by high-speed camera. Similar to the water droplets impacting on soap bubbles, the droplet with higher viscosity rebounds from the soap bubble at low Weber number and passes through the large soap bubble at high Weber number. At high Weber number with small soap bubbles, the coalescence of the soap bubble with the highly viscous droplet mostly occurs, which is different from the “bubble bursting” for the impact of water droplets on soap bubbles reported previously. With the negligible viscous dissipation of droplets on soap bubbles, a general energy balance model is established to capture the transition of different impact behaviors for both low-viscosity and high-viscosity droplets impacting on soap bubbles. Increasing the viscosity of the droplet is found to suppress the bursting of small soap bubbles while promote the coalescence of the droplet with the soap bubble, and even the “passing” of the droplet. The dependence of the impact outcome on the viscosity of the droplet in the regime of small soap bubbles and high Weber number can be interpreted by the three-phase Taylor-Culick retraction.

papers.title: Three-dimensional wake transitions of a square cylinder in sinusoidal oscillatory flows
papers.abstract: The three-dimensional wake transition of a square cylinder in a streamwise sinusoidal oscillatory flow with non-zero mean velocity is investigated numerically using direct numerical simulations and Floquet stability analysis. Sinusoidal flows with different oscillation amplitudes a and frequencies f, namely (a=0.1, f=0.15), (a=0.2, f=0.15), and (a=0.1, f=0.3), are compared with steady smooth flows (a=0, f=0) to examine the influence of sinusoidal fluctuations. The imposed sinusoidal oscillations modulate the topology of the two-dimensional base flow and force the wake to shed vortices at either the oscillation frequency or its subharmonic within a finite Reynolds number (Re) range. At large oscillation amplitudes, the flow becomes asymmetric and the onset of three-dimensionality occurs earlier, with a critical transition at Re > 139.9. In contrast, the high-frequency sinusoidal oscillations stabilize the wake and significantly suppress the development of three-dimensional instabilities, delaying the critical transition to Re > 210.4 and narrowing the unstable range of spanwise wavelength. Compared with the temporally periodic instabilities observed in smooth flows, i.e., mode A and mode B instabilities, the double-period instability mode (mode C) emerges in the low-frequency sinusoidal flows, and the quasi-periodic instability mode (mode QP) arises under high-frequency oscillations. The odd and even reflection–translation symmetries of Floquet modes in smooth flows are broken when sinusoidal oscillation is applied. Furthermore, the imposed sinusoidal oscillations lead to supercritical or subcritical three-dimensional wake transitions, depending on the oscillation parameters.

papers.title: Synergistic hydrodynamic interactions and propulsion efficiency of fish schools in oblique flows
papers.abstract: The flow structures surrounding a school of fish in an oblique flow environment are subject to mutual interference, resulting in complex turbulent formations. This leads to a significantly uneven distribution of efficiency experienced by different parts of the school. To investigate the impact of complex turbulent formations in oblique flow environments on fish interactions and to explore the swimming efficiency of a school of biomimetic underwater robots, this study focuses on analyzing the effects of inter-fish spacing, swimming angle of attack, and Strouhal number on the swimming efficiency of the school. A self-developed Central Processing Unit/Graphics Processing Unit heterogeneous parallel accelerated Ghost Cell Method was employed to numerically simulate the swimming of four fish arranged in a diamond formation. The effects of the angle of attack, inter-fish spacing, Strouhal number, and other factors on the swimming efficiency and turbulent structure of a school of fish were analyzed. The study revealed that at a low angle of attack (10°), the school of fish exhibited a significant flow synergistic optimization effect, with the amplitudes of fluctuations in the normal force coefficient (CN) and the tangential force coefficient (CT) being significantly reduced. As the angle of attack increased to 20° and 30°, the flow separation effect intensified. However, the schooling fish effectively suppressed the main fluctuation components of the normal force and enhanced the modulating effect of high-frequency vortex shedding on the surface pressure through vortex-phase interference and vortex redistribution mechanisms. Inter-fish spacing significantly influenced the synergistic effect and propulsion efficiency of schooling fish. At a medium spacing (ds = 0.6L), the schooling fish exhibited an optimal synergistic effect, with the smallest amplitude of fluctuations in the tangential and normal force coefficients and the highest propulsion efficiency among all the spacings. This study not only revealed the synergistic mechanisms of multiple fish swimming in oblique flow but also provided a theoretical basis for the design and optimization of a biomimetic underwater robot swarm. By optimizing parameters such as the angle of attack, Strouhal number, and inter-fish spacing, the synergistic effect and propulsion efficiency of schooling fish can be significantly enhanced. Future research can further explore the swimming characteristics of fish schools under more parameter combinations and optimization strategies for practical application.

papers.title: Insights into freestanding MgO monolayer membranes for efficient purification of SF6, C2F6, and C3F8 from gas mixtures: Density functional theory calculations and molecular dynamics simulations
papers.abstract: The efficient separation of SF6/N2, C2F6/N2, and C3F8/N2 gas mixtures using membrane technology is essential yet challenging, primarily due to the well-known trade-off between permeability and selectivity, which hinders the recovery of SF6, C2F6, and C3F8. To address this challenge, novel two-dimensional materials have been explored for the design of high-performance membranes. Here, we systematically investigated the highly selective separation of SF6/N2, C2F6/N2, and C3F8/N2 mixtures using freestanding graphenylene-like magnesium oxide (g-MgO) monolayer membranes through a combination of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. MD results reveal N2 permeances of (1.80 ± 0.05) × 107, (1.78 ± 0.04) × 107, and (1.78 ± 0.03) × 107 GPU (i.e., gas permeation unit) for SF6/N2, C2F6/N2, and C3F8/N2 mixtures at 300 K, respectively, which significantly exceed those reported for conventional zeolite and ZIF-8 membranes. DFT calculations further demonstrate N2 molecules permeate the g-MgO membrane with a small energy barrier of 0.237 eV, which is attributed to the absence of electron overlap between N2 and membrane, resulting from the smaller kinetic diameter of N2 compared to the effective pore size (4.11–5.08 Å) of g-MgO. Moreover, the g-MgO membrane exhibits high selectivity for SF6/N2, C2F6/N2, and C3F8/N2, reaching orders of 1017, 103, and 1032, respectively, at 300 K, surpassing the performance of most existing membranes. Our results indicate that the g-MgO membrane simultaneously achieves high permeability and high selectivity for the separation of these mixtures, effectively overcoming the traditional permeability-selectivity trade-off. These findings position the freestanding g-MgO monolayers as highly promising candidates for the purification and recovery of SF6, C2F6, and C3F8.

papers.title: Diffusio-osmosis of surfactant solutions: Molecular modeling and interfacial physics
papers.abstract: Diffusio-osmosis is an important transport mechanism at the micro/nanoscale, with applications such as chemical injection-based enhanced oil recovery. Here, we investigate the diffusio-osmosis of surfactant solutions, a class of diffusio-osmosis where solutes are mainly contact adsorbed on solid surfaces. We compute the diffusio-osmosis using molecular dynamics simulations and delineate the limitations of classical continuum models in predicting such transport. We adopt model surfactants whose tail groups exhibit a stronger affinity to solid walls than their head groups. For dilute solutions of such surfactants, the strength of diffusio-osmosis is independent of the surfactant concentration and is generally enhanced when tail groups interact more strongly with solid walls or when head groups become smaller. As the surfactant concentration increases beyond a critical value, the strength of diffusio-osmosis decreases, initially rapidly and then slowly, with increasing surfactant concentration. The classical continuum model for diffusio-osmosis can predict these trends, but quantitative discrepancies are also evident. These discrepancies arise mainly from two interfacial effects neglected in those theories: the loss of flow driving force due to the intermittent adsorption of surfactants on walls and the deviation of the viscosity of interfacial fluids from bulk values due to the formation of surfactant nanostructures near walls. The insights from the present study are relevant to the broad class of diffusio-osmosis where the contact adsorption of solutes is important.

papers.title: Dynamics of impacting droplets on hydrophobic concave surfaces
papers.abstract: The dynamic behaviors of droplets impacting hydrophobic concave substrates are investigated via high-speed photography. The effects of the Weber number (We) and the curvature (k) on the morphological evolution of droplets impacting hydrophobic concave substrates were observed. The maximum spreading arc length (Lmax), maximum jet height (Hmax), and rate variations during the spreading and retraction stage of impacting droplets were experimentally quantified. Meanwhile, the critical impacting parameters for producing satellite droplets on different curvature concave surfaces are also quantitatively expressed. Moreover, a prediction model for the Lmax of droplets impacting varied concave substrates was innovatively established based on energy analysis of impacting droplets, which was proven to present good accuracy by experimental data. The results revealed that concave surfaces suppress the spreading of the droplet while obviously enhancing the retraction stage. The Lmax and Hmax of the droplet decrease with the increase in k due to more energy dissipation. As the We increases, the Lmax increases, and the Hmax decreases. Furthermore, when the We is fixed at 90, as the k increases from 0.0606 to 0.1667 mm−1, the spreading rate of the droplet decreased from 3.1 to 2.6 m/s, and the retraction rate increased from 0.7 to 0.78 m/s. Additionally, it was observed that We promotes the formation of satellite droplets, while k suppresses the formation of satellite droplets. Simultaneously, the critical We and k parameters for generating satellite droplets were also provided. Some references are provided for designing functionalized special-shaped hydrophobic surfaces with controllable droplet wetting and dynamic behaviors.

papers.title: Impact of the inclined wall on the bubble dynamics within confined spaces
papers.abstract: The present paper systematically investigates the bubble dynamics near the inclined wall within confined spaces. Based on the high-speed photography experiments, the typical phenomena of the bubble collapse jet, centroid motion, and splitting near the inclined walls are observed, and the effects of the bubble position and wall parameters on the bubble collapse dynamics are quantitatively analyzed. Based on the conformal transformation and the image method, a theoretical model of the bubble Kelvin impulse near an inclined wall within confined spaces is established. A quantitative analysis of Kelvin impulse and the Bjerknes force is conducted, mutually validating the observed experimental phenomena. The results show that the bubble splitting process varies from symmetrical splitting to asymmetrical splitting, and the jet always points toward the adjacent flat wall. In addition, both the displacement and direction of the bubble centroid motion closely correspond to variations of the Kelvin impulse, revealing that the angles of the inclined walls influence the bubble migration.

papers.title: Erratum: “Vibrational-state-resolved relaxation and chemistry of carbon monoxide and nitrogen mixtures from 2000–10 250 K probing carbon monoxide in the ground to twelfth excited vibrational levels” [Phys. Fluids 37 , 096112 (2025)]
Analytical study of self-similar motion following shock waves in magnetized, non-ideal, self-gravitating gas with variable density
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the evolution of a blast wave propagating through a self-gravitating, non-ideal gaseous medium subjected to an azimuthal magnetic influence. A power series approach is applied to formulate approximate solutions for the primary flow quantities, utilizing Sakurai's analytical technique. The study presents both zeroth- and first-order approximations, including explicit expressions for the zeroth-order terms. To examine the nature of the resulting flow structure across the shock boundary, graphical analyses are conducted for key variables such as density, velocity, pressure, magnetic influence, and mass distribution, based on the zeroth-order profiles.

papers.title: On the suppression of satellite Bingham viscoplastic liquid droplets in a co-flow focusing upon actuation
papers.abstract: When liquid jets undergo breakup, they generate main as well as undesirable satellite droplets due to nonlinear effects. Therefore, the elimination or at least suppression of these satellite droplets is desirable due to the intrinsic nature of jet liquids. In this paper, we study the externally imposed velocity-modulated disturbed non-Newtonian viscoplastic liquid jet breakup in the co-flow focusing process. The one-fluid Navier–Stokes equations are solved using the finite element method, and the liquid–liquid interface is tracked at fixed grids using the level set method. The non-Newtonian viscoplastic behavior of the jet liquid is added via the Papanastasiou–Bingham model. It is found that higher yield stress significantly retarded jet breakup and suppressed the generation of satellite droplets. The jet liquid flow rate plays no role in the retardation or suppression of satellite droplets. At low amplitudes and frequencies, satellite droplets are generated, which are eliminated at higher amplitudes and frequencies. However, at greater frequencies than a critical frequency, the jet breakup length increases, which delays the formation of main droplets. The jet is unstable at low densities, while stable at higher densities. However, density does not play a significant role in the suppression/elimination of satellite drops. This work provides valuable insights into the generation of monodispersed drops, relevant to applications such drop-on-demand generation.

papers.title: Energy loss characteristics of gas–liquid two-phase flow in pump-turbines under pumping mode
papers.abstract: In gas–liquid two-phase flow within the pump mode of a pump-turbine, a trade-off was observed between the cavitation control and intensified energy dissipation due to gas-phase introduction. This study integrated experimental research with a Computational Fluid Dynamics-Population Balance Model (CFD-PBM) coupled model to investigate the influence mechanisms of air-injection concentration and flow conditions on energy loss. The reliability of the CFD-PBM numerical method for simulating gas–liquid two-phase flow in the pump mode of a pump-turbine was validated. Air-injection concentration was found to redistribute energy losses across flow passages. The primary energy dissipation zone, influenced by gas-phase accumulation, migrated from the double-row guide vanes to the runner passage as the air-injection concentration increased. Furthermore, due to gas-phase aggregation in low-pressure regions, energy dissipation on the low-pressure surface remained consistently higher than that on the high-pressure surface. Under constant air-injection conditions, flow rate magnitude affected entropy production migration. The runner passage persisted as the dominant energy dissipation zone across all flow rates, while the secondary dissipation zone shifted from the guide vane passage to the stay guide vane passage as the flow rate increased. Localized high entropy production regions induced by gas-phase accumulation in the runner blade channels were governed by bubble size, pressure gradient, liquid-phase backflow, and interphase interactions.

papers.title: Optimizing coupled diesel oxidation catalyst and particulate filter for enhanced emission reduction
papers.abstract: Diesel engines dominate non-road machinery applications but generate environmentally hazardous emissions, particularly nitrogen oxides and particulate matter. Therefore, investigations on the performance of an integrated diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC) and diesel particulate filter (DPF) system are conducted, focusing on the effects of critical parameters such as catalyst composition, oxygen content, exhaust velocity, and operating temperature. The results revealed that palladium (Pd) content in the catalyst enhances C3H6 conversion, with a 4.83% higher conversion rate compared to platinum (Pt) at an oxygen mass fraction of 0.04. An orthogonal test design is employed to identify the key factors influencing DOC+DPF conversion, with inlet velocity showing the greatest gray correlation with carbon particle conversion, followed by oxygen content, inlet temperature, and catalyst ratio. Additionally, NO oxidation efficiency peaked under moderate temperatures and increased with Pt catalyst content. This study indicates the importance of synergistic optimization of operating conditions, catalyst composition, and system parameters to enhance pollutant conversion efficiency. These findings establish quantitative relationships between operational variables and system performance, providing valuable insights for optimizing aftertreatment configurations in heavy-duty applications.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of air-assisted liquid injection in supersonic crossflow
papers.abstract: This study experimentally investigates the dynamics of liquid injection in a Mach 2.1 supersonic crossflow for two configurations: liquid-only injection and liquid injection with upstream air assistance. High-speed back-lit imaging and Z-type shadowgraphy were employed to examine jet breakup, penetration, and the associated shock structures. The results show that air assistance increases liquid column penetration primarily through a shielding effect and promotes earlier breakup due to direct interaction with the upstream gaseous jet. This impingement of the gaseous jet on the liquid column results in local shearing, leading to droplet entrainment into the recirculation zone formed in the inter-jet spacing, a feature absent in the liquid-only injection case. Shadowgraph images reveal that surface instability waves at the liquid–gas interface give rise to micro shocks, which convect downstream along with the instability waves. Jet boundary tracking indicates that the dominant frequency of surface oscillations increases from 2344 Hz in the liquid-only case to 3422 Hz in the air-assisted case, underscoring the stronger interfacial instabilities induced by gaseous injection. Dynamic mode decomposition reveals that jet oscillations are dominated by a shear oscillation mode in the liquid-only injection case, whereas in the air-assisted injection case, both shear and flapping modes play significant roles in jet destabilization. The elevated shear oscillation frequency in the air-assisted case signifies stronger unsteadiness and earlier fragmentation, consistent with interface tracking results. Overall, the findings show that upstream air injection enhances penetration, accelerates breakup, and increases interfacial unsteadiness, highlighting its potential for improved air-fuel mixing in high-speed combustion applications.

papers.title: Poiseuille flow with stochastically perturbed boundary
papers.abstract: We investigate, for the first time, the influence of stochastically perturbed boundaries on the flow of an incompressible Newtonian fluid. Two canonical configurations are examined: planar channel flow and axisymmetric pipe flow. The boundary perturbations are modeled as zero-mean stochastic processes, incorporated via a deterministic framework in which the characteristic spatial frequency of the boundary roughness is assumed to be asymptotically large compared to the intrinsic length scales of the flow. Asymptotic expansions for the pressure field are derived under these assumptions, and the implications of the stochastic boundary forcing on the global discharge are analyzed.

papers.title: Steady waves on an axisymmetric ferrofluid jet: A weakly nonlinear theory
papers.abstract: We examine axisymmetric periodic waves that propagate along the surface of an inviscid ferrofluid jet under the influence of an azimuthal magnetic field, using both theoretical and numerical approaches. Our analysis takes into account the competing forces of the magnetic field and surface tension. By applying the Dirichlet–Neumann operator (DNO) expansion to the free-surface boundary conditions, we derive a fully dispersive model known as the cubic DNO-truncation model. This model demonstrates strong agreement with numerical results obtained from the full Euler equations for small to moderate amplitude traveling waves across a wide range of physical parameters. Using the cubic DNO-truncation model, we first develop perturbation series solutions for periodic waves by modifying the Stokes expansion to suit the axisymmetric configuration. In non-resonant cases, we observe that within a narrow range of the magnetic Bond number, the third-order Stokes wave solutions closely align with numerical results from both the DNO-truncation model and the primitive Euler equations, even for moderate amplitude waves. However, for Wilton ripples, the asymptotic solutions diverge from the numerical results, even at small amplitudes.

papers.title: Impact of trailing-edge cracking on the dynamic stall of airfoils
papers.abstract: Offshore wind turbines are highly vulnerable to lightning strikes during operation. Such events can cause cracking at the blade trailing edge, compromising both the aerodynamic performance and structural safety of the turbines. Moreover, regulations of the angle of attack during operation can induce dynamic stall. While existing research has focused on loads and material properties of damaged airfoils, this study numerically analyzes trailing-edge crack (TEC) height and depth effects on the S809 airfoil dynamic stall. By comparing the vortex evolution of airfoils with different crack severities, the intrinsic mechanisms by which TEC influences dynamic stall are investigated. The results show that, during dynamic stall, changes in the drag coefficient lag slightly behind changes in the lift coefficient. A small crack height causes the onset of dynamic stall to occur earlier. However, as crack height increases, the development of the trailing-edge vortex (TEV) during the upstroke stage is suppressed, which delays dynamic stall and leads to improve aerodynamic performance. The influence of crack depth on dynamic stall is smaller than that of crack height, and crack depth does not alter the dynamic-stall angle. During the upstroke stage, a larger crack depth reduces the vorticity of the TEV and suppresses its growth, improving the aerodynamic performance of the cracked airfoil. Conversely, during the downstroke phase, the cracked trailing edge promotes the development of TEV, substantially increasing their vorticity as well as the extent of the affected flow area. This enhanced vortex activity raises energy dissipation and leads to a sharp degradation in aerodynamic performance.

papers.title: Interaction and combined cooling effects of mid-passage gap leakage with blade coolant in suction side and corner cooling
papers.abstract: With the increase in turbine inlet temperatures, effective cooling is essential for all regions of the turbine. However, most previous studies have focused on the thermal protection of individual components, often neglecting marginal areas. From the perspective of multi-zone interactions within the cascades, this study numerically investigates the combined cooling effects between mid-passage gap (MPG) leakage and blade coolant, with a focus on the suction side (SS) and corner cooling. An interesting corner cooling phenomenon is observed, involving interactions among the blade film coolant, leakage flow, and secondary flow. Results show that corner cooling is enhanced when the coolant is either guided by a counter leakage vortex or when the vortex is weakened by leakage. The combined effects of MPG leakage and blade coolant expand the cooling coverage on the suction side and contribute to achieving full surface thermal protection. Additionally, while a compound angle improves blade cooling, its effect is limited and mainly improves the peak value of laterally-averaged cooling effectiveness (ηl). When the blowing ratio of blade coolant (Mb) increases from 0.5 to 1.5 at leakage mass flow rate (MFRg) = 1%, the peak value of ηl on the blade suction side increases by 51%. Under this condition, when film holes are with a compound angle (β) value of 30°, the peak value of ηl further increases by 17.9%. These findings highlight the importance of considering the synergistic effects of passage vortices and leakage flows in future blade cooling designs to achieve more comprehensive and effective suction-side coverage.

papers.title: Effect of burden layers on hydrate exploitation through the horizontal well
papers.abstract: The mass and energy transfer between the burden layers and the hydrate layer will directly affect the gas production and reservoir mechanical response during the depressurization. At present, numerous studies have focused on the impact of the hydrate layer itself. To explore the effect of burden layers on hydrate exploitation, this paper predicts the gas production and seabed settlement using a coupled thermal-hydrological-mechanical-chemical simulator. The simulation results indicate that the hydrate decomposition edge reaches the burden layers (breakthrough), leading to a significant decrease in the gas production rate. This is primarily contributed to the fact that more fluid in the burden layers flows toward the wellbore, inhibiting the gas hydrate decomposition. The horizontal well should be located in the lower middle of the hydrate layer, which can effectively utilize the formation pressure without producing a breakthrough. However, the burden layers are subject to a pressure drop whether a breakthrough occurs or not, resulting in the burden layers' settlement. And, the burden layer settlement increases significantly with the decrease in the permeability. As a result, employing artificial impermeable barriers within burden layers to improve gas production may raise safety issues. In conclusion, this paper elucidates the mechanism of burden layers' influence on gas hydrate exploitation, which is of significance for the design and optimization of plans.

papers.title: Vibration effect on the localization of a gas bubble in a viscous liquid
papers.abstract: The paper investigates the dynamics of a gas bubble in a viscous, incompressible liquid in a container undergoing translational vibrations in the absence of gravity. In most earlier works, the interaction of the solid, liquid, or gaseous inclusion with the wall was considered for the case when the container size substantially exceeds the size of the inclusion, or for the case of a flat wall. In contrast, the present study examines bubble dynamics when the dimensions of the container and the bubble are comparable, such that confinement effects become important. The modeling is carried out by volume of fluid method using high-order discretization schemes. The influence of the vibration parameters, container shape, viscosity and surface tension, and the ratio of bubble size to that of the container on the pulsation and average flows and bubble deformation is investigated. It is shown that the confinement effect has a significant influence on the bubble dynamics. Additionally, it is found that in these conditions, the role of the shape of the container (the wall curvature) becomes crucial, especially at moderate vibration intensity. Specifically, it is demonstrated that, in the cases of a cylindrical container of circular cross section and a spherical container, there arise new quasi-equilibrium positions of a bubble at significant distances from the container walls and its center, while in the case of a cylindrical container of square cross section, such equilibrium states are absent.

papers.title: Effects of fluid viscosity and microfin features on laminar flow-driven heat transfer in microchannels
papers.abstract: Microchannels possess enhanced thermal convection due to its greater surface-to-volume ratio. Empirical evidence depicts that flows in microchannels are an effective means of dissipating heat flux from small, localized heat source points over a larger surface area. It formulates symmetric heat distribution, holding promising applications for tiny biological regulators. The size, shape, structures, and density distribution of heat sources in microchannels greatly influence heat distribution, whereas the medium of heat transfer was found to have a marginal effect in the case of a minute viscosity difference between two fluids. The thermo-fluid coupling effects in microchannels are highlighted to evaluate the modulation of temperature and variations of velocity within the working fluid. The effect of heat distributions on fluid flow in the presence of micro-fins within a microchannel was studied numerically in the presence of both Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluid, while considering the case of two different fin configuration conditions, i.e., decreasing inter-fin distance with decreasing fin height, and increasing inter-fin distance with increasing fin height. The flow domain was considered to have inlet boundary conditions: pulsatile flow (time varying inlet velocity and fin's temperature). Whereas, fins of different shapes: rectangular, elliptical, and conical shapes, were considered in the study. The local Nusselt number was found to be influenced by the effective surface area and boundary layer thickness linked to the varied micro-fin structures, as well as the pressure drop caused by the varying fin separation lengths. In the case of decreasing inter-fin distance, the highest Nu was found to be 30.41 and the lowest Nu was found to be 7.19 for non-Newtonian fluid for conical fins. In the case of increasing inter-fin distance, the highest Nu was found to be 30.40 and the lowest Nu was found to be 7.20 for non-Newtonian fluid for conical fins.

papers.title: Dynamics of cavitation bubble generated by low voltage discharge under hypobaric conditions
papers.abstract: A combined experimental and theoretical study is conducted on cavitation bubble dynamics under hypobaric conditions, focusing on the collapse mechanisms of bubbles with radii of ̃O(10–25) mm generated by low-voltage discharge (LVD). Experiments are performed over ambient pressures of 0.02–0.1 MPa to identify conditions for jet-free neutral collapses, where buoyancy effects remain negligible. In the first oscillation cycle, reduced ambient pressure delays bubble evolution, yielding a larger maximum radius and longer collapse time while preserving spherical geometry, indicative of inertia-dominated collapse. In the second cycle, decreasing ambient pressure enhances surface instabilities, and buoyancy-induced asymmetry intensifies near collapse, producing stronger upward-directed jets, whereas at 0.05 MPa, jet formation is suppressed and a neutral collapse is observed. Theoretical interpretation is limited by the loss of early radius and velocity data from overexposure in LVD. These are recovered using discrete weighted orthogonalization (DWO), enabling reconstruction of radius and wall-velocity histories with orthonormal polynomial expansions. Internal pressure is estimated using an inverse Gilmore model and expressed in virial form, fitted separately for the expansion and collapse phases to capture thermodynamic asymmetry. The virial model is coupled with the Gilmore equation for forward simulations, along with Noble–Abel stiffened-gas equation of state for the liquid phase to predict the temporal evolution of bubble radius, internal pressure, and temperature. This DWO–Gilmore–Virial approach successfully reproduces radius–time histories under hypobaric conditions with high accuracy, enabling deeper insights into the governing bubble dynamics. Internal pressure and temperature estimates show consistency with Rayleigh collapse predictions at specific polytropic exponents. The framework provides a robust tool for applications in underwater blasts, medical therapy, and bubble propulsion.

papers.title: Flow analysis and thermochemical insight during supercritical water gasification of polypropylene particles
papers.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive numerical investigation of polypropylene particle gasification in supercritical water using particle-resolved direct numerical simulations in both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) configurations involving a single particle or three particles in interaction. The results are analyzed systematically to assess the effects of dimensionality, particle position, and particle Reynolds number (Rep = 50–125) on flow dynamics, interfacial heat and mass transfer, and species distribution. 3D simulations reveal higher drag coefficients, Nusselt numbers, and Sherwood numbers than 2D simulations, primarily due to thinner boundary layers and weaker Stefan flow. While 2D simulations capture general trends, 3D modeling is essential to resolve boundary layer development and wake interactions accurately. In multi-particle arrangements, downstream particles experience significant shielding in 2D, whereas 3D wake structures mitigate these effects. Species H2 shows complex, nonlinear behavior due to high diffusivity and strong coupling with local flow, unlike the approximately linear temperature trends of CO2, CO, and CH4. Higher particle Reynolds numbers enhance convective transport but reduce residence time, heat release, and surface reactions, slowing particle shrinking rates. These findings provide key insight into supercritical water gasification and support the development of predictive models and scalable reactor designs for plastic waste conversion.

papers.title: A novel micro-vibration prediction method for an aerostatic thrust bearing by using Ω-vortex identification
papers.abstract: In this paper, an Ω-vortex identification method is proposed to predict the micro-vibration of an aerostatic thrust bearing. It can identify vortex structure and corresponding spatial distribution in bearing gas film accurately, quantifying vortex region area by the Ω iso-surface. Four methods are used to predict the micro-vibration of nine aerostatic thrust bearings according to the flow fields obtained by large eddy simulation (LES). The experimental results indicate that the prediction accuracy is 66.7% for the maximum gas flow velocity method, 83.3% for the maximum gas pressure difference method and gas pressure fluctuation method, and 100% for the Ω-vortex identification method. The proposed method is helpful for micro-vibration prediction and provides guidance for structure optimization to suppress vortex and micro-vibration of an aerostatic thrust bearing.

papers.title: Experimental and simulation studies on spray characteristics of different injector configurations under supersonic incoming flow conditions
papers.abstract: Experimental and three-dimensional simulation studies were performed to investigate the atomization of transverse jet injection under a freestream Mach number of 1.8, using circular, semi-circular, and square injectors. Systematic comparisons of initial spray patterns revealed distinct morphological differences among the three injector geometries. Detailed analysis was performed on the dynamic instability during jet initiation and the subsequent bow shock formation process. Particular attention was given to the recirculation zone developing, with its formation mechanism. Using zonal analysis, the global spray structure and flow field evolution were qualitatively characterized. Results show that higher injection pressure drops significantly increase the bow shock angle and spray penetration depth. Under equal pressure drops, circular injectors generated the largest bow shock angles and penetration depths, whereas semi-circular ones yielded the lowest. At constant mass flow rates, semi-circular injectors resulted in the highest bow shock angles and penetration depths, followed by square and then circular injectors. Analysis of droplet size distribution revealed a characteristic stratification pattern, with larger droplets concentrated at the core and smaller ones dispersed toward the edges. Injector geometry profoundly affected spatial distribution: semi-circular injectors demonstrate a noticeable narrowing effect in spray dispersion, whereas square injectors exhibit localized aggregation phenomena of larger spray particles within their spatial distribution. Droplet size measurements confirmed that square injectors produced larger Sauter mean diameters than the other geometries. Proper orthogonal decomposition analysis identified three dominant fluctuation modes: the first-order mode was governed by low-frequency oscillations, while the second and third modes exhibited streamwise shear-layer instabilities characteristic of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortices.

papers.title: The effect of porosity in a row of barriers on mitigation of flow dynamics and barrier interaction: Viscoplastic debris flows in a flume
papers.abstract: Viscoplastic debris flows, characterized by a finite yield stress and plastic viscosity, pose serious threats to infrastructure and communities in mountainous and flood-prone regions. Engineered barriers are commonly deployed to reduce flow velocity, trap sediments, and dissipate kinetic energy. Yet, the influence of barrier porosity and channel slope on the behavior of viscoplastic debris flows is not well understood, limiting optimized design strategies. This study employs three-dimensional Computational Fluid Dynamics simulations of dam-break-driven viscoplastic debris flows to investigate the effects of porosity in a single row of uniform barriers. Porosity, defined as the spacing between barriers of fixed geometry, varies from ϕ=0.3 to 0.9. The impact of channel inclination is also examined for θ=0°, 5°, 15°, 30°, and 45°, enabling assessment of flow redirection and force attenuation. Analyses of velocity fields, pressure distributions, and shear stresses provide detailed insights into fluid–structure interactions. Results show that both porosity and slope strongly control flow dynamics and energy dissipation. The runout length of viscoplastic flows decreases significantly with decreasing porosity, with reductions of up to tenfold between ϕ=1 and ϕ=0.3. Lower porosities elevate barrier forces while reducing downstream wall loads, whereas steeper slopes consistently amplify forces on barriers and end walls. At ϕ=0.3–0.4, stagnant, unyielded zones develop, generating localized stresses tracked over time. These findings offer critical guidance for designing barrier systems, supporting more effective mitigation of debris flows, landslides, and associated natural hazards.

papers.title: The effect of porosity in a row of barriers on mitigation of flow dynamics and barrier interaction: Water floods and viscoplastic debris flows in a complex terrain
papers.abstract: Floods, whether water-dominated or viscoplastic debris, pose significant risks to communities and infrastructure in steep terrains. Protective barriers are commonly implemented to reduce flow velocities, limit run-out distances, and mitigate impact forces; however, the influence of barrier porosity on downstream loading remains insufficiently quantified. This study employs three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations over the real topography of Hobart, Tasmania, to examine porosity-controlled barrier performance in dam-break scenarios. Porosity is varied from ϕ=0.3 to 0.9 by changing the number of barriers within a fixed reference volume, while the geometry of each barrier is held constant. Two flow types are analyzed: Newtonian water floods and non-Newtonian viscoplastic debris flows with finite yield stress. Key hydrodynamic indicators including velocity fields and pressure and shear forces on both the end wall and barriers are evaluated. For water floods, end wall pressure reductions relative to the barrier-free case (ϕ=1) range from negligible at ϕ=0.3 to approximately 25% at ϕ=0.5. End-wall shear forces decrease by 59%–61% at low porosities (ϕ=0.3–0.4). Barrier pressure and shear forces peak at ϕ=0.8, whereas lower porosities reduce barrier loading by 32%–74%. For debris flows, low-porosity configurations (ϕ=0.3) reduce end wall pressure by 92% and shear by 37%, while intermediate porosities (ϕ=0.6–0.7) minimize barrier forces. End-wall shear force displays a non-monotonic variation with porosity in debris flows, with local maxima at ϕ=0.6–0.8.

papers.title: Migration of pulsating buoyant bubbles beneath a free surface
papers.abstract: This paper presents a systematic investigation of bubble migration behavior beneath a free surface through a combination of experimental, numerical, and theoretical approaches. In the experiment, it is observed that the bubble subject to a large buoyancy effect transitions into a stable upward-migrating vortex ring after jet penetration, which subsequently interacts with the free surface and produces distinct jetting phenomena. Through numerical simulations based on the boundary integral method, we quantitatively determined the Kelvin impulse I and migration displacement d of the bubble at the end of its first cycle across a broad parameter space with stand-off distance (γ) ranging from 0.5 to 8 and buoyancy parameters (δ) from 0.02 to 0.4. It is observed that for bubbles with sufficiently weak buoyancy, the displacement during the first cycle tends to follow d∼γ−1.77 when γ is relatively large. In contrast, for bubbles situated far from the free surface, where buoyancy dominates the migration, the displacement follows a scaling relationship of d∼δ1.1. Special emphasis is placed on the reversal of migration direction observed in buoyant bubbles at relatively small stand-off distances. These initially downward-migrating bubbles eventually undergo directional reversal and ascend due to the dominant effect of buoyancy in the long run. By employing a theoretical framework based on Kelvin impulse theory, we demonstrate that this directional reversal is not solely attributable to the interplay between Bjerknes and buoyancy forces but is also modulated by the temporal variation in the bubble's added mass resulting from its volumetric oscillations.

papers.title: Noise reduction mechanism of a three-element airfoil with a swept-angle based on lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the noise reduction mechanism of a three-element airfoil with a swept angle. It analyzes the impact of the swept angle on airfoil noise through numerical simulations validated by wind tunnel experiments. An in-house high-precision numerical scheme based on the lattice Boltzmann method combined with the parallel computing capabilities of graphics processing units is used to directly simulate the unsteady vortices around the airfoil. The study finds that the noise reduction effect of the swept angle is not solely attributed to the decrease in effective incoming flow velocity, the sweepback effect introduces a spanwise phase difference during vortex shedding, which weakens the spanwise coherence of the vortex structures. Meanwhile, the breakdown into smaller vortex structures leads to an increase in broadband noise which compensates exactly the additional reduction of the low frequency spectrum pressure level. Based on the Lamb vector ω×u in the vortex-acoustic theory and combined with the dynamic mode decomposition method, this paper conducts a study on the quantitative relationship between the evolution of vortex morphology and noise changes.

papers.title: Data-driven global optimization and mechanism analysis of flapping motion for a hybrid underwater robot
papers.abstract: This study focuses on the flapping propulsion performance of a new type of hybrid-driven underwater robot. For this specific configuration of the robot, the optimal motion parameters cannot be directly obtained from biomimetic approaches. Therefore, we systematically analyzed the influence of pectoral fin motion parameters (frequency, phase difference, and amplitude) on thrust and lift characteristics using computational fluid dynamics (CFD), revealing the independent effects of each parameter. Based on the CFD simulation data, a machine learning model based on the Light Gradient Boosting Machine was developed to establish an accurate mapping between the motion parameters and hydrodynamic performance. The model demonstrates high accuracy in predicting thrust and lift coefficients, which satisfies the requirements of global optimization. The global optimal set of motion parameters for this specific robot configuration was obtained through optimization algorithms. Furthermore, by visualizing the vortex structures and pressure cloud maps of the flow field under optimal conditions, the origin of its superior hydrodynamic performance was interpreted from the perspective of flow mechanisms. The results demonstrate that collaborative parameter optimization can significantly improve propulsion efficiency and motion stability. This study provides an important theoretical basis and data support for motion control and performance optimization of this type of hybrid-driven underwater robot.

papers.title: Stability analysis of tilting pad journal bearings with flexible bases under sinusoidal loads
papers.abstract: The tilting-pad journal bearing (TPJB) is widely used in gas turbine rotor systems due to its high load capacity and stability. However, high temperatures can cause significant thermal deformation of the bearing base, which will reduce the reliability of TPJBs. This study develops a novel transient lubrication model for TPJBs with a flexible base and applies an improved stability criterion. Stability under sinusoidal loads is compared between rigid and flexible bases, and stability boundaries under varying parameters are determined. The results show that the flexible base significantly reduces the stability of TPJBs, while increasing the length–diameter ratio and preload coefficient raises the critical load amplitude. The study provides theoretical guidance for TPJB design and selection.

papers.title: Reduced-order characterization of spatiotemporal dynamics in merging buoyant diffusion flames
papers.abstract: The nonlinear dynamics of interacting diffusion flames play a decisive role in flame synchronization, unsteady heat release, and the onset of combustion instabilities in practical combustors. In this work, the spatiotemporal evolution of three buoyant diffusion flames is experimentally investigated as a canonical surrogate for multi-injector flame interactions. High-speed imaging (250 fps) and shadowgraphy reveal self-sustained oscillations characterized by vortex roll-up, periodic contraction, and flame-sheet detachment. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) are employed to extract reduced-order representations of the governing modes. POD analysis indicates that the first few modes capture the dominant coherent structures, with secondary modes resolving fine-scale instabilities and harmonic content. The associated temporal coefficients exhibit a fundamental frequency of approximately 11 Hz, with higher harmonics linked to vortex breakdown and energy cascading. Complementary SPOD analysis isolates frequency-resolved spatial modes that are orthogonal in both space and time, thereby identifying the coherent oscillatory mechanisms driving the instability. The synergy of POD and SPOD reveals the multiscale coupling between shear-layer vortices, heat release fluctuations, and flame-surface oscillations. These results advance the mechanistic understanding of merging flame dynamics and provide a physics-based framework for reduced-order modeling of unsteady multi-flame combustion systems.

papers.title: Fluid structure interaction mechanisms of wings with membrane-skeleton structures under low Reynolds number conditions
papers.abstract: Membrane-skeleton structures, valued for their lightweight properties, are increasingly used in unmanned air vehicles (UAVs). However, systematic research on the coupling effect of membrane pretension and aerodynamic characteristics on structural deformation, as well as the resulting impact on aerodynamic performance, remains insufficient. To address this research gap, this study focuses on membrane-skeleton wings with airfoil structures, and the core innovation of this study lies in adopting a technical approach that combines bidirectional fluid–structure interaction (FSI) simulation and gust response analysis to systematically explore the regulatory mechanism of membrane pretension on wing performance. In this study, the finite element method and finite volume method are used to solve structural dynamics and fluid dynamics problems, respectively. Bidirectional FSI is utilized to achieve iterative coupling between pressure and deformation; verification via low-Re wind tunnel experiments shows that the predicted flow field and deformation results have good reliability. Results show that at low pretension, wing segment aerodynamic performance improves significantly compared to the saturated pretension case: lift increases by approximately 3%–4%, with reduced drag. Under gust excitation, flexible full-wings exhibit lower load fluctuations than rigid ones, as the membrane-skeleton full-wing's peak lift decreases by approximately 9%. Pretension has minimal effect on gust response: the differences in peak deformation and peak lift under gust conditions are less than 0.8% and 0.5% of their respective maximum values across different pretension conditions, respectively. These findings clarify deformation mechanisms dominated by aerodynamics and membrane pretension, advancing the optimization of membrane-skeleton wings for the efficient low-Re UAV design.

papers.title: Hydrodynamics and trajectory for vertical water entry of truncated head-type projectiles
papers.abstract: A trajectory control method is proposed for the rapid leveling of the projectile after water entry through an asymmetric head-type design. The hydrodynamic and trajectory characteristics of truncated head-type projectiles were investigated using high-speed experiments and numerical simulations based on Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) equations coupled with the volume of fluid (VOF) method. The effects of truncation angle and water-entry velocity were systematically examined. The results show that all truncated head-type projectiles exhibited rightward-deflected trajectories, with larger truncation angles producing greater lateral deviation and trajectory curvature. This behavior is attributed to asymmetric water impact, where non-uniform flow around the projectile generates distinct cavities at the head and tail, respectively, resulting in lateral forces and yaw moments. The initial impact induced sharp peaks in drag, lateral force, and yaw moment coefficients. As the projectile interacted with the cavity surface, projectiles with larger truncation angles experienced earlier cavity collisions and faster stabilization. In contrast, variations in water-entry velocity had little influence on centroid trajectories and hydrodynamic coefficients at comparable penetration depths. An empirical trajectory model was developed by decoupling the equations of motion to relate trajectory curvature to truncation angle. The model demonstrated excellent agreement with numerical results, providing a reliable predictive tool for the design and control of water-entry projectiles.

papers.title: Electromagnetic flow instabilities and heat transfer in a toroidal duct
papers.abstract: The dynamics and heat transfer of an electrically conducting fluid in a toroidal duct with square cross section is numerically analyzed. The flow is driven by an azimuthal Lorentz force produced by the interaction between the radial electric current density, and a constant and uniform magnetic field imposed in the axial direction. For the heat transfer analysis, the temperature distribution of the fluid confined within the toroidal duct depends on a non-uniform volumetric internal heating that emulates the exponentially decaying heating profile typical to blanket conditions of a fusion power reactor. Dimensionless equations that govern the magnetohydrodynamic flow and heat transfer are solved using the spectral element method, and the resulting control parameters involved are the Hartmann (Ha) and Reynolds (Re) numbers. This paper aims to identify the flow characteristics that affect heat transfer under forced convection conditions, with a focus on the interaction between Lorentz and viscous forces. Furthermore, the study explores how different flow patterns that depend on the interaction parameter N=Ha2/Re in the range 0.1<N<3.6, influence the overall heat transfer rate quantified by a global Nusselt number. It is shown that flow instabilities identified as symmetric or asymmetric in the r and z planes, depends on the magnetic strength at a given Reynolds number, Re=2000. We also identify the onset of the secondary flow and determine the critical interaction parameter, N, required to maximize or minimize convective heat transfer, as well as the stationary flow patterns responsible for such behavior.

papers.title: Study on aerodynamic characteristics and stochastic vibration analysis during train passage over bridge under crosswind
papers.abstract: The growing demand for high-capacity rail transit has led to the adoption of lighter and faster trains operating on long-span bridges, where strong crosswind-induced train–bridge interactions present considerable risks to operational safety. This study develops a stochastic analysis framework to assess the aerodynamic performance of train–bridge systems under crosswinds by integrating computational fluid dynamics with a coupled vibration approach. A three-dimensional interaction model is established using the k-omega shear-stress transport turbulence model to resolve complex flow fields and unsteady aerodynamic loads under high-speed conditions. The probability density evolution method is employed to solve the stochastic dynamic equations, quantifying system vibrations and evaluating running safety indices. Results reveal that the lateral response of the train–bridge system increases exponentially with wind speed. Owing to aerodynamic coupling between the moving train and crosswinds, both vehicle and bridge aerodynamic coefficients show significant sensitivity to increasing Reynolds numbers. Changes in cross-sectional parameters can cause force coefficient amplitudes to vary by over 40% compared to baseline values. Large bridge pylons induce notable aerodynamic shielding effects, where spatial pressure gradients between windward and leeward sides reduce the resultant aerodynamic forces across the coupled system by up to 50%. These findings offer valuable insight for the aerodynamic design and safe operation of long-span rail bridges in wind-prone regions.

papers.title: A comprehensively validated three-step global mechanism for high-fidelity simulation of oblique detonation waves in n-decane–air mixtures
papers.abstract: This study presents a new three-step global chemical mechanism for n-decane/air combustion, specifically optimized for efficient simulation of oblique detonation waves (ODWs). The parameters in the global mechanism were specially formulated to enable predictions of essential features in ODWs, including ignition delays, heat release distribution, and detonation velocity with substantially reduced computational cost while preserving fidelity. Comprehensive validations are conducted through extensive numerical simulations, supported by direct comparisons with experimental shock tube data and a skeletal mechanism (Skel40). The proposed mechanism was found to demonstrate predictive robustness across a wide range of combustor conditions, spanning initial temperatures from 600 to 1600 K, pressures from 10 to 1000 kPa, and equivalence ratios from 0.5 to 1.6. As demonstrated in two-dimensional simulations of ODWs, the proposed three-step mechanism predicts key features consistent with those from Skel40 but with a 56-fold improvement in computational efficiency. This new capability provides a reliable and convenient alternative for system-level detonation modeling.

papers.title: Analysis of operating pressure and injection–production frequency on the tightness of full-stratum salt cavern hydrogen storage
papers.abstract: Salt caverns possess superior tightness and are ideal sites for storing gases, such as natural gas and hydrogen. Compared with natural gas, hydrogen has a smaller molecular size and is more prone to leakage; therefore, the simplified stratigraphic models commonly used in previous storage studies are no longer sufficient to characterize tightness under long-term cyclic injection–withdrawal. Considering the geological conditions of the Pingdingshan area, we establish a full-stratum digital model of a salt-cavern hydrogen-storage facility and, using single-factor analysis together with response-surface-based multi-factor analysis (Response Surface Methodology, Box-Behnken Design), investigate how the minimum operating pressure, maximum operating pressure, and injection–production frequency affect tightness after 100 years of continuous operation. The results show that (1) Increasing the minimum operating pressure can not only suppress hydrogen backflow but also intensify gas leakage, thereby increasing the leakage rate. In contrast, increasing the maximum operating pressure slightly increases hydrogen leakage but reduces the overall leakage rate. (2) Increasing the injection–production frequency significantly boosts the working gas volume and reduces the hydrogen leakage rate. In this study, when the minimum operating pressure is 6.93 MPa, the maximum operating pressure is 16.17 MPa, and the annual injection-production frequency is increased to 4 times, the salt cavern meets the tightness evaluation standards. (3) Response surface analysis indicates that injection–production frequency is the most influential factor affecting hydrogen leakage, with its interaction with minimum pressure being particularly significant. Furthermore, a multivariate regression model is established to quantify the relationship between operating conditions and cumulative leakage rate, providing a theoretical basis for optimizing hydrogen storage design.

papers.title: Agglomeration characteristics under the effect of non-uniform particle sorting on a rough bed surface
papers.abstract: Non-uniform sediment grain activity significantly influences riverbed evolution and stability. To examine the agglomeration characteristics of non-uniform particles due to water flow sorting, we conducted a flume test using various particle sizes. The motion of non-uniform particles was recorded using high-definition camera technology under different hydraulic conditions. The structural characteristics of agglomerates were analyzed using multi-target tracking technology and particle image velocimetry. The experimental results indicate that the transport velocity of large particles correlates positively with water depth, whereas that of small particles first increases, then decreases, and subsequently increases with water depth. Under the action of sorting, particles form four types of agglomerates: strip, curve, triangle, and rhombus. The head of the strip structure captures particles, leading to a pileup, while the particle crowding force in the tail weakens. Large particles move under the action of water flow, transforming the strip structure into a curve type. The tail of the curve structures are displaced by water flow interference, evolving into closed triangle and rhombus structures. The average velocity at the tail end of strip and curve structures is higher than that of triangular and rhombic structures. They are significantly affected by water flow and have relatively weak stability. Rhombic structures are the most stable, followed by triangle structures. We systematically revealed the agglomeration characteristics and evolution law of non-uniform particles under the action of water flow sorting, providing a quantitative basis for the regulation of riverbed stability.

papers.title: Laboratory simulation of slowflows
papers.abstract: Slowflows occur widely in both industrial settings and geophysical environments, with earthflows representing a slow, viscous downslope movement of water-saturated fine materials. This study presents novel laboratory simulations to model such flows using a highly viscous molten jaggery as a viscous analogue for natural earthflows. Although jaggery lacks granular and plastic constituents, its viscosity falls well within the range of certain natural earthflows, allowing it to represent essential aspects of viscous mass movements. Experiments were conducted on low to moderately inclined chutes, mimicking natural terrains. Flow dynamics, such as the evolution of flow velocity, depth, and deformation, are exclusively analyzed. Results reveal tongue-shaped, centrally thickened flows with a frontal bulge and rear depression. These behaviors are consistent with large-scale simulations of earthflows. Flow evolution displayed a kinematic transition: initial acceleration is driven by free-surface pressure gradients, followed by deceleration, leading to a near steady velocity. Flow geometry evolves rapidly with increasing slope. Velocity patterns are governed by the interplay among the gravitational, free-surface pressure gradient, and the viscous forces. The front motion is well-described by combining a power law with a hyperbolic tangent function. Overall, molten jaggery proves to be a simplified, yet, dynamically meaningful analogue of viscous earthflows. Experimental results of the molten jaggery may be utilized for the validation of existing earthflow models. Here, we only consider the viscous material, not including the plastic behavior. However, further extensions of the present study to real heterogeneous, visco-plastic natural materials are needed to widen the scope of the present study.

papers.title: Study on the evolution of near-wall jet induced by serial collapse of twin bubbles and its load amplification characteristics
papers.abstract: Bubbles are commonly found in both natural environments and engineering applications. Since they rarely exist in isolation, more complex jet phenomena can emerge due to multi-bubble interactions. In particular, the collapse of two bubbles near a rigid wall generates high-speed jet loads directed toward the wall. These jet characteristics can be regulated by controlling bubble interactions, and the jet enhancement effect resulting from two-bubble coupling holds great promise for practical applications. This study investigates the variation in jet loads from near-wall double bubbles using both underwater spark experiments and numerical simulations. A numerical model was developed to simulate two-bubble interactions near a rigid boundary, accurately capturing the full dynamic process of bubble generation, expansion, collapse, and jet formation. It also predicts the wall loads induced during bubble coupling and collapse. The simulation results closely match the experimental observations of bubble dynamics and wall pressure, confirming the model's accuracy. On this basis, the effects of bubble–wall distance (γw), bubble–bubble distance (γb), and detonation time difference (τ) on bubble-induced loads were further explored. The results reveal that the spatial arrangement and timing of the explosions significantly influence bubble motion, jet formation, and wall pressure. Under optimal conditions (γw=1.2, γb=1, τ=1), a coordinated collapse mechanism substantially enhances the peak pressure. Additionally, a global sensitivity analysis based on the Kriging surrogate model and Sobol method was conducted to quantify the influence of spatial arrangement and initiation timing. The results indicate that the bubble–wall distance γw has the greatest influence, followed by the bubble–bubble distance γb, while the detonation time difference τ has the least effect.

papers.title: Computational aeroacoustics of a heated supersonic jet exhausting an aerospike nozzle
papers.abstract: Implicit large eddy simulations are deployed to simulate the flow of an aerospike nozzle jet at a nozzle pressure ratio = 3 and four temperature ratios (TR) = 1, 3, 4, and 7. The large eddy simulation (LES) calculations are completed by aeroacoustic computations based on the Ffowcs Williams-Hawkings equation. In the supersonic jet exhausting the aerospike nozzle, two shock-cell structures are observed: an annular and a circular one. Higher TR leads to longer shock cells in the annular jet region. In the meantime, the shock cell count in the circular part of the jet decreases with increasing jet TR. Supersonic convection velocities of turbulent structures are detected with increasing TR by means of two-point cross-correlations, indicating the presence of Mach waves. Furthermore, high skewness and kurtosis of the pressure signals along the Mach wave propagation direction indicate crackle noise at higher TR. Screech noise is observed in the near-field signature of the supersonic jets. This sound component has a pronounced multi-peak behavior. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition of the azimuthally decomposed pressure fields and space–time Fourier transforms of the pressure fluctuations are used to identify the most amplified wavepackets propagating downstream and the upstream waves responsible for closing the screech feedback loop. The simulation results exhibit close correspondence with the theoretical neutral waves predicted by the vortex sheet model. In the cold case, the main screech feedback loop involves only the annular shock-cell structure, whereas at higher TR, both shock-cell structures contribute to the feedback mechanism.

papers.title: Gas properties' impact on flow dynamics and thermal characteristics in a Hartmann–Sprenger tube
papers.abstract: The Hartmann–Sprenger (H–S) tube has attracted considerable attention due to its applicability in acoustics and ignition studies. Although its operational mechanisms have been extensively investigated, the influence of gas properties on its performance remains insufficiently characterized. This study numerically examines the flow and thermal behavior of eight different gases and hydrogen–oxygen mixtures in an H–S tube over different nozzle pressure ratios (NPRs), using a two-dimensional axisymmetric model with explicit time discretization and a second-order upwind spatial scheme. The results show that the gas specific heat ratio and molecular mass primarily govern the temperature evolution, response time, and transition from initial transients to quasi-harmonic oscillations, whereas the overall pressure amplitude depends mainly on NPR and geometry constraints. Monatomic gases yield higher temperature rises, but the maximum pressure remains relatively insensitive to gas type under identical driving conditions (NPR). When the time histories are normalized by the characteristic sound speed factor (γ/M), the pressure and temperature oscillations of different gases exhibit similar phase patterns, indicating a scaled dynamic correspondence. Also, by normalizing temperature records using γ, all gases show almost the same levels for temperature, indicating similar changes in normalized thermal energy. These results provide a physically interpretable framework linking thermodynamic properties to oscillation frequency, temperature rise, and response time, supporting more informed selection of working gases for ignition or resonant-tube applications.

papers.title: Formation mechanism and control of microclimate zone with low velocity ratio jet in coal mining face
papers.abstract: Optimizing cooling efficiency in confined spaces with high-temperature crossflows, such as underground mines, remains a major challenge. This study investigates the formation and control of localized head–neck microclimates using multi-stage, low-velocity-ratio (R) jets in crossflow. The work establishes a vortex-structure–guided spacing principle that links the evolution of hairpin vortices to the continuity of cooling zones. Experimental flow visualization combined with large-eddy simulation reveals that the evolution and breakdown of hairpin vortices divide the flow field into four regions—strong attachment, weak attachment, fragmentation, and dissipation—each with distinct cooling characteristics. Based on this classification, a variable-spacing strategy is proposed, positioning downstream jets within the weak attachment zone of upstream vortices to effectively utilize residual cooling energy and maintain a continuous low-temperature region. Compared with uniform-spacing arrangements, the proposed design reduces the dimensionless temperature decay rate by 54.4% at the fifth-stage jet and suppresses excessive mixing, leading to lower energy dissipation and extended cooling coverage. These findings provide new insights and practical guidance for airflow management in mitigating heat hazards at coal mining faces.

papers.title: Lattice Boltzmann-immersed boundary method simulation of liquid bridge between two moving particles
papers.abstract: Accurate modeling of liquid bridge dynamics between moving particles is critical for understanding particle agglomeration, coating, and flotation processes; however, resolving the coupled fluid–particle interactions at realistic scales remains challenging. In this work, we develop a coupled lattice Boltzmann-immersed boundary method (LBM-IBM) framework to investigate the transient formation, evolution, and rupture of liquid bridges between two moving particles. The effects of droplet diameter, Reynolds number, Bond number, particles' diameter ratio, and eccentricity ratio are systematically analyzed. The study identifies distinct stages of particle motion: an initial stage dominated by hydrodynamic forces, a collision-dominated stage, and a final stage governed by gravity and capillary forces, with further sub-stages arising from capillary effects. A liquid ring forms for sufficiently large droplets and its size increases with rising eccentricity. The rupture of the liquid bridge is delayed when viscosity, gravitational effects, or particle asymmetry increase. Occasional cavitation bubble formation is also observed. This work demonstrates that the LBM–IBM coupling enables accurate resolution of microscale fluid–particle interactions and can provide quantitative insights relevant to spray coating, dust removal, and fine particle flotation, addressing a critical gap in current multiphase modeling approaches.

papers.title: Investigation into the stall inception of low specific-speed centrifugal pumps
papers.abstract: Stall in centrifugal pumps can induce adverse effects on unit operation, such as operational instability and low–frequency pressure pulsations. In deep stall, a substantial increase in energy demand is required to restore the impeller's internal flow to a stable condition. However, the onset and evolution mechanisms of stall remain poorly understood. Clarifying the characteristics and mechanisms of stall inception is therefore of significant importance. In this study, high–fidelity numerical simulations were conducted to investigate the topological evolution of three–dimensional flow structures within the impeller during stall inception, with the objective of elucidating its formation mechanism. Through combined qualitative and quantitative analyses, internal flow–field characteristics and circumferential flow–rate distributions were systematically compared under stall and non–stall conditions. The results indicate that the circumferential coefficient of variation (CV) of the single–passage flow–rate coefficient is highly sensitive to variations in operating conditions.
