During the dynamic transition from non–stall to stall conditions, the evolution of internal flow patterns within the impeller closely follows the trend of the CV curve. This correlation enables precise identification of stall inception and reveals its spatiotemporal characteristics. Moreover, transient analysis of the slip–angle distribution reveals that alternate stall in centrifugal impellers is driven by the combined action of a separation vortex and a corner vortex. The corner vortex, generated at the junction between the shroud and the blade suction surface, plays a dominant role during stall inception. These findings provide valuable guidance for preventing centrifugal pumps from entering stall conditions and for extending their range of stable, efficient performance.

papers.title: Effect of a wavy-type combustion chamber on fuel–air mixing and power performance of an aviation piston engine
papers.abstract: A new wavy-type combustion chamber was designed to solve the problems of difficult atomization and poor combustion stability of aviation kerosene. The effects of structural parameters of the wavy-type combustion chamber on fuel–air mixing and power performance of the aviation kerosene direct-injection piston engine at 5500 rpm and full-load cruise were systematically studied. The results show that in-cylinder maximum turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), explosion pressure, and heat release rate first rise then decline with increasing central boss depth, with Configuration A3 (2.65 mm) as the optimal design. In contrast to the poorest-performing A1, A3 delivers 2.9% higher TKE, 15.8% greater maximum explosion pressure, and 17.3% enhanced maximum heat release rate, with the maximum knock factor dropping to 2.5 at 1 °CA after top dead center (significant knock suppression). Analogously, the three parameters follow the same trend with increasing side boss depth, with B3 (3.3 mm) optimal. In contrast to B1, B3 achieves 3.2% higher maximum TKE, 15.8% greater maximum explosion pressure, 19.3% enhanced maximum heat release rate, and a knock factor of 3.0 (effective knock mitigation). The wavy-type combustion chamber attains optimal performance with 2.65 mm central boss and 3.3 mm side boss, outperforming the open-type by 8.6% in maximum explosion pressure and 2.6% in maximum heat release rate. The design and research of the wavy-type combustion chamber contributes to improving the combustion process of the engine and further enhancing the overall performance of the engine.

papers.title: The coupling mechanism between the transient rotary speed and the flow field of the flapping-wing rotor via dynamic fluid–body interaction modeling
papers.abstract: To help understand the flow field mechanisms behind the entire process of a flapping-wing rotor (FWR) from startup to dynamic equilibrium of rotary motion, this study develops a dynamic fluid–body interaction (DFBI) model to predict the aerodynamics of the FWR, wherein the DFBI model is used to accurately realize the wing's motions within the simulation. The computational fluid dynamics model in this work is rigorously validated through grid independence studies, time-step independence studies, model independence studies, and comparison with prior data. An experimental lift measurement platform is also constructed. Based on these tools, this study investigates the coupling mechanism between transient rotary speed and flow field and the effect of reduction ratio on the FWR's aerodynamic performance. Key findings indicate that rotary motion significantly suppresses negative lift during the upstroke. In addition, releasing the rotary degree of freedom alters vortex dynamics, shifting the leading-edge vortex core and affecting its structure during downstroke and upstroke. A reduction ratio of 28 is identified as optimal, yielding approximately 20% higher average lift compared to a reduction ratio of 24.5. Overall, this work facilitates the understanding for the FWR's dynamic equilibrium of rotary motion and offers valuable design guidance for further enhancing the lift performance of the FWR.

papers.title: Graph neural network modeling of free-surface flows in non-Newtonian power-law fluids
papers.abstract: In this study, we propose a graph neural network (GNN)-based numerical model for efficiently predicting the flow behavior of non-Newtonian fluids with free surface dynamics. Conventional numerical approaches, such as the finite element method, often suffer from computational inefficiency and convergence issues when simulating non-Newtonian fluids whose viscosity varies dynamically with the local shear rate. To overcome these limitations, particle-based methods such as smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) have been developed, offering greater robustness for complex free-surface flows. However, SPH remains constrained by hardware-dependent scalability, as even parallelization techniques using graphics processing units (GPUs) are limited by system-specific constraints and computational cost. To address these challenges, we extend the SPH framework by introducing a graph neural network (GNN)-based model, which achieves efficient, data-driven prediction of non-Newtonian fluid dynamics. In this work, we focus on power-law fluids, one of the simplest models of non-Newtonian behavior. Our GNN model is trained on SPH simulation data, learning the effects of particle accelerations in the presence of SPH particle interactions based on the fluid's power-law model parameters. We demonstrate that the GNN significantly accelerates computations while maintaining reliable accuracy in benchmark tests, including dam-break and droplet impact simulations. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that the GNN reduces computation time by approximately 30% compared to conventional SPH simulations, while maintaining comparable accuracy across benchmark problems such as dam-break and droplet impact cases. The results highlight the potential of GNN-based frameworks for simulating non-Newtonian free-surface flows, paving the way for future data-driven non-Newtonian fluid modeling.

papers.title: Sound-vortex conversion on droplets: Unraveling acoustic quantum vortices for vortex energy analysis
papers.abstract: Vortices—a universal motion form with analogous rotational traits—exist in both quantum fluids (e.g., superfluid helium, Bose–Einstein condensates) and classical fluids (e.g., water). However, current theories explain quantum and classical vortices in isolation (via quantum mechanics and classical fluid mechanics, respectively), creating a gap in understanding their shared energy features. To address the core question “Do vortices have common energy characteristics transcending quantum and classical theories?” this study provides rigorous experimental and theoretical evidence: energy quantization (a core quantum trait) emerges in sound-excited water vortices (classical vortices) at the micrometer-to-millimeter scale. This energy quantization modulates the adjacent microfluidic environment, endowing acoustic vortices with topological robustness and driving two typical collision modes (“head-to-head” and “side-by-side”). Notably, this quantum-like behavior in classical water-based vortices is independent of quantum mechanical mechanisms. The study establishes a top-down vortex energy analysis approach, which interprets the energy of vortices within the host field using the intrinsic angular momentum constraint of the entire host fields. Critically, the intrinsic irrotational nature of these fields may consistently endow the vortices they generate—whether quantum or classical—with three shared characteristics: energy quantization, topological robustness, and hydrodynamic entanglement.

papers.title: On breakup in droplet collision and coalescence: Surfactant-induced suppression
papers.abstract: For collision between two droplets with sufficiently large Weber numbers (We), regimes of coalescence (III), reflexive separation (IV), and stretching separation (V) after temporary coalescence have been identified in accordance with specific ranges of the impact parameter (B) and Ohnesorge number (Oh). Recognizing that prevention of droplet breakup is critical for various applications, here we discuss the mechanism governing the transition between the breakup regimes and experimentally study the influence of surfactants on the response in the various regimes. It is shown that, compared to the surfactant-free case, adding surfactant substantially delays the occurrence of regime IV, requiring notably larger critical We (Wec) for the transition between regimes of coalescence III and IV. By increasing the surfactant concentration (Φ) over the critical micelle concentration (CMC), Wec decreases although it is still significantly larger than that of surfactant-free cases, even when Φ is 40 times the CMC. Similar suppression with surfactant addition is also observed for the transition between regimes III and V, showing at least 45% larger B required to reach regime V as compared to the surfactant-free cases. Furthermore, by comparing the collision sequences with and without surfactant, with similar values of B, Oh, and We, the nondimensional maximum length of relaxation (Lm) in the surfactant-free cases is substantially larger than that with surfactant addition. The results demonstrate significant effects of surfactant addition in droplets on the suppression of further breakup after merging.

papers.title: A two-phase flow and heat transfer model for microencapsulated phase change material suspensions
papers.abstract: This study investigates the flow and heat transfer characteristics of microencapsulated phase change material suspensions in a square cavity by developing a coupled two-phase flow model that integrates the lattice Boltzmann method and discrete element method. The partially saturated cell method is employed to simulate the solid–liquid interface, while the effective specific heat method is adopted to capture the phase change behavior of microcapsule particles. A comprehensive analysis is conducted to examine the effects of microcapsule concentration, Rayleigh number, phase change temperature, and particle size on the suspension's flow and heat transfer performances. The results reveal that the inclusion of microcapsule particles significantly enhances the effective specific heat capacity of the suspension. Particle aggregation behavior is primarily influenced by the Rayleigh number. At lower Rayleigh numbers, particles are randomly distributed, while rapid aggregation occurs due to thermophoretic forces at high Rayleigh numbers. At a certain microcapsule concentration, the suspension achieves an optimal balance between heat capacity enhancement and flow stability. The results indicate that the microcapsule particles with a diameter of 75 μm can effectively release latent heat while avoiding the pronounced fluctuations associated with larger particles. Furthermore, the highest latent heat release efficiency is observed when the phase change temperature is close to the average cavity temperature. This study demonstrates that the Rayleigh number plays a pivotal role in governing the transition of the flow regime from laminar to turbulent by modulating the buoyancy-to-viscous force ratio, which in turn influences particle aggregation and heat transfer intensity of microencapsulated phase change material suspensions.

papers.title: Water-sheet atomization and spray characterization from convergent nozzles
papers.abstract: This study investigates atomization in water-sheet sprays issued from convergent nozzles. High-speed shadowgraphy is used to map breakup regimes, and laser diffraction is used to quantify droplet-size distributions across systematic variations of the flow rate, nozzle outlet aspect ratio, and convergent angle. Within the Weber number-angle (We–θ) space, two stable regimes and a third, unstable one are identified, with the latter exhibiting chaotic atomization and further subdividing into three sub-regimes. The droplet-size distributions are often bimodal, with a large-drop peak linked to rim-driven pinch-off and a fine-drop peak associated with sheet-driven atomization. Moreover, power-law correlations are developed for breakup length, Sauter mean diameter (d32), and number-mean diameter (d10). These scalings reflect the interplay of inertia, surface tension, and viscosity, where stronger aerodynamic/viscous forcing (higher capillary number) yields finer sprays (smaller d32 and d10) while pushing breakup downstream, with the nozzle geometry modulating these trends: larger outlet aspect ratios slightly lengthen breakup yet suppress droplet sizes, whereas larger convergent angles shorten breakup and further reduce characteristic diameters. These results provide a predictive framework for estimating breakup length and droplet sizes across various operating conditions, enabling the design of compact sheet-spray devices.

papers.title: Particle size non-uniformity governs the dynamics and seismic response of rock avalanche granular flows: Insights from laboratory experiments
papers.abstract: Rock avalanches are highly destructive geological hazards characterized by complex dynamic behaviors, and their granular flow processes are strongly influenced by particle size distribution. To reveal the effects of particle size non-uniformity on the kinematic, depositional, and seismic characteristics of granular flows, a controllable granular flow collapse simulation system is designed. Five gradation conditions are constructed by varying the particle size non-uniformity coefficient (Cu), and the particle motion is quantitatively analyzed using particle image velocimetry, multi-view three-dimensional reconstruction, and seismic signal monitoring techniques. The results show that Cu is a key factor controlling the dynamic evolution of granular flows. As Cu increases, the maximum mean velocity (Vmax), runout distance (R), and both deposit length (L) and width (D) increase significantly, indicating that particle size non-uniformity enhances flow mobility and energy transfer efficiency. In terms of depositional morphology, the deposits evolve from a typical fan-shaped structure to a transitional pattern and finally to a “W”-shaped double-peaked structure with increasing Cu. Seismic signal analysis reveals that the peak ground acceleration, mean envelope value, and Arias intensity all increase markedly with higher Cu, while the spectral characteristics of the signals shift from high-frequency dominance to multi-frequency coupling, indicating that particle size non-uniformity intensifies inter-particle collisions and frictional interactions. Correlation analysis further shows that the seismic signal parameters are significantly and positively correlated with the kinematic parameters (R, Vmax) and depositional parameters (L, D), demonstrating that seismic signals effectively reflect the flow intensity and depositional characteristics of granular flows.

papers.title: Mechanisms of energy retention and instability suppression in rotating jets with inlet guide vanes
papers.abstract: Rotating jets are widely employed in energy and environmental equipment, and their instability can weaken jet energy-retention characteristics and induce severe energy loss. The regulatory effect of inlet guide vanes (IGVs) on energy retention and instability in rotating jets was investigated using delayed detached eddy simulation, combined with vortex dynamics and entropy production theory. A comparative analysis was conducted between a conventional submersible guided thruster (SGT) and an integrated inlet-guide-vane submersible thruster. Results demonstrate that the IGV-induced counter-prewhirl effectively disrupts the spatial coherence among the tip leakage vortex (TLV), hub vortex (HV), and vortex ring (VR), fundamentally reshaping the energy-transfer pathways. The IGVs strengthen the shear interaction between the HV and the main flow, accelerating HV dissipation and reducing TLV–HV coherence. Quantitatively, the onset of deep instability is delayed from 3.5D to 6.5D downstream, and the peak entropy-production intensity decreases by 22%. In addition, IGV-induced short-wave perturbations promote TLV circumferential breakdown, suppress pitchwise vortex pairing, and nearly eliminate VR-driven HV oscillations. Consequently, approximately 50% of the initial available power is preserved at z/D > 12, representing a 20-percentage-point improvement over the SGT. This study clarifies the dual role of IGVs in regulating jet energy decay and instability, providing guidance for hydrodynamic equipment optimization and energy efficiency enhancement.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical investigations of incidence angle and cross-sectional aspect ratio effects for the flow over wall-mounted rectangular cylinders
papers.abstract: In this study, both experimental and numerical methods (large eddy simulation, LES) are used to investigate the flow over wall-mounted rectangular cylinders with various cross-sectional aspect ratios (CR = 1–4, representing the ratio of the sides of the cylinder cross section) and incidence angles (α = 0°–90°). The Reynolds number is defined using the free-stream velocity and the projected width of the cylinder in the flow direction, i.e., Rew = (12–48) × 103. The experimental results of surface pressure and the Strouhal number (obtained through hot wire measurements) are used to validate the numerical results. This comparison shows a good agreement between both experimental and numerical results. A single frequency is found for all positions along the cylinder height and also at the other places employed for any given CR and α. The experimental and LES results of the present study confirmed this finding. It is observed that there is a maximum Strouhal number (Sta) at a specific angle (critical angle, αc) for each CR, i.e., αc = 15°, 10°, 5°, and 0° for CR = 1, 2, 3, and 4, respectively. Interestingly, for any CR, where St reaches its maximum value at the critical angle, the drag coefficient (C¯D) reaches its minimum value due to the formation of the maximum length of the separation bubble on the lateral surface, as well as the creation of a narrow-width wake flow.

papers.title: The coupled influences of angle of attack and rotational motion on the cavitation flow around a cylinder vehicle
papers.abstract: In this study, the detached eddy simulation (DES) turbulence model coupled with the Schnerr–Sauer cavitation model is employed to numerically investigate the cavity evolution of a rotating underwater vehicle at different rotational speeds and angles of attack. The results reveal the coupled influences of rotation and angle of attack (AOA) on the cavitation flow field characteristics surrounding the vehicle. Specifically, the angle of attack causes the fluid from the upper side of the vehicle to migrate gradually toward the lower side along the body surface, thereby generating two additional streamwise vortices of equal magnitude but opposite direction, leading to a symmetric twin-vortex (TV) structure in the wake. However, the rotation of the vehicle strengthens the vortex with the same rotation direction while weakening that with the opposite direction, thereby resulting in an asymmetric twin-vortex structure, or even a single-vortex structure. Therefore, the internal pressure distribution of the cavity is modified, which subsequently changes the phase transition process between liquid water and vapor. Moreover, cavity evolution analysis shows that the angle of attack predominantly affects the shape of the cavity along its upper and lower surfaces, whereas rotation primarily influences its lateral shape. By modifying the Savchenko empirical formula, a predictive model for the cavity profile under non-zero angle of attack conditions is derived. The analysis demonstrates that the critical wetted angle of attack is inversely proportional to both the cavitation number and the aspect ratio, thereby revealing the constraint relations among aspect ratio, cavitation number, and angle of attack on supercavitating conditions.

papers.title: Erratum: “Optimization of magneto-thin film bioconvection flow of bi-viscosity Bingham fluid with swarm microorganism using machine learning-integrated numerical simulations” [Phys. Fluids 37 , 092026 (2025)]
On phase transition dynamics of ammonia droplet under high pressure conditions
papers.abstract: The phase transition dynamics of ammonia droplets under high-pressure conditions, representative of advanced engine combustors, exhibit a remarkable complexity driven by drastic variations in thermophysical properties and the progressive diffusion of the vapor–liquid interface. This phenomenon renders classical evaporation models inadequate for accurately predicting the critical fuel–gas mixing process. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a high-pressure transient phase transition model that could capture the complete lifecycle of a single ammonia droplet in a nitrogen environment, from injection to full mixing. Results show that the process is not simple evaporation but instead evolves through three continuous stages governed by distinct physical mechanisms, i.e., a classical two-phase stage, a previously overlooked transitional two-phase stage, and a supercritical single-phase mixing stage. The latter two stages prove to be particularly critical. During the transitional stage, a rapid interface thickening and a sharp reduction in surface tension not only challenge the validity of the classical phase-equilibrium assumption but also lead to a dramatic collapse in the droplet's stability against external perturbations. Upon entering the supercritical stage, the efficient conversion from a liquid-like to a gas-like fluid is driven by a pseudo-boiling phenomenon, resulting in mixing rates far exceeding those dictated by conventional evaporation. These findings provide a deeper physical understanding of high-pressure fuel phase transitions and establish a critical theoretical basis for developing high-fidelity computational fluid dynamic sub-models to enable precise prediction and control of ammonia spray combustion.

papers.title: Stability analysis of thin film flow on a heated cylindrical surface with effects of heat flux and exponentially varying viscosity
papers.abstract: In paper production, a hollow, uniformly heated Yankee cylinder is often used to dry thin films of paper pulp. To model this drying process, we analyze the gravity-driven, axisymmetric flow of an incompressible Newtonian thin film outside of a vertically oriented, hollow cylindrical wall. An infinitely long wall of small thickness is considered, with a small heater inserted into the inner side to maintain a uniform temperature. The temperature gradient between the heated wall and the liquid generates a steady radial heat flux. Heat loss from the inner surface to the ambient air influences the thermal gradient, a vital aspect overlooked in previous studies. Since viscosity is temperature-dependent, it is assumed to vary exponentially with the local temperature gradient. Using the long-wave expansion approach, we derive a Benny-type nonlinear partial differential equation governing the leading-order evolution of film thickness. A normal mode linear stability analysis determines the complex growth rate of disturbances, employing viscosity variation, heat flux, and heat dissipation at the wall–liquid and wall–air interfaces. The analysis confirms the stabilizing role of the wall Biot number, Bw, and cylinder radius R, while the viscosity coefficient Kμ exerts a destabilizing effect. The effects on steady traveling wave profiles are also analyzed.

papers.title: From stationary to vibrating hyperbolic paraboloid membranes: Evolution of flow fields and wind load under oblique and diagonal winds
papers.abstract: This study investigates the mechanism of self-excited wind-induced vibrations in hyperbolic paraboloid membrane structures, focusing on the fluid–structure interaction (FSI) effects and aerodynamic instability under varying wind angels. To explore the underlying mechanism of the FSI effect, large eddy simulation and the dynamic mesh technique are employed to model the unsteady flow fields, and the results are validated against wind tunnel test data, demonstrating good agreement in both mean and fluctuating wind pressure distributions. The findings reveal that at a 0° wind angle, conical vortices form symmetrically at the windward leading edge, leading to significant pressure gradients. Structural vibration does not notably alter the mean flow field or mean wind pressure but increases fluctuating wind pressure in the mid-span region due to vortex spreading. At a 45° wind angle, the mean flow field exhibits distinct conical vortices, and structural vibration reduces the size of separation vortices while increasing their curvature, resulting in higher wind pressure magnitudes and reduced gradient distribution ranges. Instantaneous flow field analysis shows that structural vibration induces vortices to move toward the mid-span or trailing edge, significantly increasing fluctuating wind pressure in these regions. Furthermore, the correlation between wind speed and fluctuating wind pressure is analyzed, revealing that structural vibration enhances the correlation in the mid-span and trailing edge regions, particularly at a 45° wind angle. These insights provide a deeper understanding of the wind load generation mechanisms and FSI effects in hyperbolic paraboloid membrane structures, offering valuable guidance for the wind-resistant design of such flexible structures.

papers.title: Data-driven reduced modeling of droplet shape evolution on inclined surfaces using the Onsager principle
papers.abstract: The motion of a droplet on an inclined surface involves complex interfacial dynamics in which contact line motion and shape evolution play a critical role. Classical continuum-based and reduced-order models can describe droplet behavior at small inclination angles but fail to capture essential morphological features—such as the sharp rear corner—observed experimentally at larger tilts. To address this limitation, we propose a data-driven reduced-order framework that integrates the Onsager variational principle with functional principal component analysis (FPCA). By extracting dominant basis functions directly from experimental droplet profiles, the method reduces computational cost while retaining physical interpretability. Numerical experiments show that the model accurately reproduces droplet morphologies across a broad range of inclination angles, correcting the unrealistic conical shapes predicted by previous formulations while maintaining the same degrees of freedom as the classical reduced model. More broadly, the approach provides a systematic strategy for embedding experimental data into variational modeling, offering new opportunities for predictive and efficient analysis of complex interfacial flows.

papers.title: The influence of boundary conditions and interfacial slip on the time taken to achieve a nonequilibrium steady-state for boundary-driven flows
papers.abstract: In this study, we investigate the equilibration time to attain steady-state for a system of liquid molecules under boundary-driven planar Couette flow via nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD) simulation. In particular, we examine the equilibration time for the two common types of boundary-driven flow: one in which both walls slide with equal and opposite velocity (±û/2), and the other in which one wall is fixed and the other moves with twice the velocity (û). Both flows give identical steady-state strain rates and, hence, flow properties, but the transient behavior is completely different. We find that in the case of no-slip boundary conditions, the equilibration times for the counter-sliding walls flow are exactly four times faster than those of the single-sliding wall system, and this is independent of the atomistic nature of the fluid, i.e., it is an entirely hydrodynamic feature. We also find that systems that exhibit slip have longer equilibration times in general, and the ratio of equilibration times for the two types of boundary-driven flow is even more pronounced. We analyze the problem by decomposing a generic planar Couette flow into a linear sum of purely symmetric and antisymmetric flows. We find that the no-slip equilibration time is dominated by the slowest decaying eigenvalue of the solution to the Navier–Stokes equation. In the case of slip, the longest relaxation time is now dominated by the transient slip velocity response, which is longer than the no-slip response time. In the case of a high-slip system of water confined to graphene channels, the enhancement is over two orders of magnitude. We propose a simple universal relation that predicts the enhanced equilibration time, which agrees well with our NEMD results for simple Lennard-Jones fluids and the water–graphene system. The implications of this significant speed-up in attaining steady-state, which is especially pronounced in the presence of slip, are discussed in general.

papers.title: Molecular dynamics study of the desublimation and frost formation of carbon dioxide on cryogenic nanostructured surfaces
papers.abstract: The microscopic investigation of carbon dioxide (CO2) desublimation and frost formation on cryogenic surfaces is crucial for advancing cryogenic carbon capture technology, yet remains difficult to resolve directly in experiments. While macroscopic frosting behavior is well documented, the molecular mechanisms of CO2 desublimation, particularly on nanostructured surfaces, are still underexplored compared with those of condensation. Here, we employ molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the frosting process of gaseous CO2 on cryogenic nanogroove surfaces. The results reveal that CO2 undergoes three distinct stages: adsorption and aggregation, crystal nucleation, and crystal growth, ultimately forming an ordered Pa3 phase crystal structure consistent with experimental dry ice. By analyzing the energy evolution and structural kinetics, we identify a critical design trade-off: increasing the interaction coefficient α and groove depth H significantly enhances surface affinity and heat transfer, thereby shortening the nucleation time and accelerating frost formation, for example, reducing the nucleation time from 5.3 to 2.2 ns as the surface becomes more CO2-philic. However, these modifications also strengthen interfacial adhesion, making the frost layer more difficult to detach. Consequently, we propose that surface design must be tailored to the operational cycle: high-affinity, rough surfaces are preferable for continuous high-throughput capture, whereas lower-energy surfaces are more suitable for systems requiring frequent, low-energy regeneration. These insights provide theoretical guidance for optimizing both the efficiency and defrosting performance of cryogenic carbon capture heat exchangers.

papers.title: Ultrasonic three-dimensional reconstruction and measurement technology for complex propellant free surfaces
papers.abstract: In microgravity, the free-surface morphology of propellants inside metallic tanks becomes highly complex, while conventional optical and capacitive measurement methods face significant limitations: optical techniques cannot penetrate opaque metal walls, and capacitive sensors are easily affected by wall conductivity. Ultrasonic techniques offer a promising alternative; however, most existing approaches are confined to two-dimensional planar detection and are inadequate for reconstructing intricate three-dimensional (3D) free-surface morphologies. To address this challenge, we propose a three-dimensional reconstruction method for complex propellant free surfaces based on the principle of multipath ultrasonic reflection. A multi-channel, array-based ultrasonic system was developed to enable synchronous tomographic acquisition. Building on ultrasonic reflection tomography, an elliptical reflection element method was formulated and implemented. To experimentally validate the method under terrestrial conditions, solid–liquid interfaces were employed as surrogates for gas–liquid interfaces. Experiments involving three representative surface models achieved a minimum relative error of 2.68% and a maximum below 6.17%. The results demonstrate that the proposed ultrasonic approach enables accurate three-dimensional reconstruction of free-surface morphology within closed metallic tanks.

papers.title: Deformation and breakup of an electrohydrodynamic falling droplet in viscous fluids under vertical/horizontal electric fields
papers.abstract: Droplet dynamics is a class of phenomena ubiquitous in both natural and industrial processes. In this paper, we developed a phase-field lattice Boltzmann method to investigate the electrohydrodynamic falling droplet under vertically and horizontally applied electric fields. The electric field model is based on the leaky dielectric theory, and numerical results are validated by Taylor's theory, showing good agreement under small deformation conditions. It was found that the vertical electric field suppresses the depression at the droplet tail. When the intensity of the electric field is high, the droplet stretches along the electric field direction, which ultimately results in the droplet breakup. In contrast, a horizontal electric field drives lateral expansion, which facilitates the formation of a crescent-shaped structure, followed by the bubble breakup. An increase in the conductivity ratio enhances the lateral deformation of the droplet, while an increase in the dielectric constant ratio suppresses the occurrence of lateral deformation. This study reveals the regulatory mechanism of electric fields on droplet morphology and motion, providing a theoretical basis and numerical foundation for droplet manipulation in complex multi-physical field environments.

papers.title: Erratum: “Early-time resonances in the three-dimensional wall-bounded axisymmetric Euler and related equations” [Phys. Fluids 36 (9), 097159 (2024)]
Study on cavitation number and cavitating flow characteristics in a narrow rectangular Venturi tube
papers.abstract: This study investigates the applicability of different cavitation number definitions and the influence of Venturi geometry on cavitating flow dynamics within a narrow rectangular Venturi tube. Experiments were conducted in a closed-loop water tunnel using high-speed imaging and grayscale-based image processing to characterize cavity morphology and shedding behavior. Three kinds of cavitation numbers were evaluated. The results demonstrate that the inlet cavitation number fails to reflect cavitation intensity due to strong blockage effects, while the outlet cavitation number captures overall growth trends but lacks sensitivity to transitions in shedding mechanisms. In contrast, the pressure-drop cavitation number provides accurate and robust characterization of cavitation intensity and effectively identifies regime transitions between reentrant-jet- and shock-wave-dominated shedding. Geometric effects were also examined: larger divergence angles promote periodic large-scale cloud cavitation shedding due to stronger adverse pressure gradients, while smaller angles lead to quasi-steady cavitation with tail-dominated collapse. Furthermore, reducing throat height increased cavity length by weakening reentrant jet penetration. These findings provide new insights into the appropriate scaling of cavitation number in confined Venturi flows and advance the understanding of geometry-induced modulation of unsteady cavitation dynamics.

papers.title: Hydrodynamics of squirmers: A review on Stokesian principles, analytical frameworks, and recent advances
papers.abstract: Squirmer hydrodynamics forms the basis for analyzing self-propulsion in viscous environments, bridging biological and artificial microswimmers through a unified representation that relies on surface slip velocities and their induced flow fields. This review outlines detailed aspects of squirmer modeling and dynamics, highlighting the role of swimming modes and their influence on propulsion efficiency and flow topology. Analytical tools central to microhydrodynamics, such as Faxén's laws, multipole expansions, the Lorentz reciprocal theorem, the zero-force and zero-torque criteria, Stokesian dynamics, and the formulation of mobility matrices, are systematically reviewed for their application in studying swimmer–fluid interactions. The review also examines the role of confinement, addressing motion within complex geometrical environments and near solid boundaries, where hydrodynamic interactions significantly alter trajectories, stability, and collective behavior. Particular attention is given to the modification of squirmer locomotion and reorientation dynamics in proximity to walls, along with near-field lubrication effects. The review also presents recent advancements in the field, encompassing topics such as collective dynamics and pairwise swimmer interactions under various boundary and flow conditions. Overall, the analysis provides a comprehensive microhydrodynamical perspective, integrating classical theory with modern computational approaches, thereby offering a unified framework for understanding and predicting the behavior of microswimmers in complex fluidic environments.

papers.title: Enhanced large-scale motions and suppressed very-large-scale motions in a rotating annular flume
papers.abstract: This study presents an experimental investigation into how Prandtl's first-kind secondary currents, induced by streamline curvature, modulate large- and very-large-scale motions (LSMs and VLSMs). While previous research has shown that Prandtl's second-kind secondary currents (driven by turbulence anisotropy) can suppress VLSMs and promote secondary current instabilities (SCIs), the effects of Prandtl's first-kind secondary currents on these motions have remained unexplored. We address this gap using a rotating annular flume to subject LSMs and VLSMs to controlled secondary flows. Our experiments reveal a dual and competing role for these currents: they enhance the energy of LSMs, while simultaneously suppressing that of VLSMs. Counterintuitively, the characteristic streamwise length of the attenuated VLSMs increases with the strength of the secondary circulation. We attribute this elongation to a rotationally induced inverse energy cascade, which reorganizes the turbulent structures. Furthermore, the VLSMs are observed to span the entire flow depth, indicating that the secondary currents, while disrupting the energetic coherence of VLSMs, concurrently redistribute their momentum across the water column. These findings demonstrate that curvature-induced secondary flows fundamentally alter the multiscale dynamics of turbulent flow, not by simple disruption but by actively reorganizing turbulent structures into longer, more vertically coherent patterns.

papers.title: An advanced reduced-order model for real-time and high-accuracy computation of industrial gas–solid flow systems
papers.abstract: Gas–solid flow systems are ubiquitous in science and engineering. To accurately simulate their phenomenon, the discrete element method coupled with computational fluid dynamics (DEM–CFD) method has become the standard numerical approach. However, the traditional high-fidelity physical DEM–CFD method (i.e., the full-order model, FOM) suffers from prohibitive computational cost. To solve the problem regarding the computational cost of FOM, the data-driven reduced-order model (ROM) has been proposed. Nevertheless, the conventional ROM developed for accelerating the DEM–CFD method cannot predict the aperiodic transient gas–solid flow systems, which is essential to understand plenty of scientific phenomena. This is because the conventional ROMs are commonly based on regression approaches, often requiring periodic or quasi-periodic patterns of considered systems to be learned. To resolve the essential problem for the existing ROMs, an advanced ROM approach, namely, Flattened Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) coefficients ROM (FlaP-ROM), is proposed for parametrized real-time DEM–CFD simulation of aperiodic gas–solid flow systems. Specifically, to avoid the traditional regression, the POD coefficients are flattened to one feature and directly mapped by a fully connected neural network in the parameter space. Validation tests are performed in two large-scale aperiodic transient gas–solid flow systems: a jet fluidized bed and a die-filling. Through the validation tests, FlaP-ROM exhibits excellent accuracy and efficiency in characterizing the flow dynamics and macroscopic properties in a wide range of aperiodic transient gas–solid flow systems.

papers.title: Efficient and flexible adaptive particle refinement for free-surface flows based on the regularized high-order diffusive smoothed particle hydrodynamics scheme
papers.abstract: The aim of the present work is the investigation of an adaptive particle refinement (APR) approach that enables large variations in particle size even in the presence of a free surface. In the smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) literature, the existing APR or similar multi-resolution techniques can be categorized into three main approaches, essentially driven by the discrete differential operators selected. When a conservative formulation is retained, either variable smoothing-length techniques or buffer regions are generally employed. By contrast, in formulations using accurate but non-conservative SPH operators, large variations of the particle size are achievable without requesting any specific treatment. However, because of the difficulties of such formulations in addressing the free surface, they have so far been restricted to internal flows. Recently, a regularized high-order diffusive (RHOD)-SPH approach has been derived in the context of single resolution. In this approach an accurate formulation is used inside the bulk of the fluid, whereas a conservative one is preferred in the free-surface region. In the present paper, the ingredients required in the RHOD-SPH approach are extended to APR. Specifically, the Riemann-based diffusive terms and particle shifting technique are generalized to deal with particles of different sizes. A particle-splitting procedure is employed to enlarge the range of applications of the approach. The formulation is validated on six different test cases, with comparisons to both single-resolution and reference results.

papers.title: Enhanced mass transfer in microgeometry using pulsating velocity inputs: Hydrodynamic analysis and numerical simulation
papers.abstract: The current work focuses on the performance of hydrodynamics and mass transfer in a microchannel. A hydrodynamic model is developed for a gas–liquid (CO2–water) system and slug flow pattern. For the first time in literature, a concept of pulsating velocity input is introduced in an enhanced cross-T-junction microchannel to study the mass transfer using the physical absorption mechanism in ANSYS FLUENT R2 2024. The mass transfer model is associated with the hydrodynamic model and some user-defined functions in FLUENT. This work demonstrates that incorporating obstructions and applying trapezoidal and sinusoidal wave inputs improve the CO2 absorption rate. The obtained data are further compared with the plain T-junction microchannel in terms of mass transfer coefficient. Solubility of CO2 in three different solvents (ethyl alcohol, water, and ethylene glycol) has been revealed in an enhanced cross T-junction microchannel at two different temperatures, i.e., 298.15 and 303.15 K. The numerical simulations illustrate that an increase in temperature has an adverse effect on the mass transfer rate.

papers.title: Dynamic response of a freely movable downstream cylinder in the upstream wake by an oscillating fin
papers.abstract: Extensive studies for the dynamic response of downstream structures to von Kármán wakes generated by upstream structures have been performed thus far. However, a critical gap remains in how a downstream structure responds to thrust-generating wake patterns typically produced by swimming fish in nature. To bridge this crucial gap, numerical simulations are performed on a system consisting of an upstream flexible fin and a downstream rigid cylinder vibrating freely in the cross-stream direction to investigate the interaction of the cylinder with various upstream wake patterns. The various wake patterns are generated by the heaving motions of the fin as the cylinder-diameter-based dimensionless heaving amplitude and frequency are varied. When the von Kármán wake is generated behind the fin, not only the slaloming motion of the cylinder and constructive vortex-to-vortex interaction shed from the fin and the cylinder (hereafter, SC mode) but also the interception motion of the cylinder and mixed constructive and destructive vortex-to-vortex interaction (IM mode) dominate. For a reverse von Kármán wake, both the slaloming motion of the cylinder and destructive vortex-to-vortex interaction (SD mode) and IM mode are prominent. When vortices consisting of the von Kármán wake or reverse von Kármán wake are aligned near the centerline, the SC + SD + IM mode arises. Because the induced velocity created by the destructive vortex-to-vortex interaction plays an important role in the generation of a large pressure difference around the cylinder, the dynamic response of the cylinder to the upstream wake is rank-ordered as SD, IM, and SC modes.

papers.title: Aerodynamic mechanisms behind enhanced gliding efficiency of slotted wingtips
papers.abstract: The remarkable flight capabilities of birds are made possible by the aerodynamic contributions of their diverse wing structures. However, the mechanisms that enable slotted wingtips to achieve high aerodynamic performance remain unclear. Focusing on slotted wingtip configurations, which are frequently observed in gliding and flapping birds, this study numerically investigated their aerodynamic advantages and underlying mechanisms using computational fluid dynamics. Based on prior experimental models, we performed a two-step optimization combining two-dimensional global and three-dimensional local searches to identify high-performance configurations. The resulting slotted-tip device improved the lift-to-drag ratio compared with both the base wing and the single-tip device. Through an isolated vortex analysis using Lamb–Oseen models, we revealed that the slotted structure helps reduce the aerodynamic influence of the wingtip vortices. This is achieved not only by shifting the vortex positions away from the wing but also by reducing the net circulation through vortex splitting. Despite the geometric simplifications made, our results are consistent with prior experimental measurements and provide insights into the functional advantages of the slotted wing morphology. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of avian flight and offer valuable design cues for bioinspired aerial robots.

papers.title: Constructal design of porous-filled tree-shaped networks for optimal fluid transport: An analytical approach
papers.abstract: In this article, a general mathematical framework is developed for the flow distribution in a porous-filled tree-network with rigid and impermeable walls using the Darcy–Brinkman model. The governing model equations, incorporating heterogeneous permeability, are solved by the wavelet collocation method for flow in a single tube. Further, the local study has been extended to a tree-shaped network by electrical circuit analogy. Mathematical analysis is performed for various fluids in single and two-layer fluid flow with different permeabilities to evaluate the flow variables responsible for the flow resistance. The developed theory is used to establish the mathematical relationship associated with the optimal flow in a self-symmetric, porous-filled, tree-shaped network. The explicit expression of the optimal geometry for flow transport is obtained in terms of the tube aspect ratio, tube length, and branching angle between the parent and daughter branches, using rational function approximation. It is observed that the optimal flow has strong dependencies on the permeability of the porous matrix, offering various applications in natural and engineered fluid transport phenomena.

papers.title: Effects of higher and lower angle isolated dunes on very-large-scale motions in open channel flows
papers.abstract: Dunes are ubiquitous riverbed forms, yet how they modify the most recently documented energy-containing turbulent structures—very-large-scale motions (VLSMs)—remains unclear. To address this issue, high fidelity experiments were conducted in open-channel flows (OCFs) over isolated dunes with contrasting morphologies. Time-resolved, long-duration, and high-resolution velocity fields with extended streamwise coverage were obtained using an in-house multi-camera particle image velocimetry system, enabling detailed quantification of dune effects over long distances with fine spatial resolutions. Consistent with canonical OCFs, VLSMs are evident in both dune cases upstream of the lee face, where dune effects are minimal, as revealed by the bimodal features of the streamwise velocity spectrum, indicating two dominant energy-containing turbulent structures: large-scale motions and VLSMs. The scales and strength of these motions are comparable to those in canonical OCFs. In contrast, over the lee face and downstream side, pronounced dune morphology–dependent effects emerge. For low lee-slope dunes, VLSMs persist throughout the flow depth, whereas for steep dunes, their spectral signature is eliminated in the near-bed region and remains only near the free surface. Furthermore, the strength of VLSMs, measured by their contributions to streamwise turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) and Reynolds shear stress (RSS), is substantially reduced: from 60% to 30% for TKE and from 50% to 15% for RSS in the near-dune region. With increasing distance downstream, dune effects weaken, and VLSM strength gradually recovers.

papers.title: Ferrofluid flow over a rotating disk with sinusoidal vertical reciprocation
papers.abstract: The current study investigates ferrofluid flow over a rotating disk undergoing sinusoidal vertical reciprocation. Oscillatory slip is introduced to represent the wobbling nature of the disk, while a magnetic field-dependent (MFD) viscosity is incorporated to mitigate this effect. By applying similarity transformations, the coupled transport equations for flow and heat transfer are reduced to a system of nonlinear ordinary differential equations and computed through a built-in MATLAB solver. Representative plots of velocity fields, streamlines, isotherms, velocity, and thermal profiles are provided to demonstrate the physical mechanisms. The results show that the MFD parameter acts as a stabilizer with damping fluctuations in velocity and temperature distributions. Enhanced disk reciprocation consistently amplifies velocity magnitude, where streamline patterns exhibiting sharper bending and greater outward momentum transport under stronger reciprocation. The oscillatory amplitude of radial velocity is suppressed under stronger ferromagnetic interactions. Disk rotation strengthens tangential transport through centrifugal shear, and reciprocation and oscillatory slip enhance thermal transport. Moreover, increasing oscillatory slip produces a distinctive horseshoe-shaped high-shear region for the skin friction coefficient. These findings highlight the practical control strategies for ferrofluidic devices such as magnetic dampers, adaptive lubrication systems, vibration-responsive cooling, and microfluidic mixers.

papers.title: Numerical study on aerodynamic characteristics of finite-length tandem rotating cylinders
papers.abstract: Aerodynamic interference in flow around tandem rotating cylinders (e.g., Flettner rotors) is characterized by significant complexity for engineering applications. Large eddy simulation is employed to investigate aerodynamic characteristics of finite-length tandem cylinders at a subcritical Reynolds number of 3900, with focus placed on spacing ratios (L/D) of 3, 4, and 5 and speed ratios (n) ranging from 0 to 5. For stationary cylinders (n = 0), three distinct flow regimes are identified. When rotation initiates (n = 1), flow instability is intensified. The key phenomenon of “drag reversal” emerges at n ≥ 2. This transition is attributed to coupling between the blockage effect and the rotational action. At the critical speed ratio (n = 3), vortex shedding is suppressed. At high-speed ratios (n > 3), the flow transitions into a rotation-dominated regime, where a secondary instability mode is activated. A synergy between blockage effects and rotational action is revealed, enabling relative optimal operation at L/D = 3 and n = 3 with high lift-drag ratio and achieving minimal fluctuating loads. Critical theoretical and practical guidance for optimizing tandem cylinder flow configurations in Flettner rotors is provided with these findings.

papers.title: Unraveling the dynamics of pulsatile flow under pathophysiological conditions in curved tubules of kidney
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a critical global health challenge that requires a deeper understanding of kidney physiology and pathology to develop effective therapeutic strategies. This necessitates a thorough exploration of fluid dynamic interactions within the elastic kidney tubules. This study introduces a biomechanical model to investigate the dynamics of fluid flow in elastic kidney tubules while incorporating their physiological curvature characteristics. We present a numerical model to analyze pulsatile flow dynamics in the kidney tubules, incorporating curvature and compliance variations. A finite-element framework is used to evaluate flow parameters across varying wall stiffnesses, with validation against data from the literature. Our findings highlight that both curvature and tissue stiffness significantly impact fluid dynamics. Higher stiffness reduces peak axial velocity, while convex regions exhibit greater velocity and fluid shear stress (FSS) than concave regions. Relative to straight tubules, curvature leads to greater than an order of magnitude decrease in FSS, with concave regions producing the most pronounced suppression. Increased stiffness further decreases wall displacement, reduces von Mises stress, and lowers FSS due to reduced compliance. The relationship between stiffness and FSS suggests that mechanical forces within the tubule microenvironment are strongly influenced by tissue elasticity. As CKD progresses, renal tubules become stiffer, which alters these mechanical forces that further alter fluid dynamics, and contribute to the pathological conditions of the tubule structure. The complex interrelationships among kidney architecture, fluid structure interaction, and pathology highlight the therapeutic importance of taking curvature into account when figuring out how kidney disease progresses and creating tailored treatments.

papers.title: Effects of injection angles and ignition timing on combustion characteristics in a hydrogen/ammonia dual direct injection rotary engine based on orthogonal analysis
papers.abstract: The potential application of hydrogen-ammonia blended fuel in rotary engines and the critical role of in-cylinder dual direct injection technology in fuel distribution and combustion control are well-recognized. However, the coupling effects of hydrogen/ammonia injection angles and ignition timing remain unclear. To identify the most significant injection strategy and ignition strategy affecting engine combustion parameters, this study investigates the impacts of hydrogen injection angle (θ2_H2), ammonia injection angle (θ1_NH3), and ignition timing (IT) on combustion characteristics and emission performance using an orthogonal experimental design based on CONVERGE three-dimensional simulations, with the accuracy of the numerical model validated through experimental verification. Results indicate that the order of influence on in-cylinder pressure, quantified by range (R) and variance analysis, is θ2_H2 (R = 1.1269) > θ1_NH3 (R = 0.7002) > IT (R = 0.4835). Using the normalization method, the optimal parameter combination is determined as θ1_NH3 = −60°, θ2_H2 = 0°, and IT = 10 °CA before the top dead center. Hydrogen exhibits a significant influence with a contribution rate of 51.14%. This optimal combination reduces NOx emissions by 62.6%, yields a maximum in-cylinder pressure of 3.05 MPa, and increases the combustion heat release rate by 32.5%. It clarifies the effect of parameter optimization on ammonia-hydrogen stratified combustion and pollutant formation, thereby providing strategies for the engineering design of injection systems.

papers.title: Rapid prediction of cell-free layer thickness: A semi-analytical hemorheological model for blood flow in stenosed vessels
papers.abstract: Hemodynamic characteristic parameters are closely associated with the onset and progression of cardiovascular diseases. Constructing a hemorheological prior model with complete physical significance remains a critical challenge in this field. In particular, the Fåhraeus–Lindqvist effect and the associated cell-free layer (CFL) in microcirculation are essential for understanding blood flow behavior. This study establishes a constitutive model of blood flow in microvessels based on multiphase flow theory, where flow velocity is expressed as a function of shear rate, and the shear rate is used as the independent variable to analyze flow field structure within circular vessels. By introducing an analytical solution of the velocity field in stenosed vessels in bipolar coordinates, an efficient prediction method for CFL thickness is proposed. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations demonstrate that within the same vascular cross section, velocity cores exhibit a slight eccentric distribution. Under low-shear conditions, red blood cells tend to form rouleaux aggregates, which are larger in volume and higher in rigidity, limiting their migration toward the vessel wall and leading to CFL thickening. Such aggregation simultaneously reduces disturbance diffusion, thereby enhancing CFL stability and further increasing its thickness. Hematocrit (Hct) is identified as the dominant factor influencing CFL thickness. Shear stress exerts a significant positive effect, with a standardized regression coefficient of 0.1735 and a random forest feature importance of 0.3786, indicating its strong role in promoting CFL formation and development. Although plasma viscosity (μ) has a relatively weaker influence, its effect on CFL thickness demonstrates strong linear interpretability.

papers.title: Development of high-hydrophobic ZnO nanowires on metal surface for graded wetting and no-voltage droplet displacement by negligible tilt angle
papers.abstract: A highly hydrophobic ZnO nanowire (NW) surface with a wettability gradient is fabricated on a NiSi/Si substrate using a novel voltage-assisted double-step chemical bath deposition technique. X-ray diffraction analyses confirmed the formation of c-axis oriented ZnO NWs. Detailed morphological and compositional characterization using field emission scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive spectroscopy, and atomic force microscopy signifies a progressive increase in NW areal density, Zn/O stoichiometric ratio, and effective surface roughness from the positive to grounded terminal of the biased NiSi strip. This morphological gradient resulted in a tunable wettability profile, studied with static contact angles of water ranging from 130.15° to 142.72°. The obtained hydrophobic nature is attributed to the stoichiometric ratio, morphological variations, and enhanced surface roughness. Furthermore, tilt-induced no-voltage droplet displacement is observed and analyzed. Additionally, this droplet movement behavior is compared with that on a Teflon surface. The current study utilizes a simple, cost-effective approach to fabricate high-hydrophobic ZnO nanowires on a metal surface with a wettability gradient. Such development is critical for advanced, energy-efficient microfluidics integrated biosensor systems.

papers.title: Effects of flexible surface deformation on aerodynamic characteristics of a high-aspect-ratio wing
papers.abstract: The aeroelastic deformation of high-aspect-ratio wings in lightweight solar-powered unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) inevitably causes deviations between their designed and real-world flight performance. The implementation of flexible membrane skins brings the wing a more complex fluid–structural coupling deformation problem. This study presents a high-fidelity bidirectional aeroelastic analysis on the high-aspect-ratio wing of a solar-powered UAV. The research aims to conduct an in-depth and comprehensive investigation of the combined influence mechanism exerted by the deformation of the wing's main structure and flexible skin on aerodynamic performance, laminar flow characteristics, and flow separation behavior. The results indicate that the wing deformation, primarily that of the flexible wing surface, causes an earlier laminar–turbulent transition, an increase in the drag coefficient, a severe deterioration of the stall characteristics, and thereby a notable degradation in the aerodynamic performance. The findings of this work significantly contribute to filling the knowledge gap in the coupling interactions between the flexible wing surface and flow field at a Reynolds number around 3 × 105, and provide a crucial theoretical foundation for the aerodynamic design and flight performance optimization of solar-powered UAVs. The loosely coupled analysis method developed in this study can serve as a reliable and accurate analysis tool for the evaluation of next-generation solar-powered UAVs during the design phase.

papers.title: Measurement uncertainty and sensitivity analyses on freestream parameters in a hypersonic impulse facility: A perturbation-based framework
papers.abstract: Quantifying measurement uncertainty in short-duration impulse facilities is critical for data credibility but remains particularly challenging due to rapidly evolving, high-enthalpy flow conditions with limited diagnostic time scales. This study systematically develops and demonstrates a robust, generalized perturbation-based framework to estimate uncertainties in key measured quantities and assess their sensitivity to derived freestream parameters in a shock tunnel. The sensitivity analysis reveals that freestream parameters, such as static pressure, temperature, density, and velocity are highly sensitive to tunnel shock speed (Us) and stagnation pressure (P5), while showing moderate dependence on the driven-tube fill pressure (P1), and temperature (T1). The effect of stagnation enthalpy on these sensitivities is also examined and found to have minimal influence across the studied range (2.4–7.5 MJ/kg). By conducting systematic experiments in such a facility, the repeatability errors in surface heat flux and pressure-derived coefficient (CP) are found to be well within the predicted uncertainty bounds of ±10% and ±9.5%, respectively, underscoring the robustness of the framework. The proposed methodology establishes a seamless approach for uncertainty evaluation in impulse facilities and supports more reliable interpretation of aerodynamic data under transient, high-enthalpy conditions, with potential applicability to future hypersonic test strategies.

papers.title: Three-dimensional flow characteristics around a finite wall-mounted conical cylinder
papers.abstract: This paper presents the numerical results of three-dimensional flow characteristics around a finite wall-mounted conical cylinder with an aspect ratio fixed at AR = 4 and the end diameter ratio (D1/D2) ranging from 0.5 to 1.0 at a low Reynolds number, Re = 50–500. The flow characteristics are discussed in terms of time-averaged streamlines, distribution of singular points, topological structures, three-dimensional mean streamwise vortices, and instantaneous spanwise vortices. Compared to an infinite height configuration, the downwash flow caused by the free-end suppresses the formation of the Kármán vortex street in the wake. The critical Reynolds number for horseshoe vortex formation exhibits a significant dependence on D1/D2, decreasing to Re = 150 when D1/D2 = 0.5. Two distinct topological patterns are identified in the time-averaged streamline behind the cylinder. Three flow patterns above the free-end of the finite conical cylinder are demonstrated, providing additional insights into flow structures on free-end surfaces. The stable Quadrupole, Sextupole, and Octupole types of time-averaged streamwise vortices are compared across different Re and D1/D2. Furthermore, this work not only reconciles the time-averaged and instantaneous interpretations with the solenoidal condition of the vorticity field but also clarifies the fundamental mechanisms behind the topological transition from hairpin to braid vortices driven by strain rate.

papers.title: Control of streams generated by pulse-periodic laser breakdown in the intersected focused beams in high-pressure xenon
papers.abstract: This paper reports the possibility of stabilizing and enhancing characteristics of pulse-periodic optical discharge (PPOD) in high-pressure xenon. The aim of this study was to explore the potential of using PPOD plasma as a high-brightness broadband UV radiation source for various applications. A new configuration to sustain PPOD was investigated, where two focused laser beams of a pulse-periodic fiber laser at a wavelength of 1.064 μm intersect at their focal waists. PPOD located in a single focused laser beam generally generates turbulent gas flow directed along the optical axis toward the laser beam that deteriorates the wavefront of the incident beam. PPOD sustained at the intersection of the two focused beams was shown to induce gas flow directed aside from the optical axes of the incident beams. This helps to increase the stability of the PPOD plasma from pulse to pulse. Data on the maximum spectral brightness of PPOD plasma radiation and stability have been obtained. Both estimates of the maximum electron concentration in the plasma from the measured maximum brightness and from the defocusing of laser radiation in the plasma give the value about Ne ≈ 2 × 1019 cm−3. It has been found that during PPOD with the repetition rate in the range fp = 20–21.3 kHz, resonant acoustic oscillations occur in the discharge volume, leading to a significant change in the pattern of gas streams around PPOD.

papers.title: Analysis of wave phenomena in shallow water with rational solutions of the (1 + 1)-dimensional Korteweg–de-Vries–Calogero–Bogoyavlenski–Schiff equation
papers.abstract: Understanding the behavior of shallow-water waves plays an important role in many areas of science and technology, such as oceanography and optical telecommunications. This study presents an analytical exploration of the (1+1)-dimensional Korteweg–de-Vries–Calogero–Bogoyavlensky–Schiff equation, through which a variety of rational solutions are obtained. Using mathematical methods, several wave structures are identified and categorized, like lump interactions, rogue waves, periodic kink configurations, and breather-like structures. The classification of such waves elucidates and collates their significance in the physical world and further constructs a cohesive framework for the understanding of transitions in integrable systems. Special attention is given to complex nonlinear interactions including kink-crossing phenomena and the development of M-shaped wave profiles. The results provide a detailed interpretation of the evolution of nonlinear wave motion in shallow-water waves and enhance the understanding of integrable systems.

papers.title: Study on rheological, atomization, and transport properties of particle-laden gels
papers.abstract: This study investigates the rheological, transport, and atomization properties of particle-laden gels through combined experimental and numerical approaches. Hydroxyethyl cellulose-based gels incorporating ceramic microspheres (10 μm) were prepared. Their rheological properties were characterized using a rotational rheometer to obtain viscosity curves. A rheological model for particle-laden gels was established based on the Krieger–Dougherty model. A variable-diameter pipeline was designed to study transport pressure drops under varying flow rates and flow directions. Y-jet injectors were employed to analyze atomization characteristics, including Sauter mean diameter), injector pressure drop, spray patterns, spray cone angles, and spray velocity fields. The measured viscosity curves (for both particle-laden and particle-free gels) were successfully simulated, demonstrating good agreement between experimental and computational results. Transport results reveal that, at identical flow rates, the pressure drop for particle-laden gel flowing from the small-diameter to the large-diameter section exceeds that observed in the reverse direction. For Y-jet injectors, structural parameters significantly influence atomization performance: an increased gas–liquid ratio notably reduces the SMD within the spray field. However, an excessively long mixing section hinders complete gel atomization. When successful atomization occurs, a longer mixing section yields a larger spray cone angle and higher injection velocity, albeit with a slight increase in SMD. In the spray field, a longer mixing section facilitates a more concentrated droplet size distribution. Furthermore, the influence of a Venturi tube on the injector's atomization characteristics was investigated.

papers.title: Hybrid loss-based convolutional encoder–decoder neural networks for the robust topology optimization of porous heat exchangers
papers.abstract: Deterministic topology optimization (DTO) for cooling microchannels has been widely studied in recent years. However, for the robust topology optimization (RTO) of comprehensive heat transfer performance under the condition of extensive random uncertainties in boundary conditions and material properties, no research has been conducted due to the high computational cost of conjugate heat transfer simulations in complex topological structures. To address this research gap, this study establishes a fluid-thermal RTO model for porous heat exchangers, where the random uncertainties of porosity and inlet velocity are considered. For solving the RTO model, an adaptive convolutional encoder–decoder neural network (CNN) approach is developed by proposing a hybrid data-physics-informed loss function and adaptive updating strategy to capture the topological characteristic features in each RTO iteration and reconstruct the primal physical fields corresponding to the specific realization of random porosity and inlet velocity. The results of solving both DTO and RTO demonstrate that the proposed adaptive updating strategy of CNN can maintain both the hybrid loss function and absolute prediction errors within acceptable thresholds. When the flow dissipation constraints are, respectively, set to 2, 10, and 20 times that of conventional straight single-channel designs, the RTO configurations can achieve reduction in average temperature mean of 11.25%, 14.48%, and 16.88%, along with the decrease in average temperature standard deviation of 31.02%, 27.08%, and 25.15% compared to DTO configurations, respectively. Furthermore, as the inlet velocity mean is increased from 0.05 to 0.30 m/s, the RTO configuration exhibits excellent potential in both mean and robustness of heat exchange performance, and it achieves the relative reduction of 12.26%–15.62% and 12.35%–31.04% in mean and standard deviation of average temperature compared to the DTO configuration, respectively.

papers.title: A high-performance chemistry solver for reactive flow simulations in OpenFOAM
papers.abstract: Reactive flow simulations with detailed chemical kinetics encounter significant computational challenges due to stiff, nonlinear combustion processes. This work presents a high-performance, central processing unit accelerated lightweight chemistry solver for OpenFOAM, an open-source software for computational fluid dynamics, that integrates code-level optimizations—including vectorized reaction rate evaluation, novel Jacobian construction for elementary reactions, and optimized matrix operations—with dynamic load balancing for multi-core scalability. In addition, the solver is fully compatible with the OpenFOAM ecosystem, requiring no external libraries or mechanism-specific code generation, thereby ensuring ease of integration and broad applicability to diverse chemical mechanisms. This solver is rigorously validated based on a hierarchy of test cases, including zero-dimensional autoignition, two-dimensional counterflow diffusion flames, and large eddy simulations of turbulent jet flames. Comprehensive benchmarks against the standard OpenFOAM chemistry solver demonstrate that the proposed solver can achieve up to an order-of-magnitude acceleration across a range of stiff ordinary differential equation algorithms, tolerance settings, and chemistry mechanisms from 10 species to 255 species, meanwhile maintaining solution fidelity. Cross-architecture robustness, superior computational efficiency compared with state-of-the-art solvers (e.g., DLBFoam), and good parallel scalability have also been validated for the proposed solver. This proposed solver presents the capability of significantly extending the practical feasibility of high-fidelity simulations with detailed chemistry.

papers.title: Interpretable surrogate modeling of extrusion flows with deep learning
papers.abstract: Predicting the deformed shape of nested co-axial streams after extrusion through a shaped nozzle is a bottleneck for microparticle and microfiber fabrication as well as other extrusion processes, due to the need for fully resolved three-dimensional (3D) computational fluid dynamics simulations requiring significant expertise, computational resources, and time. We recast this problem as an image translation task, mapping a two-dimensional (2D) nozzle shape to a 2D output cross section of a shaped flow. By doing so, we bypass meshing and 3D solvers by using a deep learning (DL) U-Net model to predict fully miscible, low Reynolds number (Re=1) extrusion flow shapes, achieving 450× speedup with second-scale prediction times. The DL model approximately conserves mass and achieves a mean intersection over union of 0.9757 on a held-out test set of nozzle shapes. Saliency-based interpretability analysis of the DL model shows that such extrusion flows are robust to variations in nozzle wall thickness and, for low to moderate inner flow rates, to the shape of the outer flow wall. This robustness, along with the DL model's speed and accuracy, enables efficient and practical data-driven design of co-axial extrusion devices and highlights the broader potential of interpretable surrogates in microfluidic flow engineering.

papers.title: Impacts of panel vibration and fluctuating backpressure on shock train behavior in scramjet isolators
papers.abstract: Considering the weight limitations of hypersonic vehicles and the requirements of thermal protection structure design, the adoption of thin-walled structures in scramjet isolators is an inevitable choice. However, the pressure pulsations generated in the combustion chamber, coupled with panel vibrations induced by thin-walled structures, generate unsteady effects on the shock-wave/boundary-layer interaction in an isolator. This study focuses on this problem by utilizing the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations and dynamic grid technology to investigate the combined effects of wall panel vibrations and fluctuating backpressure on shock train structures, wall aerodynamic loads, and aerodynamic performance. The effects of vibration location and frequency of the panel structure are systematically investigated. The results indicate that the oscillation frequency of the flow field is a combination of the backpressure pulsation frequency and the wall panel vibration frequency, and the shock train exhibits a periodic alternation between large-amplitude and small-amplitude oscillations. The panel vibration will cause greater non-uniformity of the outlet flow, increase the wall pressure oscillations load and amplitude increase in the shock train, reducing the ability of the isolator to resist backpressure. The influence of panel vibration strongly depends on its position and frequency: upstream wall vibrations exert the most significant effect on shock train amplitude and pressure fluctuations, while low-frequency vibrations (f < 400 Hz) intensify oscillations more markedly than high-frequency vibrations (f ≥ 400 Hz).

papers.title: Hamilton–Jacobi equation for a wrinkled flame front
papers.abstract: A model equation of the Hamilton–Jacobi type is proposed to describe the propagation of a wrinkled premixed flame front. For periodic front disturbances, the proposed equation has simple analytical solutions. Using the model equation, the dynamic properties and shape of the wrinkled flame front are investigated. It is shown that three characteristic periods can be distinguished in the process of development of a periodic wrinkled front: the induction period, the period of accelerated front motion, and the period of steady-state motion of the cellular flame. It is shown that during the period of accelerated flame motion, the process of its propagation can be approximately considered self-similar, in which the average velocity of the wrinkled front changes with time according to the law t1/2. The shape of stationary flame front cells is obtained. Two-dimensional stationary flame front cells are investigated. The results of calculations by the proposed model equation are compared with the results of calculations by the well-known Michelson–Sivashinsky (MS) equation and with calculations within the context of a hydrodynamic theory. It is shown that the normalized shapes of stationary cells calculated by all three models are very close, but the cell amplitudes predicted by them differ significantly. Thus, the cell amplitudes calculated by the model equation agree well with the calculation within the context of a hydrodynamic theory for realistic expansion ratios of combustion products but are approximately 1.5–1.7 times greater for unrealistically small expansion ratios, while the amplitudes calculated by the MS equation agree well with the calculation within the context of a hydrodynamic theory for unrealistically small expansion ratios of combustion products (for which the MS equation was obtained), but give significantly overestimated results for realistic values of expansion ratios. A comparison of the calculation results using the model equation with known experimental data on the stationary and non-stationary propagation of cellular flames was performed.

papers.title: Wetting dynamics of oil/water compound droplets on multilevel wettability-patterned surfaces
papers.abstract: Oil/water compound droplets with core–shell structures are crucial in open-surface microfluidic devices, particularly for applications in droplet-based reactors, emulsification, and material synthesis.
