While previous studies have investigated urban water bodies, they often lack clear theoretical discussions on simulation methodologies, fail to compare simulation results with observational data, and have not systematically quantified the impacts of water bodies on the surrounding wind, heat, and moisture environment. This research aims to address these gaps by providing a comprehensive analysis of their microclimatic effects. Leveraging computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations and field measurements, the research first provides a comprehensive comparison of various mass transfer equations for modeling water body evaporation, a process critical for accurate microclimate predictions. This study also emphasizes empirical validation, cross-referencing simulation results with data from wind tunnel experiments and field measurements. The methodology encompasses analyzing key environmental variables, including wind speed, air temperature, relative humidity, and the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), between campus areas with and without water bodies. The dual-validation process strengthens the reliability of CFD simulations, offering insights into the cooling potential of water bodies under realistic conditions. Results highlight the accuracy of different mass transfer equations, validating their applicability for urban water body evaporation and demonstrating how water bodies can alleviate heat stress, improve pedestrian comfort, and contribute to sustainable urban design. This study underscores the value of integrating CFD models with empirical data, providing actionable insights for urban planners and contributing to urban climate modification strategies.

papers.title: Thermal-hydraulic characteristics of subsurface seepage in multilayer saturated soil using a hybrid lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: Fundamental research on fluid seepage has become a hot topic in numerous scientific and engineering fields. However, the current understanding of seepage in complex layered porous structures and the influence of temperature on seepage remains incomplete. In this study, to investigate the flow and heat transfer characteristics of subsurface seepage in saturated soils with a multilayer structure, a thermal-flow coupled lattice Boltzmann model was developed by using a multiple relaxation time operator and the Runge–Kutta fourth-order difference scheme. This study investigates the effects of inflow velocity, inflow temperature, and solid substrate size on pore-scale flow and heat transfer within multilayer porous media. Results show that higher inflow velocity increases permeability and enhances heat penetration into colder soil layers, with inertial effects and fluid–solid interactions requiring larger pressure gradients. At constant porosity, larger solid substrate diameters yield higher permeability due to wider pore throats and reduced viscous resistance. Elevated inflow temperatures decrease fluid viscosity, promote pore-scale flow, and accelerate thermal equilibrium. For layered porous media (LPM), changes in porosity lead to variations in the number and structure of internal preferential flow paths, which in turn affect the displacement process of the high-temperature fluid. Besides, based on Pearson's theory and chi-square test, the analysis found that the pore-scale velocity distribution followed a lognormal distribution. The results enhanced the understanding of the coupled mechanisms between seepage and heat transfer in LPM and provided a theoretical basis for engineering applications involving subsurface thermal hydraulic processes.

papers.title: Design and performance of microfluidic devices for viscoelastic-controlled encapsulation
papers.abstract: Microfluidic encapsulation enables the isolation of particles or cells within picolitre-sized droplets, forming the foundation for a wide range of applications in biology, medicine, and materials science. From droplet-based single-cell ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing to long-term three-dimensional cell culture in microgels, the ability to efficiently encapsulate one or more objects per droplet is essential for throughput and downstream analysis. However, random encapsulation governed by Poisson statistics results in high fractions of empty droplets and undesired multiple occupancy, limiting the efficiency of current workflows between 20% and 36%, depending on the initial loading. Viscoelastic encapsulation provides a passive and scalable alternative to active sorting or inertial ordering approaches. By exploiting elastic and shear-thinning effects, objects self-organize into equally spaced trains along the channel centerline, enabling frequency-matched droplet formation. Despite its promise, only two studies have explored this phenomenon, with limitations including large droplet sizes, filament formation, and confinement constraints that restrict applicability to small biological objects. In this work, we introduce improved microfluidic platforms for viscoelastic-controlled encapsulation and co-encapsulation, demonstrating single-encapsulation efficiency up to 74% and co-encapsulation efficiency up to 46%. We design new device geometries, develop optimized hyaluronic acid formulations, and demonstrate high-efficiency encapsulation of both rigid particles and live Tetraselmis suecica algae. Our platform achieves encapsulation efficiencies well above Poisson statistics, reduced multi-occupancy, and droplet generation frequencies up to 2 kHz. These results establish viscoelastic encapsulation as a practical solution for high-throughput single-cell workflows, offering a robust path forward for droplet-based diagnostics and analytical platforms.

papers.title: Thrombosis risk in coronary aneurysms: Insight into platelet collision hotspots and inflammatory wall roughness
papers.abstract: Thrombosis is a major complication of coronary artery aneurysms, particularly in patients with Kawasaki disease, yet the biomechanical triggers remain insufficiently understood. This study employs a particle-resolved computational fluid dynamics–discrete phase model framework to quantify the effects of inflammation-induced endothelial roughness and impingement of the upstream flow on platelet-wall collision behavior, a critical initiating step in the formation of thrombuses. Using idealized aneurysm models with parametrically defined surface irregularities and varying inflow orientations, we demonstrate that greater roughness severity markedly amplifies platelet collisions, particularly at protruding surface crests. Furthermore, altered inflow angles induce asymmetrical jet impingement and vortical structures, concentrating platelet impacts within specific aneurysmal regions, consistent with clinical thrombus distribution patterns. Quantitatively, increasing the inflow angle to 90° amplified platelet–wall collisions by 22.5-fold compared to the 0° baseline, while augmenting the inflammatory roughness height from 0.05 to 0.1 mm resulted in a 2.79-fold rise. In contrast, macroscopic geometric parameters, such as aneurysm aspect ratio, exhibit limited influence during the thrombogenic phase. Variations in the macroscopic aneurysm aspect ratio led to negligible changes in collision counts (<8.3%). Collectively, these findings highlight the dominant roles of inflammatory remodeling and hemodynamic disturbances in governing thrombosis risk and suggest their incorporation into future risk stratification strategies for Kawasaki disease associated coronary artery aneurysms.

papers.title: PIV characterization of supersonic two-phase flow in a solid rocket motor using a visual nozzle
papers.abstract: The performance of a solid rocket motor directly determines the range and speed of weapon systems. As a critical component of the motor, the nozzle plays a significant role. The velocity distribution of the internal supersonic two-phase flow field significantly influences motor performance. However, experimental investigations on the velocity characteristics of the two-phase flow fields for solid rocket motor nozzles remain relatively scarce. To obtain the velocity distribution of the supersonic two-phase flow field within the nozzle of a solid rocket motor, a visual nozzle was designed to enable direct observation of the internal flow. Experimental systems were established for both cold-flow experiments and hot-firing experiments of solid propellant motors. Using the particle image velocimetry (PIV) technique, online measurements of the nozzle flow field velocity distribution were carried out under both conditions. The results indicate that the visual nozzle sealed with quartz glass enables online velocity measurements inside the nozzle under cold-flow conditions, with the maximum time-averaged axial velocity reaching 600 m/s. Under hot-firing conditions, the visual nozzle sealed with a truncated metal cover plate allows successful online velocity measurements of the internal flow field, with the maximum time-averaged axial velocity reaching 1000 m/s.

papers.title: Typhoon multi-stage effects on coupled dynamic responses of a 15 megawatt floating offshore wind turbine
papers.abstract: The global wind power industry is increasingly adopting large-scale, deep-water offshore facilities, such as floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs), which are more susceptible to typhoon impacts. Characterizing the dynamic response of FOWTs to typhoons is therefore essential for ensuring their structural safety. This study assesses the dynamic responses of the International Energy Agency 15 Megawatt (MW) FOWT under Typhoon Hagupit using Open-source Fatigue, Aerodynamics, Structures, and Turbulence. The investigation focuses on the coupled effects of yaw error and wind-wave misalignment (WWM), and the impacts of the typhoon's multi-stage evolution characteristics. Key findings include: (1) Among the five stages of typhoon passage, the front eyewall stage induces the most critical dynamic loads and responses on the FOWT. (2) Power spectral densities of platform motions reveal intricate coupling mechanisms. (i) Response coupling: surge and pitch: wave-driven within the 0.05–0.15 Hertz (Hz) band; sway and roll: wind-driven at 0.007 Hz. (ii) Structural coupling: platform pitch ↔ 1st tower fore-and-aft (FA) mode (0.524 Hz); platform sway/roll ↔ first tower side-to-side (SS) mode (0.535 Hz). (3) Yaw error and WWM under typhoons strongly amplify loads, especially the yaw error. Relative to the baseline (0° yaw error and 0° WWM), the maximum coupled effects increase the blade edgewise moment up to 26–35-fold. Overall, the yaw error should ideally be maintained within ±5°; the identified structure coupling highlights the importance of avoiding resonant interactions during the design phase. These analyses provide critical insights for anti-typhoon design, yaw-control optimization, and coupled-load mitigation under typhoons.

papers.title: New insights on rotor and stator interactions induced by unstable flows during the turbine runaway transients of three pumped-storage units
papers.abstract: Rotor and stator interactions are common unstable phenomena in rotational machinery that can induce complex pressure fluctuations; however, the formation mechanism of some low-frequency rotor and stator interactions between the unstable flow (backflow vortices) and the structural components in the static zone (guide vane) and rotational zone (impeller) is yet to be revealed. To investigate this issue, turbine runaway transients for three pump turbines with different specific speeds were simulated employing one-dimensional and three-dimensional coupled flow simulation methods. The formation mechanisms of pressure fluctuations were revealed by combining time-frequency and internal flow field analyses. The results suggest that, besides the frequency components of the pressure fluctuations induced by the conventional rotor and stator interactions between the structural components (a rotating impeller and a static guide vane), the pressure fluctuations also contained two new frequency components. They were induced by the new rotor and stator interaction between the unstable flow (backflow vortices) and the structural components in the static zone (guide vane) and rotational zone (impeller). The new rotor and stator interaction between the unstable flow and the structural components is defined as the generalized rotor and stator interaction. Consequently, all the frequency components of the pressure fluctuations during the turbine runaway transients of the three pump turbines were attributed to the proposed generalized rotor and stator interaction. They found an important theoretical value in understanding and suppressing the pressure fluctuations in pumped storage units.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of impeller clearance effects on flow-induced excitation characteristics in the high-pressure first stage of marine steam turbine
papers.abstract: The impeller clearance parameters of marine steam turbines are critical design factors that ensure the efficiency and operational stability of the turbine unit, directly influencing the steam flow excitation characteristics within the unit. Based on structural characteristics and their impact on turbine performance, impeller clearances are categorized into axial clearances and tip clearances. Addressing the limitations of existing research on the analysis of dual-clearance coupling effects and the lack of studies on the correlation between transient vortices and excitation force spectra, this paper employs numerical simulations to investigate the influence of different clearance configurations on the internal flow field. The results indicate that expanding the tip clearance increases leakage flow while significantly enhancing rotating instability and reducing the amplitude of the rotating frequency. The axial clearance influences the amplitude of the blade pass frequency by affecting the vortex structure on the blade surface. The interaction between two clearances influences the flow field structure by regulating the leakage flow path and the intensity of wake disturbances. The study reveals the independent mechanisms and synergistic effects of axial clearances and tip clearances on excitation characteristics, providing theoretical support for the optimization design of turbine impeller clearances and vibration control.

papers.title: Riemann solutions of nonhomogeneous generalized Chaplygin gas Euler equations of compressible fluid flow modeling acoustic generation and their limiting behaviors
papers.abstract: This article aims to solve Riemann problem for the generalized Chaplygin gas Euler equations of compressible fluid flow with zeroth-order terms modeling acoustic generation and analyze limiting behaviors of the solutions as the pressure approaches to zero. Thanks to variable substitution method, the Riemann solutions with five kinds of different structures involving delta-shocks are constructed, even though the nonhomogeneous generalized Chaplygin gas Euler system is strictly hyperbolic with two characteristic fields being genuinely nonlinear. The generalized Rankine–Hugoniot relation and delta-entropy condition of the delta-shock are clarified. Unlike the homogeneous case and nonhomogeneous case involving a single friction term, all waves containing rarefaction waves, shocks, and delta-shock are bent into curves and propagate at an exponential rate. Additionally, it is proved that delta-shock and vacuum of the zero-pressure Euler equations including the same zeroth-order terms can be formed as the limits of shocks and rarefaction waves of the nonhomogeneous generalized Chaplygin gas Euler equations.

papers.title: Regional nonlocal modeling of steady-state vertical suspended sediment distribution
papers.abstract: Understanding the vertical distribution of suspended sediments is crucial for the accurate prediction of sediment transport in both laboratory and natural river environments. Classical local diffusion models, such as the Rouse equation, and global fractional models often fail to fully represent the regional nonlocal transport processes induced by complex flow structures. This study develops a peridynamic differential operator (PDDO)-based regional nonlocal model for characterizing the vertical suspended sediment transport process. The proposed framework captures regional nonlocal diffusion while adhering to the physical constraint that near-bed entrainment processes can hardly transport particles instantaneously to the free surface, by introducing a finite interaction domain. The model formulation allows flexible specification of the interaction horizon and weight function, enabling the description of intermediate-scale particle motions between purely local and fully global regimes. Laboratory flume experiments and field measurements are employed to evaluate the model performance. Applications demonstrate that the PDDO model achieves superior agreement with measured concentration profiles compared to both the classical Rouse equation and the global fractional model, accurately reproducing sediment concentration patterns in near-bed, mid-depth, and upper water column regions. This study highlights the potential of the PDDO framework as a physically consistent and flexible tool for modeling suspended sediment transport across multiple spatial scales.

papers.title: Large eddy simulation of fillet radius effects on flow characteristics in a square-section diffuser
papers.abstract: This study employs large-eddy simulation to investigate the internal flow characteristics and three-dimensional separation mechanisms in a square-section diffuser with four fillet-radius (r = 0%D, 10%D, 20%D, and 30%D). Time-averaged, instantaneous, and fluctuating flow fields are analyzed to elucidate the effects of fillet radius on diffuser performance, corner separation, vortex evolution, and Reynolds stresses. The results show that increasing r leads to a quadratic increase in pressure recovery efficiency ηp, while both the total-pressure loss coefficient ζ and mean separation volume ratio exhibit exponential decay. At r = 0%D, the diverging section exhibits a localized separation bubble and large-scale three-dimensional corner separation, giving rise to strong secondary flows. As r increases, the bubble size remains nearly unchanged, but corner separation is progressively suppressed—from significant reduction at r = 10%D to full elimination at r = 30%D. The associated secondary-flow intensity and turbulence levels are substantially reduced, as evidenced by decreased Reynolds normal stresses. In contrast, the Reynolds shear stresses exhibit limited variation, indicating that fillet radius primarily alters turbulence production rather than velocity fluctuation coupling. These findings elucidate the physical mechanism by which corner geometry governs three-dimensional separation and turbulence, providing high-fidelity reference data for diffuser optimization, corner-flow control, and turbulence-model benchmarking.

papers.title: Machine learning-base analysis and prediction of non-isothermal viscoelastic polymer film casting process
papers.abstract: Predicting film thickness and width is of critical importance in polymer film casting process as they are key indicators reflecting rheological defects such as neck-in phenomenon and edge bead effect. Recently, our direct numerical simulations [Gong et al., Phys. Fluids 37, 093104 (2025)] have revealed that heat transfer coefficient, viscosity, and relaxation time are key factors affecting film dimensions in film casting, consistent with experimental observations. Building on this foundation, this work adopts a data-driven approach to develop predictive models. Machine learning algorithms can make predictions by self-learning from pre-existing experimental or computational data, and progressively improve prediction accuracy with minimal, if any, human intervention. In this paper, a dataset of about 200 polymer film casting cases is generated by means of numerical simulation, and the performances of six common machine learning models are systematically evaluated and compared in the task of film thickness and width prediction. The results show that the gradient boosting decision tree model exhibits optimal prediction ability under complex conditions. This model is able to predict final film thickness and width with high accuracy (correlation coefficient R2 > 0.99). Additionally, relaxation time is found to have the greatest effect on the prediction results through significance analysis. On this basis, a new machine learning model is developed through hyperparameter tuning, which further improves the prediction accuracy. This study extends the application of machine learning methods in the field of film casting, which is conducive to optimizing the processing procedure and reducing material waste.

papers.title: Self-sustained tumbling of bluff bodies at low speeds
papers.abstract: Many objects such as low length-to-diameter ratio cylinders and some planetary entry capsules are known to experience spontaneous and/or self-sustained “tumbling” rotations about a transverse axis. This study quantifies the tumbling frequency and the associated lateral aerodynamic (Magnus) force as well as increased drag for a range of geometries in subsonic flow. Experiments were conducted using a unique wind tunnel magnetic suspension system, hence are free of support interference. All non-spherical geometries exhibited sustained tumbling behavior with the tumbling frequency proportional to flow velocity. It was found that certain geometries exhibit multiple stable “lock-in” frequencies.

papers.title: Aerodynamics of spanwise leading-edge damage on a transport wing at transonic conditions
papers.abstract: Bird strikes introduce localized leading-edge damage that can significantly alter aerodynamic performance at transonic conditions, yet comprehensive characterization of these effects remains limited. This study addresses this gap by utilizing a coupled finite element method–smooth particle hydrodynamics approach for bird impact with high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics analysis of a modern swept-wing transport configuration at Mach 0.7 and 0.85. The investigation considers three spanwise damage locations (inboard, mid-span, and tip), with the inboard station further evaluating strike orientations (0°, ±30°). Results reveal that inboard damage causes the most severe degradation, including λ-shock collapse, spanwise load redistribution (with lift deficits up to ΔCL≈−0.5), and suppression of the baseline pitch-break (ΔCM≈−0.13 and −0.10 at Mach 0.7 and 0.85). Mid-span dents result in localized suction collapse and confined drag increments, while tip dents remain strictly local with negligible global influence. The +30° orientation exhibits favorable pressure drag characteristics at higher incidences, in contrast to the 0° orientation, which exhibits the strongest performance degradation. Viscous drag remains elevated at low incidence (∼ 20 counts), but decreases at moderate angles due to premature separation, with differences vanishing post-stall. Overall, the study highlights how damage location and orientation govern post-impact aerodynamics, providing insights relevant for certification standards and operational safety.

papers.title: An optimized contact upwind flux splitting scheme based on characteristics
papers.abstract: The Flux Vector Splitting (FVS) scheme tends to produce numerical transition zones and nonphysical oscillations when initialized with mathematical discontinuities. Although the Upwind Flux Scheme based on Characteristics (UFSC) can alleviate such errors, it still exhibits limitations in handling stationary contact discontinuities and high-Mach number shock waves. To overcome these issues, this paper proposes the Optimized-Contact UFSC (OC-UFSC), which achieves strict preservation of stationary contact discontinuities through an improved decoupling strategy. Furthermore, by incorporating a shock detector with the Van Leer scheme, a hybrid scheme OC-UFSC+V, is constructed to enhance stability under high-Mach number shocks. Comparative analyses against the FVS and Flux Difference Splitting (FDS) schemes in both one- and two-dimensional benchmark tests demonstrate that OC-UFSC+V resolves contact discontinuities sharply, expansion waves, and shock waves. Compared with the FVS scheme, it preserves the accuracy of linear and quadratic flows, matches the resolution of FDS schemes, and effectively avoids the common Carbuncle phenomenon in FDS. Overall, OC-UFSC+V exhibits superior resolution and stability.

papers.title: Power extraction from vortex-induced vibration of two rigidly coupled cylinders in staggered arrangement
papers.abstract: Vortex-induced vibration (VIV) of coupled cylinders offers a promising route for clean energy harvesting through fluid–structure interaction. This study numerically investigates power generation from two rigidly coupled cylinders arranged in staggered configurations over spacing ratios L, T=2.0−4.0, damping ratios ζ=0.04−0.28, and reduced velocities U*=3.0−8.5 at Re = 150 and m*=2.0. The results reveal that vibration amplitude and power output exhibit strong non-monotonic dependence on U* and ζ, with optimal performance at intermediate damping. Additionally, the maximum vibration amplitude decreases with increasing T. Maximum average power is obtained at an intermediate damping value, referred to as the optimal mass–damping parameter (α=m*ζ). The optimal α for all arrangements, except for the L=3.0,T=2.0, is recorded at α=0.32. The configuration L=2.0,T=3.0 yields the maximum average power (0.28) and power density (0.02), nearly twice that of a single cylinder, while L=3.0,T=2.0 achieves the highest power extraction efficiency (0.075). Overall, the findings demonstrate that appropriate staggered arrangements can significantly enhance power generation efficiency, offering useful design insights for compact VIV-based energy harvesters.

papers.title: Analysis of modulation of wake–wave coupling by pycnocline structure in stratified flow
papers.abstract: Nonlinear pycnoclines are frequently encountered by underwater vehicles operating in the ocean. This study investigates the impact of pycnocline strength on the dynamics of the cylinder wake. Using large eddy simulation, the research investigates how varying pycnocline strength within hyperbolic-tangent density stratification influences wake evolution and internal wave characteristics. The study reveals the combined effects of pycnocline strength and incoming flow velocity on the wake, as well as the key role of internal waves in energy dissipation under two-dimensional constraints. When buoyancy predominates in wake evolution, the internal waves are primarily Lee waves. Enhanced stratification suppresses internal wave development, accelerates wake energy decay, and inhibits vortex shedding and recirculation. Conversely, when both buoyancy and inertial forces are influential, internal waves consist of Lee waves and coherent waves. Weak stratification promotes internal wave radiation, with a more pronounced leeward wave range, whereas strong stratification suppresses this effect. The rate of energy dissipation in the wake exhibits a nonlinear relationship with stratification strength. Weak stratification may induce wake-wave resonance, leading to faster decay, while strong stratification results in a distinct envelope structure. When inertial forces dominate, substantial stratification delays wake energy decay by inhibiting internal wave radiation. Coherent structures, induced by vortex shedding and other instabilities, significantly enhance the modulation of wake energy by internal waves.

papers.title: Jet dynamics of two cavitation bubbles adjacent to a rigid wall
papers.abstract: Cavitation bubbles in fluids frequently induce persistent cavitation erosion, which seriously impacts the service life and efficiency of hydraulic machinery. This study employed the multiple image method to analyze the jet behaviors induced by the collapse of two bubbles adjacent to the wall and conducted verification through high-speed photographic experiments. The variations of jet characteristics with the spacing of the two bubbles (L*) and the bubble-wall spacing (H*) were analyzed. Then, the parameter conditions for the jet directly colliding with the wall were quantitatively examined. Also, the dominant range and mechanisms of the bubble–bubble interaction and the bubble–wall interaction on the jet behaviors were discussed. The results are summarized as follows: (1) The phenomenon of a jet colliding with the wall non-vertically occurs within a wide parameter range of L*, which can exceed 10 times the maximum bubble radius. (2) As L* increases or H* decreases, there occurs a transition from jets colliding with each other to direct impact against the wall. For the critical situation, a quasi-linear relationship exists between L* and H*. (3) The L*-H* parameter space describing the dominant role of the bubble and the wall for jet behaviors is divided into three feature regions: the bubble-dominated region, the wall-dominated region, and the co-dominated region.

papers.title: A framework for physical dominant dynamic mode decomposition mode selection of unsteady flows with rank stability
papers.abstract: Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) is a powerful data-driven technique for identifying low-dimensional representations of complex flows. However, existing dominant mode selection methods suffer limitations of lack of physical interpretability across different truncation ranks. To address this, a novel framework with rank stability is introduced to select the dominant modes through cohesive and multi-stage processes. The framework begins with the construction of a stabilization diagram by applying DMD across a range of truncation ranks to visualize all potential modes. Then, a Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise algorithm, coupled with automated hyperparameter optimization, is employed to objectively identify candidate clusters from the stabilization diagram. Finally, these candidates are filtered by using the coefficient of variation criterion to ensure the physical consistency of retained modes. The proposed framework was validated by three benchmark cases of increasing complexity, i.e., a laminar cylinder flow (Re = 60), a transitional cavity flow (Re = 3000), and a practical case of transonic buffet over a NACA 0012 airfoil (Re = 3 × 106). Comparative results demonstrate the advantage of our method in consistently identifying physical modes, compared to the amplitude method, the I-criterion and the optimization-based sparsity-promoting DMD method. It provides a robust framework for identifying dominant flow structures in multiple flow regimes, making it a valuable tool for data-driven fluid dynamics research and engineering.

papers.title: Two-phase flows in rough channels using the lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: Two-phase flows in rough-walled channels play an important role in porous media transport, multiphase fluid displacement, and drag-reduction technologies. In this work, we employ the free-energy lattice Boltzmann method to simulate immiscible fluids in complex geometries. A novel method is proposed to impose boundary conditions at the rough wall and to ensure mass conservation. We systematically study the effects of external driving force, roughness geometry, surface wettability, and viscosity ratio on the configuration of stable states and the velocity field. The study reveals rich dynamical behavior, including multiple coexisting stable states and hysteresis phenomena, where identical parameters yield different states depending on initial conditions. Phase diagrams are constructed to map the regimes of these states. Analysis of velocity profiles shows that fluid confinement in wall grooves may suppress bulk transport via vortex-induced dissipation, while low-viscosity phases can act as lubricants to enhance flow. These results not only advance our understanding of two-phase flow in rough geometries but also provide insights for optimizing transport and control in porous media, coating, and microfluidic applications.

papers.title: Flux-controlled wall model for large eddy simulation integrating the compressible law of the wall
papers.abstract: Recent advances in velocity and temperature transformations have enabled recovery of the law of the wall in compressible wall-bounded turbulent flows. Building on this foundation, a flux-controlled wall model (FCWM) for large eddy simulation (LES) is proposed. Unlike conventional wall-stress models that solve the turbulent boundary layer equations, FCWM formulates the near-wall modeling as a control problem applied directly to the outer LES solution. It consists of three components: (1) the compressible law of the wall, (2) a feedback flux-control strategy, and (3) a shifted boundary condition. The model adjusts the wall shear stress and heat flux based on discrepancies between the computed and target transformed velocity and temperature, respectively, at the matching location. The proposed wall model is evaluated using LES of turbulent channel flows across a broad range of conditions, including quasi-incompressible cases with bulk Mach number Mb=0.1 and friction Reynolds number Reτ=180–10 000, and compressible cases with Mb=0.74–4.0 and bulk Reynolds number Reb=7667–34 000. The wall-modeled LES reproduces mean velocity and temperature profiles in agreement with direct numerical simulation data. For all tested cases with Mb≤3, the wall model achieves relative errors of |εCf|<4.1%, |εBq|<2.7%, and |εTc|<2.7% in friction coefficient, non-dimensional heat flux, and centerline temperature, respectively. In the quasi-incompressible regime, the wall model achieves |εCf|<1%. Compared to the conventional equilibrium wall model, the proposed FCWM achieves higher accuracy in compressible turbulent channel flows without solving the boundary layer equations, thereby reducing computational cost.

papers.title: Closed-loop machine learning control of a cavity flow using adaptive plasma actuators at moderate Reynolds number
papers.abstract: A real-time machine learning control of the cavity flow was experimentally implemented at a moderate Reynolds number of 48 000, operating at a 4 kHz interaction frequency. A fast-response dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuator and a hot-wire anemometer probe were served as the flow perturbation device and the state sensor. Aiming to achieve maximum attenuation of the single-tone cavity noise, the particle swarm optimization (PSO) and genetic programming (GP) algorithms were employed to identify optimal actuation parameters within an open-loop framework and derive an optimal closed-loop control law, respectively. This approach yielded three distinct effective control strategies characterized by unique shear-layer vortex dynamics. The first strategy, identified via PSO as the optimal unsteady periodic actuation, modifies the noise spectrum through a “partial-escape partial-clipping” mechanism applied to shear-layer vortices, shifting the dominant characteristic frequency from St = 1.606 to St = 1.2. The second strategy, involving steady high-intensity plasma actuation, significantly suppresses shear-layer instability. This results in the near-exclusive “complete escape” of nascent vortices above the cavity trailing edge, with minimal clipping effect observed. In contrast, the third conditional actuation strategy, derived via GP, employs a novel manipulation approach: vortices are actively directed either downward into the cavity or upward, bypassing the downstream corner entirely. This alternation between “complete-escape” and “complete-clipping” mechanisms induces a 94% attenuation in the modal noise peak. Notably, the associated power consumption for this strategy is merely 31% of that required for the steady actuation strategy.

papers.title: Vortex-induced vibration characteristics and force modeling of segmented steel-concrete hybrid wind turbines tower in high-altitude cold region
papers.abstract: The low air density and rarefied atmosphere in high-altitude cold regions cause significant variations in Reynolds numbers compared to conventional low-altitude environment, posing challenges for accurately predicting wind-induced vibrations of segmented steel-concrete hybrid towers (SSCHTs). Traditional vortex-excited force models often neglect the influence of critical environmental factors in such regions, which limits their applicability for vibration prediction under extreme wind conditions. To investigate the impact of high-altitude cold environments on vortex-induced vibration (VIV) mechanisms and to develop corresponding modeling strategies, a multi-parameter coupling model integrating altitude, temperature, air density, and Reynolds number is established to analyze their effects on aerodynamic characteristics. Based on this framework, aerodynamic load time histories obtained from computational fluid dynamics simulations are applied to the finite element structural model to investigate the wake evolution and structural VIV response of SSCHTs under representative conditions. Furthermore, a trigonometric series-based lift oscillator model is proposed for vortex-excited force tailored for high-altitude cold environments and validated against aerodynamic force data under varying elevations, temperatures, and tower cross section conditions. The results indicate that vortex shedding frequencies generally decrease in high-altitude cold regions, and lateral aerodynamic forces are reduced at all heights—with a reduction of 48.3% at the tower top. However, the peak lateral displacement at the tower top remains comparable to that in conventional regions, and the lock-in wind speed is similar. While the classical lift oscillator model demonstrates good accuracy under conventional conditions, its performance deteriorates in high-altitude cold regions. In contrast, the proposed trigonometric series model shows enhanced adaptability and reconstructs the waveforms of lift coefficient more accurately, with correlation coefficients exceeding 0.94.

papers.title: An eigenvalue-based method for computing the relaxed pressure in compressible multiphase flow with N phases
papers.abstract: The modeling of compressible multiphase flows is a decades-old area of study with many applications across various fields. Many of these application areas use stiff pressure relaxation. This process involves the solution of a nonlinear system with N+1 equations and N+1 unknowns, where N is the number of phases. The resolution of this system with general equations of state (EOSs) is difficult. Furthermore, nonlinear systems can admit multiple solutions, and current solution methods do not address this possibility. Very recently, a thermodynamic relaxation method was introduced, which effectively maps a relatively simple predictor equation of state onto a more complex target equation of state. In this context, the target EOSs are the chosen EOSs for the thermodynamic model. This thermodynamic relaxation has the benefit of simplifying the stiff pressure relaxation system of equations. In this article, we show this system reduces to a polynomial of degree N, which can be recast as an eigenvalue problem through the use of the associated companion matrix. We show that although this eigenvalue method is generally less efficient than Newton–Raphson iteration, it does not suffer from convergence issues and finds all N roots of the polynomial. Hence, the method provides a fail-safe for root-finding iterative methods and a way to address the issue of multiple solutions to the nonlinear system of equations in stiff pressure relaxation.

papers.title: Aerodynamic shape optimization using the adjoint method combined with an inverse design approach for non-parameterized geometries
papers.abstract: Most aerodynamic shape optimization frameworks operate directly on surface meshes, yielding optimized meshes rather than true computer-aided design (CAD) geometries. This CAD-free strategy requires remeshing and CAD reconstruction, which often introduces geometric inconsistencies. Direct CAD-based optimization can avoid these issues but typically depends on manually built, precisely parameterized models, making it laborious and error-prone. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes an adjoint-based aerodynamic optimization framework combined with an inverse design approach for non-parameterized geometries. Starting from neutral-format models such as STEP files, the method reconstructs parameterized CAD geometries through automated inverse modeling, enabling the definition of design variables and velocities. These are directly linked to adjoint sensitivities from DAFoam, establishing a consistent loop between geometry and flow analysis. The framework's accuracy and efficiency are demonstrated on the NACA0012 airfoil, the ONERA M6 wing, and the Rotor 37 blade, showing reliable aerodynamic improvements across different configurations.

papers.title: A geometry-informed eddy viscosity formula with sublinear geometric scale dependence
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the limitations of traditional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) models, particularly their inability to accurately predict Kolmogorov flow, a fundamental flow driven by sinusoidally varying forces. Despite being known for over 70 years, the Kolmogorov flow has not been extensively utilized in the development of turbulence models. Existing RANS models, such as the standard k−ε and k−ω shear stress transport, fail to capture key flow characteristics of the Kolmogorov flow, leading to an unbounded growth (inflation) of the turbulent length scale. This paper proposes a new eddy viscosity formulation to address these issues. The proposed model introduces a geometry-informed (GI) eddy viscosity formulation, which incorporates a power function dependent on the geometric filter size to avoid the unphysical turbulent inflation in Kolmogorov flow. The GI eddy viscosity model was coupled with the k−ε transport equation and tested in channel flow, the Kolmogorov flow, and flow over a backward-facing step. The results demonstrated that the new model outperforms traditional models in some tests, providing better predictions of turbulent kinetic energy, and it also mitigates turbulent inflation. The study concludes by highlighting the potential for further model improvements and future validation using the time-varying Kolmogorov flow data.

papers.title: Investigation of viscous effects on a rectangular barge undergoing roll and heave motions in regular waves: A physics-informed neural network approach
papers.abstract: This study examines viscous effects on a rectangular barge undergoing coupled roll and heave motions in regular waves by reconstructing flow and pressure fields using a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework based on particle image velocimetry (PIV) data. Three neural network models were developed to infer the water volume fraction, velocity, and pressure. The velocity model employed a stream-function formulation to inherently satisfy the continuity equation, while the pressure model incorporated the Navier–Stokes equations with a zero-gauge pressure boundary condition in the air phase. The models were fine-tuned using the limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (L-BFGS) optimizer following initial training with Adam. The PINN-reconstructed velocity and vorticity fields closely matched experimental measurements, confirming the reliability of the approach. The results show that vortices generated near the barge coincide with local reductions in dynamic pressure, and that increasing wave height intensifies vortex strength, resulting in larger viscous effects without altering the overall vortex evolution. Under waves at the natural roll period, higher wave heights primarily increased roll damping, explaining the nonlinear roll response observed experimentally. These findings provide insight into vortex-driven mechanisms of viscous roll damping and enhancement and demonstrate the capability of PINNs for high-fidelity flow reconstruction in complex wave-structure interactions.

papers.title: Three-dimensional cage-engineered biphilic surfaces controlling thermal-fluidic interactions for boiling enhancement
papers.abstract: Boiling two-phase transition is recognized as an efficient cooling strategy for high-heat-flux applications like data centers, power plants. To enhance the comprehensive heat transfer performance of boiling phase-change, this study proposed a three-dimensional (3D) cage-engineered biphilic surface that synergistically enhances nucleate boiling initiation, heat transfer coefficient, and critical heat flux. The 3D cage structure facilitates vapor escape, while the copper foam pillars with superhydrophilic CuO nano-coatings simultaneously enhance active nucleation site density and, acting as liquid reservoirs, ensure sustained surface re-wetting even during dryout conditions. This multifunctional design addresses fundamental limitations of conventional boiling surfaces by decoupling liquid supply and vapor removal processes. Compared to a flat copper surface, the hybrid structure triggered the onset of nucleate boiling 6.5 °C earlier while achieving 87% higher maximum heat transfer coefficient. Notably, the novel design elevated critical heat flux to 232% above the baseline of a flat copper surface through enhanced liquid replenishment and two-phase bubble dynamics. The demonstrated performances advanced the surface engineering strategy for extreme thermal management, showing particular promise for the strict cooling demands of high-power applications.

papers.title: Dynamic stall induced by a periodic transverse gust of an airfoil at transitional Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: The aerodynamic response of an airfoil to periodic (harmonic) transverse gusts at transitional Reynolds numbers (Rec≈105) is investigated experimentally in a low-speed wind tunnel, with particular emphasis on gust-induced dynamic stall. A gust generator employing two motor-driven vanes produces periodic transverse gusts. The downstream flow is characterized under both static and dynamic conditions before mounting a stationary test wing. The wing, equipped with an internal six-component balance at mid-span, is first examined in uniform freestream, and then under gust excitation across pre- and post-stall regimes. In the pre-stall regime, the measured lift matches linear predictions from Küssner's and Sears functions. In the post-stall regime, the effective angle of attack, defined as the geometric wing angle plus the gust angle, enables qualitative comparison with pitch-induced dynamic stall. The gust angle is defined by treating the transverse gust as an equivalent camber-induced downwash and computing it from a thin-airfoil downwash integral. Around a static stall, transverse gusts drive the wing into deep post-stall, where pronounced nonlinear effects emerge, including lift enhancement and hysteresis in both lift and moment. These behaviors are attributed to alternating upwash and downwash induced by transverse gusts, analogous to the upstroke and downstroke hysteresis observed in pitch-induced dynamic stall. At a comparable reduced frequency, the similarity of lift and moment responses highlights an analogy between the gust-induced and classical pitch-induced dynamic stalls. Parametric variations in gust amplitude and Reynolds number further delineate the dynamics. The influence of flow transition is revealed by mounting a leading-edge transition strip under both uniform freestream and gusty conditions.

papers.title: Influence of particle-to-fluid density ratio on horizontal particle-laden pipe flows across distinct gravity regimes
papers.abstract: This study investigates the combined effects of particle-to-fluid density ratio (ρr) and fluid Froude number (Fr) on particle–fluid interactions in horizontal pipe flow, where gravity acts transverse to the mean flow direction. Simulations were conducted for three particle-to-fluid density ratios, ρr=1000, 2500, and 8000, corresponding to low [e.g., poly-methyl methacrylate (PMMA)/plastic], intermediate (e.g., glass beads), and high-density (e.g., copper or heavy metal dust) particle regimes in air, respectively, in three distinct gravity regimes: microgravity (negligible gravity influence), terrestrial gravity (moderate gravity influence), and enhanced gravity (high gravity influence), with a constant mass loading (characterizing the particle-to-fluid mass flux ratio) of Φm=0.4 and a constant particle diameter, dp =40 μm. For the fixed particle size, variations in particle density result in a Stokes number (Stk) range from 11 to 88, representing the ratio of particle to fluid response times. A four-way coupling regime was used, and the coefficient of restitution was set to 0.97 for the interaction of particle–particle and particle–wall. For Fr=17, increasing ρr reduces the asymmetry in the fluid velocity profile about the centerline, as well as a decrease in secondary flow motion due to higher Stokes and fluid Froude numbers, with the highest secondary flow magnitude observed for the lowest density ratio, decreasing as the density ratio increases. A similar trend is observed for the particle velocity. In addition to Fr, the particle Froude number (Frp) is also used, representing the balance between bulk fluid velocity and particle settling velocity, thereby providing a complementary measure of particle response to gravity and its role in secondary flow motions. At higher fluid Froude numbers (Fr=68 and ∞), inertial effects dominate over gravity, and the fluid and particle velocity profiles show negligible variation with ρr. One of the key findings of the study shows that as the fluid Froude number reaches, Fr=68 and above, the flow-related characteristics such as fluid velocity, particle velocity, and turbulent kinetic energy are independent of the density ratio, and they are solely governed by inertia rather than gravity.

papers.title: Development of an analytical model for droplet entrainment rate in gas–liquid annular flow
papers.abstract: The droplet entrainment rate is a core parameter for the optimal design of the mass and heat transfer efficiency in annular flow. However, the existing mechanism models assume that the crest of the shear disturbance wave is the whole process of droplet entrainment, which is inconsistent with the results of visual experiments; the calculated values of the disturbance wave frequency deviate greatly from the experimental values, resulting in the prediction results being several orders of magnitude higher than the experimental values. Thus, this work determines the hierarchical characteristics of the droplet entrainment process based on the summary of indirect experimental observations in the existing literature and the optimization of force balance logic in mathematical modeling: shearing the disturbance wave crest, boundary layer separation on the windward side of the disturbance wave, and shearing the ripples. The transition boundaries of the three types of entrainment mechanisms are defined using the Weber number combining the gas-phase momentum and the liquid film thickness. New correlations of the disturbance wave frequency in different types are constructed, using the mathematical structural forms of the arctangent, logarithmic, and sigmoid functions are, respectively, used to reproduce the non-linear frequency change law with the Weber number as the core. Combining the mechanical analysis of the local interfacial wave structure in different types, a new mechanism model of droplet entrainment is constructed. The new model was validated with 403 sets of data from nine datasets, and the prediction results showed that the root mean square error and mean absolute error were 12.4% and 9.8%, respectively.

papers.title: Numerical investigation on a shock-accelerated heavy gas reactive concentric cylinder
papers.abstract: The reactive shock-concentric-cylinder interaction (RSCCI) is investigated numerically to uncover detonation initiation mechanisms and interface evolution. The H2–O2–Xe heavy gas cylinder (molar ratio 2:1:3.67) with a concentrically imbedded N2 cylinder is impacted by a Mach 2.83 shock wave. The ensuing behaviors of six concentric cylinders, with inner cylinder radius (rin) to outer cylinder radius (r) ratios varying from 0.250 to 0.875, are examined. Compared to the reactive shock-cylinder interaction (RSCI), the inner cylinder in RSCCI alters the shock convergence pattern and, therefore, the ignition instant and location. As rin increases, particularly when rin = 0.750r, the detonation initiation occurs 43.53% earlier than in RSCI, flame filling time is reduced by 23.11%, and final combustion completeness reaches 0.9560, improving by 1.16% over RSCI. A large inner cylinder results in a more flattened post-shock concentric cylinder interface shape in the streamwise direction but a more expanded shape in the spanwise direction. It also reduces the post-shock cylinder area. To have an effective cylinder area expansion, rin < 0.500r is found to be imperative. A large inner cylinder also reduces the combustible gas consumption rate, leading to a lower asymptotic average temperature and weakened combustible gas expandability. Convenient theoretical methods are provided to accurately predict the early-stage inert cylinder area, the late-stage reactive cylinder areas in the RSCI case and RSCCI cases with smaller inner cylinders, and finally, the total absolute circulations under reactive conditions. This work is expected to provide theoretical insights that are beneficial to the scramjet combustor design.

papers.title: Ferrofluid dynamics with a free energy magnetic model in the simplified lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: This study presents a simplified lattice Boltzmann method, integrated with an energy-based phase-field formulation, to simulate ferrofluid dynamics under a uniform magnetic field. Unlike conventional approaches that impose magnetic body forces directly within the momentum equations, our model introduces magnetic field effects through a free energy framework, where magnetic contributions are embedded into the interface dynamics via the total energy functional. This coupling strategy improves the consistency between interfacial motion and magnetic influence while naturally localizing magnetic effects at the interface and preserving the numerical efficiency of the lattice Boltzmann scheme. The method is applied to benchmark problems, including droplet deformation and coalescence under varying magnetic field strengths, showing good agreement with experimental observations. Simulations demonstrate the model's ability to capture complex magneto-hydrodynamic interactions, resolving detailed velocity fields, magnetic flux distributions, and interfacial evolution. This approach provides a robust and reliable platform for investigating multiphase ferrofluid flows under external magnetic fields.

papers.title: A review of fluid–solid interaction experimental techniques: A comprehensive classification, development, and future directions in geo-energy science
papers.abstract: Laboratory-based experimental equipment provides valuable insights into the physicochemical interactions among gas, liquid, and rock in surface and subsurface environments. They help elucidate key processes such as enhanced hydrocarbon recovery, fluid–solid reactions, and CO2 sequestration. This work reviews experimental equipment used to study gas–liquid–rock interactions at varying reservoir conditions. It classifies the equipment by structural design, operating conditions, and functionality. A comparative analysis is conducted to evaluate their performance, strengths, limitations, and the technical challenges currently faced in the field. Static and stirred equipment are suitable for elucidating ex situ material migration characteristics, while core flooding equipment excels in replicating in situ fluid transport and fluid–solid interactions. Recent technical cases indicate that the utilization and development of these setups have gained widespread attention, and certain progress has been made in experimental techniques. Besides the overview of existing experimental techniques, this review introduces an innovative in situ dynamic core flooding setup featuring gas–liquid premixing and injection under controlled temperature, pressure, and stress fields. The equipment is capable of providing injection pressures of 0–65 MPa, confining pressures of 0–75 MPa, and temperatures of 0–250 °C. It adopts a premixing injection approach inspired by the Iceland CarbFix project, ensuring complete gas–liquid mixing and thereby substantially improving interaction efficiency. The findings indicate that developing more realistic and efficient experimental systems is essential for advancing research and innovation in geo-energy science.

papers.title: Limit behaviors for Riemann solutions of the generalized Chaplygin gas Euler equations with zeroth-order terms modeling acoustic generation
papers.abstract: This article solves the Riemann problem for the nonhomogeneous generalized Chaplygin gas Euler equations modeling acoustic generation in a fluid by forcing, and constructs five kinds of non-self-similar solutions with the use of variable substitution. It is found that though the considered system is strictly hyperbolic with two characteristic fields being genuinely nonlinear, the delta-shock occurs in the solution. Using the generalized Rankine–Hugoniot relation and delta-entropy condition, the position, propagation speed and strength of the delta-shock are derived. Unlike the previous studies on the generalized Chaplygin gas Euler equations, all waves propagate at an exponential rate. Besides, it turns out that when the parameter A modeling the strength of pressure falls to a quantitative value, the solution formed by two shocks of the considered system tends to a particular delta-shock solution of the considered system; when A drops to zero, the delta-shock solution tends to that of the nonhomogeneous zero-pressure Euler system containing same zeroth-order terms; when A approaches to zero, the solution composed of two rarefaction waves of the considered system tends to the solution with vacuum of the nonhomogeneous zero-pressure Euler system including same zeroth-order terms.

papers.title: Inter-stage flow characteristics analysis of a multistage centrifugal pump with symmetrical impeller arrangement
papers.abstract: Low-specific-speed multistage pumps are widely used in the chemical, electric power, and other fields. The symmetrical impeller arrangement structure brings stability advantages for multistage centrifugal pumps, but its inadequate structural design causes high hydraulic losses. Therefore, this paper takes the vertical multistage centrifugal pump with a symmetrical impeller arrangement structure as the research object. Through unsteady numerical simulation and test verification, the effects of the inlet flow condition on the intra-stage flow characteristic differences are analyzed, indicating the optimization direction for the structural design of multistage centrifugal pumps. This research shows the influence mechanism of the matching difference between the blade profile and the inlet flow pattern caused by the variation of the inlet flow angle on the inter-stage flow characteristics difference. This research shows that the direct cause of the asymmetric flow phenomenon is the flow structure difference caused by the uneven pre-rotation at the inlet. Our results enhance the understanding of internal flow mechanisms in multistage pumps and provide a clear direction and theoretical basis for the structural optimization of multistage centrifugal pumps.

papers.title: Acoustics of humid porous media: Effects of precondensation and molecular diffusion on their effective properties
papers.abstract: A theoretical approach is developed to describe the acoustic behavior of humid air-saturated porous media. Humid air is here considered as a binary mixture of dry air and water vapor, in which water vapor is likely to precondense (i.e., to be adsorbed) on a solid wall. The formulation of the acoustic problem includes the Navier–Stokes, mass conservation, heat diffusion, and mutual diffusion of water vapor in air equations. The boundary conditions account for the velocity continuity and the mass and heat flux conservation at the gas–liquid–solid interfaces. Indeed, precondensed water vapor forms a thin liquid film on the walls that undergoes thickness variations, resulting in non-zero vibration velocity at the liquid–gas interface. This film also acts as a mass and heat source. Its overall behavior is determined by the expression of its thermodynamic equilibrium with water vapor. The problem is analytically solved for straight pores having a constant cross section shape. The results obtained highlight the specific contributions of precondensation to the dynamic behavior of simple porous structures. These contributions, which are significant under extreme environmental conditions, essentially result in increasing the low-frequency limit of the normalized dynamic compressibility. Based on this analysis, a simple generalization to porous media is also proposed.

papers.title: Effect of corner film flow on two-phase relative permeability: A pore-scale perspective
papers.abstract: Corner film flow governed by dimensionality and wettability profoundly impacts displacement patterns, yet its effect on relative permeability remains unclear. We use a multiple-relaxation-time color-gradient lattice Boltzmann model with geometric wetting boundaries to examine, under identical pore structures, how capillary number, wettability, and viscosity ratio modulate the influence of wetting films on relative permeabilities. We find that in 3D (three-dimensional) capillary bridges link corner films into secondary pathways that increase wetting connectivity and strengthen interfacial viscous coupling. Increasing capillary number raises the relative permeabilities of both phases in 2D (two-dimensional) and 3D. At high capillary number or high wetting saturation, bulk flow dominates and the difference in wetting permeability shrinks, whereas the non-wetting permeability remains higher in 3D than in 2D due to stronger viscous coupling. Decreasing the contact angle enhances viscous coupling and weakens non-wetting–solid interactions, thereby increasing the non-wetting relative permeability and widening the 3D over 2D gap. The wetting-phase response to wettability depends on the presence of films and saturation. Increasing the viscosity ratio markedly elevates the non-wetting relative permeability, with the larger interfacial area in 3D further amplifying viscous coupling. The wetting-phase relative permeability decreases with viscosity ratio, yet at very high viscosity ratios the initial phase configuration becomes influential. This study clarifies the dimensional mechanisms governing relative permeability, especially the controlling role of wetting films, which is critical for judging when multiphase-flow physics can be simplified.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of the turbulent boundary-layer footprint on the wake of a wing section
papers.abstract: This experimental study examines the downstream wake development influenced by attached turbulent boundary layers under adverse and favorable pressure gradients (APG, FPG) on the suction and pressure sides of a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 4412 airfoil. Experiments were performed at a chord-based Reynolds number of Rec=400 000 and angles of attack of 5° and 8°. Surface pressure scans and hot-wire anemometry were used to characterize boundary layer and wake profiles, extending three chord lengths downstream of the trailing edge. The key contributions are: (i) demonstrating a strong memory effect whereby upstream boundary-layer characteristics persist into the very-near- and near-wake; (ii) establishing a unified inner/outer velocity scaling framework that enables direct comparison of boundary-layer and wake profiles; and (iii) identifying distinct suction- vs pressure-side routes to self-similarity driven by the sign of the pressure gradient. Inner scaling of wake velocity profiles using friction velocity and viscous length scale proves valid only within the very-near-wake. In contrast, outer-scaled velocity-defect profiles using the Zagarola–Smits velocity reveal self-similarity on the suction side from the trailing edge across the entire wake region, whereas pressure-side profiles retain significant upstream influence initially, with self-similarity emerging from the near-wake onward. Turbulence analysis via streamwise velocity variance and premultiplied power spectral densities further shows distinct development patterns on the suction and pressure sides of the wake. The APG on the suction side promotes early development of wake-type structures and self-similarity, while the FPG on the pressure side preserves boundary-layer features deeper into the wake. These findings demonstrate how upstream pressure gradients modulate the transition from boundary-layer-dominated to wake-dominated behavior, providing new physical insight into wake development and supporting improved aerodynamic modeling and wake prediction for aeronautical and wind energy applications.

papers.title: A wall-modeled large eddy simulation method with a generalized wall function for flux reconstruction solver
papers.abstract: This study incorporates the generalized wall stress function proposed by Shih et al. into a high-order flux reconstruction (FR) solver for wall-modeled large-eddy simulation (WMLES). The wall model accounts for non-equilibrium effects induced by favorable and adverse pressure gradients in turbulent flows via the generalized wall stress formulation. Unlike previous approaches, which estimate wall shear stress based on the tangential velocity at the interface between the first and second off-wall cells in high-order discontinuous Galerkin or FR frameworks, the present model evaluates the wall shear stress at the first solution point within the wall-adjacent element. Furthermore, a no-slip wall boundary condition is enforced, in contrast to the slip condition applied in earlier studies. To achieve a balance between numerical stability and accuracy, a hybrid approach combining weak-prescribed and weak-Riemann methods is developed for computing inviscid wall fluxes. Detailed procedures for implementing the generalized wall function and treating inviscid and viscous fluxes at the wall are thoroughly described. The solver and wall model are validated in fully developed turbulent channel flows at friction Reynolds numbers 2000, 5200, and 10 000. Performance of the generalized wall function is further assessed in simulations of flow over a periodic hill at Reynolds numbers of 10 595 and 37 000, which are characterized by strong pressure gradients. Numerical predictions show favorable agreement with experimental measurements and high-fidelity reference datasets, demonstrating the proposed WMLES approach's capability in accurately predicting non-equilibrium turbulent flows under adverse and favorable pressure gradients.

papers.title: Shoulder-attached cavity dynamics and hydrodynamic characteristics of underwater vehicles
papers.abstract: When an underwater vehicle rapidly exits the storage tube, the residual gas near the tube mouth forms an attached cavity around the shoulder of the vehicle. This cavity significantly influences the motion stability and hydrodynamic loading of the vehicle. In this study, numerical simulations were conducted to investigate the formation mechanism of the attached cavity and to evaluate the effects of various head shapes on the evolution of the transient flow field and the hydrodynamic performance of the vehicle. The results indicate that flow separation at the shoulder initiates the development of the attached cavity. The subsequent shedding of the cavity induces a periodic hairpin vortex and strong pressure fluctuations. As the shoulder geometry becomes more streamlined, the gas volume within the cavity decreases, the asymmetry becomes more pronounced, and the cavity shedding mode changes. The dominant shedding frequency tends to increase, while the amplitude diminishes, indicating a transition toward a more unstable flow state, with an intermediate configuration likely exhibiting a transitional regime in which multiscale shedding coexists. This complex evolution of the cavity directly affects the overall hydrodynamic loading characteristics of the vehicle. This study offers a significant reference point for the prediction of multiphase cavitating flows and the design of motion stability of underwater vehicles.

papers.title: A hybrid data assimilation method for scale-resolved flows combining ensemble Kalman filter and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition
papers.abstract: To improve the accuracy of low-fidelity (LF) flow-field data using limited high-fidelity (HF) observations, a novel data assimilation method based on the hybridization of the gappy proper orthogonal decomposition (Gappy POD) and the offline ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) methods is proposed. Specifically, to address the limitation that the performance of the Gappy POD strongly depends on the resolving capability of the POD basis, the proposed method first applies the offline EnKF to update the POD basis, followed by modification of the reduced coefficients via Gappy POD. This process can be repeated in an iterative manner until convergence is reached. A Gappy POD-based strategy is employed to determine the sparse sensor locations. The performance of three data assimilation methods, i.e., the Gappy POD method, the iterative offline EnKF method, and the hybrid EnKF-Gappy POD, is evaluated on a circular cylinder flow with the Reynolds (Re) number being 3900 and a square cylinder flow with the Reynolds number being 22 000. The results demonstrate that all the assimilation methods are able to effectively reduce the discrepancy between LF and HF data, with the hybrid method being the most reliable across all the cases. Furthermore, the assimilation accuracy of the hybrid method is shown to be primarily influenced by the number of sensors and the intrinsic complexity of the flow field data. The results indicate that the proposed hybrid method can reduce the dependence of the assimilation performance on the initial data, thereby broadening the applicability of the assimilation framework and improving its effectiveness for unsteady, nonlinear, and high-dimensional complex flows.

papers.title: On the excitation force characteristics of a pre-deformed composite rotor in a pump-jet propulsor
papers.abstract: Rotor excitation forces in pump-jet propulsors (PJP) induce low-frequency hull vibrations and amplify flow-induced vibrations, consequently increasing flow-field pressure pulsations and degrading the acoustic performance of the propulsion system. Through rational design, composite rotors can utilize fluid–structure interaction (FSI) effects to mitigate PJP excitation forces and achieve a more gradual variation in flow-field pressure pulsations. This study designs two pre-deformed composite rotors based on a steady-state FSI algorithm and subsequently analyzes their excitation forces and flow-field pressure pulsation characteristics using a transient FSI approach. The results demonstrate that: (1) the pre-deformation design enables the composite rotors to maintain propulsive performance comparable to their metallic counterpart under design conditions; (2) the −30° ply angle rotor develops FSI deformation that reduces the pitch angle, resulting in significant reductions of 30.7% and 46.6% in axial excitation force at the rotor blade passing frequency (RBPF) and stator blade passing requency (SBPF), respectively; (3) conversely, the +30° ply angle rotor undergoes deformation that increases the pitch angle, leading to substantial increases of 167.6% and 224.1% in axial excitation force at RBPF and SBPF; (4) internal flow-field pressure pulsations concentrate at RBPF, influenced by leading-edge deformation and radial shift of excitation forces; (5) external pulsations focus at the shaft frequency with an “∞”-shaped directivity pattern, showing azimuth-dependent amplitude variations up to 84% increase at 90° and 84% decrease near 0° azimuth, due to mass distribution and bending–torsion coupling effects.

papers.title: Cavitation evolution characteristics of a hyperelastic nose rigid–flexible combined cylinder during vertical water entry
papers.abstract: A hyperelastic rigid–flexible combined cylinder comprises a hyperelastic nose and a rigid cylindrical body. With low density, high flexibility, and excellent load-bearing capacity, hyperelastic material shows promising applications in water-entry weapon systems and maritime aircraft recovery. The kinetic energy of the rigid–flexible combined cylinder entering the water is greater than that of the pure hyperelastic body, and the deformation of the hyperelastic nose is limited by the rigid body. Although numerous research have been conducted on the water-entry process of pure rigid and pure hyperelastic materials, studies on the rigid–flexible combined cylinders remain limited. Using high-speed photography technology, this paper investigates cavitation evolution characteristics during vertical water entry of rigid–flexible combined cylinders. The findings reveal three distinct stages of cavity evolution driven by the deformation of the hyperelastic nose. Furthermore, the paper analyzes how the Froude number and shear modulus influence key parameters including length, diameter, and duration of the primary and nested cavities during water entry. These insights provide valuable references for future design optimization of rigid–flexible combined cylinders.

papers.title: Direct prediction of capillary pressure curves from cross-size digital rock images based on a spatial pyramid pooling convolutional network
papers.abstract: Capillary pressure is a determining factor in the distribution and migration of fluids in porous media, directly influencing reservoir permeability, fluid saturation, and recovery efficiency. Conventional experimental and numerical methods are costly and limited in capturing complex pore structures. Existing data-driven methods, while addressing some limitations, neglect essential physical constraints and rely on pre-computed parameters rather than directly predicting from images, resulting in inadequate adaptability to cross-size data. We hereby propose a novel physics-informed deep learning framework, namely the three-dimensional spatial pyramid pooling convolutional long short-term memory-convolutional neural network with physical information embedding (3DSPP-ConvLSTM-CNN-PI). This model can directly predict capillary pressure curves from digital rock images of various sizes without the need for intermediate parameter calculations. The model uses a 3DSPP module to adaptively capture cross-size pore geometric features and explicitly embed critical physical parameters, such as computed tomography resolution, interfacial tension, and contact angle distribution. The model is trained on 1512 capillary pressure-saturation curves extracted from five digital sandstone samples and tested on 303 unseen data cases, achieving superior performance [R2 = 99.3%, mean absolute error = 2.89%, root mean square error = 4.46%] compared to baseline and support vector regression models. Validation on three new sandstone types demonstrates robust generalization and inference speeds over 90% faster than pore network simulations. This highlights the model's precision, efficiency, and practical capability in predicting the seepage characteristics of porous media.

papers.title: Flow development in the entrance region of slender converging pipes
papers.abstract: This work presents an analytical investigation of the hydrodynamic entrance region in axisymmetric laminar flows through slender converging pipes. Extending previous analyses for straight pipes, the model radially divides the flow into a viscous wall region and a central core where both inertia and viscous effects are important. This study analyzes the impact of the inlet Reynolds number and inlet angle on the developing velocity profile and pressure drop. Results show that a converging geometry, which imposes a favorable pressure gradient, significantly shortens the hydrodynamic entrance length compared to a straight pipe. Analytical solutions show good agreement with numerical simulations.

papers.title: Transferability investigation of the tandem impeller on the performance of a low specific speed centrifugal pump
papers.abstract: Tandem blades can generate a new thin boundary layer on the rear blades and are regarded as an effective approach to suppress flow separation in radial blade channels. Previous studies have shown that tandem blades can increase the head of centrifugal pumps without sacrificing efficiency; however, the applicability of this improvement to pumps with different specific speeds has not been fully validated. To address this gap, the present study investigates the hydraulic performance and internal flow characteristics of a low specific speed centrifugal pump equipped with a tandem impeller through a combination of experiments and computational fluid dynamics (CFD). First, the head and efficiency of a low specific speed centrifugal pump with regular blades were measured by experimental methods, and the accuracy of CFD was verified. Then, the regular blades were modified to tandem blades based on the method proposed by Fensterseifer, and the full model of tandem impellers with different blade angles was simulated by CFD. Next, experimental measurements of the centrifugal pump with an optimal tandem blade impeller were performed. Both CFD and experimental results confirm that the head-increasing effect of the tandem impeller can be successfully transferred to the low specific speed centrifugal pump, provided that an appropriate combination of rear-blade inlet angle and circumferential offset is adopted. The reason for the increased head of the tandem impeller is that the fluid flow angle at the impeller outlet is increased, and its uniformity is improved, which results in a higher absolute circumferential velocity component cu,22. Nevertheless, the adverse pressure gradient near the blade gap induces locally unstable flow structures, resulting in increased torque and partially offsetting the efficiency gain. Finally, the positive effect of the tandem impeller on the performance is also verified in the low specific speed centrifugal pump.

papers.title: Investigation on the enhancement mechanism of crescent-shaped dune configurations on film cooling effectiveness of turbine endwalls
papers.abstract: A configuration design that enhances the film cooling performance of gas turbine turbines through crescent-shaped dunes was proposed. Four types of film cooling structure models, i.e., concave configuration, convex configuration, composite configuration, and cylindrical holes, were constructed. A combination of numerical simulation and experimental validation was used to investigate the cooling effectiveness and flow field structure under different blowing ratios.
