By arranging the geometric concave and convex structures of the crescent-shaped dune in the downstream region of the film holes, the surface adherence of the cooling jet is significantly enhanced. The cooling effect is enhanced with the increase in the blowing ratio. This situation is more significant in the downstream region of the film holes. The convex configuration and composite configuration induce the generation of anti-kidney vortex pair, significantly improving the near-wall coolant coverage. This anti-kidney vortex pair suppressed the lift separation effect of the conventional kidney vortex and decreased the doping intensity of the coolant and the mainstream. The composite configuration shows significant advantages in cooling effectiveness and flow field control performance. Moreover, its area-averaged cooling effectiveness is improved up to 272%.

papers.title: Sharp-enforced physics-informed neural network for inverse hydrodynamic lubrication problem with film thickness discontinuity
papers.abstract: Thin film lubrication is crucial in hydrodynamic lubrication, and film thickness measurement is essential for assessing lubrication conditions, optimizing tribological interfaces, and extending the service life of mechanical components. However, directly quantifying film thickness under high-pressure conditions remains a significant challenge. This study proposes an inverse approach based on Physics-Informed Neural Networks to reconstruct film thickness using sparse pressure data. Forward and inverse models based on Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KAN) and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) are developed, and their solving performance is compared. MLP-based model and KAN-based model exhibit significant advantages in addressing lubrication problems. In solving the forward problem, both models achieve an accuracy on the order of 10−4 or lower. However, KAN-based model attains higher accuracy with fewer neurons and fewer iterations. Furthermore, both frameworks successfully reconstructed the full-field pressure distribution and accurately predicted the film thickness from sparse pressure measurements. It was found that data from different regions significantly affect the accuracy of film thickness prediction. The study revealed that data from different regions significantly affect the accuracy of film thickness predictions. When the input data originate from within the discontinuous interface, the network fails to provide an accurate solution. Data points located directly on the interface result in the lowest film thickness error, with a prediction error on the order of 0.02%. For data points outside the interface, the film thickness prediction error increases with distance from the interface. However, the error in the pressure field remains comparable to that obtained from points on the interface, also remaining around 0.04%. In conclusion, the hybrid-driven method proposed in this paper, which combines limited data with physical information, provides a new approach for film thickness measurement.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of the formation and collapse process of a freely closed ventilated supercavity
papers.abstract: Experimental investigations were conducted to examine the formation and collapse of a freely closed ventilated supercavity. Within the tested parameter range, five distinct closure modes were identified: foam cavity (FC), hybrid foam and re-entrant jet (FCRJ), re-entrant jet (RJ), hybrid twin vortex and re-entrant jet (TVRJ), and twin vortex (TV). During the cavity formation process, the closure mode evolves from FC to FCRJ, RJ, TVRJ, and finally to TV, while the collapse proceeds in the reverse sequence. The cavity formation speed increases with the ventilation coefficient CQ, whereas variations in the Froude number Fr primarily affect the collapse speed. The transient gas-leakage rate, cavity geometry, and closure mode form a closed–loop interaction, while Fr and the ventilation rate act as external regulators: closure mode and Fr affect leakage, leakage and ventilation shape the cavity, and the cavity shape then feeds back to the closure mode. During formation and collapse, the internal pressure is higher in FC, lower in RJ, and increases gradually as the cavity elongates. High-frequency pressure energy dominates in the FC state, vanishes in RJ, and reappears as evenly spaced peaks in the TV mode because of standing-wave resonance.

papers.title: Quantifying contributions of very large-scale motions to the time variability of sediment entrainment
papers.abstract: The influence of very-large-scale motions (VLSMs) on the entrainment of sediment particles on riverbeds remains to be better understood, particularly regarding their contribution to the overall entrainment variability. To further explore this problem, a synchronized flow-sediment measurement system was developed to simultaneously capture flow velocity fluctuations and the entrainment of sediment particles at the bed surface. Experiments were conducted under various flow conditions using three sets of uniform sands with distinctly different grain sizes. Frequency-domain coherence analysis and pre-multiplied spectral analysis were employed to investigate the interactions. The results reveal significant coherence between flow velocity fluctuations and the entrainment of sediment particles in the normalized frequency range of U/(fh)>10. Furthermore, spectral energy integration shows that VLSMs contribute approximately 33% of the total variability of the entrainment of sediment particles. These findings underscore the critical role of VLSMs in modulating sediment entrainment. This study offers quantitative insights into the VLSM contribution to the entrainment of sediment particles and provides experimental evidence supporting a deeper understanding of flow-sediment interactions driven by VLSMs.

papers.title: Metachronal coordination as a mesoscale phenomenon
papers.abstract: Metachronal coordination is a highly efficient natural strategy for swimming across scales, yet mimetic systems replicating this form of propulsion remain rare, limiting our ability to explore its underlying physics. Here, we investigate a minimal magneto-capillary system consisting of seven beads that exhibit metachronal-like motion when actuated by either a rotating or Lissajous-type oscillating magnetic field, resulting in net rotation or translation of the assembly, respectively. By systematically varying the driving frequency, we identify two distinct swimming regimes, both experimentally and theoretically. At low frequencies and negligible Reynolds numbers, propulsion arises from individual bead rotations phase-locked to the external field, constituting a linear, quasi-static regime. At higher frequencies, where the Reynolds number of the appendages exceeds unity, the dynamics transition to a deformation-dominated metachronal regime. Notably, optimized propulsion emerges near a mechanical resonance, underscoring the increasing role of inertia. While demonstrated on a specific design, we hypothesize that the existence of these regimes and the crossover between them may be a general feature of mesoscopic swimmers in nature.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of leakage performance and bristle mechanical characteristics of brush seals under rotational conditions
papers.abstract: Brush seals have gained prominence as an effective alternative to conventional labyrinth seals in gas turbine engines due to their superior sealing performance. Their flexible bristles accommodate rotor eccentricity, enhancing sealing adaptability. However, under high pressure load and high rotor rotational speeds, the bristles are susceptible to severe elastic deformation, which can lead to hysteresis effects, instability, and degradation in sealing efficiency. This study designs a high-speed visual brush seal rig and combines it with fluid–structure interaction simulations to investigate the bristle mechanics and leakage behavior under rotational speeds ranging from 0 to 6600 rpm. The effects of front plate and radial clearance between bristle tip and rotor on leakage, windage heating, and hysteresis are then systematically examined. First, for brush seals without a front plate, the results indicate that higher rotational speeds reduce leakage but increase windage heating and suppress the hysteresis behavior of the bristles. Under operating conditions of 3000 rpm and a pressure ratio of 1.55, significant bristle deformation is observed, with the radial clearance increasing by approximately 0.08 mm. When the pressure ratio decreases to 1.34, a closure effect emerges in the rear rows of bristles, accompanied by a distinct stratification phenomenon. Second, the introduction of a long front plate alters the airflow direction, increases the normal aerodynamic force on the bristles, reduces the axial force, and weakens the sealing performance, thereby elevating the leakage risk. Finally, while increasing the radial clearance exacerbates leakage, it contributes to lower windage heating and mitigates bristle hysteresis.

papers.title: Three-dimensional transition in the wake of rectangular cylinders with various aspect ratios: A direct numerical simulation study
papers.abstract: This study investigates the three-dimensional (3D) wake transition of flow around rectangular cylinders with seven aspect ratios (AR = 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5). Direct numerical simulations were performed for Reynolds numbers up to Re = 600. Ten distinct instability modes are observed, manifesting as ordered or disordered states depending on Re and AR. Based on their similarities, these modes are classified into four categories: (i) A, (ii) B, (iii) quasi-periodic, and (iv) quasi-subharmonic. The characteristics of these modes, including their spanwise wavelength and the Reynolds number range in which they emerge, are thoroughly documented for each aspect ratio. The results indicate that increasing the aspect ratio generally raises the critical Reynolds number for the onset of secondary wake transition, with values ranging from approximately Recr = 95 for AR = 0.25 to Recr = 478.5 for AR = 5. However, an earlier onset of three-dimensionality is observed at AR = 4 compared to AR = 3, a phenomenon attributed to variations in vortex shedding dynamics. Furthermore, based on interactions between leading-edge and trailing-edge vortices, three distinct vortex-shedding patterns are identified for elongated cylinders (AR = 3–5). Notably, for the smallest aspect ratio (AR = 0.25), a transition in the base flow from a von Kármán vortex street to a two-layered vortex structure near the cylinder effectively suppresses 3D instabilities, thereby reverting the flow to a two-dimensional state. The study further explores the impact of various instability modes on hydrodynamic forces and vortex shedding frequency.

papers.title: A multi-grid coupled finite element-Eulerian–Lagrangian method for fluid–structure interaction problems
papers.abstract: In this paper, a multi-grid coupled finite element-Eulerian–Lagrangian method is proposed for addressing fluid–structure interaction between large deformations in fluids and structures. This method utilizes multiple Eulerian grids to encompass the entire computational domain, employs Lagrangian particles to discretize the fluid domain, and adopts finite elements to discretize the solid domain. The multi-grid domain system calculates the structures and fluids independently, thereby avoiding the cross-interference of multiple velocity fields within a single grid domain, and facilitates the fluid–structure interaction between finite elements and particles. To address issues of nonphysical penetration and false contact between finite elements and particles, we introduce a fluid–structure interaction method based on contact mechanics in the volume domain. This method accurately applies the real contact forces at actual contact nodes, which are identified through specified contact conditions and detection mechanisms. Subsequently, the convergence, accuracy, and stability of this method are verified using representative numerical tests. Finally, we conduct experiments and simulations of shock wave impacts on elastic panels. The correlation between the numerical and experimental results demonstrates the accuracy of our method, and we provide an analysis of the variation patterns observed in both the flow field and the panel.

papers.title: Effect of porous media on flame propagation under identical laminar burning velocity
papers.abstract: To reveal the effect of porous media on methane premixed flame propagation, this study conducts a series of combustion experiments in two duct configurations, namely, configuration 1: an empty duct and configuration 2: a duct half-filled with 40-mm alumina beads. The mechanisms governing flame acceleration and pressure evolution are examined for lean and rich methane–air mixtures with identical laminar burning velocities. In the duct configuration 2, compression of the unburned mixture by the advancing flame front introduces resistance that suppresses early flame propagation. Once the flame enters the porous region, the interaction between pressure waves and the flame front induces a transition to turbulent combustion, rapidly accelerating the flame from a laminar flame velocity (2.83–9.37 m/s) to a turbulent flame velocity (16.53–36.31 m/s), accompanied by a pressure sharp rise. However, heat losses to the porous walls mitigate flame acceleration, producing a pressure plateau before the pressure sharp rise. This plateau represents a favorable window for preventing flame penetration into the porous region. Moreover, a linear correlation between characteristic flame velocities and deflagration pressures in both duct configurations highlights flame velocity as a reliable indicator for assessing pressure rise intensity. Additionally, lean-methane flames exhibit higher velocities and pressures due to the greater dependence of combustion in porous media on oxidizer, making rich mixtures more susceptible to heat loss. This study provides new insights and guidance for the transition mechanisms from laminar to turbulent flame in the porous media and the safety design of the heat storage burner.

papers.title: Origin of unsteady pressure and force oscillations in the S-region: Insights from vortex dynamics of a high-head pump turbine
papers.abstract: As a flexible regulating power source, pumped storage units play a crucial role in enabling the large-scale integration of renewable energy into power grids. Through interregional regulation, they balance the generation and consumption of renewable energy across different regions, thereby enhancing overall utilization efficiency. However, during this process, units frequently traverse or directly operate within the S-shaped characteristic region (S region), which may induce operational instability. When a high-head pump turbine enters the S region, large-scale flow separation and complex vortex inevitably develop within the flow components. The dynamic evolution of these unsteady structures induces high-amplitude pressure fluctuations and force pulsations, posing significant threats to the safe and stable operation of the unit. To elucidate the mechanisms of pressure fluctuation and force evolution in the S region, this study investigates a high-head model pump turbine through unsteady numerical simulations at representative operating points with a 12° guide vane opening. The analysis focuses on internal flow characteristics, pressure fluctuations, and runner force pulsations. The results show that unstable vortex structures, including circumferential and cross flows, develop near the runner inlet, leading to pronounced pressure fluctuations. Time-frequency analysis reveals that cross flow within the runner generates low-frequency components at 0.3 fn and 0.4 fn, while rotating stall in the vaneless space causes low-frequency fluctuations at 0.6 fn and 0.7 fn. In contrast, rotor–stator interaction produces high-frequency components at 9.0 fn. Further analysis confirms that rotating stall and cross flow are the primary sources of flow instability in the S region of pump turbines. Moreover, the runner force results demonstrate that vortex structures induced by cross flow significantly affect the radial force distribution, whereas the axial force is predominantly governed by rotor–stator interaction. These findings provide a theoretical basis for optimizing the hydraulic design and enhancing the operational stability of pumped storage units.

papers.title: Dual-stress origin of local stress minima in dense granular suspensions
papers.abstract: Dense granular suspensions exhibit a local minimum in the stress–shear rate curve during the transition from quasi-static to viscous flow, a robust yet unexplained feature of dense-flow rheology. Using a dual-stress constitutive framework that couples rate-independent (hypoplastic) and rate-dependent (viscous–inertial) stresses, we capture this behavior and clarify its physical origin. The minimum results from a dynamic shift in stress dominance from contact network support to viscous resistance, revealing a dual-stress mechanism that governs regime transitions in dense granular suspensions.

papers.title: Aerodynamic performance comparison of a novel Helical-Φ vertical axis wind turbine and conventional designs
papers.abstract: A novel Helical-Φ vertical-axis wind turbine (VAWT) is proposed as an evolution of the conventional Darrieus-Φ VAWT. The aerodynamic performance of this new design is evaluated using a three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics approach and is compared with that of conventional VAWTs in terms of power generation and aerodynamic loading. The results indicate that the Helical-Φ VAWT achieves substantially higher power coefficients than its conventional counterparts at high tip-speed ratios (TSR ≥ 3.0). It also exhibits consistently lower aerodynamic loads on both the blades and the rotor across all tested TSRs. For wake characteristics, the wake velocity of the Helical-Φ turbine recovers to the freestream over a shorter downstream distance and presents a smaller velocity-deficit region, enabling a more compact turbine array spacing in wind-farm applications. In addition, the wake velocity deficit of the Helical-Φ turbine is found to be asymmetric in both the lateral and vertical directions. Overall, the Helical-Φ turbine demonstrates clear performance advantages over conventional VAWTs, particularly in enhancing array-layout density and increasing energy yield in wind farms operating at high rotational speeds.

papers.title: Numerical analysis of ciliated transport of fluid in human organs
papers.abstract: This study investigates ciliary transport of fluids and nutrients in the human body, a process central to several physiological functions. The governing continuity, momentum, energy, and concentration equations are first established in a fixed frame using curvilinear coordinates and then transformed to a moving frame through a linear mapping. After non-dimensionalization and application of the long-wavelength and low-Reynolds-number approximations, the system is reformulated in terms of a stream function for analytical tractability. Numerical solutions computed via NDSolve in mathematica (a built-in numerical differential equation solver to integrate the system) yield the velocity field, pressure gradient, pressure rise, and streamline patterns. The results reveal the influence of ciliary motion on fluid transport efficiency, offering deeper physical insight into biological pumping mechanisms and aiding the modeling of physiological flows.

papers.title: Mechanistic insights into the oxidation-driven alteration of molten pool surface dynamics under laser irradiation in spot welding
papers.abstract: The dynamic behavior of the molten pool surface during laser spot welding significantly impacts forming quality. This study combines numerical simulations and experiments to comprehensively investigate the effect of surface oxidation in an air atmosphere on the molten pool flow behavior and solidification process during laser spot welding. Throughout the laser processing, the metal surface undergoes three stages: solid-phase heating, molten pool expansion, and molten pool solidification. The durations of solid-phase heating and molten pool expansion are similar in both argon and air, but the solidification time in air is 63.7% longer than in argon. During the early stages of processing in air, the expansion rate of the molten pool increases rapidly, with the expansion rate in air reaching twice that in argon. During the solidification process in air, within 0.3–1.2 ms after the laser is turned off, strong oscillations appear on the surface of the molten pool, and it is observed that the contraction rate of the molten pool during solidification slows down. This oscillatory behavior is the main cause of the ripple-like texture on the solidified surface in air and leads to a significant increase in roughness. During solidification, rapid oxidation and the subsequent drop in surface temperature change the temperature dependence of surface tension. The surface tension's temperature coefficient shifts from negative to positive, reversing the Marangoni flow direction from outward to inward. With extended solidification time and gravity's influence, this reduces the final residual height.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of hydrodynamics and propulsion in dense bioinspired fish schools under oblique flows
papers.abstract: Oblique inflow fundamentally reorganizes the wakes of dense fish schools, generating deflected reverse Kármán jets and multiscale vortex-bridging interactions that govern the propulsion and energetics at the group level. Using a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)-accelerated ghost-cell immersed boundary solver, we conducted two-dimensional simulations of dense bioinspired fish schools, systematically varying the Strouhal number (St), Reynolds number (Re), and lateral spacing (ds). Force decomposition in body-tangential and normal coordinates, together with wake-topology analysis, revealed a unifying mechanism: propulsion efficiency peaks when the convective transit time of the shed vortices matches the undulation period, resulting in constructive phase locking among neighbors. This condition emerges within a moderate St window and at transitional Re, where coherent reverse Kármán jets remain compact. At higher St, resonance amplifies force fluctuations and dissipates power, whereas at higher Re, additional small-scale content disrupts phase coherence, reducing school-level gains. Spacing governs the coupling strength: an intermediate, dense but non-contact arrangement (ds = 0.6L) yields the broadest efficiency maximum and increases the school-averaged efficiency by approximately 12%–15% relative to both tighter and wider spacings. Furthermore, the benefits of interaction converge as the wakes diffuse. Energetic advantages are spatially selective across the formation: individuals directly exposed to the inflow incur greater drag, whereas shielded interior or trailing positions benefit from phase locking. These results provide a macroscale framework linking inflow obliquity, wake coherence, and array geometry, thereby offering design guidance for bioinspired multivehicle formations that adapt spacing and phasing to maximize collective propulsion while minimizing energy loss.

papers.title: Wave-induced pressure distribution and force characteristics of box and rectangular girders under multiple wave conditions
papers.abstract: Tsunami events impose significant challenges to the serviceability and structural safety of low-clearance cross-sea bridges. A physical model experiments with a total of 144 scenarios were conducted to investigate the spatiotemporal evolution of surface pressure and wave-induced forces on girder structures. To supplement experimental observations and provide additional insight into wave-structure interaction mechanisms, ANSYS Fluent 2022 R1 (Fluent) was employed for two-dimensional numerical simulations. The results reveal that pressure peak positions and spatial distribution patterns are predominantly governed by submergence level and cross-sectional geometry. Wave amplitude primarily controls the magnitude of pressure and wave forces; it has a limited influence on the spatial distribution patterns. The vertical wave force component substantially exceeds the horizontal component, with the disparity exceeding a factor of 20 under emerged states. Box girders exhibit more scattered pressure peaks and up to 59% higher maximum horizontal forces compared to rectangular girders, attributed to multi-surface interactions involving cantilevered flanges and recessed webs. This study contributes to an improved understanding of wave–structure interactions and provides essential insights for the hydrodynamic design and safety evaluation of coastal bridge superstructures.

papers.title: Wake reconstruction of a building using sparse data of virtual Doppler wind lidar
papers.abstract: Understanding how wind flows in urban environments is vital for the low-altitude aviation economy, aviation safety, and building monitoring. However, even Doppler lidar, currently the most effective remote sensing tool for wind field measurement, faces challenges in urban environments due to insufficient spatial resolution and signal blockage by buildings. To solve these problems, we propose UrbanFlow-Dif, a novel artificial intelligence framework designed to reconstruct fine-scale wind information from sparse lidar data. The model learns from high-resolution simulations of airflow around buildings generated by computational fluid dynamics and uses a diffusion-based generative model, which can remove noise and recover detailed flow structures. Subsequently, the sensitivity of model performance with different scanning configurations is studied to reveal the influence mechanism of lidar position angle, spatial resolution, and scanning step angle. These results demonstrate that UrbanFlow-Dif successfully reconstructs the complex wake structures, achieving a root mean square error below 1.284 m/s even under sparsity conditions (finer than 30 m/1°). Ensemble averaging can further improve the reconstruction performance. This work provides a new foundation for fine-scale urban wind field detection and reconstruction.

papers.title: Analytical investigation of turbulent compressible flows in channels of variable cross section with shock waves
papers.abstract: This study investigates the influence of turbulence on gasdynamic processes in channels with variable cross sections. A modified form of the Hugoniot relation has been obtained for Laval nozzles operating under turbulent flow conditions. The effect of turbulence on the displacement of the nozzle's critical section is examined. Using a simplified k–ε turbulence closure, the interaction between turbulent boundary layers and shock waves is analyzed, and flow invariants governing the transition through shock structures are identified. To assess the isomorphism of second-order turbulence models, comparative calculations were additionally carried out employing the k–ω model.

papers.title: The influence of blade wrap angle on cavitation performance of 1000 MW power plant boiler feedwater pump
papers.abstract: As a universal fluid mechanical equipment, boiler feedwater pumps are widely used in fields such as electric power and energy. The impeller is one of the important components of the feedwater pump, and the shape of its blades plays a decisive role in the hydrodynamic characteristics of the impeller. The wrap angle in the blade parameters has a significant impact on the blade shape and the pressure and velocity distribution of the fluid on the blade surface. This article investigates the hydraulic cavitation performance of feedwater pumps at different blade wrap angles (BWAs) using a density-based modified filtered bubble model-discontinuous cavitation model and draws the following preliminary conclusions. On the basis of keeping the blade bottom angle constant, it was found that as the blade angle decreased, the anti-cavitation performance gradually weakened, and the speed slowed down at a certain angle. At the same time, the optimal comprehensive performance is achieved at a BWA of 130°, with stable and controllable fluctuations in instantaneous entropy production. It is recommended to prioritize the use of this range of blade angles (120°–130°) in anti-cavitation design, taking into account the balance between channel suppression of diffusion and energy loss.

papers.title: Microstructure fabrication and flow boiling enhancement of R245fa in dendritic and spherical copper powder tubes
papers.abstract: To investigate the influence of porous structure morphology on enhanced flow boiling heat transfer in tubes, two types of porous-structured tubes were fabricated using 100-mesh copper powder particles with distinct morphologies through a sintering-electrochemical deposition coupling technique: dendritic copper powder surface-enhanced tube (D-SET) and spherical copper powder surface-enhanced tube (S-SET). Experimental studies demonstrate that D-SET exhibits exceptional heat transfer performance. Its maximum heat transfer coefficient reaches 16.26 kW/(m2 K), which is 1.10 times that of the S-SET. Comparative results show that the performance evaluation criterion (PEC) of the D-SET surface is 12% higher than that of the S-SET. The maximum PEC of D-SET reaches 2.72, exceeding the value of the spherical surface. The performance enhancement is attributed to the branched microstructures formed by dendritic copper powder. These structures improve bubble dynamics and delay dryout, which strengthens phase-change heat transfer. Although the pressure drop increases by 12.3%, the D-SET surface still shows superior overall thermal performance. The results confirm that copper powder morphology plays a key role in controlling surface heat transfer. They also offer guidance for the design and application of microstructured surfaces in high-efficiency thermal management systems.

papers.title: On what can or cannot influence the small amplitude oscillations of a gas bubble
papers.abstract: The analysis presented in this paper concerns the impact of different physical quantities and conditions on the small amplitude oscillations of a single gas bubble immersed in a liquid, in the presence of an acoustic forcing pressure. Namely, effects related to the nature of the gas and its modeling, to the boundary conditions on the bubble wall, and to the size and shape of the bubble itself are studied and compared. The solutions are always determined analytically. The polytropic index and the damping coefficient are not assigned a priori but are determined from gas dynamics equations of Navier–Stokes–Fourier, and rational extended thermodynamics type. This preliminary approach facilitates the distinction between essential features and reasonable possible simplifications, also with a view to extending the model to nonlinear regimes. Furthermore, the results obtained could suggest how to prescribe the polytropic index more accurately when the gas dynamics in the bubble are reduced to a simple polytropic process.

papers.title: Characteristics of the aerodynamic force on the blades of a horizontal-axis wind turbine under wind shear and tower interference
papers.abstract: The aerodynamic forces on the full-size National Renewable Energy Laboratory 5 MW wind turbine are numerically investigated, considering the effects of wind shear and tower interference. During the operation of wind turbine, the aerodynamic forces on the blade fluctuate periodically, with the frequency quite close to the natural frequency of the blade. As the blade enters the region of high oncoming flow velocity, there is a notable blade stall near the suction surface of the airfoil, which results in a remarkable increase in drag coefficient on the blade and a plateau of lift coefficient. This significantly impacts the thrust and torque on the turbine. In addition, as the blade approaches to the tower, there is a distinct increase in pressure on the leeward surface near the root of the blade. Consequently, the interference of tower will contribute to a larger fluctuation of the thrust and torque during the blade operation. Finally, a formula model is derived to accurately predict the thrust and torque on the blade under a power-law wind profile and tower disturbance.

papers.title: Investigation on nonspherical bubble dynamics in a compressible fluid fully confined by a solid boundary
papers.abstract: This study investigates the dynamics of a nonspherical bubble confined within a spherical solid structure boundary. A bubble dynamics model accounting for fluid compressibility and solid elasticity is developed for the boundary condition of full confinement. Using this numerical model, the influence of the bubble's eccentric position, confinement size, and boundary material on the bubble's nonspherical pulsation is explored. Four bubble behavior patterns are identified: quasi-spherical oscillation, internal jet fragmentation, post-collapse jet impact, and pre-rebound jet impact. The characteristics and evolution mechanisms of these behaviors are analyzed based on flow field pressure. The wall effect and fluid accumulation phenomenon are identified as the primary factors responsible for generating local high pressure on the bubble surface, which triggers the different pulsation behaviors. Furthermore, we summarize the dependence of these behaviors on various governing parameters, and the jet dynamics at the moment of jet impact are quantitatively analyzed. Finally, the structural pressure characteristics and stress distribution induced by the bubble behaviors are studied. We find that changes in the bubble's eccentric position not only lead to variations in bubble behavior patterns but also result in significant differences in structural pressure evolution. In terms of structural stress distribution, in addition to the structure surfaces near the bubble being prone to high stress, surfaces far from the bubble are also subjected to local high stress caused by fluid accumulation, which poses potential risks to the structural strength in that region.

papers.title: Stability of soluble surfactant-laden falling film over a hydrophobic incline in the presence of external shear
papers.abstract: The hydrodynamic stability analysis of gravity-driven, soluble surfactant-laden fluid streaming down a slippery, slanted plane in the presence of external shear force is being explored in this article. The Navier–Stokes equations are considered for the fluid flow along with the appropriate advection–diffusion equations for the concentration of different surfactant species. The monomers considered here are anticipated to dissolve in the bulk flow and can be adsorbed at the interface of air-liquid as well. Also, the adsorption–desorption kinetics of the surfactants at the free surface is taken into consideration. In order to control the instability of the soluble surfactant-laden flow, the wall slip is considered, which changes the shear rate near the wall, and an externally imposed shear stress, which directly impacts the shear-layered flow near the free surface. The Orr–Sommerfeld eigenvalue system is obtained and is solved numerically in the arbitrary wave regime using the Chebyshev spectral collocation method. An analytical solution using the long-wave approximation method in the small wavenumber regime (k≪1) is also discussed. The numerical analysis reveals the existence of temporal surface and surfactant modes. Moreover, in the high modified Reynolds number regime, for low inclination angles, another temporal mode named shear mode is observed. The external shear force initially destabilizes the surface mode, but as inertial effects grow, the shear-induced normal stress acts to stabilize it. However, the surfactant mode is a damped mode. The surfactant parameter βa, and solubility parameter Ra have destabilization effect on the surfactant mode, but for the higher values of these parameters, the flow system turns into an insoluble surfactant-laden flow. The slip parameter stabilizes the surfactant mode, but the external shear destabilizes it. Finally, the external shear triggers the shear mode instability. Although the slip parameter has exactly the opposite effect on shear mode compared to the external shear.

papers.title: An analytical equivalent permeability model for characterizing fluid flow through a bounded empty-porous system
papers.abstract: Natural fractures are critical for hydrocarbon extraction in unconventional reservoirs, but they are often cemented by minerals. Hydraulic fracturing can open these cemented fractures, creating a bounded empty-porous system with an empty region and a cement pack. However, no studies have yet characterized fluid flow in this scenario, leading to inaccurate predictions of the delivery capacity of opening cemented natural fractures (OCNFs). This study presents a novel analytical model to evaluate the equivalent permeability of OCNFs, incorporating viscous shear from fracture walls and the coupled empty-porous system. Unlike traditional Darcy's law, fluid flow in the cement pack is described using the Brinkman equation to account for effects from the porous medium, fracture walls, and viscous drag at the empty-porous interface. The model is validated through commercial software (e.g., COMSOL Multiphysics). The equivalent permeability and flow velocity profiles of OCNFs are analyzed with various impact factors. Results show that fracture wall and empty-porous interface effects become more significant as cement pack permeability increases, while their influence on fluid flow decreases with greater cement pack width. If the fracture width is large enough, these effects become negligible. Integrating the permeability predicted by both models into reservoir simulations reveals that neglecting fracture wall and interface effects leads to significant errors in well performance evaluation.

papers.title: Damage characteristics of a reinforced cylindrical shell under underwater dual-charge explosion during navigation
papers.abstract: There is a dynamic coupling relationship between the bubble period of underwater explosion and the velocity of underwater vehicles. The interaction characteristics between bubbles and structures vary under different matching relationships of these two factors. The arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian numerical method is primarily employed in this study to investigate the damage characteristics of a typical hull structure under the impact of synchronized underwater explosion loads from dual charges. The study primarily analyzes the variations in bubble and load-induced damage under different relative velocity conditions. The results indicate that relative velocity is a crucial factor in studying underwater explosion-induced structural damage. The primary effect is that the relative velocity influences the symmetry of the coalesced bubble, weakening the jet load and causing the point of action of the jet load to shift toward the rear. Therefore, the damage area of the structure increases under the navigation state, but the maximum deflection decreases. The sensitivity of shock wave load and jet load to changes in relative velocity differs. When the relative velocity (vs) exceeds 0.6, the deflection caused by the shock wave load remains almost unchanged, while the deflection caused by the jet load continues to decrease. Therefore, when the relative velocity is low, the jet load plays a dominant role in the shell damage process. However, when vs exceeds 1.8, the situation reverses, and the shock wave load becomes the primary factor. To ensure damage efficiency, the bubble period induced by charge explosion should be regulated to match the structural velocity.

papers.title: The performance of proton exchange membrane fuel cells with curved membrane electrode assemblies: Considering various gas diffusion layer and thermal contact resistance thicknesses
papers.abstract: This study investigates the influence of thermal contact resistance (TCR) and gas diffusion layer (GDL) thickness on the performance of proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) with curved membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs) under varying pressure differences, using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. These results show that increasing TCR thickness (0–3 μm) enlarges the high-temperature region at low and moderate voltages, reducing membrane water content and proton conductivity, thereby degrading performance. At high voltages, performance remains stable due to minimal thermal variation. With constant TCR, increasing pressure difference (0–30 kPa) affects oxygen transport resistance and distribution only at low voltages. GDL thickness significantly impacts performance: thinner GDLs (0.1 mm) benefit from pressure-induced gaps enhancing oxygen transport, while thicker GDLs (0.2–0.3 mm) lead to reduced pore volume and higher resistance, especially under elevated pressure, thus lowering performance. These findings reveal new insights into the interplay between mechanical deformation and multi-physical transport in PEMFCs with curved MEAs.

papers.title: The sound emission of underwater pulsed discharges stimulated by an air bubble and the dynamic behavior of the corresponding cavity after breakdown
papers.abstract: For underwater pulsed discharges, injecting an air bubble between electrodes serves as an effective external stimulation method. The bubble can significantly influence electrical parameters, sound waves, and pulsating cavities during the arc discharge and subsequent stages. Investigating the influence and mechanisms of the bubble in a single discharge event is essential for the optimized control of underwater pulsed discharges. This study utilized the schlieren optical system to record the morphology and evolution of sound waves and pulsating cavities, while hydrophones measured sound-wave intensity. A computational model based on the energy balance equation and the Gilmore model was used to describe the dynamic evolution of pulsating cavities. The results indicate that the presence of the bubble significantly alters the morphology of sound waves and the pulsating cavity, inducing transient stratification within the pulsating cavity. Furthermore, it demonstrates notable advantages in enhancing sound-wave intensity, increasing internal energy of the pulsating cavity, and improving energy conversion efficiency. The bubble guides and distorts the discharge channel, and there is an optimal bubble position that significantly enhances sound-wave intensity. The dynamic characteristics of the pulsating cavity are influenced by energy parameters and external constraints, and these parameters primarily affect the initial stage of the cavity. This study has important theoretical implications for the efficient application of underwater pulsed discharges in practical production scenarios.

papers.title: Hysteresis of the dynamic oblique shock wave induced by an oscillating ramp in supersonic flow
papers.abstract: The hysteresis of dynamic oblique shock induced by an oscillating ramp at three different motion scenarios is demonstrated by two-dimensional numerical simulations. The angle of the oscillating ramp varies between 7° and 9° in a supersonic flow with an incoming Mach number of 2.5, in which no separation flow occurs in the boundary layer around the compression corner. It is found that the dynamic flow downstream of the oblique shock exhibits a partition hysteresis phenomenon with two distinct hysteresis regions: one is in the vicinity of the ramp wall, and the other is adjacent to the oblique shock wave. The effects of centrifugal force, Coriolis force, viscous force, and the lag in dynamic shock position on these two hysteresis phenomena regions are discussed and elucidated based on a comparative analysis of viscous and inviscid results. Additionally, a method for accurately predicting the dynamic shock wave angle is proposed for the inviscid flow, with the verified error less than 0.5%.

papers.title: Effect of angle of attack on the instability-wave selectivity in hypersonic compression ramp laminar flow
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effect of angle of attack (AOA) on the convective instability of a hypersonic flow over a compression ramp at Mach 7.7, with particular emphasis on high-frequency two-dimensional Mack modes and low-frequency three-dimensional shear-layer instabilities. Combining linear stability theory (LST) and resolvent analysis, we examine how the change in AOA affects the convective instability mechanisms associated with separation bubbles. Results show that as AOA decreases from zero to negative, the separation bubble elongates, leading to increased growth rates and spatial extent of higher-order Mack modes. The negative AOA also promotes the emergence of additional shear-layer instabilities within concave high-curvature regions near the aft portion of the bubble. In contrast, positive AOAs compress the separation bubble, suppress higher-order modes, and reduce both the number and growth rates of shear-layer instability modes. Notably, at large positive AOA, the separation bubble acts as a broadband perturbation amplifier in the vicinity of the separation point for high-frequency Mack modes. For both large positive or negative AOAs, the low-frequency shear layer modes are shown to be unsteady Görtler modes. A comparison between LST and resolvent analysis demonstrated good agreement, confirming that the parallel-flow assumption underlying LST remains largely valid across multiple AOAs. These results indicate that, despite the changing bubble morphology with AOA, LST remains a valid tool for stability studies of the shock wave–boundary layer interaction (laminar flow).

papers.title: Experimental investigation on ammonia/hydrogen/air continuous rotating detonation
papers.abstract: Ammonia has garnered international attention as an ideal carbon-free fuel. However, its poor combustion characteristics limit its widespread application. Continuous rotating detonation (CRD), fueled by ammonia, offers a novel approach to ammonia utilization. In this study, ammonia–hydrogen–air CRD experiments were first conducted in a hollow chamber. Propagation characteristics and flow field structure of ammonia–hydrogen–air CRD were analyzed through pressure measurement and top-viewed optical observation. The CRD wave propagates in the single-wave mode with a velocity of 1782 m/s, which accounts for 93.2% of the corresponding theoretical Chapman–Jouguet (C–J) velocity in the selected test. The analysis of the integral of chemiluminescence intensity (ICI) conducted on high-speed images confirms the coupling structure of the CRD wave. Increasing the hydrogen mass fraction (XH2) enhances the propagation velocity and peak pressure of the CRD wave while reducing its velocity deficit, which is attributed to improved combustion characteristics and a diminished deflagration proportion. Additionally, the analysis of high-speed images and ICI of their phase-averaged images indicates that the brightness and area of the reaction zone increase initially and then decrease with increasing XH2. Notably, a transition from a sawtooth-wave mode to a single-wave mode occurs as XH2 increases from 5% to 10%. As the nozzle contraction ratio (CR) increases from 2 to 8, the peak pressure of the CRD wave decreases, and the reaction zone becomes less compact. At CR = 8, the significantly lower peak pressure causes the CRD wave to approximate a sawtooth-wave mode.

papers.title: The spatial scattering of sound by a mixing layer: Case of short waves
papers.abstract: A high-order-accurate numerical model for the modified linearized Euler equations is employed to investigate the sound scattering of a plane wave by a temporally evolving mixing layer. The model is validated against benchmark cases to ensure its accuracy. Numerical results show that, as the convective Mach number increases and the characteristic scale ratio (defined as the ratio of the incident acoustic wavelength to the mixing layer's characteristic length) decreases, the acoustic scattering behavior transitions sequentially through the resonance regime and the geometrical-acoustics regime. Correspondingly, the scattered fields exhibit higher intensity, diminished symmetry, and greater irregularity. The study further reveals that the scattering generated by a mixing layer shares key similarities with that produced by a compact vortex, particularly in terms of scaling effects observed in the resonance regime, a characteristic not found in non-compact vortices. This similarity arises because the large-scale vortical structures in the mixing layer more closely resemble a compact vortex than a non-compact one. In the resonance regime, these structures act as compact acoustic sources, generating scattered waves with relatively symmetric directivity. In contrast, within the geometrical-acoustics regime, scattering is primarily governed by refraction and distortion effects resulting from the spatially varying flow field.

papers.title: Near-wall flow recovery from particle image velocimetry using physics-informed neural network
papers.abstract: A physics-informed neural network is employed to reconstruct near-wall flow fields from particle image velocimetry (PIV) data in regions where direct measurements are inaccessible. Experiments were conducted in a vertical square duct, and four datasets were prepared with mean velocity components and Reynolds stresses measured at the duct's center plane for Reynolds numbers in the range Re=2.1×104 to 3.2×104. The Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations were incorporated in the training as physical constraints, and a two-step training strategy was introduced to address closure limitations in near-wall region with insufficient prior knowledge. In the first stage, the model was trained within the PIV domain to denoise the flow data and reconstruct pressure field through data assimilation, producing results consistent with Darcy friction coefficients at each Re. The second stage incorporated additional physical constraints, including force balance and a simplified turbulence-closure approximation, to recover the near-wall flow behavior. The final model produced velocity profiles consistent with turbulent boundary layer theory, capturing the linear viscous sublayer and the onset of the logarithmic region. The reconstructed Reynolds stresses effectively captured the strong near-wall anisotropy reported in previous studies, exhibiting peak approximately eight times larger in the streamwise direction than in the wall-normal direction. Comparisons with models trained without Reynolds stress regularization confirmed that this constraint contributes to improved Reynolds stress prediction.

papers.title: On the prediction of flow-induced noise at low Mach numbers: A comparative study of compressible, weakly compressible, and incompressible models
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of flow-induced noise at low Mach numbers (M<0.3) is hindered by the omission of weak compressibility in incompressible formulations and the heavy computational load of fully compressible schemes. To address this gap, we systematically assess an acoustic-wave-preserving weakly compressible model through three canonical cases: flow over a circular cylinder, gust–airfoil interaction, and turbulence–airfoil interaction. For benchmarking, its performance is compared against incompressible and fully compressible models, with far-field noise additionally evaluated using the Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings equation. The comparisons reveal that while all models reproduce the hydrodynamic fields, their acoustic predictions differ markedly. In particular, the weakly compressible and fully compressible models correctly capture wave propagation and provide consistent far-field noise predictions, whereas the incompressible model fails to represent acoustic radiation. Furthermore, the weakly compressible model achieves accuracy comparable to the fully compressible model for Mach numbers below 0.2, but its isentropic assumption deteriorates at higher Mach numbers. Taken together, these findings not only clarify the validity range of the weakly compressible model but also underscore the necessity of accounting for compressibility effects in low-Mach-number aeroacoustic simulations.

papers.title: Curved contraction–expansion channel design to improve particle separation performance of inertial microfluidic chips
papers.abstract: As an efficient particle separation technology, an inertial microfluidic chip has broad application prospects in biomedicine, environmental monitoring, and other fields. This paper aims to explore the influence of the curve-contraction-expansion channel structure on the particle separation performance of the inertial microfluidic chip and optimize the chip design through numerical simulation methods. The principle of the inertial microfluidic chip is introduced, and the advantages and disadvantages of the curve channel, the contraction–expansion channel, and the combination of the two are analyzed. The simulation model of the inertial microfluidic chip is established, and the influence of parameters, such as the inlet angle, channel width, channel inner diameter and overall channel curvature on the particle separation performance, is analyzed. The research results show that the curve-contraction-expansion channel structure can effectively improve the particle separation performance. The particle separation effect is best when the inlet angle is 90°, the channel width is 30 μm, the channel inner diameter is 400 μm, and the overall channel curvature is 425 μm. In addition, the article also discusses the indicators, such as particle trajectory, yield, the change of the number of outlet particles over time, and the particle focusing effect, and analyzes the influence mechanism of different parameters on the separation performance. This paper provides a theoretical basis and reference for the optimal design of inertial microfluidic chips and looks forward to its application prospects in the biomedical field.

papers.title: Methanol synthesis via direct CO2 hydrogenation in a square duct: A direct numerical simulation study
papers.abstract: Efficient production of hydrogen (H2) derivatives, such as e-methanol, is essential to achieving carbon-neutrality targets. In the present computational fluid dynamics study, we investigate synthetic methanol (CH3OH) production via direct carbon dioxide (CO2) hydrogenation in a milli-duct with a rectangular cross section. The duct involves catalytic wall reactions with CO2 and H2 as reactants. Direct numerical simulations are carried out at bulk Reynolds numbers of Reb= 100, 500, 1100, and 2200 spanning laminar and turbulent flow regimes. We investigate a high catalyst loading, corresponding to gas hourly space velocity values of 0.086, 0.44, 0.96, and 1.93 m3/(kgcat h) at these Reynolds numbers, respectively, to study the impact of turbulence on methanol production in the limit of fast, transport-limited chemistry. The numerical results consist of the following features: (1) In the turbulent case (Reb=2200), the reaction rate reaches local minima/maxima in the turbulent ejection/sweep structures observed in the proximity of the catalytic walls, respectively. (2) Turbulent mixing may significantly enhance methanol production under transport-limited chemistry, increasing the methanol mass flow rate at the outlet up to 56.4% compared to laminar flow at a matched Reynolds number. (3) The single-pass conversion efficiency of CO2 and the methanol yield across the duct decrease monotonically as the Reynolds number increases (lower residence time). In contrast, the methanol mass flow rate at the outlet increases as Reb increases (higher reactant inflow).

papers.title: Particle dispersion behavior of biomasss in a dual-stage swirl gasifier
papers.abstract: The distribution of biomass particles in the gasifier significantly influences the conversion efficiency and soot generation during gasification. Numerous studies have confirmed that a single-stage swirl combustor can significantly improve conversion efficiency and is widely used in the coal industry. However, the turbulent structures and shear layers in dual-swirl reactors are highly complex, and existing research lacks systematic investigation into the interactions of biomass particles and recirculation zones. In this paper, a novel dual swirl gasifier is built to investigate the dispersion behavior of biomass particles that would shed light on new generation high-temperature gasification. Both co-swirl and counter-swirl gasifiers with different swirl angles (40°, 50°, and 60°) are investigated. In addition, the influences of inflow rate and the physical property of biomass particles on the two-phase flow behavior are also systematically studied. The vortex structures and particle dispersion in the flow field are quantitatively analyzed. It is found that the counter-rotating vortex structures disrupt the formation of the central exhaust tube vortex, leading to poorer particle dispersion, and the injection of biomass particles apparently changes the size of the central recirculation zone. Moreover, it is also observed that the interparticle distance conforms to a normal distribution. When the biomass particle size is less than 500 μm, the interparticle distance is very small and particles tend to adhere to the wall of the gasifier. The current work provides valuable insights for optimizing the operating conditions of dual-stage gasification.

papers.title: Acoustic-based microdevice for biomedicine applications: Comprehensive parametric analysis, predictive surrogate modeling, and machine learning-based optimization
papers.abstract: Acoustofluidic micromixers are critical tools for biomedical applications due to their ability to achieve efficient, non-contact mixing at microscales. In this study, an acoustic-based micromixer incorporating sharp triangular edges is comprehensively modeled, analyzed, and optimized in an application-based manner. The process begins with parametric geometry design of the micromixer, incorporating five dimensionless parameters: edge height (h*), edge angle (α*), spacing between edges (d*), vertical offset (ϕ), and tip curvature radius (rc*). A detailed finite-element model is developed in COMSOL Multiphysics, integrating fluid flow, acoustics, and species transport under acoustic streaming in the frequency domain based on perturbation theory. A central composite design-based response surface methodology is then employed to develop a surrogate model for the mixing index (MI) and pressure drop (ΔP). A total of 152 simulations are conducted to build statistically significant models (R2 = 0.9590, F = 33.25 for MI), and the results are validated against the experimental literature. Subsequently, a Multi-Objective Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm is applied to identify Pareto-optimal designs that balance mixing efficiency with pressure losses. Key findings include a maximum mixing index exceeding 96%, with pressure drops in optimal solutions maintained between 1 and 4 Pa. Increasing both the applied voltage and the edge height each yielded over 70% improvement in mixing. The robust, validated framework demonstrates strong potential for the intelligent design of bulk acoustic-based devices in clinical and pharmaceutical micro-systems.

papers.title: A hybrid turbulence model for the taxiing seaplane
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of aerodynamic and hydrodynamic loads, as well as attitude, during high-speed seaplane taxiing is hindered by the strong nonlinear interaction between air and water flows across the free surface and the multiphase nature of the problem. To address this challenge, we propose a hybrid turbulence framework (SRH, Spalart–Allmaras + Realizable k–ε hybrid turbulence model) based on Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS)/RANS coupling, in which the computational domain is partitioned into a liquid-dominant region, a gas-dominant region, and an interfacial transitional zone. Distinct turbulence closures are assigned to the single-phase regions, while a phase-volume-fraction-based transition scheme ensures smooth parameter exchange across the interface. Validation against experimental measurements and single-model RANS simulations demonstrates that the SRH model achieves comparable accuracy at low speeds, and at high speeds reduces the mean prediction error by ∼5% relative to the single-model baseline, with up to 30% improvement in drag prediction accuracy at the highest volume Froude number (Fr▽) considered. This framework improves both aerodynamic force estimation and the resolution of aerodynamic–hydrodynamic interactions, offering a computationally efficient and physically consistent approach for high-speed multiphase flow prediction in aeronautical and marine engineering applications.

papers.title: A coupling discrete element and lattice Boltzmann method model for simulating fluid–structure interactions involving deformable and breakable solids
papers.abstract: Although fluid–flexible structure interaction problems have been extensively studied, the fracture behavior of solid systems remains largely unexplored. This study presents a coupled computational framework based on the discrete element method (DEM), immersed moving boundary (IMB) method, and lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) that integrates numerical models for fluid dynamics, solid elastic deformation, and fracture of slender, flexible structures. The approach leverages the LBM for efficiently handling complex flow phenomena and employs the DEM with rectangular particles and a parallel bond model to capture deformation and failure of flexible plates. Large eddy simulation is incorporated to model the turbulence. Fluid–solid interface dynamics are resolved using the IMB method, and the solid volume fraction in the coupled system is analytically computed to accurately capture two-way fluid–solid interactions (FSIs). Consequently, the proposed approach is capable of simulating the complete transition from continuous to discontinuous fracture in slender solid systems. The framework is validated against several benchmarks to demonstrate its accuracy and reliability. The results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in simulating the transition from elastic deformation to fracture in slender structures and in capturing complex two-way FSI, confirming its potential for engineering applications such as the analysis of submarine risers.

papers.title: Bionic design for secondary flow loss control in high-lift low-pressure turbines
papers.abstract: In low-pressure turbines (LPTs), the trend toward high-lift designs leads to increasingly complex end wall secondary flows and greater flow losses. A novel bionic blade design is proposed in this paper to mitigate the losses caused by secondary flow. To determine the design parameter range and accelerate the iterative design process, a framework based on the Bayesian Optimization (BO) algorithm is built. A low-speed wind tunnel test bench was employed to reproduce the low Reynolds number conditions experienced by the low-pressure turbine. Experiments were conducted on both the baseline and bionic blade cascades under two inlet conditions with different boundary layer thicknesses to assess secondary flow structures and total pressure loss, thereby evaluating the performance of the bionic blade. In addition, numerical simulations were also performed to reveal the inherent mechanism of the bionic blade in influencing the development and loss of secondary flow. Under high-lift design, backflow in the corner area and the interaction between secondary flow and suction-side separation worsen the flow loss of the baseline blade cascade, while the bionic blade effectively mitigates these effects, reduces the spanwise extent of secondary flow, and demonstrates greater stability under varying inlet boundary layer conditions.

papers.title: A physics-informed diffusion model for super-resolution reconstruction of airfoil flow field data
papers.abstract: High-fidelity flow field data are essential for accurate evaluation of the aerodynamic performance of airfoils, as they directly affect the prediction accuracy of lift, drag, and flow separation characteristics. However, traditional methods are either computationally expensive, e.g., computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solvers, or struggle to achieve sufficient reconstruction fidelity and physical consistency, e.g., data-driven super-resolution approaches. In this paper, we propose a novel super-resolution reconstruction method based on the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM). It incorporates deformable convolutional layers and attention modules into the U-Net denoising network to enhance the extraction of airfoil features. Meanwhile, residual networks are also integrated to improve data reconstruction performance. To embed physical information, we introduce pointwise physics-informed loss functions based on the continuity and momentum residuals to enforce physical consistency. We select various airfoils from the public University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) airfoil database, generate computational grids using Gmsh, and obtain high-fidelity flow field data through OpenFOAM simulations for model training and validation. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method can accurately predict characteristics of the flow field data around the airfoils, with computation time being only 23% of that required by traditional computational fluid dynamics software. Moreover, our method outperforms other deep learning models in terms of generation accuracy and generalization ability. This indicates that the proposed method offers significant advantages in computational efficiency and generation accuracy, providing a new solution for airfoil flow field data reconstruction.

papers.title: Numerical study on the enhanced wall-to-fluid heat transfer caused by the bubble wake
papers.abstract: This numerical study investigated the wall-to-fluid heat transfer enhancement caused by an air bubble rising with an oscillatory trajectory. The geometric volume of fluid method, isoAdvector, is used to simulate a bubble rising near a heated wall in a static fluid, considering different bubble–wall distances (S), Galilei (Ga) number, and Eötvös (Eo) number. The results indicate that when the distance between the bubble walls is relatively small, the repulsive force from the walls predominates, causing the bubble to move away from the wall and thereafter spiral upwards initially. As the distance increases, the bubble movement approaches a stable periodic spiral trajectory, and the influence of wall disturbances diminishes. The rise in the quantity of Eo exacerbates bubble deformation, resulting in increased resistance and a decrease in ascent velocity. Simultaneously, the shedding frequency of the vortex increases, further disrupting the thermal boundary layer. An increase in the Ga number accelerates the shedding frequency of the tail vortex and significantly amplifies the disturbance intensity of the flow field. Compared to the case of S = 4D, the mean maximum Nusselt number on the wall surface increases by 27.07% and 11.70% for S = 2D and S = D, respectively. Compared to Ga = 50, the mean maximum Nusselt number at the wall increases by 187.58% and 238.71% for Ga = 279.58 and 559.17, respectively. Compared to Eo = 0.54, the average maximum Nusselt number of the wall for Eo = 1 and Eo = 5 increases by 2.69% and 17.16%, respectively.

papers.title: Physics-constrained uncertainty quantification of Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes model in a centrifugal compressor with adaptive non-uniform perturbations
papers.abstract: The performance prediction of centrifugal compressors using Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes models often show significant deviations from experimental results, mainly due to structural uncertainties arising from the linear eddy viscosity assumption. This study develops a physics-constrained framework for turbulence model uncertainty quantification (UQ) in the numerical simulation of a shrouded centrifugal compressor. The framework introduces an adaptive non-uniform perturbation strategy within the barycentric map, enabling simultaneous modification of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Reynolds stress anisotropy tensor. Compared with conventional uniform perturbation methods, the adaptive approach not only improves numerical convergence under large perturbations of turbulent kinetic energy production but also ensures more consistent performance predictions across the entire operating range. The results indicate that, after introducing eigenvector perturbations, the predicted uncertainty interval covers most of the experimental data at three different rotational speeds, despite obvious discrepancies between baseline shear stress transport model (k–ω SST) predictions and measurements. Furthermore, the investigation of flow structure and entropy generation is conducted to elucidate how different perturbations influence internal flow characteristics and loss mechanisms. Overall, this study presents the first application of a physics-constrained UQ framework with adaptive non-uniform perturbations to centrifugal compressors, establishing reliable uncertainty bounds for performance prediction and clarifying the role of anisotropic turbulence limiting states in flow separation mechanisms.

papers.title: Effect of flame stretch on the transition boundary of “explosive transition of deflagration”
papers.abstract: Recent investigations have shown that mixtures with Le > 1 are characterized by a temperature limit for sustaining a one-dimensional, stretch-free, highly preheated premixed flame. This limit is attributed to the chemical reactions occurring in the preheat zone under such extreme conditions. Beyond this, volumetric autoignition, termed as “explosive deflagration transition (ETD),” can occur. A previous two-dimensional simulation [Morii et al., “Two-dimensional laboratory-scale DNS for knocking experiment using n-heptane at engine-like condition,” Combust. Flame 223, 330–336 (2021)] for an nC7H16/O2/Ar mixture, which quantitatively reproduced an experiment, shows that knock onset aligns with ETD. In this study, we used a counterflow configuration to systematically vary the residence time of highly preheated premixed flames and investigated the flame stretch effects on ETD. A conceptual framework showed that the reaction progress in a zero-dimensional ignition system is equivalent to that in a one-dimensional stretched flame with Le = 1. This framework was extended through simulations of highly preheated stretched flames for a lean C3H8/O2/He mixture, as a representative mixture with Le > 1, consistent with ETD conditions. The three reaction front modes were identified: (I) conventional premixed flames, (II) flames influenced by preheat-zone reactions, and (III) a front governed by autoignition chemistry. Further analysis expanded the concept of Zel'dovich's spontaneous ignition front into a propagating stretched flame. Then, the mode (III) was revealed to correspond to the spontaneous ignition front. The transition from mode (I) to mode (II) marked the boundary of ETD, with the boundary temperature increasing with increasing stretch rate. These results suggest potential knock limit extension due to the stretch effect in engine combustion.

papers.title: Alternating-current induced-charge electrokinetic interactions of two-dimensional cylindrical conductive microparticles near ideally polarizable electrodes: A fully transient numerical investigation incorporating in-liquid multi-body contact
papers.abstract: Induced-charge electrokinetics (ICEK), including induced-charge electroosmosis (ICEO) and induced-charge electrophoresis (ICEP), is critical for microfluidic fluid/colloidal manipulation, yet the coupled behaviors of ICEO fluid convection and colloidal ICEP under alternating-current (AC) fields—featuring multiple interfacial charge relaxation mechanisms—remain underexplored. Via full-transient simulations of ideally polarizable two-dimensional (2D) cylindrical conductive particles (radius R = 5 μm) and AC-powered planar electrodes in a rectangular microfluidic chamber, this study finds: single particles stably suspend below fRC−P (particle–electrolyte interfacial double-layer relaxation frequency) via balanced repulsive dielectrophoresis (DEP)/AC-electroosmosis (ACEO) and attractive ICEP, but contact electrodes above fRC−P due to induced electrical double layer short-circuiting; multiple particles show horizontal mutual repulsion, vertical chaotic dispersion (≤fRC−DE, electrode relaxation frequency), near-electrode ordered dispersion (fRC−DE–fRC−P), and stable pearl chains (≫fRC−P); a 4 × 4 array has chaotic dispersion (≤fRC−DE), layered staggered dispersion (fRC−DE–fRC−P), and chained dispersion (≫fRC−P). A novel repulsive DEP between leaky dielectric particles and polarizable electrodes is also identified, confirming AC frequency as a key ICEK regulator and providing a framework for optimizing microfluidic particle sorting/assembly.

papers.title: Efficient dual-synthetic-jets-based lift enhancement strategy generated by deep reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Distributed dual-synthetic jet actuators (DSJAs) are first integrated with a plain flap for improving the lift enhancement control ability. Two control methods (flow separation control and virtual gurney flap control) and their coordinated control are numerically investigated. A hundred-environment parallel deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework integrating long short-term memory (LSTM) networks is first constructed and applied to optimize the control strategy with the objective of maximum lift enhancement effect. Notably, the parallel number is the highest in publications, indicating the best computing efficiency. Results show that the lift enhancement ratio of flow separation control (98.44%) is more than ten times that of virtual gurney flap control (9.05%) under the same energy consumption. Simultaneous operations of separation control and virtual gurney flap control could realize a lift enhancement ratio of 91.14%, which is instead less than that of only separation control. The optimal performance is not achieved by the simultaneous maximum-voltage activation of all DSJAs. The best control strategy, with a lift enhancement ratio of 115% (larger than the sum of the individual effect produced by separation control and virtual gurney flap control alone), is generated by DRL framework. Under control of this strategy, distributed DSJAs operate in a pulse mode and achieve a better lift enhancement effect with a higher effectiveness-cost ratio (2.46 times that of coordinated control) and lower energy consumption (less than half of coordinated control).

papers.title: The nonlinear saturation amplitude of two-mode Rayleigh–Taylor instability in plane geometry
papers.abstract: A weakly nonlinear theoretical model is established for the two-dimensional incompressible two-mode Rayleigh–Taylor instability (RTI). An exact third-order analytical solution of the small perturbed interface is derived. The root mean square of all perturbation amplitudes is employed to define the nonlinear saturation amplitude (NSA) of the two-mode RTI. It is found that the two-mode feedback becomes significant in affecting the nonlinear saturation of both modes and even their rms amplitudes within specific ranges of the wavenumber ratio and initial amplitude ratio. The dependence of the NSA of rms amplitude on the Atwood number, the wavenumber ratio, and the initial amplitude ratio is obtained. When two-mode feedback becomes noticeable, an approximate analytical solution for the NSA of rms amplitude is derived and compared with the Haan model at different wavenumber ratios. In addition, a fitting model for the NSA of the rms amplitude over a wider range is obtained using the least squares method. Finally, the theoretical model is compared with the numerical simulation using high-order and low-dissipation methods and exhibits good agreement in the linear and weakly nonlinear stages.

papers.title: Effect of fin size and angle of attack on the structural evolution of cavity and flow field characteristics on high-speed horizontal water entry of a large-caliber vehicle
papers.abstract: To investigate cavity evolution and hydrodynamic forces of a large-caliber vehicle with fins during high-speed horizontal water entry, an experimental platform was established. The cavity evolution process was captured by high-speed photography. On this basis, detached-eddy simulation was employed to analyze cavity evolution and hydrodynamic forces. The effects of fin size and angle of attack (AOA) on flow field characteristics were also systematically examined. Results show that horizontal water entry of a vehicle at a nonzero AOA exhibits periodic tail-slapping accompanied by cavity deformation at each slap position. The cavity exhibits three distinct patterns: (1) the front section shows a regular tail-slapping cavity; (2) the middle section displays necking phenomena with a rough surface, linked to Kelvin–Helmholtz instability; (3) the rear section collapses into dispersed bubble clusters dominated by Rayleigh–Taylor instability. Analysis of the coupled relationship between pressure and turbulent kinetic energy, from the perspective of energy conservation and transformation, reveals the mechanisms of cavity collapse and recovery. Moreover, larger fins increase tail-slapping frequency, resulting in greater cavity deformation. When the mean aerodynamic chord doubles, the lateral acceleration (ay) increases by more than 100%. Increasing AOA promotes the integration of small-scale vortex blobs into large-scale vortex tubes, with the vortex core volume expanding due to the amplified tail-slapping motion. When AOA = 3° increases to 9°, the ay increases to approximately 8 times the original value.

papers.title: High-order spectral-element modeling of ferrofluid droplet migration, coalescence, and breakup in non-uniform magnetic fields
papers.abstract: We present a high-fidelity numerical framework for simulating multiphase ferrofluid dynamics by coupling the Navier–Stokes, Cahn–Hilliard, and Maxwell equations within a spectral element method (SEM) discretization. To overcome the computational challenges of high-order interface dynamics and variable material properties, we introduce an accelerated algorithm that decomposes the fourth-order Cahn–Hilliard equation into two Helmholtz equations and employs constant-coefficient formulations for both pressure and magnetic potential solvers. This strategy reduces computational cost by more than 50% while preserving accuracy for two-phase flow. The model is validated against several classical benchmarks: bubble rising without magnetic fields, magnetic field distribution around cylinders, and ferrofluid droplet deformation under uniform fields. Excellent agreement is observed with analytical solutions, numerical benchmarks, and experimental measurements.
