Further investigations under non-uniform magnetic fields generated by permanent magnets reveal rich ferrofluid droplet behaviors, including elongation, zigzagging, filamentation, and binary or ternary breakup, controlled by magnet geometry and field strength. Systematic studies of droplet migration demonstrate the critical influence of magnetic Bond number, susceptibility, and initial offset on interfacial dynamics and trajectory. Multi-droplet interactions highlight the roles of magnetic coupling and hydrodynamic effects in coalescence and separation. These results confirm that the proposed SEM-based multiphase ferrofluid solver is accurate, efficient, and versatile, providing a powerful tool for the study and design of ferrofluid-based microfluidic and biomedical applications.

papers.title: Three-dimensional conservative phase-field lattice Boltzmann simulations of droplet generation in a flow-focusing microdevice
papers.abstract: Microfluidic droplet devices have been extensively studied because of their wide range of applications, particularly in canonical geometries, such as T-junctions and flow-focusing configurations. In this work, we present a three-dimensional phase-field lattice Boltzmann framework based on the conservative Allen–Cahn equations, capable of accurately simulating both binary and ternary fluid systems in contact with arbitrary shaped solid surfaces. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to perform three-dimensional simulations of droplet generation in flow-focusing microfluidic devices with three immiscible phases and wettability using a phase-field approach. The method applies non-equilibrium bounce-back boundary conditions at inlets and outlets to properly enforce mass conservation and employs a method based on the bounce-back scheme on rigid walls that are not conformal to the lattice grid to handle wettability on complex geometries. This treatment ensures mass conservation even in the presence of staircase approximations on curved boundaries. The wettability model is validated through droplet spreading tests on both flat and curved surfaces, and spurious currents near triple junctions are analyzed to assess numerical accuracy. Then, a comprehensive parametric study on droplet generation in a flow-focusing microdevice is presented, exploring the effects of capillary number, flow rate ratio, viscosity ratio, and contact angle on droplet size, morphology, and production frequency. Finally, a preliminary study on the generation of multicomponent droplets is conducted to demonstrate that the developed solver is a robust and versatile tool, well suited to advancing the understanding of multiphase microfluidic flows and facilitating the interpretation of the experimental data.

papers.title: Hypersonic flow field and heat flux prediction model based on physics-informed neural networks with positional encoding
papers.abstract: The calculation of flow fields and aerodynamic heat under hypersonic flow conditions faces challenges such as low computational efficiency and stringent grid requirements. In contrast, the physics-informed neural network (PINN) model exhibits advantages such as adhering to physical laws, being mesh-free, and having high computational efficiency. Given that neural network models tend to smooth out the data distribution at locations with large gradients and strong discontinuities in hypersonic flow fields, this paper develops a PINN model with high-frequency positional encoding (PE-PINN). This model maps coordinate information to a high-dimensional space, enhancing the network's capability to capture high-gradient features. Furthermore, in the process of modeling two-dimensional flow fields, the PE-PINN model incorporates a shock wave attention module to capture shock wave positions and weighted enhancement of features in shock wave regions, allowing the network to better capture areas with large gradient data distributions in hypersonic flow fields. Compared with the traditional PINN model, the PE-PINN maintains the same prediction efficiency while improving the accuracy of shock wave position characterization from 91.2% to 99%. It successfully simulates the large gradient temperature distribution near the wall, achieving aerothermal prediction with 65.96% and 72.34% efficiency improvements compared to traditional numerical simulations using the PINN and PE-PINN models. This provides an effective method for rapid iterative calculations of fluid–structure interaction in the thermal protection systems of hypersonic vehicles.

papers.title: Artificial neural network-based subgrid-scale velocity enrichment model used for large-eddy simulation of particle clustering and collision rates in isotropic turbulent flows
papers.abstract: This study extends our previously proposed artificial neural network (ANN)-based subgrid-scale (SGS) model [Tan and Jin, Phys. Fluids 36, 085170 (2024)] to improve the predictive accuracy of large-eddy simulation (LES) for particle clustering and collision rates. The model integrates a linearized SGS velocity equation with an ANN closure that represents the effects of SGS self-interaction and the pressure gradient, thereby bridging physics-based and data-driven approaches. Using the large-scale velocity and velocity gradient tensor as inputs, the model predicts their combined SGS contribution; SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis is employed to interpret the relative importance of these input features. By solving the linearized governing equations informed by the large-scale flow, we reconstruct the SGS flow fields. The novel contribution of this work lies in validating the dynamic interaction between inertial particles and the reconstructed SGS motions, which is critical for accurately predicting particle clustering, relative motion, and collision rates. In an a priori study, the model's performance in reconstructing SGS fields is validated through analysis of flow structures and probability density functions of velocity gradients. Furthermore, predictions of particle statistics—including the radial distribution function, radial relative velocity, and collision kernel—are compared with results from direct numerical simulation (DNS) and filtered DNS. The results demonstrate that the hybrid physics-informed ANN model effectively reconstructs small-scale velocities and significantly enhances the prediction accuracy of particle clustering and collision statistics in LES.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic analysis of oscillating water column under the influence of surface tension and uniform current
papers.abstract: This study examines the hydrodynamic response of an offshore oscillating water column (OWC) device under the combined influence of surface tension and uniform current, factors that are often overlooked but play a vital role in its hydrodynamic performance. A linear wave–structure interaction model is developed and solved using both analytical and numerical approaches. Analytically, the eigenfunction expansion method combined with an algebraic least squares technique is employed, eliminating the need for eigenfunction orthogonality and explicit mode coupling. Numerically, the problem is addressed using the boundary element method and the finite difference method. The analysis provides new insights into the interaction of capillary-gravity waves with a uniform background current and highlights their effects on the efficiency, conductance, and susceptance characteristics of OWC. The results demonstrate that resonance behavior is highly sensitive to both environmental and structural parameters. In the absence of current and surface tension, sharp resonance peaks appear at specific chamber widths, leading to higher efficiency. However, increasing current velocity and surface tension smooth out the peaks, producing broader but less pronounced resonance bands. Following currents shift the resonance toward higher frequencies, while opposing currents cause a shift to lower frequencies. Surface tension also stabilizes the susceptance response by flattening abrupt variations, thereby enhancing operational reliability. Structural parameters, particularly chamber width and wall drafts, significantly affect the hydrodynamic performance. At higher wave frequencies, a decrease in the front wall drafts leads to an increase in efficiency. These findings provide valuable guidance for improving OWC efficiency under the influence of both surface tension and uniform current.

papers.title: Influence of dilatation structures on particle transport in compressible turbulent channel flows
papers.abstract: The influence of dilatation structures on particle transport in supersonic channel turbulence is investigated by direct numerical simulation with nominal Mach number Ma=4.7, and friction Reynolds number Reτ=859. Eulerian-Lagrangian point-particle approach is employed for tracking the particles with nominal Stokes numbers St0+=1∼1000. We find that the dilatation structures are primarily localized in near-wall low-speed streaks, with a stable convective velocity of approximately 34uτ. Expansion regions (θ′>0) induce off-wall fluid motion and positive wall-normal acceleration of particles, while compression regions (θ′<0) cause toward-wall fluid motion and negative particle wall-normal acceleration. Large-inertia particles (St0+=200) respond weakly to the dilatation structures, whereas small-inertia particles (St0+=1) exhibit rapid responses with downstream-shifted acceleration and velocity distributions. Dilatation structures exert a subdominant influence on particle transport relative to the sweep and ejection events, with their induced particle transport being approximately 1/3 that of the latter and particle wall-normal transport distances less than one viscous scale. This limited effect of dilatation structures arises from short interaction time during which particles go through dilatation structures rapidly due to the streamwise velocity differences between the particles and the structures, as well as cancelation by adjacent structures with opposite fluid motions.

papers.title: Performance simulation of fuel cell-turbo compound electric power system
papers.abstract: The emerging demands of electric vertical takeoff and landing and flying cars require power systems to have high takeoff and landing power and high cruising efficiency. Existing power solutions, including pure electric, turbo-electric, piston engines, and fuel cell, face significant challenges in meeting these requirements. We proposed a fuel cell-turbo compound power system, providing a very promising configuration for solving this problem. This study established the simulation models of this structure. The accuracy of the typical component model was verified through relevant experimental data. On this basis, the system performance under typical working conditions was further analyzed. The results show that both the energy recovery efficiency and the output power of the system have been substantially improved. Under the working conditions of high rotational speed and high flow rate, the maximum output power of the system can reach 367.8 kW, meeting the high-power demand during takeoff and landing. Under the working conditions of low rotational speed and low flow rate, the system efficiency can reach up to 43.38 % at most, meeting the high-efficiency requirements during cruising. In addition, the variation of rotational speed and the proportion of hydrogen participating in combustion play a crucial role in the system performance. Although increasing combustion chamber hydrogen can help enhance power output, excessive utilization of hydrogen can lead to performance degradation. These findings provide important insights for the optimization of the compound power system of the next generation of aircraft.

papers.title: Mechanism of gas-saturated liquid flow anomaly near to phase transition point
papers.abstract: During oil field development, the flow of gas-saturated fluids is commonly observed. Gas-saturated fluids at pressures above the saturation pressure (i.e., in the pre-transitional phase state) are typically studied as homogeneous liquids, since classical phase transition theory assumes supercritical nucleation of particles of a new phase. However, experimental studies have revealed an anomaly in the flow of gas-saturated Newtonian fluids: a sharp increase (by a factor of 2–3) in the flow rate occurs when gas-saturated liquids flow through a porous medium and reducing the pressure at the outlet of the porous medium to a level close to the gas release pressure. Understanding the mechanism behind this anomaly is of significant importance for optimizing oil field development. To identify the mechanism governing the flow of gas-saturated fluids in the pre-transitional phase state and to explain the observed anomaly—specifically, the sharp increase in fluid flow rate—the “slip effect” is proposed as the underlying mechanism. A numerical solution for the flow of gas-saturated fluids in the pre-transitional phase state, accounting for the slip effect, has been obtained. The solution has been compared and analyzed with the experimental data. A mechanism for the anomalous flow of gas-saturated fluids under pre-transitional conditions is proposed.

papers.title: Learning from theory: Rapid predictions of vibration-driven droplet motion in asymmetric pores
papers.abstract: Seismic and acoustic vibrations can mobilize trapped non-wetting droplets, but predicting the coupled capillary–inertial response across realistic pore shapes is prohibitive at scale. We leverage a validated single-channel momentum theory to programmatically generate a high-fidelity dataset and train a physics-informed time-series neural network for time-resolved motion in asymmetric pores. Using only 3000–5000 training samples, the surrogate attains 2%–5% test error. On the same hardware, it reduces wall-clock time per case from 75 to 87 s for the mechanistic solver to less than 0.6 s, with the fastest cases completing in less than 0.3 s; this corresponds to 124–156 times acceleration and makes ensembles of thousands of pores tractable. Large surrogate ensembles reveal how frequency, peak acceleration, and geometric asymmetry govern mobilization and hysteresis, providing immediately usable constraints for models and for designing vibration strategies in enhanced recovery, groundwater remediation, and geologic carbon storage.

papers.title: Aerodynamic performance improvement of vertical axis wind turbines in a hybrid configuration
papers.abstract: Because of wake losses and variations in wind speed, turbines often operate below their rated power, making efficiency improvements crucial for enhancing overall generation. This study introduces a novel design that integrates small turbines around a wind turbine tower to harness aerodynamic interactions and enhance overall system performance. A three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics based parametric study was conducted, considering four angular placements (0°, 30°, 60°, 90°), varying wind speeds (4, 6, 8, and 10 m/s), turbine height along the tower, and dual-turbine configurations. Performance was evaluated through power, torque, drag, and lift coefficients as well as flow field analysis. Results show that increasing wind speed enhances turbine performance, with the highest power coefficient (Cpower) of 0.5487 obtained at 90° under 8 m/s due to stronger local velocities and attached flow. Conversely, the 0° position yielded the lowest Cpower 0.07641 at 4 m/s because of tower-induced stagnation. Height variation along the tower, considering decreasing tower diameter and increasing wind speed, shows that the turbine at the upper elevation obtained the highest CPower of 0.4829 at D = 3.0 m, V = 10 m/s, while the lower section, benefiting from larger tower diameter, obtained CPower of 0.4055 at D = 6.0 m, V = 4 m/s. Dual-turbine analysis confirmed that configurations of T1: 45° and T2:90° obtained an improved total power coefficient (Cp-total), while closely spaced cases T1:30° and T2:90° were affected by a strong stagnation region. The total improvement efficiency analysis revealed that integration at 90° improved the horizontal axis wind turbine efficiency by 0.85%.

papers.title: Simulations of two-phase methane/oxygen rotating detonation wave at cryogenic condition
papers.abstract: This paper numerically investigates rotating detonation waves in a gaseous methane/cryogenic liquid oxygen mixture using a non-premixed injection pattern. Distinct differences are observed between the liquid-oxygen detonation engine and traditional liquid-fueled detonation systems: (1) the rotating detonation wave exhibits a strong propensity to form a counter-rotating mode at near-stoichiometric conditions, and (2) a considerable parasitic flame anchors near the inlet, reducing the detonation fraction. Both the counter-rotating mode, characterized by the coexistence of counter-propagating primary and secondary shocks, and the one-wave mode are observed; the specific mode depends on the initial oxygen droplet diameter and the global equivalence ratio. Significant local explosions occur near oxygen droplets immediately behind the leading shock, inducing numerous retrograde shocklets. These shocklets couple with the parasitic flame in the vicinity of the oxygen cluster, facilitating the formation of a secondary shock. Increased gaseous methane mass flow rate (e.g., ϕ = 2.0) or decreased global reactivity (e.g., ϕ = 0.25) reduces the secondary wave strength, resulting in a dominant one-wave operating mode. In the counter-rotating mode, the presence of secondary shocks substantially decreases the total pressure gain due to multiple shock collisions. The maximum mean thrust is observed at ϕ = 2.0, while the minimum is found at ϕ = 0.25. However, variations in the methane mass flow rate lead to an inverse trend in specific impulse. Stable propulsive performance is found in the one-wave mode compared to the counter-rotating mode.

papers.title: An efficient immersed boundary–dynamic wall function model based on adaptive cartesian grids
papers.abstract: Compared to traditional body-fitted moving grids and overset grids, adaptive Cartesian grids offer significant advantages, including no need for grid deformation, highly automated generation process, natural adaptability to complex geometries, and ease of implementing solution-based adaptive mesh refinement. However, in high Reynolds number simulations involving large motions, these grids face the issue of “grid catastrophe” due to the extreme grid resolution required for turbulent boundary layer simulation. To address this, we employ the immersed boundary-dynamic wall function model combined with an implicit dual-time-stepping method, effectively resolving near-wall flow structures without significantly increasing grid count. To handle the assignment of newly emerged Eulerian cells during motion, a three-point interpolation method is used for flow field initialization. This computational framework has been validated through a series of steady-state benchmark cases. Through simulations of typical dive processes and typical pitching airfoil benchmarks, we demonstrate the high efficiency and fidelity of our method in solving turbulent flow fields under dynamic boundary conditions at subsonic and critical sonic speeds. This method provides efficient and reliable numerical simulation support for the aerodynamic design and optimization of various new aircraft.

papers.title: Single-particle transport in spherical and non-spherical particle-packed porous media
papers.abstract: Fine particle transport in porous media governs contaminant migration and the internal stability of geotechnical structures. While skeleton particle morphology significantly affects transport mechanisms, investigations comparing these processes in spherical and non-spherical particle-packed porous media remain limited. This study used the discrete element method coupled with lattice Boltzmann method and planar laser-induced fluorescence experiments, to investigate single-particle transport under different hydraulic gradients (i = 0.000 17–0.0017) and size ratios (dn/D = 0.133–0.4). Results revealed that compared with spherical particle-packed media (SPM), non-spherical particle-packed porous media (NSPM) exhibit higher porosity and superior pore connectivity, more complex pore networks and more tortuous high-velocity flow channels. Particle transport trajectory complexity in NSPM is greater than that in SPM, exhibiting stronger transverse dispersion, greater velocity fluctuations, and random directional changes. The passage probability is 3.4%–7.8% greater for fine particles in NSPM than in SPM under varying dn/D at constant i and 3.3%–7.0% greater under varying i at constant dn/D; however, longer and more variable transport times, while increasing hydraulic gradient, can increase the passage probability and reduce the transport time. The particle transport trajectory tortuosity in NSPM is greater than that in SPM. At a constant i of 0.000 85, as dn/D increased from 0.133 to 0.4, the average tortuosity increased from 1.22 to 1.33 in SPM and from 1.53 to 1.59 in NSPM. At a constant dn/D of 0.267, as i increased from 0.000 17 to 0.0017, the average tortuosity increased from 1.20 to 1.40 in SPM and from 1.42 to 1.72 in NSPM.

papers.title: Energy dissipation characteristics of reversible mixed-flow pump at pump and turbine modes based on entropy production theory
papers.abstract: This study investigates the energy loss characteristics and pressure pulsation patterns of a reversible mixed-flow pump (RMFP) at both pump and turbine modes through numerical analysis. The results demonstrate that: in pump mode, the volute domain exhibits the highest entropy production rate at 80% of the design flow rate, with significant energy loss occurring at the impeller shroud region (Span = 0.8) due to flow separation. Under turbine mode, the impeller domain dominates entropy production, and the hub region (Span = 0.2) shows maximum entropy generation rate at low water head, indicating reduced energy conversion efficiency. Pressure pulsation analysis reveals that the dominant frequency at the point near the volute tongue is 6× rotational frequency in both modes. However, the pulsation amplitude in pump mode is primarily governed by the impeller tongue interaction, whereas in the turbine mode it stems mainly from high-potential-energy fluid impact in the inflow passage. The study elucidates the key loss mechanisms of RMFP under different operational modes, providing the theoretical foundations for optimal design.

papers.title: Natural convection in an evaporative air–water system inside a cavity heated by an immersed porous medium
papers.abstract: We report on numerical results of natural convection inside a cavity that is partially filled with water and heated by an immersed porous medium. The part of the cavity above the water is occupied by air. The heat provided by the porous medium generates thermal convection in the water and the air. While water evaporation at the free surface generates convection of vapor in the air too. The porous medium is treated as a continuum and the flow inside and outside of it is modeled via the one-domain approach. Herein, we consider two cases at different Rayleigh numbers. In the first case, the flow is laminar in the air and transitional in the water, and in the second one, the flow in both phases is turbulent. Our simulations predict that thermal convection in each phase is organized in a single or dual-roll large scale circulation. Water descends from the free surface along the edges of the cavity and near the bottom it moves mostly around the porous medium. Overall, the presence of the porous medium increases circulation, hence, convective heat transport. On the other hand, the free-surface temperature and evaporation rate are essentially constant and subject only to small-amplitude fluctuations. Furthermore, the convective structures of the two fluids interact with one another at the free surface, and the main roll of the water exerts a low-frequency modulation to those in the gas. These findings can be relevant to industrial applications of water pools.

papers.title: Investigation of vortex-induced vibration of a circular cylinder near a wavy wall with the local domain-free discretization method
papers.abstract: Vortex-induced vibration of a circular cylinder in proximity to a stationary wavy wall at a Reynolds number of 150 is investigated, using an immersed boundary method, called the local domain-free discretization method. The cylinder is elastically mounted and can only oscillate in the transverse direction, with a mass ratio of m*=8/π, zero structural damping (ζ=0), and a reduced velocity Ur ranging from 2 to 9. The effects of wave height h/λ and gap ratio G/D between the cylinder bottom and the wavy wall are studied. Results show that the cylinder responses are significantly affected by the wavy wall. For a small G/D, the cylinder response amplitude Aave basically increases with Ur and h/λ due to collisions between the cylinder and the wavy wall. Even though the lock-in region is unclear, Aave is still large at high Ur. The positive vortices on the lower side of the cylinder are obviously suppressed by the wall. At G/D=1, Aave curve exhibits three distinct branches, i.e., “initial,” “upper,” and “lower,” mainly corresponding to “2S,” “2P,” and “2S” vortex shedding modes. Compared with the unbounded case, the lock-in region is narrowed, whereas the vibration is enhanced. For G/D=2, the lower branch turns unobvious. The lock-in region is broadened with a stronger cylinder vibration compared with the unbounded case. The merging between the vortices shed from the cylinder and the induced secondary ones is precluded, giving rise to complex “2S+S” and “2P+S” shedding modes.

papers.title: Boltzmann kinetic scheme for Knudsen flow in a micro in-plane radiometric actuator: Shakhov model with heat flux specified walls
papers.abstract: A fixed-surface heat flux boundary condition was implemented using the Shakhov–Boltzmann kinetic model. Our approach is tested by simulating a fixed heat flux boundary condition in a Micro In-plane Knudsen Radiometric Actuator (MIKRA) device, across the range of Knudsen number (Kn = 0.3–11.49), designed for extreme, vacuum-like environments. Simulation results, compared with laboratory measurements under identical heat-flux conditions, show strong agreement, confirming the model's ability to accurately predict rarefied gas dynamics. Surface temperatures on both hot and cold MIKRA arms are predicted within 1% error for moderate Knudsen numbers (Kn < 4.64), with accuracy decreasing to 3%–5% at higher Knudsen numbers (Kn > 4.64) due to radiative effects beyond the model's conductive framework. Notably, the overall mean absolute percentage error is 2.07%. Experimental force validation indicates the model's improved performance, especially vs Direct Simulation Monte Carlo, in the sensor-relevant Knudsen regime. Our work lays a strong computational foundation for rarefied microscale gas simulation with direct experimental validation. A thorough parametric study addresses accommodation coefficients and microscale rarefaction effects, including one- and two-dimensional flow profiles, velocity contours, and core phenomena like thermal creep and the Knudsen layer. Also, the variation of accommodation coefficients for both arms is discussed, and a comparison is drawn. Parametric analysis reveals that asymmetric accommodation coefficients on hot and cold sensor arms produce a synergistic effect: increasing the hot arm coefficient while decreasing the cold arm coefficient enhances Knudsen effects. The fixed heat flux boundary condition is also compared with the fixed heat flux boundary condition to see the difference in findings.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of turbulent drag reduction by streamwise–spanwise discontinuous microgrooves in natural gas pipelines
papers.abstract: During high-pressure natural gas transportation, significant frictional losses arise due to turbulence-induced wall shear. Conventional bionic microgroove surfaces can suppress near-wall vortical structures and thus reduce drag to some extent; however, their effective drag-reduction range is limited, and they tend to deteriorate or even reverse to drag enhancement under high Reynolds number conditions. To address this limitation, a novel streamwise–spanwise two-dimensional discontinuous microgroove inspired by the tactile paving pattern (“blind path”) is proposed in this study. A 45° smooth transition angle is introduced in the groove design to mitigate local flow separation. Based on large eddy simulation combined with the wall-adapting local eddy-viscosity subgrid-scale model, the drag-reduction performance of the proposed two-dimensional discontinuous groove and the conventional alternating-width semicircular groove was comparatively evaluated over the Reynolds number range of Re = 1.30 × 105–6.54 × 105. The results indicate that the discontinuous groove achieves a maximum drag reduction of 18.08% at Re = 2.0 × 105, outperforming the traditional configuration and maintaining effectiveness across a broader Reynolds number range. Mechanistic analysis reveals that the proposed groove effectively suppresses the formation of quasi-streamwise vortices in the near-wall region and displaces the high-disturbance zone away from the wall, thereby significantly reducing wall shear stress and velocity fluctuations.

papers.title: Learning non-ideal vortex flows using the differentiable vortex particle method
papers.abstract: Vortex flows are ubiquitous in both natural processes and engineering applications, including phenomena such as typhoons, water currents, and aerospace fluid dynamics. The vortex particle method (VPM), a computational approach grounded in vortex dynamics, has been extensively applied in aerodynamics, oceanography, turbulence, and aeroacoustics. With the recent introduction of machine learning into computational fluid dynamics, a hybrid framework known as the differentiable vortex particle method (DVPM) has been proposed, which integrates the vortex particle method with deep learning to enable efficient learning and prediction. However, the original formulation of DVPM is limited to ideal vortex flow conditions, such as inviscid flows without non-conservative body forces, which significantly restricts its practical applicability. In this study, we extend the differentiable vortex particle method beyond idealized flow scenarios to encompass more realistic, non-ideal conditions, including viscous flow and flow subjected to non-conservative body forces. We establish the Lamb-Oseen vortex as a benchmark case, representing a fundamental viscous vortex flow in fluid mechanics. This selection offers significant analytical advantages, as the Lamb-Oseen vortex possesses an exact analytical solution derived from the Navier–Stokes (NS) equations, thereby providing definitive ground truth data for training and validation purposes. Through rigorous evaluation across a spectrum of Reynolds numbers, we demonstrate that DVPM achieves superior accuracy in modeling the Lamb-Oseen vortex compared to conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). Our results substantiate DVPM's robust capabilities in modeling non-ideal vortex flows, establishing its distinct advantages over contemporary deep learning methodologies in fluid dynamics applications.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of viscoelastic thermal convection in entangled polymer solutions: Elliptical cylinder effects within a square enclosure
papers.abstract: This study numerically explores natural convection heat transfer of linear entangled polymer solutions in a square cavity with an elliptical cylinder, using the Rolie-Poly model to describe the solution's rheological properties. It analyzes how geometry and fluid rheology jointly affect flow and heat transfer, finding that both exert significant impacts. In the stable convection, the elliptical cylinder with an axial length ratio of 1:2 has the highest heat transfer efficiency. The rotation effect is significant, and the heat transfer efficiency is the worst at 45° and the best when placed vertically. At Ra=106, the cylinder with an axial ratio of 1 performs well, and increasing the rotation angle of elliptical cylinders further enhances heat transfer. The Weissenberg number (Wi) has a nonlinear effect on the average Nusselt number (Nu), with Nu almost unchanged when Wi>25. Lower polymer viscosity ratio (β) reduces flow stability but improves heat transfer. When the relaxation-time ratio exceeds the threshold value (ξ=5), Nu oscillates periodically, caused by model asymmetry and shear-thinning effect. Here, the shear-thinning effect dominates the flow-field evolution, reducing viscous dissipation, lowering system instability threshold, and inducing oscillations. This study provides a novel design insight for optimizing viscoelastic thermal convection in cavity-column structures for industrial applications.

papers.title: Rebound dynamics of double-droplet impact on a superhydrophobic spherical surface
papers.abstract: The impact of double droplets on a fixed canonical curved surface is a common yet complex phenomenon, in which the intrinsic relationship among inter-droplet interactions, rebound dynamics, and geometric constraints of the surface has not been fully elucidated. To address this, the three-dimensional multi-relaxation-time Shan–Chen lattice Boltzmann method is employed to simulate simultaneous and non-simultaneous double-droplet impacts on a superhydrophobic spherical surface. This study elucidates the formation mechanisms of the complete-coalescence rebound (CCR), partial-coalescence rebound (PCR), and no-coalescence rebound regimes, evaluating the effects of the Weber number and droplet spacing on contact time, restitution coefficient, and centroid offset. For simultaneous impacts, the results show that the contact time exhibits a U-like dependence on the horizontal spacing, reaching a minimum in the PCR regime. This is attributed to a fundamental transition in the retraction mechanism: from the inefficient “sides-first, center-last” liftoff in the CCR regime to the highly efficient “center-led, sides-follow” detachment in the PCR regime. The restitution coefficient decreases with increasing horizontal spacing. For non-simultaneous impacts, both horizontal and vertical spacing enlarge the contact time and centroid offset. Moreover, a threshold Weber number (We ≈ 41) is identified, above which lamella rupture driven by strong inertia markedly prolongs the contact time.

papers.title: Experimental study on the damage and permeability characteristics of similar natural gas-bearing coal–rock composites
papers.abstract: Investigating the damage and permeability characteristics of gas-bearing coal–rock composites is essential for understanding the mechanisms driving dynamic disasters in coal and rock gas composites. This study focuses on the uniaxial compressive strength of natural coal–rock specimens, from which similar natural composites with transition interfaces were created using the pouring-core sampling method. We conducted mechanical-seepage experiments on gas-bearing coal–rock composites under various confining stresses, gas pressures, and stress paths. The results show a positive correlation between the specimens' compressive strength and confining stress; as confining stress increases, both total input energy and elastic strain energy of the specimens increase, while dissipated energy decreases. When specimens reach instability, they require more energy to maintain this state. At peak strength, the stored elastic strain energy in the specimens gradually increases. Furthermore, higher gas pressure reduces the specimens' bearing capacity. At peak strength, specimen strain decreases, resulting in diminished deformation capacity. Among different testing paths, specimens exhibit the highest strength under the loading axial stress path, while the lowest strength occurs under the compound loading axial and unloading confining path, exhibiting significant deformation and expansion. In contrast, under the unloading confining stress path, specimen strain is minimal, and the overall energy required for specimen instability—including elastic strain energy and dissipated energy—remains relatively low.

papers.title: Effect of axial misalignment on lubrication behaviors of thrust bearings with different cavity structures
papers.abstract: To solve the problem of unclear anti-misaligned performance of four different thrust bearings, the computational models for the fluid domains of the four types of cavity-structured thrust bearings were established. The variations in reliability, cooling performance, and dynamic characteristics of the four types of bearings under different operating conditions were discussed. The influence mechanism of misalignment on the oil film characteristics was revealed. The anti-misaligned performance of different bearings was compared. The results indicate that as the misaligned degree (MD) increases, the pressure distribution range of Nos. 2 and 3 pads of the bearing slightly expands, while the pressure distribution range of the remaining pads significantly decreases. Under different operating conditions, as the misaligned degree increases, the minimum film thickness and Sommerfeld number significantly decrease, while the maximum pressure, maximum shear stress, and stiffness notably increase. The temperature rise, maximum temperature, and damping generally show a slight reduction. When the rotational speed decreases or the axial external load increases, the influence of the misalign degree on the lubrication characteristics of the thrust bearing becomes more pronounced. The taper-pocket thrust bearing (TPTB) exhibits the best anti-misaligned performance. The findings provide theoretical guidance for the design and optimization of thrust bearings.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of wide-area Kelvin's ship wake based on high-order spectral method
papers.abstract: The surface wake generated by a vessel sailing on the water surface can persist for kilometers and may disclose navigation parameters. Conventional viscous flow models entail high computational costs for large-scale wake simulation, while potential flow methods also struggle to efficiently capture kilometer-scale wake structures. In this study, the open-source software high-order spectral (HOS)-Ocean, based on the HOS method, is extended to simulate the wide-area wave wakes by inducing a moving surface disturbance. The ship is simplified by a moving two-dimensional (2D) Gaussian pressure distribution. A preliminary analysis is conducted on the effects of pressure distribution steepness, HOS order, and the use of an equivalent inflow condition. Wake structures under varying Froude numbers Fr (based on ship length or water depth) and heading angles θ are analyzed using power spectral density derived from 2D discrete Fourier transform. A preliminary investigation into the effects of environmental waves on wakes is conducted. Results demonstrate distinctive spectral signatures and validate the proposed approach, providing an efficient and reliable framework for wide-area wake prediction in surface vessel operations.

papers.title: Jet-induced mixing mechanisms in a novel pond geometry
papers.abstract: This study examines the mixing performance of a novel raceway pond design actuated by lateral oscillating jets, using computational fluid dynamics simulations with passive scalar transport modeling as a theoretical framework for quantifying homogenization. Two jet operation strategies are investigated: a fixed single-configuration mode (case 1) and a time-alternating configuration mode (case 2). Mixing efficiency is evaluated through time-resolved concentration fields and quantified using complementary indicators, namely, the scalar variance, the L2 norm of concentration gradients, and the mix-norm. The results show that alternating jet actuation (case 2) significantly enhances homogenization. Specifically, the scalar variance decays 41% faster, and the mix-norm decreases over twice as rapidly compared to case 1. The gradient norm exhibits a pronounced rise followed by rapid decay once jet switching is initiated at 20 s, indicating accelerated filament stretching and breakup of unmixed regions. As a result, case 2 reaches a near-uniform concentration state approximately 30% earlier than case 1. The improved performance is attributed to the periodic disruption of coherent vortical structures, which intensifies Lagrangian stretching and folding and thereby accelerates diffusion-driven mixing. These findings highlight the potential of time-modulated jet operation to improve operational efficiency in microalgal raceway ponds while offering a mechanically flexible alternative to conventional mixing technologies.

papers.title: Hybrid phase-field lattice Boltzmann method for two-phase flows
papers.abstract: Accurate simulation of two-phase flows remains challenging due to the complex interfacial dynamics. The phase-field lattice Boltzmann method (PF-LBM) provides a powerful framework for such problems. However, conventional double-distribution-function models incur high memory costs, and finite-volume-based hybrid methods may suffer from grid-induced anisotropy. To address these limitations, a new hybrid PF-LBM is developed to improve isotropy and numerical accuracy for incompressible two-phase flows. In this approach, an improved finite volume method is employed to solve the conservative Allen–Cahn equation, where the flux formulation is reconstructed using the lattice Boltzmann (LB) mechanism to incorporate the effects across all discrete velocity directions. The hydrodynamics are solved using a velocity-based LB model equipped with a central-moment multiple-relaxation-time collision operator, enabling robust simulation of high-Reynolds-number flows. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed hybrid scheme attains higher accuracy and improved fidelity in capturing complex interfacial deformations and topological transitions than the conventional finite-volume-based hybrid method.

papers.title: Numerical study of landslide-induced surge waves based on the volume of fluid–discrete element method coupling method
papers.abstract: Landslide-induced surge waves involve complex fluid–solid interactions, making accurate and efficient numerical simulation methods crucial. This study proposes a volume of fluid–discrete element method (VOF–DEM) coupling method, in which the VOF method is embedded within a two-way-coupled computational fluid dynamics–DEM framework. Turbulence is modeled using a Reynolds-stress model, extending the approach to particle-laden, turbulent free-surface flows. In parallel, a virtual dual-mesh porosity algorithm is introduced to compute local fluid porosity with high accuracy. The coupled method is validated by comparing simulated particle column collapses with experiments results. The findings demonstrate that the method effectively captures landslide downslope velocity, surge waveform evolution, propagation characteristics, and deposition morphology. Applied to the RongSong deposit landslide at the RuMei Hydropower Station, the simulation successfully reproduces the landslide motion and surge waves generation and propagation. The results provide reliable physical insights for predicting and mitigating landslide-induced surge waves hazards in mountainous reservoirs.

papers.title: Analysis of deformable bi-cuspid valve dynamics in pulsatile flow using a coupled peridynamics–lattice Boltzmann-immersed boundary framework
papers.abstract: Multi-leaflet valves enable passive, one-way fluid transport and are increasingly applied in biological systems, soft robotics, and other industrial applications to prevent backflow. Despite extensive studies on biological valves, understanding the coupled fluid–structure dynamics of biological and synthetic bi-cuspid valves under material degradation and flow conditions remains limited. This work investigates operational modes of bi-cuspid valves using a strongly coupled framework combining the cascaded lattice Boltzmann method for fluid flow and bond-based peridynamics for solid mechanics modeling. The scheme is validated against other numerical data and applied to two-dimensional valve models subjected to pulsatile inlet conditions. Systematic variations in Young's modulus (E) and Reynolds number (Re) reveal their influence on leaflet deformation, aperture size, and flow features such as jet formation, recirculation zones, and inversion during reverse flow. Flexible leaflets (low E) exhibit larger apertures and higher variability, with increased risk of wall contact and asymmetry, while stiffer valves (high E) promote regular motion but reduce opening, enlarging stagnation regions. Higher Re amplifies the aperture and jet velocity, altering downstream flow separation. Simulations highlight the necessity of multi-cycle analysis to capture transient dynamics and inversion phenomena. These findings offer insights into the design of robust soft valves for applications that require controlled unidirectional flow under complex operating conditions.

papers.title: Flow field reconstruction in turbine cascades based on self-adaptive loss physics-informed neural networks under sparse data
papers.abstract: A self-adaptive loss physics-informed neural network (SAL-PINN) method is proposed to address the challenges of limited generalization capability exhibited by purely data-driven neural networks under sparse data conditions and the insufficient accuracy of standard physics-informed neural networks in capturing complex flow details. This method enables high-fidelity reconstruction of the plane turbine cascade flow field with limited measurement points. By incorporating a dynamic weight balancing mechanism, SAL-PINN adaptively adjusts the loss function weights for regions characterized by different numerical scales within the flow field, thereby facilitating targeted reinforcement learning for critical regions. This approach yields excellent performance in predicting both global flow structures and local flow details. The results demonstrate that under sparse data conditions, SAL-PINN achieves a further reduction in prediction errors for key physical quantities across the entire field by approximately 1.5%–2.0% compared to the standard physics-informed neural networks. In boundary regions with complex flows, the error reduction is even more pronounced, reaching 12.0%–25.4%. This study also systematically evaluates the models' sensitivity to data volume, revealing that the incorporation of physical information significantly reduces their dependence on data, while the adaptive weighting mechanism further diminishes this sensitivity. This work provides an effective solution for achieving high-accuracy flow field reconstruction with minimal data, offering significant potential for engineering applications, particularly in scenarios where experimental measurements are high-cost.

papers.title: Multi-objective optimization of guide-vane closure scheme with the consideration of pressure pulsations during the pump power trip of pump-turbines
papers.abstract: To overcome the challenges associated with ensuring a power supply–demand balance, pumped-storage technology has been widely applied to regulate grid load fluctuations and enhance power system stability. This study focused on mitigating the pressure pulsations and complex flow phenomena caused by guide-vane closure during the pump-trip process of pumped-storage units. A multi-objective optimization framework based on the second-generation non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm was proposed, integrating a one- and three-dimensional coupled numerical model and a modified Suter-transform method to refine four-quadrant characteristic curves. The two-stage guide-vane closure pattern was optimized with the following four objectives: minimizing the spiral-casing pressure peak, draft-tube pressure fluctuation, unit speed overshoot, and pressure fluctuation. A response surface surrogate model was introduced to accelerate computational convergence. The results demonstrated that the optimized closure pattern effectively reduced the maximum reverse rotation speed to below the rated unit speed. In addition, the duration of the pump-braking mode, dominant frequency components of the pressure pulsations, and axial hydraulic-thrust fluctuations were significantly suppressed. Short-time Fourier transform and flow-field vector diagrams revealed that suppressing the pressure vortices in the vaneless zone and backflow at the runner inlet effectively mitigated the dynamic hydraulic loads. This method provides a practical approach for enhancing the operational stability and prolonging the service life of pumped-storage units.

papers.title: Evolution and dynamics of vortex rings in a confined and asymmetric region
papers.abstract: Vortex ring evolution in confined asymmetric geometries is critical to biological and engineering flows, yet the combined effects of confinement and asymmetry introduce dynamics not captured by studies of either factor alone. This study employs numerical simulations to investigate the three-dimensional evolution of vortex rings under such combined conditions, focusing on the roles of eccentricity (ε), Reynolds number (Re), and stroke ratio (L/D0). The evolution of the primary vortex ring (PVR) before transition into turbulence proceeds through three stages: symmetric growth, asymmetric inclination, and reorientation toward the confinement axis. The inclination arises from asymmetric interactions between the PVR and the boundaries. This interaction generates a boundary vortex ring (BVR) of unequal strength on the near-wall and far-wall sides, causing a differential circulation decay that drives the inclination. The reorientation stage is initiated as the PVR–BVR interaction strengthens with the growing inclination. This interaction promotes vorticity annihilation between opposite-signed segments of the PVR, and it is this annihilation-induced circulation loss that primarily redirects the vortex trajectory. Based on the slug model and the circulation-decay model for confined symmetric vortex rings, a scaling model is developed that quantitatively links the asymmetric circulation decay to the evolving inclination angle, showing good agreement with the simulations. The present study reveals the evolution and dynamics of vortex rings under confined asymmetric region, providing insight into vortex-mediated transport and dissipation in environments such as intracardiac filling.

papers.title: Viscoelastic sub-diffusive channel flow in a transverse magnetic field
papers.abstract: We report the temporal linear stability as well as the nonlinear stability, via direct numerical simulations, of the viscoelastic sub-diffusive plane Poiseuille flow subjected to an external magnetic field. The fluid is described by the fractional upper-convected Maxwell constitutive model. Linear stability analysis reveals the critical conditions under which viscoelastic sub-diffusive flow transitions from stable to unstable regimes. Direct numerical simulations are shown to quantify the transitional pathway to the formation of the stable macrostructures. The spatiotemporally stable macrostructures within this flow paradigm are shown to be relevant to the experimentally observed transition of flow instability in sub-diffusive axisymmetric channel flows.

papers.title: Physics and dynamics of particle migration in zigzag inertial microchannels
papers.abstract: Effective manipulation and separation of particles in inertial microfluidics is essential for a broad range of biomedical, clinical, and industrial applications. Among serpentine geometries, zigzag microchannels offer unique advantages, including high separation efficiency and purity, compact design, scalability, portability, and improved resolution for focusing small particles. However, the underlying physics governing particle migration in these structures remains poorly understood. This study aims to elucidate the mechanisms of particle migration in zigzag inertial microchannels by examining how Reynolds number and channel geometry, specifically height and width, affect the interplay between inertial lift and lateral drag forces. A combined numerical and experimental approach was employed to analyze particle migration under different flow and geometric conditions. Results show that reducing channel height enhances shear-gradient lift forces, enabling completion of the first migration stage, while the balance between rotation-induced lift and lateral drag determines the final focusing pattern. Increasing channel width, in contrast, causes only minor changes in hydraulic diameter in high aspect ratio channels (H ≪ W) and leaves the shear rate nearly constant across most of the cross section, resulting in weaker effects on particle focusing. At Re = 50, 3 μm particles achieve side focusing only at smaller heights, whereas 15 μm particles transition from double-stream to single-stream focusing as the force balance shifts. These findings establish a mechanistic framework for predicting particle migration and optimizing geometry for precise alignment. Such insights are directly relevant to applications such as flow cytometry and rare-cell analysis, where accurate focusing improves detection performance and efficiency.
